14443-sketches-in-the-house-the-story-of:
T. P. O'Connor, Irish nationalist member of Parliament, wrote these 1893 sketches of a memorable House of Commons session, covering debates, personalities, and late-night divisions. O'Connor sat in the House himself and knew its floor.

He profiles speakers who could hold a friendly, hostile, or merely indifferent audience, recalls Parnell speaking to an almost empty chamber, and captures the wit and weariness of parliamentary life. The sketches are journalistic rather than formal history, full of anecdote. They give a lively inside view of Westminster in the Home Rule era. O'Connor's sketches first ran as journalism before book publication.
20333-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, the London Charivari, for January 28, 1893, opens volume one hundred and four. A shooting joke sets guns in a wood full of pheasants for sport. Beaters move at the far end while guns wait at their posts. Suddenly a commotion breaks in the middle of the wood.

Pheasants rise long before the beaters have come anywhere near them. Birds sail away unshot to right and left in comic disorder. Punch turned such country mishaps into crisp weekly humor. Readers get cartoons, jokes, and verses from Britain's famed comic paper. Cartoons by famed artists shared these pages with the jokes each week.
20538-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, London's comic weekly, dated this issue February 4, 1893, in its 104th volume. Between cartoons and jokes, its verse writers took up the questions of the day. One poem speaks in Irish dialect about the new moves to restrict immigration to America.

The singer complains that the welcome is a bit thin. They will not stop cabin passengers, big-wigs, and British peerage, he says. But they do not want the poor devils who crowd over in the steerage. The poem shows Punch turning a hard policy debate into song, with sympathy for the steerage passenger.
20704-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch dated this issue January 21, 1893, opening the magazine's 104th volume. Punch filled its winter pages with hunting jokes, society cartoons, and verses on the season. Field sports gave its artists and writers rich material in January.

One sketch studies the beater at a shoot. It is curious to note with what venomous hatred the beater regards the bunny. Pheasant or partridge he is careless of, and even the hare counts for little beside it. But let him once set eyes on a rabbit, and his whole being seems to change. Punch turns country custom into comedy.
21598-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch mocks a school board craze in its January 14, 1893 number, volume one hundred and four. A fund, the papers said, would supply schools with Union Jacks to raise loyalty. Punch stages a School for Patriotism in a room decked with flags.

The teacher races from Trafalgar to Waterloo, with hornpipes between the battles. Pupils chant Rule, Britannia on command and drill a Union Jack war dance. The joke bites at rote teaching and cheap flag-waving alike. Around the sketch sits a full Punch week of verse, gossip, drawings, cartoons, and comic turns on the news.
21818-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
London laughs at itself in this February 11, 1893 number of Punch, the famous comic weekly. The lead poem, The Last Woman, answers news that the dreaded crinoline has appeared again in fashionable quarters. Its speaker dreams of empty streets in Regent Street and Belgravia, with the ghosts of old fashions drifting round one lone survivor.

The rest of the issue mixes comic verse, jokes, sketches, and drawings in Punch's house style. Fashion, politics, and manners all take their turn under the rod. A single number cannot hold the whole of Punch, but it shows the weekly at its weekly work. For readers now, it is a small time capsule of what made Londoners smile in 1893.
22133-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch's weekly number for February 18, 1893, volume 104, keeps the old comic paper's routine. A mock playbill poem opens the fun: a corpse lies stiff on property rocks below a revolving cliff. The villain threw the deceased down; the hero Jack gets blamed anyway. Punch readers loved such burlesque of stage melodrama.

Jokes, verse, social sketches, and the famous cartoons fill the rest. Politicians and fashions of February 1893 take their weekly ribbing. Punch assumed a reader who knew the news and the theatre bills alike. Preserved alone, this issue is a time capsule of London humour in the last decade of Victoria's reign.
22380-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 104, is dated March 4, 1893. The comic weekly here reports a divorce court exchange. Mr. Inderwick, a barrister, begins by denying he wishes to make a joke.

Despite that pathetic announcement, his ruling passion proves too strong. Artists' models, he asks, are not always models of virtue? The judge passes the line without any comment. Punch notes the joke was not new, by any means. The barrister had apologized beforehand and could not help himself. Readers get Victorian courtroom humor in miniature. The magazine fed on such small public embarrassments every single week.
22486-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, volume 104, dated February 25, 1893, stages a mock lodge debate. A speaker bows out of an argument among the brethren present. Gentlemen, he says, can worry it out among themselves.

When you have agreed, he tells them, let me know. A second speaker notes they never did let him know. They went and elected another Johnny instead, he complains. Deuced bad taste, the inquirer calls the whole proceeding. Talk then shifts to the agricultural depression of the day. What does it mean, the inquirer demands to know. Punch mixes lodge comedy with farm politics in one scene. Readers get its weekly blend of jest and current complaint.
22645-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, appears here in its issue of March 18, 1893, from volume 104 of the magazine. The catalog record names no editor. Victorian Punch mixed political satire with domestic comedy, and its jokes assumed readers who followed Parliament, dynamite scares, and socialist agitation in the papers.

The sample tells of a man twice taken for a dynamiter, socialist, or agitator because he carried a black bag holding only sandwiches and cake. Refusing to open it landed him in the Clock Tower until he apologized. Such sketches turned public anxieties into drawing-room farce. Cartoons, verses, and prose fill the number. It preserves the comic voice of confident, clubbable Victorian Britain.
22671-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, presents its issue of April 8, 1893, from volume 104. The catalog record names no editor. Among its jokes, this number defends an old City of London custom: the turtle feast. Aldermen in the Maria Wood caught a turtle, and the captor ate all the green fat.

With mock devotion, the magazine hopes the day is far off when a socialistic government lays a desecrating finger on these ancient civic customs. The joke cuts two ways: affection for ritual, and a sly portrait of well-fed city fathers. Around it stand the usual cartoons, verses, and comic paragraphs. The issue is a slice of Victorian London laughing at itself while guarding its dinners.
22691-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, presents its issue of March 11, 1893, from volume 104 of the magazine. The catalog record names no editor. Politics fills this number's sample sketch, in the voice of an angry patriot who loves his country and hates what the government is doing to it.

Everything is to be turned inside out, he fumes, by some blessed new law about elections, a Registration Bill or something of that sort. Tinkering and pottering have gone far enough, and the confounded County Council interferes with everything. The sketch catches the grumble of the respectable voter in any age. Around it, cartoons and comic verse do the magazine's usual work. The issue is Victorian Punch in its natural habitat: Parliament, the suburbs, and the club.
22698-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, offers its issue of April 1, 1893, from volume 104 of the magazine. The catalog record names no editor. An April number invited foolery, but the sample sketch aims at a perennial target: the public man of defective education posing as a guardian of morals.

Such a man, Punch sneers, would be the very one to sponsor a bill for preserving public morals. He hopes to gain the basic knowledge his own schooling missed. No awkward case from his past, the writer hopes, will rise against him in debate. The rest of the issue runs to the usual cartoons, comic verse, and society jokes. It is Punch in its high Victorian confidence, certain that humbug is eternal.
22724-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, presents its issue of March 25, 1893, from volume 104. The catalog record names no editor. The sample scene is military comedy, with an officer soothing the wounded pride of subordinates whose grand titles outrun their real commands.

You may still call yourselves Majors, the speaker allows, not that I call you so myself. Your superior can look after you, and after those two half battalions each of you supposedly commands. The joke turns on the gap between rank and reality, a gap Punch's readers in the services knew well. Cartoons, verses, and sketches of town and country fill out the number. It is a routine week of Victorian Punch, which is to say a well-filled one.
23604-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, the London comic weekly edited by Sir Francis Burnand, filled this issue of mid April, eighteen ninety three, with jokes, verse, sketches, and cartoons. A frontispiece shows a gallant volunteer officer in a perilous spot, his hired charger choosing ford waters over a bridge and refusing to come out, rear, or lie down.

A verse on political meetings follows, with a crowded, gas lit, stuffy hall, a prosy speaker, and a mob that loves to stamp and bawl, while Mr. G. attacks the British constitution. Punch keeps its Victorian wit, laughing at volunteers, speakers, and politics in turn. Modern readers will enjoy the issue as a lively snapshot of London humour in the eighteen nineties, confident, clubmanlike, and ready with a punch line.
24398-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
This number of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 104, edited by Sir Francis Burnand, is dated April 22, 1893. Its Booking-Office column reviews The Earth Girl, a one-volume Hugoesque romance by Wyatt and Ross, bound in pale grass-green with a blood-red title. The two authors studied Victor Hugo's romances for the grand old master's style, and set out, like the Pickwickian fat boy, to make readers' flesh creep.

Their heroine, Terra, begins as Terra Incognita, never Terra Firma, and ends sent back whence she came, the Earth-to-Earth girl. The scene lies chiefly on the island of Breke. The wild girl first sees light in a cavern, brought up on raw eggs from the sea-bird's nest, uncooked herbs, and raw fish. No tea, coffee, milk, or liquors reach her family of three, Pa, Ma, and the infant phenomenon. Readers get Punch laughing at a lurid romance.
24408-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
This number of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 104, edited by Sir Francis Burnand, is dated April 29, 1893. It opens with a cartoon, What Our Artist, the very shy one, has to put up with. An affable stranger greets the artist, digs him with an umbrella, and praises a racy bit about the cat and the fiddle. The artist, fearing he has not the stranger's acquaintance, earns a second dig and a cry of hoity-toity pride.

Next come stray thoughts on play-writing, from the commonplace book of The O'Wilde. The play, it says, is not the thing; the point is an immense assortment of irrelevant epigrams. Examples follow: be virtuous and you will be a county councillor. Nothing is so dull as a life of virtue except a career of vice. Virtue is the weakness of the masses acting under their circumstances. Readers get Punch teasing Wilde.
25767-picture-and-text-1893:
Henry James writes Picture and Text, published by Harper and Brothers in 1893, gathering papers on art and illustration first printed in magazines. Two papers came from Harper's Magazine, one title altered from Our Artists in Europe, the other on Mr. Sargent with portraits reproduced.

Notices of Mr. Abbey and Mr. Reinhart came from Harper's Weekly, Mr. Alfred Parsons from an exhibition catalogue introduction, Daumier from the Century, and After the Play from the New Review. James argues book and magazine illustration, born in his time in variety and richness, changed how readers see art and artists.
26385-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
This number of Punch, dated January 7, 1893, offers the weekly magazine's usual mix of jokes, verse, and pictures. An opening squib plays on a Times letter about salmon written by a man named Ffennell, a fanciful spelling of fennel, the herb served with the fish. The Song of the Shirt appears in a very latest version, recast as a clerk's lament over laundresses who scrub, lime, and wire-brush his linen to rags.

Further pages carry short jokes, songs, and elegiac verse, including a poem recalling Montagu, a cordial comrade and champion now dead after long pain. The poem also recalls the schooldays, field sports, and club life that gaiety once filled. Published at 85 Fleet Street by Bradbury, Agnew and Company, the issue captures London humor at the start of 1893.
26454-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for May 6, 1893, edited by Sir Francis Burnand, opens with a pathetic lament from a repentant subscriber to the Anti-Advertisement League. Gifted with decent taste, he once reviled crude posters ten feet high and signs swinging in the sky, and he gladly paid his half-crown to Mr. William Black's League. Now his oath bars him from every shop that advertises.

The lamenter cannot buy toilet soap without saponaceous aid against London smuts, nor furnish his villa while upholsterers' puffs persist. An operatic note follows, finding little magic in The Magic Ring until act two, when Monkhouse and Kaye, Susie Vaughan, and Marie Halton turn burlesque into comic opera. The issue keeps Punch's weekly mix of verse, jokes, and stage talk.
26708-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 104, dated May 13, 1893, was edited by Sir Francis Burnand. It is a single weekly number of the satirical magazine, mixing jokes, verses, dialogues, and parliamentary sketches with illustrations, in the magazine's familiar Victorian voice.

Mixed Notions number ten debates the Behring Sea arbitration, as well-informed men confuse mare clausum, Paris, and the French president, Baron de Courcel. Other pieces include In Memoriam, The Devil's Own, English as She Is Spoke, Mr. Symple-Stutter's Speech, and Mr. Gladstone's Change of Name. Essence of Parliament, extracted from the diary of Toby, M.P., watches Gladstone speak in a low conversational tone before a breathless crowded House.
26769-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 104, dated May 20, 1893, was edited by Sir Francis Burnand. Its opening piece covers the opening of the Imperial Institute, with splendid Imperial Show weather, real Queen's weather. A panegyric follows, which the editor regrets he must omit for lack of space. He suggests it might sell as a pamphlet for one shilling.

The narrator, among the humblest distinguished guests, sits behind a charming young lady and her deaf grandmother. The granddaughter misidentifies the Archbishop of Canterbury as the Lord Chancellor, Lord Salisbury as General Roberts in a naval uniform, and Sir William Harcourt as Sir Edward Leighton. The narrator will not dispel the harmless illusion, lest the granddaughter be cut out of the will. Other pieces include the man who went, the booking-office, and more power to Miss Cobbe.
27493-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Volume 104 of Punch, or the London Charivari, dated 27 May 1893 and edited by Sir Francis Burnand, shows the weekly in full Victorian form. Its opening piece appeals for inspiration, since Mr. Lewis Morris has been asked to write an ode on the approaching Royal Marriage.

Further items mock the Chief Secretary's musical performance, as Mr. John Morley, accompanied by the Under Secretary, arrives at Kingston and goes to Bray. A water carnival prompts a joke about giving Old Father Thames a soap-and-water carnival. A cartoon called A Reserved Seat closes the sample, with a mistress asking Jim how he liked the show. The issue is light, topical satire.
33771-mcclure-s-magazine-vol-1-no-2-july:
McClure's Magazine for July 1893, volume one, number two, shows a young magazine assembling star contributors. Edward E. Hale writes an afternoon with Oliver Wendell Holmes, Stanley J. Weyman contributes In the Name of the Law, and Thomas Hardy offers John Horseleigh, Knyght. Rudyard Kipling gives The Merchantmen, and Cleveland Moffett and W. H. Gilder report on Peary's expedition and the north magnetic pole. Hugh Robert Mill races to the North Pole on paper.

Further pieces include human documents, wild beasts by Raymond Blathwayt, and Monsieur de Blowitz by W. Morton Fullerton, a reviewer tracked by Dr. William Wright. They also include romantic stories from the Brontë family history and a strange story of lost years. Illustrations show Holmes's Cambridge and Boston homes, Edison, Nansen, Peary, and Greely. The issue captures McClure's at its launch: literary, adventurous, and eager for the modern world.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: Thomas Jefferson's papers open this first volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. Born in Virginia in 1743, Jefferson entered William and Mary, practiced law, and sat in the House of Burgesses before the Revolution. The volume prints his messages and state papers as president. Richardson's series gives the public a full official record of each presidency.
a-select-bibliography-of-chemistry-1492-:
A Select Bibliography of Chemistry, 1492-1892, compiled by Henry Carrington Bolton and published in 1893, lists the literature of chemistry across four hundred years. Bolton, a chemist and bibliographer, gathered the books and papers of his science from its early printed works in 1492 to the professional journals of his own century. The result is a map of everything a chemist around 1893 might need to find.

Bibliographies like this one were working tools: they told researchers what existed, and where a subject had been treated before. Bolton's select list covers the whole span from incunabula to modern periodicals. It remains useful to historians of chemistry, who use it to trace how the science's literature grew and organized itself.
arxiv-2509-00693:
Arun Vignesh Malarkkan leads a team of four authors on privacy in data preparation. Domain data often contain sensitive attributes about people. Rules such as HIPAA and GDPR govern much of that data. Clear feature engineering is also needed for trust. Yet standard engineering can leak privacy while it chases accuracy.

The team frames the task in exact terms. Features should be reshaped to raise target prediction. At the same time, they should lower prediction of sensitive traits. Their DELTA framework first uses reinforcement learning to find useful transforms. It then uses a variational sequence model with a split latent space. That split keeps utility signals apart from privacy signals. Across eight datasets, accuracy rises while leakage falls.
arxiv-2509-01093:
Large language models answer questions well on familiar text, but real writing changes over time. Yulong Wu, Viktor Schlegel, and Riza Batista-Navarro ask how that natural drift in wording affects question answering. They built edited variants of reading passages from known test sets, written by people, and scored how close each variant stayed to text seen in training.

Across six data sets and eight models, scores fell as passages drifted from their trained forms. On one yes-no test, average accuracy dropped by more than thirty points from the closest to the most distant group. The needed facts were still present in the passage. Wu and the co-authors warn that models may grasp wording more than meaning.
arxiv-2509-01193:
Fine-tuning large pre-trained models for many users at once is costly, and low-rank adapters offer a cheaper path because only small added parts are trained. Sheng Lin, with seven co-authors, studies joint fine-tuning where several adapters share one base model. Two forms of data unevenness slow that joint work down.

Sequences vary in length, and the data are skewed, so a single setup wastes resources. Their framework, LobRA, runs model copies with different resource use and parallel setups matched to each workload. A second design tackles the skew in the data itself. Lin and the team aim to let service providers handle many fine-tuning requests together at lower cost, without training each task alone.
arxiv-2509-01393:
Formulaic alphas are math-defined trading signals built from price, volume, sentiment, and other data, and language models can now draft many of them. Qizhao Chen and Hiroaki Kawashima tackle the next problem: how to weight those signals as markets change. Their framework uses reinforcement learning, guided by a method called PPO, to adjust the weights in real time.

A DeepSeek model generated fifty alphas for ten stocks, and the learning agent then blended them live. The tuned strategy did not always give the highest total returns, but it achieved higher Sharpe ratios, a measure of return per unit of risk, and smaller worst drawdowns in most cases. Against equal-weighted, buy-and-hold, random, and momentum baselines, the approach showed steadier risk-adjusted performance, a trait valued in quantitative trading.
arxiv-2509-01793:
Aryan Amit Barsainyan, Jing Yu Lim, and Dianbo Liu build STORI, a test bench for learning agents in random worlds. Agents that learn by trial, called reinforcement learning agents, shine in games but transfer poorly to real settings. Real systems bring noisy sensors, shifting rules, and partly hidden state. Past benches rarely capture that mix, and no shared sorting of random types existed.

STORI adds varied random effects to a classic game bench in a planned way. The authors sort randomness into five types and test two leading model based agents. Both agents badly underrate how much the world varies and falter under corrupted actions. Code and data are public, giving teams a shared base for sturdier agents.
arxiv-2509-01893:
Zhongrui Chen leads six co-authors on scheduling data center jobs that need many servers at once and cannot pause mid-run. Pausing such jobs costs heavy save and reload work, so systems avoid it. First come first served rules can idle many servers and slow replies. A known rule that favors big jobs keeps use high but makes wait times swing wildly.

Their Quickswap family keeps the big job bias but grants turns to other jobs at set intervals. Proofs cover stability and average reply time, with dramatic gains in the simplest case. Simulations on real workloads, with tuned variants, beat both rival rules by wide margins. The design aims for high use without unfair waits.
arxiv-2509-01993:
Pratik Khandagale leads four co-authors in showing that dipolar forces can collapse a dielectric polymer chain under a strong electric field. A polymer chain pinned at both ends folds sharply toward its center in their study. Dipolar interactions act across distance, and monomer polarization depends on direction, traits past theories could not include. Real polymers carry both traits, so the gap mattered.

Once collapsed, many monomers crowd the center and spike the local field and polarization by huge factors. The collapse responds to field direction and to how far the chain is stretched. The effect suggests fast actuators and sensors driven by field alone. It also exposes physics behind instabilities and electrical breakdown in insulating polymers.
arxiv-2509-02193:
Daniel Isla leads six co-authors in probing primordial black holes inside the main lens galaxy of a doubly imaged quasar. Primordial black holes formed just after the Big Bang could supply part of galactic dark matter. The lens galaxy sits between us and a distant quasar whose light it splits and magnifies. Sixteen years of microlensing variability in that system carry the probe signal.

Ninety simulated scenarios mix smooth matter, stars, and black holes in varied shares. None reproduces the full observed signal, a sobering check. Long term variability alone favors a small mass share in black holes near the mean stellar mass. Strong limits on Jupiter mass black holes need a source size measurement. Far longer light curves would constrain heavier populations.
arxiv-2509-02293:
Yidong Chen, Marius Junge, and Nima Lashkari wrote a 2025 quantum gravity paper on third quantisation, a framework where whole universes can be created and destroyed, much like particles in field theory. Gravity's path integral sums over changing topologies, which motivates the picture.

The authors argue that topology change is rare, so its effect on very late-time physics follows a universal Poisson process, a standard model of random rare events. That process explains the plateau seen in multi-boundary spectral statistics. For closed baby universes, counts follow a coherent state. Open universes need a noncommutative version, which the authors build as an operator algebra construction called Poissonization. Toy models and two-dimensional gravity examples fit the framework exactly.
arxiv-2509-02393:
Arnd Hartmanns and Robert Modderman present a 2025 formal methods paper on computing reachability chances in discrete-time Markov chains, models where a system jumps between states with fixed probabilities. Model checking asks how likely the system is to reach a goal state.

One route sums the probability of all paths from the start to the goal. Splitting that sum into path abstractions, local reachability pieces, helps when refining counterexamples. The authors complete an earlier 2010 approach and prove the split gives the same total. They also show the split need not follow the chain's strongly connected parts; any finite chain of state sets works. Their proofs recast the chain using a free monoid structure, keeping them short, and a reference implementation is included.
arxiv-2509-02493:
Raj Kiriti Velicheti, Subhonmesh Bose, and Tamer Başar present a 2025 game theory paper on incentive design, where a principal shapes an agent's rewards through a committed policy. When the agent knows more than the principal, the principal pays an information rent for that advantage.

The authors study this asymmetry systematically in matrix games and in quadratic Gaussian games. They show the principal benefits from shrinking the knowledge gap. Two routes are compared: letting the agent shape the principal's belief through information design, or paying to acquire information directly. Surprisingly, agent-shaped beliefs can help the principal. Adding uncertainty always raises the principal's cost, but the paper gives solutions for each case, clarifying when information gathering pays.
arxiv-2509-02693:
Dhayaa Anbajagane and Hayden Lee present a 2025 cosmology paper on cosmological collider physics, where heavy particles active during inflation leave distinctive non-Gaussian marks in the initial density field. Those marks could reveal particles far beyond any accelerator's reach.

Earlier studies of such signals relied on perturbation theory, valid only while density contrasts stay small. The authors built a method to run full simulations with arbitrary three-point signals in the starting conditions. A suite of over thirty templates is evolved into the strongly nonlinear regime. They detail effects on matter clustering, halo counts, and halo bias. Forecasts for Rubin Observatory lensing show the lensing field's second and third moments give limits that rival and complement microwave background results. Data products are released publicly.
arxiv-2509-02793:
Elliot Granath wrote a 2025 geometry paper on when a shape can carry a metric of positive scalar curvature. A metric is a rule for measuring distance, and scalar curvature summarizes how space bends at each point. For certain closed shapes called Spin manifolds, an older theorem tied the question to a single invariant, a number that stays fixed under change.

Granath extends that line of work to Spin^c manifolds, a slightly broader class. He shows the kernel of the related invariant splits into images of two transfer maps, which are ways of building new shapes from old ones. Along the way he revisits details of the earlier proof and offers alternate arguments for some steps.
arxiv-2509-02893:
Tian-Xiao He wrote a 2025 mathematics paper, the second in a series, on arrays of numbers known as multiple Riordan arrays. These arrays package whole families of sequences into one structured table. Combinatorialists use them to track counting patterns and how sequences transform into each other.

He defines a broader family called multiple almost-Riordan arrays, allowing a few entries to break the usual pattern. He then shows that all such arrays together form a group, meaning they can be combined and undone under one rule. The paper works out sequence descriptions for these arrays and builds their production matrices, which generate one row from another. It also defines a compressed form of the arrays and describes its sequences.
arxiv-2509-02993:
Chao Fan and 8 co-authors proposed a 2025 network called SPENet for medical image segmentation with very few labeled examples. Segmentation means painting each pixel with a class label, such as tumor or healthy tissue. Clinics often cannot supply the thousands of marked scans that standard models need.

SPENet compares a labeled support image with a new query image through prototypes, which are summary patterns of each class. One module builds both a global prototype and several local ones, catching variation inside a class. Another module uses the query image to polish those support prototypes and drop misleading ones. Across three public datasets, the network beat leading rivals at this few-shot task.
arxiv-2509-03193:
Maximilian Neidhardt and 4 co-authors built a 2025 endoscope that measures tissue stiffness at high speed, paired with deep learning. Stiffness signals disease in soft tissue, yet standard imaging cannot easily measure it during minimally invasive surgery. Their fiber scanning probe images complex wave fields rippling through tissue in many directions and frequencies.

A conical scan pattern samples fast while keeping three-dimensional information. A spatio-temporal neural network turns those wave movies into local elasticity maps in real time. Training used rubber-like phantoms of known stiffness. Against conventional phase tracking, their two-dimensional scans cut average error roughly in half. A fuller three-dimensional method cut error far more when wave direction was unknown. Tests on pig tissue showed the approach works outside phantoms.
arxiv-2509-03393:
Taisiya Khakharova, Lucas Sakizloglou, and Leen Lambers explored graph-based offline reinforcement learning for sepsis treatment in 2025. Sepsis is a life-threatening response to infection, and choosing fluid and vasopressor doses for each patient is genuinely hard. Learning treatment policies from past records, without live experimentation, is called offline reinforcement learning.

Earlier studies used ordinary tabular patient data. This team instead models records from a well-known intensive care dataset as a graph with several node types that changes over time. Two graph neural network encoders learn patient state representations while decoders predict the next state. Those representations feed a policy learning algorithm designed for offline data. Experiments confirmed the approach's potential while exposing how hard representation learning is here.
arxiv-2509-03593:
AT2020adpi, a bright flare from the centre of a distant galaxy, is examined in a 2025 research paper by Paarmita Pandey and fifteen co-authors. Such nuclear transients can signal a star being torn apart by a supermassive black hole, or an episode of feeding by the black hole itself. Telling those apart is notoriously hard.

Observations span optical, ultraviolet, infrared, and spectroscopic data taken around the flare's peak. Its energy output fits a power-law shape and rivals luminous active nucleus flares. A strong mid-infrared flare arrived about 210 days later, read as an echo from hot dust roughly a fifth of a parsec away. Spectra mix broad hydrogen and helium lines with iron and magnesium features in an unusual combination. The authors conclude the event was likely an accretion episode, triggered by a star disrupting within a disk or by instability in an active nucleus.
arxiv-2509-03693:
Designing artificial intelligence explanations that help people spot misinformation is the focus of a 2025 research paper by Yeaeun Gong and four co-authors. Most explanation tools describe only content features, like wording and sentence structure. The authors argue readers also judge claims by social context: who shared the item, how others reacted, and what surrounds it.

Three explanation styles are compared: content alone, social alone, and a combined form where the two either agree or conflict. Two online crowdsourcing experiments test them, one on COVID-19 material and one on political material. Explanations generally improved detection of false items. Effectiveness depended strongly on whether the content and social explanations aligned. Order also mattered: showing content first versus social first changed accuracy, and the effect differed between the health and politics studies. The findings give designers concrete guidance for explanation interfaces.
arxiv-2509-03793:
Prathamesh Devadiga and two co-authors devote a 2025 research paper to SAMVAD, a multi-agent system that simulates judicial deliberation in India. Real studies of court panels face heavy ethical and practical barriers, since actual deliberations are closed. A simulation offers a safer way to explore how benches reason together and reach verdicts.

Agents powered by large language models play the judge, prosecution counsel, defence counsel, and several adjudicators forming the bench. A retrieval step grounds their arguments in key Indian legal texts, from the penal code to the constitution. That grounding lets the judge and counsel produce legally sound instructions and arguments with sources attached. Adjudicators then deliberate over case facts, instructions, and arguments across several rounds, working toward a consensus verdict. The paper details the architecture, message protocols, and simulation workflow. A full evaluation plan covers performance, quality of deliberation, and consistency of outcomes.
arxiv-2509-03893:
Stefan Stojanov and four co-authors study weakly-supervised learning of dense functional correspondences between images in a 2025 research paper. A correspondence matches each point on one object to the matching point on another. Across different categories, shared function can guide the match: parts that do the same job often look and sit alike, even on unlike objects.

Their definition of dense functional correspondence formalises that idea. Vision-language models first pseudo-label images from many views, identifying functional parts without hand annotation. Dense contrastive learning, driven by pixel-level matches, then distils functional and spatial knowledge together into one new model. That model can establish correspondences on fresh image pairs directly. Synthetic and real benchmark datasets are curated for the task. Against baselines built from ready-made self-supervised image features and grounded vision-language models, the new approach shows clear advantages for shape reconstruction and robot manipulation uses.
arxiv-2509-03993:
In a 2025 mathematics paper, Yuki Kondo and one co-author compute the generic degree of the generalised Verschiebung map in rank two. In positive characteristic, the Frobenius map raises coordinates to the p-th power and pulls bundles back along it. The Verschiebung is the induced map on moduli spaces of stable bundles, and its generic degree counts preimages over a typical point.

Earlier work on dormant opers supplies the key input. A conjecture of the second author predicted a direct link between counting higher-level dormant opers and these degrees, and the rank two case is resolved affirmatively here. Consequently, for general curves of genus above one in characteristic above two, the degrees can be determined explicitly by counting certain combinatorial objects. One degree is computed, for genera three through ten, as a polynomial in p. Such explicit formulas turn an abstract moduli question into concrete, checkable data.
arxiv-2509-04493:
Brian Hopkins, writing alone, revisits three classical ways of splitting whole numbers whose counts follow the Fibonacci sequence in a 2025 mathematics paper. Compositions are ordered splits of a number into parts, and restricted families of them have been known since ancient India and nineteenth-century England to number exactly the Fibonacci counts. Hopkins proves those enumeration results with tiling arguments, covering a number with domino-like pieces, and shows how the same tilings prove several Fibonacci identities combinatorially.

MacMahon's notion of conjugation, a way of flipping a composition's diagram, enters next. For every target number from two onward, the compositions contain subsets whose sizes obey the Fibonacci recurrence. Classical counting thus still yields fresh structure.
arxiv-2509-04593:
Aditya Gahlawat and five co-authors steer uncertain systems safely by guiding their whole probability clouds in a 2025 research paper. Covariance steering guides a system so its spread of possible states lands in a safe shape. Real systems face unbounded random disturbances plus model errors tied to state, making future distributions unknown and potentially wild. Their method pairs an L1-adaptive control layer, which robustly handles the uncertainty, with certificates in the Wasserstein metric, a distance between probability distributions.

Those certificates feed the high-level steering, guaranteeing safety without assuming finite samples from the true spread or pre-known ambiguity sets that rival methods impose. Nonlinear stochastic processes gain predictable, cautious control with proof. Uses include vehicles and robots working amid deep uncertainty.
arxiv-2509-04693:
Soft glassy materials that contain actively rotating parts can respond to shear in odd, sideways ways. Debarghya Banerjee and one co-author model that response in a 2025 soft matter paper. Their chiral soft glassy rheology model treats the material as actively rotating inclusions inside a glassy matrix.

For steady shear, they find an odd viscosity that grows, counterintuitively, as the active rotation frequency falls. For oscillatory shear, they find an odd viscoelastic spectrum shaped by resonance effects and glassy power laws. The work helps explain how odd viscoelasticity, a gap between odd fluids and odd solids, can emerge.
arxiv-2509-04793:
Planet-hunting surveys produce far more light curves than human vetters can check quickly. Bibin Thomas, lead author with five co-authors, present a hybrid deep learning classifier for that task in a 2025 paper. The model combines convolutional networks, bidirectional recurrent layers, and attention, and it trains on Kepler DR25 data.

Attention visualisations highlight the entry and exit phases of transits, matching astrophysical expectations. Applied to candidate signals, the pipeline flagged a set for false positive analysis, after which the authors report several statistically validated candidates and three robust exoplanets. Its fast inference suits triage for TESS and future PLATO work.
arxiv-2509-05193:
Skipping the first few steps of a system's behaviour can reveal simple structure, Bastien Dubail and two co-authors argue in a 2025 reinforcement learning paper. Many learning methods assume a low-rank form, meaning a large table can be rebuilt from a few patterns, for a measure of future states.

The authors show the plain measure lacks that form, while the shifted version, which starts after some early transitions, often has it. They give accuracy guarantees for estimating it from sampled entries and link the needed shift to how fast the system mixes. Tests in goal-based learning support the claim: shifting improves performance.
arxiv-2509-05593:
A thermodynamic identity for charged black holes survives exotic entropy rules, Hai-Long Zhen and four co-authors report in a 2025 gravity paper. Their black holes sit in anti-de Sitter space, carry electric charge, and are immersed in perfect fluid dark matter.

The investigation runs in two frameworks: restricted phase space thermodynamics and a dual conformal field theory picture. Non-extensive entropy forms, which generalise the usual entropy rule, are examined systematically. In both frameworks the Goon-Penco relation, linking a change in the black hole's extremality to a change in its temperature under charge variation, still holds. The authors present that persistence as evidence the relation is universal.
arxiv-2509-05693:
Judging a risk score for patients who entered a study late and may leave early is widened by Kendrick Li and six co-authors in a 2025 statistics paper. Time-dependent ROC analysis measures how well a blood marker separates future cases from non-cases, but left truncation and right censoring distort the data.

The authors build several tools that extend an earlier limited approach, for both plain and driver-based truncation. They also add weighted tools for sensitivity and specificity, and for the area under the curve, that correct for both distortions at once. Simulations test the tools in depth. A case study scores a death-risk model for elderly kidney failure patients using national transplant data.
arxiv-2509-06393:
Talking to a chatbot that talks like you lifts engagement in mental health support, find Mehrnoosh Sadat Shirvani and six co-authors in a 2025 paper. Therapy chatbots work, but users drift away. Borrowing from journaling and empty-chair techniques, the authors design self-clone chatbots that mirror each user's own support strategies and conversational patterns, turning self-talk into dialogue.

In a semi-controlled experiment with one hundred eighty people, self-clones produced much higher emotional and cognitive engagement than a generic counselor persona. Believability of the clone mediated the effect, and the authors stress the balance between a convincing self-likeness and keeping interactions positive. Self-clones are offered as a promising engagement strategy for digital mental health.
arxiv-2509-06893:
Swarms of drug-carrying nanobots treating cancer spread across many sites are modeled by Noble Harasha and one co-author in a 2025 theoretical paper. Nanobots promise targeted delivery with less toxicity, but diffuse cancer presents several distinct sites at once. Payloads must be divided among sites according to need, which requires coordination.

A mathematical model describes the agents and their chemical environment, with movement based on experimental findings: the bots noisily climb and descend chemical gradients. Three algorithms are compared. The first simply follows natural chemical signals around each site and works unless signals are weak. The second amplifies those signals, speeding treatment but lowering eventual success except for concentrated cancers. The third also releases a counter-signal that repels bots from sites already treated enough. Simulations show the third algorithm performing well across all cancer patterns tested.
arxiv-2509-06993:
Zirui Xu and 6 co-authors describe the winning answer to a geospatial embedding challenge in a 2025 technical report. The EarthVision Embed2Scale challenge at CVPR 2025 aims to develop foundational geospatial models that embed hyperspectral geospatial data cubes, stacks of satellite imagery across many wavelengths, into embedding vectors. Such vectors should facilitate various downstream tasks, including sorting and regression.

Their new method, called the Geospatial Foundational Embedder, was the top-ranked winning answer on the challenge, according to the report. The work is presented as a technical report introducing the method rather than a full experimental study. It addresses data from the SSL4EO-S12 data set, a standard self-guided learning benchmark for Earth reading. Winning a shared challenge gives evidence the approach compared favorably against other submitted foundational embedding methods.
arxiv-2509-07293:
Miguel Saavedra-Melo and 5 co-authors test a simpler way to control reconfigurable intelligent surfaces in a 2025 paper. These surfaces are panels that steer reflected radio waves and are candidates for next-generation wireless networks. Conventional designs need bulky control wiring for every element. The wave-controlled design instead uses standing waves on a single transmission line to create the needed bias voltages.

The team builds such a surface and its biasing line, then compares theory against bench measurements. The standing wave does generate the correct voltages, but the results also depend on impedance matching, a tuning factor the theory had missed. With a single standing wave frequency, the surface steers a beam to angles near broadside, straight out from the panel. Simpler control could make these surfaces cheaper and thinner for future base stations.
arxiv-2509-07393:
Akihito Hora, writing alone in 2025, follows how random stacks of Young diagrams change over time. Young diagrams are staircase shapes made of boxes that encode symmetry data in algebra. Here several diagrams evolve together as boxes jump between them under a branching rule tied to wreath products, group constructions that mix a finite group with symmetric groups.

Under suitable scaling, averaged limit shapes emerge, smooth outlines that the random diagrams follow on average. Hora describes how those macroscopic shapes evolve in time using Voiculescu's R-transforms and free Lévy measures, tools from free probability theory. Both diffusive scaling, where motion spreads like heat, and a non-diffusive kind are covered. The microscopic dynamics even allow waiting times that are not exponential, a flexibility most such models lack. The work links random diagram growth to deep probability theory.
arxiv-2509-07893:
Peter K. Friz and 1 co-author characterise a similarity measure for random paths in a 2025 probability paper. The expected signature kernel compares probability laws on path space and feeds a standard test for whether two distributions differ. Rough paths theory supplies the tools for handling paths too irregular for ordinary calculus.

For group-valued Lévy processes, a broad class of jumpy random motions, the kernel turns out to be one component of the solution to an extended Goursat-type system of equations. The authors describe the continuous case exactly, where the system stays finite-dimensional, and treat jumps separately. A computable formula for the kernel helps statisticians compare collections of streams, from handwriting samples to financial price paths, with mathematical confidence.
arxiv-2509-08193:
Computing is shrinking into disposable items like food packaging and medical patches, where chips must be nearly free. Shvetank Prakash and 15 co-authors present FlexiFlow in a 2025 research paper. FlexiFlow is a design framework for such item-level intelligence. It uses flexible electronics, which cost far less than silicon but run slowly and hold few gates.

The key insight is lifetime: these items operate for wildly different spans, up to a thousandfold variation. That changes the best architecture for each product. The framework includes a workload suite, tiny RISC-V cores at several bit widths, and a carbon-aware selection model. Lifetime-aware design cut the carbon footprint substantially in their tests. The team even taped out a real chip using open tools. Their work rethinks computer design for a trillion-item scale.
arxiv-2509-08293:
Abdelaziz Belaada and 3 co-authors define a new class of operators between ordered spaces in a 2025 maths paper. The operators take several inputs at once, so they are multilinear. They are also positive, which means they respect the order of the spaces. The class extends old ideas of domination and summability to this richer setting.

A theorem in the style of Pietsch describes the class through a single ruling measure. A version for polynomials follows. Last, a tensor form recasts the operators as plain dual objects on a completed tensor space. Such recasts are the workhorse of analysis. They turn hard multi-input problems into linear ones on a bigger space, where stock theorems apply.
arxiv-2509-08393:
Young stars drag planet-forming disks into shapes set by their magnetic fields, model D. Steiner and 2 co-authors in a 2025 astrophysics paper, first in a series. The inner tenth of an astronomical unit matters most for the disk's long-term evolution, yet large-scale field topology there is poorly understood. Field transport inside the disk shapes how material accretes onto the star.

Steady-state solutions combine a one-plus-one-dimensional hydrodynamic disk with two field sources: a stellar dipole that truncates the disk's inner edge and a fossil field inherited from the parent cloud. Dependencies on the stellar field are mapped explicitly. Planet formation begins in exactly this magnetised inner region, so its steady states constrain every later chapter.
arxiv-2509-08593:
Using language models to grade other language models creates a regress: who grades the graders when no ground truth exists? Andrés Corrada-Emmanuel answers with logic rather than more graders, in a 2025 research paper written alone. Disagreement between judges carries information. If two judges disagree about a third model's work, they cannot both be perfectly right.

Corrada-Emmanuel formalizes that idea as a linear programming problem over answer counts for any finite test. From agreement patterns alone, the method computes the only possible values of each judge's grading ability. It then raises alarms when a judge must be violating a user-set accuracy requirement. The alarms carry no false positives, a strong guarantee. Such no-knowledge checks could keep automated evaluation honest as models increasingly judge models in industry pipelines.
arxiv-2509-08793:
Weizhe Liu and 25 co-authors report frequent extreme galaxy outflows among bright early quasars in a 2025 paper. Quasars are very bright centers of young galaxies. Fast outflows may shut down star formation, a process called quenching.

Observations with the James Webb Space Telescope find very fast outflows in six of twenty-seven quasars at high redshift. Speeds and energy rates far exceed those in lower redshift samples. The outflow rate is several times higher than in comparison groups. Some flows could reach beyond the galaxy into surrounding gas. The authors argue quasar feedback likely plays a strong role in regulating early massive galaxies.
arxiv-2509-09193:
Haoxiang Luo and 11 co-authors survey AI reasoning for wireless networks in a 2025 paper. Old deep learning tools act as closed boxes and lack step by step reasoning. Wireless nets, though, face hard choices at many layers, from radio links to apps.

Reasoning based AI, such as large language model agents, can plan, recall, use tools, and act across layers with little human help. The survey sets up a task taxonomy for wireless work. Each net layer is checked for pain points and for gains reasoning tools can bring. Gaps and next steps close the survey. Its aim is to guide the merger of reasoning AI with next generation wireless nets.
arxiv-2509-09293:
Dharam V. Lal and 5 co-authors describe the superMIGHTEE project and its first data release in a 2025 paper. The project combines MeerKAT data from South Africa with upgraded GMRT observations from India to image the deep radio sky. Sensitivity reaches a few microjanskys across a wide frequency range.

Total intensity images cover deep fields at two frequencies, with catalogs of tens of thousands of radio sources. Source redshifts extend far, with a median around one. Broadband spectra show a shift from active galactic nucleus dominated sources to star forming galaxies at faint flux levels. Later releases will add polarization and spectral line products. The dataset targets galaxy evolution over cosmic time.
arxiv-2509-09493:
Ignacio Amores-Sesar and 3 co-authors revisit trust in distributed systems in a 2025 paper where each participant may trust others differently. Ordinary quorum models force everyone to share the same trust assumptions. Under purely personal assumptions, classic guarantees turn out to be too weak, and basic tasks such as reliable broadcast and consensus become impossible without something stronger added.

Earlier fixes, the authors argue, added so much that the freedom of personal trust was effectively lost. Their new characterisation of asymmetric problems supports fresh algorithms for broadcast and consensus under weaker demands. Because the approach is general, it can be carried over to other core problems in systems built on asymmetric trust.
arxiv-2509-09593:
Bangzhao Shu and 7 co-authors test how well language models read fine-grained human feelings in a 2025 benchmark study. Models are now common in mental health research, yet most emotion tests sort text into a few broad boxes. Real self-description is far richer, and that mismatch can hide how poorly a model truly tracks what a person says they feel.

The team built EXPRESS, a data set from Reddit communities holding 251 self-disclosed emotion labels, then broke predictions down into eight basic emotions for close comparison. Across popular models and prompt styles, matching human labels stayed hard. Some outputs fit emotion theory neatly while still missing context cues that human readers catch, hence the title's charge of fluency without feeling.
arxiv-2509-09693:
Measuring the eyelid's landmarks precisely guides surgery for drooping eyelids, but specialists are scarce where need is common. George R. Nahass and 11 co-authors built Glorbit, a browser-based measurement platform, in a 2025 research paper. The application automates periorbital measurements such as margin reflex distances and fissure height. It was designed from the start for low-resource clinics.

An AI segmentation model sits inside a modular pipeline backed by secure, site-specific cloud storage. The app works offline, preprocesses images locally, and uploads through authenticated logins. A simulated enrollment study with fifteen volunteers ran the full workflow without error on laptops, tablets, and phones. Sessions averaged about one hundred seconds, and usability scores were uniformly high. Standardized eye measurements from any browser could feed future triage tools and bring specialist-grade assessment to clinics that have none.
arxiv-2509-10093:
Laura Bragagnolo and 3 co-authors improve the parsing of crowded human figures in this 2025 paper. Multi-human parsing labels each body part in an image and assigns it to the right person. Leading methods do well on public data sets but break down when bodies overlap, a common case in real scenes.

The team's insight is that people hidden from one camera angle may stand apart from another. They train models with several views at once, using weak supervision on instances and a loss that forces agreement across views. They also describe a semi-automatic way to build training masks from color, depth, and skeleton data. In heavy overlap tests, the approach lifted parsing scores by a clear margin over the base model.
arxiv-2509-10193:
In Italy, did a temporary tax break create lasting permanent jobs? Michele Cantarella, Maria Cristina Maurizio, and Francesco Serti tackle that question in this 2025 economics paper. They study payroll tax exemptions that rewarded firms for converting temporary contracts into permanent ones, using detailed work histories from Tuscany.

A 2018 change in who qualified for the exemption lets the authors separate the policy's effect from other trends. Conversions rose right after the incentive appeared, yet the gain faded quickly and looks like hiring that firms simply moved earlier. Over the medium term they find no lasting effect on job security, staying with the same firm, or total time in work, for any group of firms or workers.
arxiv-2509-10293:
Yinan Wang and five co-authors introduce OpenCSP, a machine learning framework for predicting crystal structures under pressure, in this 2025 materials paper. Most large atomistic models train on calm, near-ambient data, so their stress predictions falter at the crushing pressures found inside planets, exactly where new crystal forms appear.

OpenCSP pairs an open, pressure-resolved dataset with models tuned jointly for energy, force, and stress accuracy. The data grow through randomized high-pressure sampling, sharpened by an uncertainty-guided loop that adds under-sampled squeezed states and drops redundant quantum calculations. Even with far less training data than leading rivals, the models match or beat names such as MACE-MPA-0 and MatterSim on stability ranking, with the biggest wins at high pressure.
arxiv-2509-10393:
Clémentine Chazal and four co-authors introduce a computable way to judge how close a method gets to its target distribution in this 2025 statistics paper. Many techniques in statistics and machine learning aim at a distribution defined by minimizing an entropy-regularised variational objective, but that flexibility hides the target's density formula, making quality hard to check.

Their measure, gradient discrepancy, and its kernel version, can be computed explicitly from samples. In Bayesian settings it coincides with the well-known kernel Stein discrepancy, which they reinterpret as the size of a variational gradient. Beyond that setting, the measure lets researchers build and compare new sampling algorithms even when densities are unavailable. The authors propose several, including a generalized Stein variational method, and prove conditions under which the measure stays continuous and controls convergence.
arxiv-2509-10493:
Ruiqi Wang and six co-authors manage radio settings for LoRaWAN, the long-range, low-power networks used by sensors, in this 2025 networking paper. A large deployment must trade off packet delivery against energy efficiency, by tuning each node's carrier frequency, spreading factor, and transmission power. Earlier methods often chase one metric or cannot keep up as channels change.

Their first framework, D-LoRa, lets nodes learn on their own by framing the choice as a combinatorial multi-armed bandit problem, split into pieces with separate rewards to keep learning cheap. A hybrid successor, CD-LoRa, adds one centralized setup pass that assigns channels and trims the options before distributed learning takes over. Simulations and field trials favor both: delivery rose by up to about eleven percent and energy efficiency by about a quarter over strong baselines.
arxiv-2509-10593:
Cervical cancer is preventable when screening reaches people, and Aoife McDonald-Bowyer with nine co-authors work on the imaging brain of a speculum-free screening device in this 2025 medical technology paper. Such devices could widen access, especially in low-resource settings, but they need software that can find the cervical os reliably to guide sampling.

The team compared five encoder-decoder networks on nine hundred-odd endoscopic frames from two hundred cases, annotated by gynaecologists. A vision transformer pretrained on surgical video, EndoViT with a DPT head, won on overlap and detection rate against convolutional rivals. Tests on phantom models kept working under varied conditions at over twenty frames per second, fast enough for real-time guidance. The study lays groundwork for devices that non-experts could use anywhere.
arxiv-2509-10793:
Eli Baum and six co-authors present ORQ in this 2025 computer security paper. ORQ runs complex analytics over private data that nobody has to reveal. Parties can pool datasets logically, while secure multi-party computation keeps every record hidden, even against malicious participants. Joins across many tables are ORQ's specialty. Under such computation, joins are normally ruinously expensive.

The system dodges the quadratic cost of secure joins by exploiting how real queries are structured. Joining and aggregating happen on the fly, with intermediate results kept bounded. Around that core sit oblivious operators, a vectorized query engine, a network layer that spreads communication costs, and a dataflow API. In local and wide-area tests, ORQ beat rival systems soundly. It ran the full TPC-H benchmark at scale factor ten, entirely under secure computation. That scale previously required leaking information, or trusting a third party.
arxiv-2509-10993:
Managers are beginning to clone themselves as AI agents, and Qing Hu with three co-authors explore that future workplace in this 2025 paper. A manager clone agent is a digital surrogate, trained on a manager's messages and decision patterns, performing managerial tasks in their place. The authors ran six design fiction workshops with twenty-three managers and workers, who invented scenarios together and argued through what followed.

They imagined four roles for clones: a proxy presence, an informational conveyor, a productivity engine, and a leadership amplifier. Their worries stacked up at individual, interpersonal, and company-wide levels, from eroded trust to flattened hierarchy. The paper collects design advice from both sides of the reporting line. It stresses that workers' perspectives and human bonds must be designed in deliberately, before the clones arrive by default.
arxiv-2509-11993:
Finding dark matter haloes in a simulation sounds simple until someone asks which particles actually belong to one. Tamara R. G. Richardson, with two co-authors, presents STRAWBERRY in 2025, an algorithm that answers the belonging question using the gravitational potential itself.

A particle counts as bound when its energy stays below the escape energy of its potential well, judged from an accelerated, or boosted, frame. The escape level is set by the nearest saddle point leading toward a deeper minimum, so no arbitrary density cutoffs are needed and every particle's gravity enters the test. Only present-moment information is used. The authors show particles typically bind between their first closest and farthest passages around a center. Bound and unbound groups also differ sharply in phase-space patterns, density profiles, and evolution. Haloes end up painted as two-component systems.
arxiv-2509-12793:
J. Gbetoho, F. Dossa and G. Avossevou solve in 2025 the energy levels of graphene in a magnetic field when space has a smallest length. Graphene is a one-atom-thick carbon sheet where charge carriers act like light, fast particles with no mass.

A hidden symmetry lets them build the full spectrum with algebra alone, without brute force. From that spectrum they work out heat traits such as heat capacity with a known math tool. They find the high-heat law holds and that heat capacity does not depend on the length shift. The work links a deep space idea to tests on a real material.
arxiv-2509-13193:
Ignasi Rosell, Antonio Pich and Juan Jose Sanz-Cillero bound in 2025 heavy resonance masses from oblique gauges in a broad non-linear theory. Oblique gauges S and T track new physics that hides in propagators. Strongly linked heavy states are the target.

Next-order terms now include odd-parity parts and fermion cuts. Fresh data bounds are folded in. When both Weinberg sum rules hold, vector masses must top a very high scale. Lighter masses in a mid range force breach of the second rule. The split sorts which strong completions remain viable.
arxiv-2509-13293:
Mengyi Gong, Christopher Nemeth and three co-authors infer soil drydown after rain in 2025 with adaptive online changepoint tools. Moisture traces split into segments with shifting forms and scales. Static models miss that piecewise life and lag real shifts.

Two extensions of Bayesian online detection are given. One uses particle filters when key parameters resist exact pooling. One learns parameters live via gradient steps inside detection. Hyper choices and cost cuts are detailed on fake data. Field sites in Austria and the United States give site drydown rates. Adaptive fits beat static rivals on those field series.
arxiv-2509-13493:
Michele Aleandri, Paolo Dai Pra and Ida Minelli study in 2025 reinforced interacting agents in competitive and cooperative settings, where choices evolve under reinforcement, network links, and environment pushes. Long-term acts and synchronization are the core asks.

In competitive irreducible networks, states converge almost surely. Bipartite graphs yield random limits; non-bipartite graphs yield fixed limits. Reducible networks split via hierarchy graphs, where upper agents see lower ones as forcing inputs. A general forced framework characterizes long acts in full. Synchronization patterns sort by graph structure in a rigorous way.
arxiv-2509-13893:
Lucas MacQuarrie and Pei Yu sharpen a test for relaxation oscillations in a 2025 dynamical systems paper. Slow-fast systems can produce relaxation oscillations, long slow drifts punctuated by sudden jumps, but the standard geometric theory does not apply to every model. Earlier work by Zhang, Wahl, and Yu, and by Yu and Wang, gave simple checkable conditions that certify such oscillations in those harder cases.

MacQuarrie and Yu present seven models that fail the existing conditions yet still display recurrent behavior, showing the tests are too narrow. Motivated by those counterexamples, they generalize the conditions into new, still simple, hypothetical criteria for recognizing slow-fast relaxation oscillations, and lay out arguments aimed at growing them into a fuller mathematical theory.
arxiv-2509-14193:
Fernando Diaz-Diaz, Karel Devriendt and Renaud Lambiotte study signed networks in 2025, where links between nodes can be friendly or hostile. Groups inside such networks take two forms. Communities hold friendly links inside, while factions split into opposing camps.

Their tool is the Gremban expansion, a step that turns a signed graph into a larger unsigned one, so standard unsigned methods can still apply. The authors work out the maths and combinatorics of that step, centred on a built in symmetry. Their main result links cuts in the expanded graph to community and faction patterns in the original. On that base they build a spectral clustering method, a grouping method based on graph spectra, that can tell the two patterns apart and extend to more than two groups.
arxiv-2509-14293:
Arash Azizi, writing alone in 2025, gives an exact account of two photon emission from a speeding detector. The detector is an Unruh-DeWitt detector, a simple model atom moving with steady acceleration. It is switched on and off smoothly with a Gaussian profile.

Azizi evaluates the relevant time ordered integrals in closed form. One spectral formula then covers all four direction pairings for the two photons. Patterns are sorted by narrow frequency gates and a resonant factor written with the Faddeeva function. As the interaction lasts longer, the gates sharpen toward the endless interaction limit. The study maps how output scales with acceleration, energy gap and duration, and describes the single photon share of the signal.
arxiv-2509-14393:
Richter Jordaan, writing alone in 2025, characterises ideally connected graphs inside two classic families. For any two vertices, many disjoint paths may join them, but never more than the smaller degree. A graph is ideally connected when that upper bound is always reached.

Jordaan settles the question for cographs and for chordal graphs separately. Ideally connected cographs turn out to be exactly those with no copy of a certain small forbidden pattern. Ideally connected chordal graphs are exactly the threshold graphs. Threshold graphs can be built vertex by vertex, each new vertex either isolated or joined to all previous ones. Clean characterisations turn a global path property into a simple structural test.
arxiv-2509-14493:
Samuel J. Bell and five co-authors test a translate then detect path in 2025 for toxic posts across tongues. Toxic content filters lack training data in most tongues. Turning text into a high resource tongue first may let strong filters do the work.

The team set translation based paths against tongue specific and multilingual filters across sixteen tongues. Translation won in most cases, most of all where the target tongue had few resources and the translation was good. Gains tracked both resource level and translation quality. At scale, good translation plus one strong filter beat bespoke models in most tests. Filters for low resource tongues may gain most from better translation.
arxiv-2509-14793:
Wen-Jie Zhang, Xi Yan, and Jun-Hong An design a quantum router built from defects in diamond in a 2025 quantum physics paper. A quantum router moves quantum information between nodes of a future quantum network. Their nodes are silicon-vacancy centers in diamond, which couple strongly to sound waves through strain, but long-distance links usually suffer from decoherence, the loss of quantum information.

The design places an array of these centers inside a diamond waveguide carrying phonons, the quanta of sound. Instead of switching signals one at a time, it can send a state from one input node to several targets in parallel, much like a home WiFi router. Lasting entanglement becomes possible when bound states form in the combined system. The scheme points toward practical solid-state quantum networks.
arxiv-2509-15293:
Dinura Dissanayake and eleven co-authors benchmark how well foundation models reason step by step in embodied settings in a 2025 AI paper. Robots and agents in the physical world must act effectively, safely, and in ways that respect spatial context. Large multimodal models understand images and language impressively, but structured reasoning for physical tasks is a different demand.

Their benchmark, FoMER, scores models across varied scenarios requiring them to read multimodal observations, weigh physical constraints and safety, and produce valid next actions in natural language. Step-by-step performance is the explicit target, since a correct final answer reached by broken reasoning fails in the real world. The study maps where today's foundation models reason soundly about bodies and spaces, and where their chains of thought snap.
arxiv-2509-16193:
Fake audio that mimics real emotion poses a growing risk, and spotting it may take more than sound alone. Mohd Mujtaba Akhtar and seven co-authors test whether models trained on many signal types beat models trained on audio alone for this task. Models that learned from mixed media should catch odd shifts in feeling that pure audio models miss.

Their tests confirm the mixed models win. They then add SCAR, a fusion method that lets model features refine each other in stages. The fused system set a new best mark for fake emotion detection, beating single models and older fusion tricks.
arxiv-2509-16393:
Banks and funds hold market data they cannot share, yet joint learning could sharpen everyone's forecasts. Manuel Noseda and three co-authors test shared learning for predicting whether volatile markets rise or fall, where partners swap only model updates, never raw data. They compare joint, solo, and fully pooled training with a shared memory-based classifier.

The shared approach matched the pooled model and clearly beat solo training. It held up when data differed across partners, when models were personalized, and when extra privacy noise was added. The results show real collective value from privacy-safe teamwork in finance.
arxiv-2509-16793:
Alexander Pukhov, Nina Elkina, and Tom Wilson present a new plasma simulation code in a 2025 paper. Their code tracks particles inside electromagnetic fields. It works in a boosted frame, one that moves with the action. That shift preserves the field structure while using gaps in scale to save computing.

Unlike quasi-static methods, the code need not split beam and streaming particles. Trapped particles are handled in a self-consistent way. The result is fast, accurate simulation of plasma wakefield acceleration. Such acceleration could shrink future particle accelerators from kilometers to rooms. Better codes help design those machines before they are built.
arxiv-2509-17193:
David Christopher and Davamani Christober wrote a 2025 arXiv paper in number theory about counting partitions. A partition splits a whole number into parts, and here the parts must come from a fixed finite set A. The paper studies how fast the count of such partitions grows as the number itself grows.

A classic estimate for this growth has been proved in several ways over the years. The authors give a fresh proof that stays purely combinatorial, with no heavy machinery. Their route uses the fact that the count, as a function of the number, is a quasi-polynomial when the part set is finite. The paper also needs the part set to share no common divisor above one, as the classic result does.
arxiv-2509-17393:
Kang-il Lee and six co-authors rethink how programs get written from examples. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from a weakness in program synthesis: training examples are few, and test inputs hide edge cases, so synthesized programs often break in the real world. Their fix lets the synthesizer peek at the test inputs while it works, a move they call transductive synthesis.

The method treats synthesis as active learning over the outputs of a finite set of candidate programs. A language model predicts outputs for chosen test inputs, and candidates that clash are struck out. A greedy maximin rule picks which inputs to ask about, keeping the query count low. On four benchmarks, from logic tasks to world modeling in MiniGrid, the method raised accuracy and cut cost next to rivals. Code is released under the name SYNTRA.
arxiv-2509-17893:
V M Schafer and 6 co-authors compare two ways to link qubits made of unlike ions. Their 2025 paper deals with trapped-ion quantum computers, where paired gates join two qubits. Each gate type has its own perks and flaws, and mixed pairs add fresh twists.

Both gates were run on calcium and strontium ions, which react to magnet fields in very unlike ways. One gate scored a bit higher on truth of output than the other, and both scored near perfect. The study maps how the control light phases behave and how stable they stay. Such maps guide which gate to pick for mixed work.
arxiv-2509-17993:
Haoxin Yang and 7 co-authors bake a copyright mark into AI image making, so fakes can be traced. Their 2025 frame, StableGuard, works with latent diffusion models, which build images from a compact code. Past marks were added after the fact, which hurts trust in checks.

A tweaked auto-encoder makes paired marked and clean images in one pass. Masked blends of the pairs train a checker net that needs no tag of how an image was faked. That net mixes mark cues, local fake traces, and tone cues. Both parts train as one, in a self-taught way.
arxiv-2509-18893:
In graph learning, linked nodes often share labels, but sometimes neighbors differ on purpose. Qinhan Hou, Yilun Zheng, Xichun Zhang, Sitao Luan, and Jing Tang study that mismatch, called heterophily, at the whole-graph level in this 2025 paper. Node-level heterophily is well studied. Its graph-level cousin, where the label describes the whole structure, was not.

The team sorts graph labeling schemes into a taxonomy and focuses on motif-based tasks. Motifs are small recurring patterns whose presence sets the label. An energy-based flow analysis yields the key insight: motif detection needs mixed-frequency dynamics, not one dominant band. Objectives based on motifs clash with global frequency dominance by design. Tests on synthetic graphs with tuned heterophily and on molecular data back the theory. Frequency-adaptive models beat frequency-dominated ones. The paper offers design guidance for graph-level networks.
arxiv-2509-18993:
Training very large language models costs huge memory and computing power, and low-rank designs try to cut both. Boao Kong and four co-authors start from a finding about what flows between the layers of such a model. The changes in layer activations, they found, are themselves low-rank, meaning a small summary captures most of them. Past low-rank methods tend to lose accuracy, add overhead, or save little memory.

Their design, CR-Net, rebuilds each layer's activations from the prior layer's output plus its low-rank change. A tailored recomputation scheme cuts the memory needed to store activations during training. In training runs from small models up to seven billion parameters, CR-Net beat other low-rank methods. It did so while using fewer resources and less memory.
arxiv-2509-19093:
Estimating a hidden state from noisy measurements, called filtering, leans on an equation named for Duncan, Mortensen, and Zakai. Yuhua Meng and three co-authors study a robust pathwise version of that equation. They prove bounds on derivatives of its solution of every order, inside weighted spaces that taper at the boundary. The weights help the estimates but blur regularity near the edge, so weighted and classical inequalities are combined to sharpen the result.

The sharper bounds back a tensor-based numerical method proposed earlier, giving it convergence guarantees. The authors then cut the method's cost when the system's drift and observation functions have a separable form. In simulations of a hard cubic sensor problem, their method beat particle filters and extended Kalman filters on accuracy and speed. It also rebuilt multi-peaked probability densities that the rival methods missed.
arxiv-2509-19493:
Can the shape of a droplet be summed up in just two numbers? Mihir Durve and three co-authors test that idea on five thousand droplets from five shape classes. Each droplet outline, traced with four hundred points, is first smoothed with wave math. An encoder then squeezes the outline down to two values, and the steps can be run in reverse to rebuild the shape.

Plotted by their two values, the droplets form ring-shaped groups, one per class. Common grouping tools such as DBSCAN split or missed those rings. The result shows both the power and the trap of shrinking shapes to two numbers. Grouping methods built for round blobs fail on rings, so shape studies need tools matched to ring-like data.
arxiv-2509-19993:
Mechanical face seals guard pumps and turbines, floating on a thin fluid film that must never collapse. Ben S. Ashby, Tristan Pryer, and Nicola Y. Bailey model what happens when the two faces are misaligned and axial shocks hit. Industry wants smaller clearances for efficiency, which leaves less room for error. Unplanned face contact means wear and early failure.
