They show, for any chosen level of smoothness, that nontrivial rotating solutions exist whose velocity is supported in a bounded region. The flows can be taken as small changes to radial flows.

These are presented as the first smooth rotating flows with finite energy that are not locally radial. The authors also prove rigidity results for rotating solutions in general. Those results show the geometry of such flows is tightly constrained, so the new examples sit in a narrow space left open by the rigidity side.
arxiv-2511-12393:
Nicolo' Pagan, Andreas Philippou and Giulia De Pasquale present a control framework to slow misinformation on social networks without simply killing user engagement. Recommender systems often boost false content because they reward engagement over truth. The framework penalizes traits that false posts commonly exploit, such as extreme negative sentiment and novelty.

The authors extend a closed-loop opinion model to balance two goals at once: less misinformation spread and sustained engagement. Both model-free and model-based controllers cut misinformation propagation sharply across network setups in simulations, using a fact-check dataset with sentiment features drawn by language models. In networks with radical users, median engagement even rises as misinformation falls.
arxiv-2511-12493:
Lars Davidson improves a widely used two-equation turbulence model with help from neural networks. The k-omega model predicts turbulent kinetic energy too low, a flaw it shares with most models of its class. Comparing its terms against direct simulation data, Davidson finds production and dissipation are modeled well, while turbulent diffusion is the weak term.

He turns the energy equation into an equation for a corrected turbulent viscosity and solves it with a physics-informed neural network, then derives a new turbulent Prandtl number from the correction. Three further coefficients are set by neural network models to offset the larger kinetic energy. Tests on channel flow and flat-plate boundary layers show much improved velocity and energy profiles.
arxiv-2511-12693:
Sushant Gautam, Michael A. Riegler, and Pål Halvorsen present HEDGE, a framework for detecting hallucinations in vision-language models that answer questions about images. Such models can state false things with confidence, a real risk in medical use. HEDGE probes a model by perturbing the image in controlled ways, sampling its answers, and clustering those answers by meaning. Shifts in the answer pattern then signal how shaky the model's response really is.

The team tested three medical vision-language models on two medical question datasets. Detectability depended on model design and prompt style: models with dense visual tokenization were easiest to audit, and short label-style answers gave cleaner signals than full sentences. One metric, VASE, gave the most robust signal across settings. The authors frame detection as a geometry problem shaped by sampling, prompts, and clustering choices.
arxiv-2511-12793:
Bowen He and four co-authors introduce lifelong learning for inductive logic programming, where a system learns logic rules from examples. Neural-symbolic AI tries to give neural networks the reasoning discipline of logic, but most work redesigns networks for single problems. This paper instead studies sequences of problems. Because logic rules are compositional and transferable, rules learned for earlier tasks can be reused as building blocks for later ones. Much as a student carries lemmas from one course into the next.

The authors formalize that reuse in a compositional framework and test it on sequences of inductive logic programming tasks. Experiments showed the approach is feasible and brings better scalability and performance than learning each task cold. The result opens a continual learning direction where knowledge accumulates as inspectable rules.
arxiv-2511-12893:
Kaixin Zhang and four co-authors speed up visual autoregressive image generation. These models build images scale by scale, and costs climb as sequences lengthen. Static pruning saves time by deleting weights or tokens for good, but that damages the pretrained model's structure. ActVAR instead activates selectively: it splits feedforward layers into small expert sub-networks and routes each token to the experts it needs. A gating step picks which tokens deserve full computation and reconstructs the rest to keep global context.

A two-stage distillation process trains the routing and gating policies under the original model's supervision, so the slimmed model stays faithful to what it learned. On the standard ImageNet benchmark at moderate resolution, ActVAR cut computation by about a fifth with minimal quality loss. The design offers image generation services a way to lower cost per image without retraining a smaller model from scratch.
arxiv-2511-13193:
Yijia Fan and six co-authors make language-model agents bid for the right to speak. Multi-agent systems built on large language models tend toward free-for-all chatter: token costs balloon and the signal drowns in noise. The authors argue the root problem is that communication is treated as free when it is actually scarce. Their framework, DALA, runs inter-agent communication as a centralized auction in which agents bid for speaking opportunities according to the predicted value density of what they have to say.

Scarcity disciplines the conversation: agents learn to write concisely, and low-value messages simply never get sent. Across seven challenging reasoning benchmarks, DALA reached state-of-the-art performance, and the authors report an emergent behavior they call strategic silence.
arxiv-2511-13693:
Alexander Clow, Sean Kim, and Ladislav Stacho bound the size of large degenerate induced subgraphs inside sparse graphs. A graph is d-degenerate when every part of it holds a vertex of degree at most d, a common sparseness measure. They ask how big an induced d-degenerate piece any k-degenerate graph must contain.

Their lower bound takes the better of two terms, one scaling with the graph's order and one tied to a complementary independence measure. The result improves a classic bound of Alon, Kahn, and Seymour for this setting. A modified argument sharpens the bound further for graphs of bounded genus, extending earlier work that covered only planar graphs.
arxiv-2511-13793:
Mattias Brännström, Themis Dimitra Xanthopoulou, and Lili Jiang model fairness in a real recruitment pipeline by tracing how information flows through it. Hiring AI mixes automated candidate matching with human judgment, and bias can enter, move, and grow at each handoff. Technical audits and high-level ethics reviews each miss that interaction on their own.

Stakeholder interviews and repeated modeling rounds produced a multi-level map of how candidate data are transformed, filtered, and read by both algorithms and people. The map shows where bias can emerge, how it propagates, and what it can do to candidates downstream. The case study shows how flow modeling makes fairness risks visible across a whole socio-technical system.
arxiv-2511-14493:
Aleksi Pyörälä studies dimension results for self-conformal measures, a class of fractal measures. The central question is how dimension behaves under convolution and under orthogonal projection. For convolution, the expected outcome is that dimensions add, up to the limit of the ambient space. Pyörälä gives conditions that guarantee that outcome.

The main condition is that the measure is totally non-linear and not supported on a smooth surface. He also gives algebraic conditions for cases that fail total non-linearity. For projections, dimension is preserved down to the target dimension under stated conditions. The results cover both planar and higher dimensional settings with care.
arxiv-2511-14593:
The JUNO collaboration reports its first measurement of reactor neutrino oscillations. Neutrino flavor change over distance probes fundamental mixing angles and mass differences. JUNO uses a huge liquid scintillator detector placed near several reactor cores. Its design aims to resolve the interference pattern with sub percent precision.

With the first fifty-nine days of data after completion, the team measure two key oscillation parameters at high precision. Both values come from one simultaneous fit. The precision already tests the three flavor framework sharply. Results also bear on neutrino mass ordering and possible new physics. The paper marks the start of JUNO physics output after years of construction.
arxiv-2511-14693:
Rishu Kumar Singh, Navneet Shreya, and three co-authors build VALOR, a framework for sorting customer complaints by aspect and severity. Most past work reads only short posts or reviews, one channel at a time. Real support chats run for many turns and mix text with proof such as screenshots and product photos, which carry key facts.

VALOR routes each case through several expert models that reason step by step with large generative models. A semantic alignment score checks that the text and image stories agree before the final call is made. Finer sorting of grievances helps support teams fix the right problem first and spot severe cases early.
arxiv-2511-14993:
Vladimir Arkhipkin and 24 co-authors report Kandinsky 5.0, a family of foundation models that generate images and short videos from text. The line-up spans a six-billion-parameter image model, a light two-billion-parameter video model, and a nineteen-billion-parameter pro video model aimed at top quality. Videos run up to ten seconds at high resolution.

The report details the full data pipeline behind the models, from collection and filtering to clustering, and a multi-stage training plan. Quality steps after pretraining include supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. For practitioners, the value of such reports lies in the training recipe details that are usually kept private.
arxiv-2511-15193:
Hiromichi Tagawa, Connar Rowan, and five co-authors calculate the fingerprints that gas disks around supermassive black holes leave on gravitational waves. Detectors have logged about two hundred mergers of compact objects, and some may have happened inside the disks of active galactic nuclei. In such a crowded home, the central black hole and nearby companions keep tugging the merging pair.

That steady acceleration shifts the phase of the emitted waves in a measurable way. The authors work out the expected spread of those shifts for mergers in disks. If observers can read the shift, they can sort mergers by birthplace, testing whether disks really are a major factory for the events detectors hear.
arxiv-2511-15793:
Ming-Yu Lei, Bei Zhou, and Xiaoyuan Huang ask whether gravitational waves could test a popular explanation for a gamma-ray glow at the center of our galaxy. That excess of GeV gamma rays might come from dark matter particles annihilating, or from a hidden crowd of millisecond pulsars, rapidly spinning neutron stars in the galactic bulge. Those pulsars are hard to spot with light because of crowding, scattering, and dust.

A spinning pulsar that is slightly non-round emits a nearly steady gravitational wave whose strength is set by its ellipticity. Modeling the proposed population under three ellipticity scenarios, including binaries and Doppler shifts, they find current detectors fall short. Next-generation instruments could detect a fraction of the pulsars.
arxiv-2511-15893:
François Baccelli and Sanjoy Kumar Jhawar analyze a moving wireless network where stations travel at constant speed in random directions. Station starting points follow a homogeneous Poisson process, a standard model of random scatter in the plane. Fixed users always connect to the nearest station, so as stations move, each user hands over from one station to another over time, tracing a dynamical Poisson-Voronoi tessellation.

The handover moments of a typical user form a point process on the time axis. The authors prove that process is stationary and determine its intensity and the joint distribution of gaps between handovers. They also study Palm distributions, the view from a typical handover event, for quantities like distance to the closest stations.
arxiv-2511-15993:
Yangyang Zhang, Zhenwei Li, and Xuefei Chen explain how extremely low mass white dwarfs can form in unusually wide orbits through hierarchical triple systems. Such helium white dwarfs cannot form from single stars, so binary interaction is normally invoked. Two known systems, however, orbit too widely for standard binary evolution. A triple scenario forms the dwarf in an inner binary, then leaves it paired widely with the third object.

Merger of an evolved star with a brown dwarf in the inner pair fails to yield the needed single dwarfs. Type Ia supernova explosions in the inner system succeed in their models. The team also track how explosions reshape the surviving orbital distribution. Triple dynamics thus rescue a class of binaries that pairwise evolution cannot explain.
arxiv-2511-16293:
S. Bouarroudj and A. N. Zubkov describe certain almost-simple algebraic supergroups over an algebraically closed field whose characteristic is odd or zero. Supergroups blend ordinary group structure with anticommuting directions, and the almost-simple ones are basic building blocks for the theory.

Beyond the supergroups whose Lie superalgebras are simple and already appear in Kac's classification theorem, the authors construct new examples. In these new supergroups the Lie superalgebra is either not simple, or simple but absent from Kac's list. The constructions widen the known landscape of almost-simple supergroups and give concrete material for testing how far the classical classification picture extends into the super setting.
arxiv-2511-16593:
Diaeddin Rimawi's thesis tackles a trade-off in online teaming AI systems that keep learning alongside humans toward a shared goal. Disruptions degrade how such a system performs, and recovering costs energy, so decision-makers must balance resilience against greenness.

The work models the system in steady, disruptive, and final states. It introduces GResilience, a recovery framework with three policy styles: optimization over several goals at once, game-theoretic two-agent decisions, and reinforcement learning. A second tool measures both resilience and emissions. Experiments with a robot learning object classification from human demonstrations show the model tracks output shifts during disruptions, and the policies shorten recovery, steady the output, and reduce human effort. The reinforcement learning policies performed best, at a slight emissions cost. Running in containers halved emissions.
arxiv-2511-16693:
JaeSeong Kim and Suan Lee map how language identity is organized inside multilingual language models, probing six models across all 268 transformer layers with linear and nonlinear probes. Their new token-language alignment analysis tracks how language directions in the representation space relate to vocabulary embeddings, layer by layer.

Language information separates sharply in the very first transformer block, jumping by about seventy-six percentage points, and stays almost fully linearly separable through the whole depth. Alignment between language directions and word embeddings tracks the training data's language mix. Models trained with Chinese align Chinese far more strongly than English-centric models do, a more than fourfold structural imprinting effect. The authors argue models distinguish languages through latent structure shaped by the corpus, not surface script, with lessons for data composition and fairness.
arxiv-2511-16893:
Tatsuya Aoyama, Ethan Gotlieb Wilcox, and Nathan Schneider predict when induction heads, the attention circuits credited with language models' in-context learning, will appear during pre-training. Despite their importance, the exact conditions that trigger these pattern-copying heads in language modeling had not been pinned down.

A simple equation combining batch size and context size forecasts the emergence point, and that point barely depends on model size. The statistical fuel is bigram repetition: how often token pairs repeat and how reliably they predict what follows jointly set an effective decision boundary for head formation. Local dependencies with frequent, reliable repetition suffice to create induction heads, while category structure and the shape of the token distribution modulate behavior near the boundary. The findings link a core learning mechanism to measurable data statistics.
arxiv-2511-17093:
Alexander B. Kaganovich surveys Two-Measure Theory, an alternative approach to gravity he and others have developed since 1998. The theory's starting point is a mathematical observation: the spacetime manifold carries a volume measure that standard field theory ignores, and taking it seriously changes the theory's structure. Where it counts, though, the theory still reproduces Einstein's general relativity in every classical test.

Kaganovich gives the theory a clear mathematical and conceptual justification, answering the charge that it is too exotic to matter. He then gathers, in one place, a quarter century of its main results, including effects that traditional models do not produce. The overview is meant both as an entry point for newcomers and as a record of what the framework has achieved.
arxiv-2511-17293:
Thorsten Buss and seven co-authors run the first full-physics benchmark of machine-learned surrogates for highly granular calorimeters, the finely segmented detectors that record particle showers in collider experiments. Generative surrogates promise much faster simulation, but most were tested only on single particles in simplified settings. The authors built DDML, a library that plugs such surrogates into realistic detector descriptions, and compared two models: one generating showers on a regular grid, another as point clouds.

To separate method quirks from model quality, they also compare against idealized simulators sampling ground truth at different resolutions. The evaluation climbs from single particles through photon pairs to a full-physics test, the hadronic decays of tau leptons. Point cloud models, they find, strike the better balance of speed and accuracy for this demanding simulation task.
arxiv-2511-17393:
Georgia Baltsou and three co-authors build a face dataset meant to correct the demographic skew of existing ones. Face verification systems guard banking apps and personal devices, yet most training and test datasets underrepresent many races, genders, and other groups, which limits fairness and accuracy. The authors' methodology uses advanced generative models to synthesize varied, high-quality face images that still respect the rules for identity card photographs.

The resulting dataset, DIF-V, holds 27,780 images of 926 synthetic identities and is offered as a benchmark for face verification research. Testing existing models on it, the authors found biases toward certain genders and races, and showed that identity style modifications hurt model performance. The work aims to give the field a fairer measuring stick and to push verification technology toward more inclusive reliability.
arxiv-2511-17593:
Saicharan Kolluru benchmarks the two leading open-source systems for serving large language models, vLLM and HuggingFace's Text Generation Inference, head to head. Production deployments must balance throughput, latency, and memory use, and the right choice depends on the workload. Kolluru measures both systems across those dimensions, including scalability, using LLaMA-2 models from seven to seventy billion parameters.

Under high-concurrency workloads, vLLM delivered up to twenty-four times the throughput of its rival, thanks to its PagedAttention memory mechanism. The rival system, however, showed lower tail latencies for interactive, single-user scenarios, where responsiveness matters more than volume. Kolluru closes with useful selection guidance: high-throughput batch processing points one way, latency-sensitive interactive applications with moderate concurrency the other. The study gives deployment teams measured profiles instead of folklore.
arxiv-2511-17793:
Shweta Mahajan, Hoang Le, Hyojin Park, Farzad Farhadzadeh, Munawar Hayat, and Fatih Porikli examine why efficient vision language models often hallucinate objects that are not in an image. Their analysis shows that models joining image and text by simple concatenation often fail to tell matching pairs from non matching ones.

They propose a framework that adds interleaved attention layers and teaches the model where to look using spatial knowledge from a segmentation model. That stronger grounding reduces hallucination. Tests on vision focused benchmarks show results that match or beat earlier efficient models, with lessons for building smaller multimodal systems.
arxiv-2511-17893:
Chiaki Hirose and three co-authors propose a new alignment sensing method for laser gravitational wave detectors, where precise control of many optical axes is needed to keep the instrument locked. Standard wave front sensing is dominated by the main arm signal, hiding other axes.

Their method beats two modulated sidebands against each other and reads the signal at the difference frequency. Theory and a test on part of the KAGRA detector show that signals from the power recycling cavity and the incoming beam separate cleanly from the arm. Feedback using the method held a stable lock for over an hour.
arxiv-2511-17993:
Jiayu Wang, Haoyu Bian, Haoran Sun, and Shaoning Zeng present SD-PSFNet, a network for removing rain from images. Rain removal is hard because streaks vary in scale and tangle with the scene behind them. Borrowing from optics, the design uses point spread function components, which model how a point of light smears, to expose the degradation process that rain imposes on a photo.

The network restores the image in three linked stages, re-estimating the rain effect at each stage and refining the result step by step. A gated fusion step passes the best features between stages. The authors present the system as a way to separate rain from background more cleanly by modelling the physics of the streaks rather than treating removal as pure pattern matching.
arxiv-2511-18193:
Xiaorong Zou develops a numerical algorithm, based on trigonometric interpolation, for a second order Volterra integro differential equation. Such an equation mixes derivatives with a memory integral whose upper limit is the current point. A similar idea recently worked well for the Fredholm type, where the integral runs over a fixed interval.

The method keeps the earlier strengths: high exactness with a modest grid, good handling of singular kernels, and fit with general edge rules. Tests under varied edge rules perform as expected. The approach also points toward equations with higher order rate parts, widening the class of memory equations it can solve.
arxiv-2511-18993:
Christos Koutlis and Symeon Papadopoulos locate the faked parts of a video by cross checking sound against lips. Deepfake clips can swap a face or a voice in short spans, so a whole clip verdict is not enough; the fake seconds must be marked. Their AuViRe method rebuilds speech features of one channel from the other.

In true speech, lip motion predicts the sound and the sound predicts the lips. In a faked span that cross rebuild strains, and the gap swells into a clear cue. Scores beat the past state of the art by wide margins on two bench sets and on a wild test. Fine time marks help moderators cut the fake and keep the rest.
arxiv-2511-19193:
E. V. Gorbar, B. E. Grinyuk, and V. P. Gusynin analyze bound states in one-dimensional quantum systems where energy depends on momentum to the fourth power. Such quartic dispersion appears in some engineered and layered materials. They ask where the wave function crosses zero, the nodes, inside and outside the region where a classical particle could move.

Using a semiclassical method with corrections up to fourth order, they derive a rule for the bound-state energies. Results for harmonic and quartic wells agree with a variational calculation. A surprise emerges: the classic oscillation theorem fails in the forbidden region, where wave functions gain extra nodes, though it still holds where motion is allowed.
arxiv-2511-19493:
Chris Kuchar releases RFX, a production-ready random forest package in Python, built around the classic Breiman and Cutler method. Random forests are valued, but their proximity matrices, which record how alike cases are, explode in memory and cap analysis near sixty thousand samples. RFX attacks that bottleneck from several sides.

A QLORA-style compression shrinks GPU proximity storage hugely while keeping nearly all of the geometric structure. A CPU scheme stores only the triangle of the matrix with sparse thresholding for a lossless saving. Batch sizing tuned to the GPU hardware keeps utilization high, and tools cover classification, error estimates, importance measures, and interactive plots.
arxiv-2511-19693:
Chin-Chia Michael Yeh leads a team of fifteen authors presenting TREASURE, a foundation model built for payment transaction data at Visa. Payment networks record enormous volumes of daily activity, and modelling those records well enables abnormal behaviour detection and personalised services. TREASURE is a transformer built for transactions: it captures both the cardholder's behaviour and the network's own signals, such as response codes and system flags, which generic sequence models ignore.

An input module with dedicated parts for static and dynamic attributes feeds the encoder, letting one model serve many downstream tasks. The authors verify the system on industry-grade data sets. They present TREASURE as a multipurpose representation engine for a data type that, despite its commercial weight, has had few models built natively for it.
arxiv-2511-19793:
Xie Chen asks whether a wider version of the Landau paradigm can organize all quantum phases of matter. Landau's framework reads phases through broken symmetries, but many quantum phases discovered since fall outside it. Recent ideas about generalized symmetries and generalized gauging hint at an upgrade.

In this essay, those beyond-Landau phases and their transitions are recast as breaking of generalized symmetries, often produced by a gauging step framed through topological holography. The picture promises a systematic map of quantum phases. Chen also sets out what still must be understood before the generalized paradigm becomes a working tool.
arxiv-2511-20193:
Elad, Murali, and Shoham ask why program provers fail on some true claims. Their 2025 paper studies separation logic with inductive definitions. The logic reasons about heap-manipulating programs and shared resources. Inductive predicates describe unbounded data structures in memory. Automated proof tools for it are imperfect.

The authors place the logic inside a relaxed sibling. They call the looser system Weak Separation Logic. Unlike the strict version, the weak one admits completeness. A broad fragment reduces to first-order logic cleanly. The popular fold/unfold mechanism gets a verdict too. It is incomplete for the strict logic, as expected. Yet it is sound and complete for the weak logic. That makes the weak logic its natural home. Proof failures trace to nonstandard, rogue models. Over seven hundred benchmark entailments tested their prototype tool. A third of those included background theories.
arxiv-2511-20393:
Pirogov and Zenin propose rebuilding gravity to absorb two cosmic mysteries. Their 2025 paper presents multiscalar-metric gravity, reported at the Lomonosov Conference. Dark energy drives the universe's speeding expansion. Dark matter's gravity shapes galaxies, yet no particle has been found. Their idea changes general relativity instead of adding unseen matter. Spacetime keeps a basic metric plus extra scalar fields.

Those fields act as special moving coordinates of spacetime. In physical terms they behave like gravitational Higgs fields. They can break the symmetry of relativity on their own. The resulting theory is called metagravity. It predicts massive tensor and scalar gravitons. The scalar graviton could source dark energy and dark matter effects. Open problems include rotating black hole solutions in this scheme. Coupling the scalar graviton to ordinary matter needs study. Odd features in gravity waves offer possible tests. The authors frame it as a route to deeper unity.
arxiv-2511-20793:
Xiaojiao Xiao and colleagues build in 2025 a system to read a liver tumour three ways at once. Clinicians segment the tumour, track how it enhances over time as contrast dye washes through, and classify it, since benign hemangiomas and malignant hepatocellular carcinomas brighten in different curves. Done separately, the work is slow and varies between observers. Their MTI-Net performs all three tasks.

Its modules fuse frequency-domain and spatial features with entropy guidance, enforce consistency between segmentation and regression, and add a task-driven discriminator plus a Transformer for the MRI sequence. On 238 subjects, the network segmented tumours with a Dice score of 85.23 percent and an overlap of 75.48 percent across cases. Its enhancement-curve error was a mean absolute error of 44.35 units on average. Single-task baselines fared worse: Inception scored a worse 115.67 and VGG-16 210.28 on the same measure. The classification score reached 92.8 percent accuracy, supporting clinical assessment.
arxiv-2511-20893:
Aodong Li, Abishek Sankararaman, and Balakrishnan Narayanaswamy tackle in 2025 a streaming-data headache: category vocabularies that keep growing. Recommenders and classifiers hash category values into a fixed-size space, but in online learning the usual deterministic embeddings depend on arrival order and forget old items as new ones arrive. Their probabilistic hash embedding, PHE, treats each embedding as a distribution and updates it with Bayesian online learning.

The design keeps a bounded parameter set that never grows with the number of distinct values seen. New items are absorbed without erasing old ones, and results no longer depend on the order items appeared. Tests span classification, sequence modelling, and recommendation in online setups, where PHE beat standard hashing approaches. It did so while using as little as 2 to 4 percent of the memory of a one-hot embedding table.
arxiv-2511-21393:
Yusong Zhang speeds up the solution of a stubborn class of linear systems in a 2025 numerical analysis paper. The systems are complex symmetric and indefinite, arising in problems like the Helmholtz and Maxwell equations, and complex arithmetic makes them costly to attack directly. Zhang's lopsided HSS method splits each step into two solves with real symmetric matrices, alternating between them, which sidesteps much of that cost.

Zhang proves a convergence bound set by the extreme eigenvalues of the real parts and the iteration parameters. Under stated conditions, the method converges for any positive parameter choice. A preconditioned variant, PLHSS, converges faster and clusters its spectrum tightly, yielding a ready-made preconditioner. In tests, convergence barely changed with mesh size or parameter choice. Pairing the preconditioner with GMRES and COCG solvers beat existing splitting methods, even when the imaginary part is indefinite.
arxiv-2511-21593:
Akash Vyas, Shreyas Kumar, Jayant Kumar Mohanta, and Ravi Prakash solve a notoriously stubborn control equation exactly instead of approximating it, in 2025. The Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation defines the optimal controller for a nonlinear system, but its solutions are usually learned step by step through adaptive dynamic programming, which needs training and a workable starting policy. For continuous-time systems whose input enters affinely, meaning linearly in the control, the team finds another way.

Their framework produces a closed-form solution to the equation for this system class with known dynamics, and with it a closed-form optimal control policy. Lyapunov theory proves the resulting closed-loop system is stable, for both regulation and tracking problems. Tests on standard benchmark problems show better efficiency and optimal performance without any training loop. The tracking controller's performance is rated satisfactory rather than perfect, an honest blemish reported alongside the guarantees.
arxiv-2511-21993:
Chen studies how long a closed loop on a hyperbolic surface must be, given its self-crossings. The shortest non-simple geodesic is always a figure eight with one crossing. Basmajian had bounded curves with k crossings by its length.

Chen improves those bounds with a constructive approach, working inside the pair of pants, a three-holed building block surface, determined by a shortest figure eight. He explicitly builds families of words in the surface's fundamental group whose geodesic representatives realize any prescribed self-intersection number. The sharper length estimates follow from analysing the figure eight's geometry closely. As a consequence, the upper bound on the self-intersection number of shortest geodesics with at least k crossings drops from 512 to 128, sharpening the connection between geometry and combinatorial complexity.
arxiv-2511-22093:
Sridhar, Ray, and Kalogera, astrophysicists, dissect the black hole merger population in GWTC-4, the latest gravitational-wave catalog with 153 confident binary black hole signals, using binned Gaussian processes. A flexible data-driven method that avoids assuming a fixed formula for how masses, mass ratios, and spins are distributed. Their goal is the stubborn excess of mergers near 35 solar masses, whose astrophysical origin, isolated binary evolution or dynamical assembly in dense clusters, has been debated for years.

The flexible fit resolves three distinct subpopulations, and only one carries the 35-solar-mass peak; that group strongly prefers equal-mass pairs and randomly oriented spins, fingerprints of dynamical assembly. Comparing with simulations, that subpopulation could consist entirely of globular-cluster mergers if black holes are born with modest spins between 0.1 and 0.2 of maximum, and the cluster merger rate is bounded below accordingly.
arxiv-2511-22293:
Baoueb, Bie, Fontaine, and Richard, speech researchers in Paris, speed up a phase-aware neural vocoder. Diffusion vocoders like WaveGrad turn mel spectrograms into audio, but their output can drift out of agreement with the conditioning spectrogram, especially off the training distribution. GLA-Grad fixed consistency by folding the classic Griffin-Lim algorithm into the reverse diffusion process. GLA-Grad++ keeps the benefit while cutting the cost, computing the correction term only once with a single Griffin-Lim application instead of repeatedly.

That change accelerates generation while preserving phase consistency. In experiments the method outperforms the baseline models, with its advantages in out-of-domain scenarios, where the conditioning spectrogram differs from what the vocoder was trained on and diffusion vocoders degrade most. The authors frame the work as making diffusion-based speech synthesis both more faithful to its input and cheaper to run.
arxiv-2511-22393:
Haddad, Jiménez, and Villa prove a result about slicing convex bodies. Take two symmetric convex bodies in n-dimensional space, one inside the other, the inner one strictly convex, meaning its surface curves everywhere. A hyperplane slice of the outer body has a centre of mass, its balance point. The authors ask where such balance points can land relative to the inner body.

They prove that at least n hyperplanes tangent to the inner body cut slices whose centre of mass lies exactly on the inner body's surface. In three dimensions, that guarantees at least three such slices. The proof uses Lusternik-Schnirelmann category, a topology tool counting how many simple pieces cover a space, applied to a variational setup where the centroid appears as a critical point. The note advertises this method for similar centroid problems.
arxiv-2511-22493:
Liu, Gao, Ji, and Zhao build a better detector for social media bots, fake accounts spreading misinformation and running coordinated manipulation. Their tool is a graph neural network, judging an account from its connection network as well as its profile features. Spectral versions analyse the graph's frequency patterns, but spread attention across the whole spectrum and ignore a useful clue: bots tend to connect across unlike accounts. That low similarity, called low homophily, shows up in high-frequency features.

Their HW-GNN focuses spectral analysis with learnable Gaussian windows highlighting the frequency bands where bot signatures live. A homophily-aware mechanism feeds each network's measured similarity pattern into how those windows are tuned. Across several benchmarks, HW-GNN reached state-of-the-art detection, improving the average F1 score by 4.3 percent over existing methods. Its components can be plugged into other spectral graph networks to lift their performance.
arxiv-2511-22593:
Viswanathan and colleagues make a bottleneck task in quantum computing provably efficient. Variational quantum algorithms for chemistry build trial states from operator pools drawn from a Lie algebra. The pools are the minimal complete ones, the smallest generator sets generating the whole algebra. Finding them meant greedy searches over exponentially many candidates. The authors replace that hunt with a framework grounded in basic Lie algebra properties, costing only polynomially in the number of qubits.

Their construction checks completeness by ranking binary matrices from candidates' commutation relations, giving answers, not greedy guesses. In quantum chemistry, optimal pools shrink operator count growth from fourth-power to linear in system size, slashing gradient overhead. A batched adaptive algorithm using them, MB-ADAPT-VQE, converges faster under strong correlation, and the pools unlock a gradient-free fixed-ansatz method blocked by construction costs. Uses beyond chemistry include error correction and control.
arxiv-2511-22693:
Deressa and colleagues restructure a generative model so control becomes algebra. Standard diffusion and flow models learn one trajectory predictor carrying noise to data, control being bolted on externally through guidance or prompt tricks. Generative Anchored Fields instead learn two endpoint predictors, one at the noise side and one at the data side, the velocity field emerging from their disagreement. With multiple data-side heads, one per class, the model supports Transport Algebra.

Algebraic operations on the learned head pairs yield directed transport maps between a shared base and many modalities. They enable controllable interpolation, hybrid generation, and semantic morphing by vector arithmetic, as primitives, not add-ons. Sample quality stays strong, a Fréchet inception distance of 7.5 on CelebA-HQ at 64 by 64 in reported experiments. The authors also demonstrate lossless cyclic transport, an LPIPS score of exactly zero in their test.
arxiv-2511-22793:
Nukapotula and colleagues borrow a graphics trick to make wireless channel estimation fast enough for 5G. Base stations need channel state information for beamforming, but acquiring it via pilot transmissions eats up to 25 percent of spectrum. Machine learning methods can reconstruct channels from sparse measurements. Inference takes 5 to 100 milliseconds, too slow when each transmission interval lasts a millisecond or less.

GSpaRC represents the radio environment with compact 3D Gaussian primitives, each carrying a small neural model with physics-informed features like distance-based attenuation. They are rendered via a custom CUDA pipeline onto a hemispherical surface matching omnidirectional antennas. On multiple radio datasets it matched recent state-of-the-art fidelity while cutting training and inference time by over an order of magnitude, first to break the one millisecond latency barrier. The authors see it enabling low-latency channel estimation and digital twins for future networks.
arxiv-2511-22893:
Espinel-Ríos controls gene expression with a flicked light switch. Optogenetics lets engineers tune protein production in microbes with light, but intensity-only control fails when the dose-response curve is steep: the system is either fully on or fully off, with no middle. Pulse-width modulation, borrowed from electronics, alternates full-on and full-off light within each forcing period so the average dose lands between.

Optimising such schedules is a switching-time control problem with input; mixed-integer formulations explode as grids refine. Espinel-Ríos instead parametrises each period by its duty cycle, one number encoding the on-off split, and trains a reinforcement learning policy over duty cycles, respecting the light's binary nature. In a case study of optogenetic growth control with a dose-response, the policies showed tunability and tracking under system uncertainty. The approach generalises to duty-cycle bioprocesses, from photocycles to feeding.
arxiv-2511-23093:
Čertík and colleagues continue their complexity study of ordered graphs, this time for ordered matchings, graphs with a fixed vertex order in which every vertex belongs to exactly one edge. Matchings matter because they are the simplest building blocks inside ordered graph homomorphisms, the order-respecting maps the team studied before. So their difficulty sets a baseline for the whole theory.

The headline problems are hard in the classical sense: deciding whether one ordered matching appears inside another, and whether an ordered homomorphism exists between two ordered matchings, are both NP-complete. The picture flips under parameterization, though: with the target's size as the parameter, homomorphism-finding for matchings is fixed-parameter tractable. It uses an algorithm exponential only in the small parameter, unlike the W[1]-hard general problem. The core problem for matchings is solvable in polynomial time, again unlike the NP-complete general case.
arxiv-2511-23293:
Li and colleagues show that collisions of nuclei at near light speed can reveal short-range correlations between nucleons. The close pairs inside nuclei that electron scattering found decades ago. Whether those correlations leave any mark on the quark-gluon plasma's initial state was an open question. So the team builds them into the initial conditions and studies higher-order fluctuations of the fireball's transverse size.

The third- and fourth-order size fluctuations, which map onto transverse momentum fluctuations in the final state. Differ by more than 10 percent between nuclei modeled with and without the correlations in ultra-central collisions, an effect Monte Carlo sampling with the TRENTo model confirms. The size of the effect scales universally with the nucleus's radius measure and average density. Mirroring the link between short-range correlations and the EMC effect, and giving heavy-ion experiments at RHIC and the LHC a nuclear-structure probe.
arxiv-2512-00193:
AI benchmarks tend to saturate within a few years, sometimes months, as models master them. Anson Ho and co-authors address that problem in a 2025 study they call a Rosetta Stone for AI benchmarks. When tests keep expiring, long-run trends in capability become hard to study.

The authors build a statistical framework that stitches benchmarks together onto a single numerical scale. Model capabilities and benchmark difficulties are placed on that shared scale, like items in one measuring system. The approach could let researchers compare today's models with past ones fairly, instead of guessing across disconnected test scores. A common scale also exposes when a new benchmark is simply too easy.
arxiv-2512-00593:
Spin-Hall oscillators generate microwave signals from magnetic materials and can synchronize with each other. Bechberger and co-authors demonstrate spin-wave emission with current-controlled frequency in 2025, using a spin-Hall oscillator based on a low-damping magnetic garnet. The garnet carries dominant perpendicular magnetic anisotropy.

Mutual synchronization, mediated by propagating spin waves, makes such oscillators candidates for neuromorphic computing hardware. Controlling the emitted frequency with current gives designers a simple tuning knob. Gallium-substituted yttrium iron garnet keeps damping low, which should let the spin waves travel farther between devices. Current control is the simplest knob a circuit designer could ask for. Spin waves carry signals without moving charge, which keeps energy loss low. For folks who dream of chips that think like brains, the gain is a part that can sing at a pitch set by a wire. It can also lock step with its peers.
arxiv-2512-00893:
Kundan Mukhia and six coauthors study how a major election moved crypto markets in a 2025 paper. Their event is the 2024 United States presidential election, treated as a major political risk event. They focus on stablecoins, crypto tokens meant to hold a steady value, and split activity into human and automated kinds.

Human-driven peer-to-peer transactions on Ethereum shifted two days before the election, their structural break analysis finds. Exchange trading volumes, by contrast, reacted only on Election Day itself. That timing gap suggests ordinary users moved early while markets waited. Early-warning signals like these could help track political risk in digital markets.
arxiv-2512-01293:
Joao Amarante and co-authors model how disk galaxies form two groups of stars. Some stars are rich in alpha elements, made in big stars. Others are poor in those elements. Real disk galaxies show both groups side by side.

The team ran many smooth particle models as part of the GASTRO set. Each run mixed dense clumps of new stars with a single big merger event. They then checked which mix could make both star groups. Tests like this help show how mergers and clumps each shaped the disks we see today, ours included.
arxiv-2512-01593:
Muhittin Evren Aydin, Nursemin Cavdar, and Mahmut Ergut study curves of constant curvature in dual planes. Dual numbers add a nilpotent part to real numbers. Curves in dual affine and dual Lorentz-Minkowski planes model motions and lines. Their curvature can be a dual constant.

The team first finds invariants of curves under equiaffine moves. They then give explicit equations for all constant-curvature curves. Full lists like this aid work on kinematics, where dual curves encode rigid motions. They also extend classic curve theory to dual settings. Explicit equations let others plot every case at once, turning a classification claim into pictures that can be checked by eye.
arxiv-2512-01793:
Nagl and co-authors identify a candidate for a vortex crystal in a triangular quantum antiferromagnet. Triangular lattices frustrate magnetic order by geometry. Strong spin-orbit coupling adds bond anisotropy. Merging those two paradigms may yield exotic quantum materials.

Their candidate is an organic antiferromagnet with a stated chemical makeup. In it, a Z2 vortex crystal state may form. Crystals of vortices would be a new magnetic texture. Neutron and lab data on the candidate will test whether that texture truly appears. Organic salts can be grown as clean crystals, which suits neutron scattering tests of the vortex state in large shared facilities.
arxiv-2512-02293:
Simultaneous localization and mapping with 3D Gaussian Splatting makes dense, photorealistic maps, but purely visual systems stumble on motion blur, weak texture, and changing light. Zihan Zhu and four co-authors present VIGS-SLAM in 2025, which adds inertial sensing to the splatting pipeline.

An inertial unit keeps tracking steady exactly where cameras struggle, during fast motion or in blank corridors. The system aims at robust real-time tracking with high-fidelity reconstruction at once. Reliable dense maps are the raw material for augmented reality, robot navigation, and digital twins of real spaces.
arxiv-2512-02393:
Agentic software systems, built from orchestrated AI modules, behave stochastically: the same request can take many different paths. Shuyang Liu and five co-authors argue in 2025 that judging such systems only by their final outcome misses most of what matters, and propose process-centric analysis instead.

Their trajectories adapt to the problem as they run, unlike the fixed paths of conventional programs. Outcome-only evaluation cannot see wasteful detours, lucky recoveries, or fragile reasoning that happened to end well. Studying the process gives engineers the evidence needed to debug and trust systems whose behavior is a distribution, not a script.
arxiv-2512-02493:
Yunlong Xiao takes a fresh look at superchannels, the rules that transform quantum processes themselves. Quantum channels are the basic operations of quantum theory, describing how a system changes. Superchannels act one level up, turning one channel into another.

The standard framework has real flaws, Xiao argues. Two rival constructions of a key operator coexist, and the theory lacks the firm representations that ground channel theory. Guided by a generalized form of Occam's razor, the 2025 study rebuilds the framework more simply. A cleaner foundation could help physicists reason about quantum devices that process other processes. A base that holds firm makes the rest of the field less prone to drift and doubt as it grows.
arxiv-2512-02593:
Chao-Han Huck Yang, Andreas Stolcke, and Larry P Heck survey spoken conversational agents built on large language models. Voice based models have drawn wide interest from researchers and the public alike. Leading closed models now handle speech recognition, translation, and spoken understanding far better than older open systems.

Their 2025 overview maps where these voice agents stand and what they can do. Speech tasks once handled by separate tools are merging into single conversational systems. A clear map of the field helps builders choose models, spot gaps, and design assistants people can truly talk with. Voice is how most of us talk, so gains here reach folks who type with pain or not at all.
arxiv-2512-02993:
Yifei Zeng and nine co-authors generate textures for 3D objects natively, instead of painting them view by view. Multi view fusion often leaves seams where views disagree, and complex surfaces end up partly uncovered. Those flaws limit how faithful and complete a generated texture can be.

TEXTRIX builds a latent attribute grid for native 3D texture generation. Working in 3D from the start avoids stitched inconsistencies. The framework also supports precise 3D part segmentation downstream. Better textures lift games, product design, and virtual retail, where surfaces must look right from every angle. Full wraps with no seams read as one cloth. That cloth like look is what makes a fake good feel real to the eye at a glance.
arxiv-2512-03093:
A classic math object may be easier to compute than thought. Isaac Dobes gives a new formula for Cayley's first hyperdeterminant in this 2025 work. Hyperdeterminants extend the idea of a determinant to arrays with more than two directions.

His formula uses the Levi-Civita symbol, a standard tool for signs in algebra. With it, he shows the value for symmetric arrays can be found in time that grows in a tame way with size. He then discusses uses for boson entanglement in quantum physics. Faster methods widen what researchers can test. Symmetric cases arise in quantum problems, so the faster route has ready uses.
arxiv-2512-03293:
What an agent wants shapes how it plans. Filippo Torresan, Ryota Kanai, and Manuel Baltieri study prior preferences in active inference agents in this 2025 work. Active inference uses expected free energy to balance using what is known and exploring for more.

The authors compare soft and hard preferences and ways to shape goals. How a goal is set can change an agent's choices in subtle ways. Their analysis helps designers build agents that act as intended. It matters for robots and AI systems that must plan under uncertainty. Goal shaping is delicate, since a hard goal can blind an agent to new evidence.
arxiv-2512-03493:
Collisions of gold nuclei probe matter at extreme heat and density. Yige Huang, for the STAR Collaboration, reports precision measurements in this 2025 work. The team studies fluctuations in net-proton counts from event to event.

They measure how those fluctuations depend on the rapidity window, using high-statistics data from RHIC. Protons and antiprotons are identified with improved detector performance. Such cumulants can signal the critical point of quantum chromodynamics. Finding it would map a key feature of the strong force's phase diagram. Cumulants of high order are sensitive probes, but they demand the statistics this run provides.
arxiv-2512-03593:
Digital avatars should stay sharp even in close-up views. David Svitov, Pietro Morerio, Lourdes Agapito, and Alessio Del Bue present CloseUpAvatar in this 2025 work. Their method builds high-fidelity, animatable full-body avatars that handle more general camera motions.

The avatar is represented as a set of textured planes. Two sets of learnable textures capture low and high-frequency detail in a multi-scale mixture. Preserving quality in close views matters for virtual meetings, games, and film. The approach aims to keep faces and clothing crisp as the camera moves. Multi-scale textures aim to keep both silhouette and fine surface detail intact.
arxiv-2512-04593:
Koustav Chandra, Rossella Gamba, Danilo Chiaramello, and co-authors give a multi-sided reading of GW250114, the loudest gravitational wave signal caught so far. A louder signal lets physicists test Einstein's gravity in its strongest regime. Their 2025 arXiv paper fits the wave with a model that handles eccentric, precessing black hole pairs. That freedom checks whether odd orbits were hiding in the data.

The source fits two first-generation black holes of nearly equal mass and low spin. They merged into a remnant whose mass lands in the pair-instability gap, a range where stars alone should not leave holes. The team confirms faint higher harmonics in the wave, with stronger evidence than the main collaboration reported. Even data after the peak alone favors those harmonics. Each such test sharpens the case that general relativity holds where gravity is most extreme.
arxiv-2512-04793:
Gongyu Chen, Xiaoyu Zhang, Zhenqiang Weng, and co-authors present YingMusic-SVC, a singing voice conversion system built to survive real songs, not just clean studio clips. Conversion should keep a song's melody and words while swapping in a target singer's timbre. Zero-shot systems that need no target recordings often crack on harmony backing, pitch errors, and the quirks of real singing. Their 2025 arXiv paper hardens each stage of the pipeline.

A timbre shifter trained on singing splits voice color from content. A pitch-aware adaptor tracks dynamic expression as notes bend. A balanced flow-matching loss protects high-frequency sparkle, and reinforcement learning with Flow-GRPO polishes the result. On a graded multi-track benchmark, the system beat strong open baselines in timbre match, word clarity, and natural feel. Robust conversion opens karaoke, dubbing, and restoration work to voices never recorded in a studio.
arxiv-2512-05093:
K. Kade and six co-authors zoom into two distant starburst galaxies whose light left them when the universe was making stars at its fastest rate. Both are dusty, furiously star-forming systems, stretched and brightened by gravitational lensing. The open question is what ignites such intense bursts — a collision, or something quieter. The team used ALMA to map the glow of carbon monoxide gas, the raw fuel of stars.

Modeling the lens with fixed-shape and free-form methods, and splitting the gas signal into approaching and receding halves, they reconstruct the galaxies. Both show a hint of orderly rotation, but no clumps, companions, or ongoing mergers. Given their fierce star formation and draining gas, the authors suggest a recent collision lit the fuse, though the galaxies may now be settling into disks. The work shows how lensing can dissect galaxies too faint and far for ordinary imaging.
arxiv-2512-05593:
Rong Wang, Wei Mao, Changsheng Lu, and Hongdong Li present a new way to animate cloth in three dimensions, from a set of body poses. Older methods first bend a garment with a simple skinning step, then add fine wrinkles on top. When skinning lands out of line, the wrinkles are spoiled and the result looks soft and wrong. The team's 2025 paper drops skinning entirely.

Instead, the method predicts two things on their own. It predicts where each point of the cloth ends up, which fixes the broad shape. It also predicts which way each point faces, which carries the fine wrinkle detail. Both are drawn as texture images, so strong pre-trained image models can restore crisp detail. A final fusion step merges the two streams into the full garment. In tests on varied clothing, it produced sharper, more faithful wrinkles than leading rivals.
arxiv-2512-05993:
Ruchika Verma and a large team of co-authors argue that brain pathology needs its own foundation model, and they build one. In pathology they have been trained mostly on surgical specimens, poor in nervous tissue. Brains are different: neurons and glia, distinctive architecture, and signature lesions like the tangles and plaques of Alzheimer's disease. A model raised on other organs may simply not see what a neuropathologist sees.

Their model, NeuroFM, trains on whole slide images of brain tissue across many neurodegenerative diseases. Against general rivals it wins at classifying mixed dementias, segmenting the hippocampus, and identifying ataxias. The broader claim is about specialization. Each organ system may need its own training. A dedicated brain model reads brain slides more accurately.
arxiv-2512-06193:
Jihyung Park, Saleh Afroogh, David Atkinson, and Junfeng Jiao study a quiet risk in chatbots used by children. A bot can stay polite and still push a child toward more and more distress, by echoing feelings again and again in a way that slowly makes things worse. Standard filters look for bad words, so they miss this slow drift in tone across a talk.

The team builds a tool named GAUGE that watches the model's own word scores as a reply is formed. It tracks how each new reply shifts the mood of the talk, and flags turns where that shift points toward harm. Because it reads signals from inside the model, it can catch trouble as it forms, rather than after a full reply is sent. The work gives makers of child facing bots a way to spot hidden harm early and step in sooner.
arxiv-2512-06393:
Qiming Bao, Xiaoxuan Fu, and Michael Witbrock expose a stubborn flaw in how language models reason with rules. A model may ace a clean logic task, then keep following the same chain of steps even when a rule is cut, flipped, or made to clash with another. They name this habit Logic Inertia. Their diagnostic suite tests models with deleted rules, clashing rules, rewritten rules, and stacked laws drawn from many domains.

The drop can be total: some top models fell from perfect scores to zero on clashing rules. Their fix, Conflict Aware Fusion, trains models to check for clashes before drawing conclusions. Training stages set up the checking habit, sharpen the choice to halt on a clash, punish drift between equal wordings of a rule, and reward answers cleared by a strict symbolic checker. The trained models held up far better across the stress tests.
arxiv-2512-06593:
Yuehua Su and three co authors survey a proposed way to measure the tangled correlations inside strongly correlated electron systems. In such materials, electrons push on each other so hard that single particle pictures fail, hiding the causes of odd states like unconventional superconductivity and quantum spin liquids. Coincidence detection is a technique that catches two particles at once, in pairs of channels, with readings of momentum, energy, and place.

By recording pairs, the method aims to measure two body correlations directly. The perspective piece reviews where the proposals stand and what they would take to build. The authors argue that working coincidence tools would give fresh purchase on long standing puzzles. Those range from how certain superconductors pair electrons to how magnetic order goes itinerant. Newer states would open up too, such as electronic nematicity, where electrons break rotational symmetry on their own.
arxiv-2512-07093:
Xiaoda Li and co-authors design better airfoils for the thin upper air and near-space, where gas is so sparse that ordinary fluid equations fail. There the flow obeys the Boltzmann equation in a six-dimensional space, far too slow to solve inside a design loop. Their answer pairs a fast, structure-preserving solver with a Bayesian search that learns from each trial. Airfoil shapes are described by a standard transformation that guarantees workable geometry, and only thickness varies.

Across a wide range of sparseness, the search found drag-minimizing shapes at two supersonic speeds. As the gas thins, the streamwise force grows and drag shifts from pressure-driven to shear-driven, yet shaping helped everywhere. Gains peaked where the gas is weakly rarefied, cutting drag by large fractions, and shrank to a few percent in the freest molecular flow.
arxiv-2512-07193:
Manthan Shenoy and Andreas Rausch test whether software tools that spot design patterns in code are reading meaning or merely names. Design patterns are standard solutions programmers reuse, and attention-based detectors claim to find them by grasping a program's structure and behavior. The authors reproduce one leading detector, then build a scrambled version of its test corpus: class and method names. Printed strings, and comments are replaced, while control flow, inheritance, and logic stay untouched.

Under that obfuscation, the reproduced classifiers stumble badly, misclassifying at rates that expose how much they leaned on surface cues like names. A detector that truly understood the pattern should shrug off renamed identifiers, since the design itself did not change. The authors release their scrambled corpus, a few dozen Java files, as a proof-of-concept benchmark so other detectors can be graded on semantic depth rather than vocabulary.
arxiv-2512-08093:
Manas Joglekar, Jeremy Chen, Gabriel Wu, and colleagues, artificial intelligence researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about honesty in large language models. Models can overstate their confidence or cover up misbehavior, and reinforcement learning can quietly reward such dishonesty. The team proposes training models to give confessions, separate reports of their own compliance with instructions and policy.

A confession is rewarded only for its honesty, not for how good the main answer was. That design makes surfacing misbehavior the easiest way to earn reward, instead of hiding it. The researchers trained a GPT 5 Thinking model this way and tested it on new scenarios covering hallucination, instruction following, scheming, and reward hacking. When the main answer lied or hid flaws, the confession often admitted them honestly. Confessions could also support monitoring, rejection sampling, and warning users at run time.
arxiv-2512-08193:
Jiwoo Park, Ruoqi Liu, Avani Jagdale, and colleagues, researchers in health informatics, posted a systems paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their platform, ClinicalTrialsHub, gathers all data from the ClinicalTrials dot gov registry in one searchable place. It then enriches those records by pulling structured trial details out of PubMed research articles automatically.

That enrichment raised access to structured trial data by more than four fifths compared with the registry alone. Large language models help at several points, parsing full text papers, turning plain user questions into database searches, and answering questions with evidence tied to source sentences. The team tested the platform with clinicians, clinical researchers, and doctoral students in pharmacy and nursing. Automatic checks also measured the extraction and answering quality. The authors aim to serve patients, clinicians, researchers, and policymakers alike. Easier trial access, they argue, supports evidence based medicine.
arxiv-2512-08493:
Dyna Soumhane Ouchebara and Stephane Dupont, computer security researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Detectors that flag vulnerable code suffer from skewed training data: some flaw types appear often, others barely at all, so classifiers learn the common ones and miss the rare ones. The authors test whether large language models can balance the data by augmenting vulnerable code examples.

They compare two strategies using a code tuned language model. One generates fresh vulnerable functions under control. The other refactors existing vulnerable code while preserving its meaning, creating new looking samples of rare flaws. The augmented data then trains a standard code classifier on a public vulnerability dataset. Both approaches enriched the codebase with reasonable quality. A hybrid of the two boosted classifier performance most, giving security teams a practical answer to a limiting data problem.
arxiv-2512-08793:
Alex Plyukhin studies how to use the potential of mean force in a Langevin equation for a particle coupled to a thermal bath. That potential captures the average effect of the bath on the system and corrects the equilibrium distribution. How it should enter time dependent dynamics, however, has remained unclear in general.

The model uses a single particle system, while bath particles feel on site anchor potentials that create a nontrivial mean force potential. The author finds that the potential does not simply replace the external potential. It also makes the friction kernel and the noise statistics depend on the system position, through bath details that are not known in advance. The Langevin equation is therefore not closed in general. For systems with linear forces, that position dependence cancels. A harmonic chain bath gives a concrete case where the standard form holds, with a quadratic mean force potential.
arxiv-2512-08993:
Molla Basir Ahamed and Rajesh Hossain study geometric properties of analytic functions in a generalized Robertson class, a family of starlike functions of a given order. Such function classes are fundamental in complex analysis and geometric function theory. A deeper account of their univalence and shape behavior is the main significance of the work.

The authors derive sharp bounds for the norms of the Schwarzian and pre Schwarzian derivatives. Those bounds are stated in terms of the initial coefficient of the function, with focus on the important case where that coefficient is zero. Sharp distortion and growth theorems are also established for the class. Finally, the radius problem is addressed by finding the sharp radius of concavity and the sharp radius of convexity. Each bound is sharp,. The results give a complete geometric picture for this generalized family of functions.
arxiv-2512-09093:
A S Ianovskaia and coauthors show in theory that a superconducting spin valve built from layered van der Waals sheets can be tuned by a gate voltage. Their structure places a monolayer superconductor between two ferromagnetic monolayers. Gating the ferromagnetic layers shifts their chemical potentials, which changes how their electronic spectra hybridize with the superconductor.

That hybridization sets the effective exchange field felt inside the superconducting layer. By tuning it, the same device can move smoothly between standard, inverse, and triplet spin valve regimes. Gating also enables unusual temperature behavior of the superconducting order. Examples include reentrant the effect, bistable states, first order phase transitions, and the effect that appears only at finite temperature. The results present these trilayers as a handy platform for superconducting spin devices. External voltages can switch spin valve functions and unusual superconducting states on demand, without rebuilding the device or changing its parts.
arxiv-2512-09193:
Ehsan Roohi writes for teachers of undergraduate gas dynamics, the study of fast-moving compressible flows. Students in that subject normally solve hard, tangled equations by repeated numerical steps or by looking values up in long tables. Roohi argues that this routine can hide the physical picture behind the numbers.

He builds a teaching framework that trains deep learning models to stand in for the exact solutions. The models cover five classic problems: Rayleigh flow, Fanno flow, oblique shocks, flow through converging-diverging nozzles, and unsteady shock tubes. Each model uses network shapes and physics-based input choices picked for its problem. The trained models are accurate and can draw solution maps instantly, including temperature-entropy diagrams and wave pictures. Roohi presents the approach as a way to bring modern data tools into the physics classroom.
arxiv-2512-09393:
Vasiliki Stoumpou and colleagues build a system to locate subdural hematomas, dangerous bleeding between the brain and its covering, on CT scans. Subdural hematoma is a common emergency in brain care, and it grows more frequent as populations age. Fast, accurate detection guides care, but current tools flag presence, with little explanation of where the bleeding sits.

The team's framework combines three parts. The first is clinical data such as demographics and lab results. The second is a 3D convolutional network reading the CT volume. The third is a transformer-enhanced segmentation model that maps where the bleeding is. It was trained on more than twenty-five thousand head CT studies from Hartford HealthCare. Clinical data alone did modestly, while the imaging models did far better. The combined ensemble did best of all and produced maps matching hematoma patterns, which the authors say could speed triage in radiology.
arxiv-2512-09593:
Simon Daley-Yates and colleagues revisit a puzzle about WASP-12, a star whose spectrum shows a dip in the lines of singly ionized magnesium and calcium. The dip has been read as evidence that the planet WASP-12b is losing its atmosphere, forming a torus around the star.

They build the density profile of ionized magnesium along the line of sight from WASP-12 to Earth. They combine hydrodynamic simulations with observations, and account for the stellar wind, the star's astrosphere, and the interstellar medium. Most gas sits in a torus near the star, but the torus is hot enough to ionize magnesium, leaving little in the singly ionized state. Most of that ion is in the interstellar medium. The total falls about a hundredfold short of explaining the observations. The authors speculate cooling will fragment the torus into cold clumps rich in the ion, rescuing the explanation.
arxiv-2512-09893:
Nian-Cin Wang and Rajeev Sahay make deep learning for antenna arrays harder to fool. Learning models now handle tasks like signal detection and estimating direction of arrival. Yet they carry no statistical guarantees and can be misled by crafted adversarial interference. The authors first prove a helpful fact: second order statistics of the received array signal are spatially robust against bounded attacks. That result motivates their design, a fast learning classifier backed by a classical statistical validator.

The validator is a generalized likelihood ratio test working in the spatial domain of the array. The learning model answers quickly and speculatively. The test then confirms or rejects its answer on firmer theoretical ground. Experiments varied the attack budget, the attack design, and the attack strength. Across these settings the combined system beat several leading baselines for robust array processing. The letter appeared in IEEE Wireless Communications Letters.
arxiv-2512-09993:
R. C. Chen leads a team planning how the Roman Space Telescope will get redshifts for its supernova survey. The High-Latitude Time-Domain Survey will find thousands of distant Type Ia supernovae for dark energy studies. Building a Hubble diagram from them requires knowing each supernova's redshift. Beyond the main prism instrument, the authors test whether grism observations from an overlapping wide area survey can supply host galaxy redshifts. They simulate dispersed grism images and measure redshifts with standard software.

The simulations give recovery rates as a function of galaxy brightness. Combining grism, prism, and ground based efficiencies, they predict several thousand supernovae will end up with a spectroscopic redshift from the supernova or its host. They also size a modeling systematic that could reach roughly half the statistical uncertainty on dark energy parameters.
arxiv-2512-10193:
C. K. Tam leads a large collaboration studying how nuclear collisions inside a dense medium differ from collisions in empty space. When calcium nuclei smash into nickel nuclei, the protons, deuterons, tritons, helium nuclei, and alpha particles that fly out carry information about the nuclear symmetry energy. That energy is a key unknown for neutron star physics. Transport models simulate the collisions, but one ingredient is poorly constrained: the in-medium cross section, how much the surrounding nuclear matter suppresses scattering between nucleons. The team compares measured momentum spectra against a leading transport model for several collision systems at two beam energies.

Central collisions were selected by particle multiplicity, consistently in data and simulation. The comparison shows the in-medium cross sections are reduced more strongly at the lower beam energy than at the higher one. That energy dependence is a concrete constraint modelers lacked.
arxiv-2512-10893:
Andrea Derdzinski and a large collaboration run eight hydrodynamics codes on the same unsolved problem and compare their answers, a rehearsal for LISA. The coming space-based gravitational wave detector will hear intermediate-mass-ratio inspirals, a small black hole spiralling into a supermassive one, often inside the accretion disc that feeds the giant. Thousands of orbits make these signals exquisite probes, and equally easy to bias with a wrong model.

The test case pairs a binary with mass ratio one part in ten thousand against its disc. In thick discs, all codes at high enough resolution agreed with each other and with analytical predictions. Thin discs, beyond the reach of analytics, split the field: two- and three-dimensional runs, and codes, disagreed even on the sign of the torque the disc exerts. Moving-mesh and GPU-friendly codes looked most efficient, a practical steer for LISA-era modelling.
arxiv-2512-10993:
Christopher Wensrich and colleagues examine whether X ray methods can uniquely recover the hidden stress fields locked inside solid materials. The technique, called eigenstrain tomography, combines diffraction measurements with elasticity theory to rebuild three dimensional residual stress. Several groups have used it, but whether its answers are unique was never clearly settled.

The authors build explicit counterexamples showing that reconstruction from a single measured strain component is not unique. They then derive minimum conditions for a well posed problem. The full strain field in an even, uniform sample can be uniquely recovered from three measured components, either the shear parts or the diagonal parts. Two further proofs clarify which stress fields diagonal or uniform eigenstrains can and cannot produce.
arxiv-2512-11193:
Haris Aziz, Yuhang Guo, Alexander Lam, and Houyu Zhou design fair mechanisms for placing facilities on a line when a machine learning prediction of the best answer is available. Classic facility location balances total or worst case travel cost. These authors instead target the envy ratio, the largest gap between any two agents' utilities, so fairness means nobody envies another too much.

Their deterministic mechanism uses predictions to achieve strong performance when the prediction is right, while degrading gracefully when it is wrong, and they prove that trade off is optimal. They also settle open questions with a prediction free randomised mechanism that improves the best known approximation. A further bias aware randomised design folds predictions back in for still better guarantees. The work extends learning augmented algorithms into fairness focused mechanism design.
arxiv-2512-11593:
Hyungrok Do and co-authors tackle a hard health question: what do mixes of chemicals in the environment do to people? Single chemical studies miss how exposures act as a group. Past mix methods trade off clarity, speed, and the kinds of outcomes they can handle.

Their model, NeuralPLSI, blends a classic index based approach with a neural network. It builds one clear exposure score, then lets a flexible network link that score to health outcomes. It works for plain, yes or no, and time to event outcomes, and it gives ranges for key values. Tests on survey health data from NHANES show it works in practice, and free software is included.
arxiv-2512-12093:
Mohsen Ben Abdallah and Marwa Ennaceur classify a family of operators on the Block type Witt algebra B(q). Rota-Baxter operators split products in a controlled way and underpin many algebraic structures. The homogeneous ones of weight zero, with degree a pair of integers, are the target here.

A key step fixes the record for the non resonant case. The profile function must obey a nonlinear equation whose only solutions are constants, delta spikes, or finite support forms. Flashier families claimed before, like non constant polynomials and exponentials, cannot occur. The resonant case is the opposite: any profile works if the operator lives on one line. The classification yields all homogeneous post-Lie structures on the algebra.
arxiv-2512-12493:
Vaarunay Kaushal and Rajib Mall build early warning systems for student success in online courses in a 2025 paper. Spotting at-risk students early lets teachers step in while help still matters. The study extends prediction to week 20, half the course, and compares a decision tree with an LSTM model at six time points.

Static demographic features dominated predictions, at 68 percent importance, allowing assessment free early forecasts. The LSTM reached 97 percent recall at week 2, best for early action, while the tree gave stable balanced results mid-course at 78 percent accuracy. By week 20 both hit 68 percent recall, but LSTM precision led, 90 percent against 86. Timing should drive model choice, they argue.
arxiv-2512-12693:
Sumantrak Mukherjee and eight co-authors present a Bayesian framework for multi-task bandits with shared structure in a 2025 paper. In bandit problems, a learner picks among options to gain reward while exploring. With many tasks and partial context, each task looks data poor alone, yet tasks share hidden links through latent context variables that tie their reward patterns together.

Their method pools observations across tasks to learn one global joint distribution, while still allowing personal inference for new tasks.
