Uncertainty splits into structural doubt about latent links and user specific doubt from thin history. A particle based approximation of a log density Gaussian process represents the joint law. Tests beat hierarchical bandit baselines, above all under misspecification.
arxiv-2512-12993:
Guillermo Castillo, Himanshu Lodha, and Ayonga Hereid present a layered strategy for teaching two-legged robots to walk over rough ground. End-to-end learning can be slow and fragile. Their method instead compresses what the robot senses about terrain into a compact code.

A convolutional encoder learns that terrain code, and a high-level policy uses it plus a simple model of the robot body to choose gaits in real time. The team studied how the size of the code affects learning and toughness, and added memory of recent terrain views. They also distilled the code from depth camera images and checked results in a high-fidelity simulator.
arxiv-2512-13193:
I. G. van Rens and co-authors measure the quantum Hall effect in graphene that was lightly treated with hydrogen. Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms. Exposing it to a cold hydrogen plasma attached hydrogen to a few percent of the layer, enough to reshape its electronic behavior.

Compared with pristine graphene, the spacing of Landau levels shrank a lot in the treated samples. Its growth with magnetic field changed from a square root pattern to a linear one. The team concludes the band structure changed from a linear Dirac type to a quadratic one, with an effective electron mass of 0.24 times the free electron mass. Calculations agreed.
arxiv-2512-13293:
Hao Fu, Wei Liu, and Shuai Zhou study how swarms of robots can travel in formation through crowds of people. Robots that move with humans must keep their shape without freezing or scattering. Reinforcement learning can help, but unpredictable pedestrian behavior makes exploration inefficient and policies timid.

Their algorithm adds a self-learning intrinsic reward that rewards coordinated exploration by the whole team. A dual sampling scheme inside centralized training sharpens both the navigation policy and that reward. Updates run on two time scales to keep the two parts from interfering. On social formation benchmarks, the method beat prior state-of-the-art systems across key metrics.
arxiv-2512-13493:
Soojeong Lee, Michael States, Keegan Bunker, and Ryan Caverly report prototype tests of CABLESSail, a solar sail that steers by reshaping itself. Cables routed along the sail's deployable booms bend the structure, changing how sunlight pressure torques the craft. That offers momentum management without extra actuators.

Small-scale tests showed cable actuation bends the booms as intended. Their new control allocation method computes the needed boom deformations for a desired torque efficiently. In simulations it stayed robust to uncertainty in the membrane shape and matched or beat existing solar sail actuators. Both advances raise the readiness of the concept for flight.
arxiv-2512-13593:
Robert Reed, Luca Laurenti, and Morteza Lahijanian tackle formal checks of dynamical systems whose rules are not fully known. Proof-based checks are hard in high dimensions, since splitting the state space grows fast with size. Learning methods can shrink the space, but their results need a guarantee to count as proof.

Their method uses convex autoencoders to cut dimension, then learns the dynamics in the small space with a kernel method. They build a finite abstraction that is sure to contain the true behavior of the real system. Results in the small space map back to the full system. Tests include a 26-dimensional system run by a neural network, with large gains in scale.
arxiv-2512-13793:
Hui Yang and Ya-Hui Zhang propose a minimal model that unites magnetism and superconductivity in bilayer nickelate. The material La3Ni2O7 shows high-temperature superconductivity, and its phase sits next to a spin-density-wave phase. A good model must capture both without added pressure or strain.

Their model couples half-filled local moments in one orbital to itinerant electrons in another, through strong Hund coupling. In the large coupling limit, it becomes a bilayer type-II t-J model. Numerical iDMRG runs on a small cylinder show period-4 stripe-like spin order from competing exchange effects. Raising interlayer exchange suppresses magnetic order and stabilizes interlayer s-wave superconductivity. The model thus frames how the two phases trade off.
arxiv-2512-13993:
Nicholas J. E. Richardson, Noah Marusenko, and Michael P. Friedlander analyze a multiscale method for discretized continuous optimization. Solving such problems at one fine resolution is routine, but per-iteration cost grows fast with grid size. Their method solves a hierarchy of ever finer dyadic grids instead.

Each coarse solution is interpolated to warm start the next finer scale, using any q-linearly convergent update as the inner solver. Convexity and smoothness carry across scales. For problems with Lipschitz-continuous solutions, two variants converge to the fine-scale solution with explicit error bounds. Total cost to a fixed accuracy is provably lower when update cost grows at least linearly with size. On density demixing problems, speedups reached four to sevenfold with far less memory.
arxiv-2512-14793:
K. M. Etmimi and two coauthors use computer models to study what happens when beryllium atoms are added to diamond. They test beryllium sitting between carbon atoms, beryllium taking the place of a carbon atom, and beryllium paired with nitrogen. For each case they work out the shape, the electric traits, and fine magnetic details.

Taking the place of a carbon atom proves easier than squeezing in between, though both paths cost energy. Adding nitrogen beside the beryllium lowers the cost further, since nitrogen atoms are smaller and strain the lattice less. Some mixes with three or four nitrogen atoms act as shallow donors. The results guide work on diamond based electronics, where such doping could help diamond carry current in a useful way.
arxiv-2512-14993:
Pranav Kakhandiki and three coauthors speed up the search for the easiest path between two stable states of a system. Such minimum energy pathways matter for designing catalysts and biomolecules. The standard method, the nudged elastic band, can need hundreds to tens of thousands of costly simulations for one path.

Their framework, NN-BAX, learns the energy landscape and the pathway at the same time. It fine tunes a foundation model step by step, choosing each new sample where it will improve the path most. On test systems ranging from simple Lennard-Jones clusters to embedded atom models, it cut energy and force evaluations by one to two orders of magnitude. Accuracy barely dropped, and the method scaled past 100 dimensions, hinting that weeks of computing could shrink to hours.
arxiv-2512-15193:
Vladan Jaguzović and a coauthor study how strongly certain analytic functions can concentrate on the sphere. The functions live in weighted Bergman classes on real space of dimension at least 2, and their moduli are log subharmonic with respect to the spherical metric. Concentration questions ask how much of a function's mass can pile into a small region.

Using the isoperimetric inequality for the spherical metric, the authors prove a monotonicity property for the super level sets of a weighted power of the function. From that they obtain sharp concentration estimates. They also solve maximization problems for convex Wehrl type functionals, a family tied to quantum phase space volumes. Quantitative stability bounds follow, measuring how far a function's modulus sits from spherical comparison profiles in terms of its concentration deficit.
arxiv-2512-15493:
Hampus Linander and co authors add a soft geometric bias to object centric world models in a 2025 paper. Physical systems are naturally described by geometric objects and their motions. Exact symmetry rules can help a model, but real systems often break those symmetries in part, so hard rules can hurt.

The team embeds object states as Clifford multivectors, which nudges the model toward sensible geometric change without forcing exact symmetry. Their soft Clifford transformer is tested on 2D rigid body motion, 3D charged particle systems, and real driving data. It beats both plain baselines and strictly equivariant models on long horizon accuracy, most clearly where symmetries are broken.
arxiv-2512-15593:
Sirio Resteghini and Cesare Straffelini study simultaneous sequential compactness in a 2025 math paper. A family of sequences converges simultaneously when one infinite subset of indices works for all of them at once. The question is how large such families can be, and in which spaces the property holds.

The authors discuss simultaneous convergence in the same space and across different sequentially compact spaces, and link the two settings. They show it holds for fewer sequences than certain cardinal bounds, depending on the weight of the space, and generalize the results to Hausdorff spaces. A final part probes whether those bounds are optimal. The work sits in general topology and set theory.
arxiv-2512-15693:
Yifei Li and co authors present Skyra, a model that detects AI generated videos and explains its verdicts, in a 2025 paper. Most detectors give only a yes or no label, which leaves users unable to judge the call. Skyra instead grounds detection in visual artifacts that people can see and check.

To train it, the team builds ViF-CoT-4K, the first large data set of AI video artifacts with fine grained human annotations. A two stage training plan sharpens artifact perception, explanation skill, and detection accuracy. Their new ViF-Bench holds 3,000 samples from over ten leading video generators. Skyra surpasses prior methods across several benchmarks in their experiments.
arxiv-2512-16093:
Jintao Zhang and seven co-authors present a speed breakthrough in an arXiv paper released in 2025. Video diffusion models create striking clips but are painfully slow. TurboDiffusion, the team's framework, speeds up the whole generation process by 100 to 200 times while keeping video quality close to the original.

Three tricks do most of the work. Faster attention methods cut the cost of comparing frames, a step distillation method reduces the number of generation steps, and 8-bit quantization shrinks the model's numbers. Extra engineering polish adds further gains. The team tested four Wan video models, including a 14-billion-parameter one at 720p, on a single RTX 5090 graphics card. They released code and model checkpoints in a public GitHub repository for others to use.
arxiv-2512-16193:
Narumi Fujii and four co-authors uncover a hidden link between delay and group effects in a paper made public on arXiv in 2025, due in Physical Review E. The Kuramoto model describes oscillators, from fireflies to generators, that sync through pairwise coupling. Real couplings take time, so signals arrive delayed.

By expanding the delayed coupling to second order, the team derived an equivalent model with no delay but with three-body interactions added to the pairwise ones. Simulations and stability analysis show both models switch into sync in the same qualitative way. In particular, the puzzling bistability of the delayed model, where sync and disorder can both persist, is explained by the three-body terms. The result reframes time delays as higher-order interactions, a fresh lens on collective dynamics.
arxiv-2512-16693:
Antoine Martinez and coauthors compare three global models of the upper air of Venus, a key step for planning future missions and computing spacecraft orbits. The three models are the Venus PCM, the VTGCM, and the Tohoku University GCM, each a full 3D climate code.

Side by side, the standard runs share broad traits but split on key points. All three miss the daytime Pioneer Venus data, giving air that is too hot high up, tied to too little atomic oxygen. Choice of solar spectrum drives much of the split over how heat tracks solar activity. The team closes with fixes, from shared solar inputs to updated heating and cooling schemes.
arxiv-2512-16893:
Kaiwen Jiang and coauthors tackle fast, expressive 3D head avatars from a single photo. Video diffusion methods animate portraits well but break 3D consistency and run slow, while 3D-aware feed-forward methods are fast yet lose facial detail.

Their pipeline turns one wild photo into an animatable 3D form in one pass. A light local fusion step joins structure and motion data, replacing heavy global attention. Motion is learned from data in a form split from the face shape, so no fixed parametric face model caps expression. The system runs at 107.31 frames per second for animation and pose control, a three to four order speed gain over the state of the art at like quality.
arxiv-2512-16993:
Alberto Salvio gives a systematic thermal field theory for rotating plasmas with fermion fields, aimed at neutron stars that spin fast. The frame allows any temperature, chemical potentials, and average angular momentum in the equilibrium state.

Both Dirac and Majorana fermions and masses are covered, extending a past scalar-field study to all fermion-scalar theories. Path-integral tools handle thermal Green functions with any number of points, in real-time and imaginary-time forms. Uses include the Fermi surface and momentum, mean energy and density, and particle output such as neutrinos from direct URCA processes. The neutrino rate grows without bound as spin nears the inverse plasma size, so rotation can lift it a lot.
arxiv-2512-17093:
Timo Pierre Schrader and coauthors teach language models to write Answer Set Programming code for logic puzzles, with a solver in the loop. ASP is strong for combinatorial search, but models saw few ASP examples in training, so their code often misses the mark.

Their method samples program continuations from the model for puzzle statements given in plain words. Since partial ASP code narrows the solution space step by step, solver feedback sorts samples into chosen and rejected ones. Fine-tuning on that curated split, plus solver-guided best-of-N search, lifted results in two prompting setups on two data sets, a recipe for other niche languages.
arxiv-2512-17393:
Uttam Tiwari and five co-authors watch a sheet of tiny spinning grains melt, refreeze in spirit, and melt again as they spin harder. The grains sit packed in a flat dish, and the walls force flaw lines, called grain boundary scars, into the crystal. Such scarred sheets belong to a class known as odd elastic solids, which push back in sideways ways.

The scars reroute the flow: currents that normally hug the rim split off from the middle of the sheet. As the team raised the share of counterclockwise spinners, the sheet began to shear itself. That self-shear built odd stresses and melted the crystal at a fixed packing density. The trick suggests new ways to make materials change state on command.
arxiv-2512-17793:
Paul Darius, Thomas Hoppe, and Andrei Aleksandrov map the dangers that appear only when AI agents meet each other. A single agent can be tested alone, but fleets of agents trade, negotiate, and adapt to one another. Harms can emerge from the interaction itself, the way traffic jams emerge from careful drivers.

The team gathers systemic risk examples from the literature, then builds two scenarios to make the patterns concrete: agents running a smart power grid, and agents administering social welfare. From these they draw a taxonomy of risk types and name the behaviors that generate them. A sketch language called Agentology lets designers draw the web of agents and spot risky loops. Safety work, they argue, must graduate from single agents to systems.
arxiv-2512-17893:
Sven Benjamin Kožić and three coauthors probe a puzzle in quantum computing: why neural network guesses for a quantum system's wave pattern work well in one frame and poorly in another. They use a simple chain model whose exact answer is known. Rotating the frame moves the target answer but leaves the training terrain unchanged.

That shift alone can push training toward bad resting spots, so a run can report low energy while its wave pattern is wrong. The failure can happen even when the moved target still fits the network's reach. The lesson is that frame choice shapes training in ways builders must plan for.
arxiv-2512-18293:
Matthew Deakin, Rahmat Heidari, and Xu Deng bring a hidden cost of grid balancing into power planning math. Converters that fix lopsided voltages on local networks pay for it with a ripple of power on their inner DC link, which strains parts and can shake stability. Planning tools that set grid flows rarely model that ripple.

The team derives the ripple size for general multi terminal converters and adds it to flow planning as a firm limit for common two level designs. Case studies show both the neutral wire current and the ripple must be tracked, with a trade between bigger capacitors and bigger switch legs. Time based runs on a four wire grid converter confirm the algebra holds.
arxiv-2512-18493:
Zisheng Chen, Zirui Zhu, and Xiangyang Li test whether small quantum processors can help catch cyber attacks today. Detection models face shifting traffic, tight feature budgets, and noisy data, and even strong classical systems miss rare attacks when patterns drift. Their capstone report, posted to arXiv in December 2025, builds a hybrid design instead of a purely quantum one.

A compact neural network first compresses the security data, then a few features go to quantum heads of two to four qubits, built as quantum support vector machines and variational circuits. On intrusion detection (NSL-KDD) and spam filtering (Ling-Spam), the hybrids match tuned classical models and modestly cut missed attacks on hard cases. The best four-qubit model also ran on a real IBM Quantum device, where results tracked the simulator closely.
arxiv-2512-18593:
Amit Barman, Atanu Mandal, and Sudip Kumar Naskar build translation tools for Indian law. Most legal and court documents in India are written in English, which locks out citizens who read only Hindi or other languages. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and prepared for the JUST-NLP 2025 shared task, compares two ways to train an English-Hindi legal translator.

One strategy fine-tunes the pretrained OPUS-MT model on legal text. The other trains a transformer from scratch on the legal corpus alone. Scored with SacreBLEU, chrF++, COMET, and other metrics, the fine-tuned model wins clearly, reaching a SacreBLEU of 46.03 and beating both the baseline and the from-scratch systems. Domain adaptation, they conclude, is what makes legal machine translation good enough to widen access to justice.
arxiv-2512-18893:
Alejandra Martinez, Dennis Novy, and Carlo Perroni test whether firms, like people, befriend their friends' friends. In social networks that tendency is called transitivity, and it clusters relationships. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, develops a way to detect and measure the same pattern in firm-to-firm trade, using systematic departures from conditional independence between trading relationships.

Applied to Colombia-U.S. exporter-importer data, the method finds transitivity is real and economically meaningful: sharing a trading partner makes two firms more likely to trade with each other. Counterfactual exercises show this clustering shapes how the whole network adjusts when costs shift. For trade policy, the lesson is that shocks travel along a web woven partly by introductions, so the structure of who knows whom belongs in the model.
arxiv-2512-18993:
Xiaotong Xu and co-authors grew crystals of iron placed inside niobium diselenide, and varied the iron share across a wide range. The work links how much iron is present to how the atoms order themselves. It also tracks how the magnetic state changes with that order.

As iron content rises, the material passes from simple paramagnetism to a spin glass, then to long-range antiferromagnetism, and back to a spin glass. The strongest magnetic order appears near one quarter iron, where iron atoms form a neat superlattice. Measurements of structure, magnetism, and transport support the map, which helps guide future tuning of layered magnetic materials.
arxiv-2512-19093:
Peiqing Lu, Yuan Zhang, Haoyun Zhang, and Jiasen Zheng built HERALD, a system for solving math problems written in two languages. Language models read problems well but often slip on exact calculation. HERALD joins several models, including NuminaMath-7B-TIR, GPT-4o, and Mistral-7B, with external math tools.

Adaptive routing sends each problem down a suitable reasoning path, and tool-based reinforcement learning decides when to call a calculator or symbolic tool. Knowledge distillation then compresses the ensemble so answers come faster. Confidence checks and dual-path verification guard the final result. The authors report gains in accuracy, stability, and clarity for bilingual problem solving.
arxiv-2512-19193:
Fabrizio Tavecchio and four co-authors measured polarized light from two extreme blazars, jets of active galaxies pointed near Earth. These BL Lac objects shine from radio to X-rays. Polarization at each band traces the magnetic field and flow pattern inside the jet.

Radio, optical, and X-ray data came from Swift, NuSTAR, and the IXPE satellite. One source, 1ES 1101-232, showed X-ray polarization about five times its optical level, matching a known trend of rising polarization with frequency. The second source gave only an upper limit near its optical level. An improved stratified shock model, the authors show, can explain both sets of data.
arxiv-2512-19393:
Eloise Lardet, Letian Chen, and Thibault Bertrand write a kinetic theory for flocks made of several species at once. Mixed self-propelled groups form patterns no single-species model can show. Their particles align or anti-align depending on the species pairing, and the theory must track each population's density and flow.

For a two-species system, linear stability analysis of the coarse-grained equations matches particle simulations well. The theory even gets the pattern length right, through a Turing-Hopf instability that blends stationary and oscillatory growth. Cyclic alignment rules across more species reproduce the same ordering seen in simulations. The framework is built to extend to richer active mixtures.
arxiv-2512-19593:
H. Göttling, L. Hoff, K. Hebeler, and A. Schwenk compute the equation of state of a neutron star's crust and outer core from chiral effective field theory, with honest error bars. Chiral theory builds nuclear forces order by order, and each order adds uncertainty that must be tracked, not ignored.

A two-dimensional Gaussian process, trained on many-body results from leading through third-next-to-leading order, evaluates energies, pressures, and chemical potentials fast, truncation errors included. Beta-equilibrated matter is followed from the neutron drip through the proton drip into the uniform phase, with surface and Coulomb corrections. The crust equations of state that result stay consistent with the underlying theory.
arxiv-2512-19793:
Ahmed Rakin Kamal and Ratul Mahanta build exact cosmos models in type IIB supergravity where time will not sit still. Their ten-dimensional solutions let the four large dimensions change with time. The six inner dimensions form any compact Calabi-Yau space, scaled by a time-based factor. Most versions switch on the full flux set. No local sources are needed anywhere.

The stress and energy in these worlds meet all four standard energy rules. That holds in ten dimensions and in the four-dimensional view. The clear cases have a negative Ricci scalar in four dimensions. That suits them to early-universe models that stretch or expand. The authors also revisit a famed no-go result. They argue that, with their new parts in place, a positive scalar is harder to rule out.
arxiv-2512-20293:
Jaykumar Kasundra and a large team present AprielGuard, a safeguard model that screens content for large language models. Many deployed systems guard safety risks such as toxicity and adversarial attacks such as prompt injection with separate tools. AprielGuard merges both jobs into one taxonomy and one learning approach.

The eight-billion-parameter model trains on open and synthetic data spanning single prompts, multi-turn conversations, and agentic workflows. Structured reasoning traces are included to make its judgements easier to interpret. Across public and in-house benchmarks, it outperforms open guardrails such as Llama-Guard and Granite Guardian. The edge is largest on multi-step, reasoning-heavy cases. Releasing the model openly is meant to support transparent, reproducible safety research.
arxiv-2512-20793:
Ian Matthias Flór, Claudia Artiaco, Thomas Klein Kvorning, and Jens H. Bardarson map where quantum information lives inside a material. In many-body systems, correlations spread across positions and sizes, and researchers want that layout without picking one measurement in advance. Their tool, a higher-dimensional information lattice, sorts information by location and scale.

An inclusion-exclusion recipe separates fresh information from repeated copies where regions overlap. Positive values mark spots gaining new information; negative values mark redundancy. Applied in two dimensions, the map behaves differently for trapped states, critical states, and the toric code, where topological order shows as one large negative value. Edge-state signatures also stand out.
arxiv-2512-21893:
Shruti Aggarwal, Trasha Gupta, R. K. Agrawal, and S. Indu test whether supervised machine learning can measure quantum entanglement without reconstructing the full quantum state. Entanglement is a central resource for quantum computing, but it cannot be read off directly from physical observables, and computing it from full state information is expensive.

The authors train models on measurement outcomes as input features, with established entanglement measures as the labels. The trained models then estimate the entanglement of new states of two and three qubits from measurements alone. The study reports that the models predict entanglement accurately without access to complete state information. The authors present the approach as evidence that machine learning can serve as an efficient, practical characterization tool for quantum information experiments, where full tomography of every state is unrealistic. The work is a proof of concept rather than a replacement for exact methods.
arxiv-2512-22293:
Tsogt-Ochir Enkhbayar tests whether warning labels in training data teach language models what to avoid, and finds they largely do not. Content flagged with warnings like do-not-use security flaws was reproduced by models at rates close to models shown the content directly, about seventy-seven percent against eighty-three percent in the reported comparison. The warning framing, meant as a guardrail, barely changed behavior.

Sparse autoencoder analysis points to the mechanism: describing something and performing it activate overlapping internal features, so the warning's context does not separate the two. A related effect the author calls stealth slip lets conversational preambles rotate activations where linear probes miss them. Prompting and inference-time steering failed to fix the problem, while training-time feature ablation worked.
arxiv-2512-22393:
Alexander Venus, Erik Leitinger, and Klaus Witrisal extend multipath-based mapping toward realistic 6G networks, where phones can map their surroundings from reflected radio signals. Joint versions fuse data from many mobile terminals for accuracy. Current methods, though, assume perfectly synced base stations sending non-interfering sequences, assumptions real 5G deployments violate even with muting patterns meant to reduce interference.

The authors jointly handle source separation, sync, and mapping inside a Bayesian system solved with the sum-product algorithm on a factor graph. A new base-station-dependent data association and sync bias model classifies features by lasting traits like reflection order. Their analysis shows little performance loss versus idealized joint methods that assume sync and orthogonal signals.
arxiv-2512-22793:
Minh Bui, Simon Monckton, and Mo Chen study reach-avoid games for drones, where a defender must catch an attacker while both maneuver around obstacles in three dimensions. Hamilton-Jacobi reachability analysis gives strong guarantees for such games, but applying it directly in three dimensions is out of reach. Earlier game solvers lacked the generality to handle full three-dimensional motion with realistic dynamics.

Their fix splits the game into a horizontal sub-game and a vertical sub-game, each solved with reachability analysis while allowing the defender acceleration. A tracking controller in each sub-game then rebuilds the full strategy, and the authors prove when the capture guarantee survives the split. Simulations show the split keeps the original problem's guarantees, and tests in the Gazebo physics simulator capture quadrotors flying in three dimensions.
arxiv-2512-22993:
C. N. Pope examines whether a recently found compactification of heterotic supergravity stays consistent once fermions are included. The background wraps the theory on a warped product involving the five-dimensional coset space known as T1,1, and it yields a four-dimensional Minkowski vacuum with minimal supersymmetry. In the bosonic sector, an earlier study found a fully consistent truncation keeping the gauge bosons tied to the space's SU(2) by SU(2) isometries.

Consistent truncation is a strong demand: every solution of the smaller theory must lift to an exact solution of the full one, with no leaked degrees of freedom. Pope shows the fermionic sector can be reduced consistently as well. The heterotic theory therefore reduces cleanly to an ungauged four-dimensional supergravity with minimal supersymmetry, coupled to SU(2) by SU(2) Yang-Mills multiplets and one scalar multiplet. Such reductions give controlled playgrounds for connecting string theory to four-dimensional physics.
arxiv-2512-23093:
Ananya Drishti and Mahfuza Farooque present Cogniscope, a tool for studying whether everyday social media use can reveal early cognitive decline. Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment erode memory, attention, and language long before standard tests catch them, and MRI scans are too costly for population-scale monitoring. Social platforms generate steady traces of behavior, but real patient data are sensitive, so the authors simulate instead.

Cogniscope generates synthetic users following varied trajectories of decline and embeds small tasks, like summarizing a video or answering light questions, inside content feeds. The interactions produce language markers such as semantic drift and disfluency, plus signals like watch time, pausing, and sharing. Tests show how detection quality shifts with data mix, noise, and window length. The generator code, settings, and synthetic datasets are released as a safe benchmark.
arxiv-2512-23293:
Toshizumi Fukui and Saiki Hoshino give singular plane curves a notion of curvature sharp enough to classify them. A plane curve that pinches or crosses itself has no curvature at the singular point, so the authors define curvature parameters for curves of finite multiplicity and build curvatures from them. Their goal is recognition: tell, from those numbers, exactly which singularity type a curve carries.

For the A-simple singularities, the standard list of simplest curve singularities, they provide criteria that fix the type from the curvature data. As a use, they examine parallel curves, the curves traced by points at a fixed offset distance from the original. Offsetting a singular curve creates new singularities, and the criteria are used to work out which types appear. The paper connects differential geometry's measurement, curvature, to the algebraic classification of singularities.
arxiv-2512-23493:
Wei Gao, Paul Zheng, Peng Wu, Yulin Hu, and Anke Schmeink tackle scheduling for industrial wireless networks that must be both ultra-reliable and fast. In these ultra-reliable low-latency settings, many devices share the channel, channel information is imperfect, and the error rate must stay below a strict bound while total data rate is maximized.

Their method decides the order in which devices are served and the modulation and coding scheme for each, adapting both to the imperfect channel knowledge. It combines a deep reinforcement learning algorithm, TD3, with Bayesian optimization that steers training and picks informative samples, countering TD3's sensitivity and the imbalance of error samples. Simulations showed faster convergence and higher total transmission rates than existing approaches.
arxiv-2512-23593:
Nikolai Beving, Jonas Marxen, Steffen Mueller, and Johannes Betz design an observer that lets steer-by-wire systems feel the driver's hands without a torque sensor. Steer-by-wire replaces the mechanical steering column with electronic signals, saving weight and enabling autonomous driving, but the driver's own grip creates high-frequency torque disturbances that degrade steering feel.

Their observer is a Kalman filter that treats the driver's passive torque as an extra state, modeled with a first-order lag, and estimates it from motor measurements alone. Both linear and extended Kalman filter versions were implemented in linear and nonlinear system models and tested in simulation. The nonlinear filter handled friction changes best, and the observer reconstructed driver disturbances with only about fourteen milliseconds of delay. Real-world validation remains future work.
arxiv-2512-23693:
Sky Wang, Justin Svegliato, Helen Appel, and Jason Eisner propose teaching language models from feedback on specific passages rather than whole answers. In their setup, an annotator reads a model response and marks the spans they liked and disliked, saying why. The model then rewrites only the disliked spans, left to right, producing a chain of steadily improving versions of the same answer.

Each adjacent pair in that chain becomes a preference example for direct alignment training, so the model learns from small, targeted edits instead of wholesale rewrites or bare thumbs-up rankings. The authors also built a data set in this format. In their experiments the approach outperformed both standard A/B preference ranking and full contrastive rewrites, evidence that structured, revision-based supervision tunes models more efficiently.
arxiv-2512-24093:
Sanchi Monga and Saswata Bhattacharya compare two semiconductors. Both are carbide antiperovskites. One contains calcium. The other contains strontium. Only that single lattice ingredient differs. The team uses first-principles calculations throughout. They ask how the swap changes excited charge carriers.

Both compounds are direct-gap semiconductors. They absorb light in the visible to near-infrared range. Their carrier dynamics diverge sharply, though. In the calcium material, the lattice moves more strongly. The energy gap swings more widely as a result. Decoherence also runs faster there. At the same time, weaker coupling holds back wasteful recombination. The payoff is a much longer carrier lifetime. It reaches about forty nanoseconds. The strontium version lasts barely two nanoseconds. Hot carriers cool within a few picoseconds in both materials.
arxiv-2512-24193:
Pieter Blok and five colleagues weigh potatoes on a moving harvester. Yield estimates guide how farmers tune their growing practices. Cameras on the harvester capture three-dimensional scans of tubers on a conveyor belt. Each tuber hides part of itself from the camera. The scans are therefore incomplete. Weight estimates based on them run systematically low.

Their network, PointRAFT, skips shape reconstruction entirely. It predicts weight directly from the partial point cloud. A height embedding adds the tuber's height as an extra geometric cue. Training used tens of thousands of scans from a working harvester in Japan. The tubers spanned four cultivars and three seasons. On held-out tubers, the mean error was about twelve grams. The system also runs fast enough for commercial harvesters. It handles up to a hundred fifty tubers per second.
arxiv-2512-24293:
Maurice Genevieva Almeida defines a new graph coloring. Vertices receive red or blue. The coloring is quasi neighborhood balanced when every vertex sees nearly equal colors around it. Red and blue neighbor counts may differ by at most one. At least one vertex must hit a difference of exactly one. Variants refine the idea further.

Uniform, positive, and negative variants depend on the extra neighbor's color. Only vertices of odd degree have such an extra neighbor. The paper gives examples of graph classes admitting each variant. Graph operations on such colored graphs are discussed. Two structural results close the study. No forbidden subgraph characterization exists for the class. Deciding whether a graph admits such a coloring is NP-complete. The notion joins the family of balanced coloring problems in graph theory.
arxiv-2512-24593:
Nhut Le and Maryam Rahnemoonfar build a three-dimensional dataset for disaster assessment. Natural disasters grow more frequent and costly. Semantic segmentation of 3D scenes could speed damage assessment. Existing models lack data from real post-disaster environments, though. The team fills that gap with drone footage of Hurricane Ian.

Aerial video from affected areas in 2022 feeds the reconstruction. Structure-from-motion and multi-view stereo turn it into 3D point clouds. Three leading segmentation models are then evaluated on the data. A fast point transformer, a point transformer variant, and a convolutional model all struggle. Their limits in disaster-stricken regions stand exposed. The findings argue for specialized 3D benchmarks and better techniques. Post-disaster scene understanding needs both before response teams can rely on it.
arxiv-2512-24993:
Josue Leon-Torres, Patrick Hendra, Yugant Hadiyal, and colleagues make quantum imaging with undetected light resilient to noise for real-time phase imaging. The technique uses quantum correlations and nonlinear interferometry so the light touching a sample need not be the light detected. Combined with digital and off-axis holography, it extracts amplitude and phase from single-photon interference.

Environmental noise and dynamic change in real settings are the main obstacle addressed. Quantum optics readers get progress toward practical imaging outside quiet laboratories. Phase imaging without detected illumination light could help with delicate samples that visible or damaging wavelengths would disturb.
arxiv-2601-00093:
Daewon Lee leads sixteen co-authors in watching how palladium hydride nanocrystals change phase as they take up hydrogen, a model system for materials that store energy or information. Their 2026 study uses liquid-phase electron microscopy to film hydrogenation live inside crystals of two shapes, a cube and a hexagonal plate. Elastic energy at the boundary between the two hydride phases was thought to steer the path, but shape effects were largely unknown.

Both shapes follow a similar sequence of nucleus growth, boundary flattening, and reverse nucleation, yet their internal boundaries align along different crystal directions. Cubes follow the ordering predicted by static elastic energy, while plates show two other alignments. Simulations show shape decides which pathways stay reachable when the system is driven far from balance. The authors offer shape as a design lever for steering transformations and improving intercalation devices.
arxiv-2601-00193:
Lisen Ding, Xiangyi Peng, and Dongling Wang design a faster solver for a wave equation with damping built in. The Benjamin Bona Mahony Burgers equation needs care in time stepping. Fine time grids give accuracy but cost a lot. Their scheme works on two time grids at once. A coarse grid handles the hard nonlinear solve first.

Interpolation then lifts that rough answer onto the fine grid. A linearized step on the fine grid corrects it. Cost drops while accuracy holds up well. The team proves key safety traits with the energy method. Conservation, unique solvability, convergence, and stability all come through. The error shrinks at a stated order in time and space. Numerical tests back the theory up. For applied analysts, the trick is reusable. Coarse work first can cheapen fine work later.
arxiv-2601-00693:
Rajiv Chaitanya M and D R Ramesh Babu improve exploration in reinforcement learning, the stage where an agent must try new actions to learn what works. Exploration is especially hard when rewards change over time or policies are high-dimensional. Their framework, ARISE, adds a compact swarm-based exploration layer on top of standard policy-gradient methods.

Actions from the policy are blended with proposals from particles that each represent a candidate trajectory, and reward variance cues tune how bold the exploration is. Gains were small on easy tasks but large on harder ones, including a forty-six percent improvement on LunarLander and strong robustness when rewards shifted mid-training. The layer is presented as lightweight, keeping the stability of the base learner.
arxiv-2601-00993:
Julian D Santamaria and two co-authors present WildIng in 2026, a way to name wildlife in camera trap photos from new places. Camera traps watch animals without bothering them, but sorting their photos by hand is slow. AI models sort them well where they were trained. Move them to a new region, and scores crash. One strong model fell from about eighty-five in each hundred right in Africa to about sixteen in America.

WildIng fights the crash by adding words to the picture. It joins image features with text that describes each species' look. Words stay steady when backgrounds, light, and plants change. The team tested the method on two data sets, from America and from Africa. It lifted a strong base model's score by about thirty in each hundred under the region shift. The work could help track species across parks and borders.
arxiv-2601-01093:
Zeguang Liu and Xin-Jian Xu study an inverse problem for the Bessel operator, a math object that shows up in wave and vibration problems. The question runs backward: from a list of measured tones, called eigenvalues, plus extra constants, can one pin down the hidden inner term that shaped them? They work on a unit interval and split the study by the range of a key parameter.

For whole-number values of that parameter, they prove uniqueness using a closedness trait of a function system built from the data. For a broader range, a density trait of the data gives uniqueness, with an added smoothness demand in some cases. They then extend several known results, once proved only for the zero case, to the full range. Such uniqueness results are the base for any method that rebuilds an unknown system from its tones.
arxiv-2601-01193:
S. P. Leka Amruthavarshini and R. Rajkumar define a new matrix for a connected graph. Its entries mark pairs of points in two ways. Neighbors get a one; pairs at the graph's full diameter distance get that value; all others get zero. The matrix squeezes local links and global reach into one object.

The authors compute the spectrum, the set of characteristic values, of this matrix for paths, cycles, and double star graphs, and find its determinant for any connected graph. They use the matrix's polynomial coefficients and values to single out a class of bipartite graphs, those whose points split into two non-linked camps. They also bound the values in terms of common graph traits. Finally, they work out the spectrum for graphs built by joining or combining smaller ones. The results add a fresh tool for reading graph structure from algebra.
arxiv-2601-01393:
Avro, Lina, and Sharmin build a custom image classification network and test it across farm and city pictures. Design choices matter, they argue, when one model must handle very different scenes. Their network adds shortcut links between layers, a squeeze-and-excite block that weighs image channels, and careful starting values to speed learning.

Five public data sets cover parked vehicles, blocked footpaths, road damage, mango types, and rice types. Against well-known networks, the custom model held its own while using modest computing power. The authors say the results show that thoughtful design, not just size, drives good results for smart city and farming tools.
arxiv-2601-01693:
Controlling gene expression inside living bacteria, a field called cybergenetics, could improve drug development and biomanufacturing. Liam Perreault and five co-authors apply data-enabled predictive control, or DeePC, to steer a bacterial system. The system has two inputs: light-based genetic switches and media concentration. It has two outputs: a target gene's expression and the host's growth rate.

Unlike AI controllers that demand large datasets and retraining for each new system, DeePC works directly from measured data without a prior model. With basis functions added to handle nonlinear behavior, the controller stayed robust when system parameters varied. It performed among the best strategies tested while using the least data, a practical advantage for laboratory biology.
arxiv-2601-02193:
Standard learning theory assumes training data are independent draws, but what if an adversary helpfully adds extra correctly labeled points? Kasper Green Larsen, Chirag Pabbaraju, and Abhishek Shetty define monotone adversarial corruptions: added points labeled by the true target function, inserted after the adversary sees the clean dataset.

Surprisingly, every known optimal binary classification algorithm can be pushed to suboptimal expected error on a fresh test point in this setting, even though the corruption only adds truthful data. Algorithms whose guarantees rest on uniform convergence, by contrast, do not degrade. The result exposes how deeply optimal learners lean on exchangeability of the data, a fragility invisible in the standard model.
arxiv-2601-02293:
Pinak Banerjee works in M theory, the framework that links the different string theories. He follows what happens when an M5 brane is reduced to a D4 brane in ten dimensional Type IIA spacetime. He begins by re deriving the motion equations and the Bianchi identities, the consistency rules, for the simpler abelian D4 brane case.

Fluxes in this setting are counted not by ordinary cohomology. They are counted by a non abelian version called cohomotopy, with a four flux in the bulk and a three flux on the M5 brane. Banerjee computes the minimal model for a step called cyclification of a key fibration, which encodes the D4 rules after reduction. Matching the two pictures leads him to conjecture a relative cohomology theory for the D4 brane.
arxiv-2601-02593:
Chunhua Qi, David J. Wilner, and Catherine C. Espaillat measure carbon and oxygen isotope ratios in the planet forming disk around the young star HD 163296, using the ALMA telescope array. Isotope ratios record where a disk's volatile material came from and how its chemistry evolved. Their method is empirical, comparing rare forms of carbon monoxide directly, without detailed disk modeling.

New observations of one rare isotopologue at fine resolution join archival data on three others. Two flux ratios rise sharply across the carbon monoxide snowline, the radius where that gas freezes out, and flatten farther out where the emission becomes optically thin. In that thin region, beam averaged intensities of the four lines give the isotope ratios directly. The carbon ratio comes out near seventy five, and the sharp transition makes this disk an especially clean case for isotopic analysis.
arxiv-2601-02893:
Hsin-Yu Hsu and six co-authors ask whether giving up symmetry can buy a stronger violation of a Bell inequality in a smaller quantum system. Bell tests measure how far quantum predictions depart from classical ones, and symmetry between the two parties is often assumed for convenience. The team studies the trade-off between party-exchange symmetry and the size of the Hilbert space, the mathematical space describing the system.

For one well-known family of symmetric inequalities, they find evidence that no trade-off is needed. For several small inequalities, though, symmetric strategies in the smallest possible space fall short of the best violation, so only asymmetric strategies reach the maximum. The results bear on the shape of the set of quantum correlations and on efforts to certify devices from Bell test outcomes alone.
arxiv-2601-03293:
Rohan Pandey studies where the roots of independence polynomials of generalized Petersen graphs fall in the complex plane. The independence polynomial counts independent sets of a graph by size, and the location of its zeros connects to deep questions in combinatorics and statistical physics. Using an exact transfer-matrix algorithm, Pandey computes the polynomials for graphs with up to thirty vertices around the cycle and four step sizes.

The numerics reveal a striking split based on parity. For odd step sizes, roots form complex conjugate patterns accumulating on closed curves; for even step sizes, the roots look strictly real and negative. Motivated by that evidence, he conjectures the polynomial is real-rooted exactly when the step size is even. The phenomenon ties the algebra of these graphs to the hard-core lattice gas model.
arxiv-2601-03393:
Edward Groot and seven co-authors ask how much weather models disagree because of their sub-grid physics, by holding everything else fixed. In atmospheric models, parameterized small-scale processes interact strongly with the resolved flow. So errors are hard to attribute. For the Model Uncertainty Model Intercomparison Project, each physics suite was coupled to the same prescribed large-scale dynamics. That dynamics came from a convection-permitting benchmark simulation. The suites were then run over the Indian Ocean for a full month.

The four suites produced strikingly similar precipitation. Correlations between models exceeded zero point nine five at the native grid. This holds even though precipitation is a dominant uncertainty that redistributes large amounts of heat. The analysis of joint probability distributions of rain and physics tendencies then turns to why the suites agree so closely, and where their tendencies still diverge.
arxiv-2601-03493:
Jinming Nian and four co-authors study a quiet choice inside automatic prompt optimization: which test examples should score each candidate prompt? Optimizers usually sample a small evaluation set at random and treat that choice as a detail. The authors argue the choice shapes the feedback signal, and therefore the final prompt, more than people assume.

Their method, SESS, picks evaluation subsets using submodular selection, a math framework for choosing items with diminishing added value. They show the goal is monotone and submodular under mild conditions, so a greedy algorithm carries guarantees. On GSM8K, MATH, and GPQA-Diamond benchmarks, chosen subsets produced better optimized prompts than random or rule-based picks. Careful test-set design can improve AI tuning without any bigger model.
arxiv-2601-03593:
Kevin Zhao and nine co-authors built Polyphony, a system that gives data center operators a new handle on rare but painful slowdowns. The target is tail latency, the worst delays users feel, across networks serving many classes of traffic at once. Polyphony works on a scale of minutes and is meant to complement, not replace, congestion control and traffic engineering.

The system watches workloads across the whole network and feeds them into a prediction engine that estimates what a configuration change would do before anyone applies it. That counterfactual step matters because modern workloads shift constantly, which defeats older tuning methods built for stable conditions and few knobs. Fewer tail events means cloud services feel steadier to customers even when demand surges.
arxiv-2601-03793:
Sethupathy Parameswaran, Suresh Sundaram, and Yuan Fang tackle zero-shot node classification in text-attributed graphs, networks whose nodes carry written descriptions, like papers with abstracts or products with blurbs. With no labeled examples at all, sorting nodes into classes is hard. Their Zero-shot Prompt Tuning framework leans on a universal bimodal conditional generator to manufacture the missing training data.

First, a graph-language model is pretrained to capture both network structure and node text. A conditional generative model then learns the joint pattern of graph and text embeddings, producing synthetic samples for each class from its name alone. Those samples support continuous prompt tuning for the classification task. Synthetic stand-ins for labels could help cold-start problems in social networks, publishing, and online retail alike.
arxiv-2601-03893:
Markus Walker and four co-authors smooth out the control signals produced by sampling-based model predictive control, a planning method that steers nonlinear systems by testing many possible futures. Random sampling makes the chosen controls jittery, which real machines dislike. Their method, deterministic sampling MPPI, extends the model predictive path integral framework with fixed, deterministic samples instead of random ones.

The design also imports iterative optimization ideas from cross-entropy method control, combining the exponential weighting of the path integral approach with the efficiency of chosen samples. Experiments showed smoother trajectories than state-of-the-art methods achieved. Smooth control is not cosmetic: jerky commands wear actuators, waste energy, and can destabilize robots and vehicles, so planners that are both smart and smooth are genuinely more deployable.
arxiv-2601-04193:
Kieran Morris and Oliver Johnson set up optimal transport on graphs in a form that mirrors a classic fluid picture. Optimal transport finds the cheapest way to reshape one distribution into another. On a graph, masses sit on vertices, yet movement happens along edges, so a discrete flow law must link the two.

Morris and Johnson propose a discrete transport equation that connects distributions on vertices and on edges together. From it they derive a discrete analogue of the Benamou-Brenier formulation for the Wasserstein distance of order one on a graph. That formulation views distance as the least action of a flow. As a payoff, they classify all shortest paths, the geodesics, for that distance on graphs, giving a full picture of how mass travels most cheaply.
arxiv-2601-04293:
Nathan Shaw and three co-authors map what is known about debugging autonomous driving systems in a 2026 arXiv systematic mapping study. Testing self-driving software has drawn heavy research, but the step after a test fails. Finding and fixing the fault — has been largely ignored, even though safety and reliability depend on it.

The study surveys the existing debugging approaches, sorts them, and exposes how fragmented the field still is. Along the way the authors propose directions for future work and clearer shared definitions and terms, so that later studies can be compared at all. Their picture is of a young research area with promising pieces but no settled practice, facing systems now nearing commercial deployment.
arxiv-2601-04393:
Eren Kocadag, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari, and Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag test whether bias can be scrubbed from word embeddings where identities overlap, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Static embeddings absorb social stereotypes from their training text. Earlier debiasing work built on the Stereotype Content Model, which rates groups by warmth and competence, handled one identity at a time; real bias is often intersectional, aimed at combinations.

The team builds compound representations for pairs of identities, by adding or joining their vectors. applies three fixes — subtraction, linear projection, and partial projection — across Word2Vec, GloVe, and ConceptNet Numberbatch. Judged by whether word neighbourhoods stay coherent and analogies still work, the mitigation carries over to the intersectional case with the semantic landscape mostly intact. The trade-off is familiar: gentler methods protect geometry but tread carefully on analogies, while stronger projections can do the reverse.
arxiv-2601-04593:
Patrick R. Behr and eight co-authors measure the harsh light falling on planets of the nearest Sun-like stars, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Far-ultraviolet radiation drives the chemistry of planetary atmospheres, so interpreting any atmosphere observation requires knowing the starlight that bathes the planet. Aboard the SISTINE sounding rocket, their spectrograph captured both stars of Alpha Centauri AB in a single exposure, with the broadest far-ultraviolet coverage taken at once.

Combining that spectrum with archival data and a new activity model, they build full energy distributions for both stars from X-ray wavelengths to the millimetre. Feeding the extremes — companion near or far, stars quiet or active — into a photochemistry code, they estimate atmospheric abundances for a hypothetical planet of Alpha Centauri A. The reassuring headline: extra atmospheric escape caused by having two suns should not trouble missions like the Habitable Worlds Observatory hunting Earth-like planets.
arxiv-2601-04793:
Josef Durech and 5 co-authors revisit asteroid Didymos in a 2026 paper about the after-effects of NASA's DART mission. In September 2022 the DART spacecraft struck Dimorphos, the smaller member of the Didymos pair, to test whether a kinetic impact could divert a dangerous asteroid. The hit changed the pair's orbital period, and Durech's team hunted for a subtler effect.

Using photometric light curves, brightness records gathered across six apparitions from 2003 to 2023, they compare rotation before and after the impact. The question is whether Didymos itself began spinning at a changed rate. Knowing every effect of an impact helps planners judge how predictable a real deflection attempt would be.
arxiv-2601-05293:
Sahaya Jestus Lazer and 3 co-authors survey how agentic AI reshapes cyber defense and cyber attack in a 2026 paper. Agentic AI marks a shift from one-step text tools to systems that can plan, act, and adapt through long tasks. Such systems hold a memory, use tools, and loop through choice after choice as they work. That free hand lets them run on their own in real settings, for good or for ill.

On the defense side, the team map gains such as round-the-clock watch, fast first aid when a breach hits, and fraud checks at scale. On the attack side, the same free hand speeds up scouting and strikes. The survey also shows trial builds for real use. Its core ask is how to keep the gains and curb the risks at once.
arxiv-2601-05393:
Tony Affolder and 25 co-authors measure how a cold noise fault affects detector modules built for the upgraded ATLAS experiment in a 2026 paper. The ATLAS inner tracker will become a full silicon detector for the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider, and its modules must exceed strict efficiency and noise occupancy targets. During pre-production, many short-strip modules showed cold noise: clusters of strips with very high noise when operated below a threshold temperature.

The team studies the fault's impact on tracking performance using a charged particle beam, part of a large collaboration effort to ensure production quality. Understanding whether cold noise spoils real tracks decides whether affected modules can be accepted, repaired, or must be rejected before installation deep inside ATLAS.
arxiv-2601-05593:
Jingcheng Hu and 19 co-authors introduce PaCoRe, a 2026 framework that scales reasoning by running many solution attempts in parallel and coordinating them. Language models usually reason in one long chain, so extra compute is limited by the context window. PaCoRe instead explores broadly and merges what the attempts find.

Each round launches many parallel reasoning trajectories. Their findings are compacted into short messages, then synthesized to guide the next round and the final answer. Training used large-scale reinforcement learning based on outcomes. The authors report strong gains across domains, including a small model surpassing a frontier system on a 2025 mathematics competition set by using roughly two million effective tokens of reasoning.
arxiv-2601-05693:
Zenghao Duan and 8 co-authors identify, in a 2026 paper, a failure mode they call circular reasoning in large reasoning models. Instead of progressing, a model can treat its own generated text as a premise for repeating itself. The result is a self-reinforcing loop that wastes computation and can end in inference failure.

Their LoopBench dataset captures numerical loops and statement loops as two distinct types. Analysis shows semantic repetition begins before exact textual repetition, and stalled reasoning triggers entry into the loop. A V-shaped attention pattern then keeps the cycle going. Using a cumulative sum algorithm to catch early warning signs, the authors predict loop onset accurately across several reasoning models.
arxiv-2601-05793:
Jie Liu and 2 co-authors address in 2026 a subtle consistency problem in predicting gravitational waves from the early universe's electroweak phase transition. Vacuum decay through bubble nucleation should not depend on the theorist's gauge choice, an arbitrary descriptive freedom. Yet naive calculations of nucleation rates often do depend on it.

Working in a 3D effective field theory of the Standard Model, the authors study gauge dependence of the transition parameters. Using power counting tied to the new-physics scale and a Nielsen identity at finite temperature, they show perturbative methods can yield gauge-independent nucleation rates and transition parameters. Depending on the counting scheme favored, that independence enables more accurate predictions of the gravitational wave signature. That care matters, since a wrong rate would spoil the forecast for the waves that reach us.
arxiv-2601-06393:
Distributed quantum sensors usually need a shared reference frame to make sense of their measurements. Hua-Qing Xu and 8 co-authors show how to do without one in a 2026 paper. When distant parties cannot align their frames, symmetry restrictions create a no-go result: locally encoded information cannot be extracted in the usual way.

Their reversed-encoding method applies to two copies of network states that are invariant under local unitaries. It circumvents the no-go theorem and also softens the decoherence-like noise caused by frame misalignment. The full quantum Fisher information, the measure of how much a state reveals about a parameter, becomes recoverable. Local Bell-state measurements prove optimal for reaching it, opening field use for distributed quantum sensing.
arxiv-2601-06693:
Umesh Dhumal uses nested drops to make tiny drug grains in a 2026 paper. Drops of water in oil in water can box in where drug grains form. In that box, grains can start and grow in a tight space.

But such nested drops are frail and short-lived in most past work. How they are mixed and what goes in them shifts their life a lot. He builds them with sound waves in a two-stage plan of his own. The drops then last long enough to serve as molds for the grains. The grains that form are rich in drug and less than a micron wide. Drug firms gain a way to make grains of like size and load. The frail point of such drops is met head-on and fixed.
arxiv-2601-06893:
Neil O’Connell and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers absorption times for discrete whittaker processes and non-intersecting brownian bridges. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The authors present evidence for a conjectural relationship between absorption times for discrete Whittaker processes and maximal heights of non-intersecting Brownian bridges. Introduction It is well known (see, for example.

[ 1 ] for a survey) that twice the square of the maximum of a reflected Brownian bridge, starting and ending at zero. Has the same law as the random variable where is a sequence of independent standard exponential random variables. And that twice the square of the maximum of. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07293:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Weidong Tang and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers Inference-Time scaling for visual AutoRegressive modeling by searching representative samples. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. While inference-time scaling has significantly enhanced generative quality in large language and diffusion models. Its application to vector-quantized (VQ) visual autoregressive modeling (VAR) remains unexplored.

The authors introduce VAR-Scaling , the first general framework for inference-time scaling in VAR. Addressing the critical challenge of discrete latent spaces that prohibit continuous path search. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07593:
Dimple Vijay Kochar and colleagues apply reinforcement learning to hardware test planning. Chip designers often rely on ad-hoc testbenches written early in the design cycle. Large language models can generate RTL code, the language that describes hardware. Whether they can reason about specifications and produce targeted test plans is far less clear. The team's 2026 preprint tests that ability.

Their method uses GRPO, a reinforcement learning algorithm, with state mutations. Mutating states during training may expose the model to more varied hardware situations. The goal is test plans that aim at real weaknesses in a design. Better automated test planning could catch chip bugs earlier and cheaper. The paper speaks to hardware verification teams watching LLM tools enter their workflow.
arxiv-2601-07993:
Damjana Kokol Bukovšek and coauthors pin down the exact region spanned by three measures of how traits move as one. Concordance measures state how strongly random values move as one. Those who use them take more than one at once to narrow the set of links that may hold. Links between distinct weak concordance measures have seen much study in recent years. Their 2026 preprint pins down the region set by Spearman's footrule, Gini's gamma, and Kendall's tau as a trio.

An exact region tells users which sets of values can show up at once. Impossible combinations expose errors in reported statistics. Ones that can occur show how much doubt stays after all three. Each measure weights disagreements between rankings differently. The paper serves those who work with rank based links in data. It completes a three-way comparison that pairwise studies could not finish.
arxiv-2601-08093: Na-Na Gao, Jian-Fu Zhang, and Jungyeon Cho study turbulence in relativistic magnetized plasma. Their 2026 arXiv paper works within relativistic force-free magnetohydrodynamics, the flow of magnetized matter near light speed. They run high-resolution simulations with a uniform background magnetic field in place. The focus is on cascade processes, where energy moves across scales in the flow. Both strong and weak cascades are covered. The study helps readers who model jets, pulsars, and other extreme cosmic flows where such turbulence shapes what telescopes see.
arxiv-2601-08493:
Kexin Bao and five co-authors present PKI, a network that injects prior knowledge into few-shot incremental learning. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets models that must adapt continually from a few new-class examples. Two challenges dominate: catastrophic forgetting and overfitting to the new classes.

Many existing methods freeze more network parts and fine-tune others with extra memory during sessions. PKI instead infuses prior knowledge directly into the network design. The aim is to keep old classes safe while new ones are learned from scarce data. Published in the journal Neural Networks, the work serves builders of systems that must learn on the job without retraining from scratch.
arxiv-2601-08693:
Yash Lapasia and a large team measure how modeling choices shift stellar masses of optically dark galaxies. Their 2026 arXiv paper follows JWST studies suggesting some high-redshift galaxies may be ultra-massive. Such claims challenge standard models of early galaxy formation and cosmology.

The authors focus on two uncertainty sources: the attenuation law for dust and assumed star-formation histories. Both choices feed the spectral fits that produce stellar mass estimates. If masses swing widely with these choices, ultra-massive claims need caution. The study gives observers a clearer error budget before early galaxy results are used to test cosmology.
arxiv-2601-08893:
Andrew Kiruluta puts forth a new base for AI that makes text and video. Top tools now cut text into tokens and pass them through layers that weigh links. Kiruluta says that path is a choice, not a law. He treats make work as a field that flows and shifts in time, held in check by set rules.

His models are called Spectral Generative Flow Models. They store the field in a mix of wave sizes, from broad swells to fine ripples. Noise then steers the field to a text or clip form. A reader gets a bold swap of base ideas. It asks if flow in a wave field can beat token steps on cost and on grace of moves.
arxiv-2601-09193:
Dev Prakash Jha and Raju George study how to steer a heat type system to full rest when it holds past states. Heat flow in a rod with memory rests on past heat, not just now. A lag makes it rest on old states too. To null control such a system means to drive it to zero at a set end time, by a push at the edge.

They set a strong form of that task. State, memory sum, and lag past must all be zero at the end. A weak form that leaves past terms live could spring back. A reader in control work gets tests for when the strong form can be done in a finite size case.
arxiv-2601-09293:
Sofiene Lassoued, Stefan Lier, and Andreas Schwung run a shop floor plan that must cope with chance. Jobs come at random times. Machines break with no warn. A fixed plan dies on the first break. The plan must be made live, as the floor shifts. Yet each step must stay doable: no job on a dead machine, no clash of times.

They model the floor as a timed net of states and moves. A learn agent then picks next steps, with a mask that blocks bad picks. The mask is the key guard: the agent can learn fast, but can not pick a step the floor can not take. A reader in plant work gets a live plan with a built in safe check.
arxiv-2601-09593:
L. Maghlaoui, P. O. Hess, F. Weber, and C. A. Zen Vasconcellos explore a cosmology where dark energy comes from geometry. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents the pseudo-complex Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker model. It extends the standard expanding-universe model inside pseudo-complex general relativity.

In this approach, the pseudo-complex structure itself produces what looks like dark energy. The Hubble parameter then drifts with time instead of staying a fixed constant H0. The paper works out the model's expansion history, including a predicted redshift drift in an appendix. A changing Hubble rate is testable, which makes the idea more than a mathematical game.
arxiv-2601-09793:
Soumadip Pakrashi, Atanu Rajak, and Sambuddha Sanyal report a freezing effect that simple theory cannot shake. Their 2026 arXiv paper shows a robust plateau where particles stay put in lattices that are driven in time and patterned in a near-periodic way. The plateau shows up no matter how the lattice starts out and no matter how it is driven.

The team combines exact Floquet dynamics, Floquet perturbation theory, and van Vleck analysis. They find one tuned ratio of drive strength to drive rate where all Floquet states stay put, despite a dense web of near-resonances. Such lattices model quantum simulators and cold-atom setups in the lab. A plateau that no protocol can break gives engineers a sure way to freeze motion on demand.
arxiv-2601-10093:
Yiding Qiu, Seyed Mahdi Azimi, and Artem Lensky built a grader for code classes. Large code classes give slow, thin notes on pupil work. Pupils need fast notes that say what is wrong and why. The team built a local tool named Mark My Works.

The tool runs two checks at once. It runs unit tests on the code. It also asks a language model to read the code and write notes. Role based prompts guide the model. It can fault style, not just right or wrong. The notes state their grounds, so pupils can see the why.
arxiv-2601-10293:
Marco Barbisan and co authors update the power design of a beam tool for a fusion test. The tool fires a fast neutral beam into a plasma. The beam lets tools read the plasma's heat, flow, and field. The test rig is RFX-mod2 in Padova.

The beam is key for two read tools. One reads light from charge swaps. One reads field pitch from light shifts. The paper gives the fresh power design for the beam source. It covers how the beam is made and fed. A sound design is a step to first runs of the tool.
arxiv-2601-10393:
Nanda Rea, Natasha Hurley-Walker, and Manisha Caleb review a new class of radio sources. They are named Long Period Transients. Each source sends radio bursts that last secs to mins. The bursts repeat with a gap of mins to hours. Their strength can reach a high mark.

The bursts are strongly polarized. Their live spans come and go. The class was found in the last few years. Much about it is still open: what the sources are, and how they burst. The review sums what is known. It maps the traits that set this class apart from pulsars and kin.
arxiv-2601-10593:
D. G. C. McKeon, F. T. Brandt, J. Frenkel, and S. Martins-Filho study supergravity in a flatland-style setting of two space dimensions plus time. They work with the first-order Einstein-Cartan action. The model includes a cosmological term, and they extend it with supersymmetry. Lagrange multiplier fields enter as part of the setup named in the title.

In this setting, the spin connection can be written as an axial vector. That choice makes the action bilinear in the quantum fields. A bilinear action can be quantized without fixed background fields. The result gives theorists a cleaner route into quantum gravity models in low dimensions, where hard problems often become tractable test cases.
arxiv-2601-10793:
Javier Lafuente-López studies metrics that change signature on a manifold. A metric sets how distances and times are measured. In some models of quantum gravity, space can pass from a Euclidean region to a Lorentzian one. That switch was first proposed by Hartle and Hawking to dodge the initial singularity of the standard cosmos.

Lafuente-López gives a one-parameter family of such signature-change models. The family generalizes Kossowski's signature type. He seeks simple local formulas near the surface where the switch happens. Clean local forms make the models easier to test and extend. The work serves theorists who model the birth of spacetime without a hard beginning.
arxiv-2601-11093:
Ashish Raj Shekhar, Shiven Agarwal, Priyanuj Bordoloi, Yash Shah, and Vivek Gupta present Integrity Shield, a system for ethical AI use in assessments. Language models can now solve whole exams from an uploaded PDF. That power threatens the reliability of grades and credentials. Watermarking is a common defense, but token-level marks fail when students use closed, black-box systems.

Integrity Shield aims at authorship transparency under those real conditions. Teachers hand out the documents; students query systems the school does not control. Any shield must work without touching the model's decoding. The work serves educators who want AI use declared and checkable, rather than banned in ways no one can enforce.
arxiv-2601-11193:
Peter von Schultzendorff and five coauthors mix physics code with learned models. Their 2026 preprint adds a learned near-well model to OPM Flow. OPM Flow is a tool that simulates flow in rock that holds oil and gas. Flow near a well is one of the hard parts to get right.

Hybrid designs pair old physics-based code with models fit to data. The learned parts can match real effects with high fidelity. They also run fast once they are trained and ready. That speed opens the door to quicker full runs of a field. It also helps model effects that physics alone does not yet explain well.
arxiv-2601-11493:
Lorenzo Lazzarino, Katherine Pearce, and Nathaniel Pritchard grade random matrix shortcuts. Their 2026 preprint deals with Generalized Nystrom approximations. Randomized methods in numerical linear algebra scale to huge matrices. They give accurate low-rank approximations at a fraction of the cost.

A key open task is to judge that accuracy cheaply. Extra passes over the matrix can cost as much as the method saves. Error estimators must work with no new matrix access. The team gives efficient estimators for the generalized case. Trustworthy error bars make random methods safe for pipelines. Engineers can then stop early when the fit is good enough.
arxiv-2601-11693:
Shane Panter and Nasir Eisty review technical lag as latent debt. Their 2026 rapid review consolidates research on the topic. Technical lag builds when systems fail to keep pace. Technology advances, and lagging systems lose quality over time.

The review clarifies definitions of technical lag first. It explores how lag is detected and quantified in code. Underlying causes and consequences come next in the survey. Current management practices for lag are also reviewed. The vision casts lag as passively accumulated technical debt. Debt that accrues by standing still reframes upgrade choices. The method was a rapid review with snowballing. Peer-reviewed studies formed the base of the synthesis.
arxiv-2601-12093:
Duarte Alexandrino, Ben Moseley, and Pavlos Protopapas speed up physics-informed neural networks for nonlinear systems. Such nets solve equations by adding the law to the training loss. They can model dynamic acts across science and engineering.

Yet they train slowly and move poorly to new problems. The team's method, named in the work, guides transfer learning with perturbation steps. Past runs can then seed new ones with care. Faster PINNs would aid real-time models of fluids, structures, and fields.  Shared starts could cut hours from each new solve task.  Speed gains grow when many like problems must be solved in a row.
arxiv-2601-12193:
Shaunak Halbe, Bhagyashree Puranik, Jayakrishnan Unnikrishnan, and their co-authors build one embedding space for many video search tasks. Users now ask for whole clips, for a brief moment in a clip, and for mixed text-image queries. Past systems train split encoders on vast data for each task.

Their system, named VIRTUE in the work, uses unified embeddings for all these tasks. One space could serve many query forms with less cost. It also lets composed queries mix modes in one search. The work tests that breadth.  One trait space also eases mixed text and clip search.
arxiv-2601-12393: Shohei Satake works on Lee codes, a tool from coding theory. He builds a new explicit family of codes of a special near perfect kind. These codes can be made as long as one likes. Long codes with good traits are prized, since explicit families are rare in this area.
arxiv-2601-12693:
