Mohoshin Ara Tahera and four co authors build a federated system for real time object detection in traffic. Intelligent transportation systems need detection that is fast, private, and secure at once. Three challenges block that goal. Traffic data differ by place, with some classes missing at some sites. Edge hardware also struggles to run large transformer models within latency limits.

The third challenge is trust: client updates may be hostile, and central aggregation is a risk. Their system, BlocksecRT-DETR, answers with decentralized federated learning. It aims to be privacy preserving and token efficient at the same time. Secure detection at the edge would help smart traffic systems scale safely. The design shows one route to that goal.
arxiv-2601-13093:
Gabriel Picavet and Martine Picavet-L'Hermitte study a special class of ideals in ring theory. Ideals are sets inside a ring that stay closed under set rules. The class here is called quasi maximal ideals, first set out by Alan and co-authors.

The pair give a full account of what marks such ideals. They also bring in a linked class, called submaximal ideals. A key tool is the conductor of a small step from one ring to a larger ring. They show that this conductor is quasi maximal in the larger ring. That fact yields a fresh way to mark such small steps. Ring staff get a sharper kit for sorting finite ring growth.
arxiv-2601-13193:
Yuxi Hu, Mengran Yuan, and Jie Zhang study if a wavy flow form stays true for long times. The flow is a one dim squeezed fluid. In this form, two old laws are swapped. Newton's law for thick flow is swapped for Maxwell's law. Fourier's law for heat flow is swapped for Cattaneo's law.

The swap gives the set a finite speed for signals, unlike the old set. The wave form at stake is a rarefaction wave, a smooth spread out fan. The team proves that small shakes of that wave fade and the wave holds for long times. Such proofs set when the new set can be trusted for real flows.
arxiv-2601-13293:
Michael Hinze, Christian Kahle, and John Sebastian Simon track the long time acts of best shape flows. Their task joins shape choice with the time flow laws of Navier and Stokes. The sought shape is held as a phase field, a smooth mark that says where fluid or wall sits.

The flow laws are run through a porous media swap, a known trick to make shape tasks firm. The field that marks shape stays fixed in time, while the flow moves. The team asks where the joint acts settle as time runs long. Such work guides tasks like pipe and wing shape, where the best form must serve a flow that never sits still.
arxiv-2601-14393:
Gor Oganesyan leads a team of eleven authors on gamma-ray burst physics in this 2026 paper. Gamma-ray bursts are the most violent explosions known. A small fraction of their X-ray photons behave in a telling way after escaping the source. The abstract in the evidence pack cuts off at that point, so the full photon path is not stated there.

The title names the paper's claim: MeV absorption in gamma-ray bursts can serve as a probe of their progenitor winds. A progenitor wind is gas blown off by the star before it burst. If burst photons are absorbed by that wind, the loss pattern records the wind's traits. Readers get a proposed new use for an absorption signal.
arxiv-2601-14493:
Matthieu Bourguignon and a team of seven co-authors study how glass breaks in this 2026 paper. Shear bands lie at the root of fracture initiation in bulk metallic glasses and amorphous polymers. For silicate glasses, past studies stressed a distinct effect: permanent volumetric strain, often called densification. The team's work tests which picture fits silicate glass.

They systematically investigate indentation-induced fracture in two families of aluminoborosilicate glasses. Indentation presses a hard tip into the surface to start cracks in a controlled way. Their title claims a universal shear localization mechanism behind fracture initiation. The tests are hands-on. A hard tip is pressed into real glass, and the cracks are then read up close. Readers get lab evidence that silicate glass may fail more like its metallic cousins than once thought.
arxiv-2601-14593:
Po-Kai Chiu and Hung-Hsuan Chen work on medical image learning in this 2026 paper. Deep learning for medical image analysis is limited by the requirement for expert annotations. Three-dimensional self-supervised methods like volume contrast learning are powerful. They partially address the labeling scarcity issue. Their high computational cost and memory consumption are barriers, though.

The team moves from volumes to slices, as their title says. They design computationally efficient contrastive learning for sequential abdominal CT analysis. Slices are the single cross-section images that stack into a CT volume. Readers get a lighter self-supervised method that still learns from the order of slices in a scan.
arxiv-2601-14893:
C. Chilarescu examines a production function that he put forward in earlier work. A production function links the inputs a firm uses to the output it makes. His 2026 arXiv paper tests what his new function can and cannot do.

One test concerns elasticity, which gauges how output reacts when an input grows. He proves that, under set limits on the inputs, the elasticity can also fall below one. He also proves that the function meets the Inada conditions under set limits. Those are the classic edge rules for such functions in economics.
arxiv-2601-15093:
Fien Apers asks whether a famous set of string theory vacua can have a holographic dual. Her 2026 arXiv paper deals with the DGKT solutions of massive type IIA string theory. These vacua split their scales apart by using very large fluxes.

Whether any scale-separated anti-de Sitter vacuum has a dual is not known. Apers studies the brane dual proposed for the DGKT case. She also studies its decoupling, the step that should isolate the dual theory. The paper tests how far that proposed brane duality can really be trusted today.
arxiv-2601-15293:
Alva Markelius, Fethiye Irmak Doğan, and co-authors ask how disabled students feel about robot help at university. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with barriers in higher education. Long procedures, poor information, and high social demands can block students from support.

The study tests robot-based support in two roles. One role gives information, a signposting role. The other acts as a sounding board for disclosure. Two embodiment types are compared as well: a physical robot and a disembodied voice agent. Students then judge which form of help they would accept in practice.
arxiv-2601-15493:
M M Abid Naziri and four co-authors test the libraries behind deep learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Libraries such as PyTorch sit under most AI applications. They are complex, and they contain bugs. Many bug-finding methods exist for them. The authors say much room for improvement remains. One core obstacle is the lack of API specifications.

Without specs, a tester cannot easily tell right output from wrong. The team's answer uses neurosymbolic constraint learning, per the title. That blends neural methods with symbolic rules. Learned constraints can stand in for missing specs. Better library tests matter beyond research. A bug deep in a shared library can quietly corrupt many models built on top of it.
arxiv-2601-15793:
Yuxuan Lei and five co-authors teach language models to simulate people in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is HumanLLM. Models have grown strong at objective tasks like math and coding. Simulating human behavior is a different, newer ambition. It carries large implications. Social science research could run on simulated subjects. Businesses could test ideas on simulated customers before spending.

The title stresses personalized understanding and simulation of human nature. A useful simulator must capture how individuals differ, not just averages. The abstract frames the motivation more than the method. Readers will find design details in the full text. The stakes cut both ways. Good simulators aid research, but shallow ones can mislead it with confident, wrong behavior.
arxiv-2601-16293:
Roche reports new tests of how stuff bounces far UV light. The 2026 preprint deals with light past the UV edge, called VUV. True bounce values count for probes that sense light in rare gas. DUNE is one such big probe now in build. Past bounce values clash much from source to source. Test terms drove much of that clash.

Fresh tests under set terms aim to pin true values down. Stuff in the tests is that used in argon and xenon probes. Firm values let teams tune probe light yield with care. They also cut doubt in probe design sums. The work is a lab note for probe builders.
arxiv-2601-16393:
Keidai Iiyama and Grace Gao track moon craft by earth GPS marks. Their 2026 preprint deals with craft that loop the moon. Earth GPS marks are weak at moon range and hard to read. Yet they could guide moon craft with no new moon net. The team builds a filter to draw orbit and clock from those marks.

The filter clones past states to hold time lags in the data. A split form of the filter keeps the sums firm and fast. Firm orbit marks are key for safe moon flight plans. The work tests earth marks as a moon guide path. It seeks high grade from low sight terms.
arxiv-2601-16493:
Yuerang Li, Zipeng Wang and Kenan Zhang bound Shimorin type sum tools. Their 2026 preprint deals with sum tools on the unit disk. Such a tool weighs a map by a fixed weight set on a line. Bounds link the in size and out size of the tool. Those links are named Lp to Lq bounds in the field.

Firm bounds tell for which size pairs the tool stays sound. Sound tools serve sums in wave, heat and chance maths. The team seeks sharp pairs for this tool class. Sharp pairs close gaps left in past bound work. The work is a pure sum study of disk tools.
arxiv-2601-16693:
Javier Sanz Rodrigo, Nicholas Kryger-Nelson, Lena Mittmann, Eugène Bertin, Ivano Castelli, and Andrea Crovetto hunt for new raw stuff to build with. Their 2026 preprint centers on metal phosphosulfides. These mixes of metal, phosphorus, and sulfur can do many jobs. Yet they are hard to cook in a lab. Past work thus stuck to one mix at a time.

The team pairs AI tools with fast lab work. Smart search can cut the trial list down. Quick cooks then test the top picks in days. This loop could open a whole class of stuff. New such mixes may serve cells, chips, and light tools.
arxiv-2601-17093:
Olha Sirikova and Alvin Chan build a three-view frame to set neural nets side by side. Teams need such sets to check and trust their nets. Past gauges gave just one view of net kinship. Their 2026 preprint joins three views in a triangle frame. One view is the still shape of the net's codes.

The next view is how nets act, by calls and links. The third view is how nets hold up when trimmed. Trim tests cut weights and watch skill hold or fall. Three views give a fuller kin map than one. Such maps help pick nets for science work.
arxiv-2601-17293:
Minh-Tâm Quang Trinh and Nathan Williams compute special elements in Hecke algebras. For any finite reductive group, such elements arise from partial Springer resolutions. The team finds them via the Harish-Chandra transform. Partial resolutions come in two kinds. The larger kind holds the deeper story, and the authors treat it with care.

Hecke algebras encode deep symmetry in representation theory. Central elements act as anchors for whole blocks of that theory. Knowing them in closed form saves long case work. It also links geometry to algebra in a tight way. The result serves pure math, where such bridges guide new proofs. Noncrossing combinatorics enters as part of that bridge.
arxiv-2601-17793:
Robin Ming Chen, Yang Lan, Yue Liu, and Zhong Wang prove a stability result for a classic wave equation. Their 2026 preprint deals with the Camassa-Holm equation, used for shallow water waves. The equation admits smooth solitons, single waves that hold their shape as they travel. It also admits multi-solitons, groups of such waves that pass through each other. The team asks whether these waves are stable in the long run.

They show that solutions starting near a soliton settle toward one as time grows. The settling holds in the energy space, up to a shift in position. The same holds for multi-solitons. Stability proofs tell modelers which wave shapes can be trusted over long spans.
arxiv-2601-17893:
Sarmistha Sarna Gomasta, Mahmood Jasim, Hossein Hadisi, Yvonne Jansen, and Pierre Dragicevic test what music does to data videos. Their 2026 preprint reports a study that was registered before it ran. Data videos pair charts and facts with story and sound to reach wide audiences. Many of them use music, yet no one had pinned down what the music changes for viewers.

The team measures three effects: how well the video persuades, how much it engages, and how it makes viewers feel. Each effect matters to people who make such videos for news, health, or public campaigns. The results can guide when music helps a message land and when it may get in the way.
arxiv-2601-18293:
A team including Saverio Braccini tests a beam monitor that never touches the beam. Their 2026 preprint deals with low-energy medical cyclotrons. These machines make isotopes for medicine, and their beams are fragile. Even a thin device placed in the beam can spoil its quality. The team studies an external fiber monitor made of cerium-doped silica fibers that scintillate. The fibers catch secondary radiation thrown off at parts the beam already passes.

They test the monitor on the 18 MeV Bern Medical Cyclotron beam line. Reading stray radiation keeps the beam itself intact. Safer, cleaner beams mean more reliable isotope supply. The work serves hospitals that depend on those isotopes.
arxiv-2601-18493:
Sara Tehrani and four colleagues build a test set for AI tools that read maps of harm from space. When floods, fires, or quakes hit, fast reads of sky shots help crews choose where to go first. Past test sets ask for coarse tags, such as which block is hit. Real crews need more: what a site does, and what harm it took.

Their set, named DisasterInsight, asks tools to judge shots by use as well as by harm. It also checks if a tool stays firm when the ask is worded in new ways. A tool that fails on a fresh word may fail in the field. The set aims to grade tools by the needs of real aid work. That could push the field toward tools crews can trust in a crunch.
arxiv-2601-18593:
Felix Ballani studies a maths shape used to draw the grains in metals and rocks. The shape splits a space into cells, one per seed point, but its walls can curve. Curved walls fit real grains more than flat walls do. The shape can also grow or shrink each cell by a weight, to match grains of unlike size.

Ballani pulls its key traits into one place. He shows how the shape acts when the whole space is stretched or sheared. He also shows what its flat cuts look like. Last, he speeds up the way shots of the shape are drawn on a grid. Fast, true shots help staff test grain models on real scans. The work makes a prized shape less hard to use.
arxiv-2601-18793:
Michael Lee and three colleagues fix a flaw that pops up when code that makes code meets code that can pause and steer its own flow. The flaw is called scope escape: made code can name a thing that is out of reach where the code will run. Such code is broke at birth. The flaw can be stopped in two ways. A strict type check can bar it up front. Or a run check can catch it late.

Type checks for this case exist in maths but are hard to build and to use in real tools. Run checks are used in the field, yet their worth was not well mapped. The team set out the run check path in full, in a long form of their work. A clear map could help tool teams pick a guard that fits their needs.
arxiv-2601-18993:
Wei Cao and eight co-authors free a camera from the path it first took through a scene. Their method replays a moving scene, shot on one plain camera, from any new path a user picks. Wide turns are hard: one camera sees only a thin slice of a moving world, so most of the scene stays unseen.

The team rebuilds the scene in full 3D plus time, then renders the new view without any training. They call the method FreeOrbit4D. Filling the unseen parts in a sound way is the core trick, and it serves film, games, and replay tools.
arxiv-2601-19193:
Van-Quang Nguyen and Takayuki Okatani teach models to answer table questions with visible reasoning. Tables in images and documents hold much of the world's data. Yet models trained on past table sets give short factual answers with no steps shown. Brief answers hide how the model got there and often miss the mark.

Their method, CoReTab, drives reasoning through code, so each step can be checked as it runs. Code based steps turn a guess into a trace a user can audit. Better table skill matters for finance, science, and any office work where numbers live in grids.
arxiv-2601-19593:
Estèphe Arnaud, Mohamed Daoudi, and Pierre Guerreschi work on planning botulinum toxin injections. These injections are the standard treatment for facial asymmetry and a common tool for facial rejuvenation. Choosing the right dose for each spot, though, still rests mostly on the clinician's intuition. Wrong doses lead to weak or uneven results.

The authors propose a framework that simulates the effect of an injection before it happens. Their method edits a learned latent model of the face in a localised way. By tying the edit size to dose, the system models dose-response: how the face changes as dose changes. Doctors could test a plan on the model first. That promises more predictable outcomes and fewer corrective visits.
arxiv-2601-20093:
Xuanyu Long and Feng Liu ask whether flat-band materials can carry a steady current. Flat bands are energy bands that barely vary, giving electrons unusual quantum geometric properties. Singular flat bands touch another band at a point, which makes their geometry especially rich. The authors study how such bands respond to a steady, uniform electric field.

They build a minimal two-band lattice model. Away from the touching point, the flat band's spectrum in the field is captured by an intraband Berry phase. The question is whether Landau-Zener tunneling between bands enables single-particle direct current. Flat-band systems are candidates for novel electronics and superconductors. Knowing if they conduct under a field is a basic, necessary fact.
arxiv-2601-20293:
Marian Douspis tests the standard picture of the expanding universe without assuming any dark energy model. The test concerns the FLRW metric, which assumes the universe is uniform at large scales, and whether space is flat or curved. He uses the latest data release from the DESI survey to run the check.

Distances come from two supernova collections, Pantheon+ and DESY5. An iterative smoothing method rebuilds the distance modulus, the comoving distance, and the Hubble parameter from the data. A model-free test of this kind can show whether the standard metric itself is failing, before new physics is invoked.
arxiv-2601-20493:
Joan Domingo-Pasarin and Xavier Ros-Oton study the regularity of free boundaries for weak solutions of generalized Alt-Caffarelli type problems. Their work is motivated by the Serrin problem, a classic question about overdetermined boundary conditions. In the problems studied, a solution satisfies one condition inside the domain and an extra gradient condition on its boundary.

Free boundaries, where the solution's regime changes, are where the geometry gets subtle. Lipschitz regularity of that boundary is a key step toward smoother conclusions. Such results feed into shape optimization and the theory of equilibria in physics. The point sounds dry, but it is not: the shape of that edge is where a proof lives or dies.
arxiv-2601-20593:
Chetan Balwe and Nidhi Gupta study the connected components of affine quadrics in A1-homotopy theory. For any smooth quadratic hypersurface over a field, they use iterations of the naive connected-components functor. Their goal is the field-valued sections of the sheaf of A1-connected components of the hypersurface.

A1-homotopy theory imports the ideas of topology into algebraic geometry, where paths are replaced by algebraic curves. Connected components in this sense are far subtler than in ordinary topology. Quadrics are a test case where explicit answers can anchor the general theory. The proofs lean on a tool kit that few fields share, and that is part of their worth.
arxiv-2601-21093:
Zhou Fan and Leda Wang study how a common training method behaves when data has far more features than old theory assumed. They follow repeated passes of mini-batch gradient descent on models built from a few hidden directions. Sample size and feature count grow together in their setup.

The authors give an exact long-run picture of the learning path. It holds for a wide range of small batch sizes and a matched learning rate. The results show which hidden directions the method learns first and how fast. That helps explain why repeated passes over data help some tasks and hurt others.
arxiv-2601-21193:
Zecheng Zhao and four co-authors speed up how platforms find the right video for a text query. Their 2026 paper studies text-to-video retrieval. It is a core service in video platforms. Dense retrieval with dual encoders leads in accuracy. Its compute and storage scale poorly with corpus size, though. Real-time systems at scale use two stages. A fast recall model gathers a small pool of candidates. A dense retriever then reranks that pool.

The authors pair generative recall with dense reranking. Their twist is learning multi-view semantic IDs for fast retrieval. Each video gets compact codes a generative model can predict from text. Good IDs make stage one both fast and accurate. The work targets the scale where brute-force search dies.
arxiv-2601-21393:
Abhijith S Parackal, Florian Trybel, Felix Andreas Faber, and Rickard Armiento run a giant screen for new crystal materials. Computer surveys can map which crystals are likely to be stable. The team lists all two- and three-element mixes up to a set cell size, which yields a vast pool of candidate structures.

Each candidate gets a fast energy check to weed out hopeless cases. Screening at this scale turns materials hunting into a numbers game with real odds. The survivors form a short list for deeper study and lab work. Such maps can speed the search for better batteries, chips, and catalysts.
arxiv-2601-21693:
Liang Li, Yu Wang, Jin-Jun Geng, Yong-Feng Huang, and Rong-Gen Cai dissect long gamma-ray bursts pulse by pulse. The team studies bursts caught by the Swift satellite that show a clear early pulse before the main event. Each precursor and main burst is measured on its own.

They compare duration, spectral hardness, fastest flicker, and spectral lag between the two parts. Both parts broadly match the class of bursts tied to collapsing massive stars. Whether the early pulse is a true warning or a separate act matters for burst physics. Pulse-level detail helps theorists test what the central engine does before it fully wakes.
arxiv-2601-21993:
Dhiogo José Correa de Sá, Carlos Pereira Lopes Filho. And Carlos Eduardo Schmiedel argue that software interfaces are too rigid for the age of autonomous agents. Agents reason in adaptive, probabilistic, context-dependent ways. System integration, by contrast, still rests on static interfaces and fixed contracts between programs.

Their 2026 preprint introduces Liquid Interfaces, a coordination paradigm where an interface is not a lasting technical artifact. Instead, interfaces are treated as temporary, formed for the interaction at hand. The idea reframes integration as negotiation rather than plumbing. If it works, systems of agents could connect, cooperate, and part without the brittle hand-built adapters that make today's integrations so costly to maintain.
arxiv-2601-22093:
Fethiye Irmak Dogan and co-authors study bias that passes between models. Social bias in generative systems is usually measured as unequal performance across groups. The authors focus on a subtler form: associational bias, where models learn stereotyped links between concepts and demographic groups even when no group is named.

A model can link doctors with men without ever being told a doctor's gender. Their 2026 preprint investigates how such associations behave when generative models communicate with each other. If bias can amplify as models talk, then multi-agent systems and model-generated training data could quietly entrench stereotypes. Tracing that spread is a step toward interrupting it.
arxiv-2601-22193:
Cyriac Antony, Alessio Martino, and Blerina Sinaimeri study a hard puzzle from the study of how species evolve. Their 2026 preprint looks at ways to map a parasite family tree onto a host family tree. Events such as shared splits, copies, host jumps, and losses link the two trees.

The hard part is to find the best map when time facts are not full. The team focus on maps where host jumps stay within a fixed short range. They probe the shape and cost of such maps. Their results guide those who build tools for this task.
arxiv-2601-22393:
Amirhossein Akbar Tabatabai and Raheleh Jalali probe the proof strength of linear logics. Proof complexity asks how long a proof must be. Their 2026 preprint notes that lower bounds for the classic sequent calculus remain a major open problem. They shed new light by isolating the power of structural rules.

They show that the rules, combined, are vastly stronger than any one alone. They prove exponential gaps that make the point sharp. The work helps map what makes proofs blow up. That map guides logic, verification, and automated proof. It is a firm step on a hard road.
arxiv-2601-22593:
Zahra Moslemi, Ziyi Liang, Norbert Fortin, and Babak Shahbaba built a transformer that learns across many kinds of graphs at once. Real graph sets differ in shape, scale, and meaning, with no shared node names. Their 2026 preprint presents the Multi-Graph Meta-Transformer for that messy case.

The frame aims to pull joint signals while keeping each graph's sense clear, so results stay interpretable. Brains, molecules, and social nets could all feed one such learner. The work is a bid for a general graph engine. It values clear reasons as much as raw scores. That breadth is the point of the design.
arxiv-2601-22693:
Jiahao Wu, Yunfei Liu, Lijian Lin, and Ye Zhu built PEAR, a tool that rebuilds a full 3D human mesh from one photo, pixel true. Such meshes drive avatars, film, and motion tools. Their 2026 preprint notes that past tools are slow, coarse in pose, and slip at the face and hands.

PEAR aligns the mesh to the image pixel by pixel, with fine detail where it counts. Expressive, well-fit meshes from a single shot would ease many crafts. The work targets the gap between a photo and a true double. Speed and fit are the tests.
arxiv-2601-22793:
A team of imaging researchers introduces a much faster way to recover phase data at busy beamline labs. Phase retrieval turns measured light patterns into images of a sample. Their method, called fast Eikonal Phase Retrieval, runs more than a hundred times faster while keeping accuracy under control.

The method grows from a math expansion based on how far light travels. A wave-optics fix and a fast filter step keep the results sharp. Speed matters at shared beamlines, where many teams queue for short slots of beam time. The scheme is built for high-throughput beamlines, where fast scans and many users demand results in minutes, not hours of computing.
arxiv-2601-22993:
Rohan Tangri and Jan-Peter Calliess design a learning method that respects a hard limit on risk. Their algorithm, VaR-CPO, optimizes a Value-at-Risk constraint directly, rather than hoping average rewards stay safe. It is built to be sample-efficient and conservative while an agent learns.

In their tests on feasible settings, the method explored safely with no constraint breaches during training. Rival methods failed to match that record. Safe learning matters where a single bad action, in finance or control, is too costly to allow. Zero violations during training is the headline property, a standard that baseline methods in the study failed to uphold.
arxiv-2602-00293: Rubio Gunawan constructs a smooth circle covering map with a physical measure on a hyperbolic repelling fixed point. Relaxing smoothness at just one point, the author also builds an example whose physical measure basin has full measure. One key technical step, a realization method of independent interest, stands out. It gives a canonical construction of a full branch map from its induced map, linking smooth dynamics to measure theory.
arxiv-2602-00593: Yifan Jiang and colleagues introduce Pix2Fact, a visual question-answering benchmark testing expert perception plus knowledge search, areas existing benchmarks judge alone. Its 1,000 4K images span eight scenarios, with questions crafted by PhD-holding annotators across disciplines, each demanding visual grounding and external knowledge. Testing ten state-of-the-art vision-language models, the best reaches only 51.7% accuracy even with visual ground truth and search tools. Failures trace to grounding errors, shallow search use, and trouble retrieving long-tail, unstructured local information, exposing limits in real visual comprehension.
arxiv-2602-00693: Marco Nurisso and colleagues examine the space of feed-forward ReLU networks, asking whether it is connected and where its singularities lie. After initialisation, training under gradient flow restricts the space to an algebraic variety arising from the homogeneous nature of ReLU activation. The study extends earlier results on general directed acyclic graph architectures, mapping connectedness through bottleneck nodes and balance conditions for specific subsets. It shows singularities are closely tied to the topology of the underlying graph and its induced sub-networks. Simple numerical experiments validate the theory.
arxiv-2602-01193: Shashini Nilukshi and Deshan Sumanathilaka survey visual word-sense picking, where pictures help pin down what a vague word means. Old word-sense work leans on text alone, while the visual form uses picture cues to fix sense with scant text. The survey tracks growth from early fusion plans through graph and contrast plans to CLIP tunes, diffusion picture-making, and language-model aid, over studies from 2016 to 2025. CLIP tunes and language-aided plans beat zero-shot baselines, yet context gaps, common-sense bias, and thin multi-tongue data persist.
arxiv-2602-01293: Hui Chen and co-authors fix antenna beam maps for sense-and-talk nets, where shape slips and hardware flaws blur angle reads. They grade calibration by angle miss, not by beam shape match, and fold that grade into a trainable loss. A team plan lets many user devices tune beams from local data in rounds, pooling updates into shared calibration knobs. Real chamber beam reads back the plan, slashing angle miss in both flat and full 3D calibration cases.
arxiv-2602-01393: Marco Benedetti and co-authors tweak the pseudo-inverse rule for Hopfield-style nets so it infers archetypal concepts from few examples. The new rule corrects for population-level example correlations rather than one training set's, cutting overfitting and aiding generalization. Mean-field replica theory ties generalization to many thermodynamic states beside standard Hopfield states. Those states appear and vanish via smooth shifts or sharp jumps, with far stronger replica symmetry breaking than the standard model. Simulations match the theory, deepening insight into memory storage and generalization in attractor nets.
arxiv-2602-01693: Kewei Hu and colleagues give agents explicit world state reasoning, instead of burying task structure inside high dimensional latent representations. Their Grounded Scene graph Reasoning approach models world evolution as transitions over grounded scene graphs. It reasons stepwise over states and spatial relations rather than mapping perception to actions. That reasoning covers action preconditions, consequences and goals in a space. Training uses a dataset supervising understanding, action planning and goal interpretation. Tests across RLBench, LIBERO, a GSR benchmark and robots show better zero shot generalization and long completion than baselines.
arxiv-2602-01893: Timur Mudarisov and colleagues view multi head attention in language models through a top-N selection lens, studying conduct in value state space. They define Precision, Recall and F-score metrics for token selection, and derive bounds from dimension and margin under assumptions. Stable value norms with a sink token, exponential similarity decay, and attention weight profiles predict a small-N regime of strongest separability. Across three models results track envelopes, selection sharpens separability, sink similarity tracks Recall, and LLaMA-2-7B heads split into Retriever, Mixer and Reset regimes.
arxiv-2602-02393:
Ruiqi Wu and 10 co-authors build an interactive world model that stays coherent for more than a thousand frames, in a 2026 arXiv paper. A world model generates video that responds to a user's actions, like a playable simulated place. Real-world training video is messy: camera poses are noisy and viewpoints rarely repeat, so long-term memory is hard to learn.

Their system, Infinite-World, compresses past frames into a fixed-size memory without needing pose estimates. A second module turns continuous motion into a three-state action label, shielding training from noisy trajectories. A short fine-tuning set, only thirty minutes of video chosen to revisit places often, activates long-range loop closure. Tests and user studies report better visual quality, action control, and spatial consistency than rivals.
arxiv-2602-02593:
Jiaxuan Zou and 4 co-authors unify the neural scaling laws that predict how model performance improves with size, data, and compute, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Existing explanations lean on specific architectures or heavy kernel machinery and lack intuitive reach. The new system views learning as progressively covering patterns drawn from a long-tailed Zipfian distribution.

A threshold called the effective frontier separates learned patterns from the unlearned tail. The authors prove that reducible loss is asymptotically set by the probability mass beyond that frontier. Precise scaling laws then follow for model size, data set size, and compute, traced to capacity, coverage, and tuning bottlenecks respectively. A max-bottleneck principle unifies them: the famous Kaplan and Chinchilla laws are not rivals but equilibrium solutions of one constrained problem under different active bottlenecks.
arxiv-2602-02693:
David L. Nidever and 16 co-authors present a 2026 overview of the Magellanic Genesis survey, a Sloan Digital Sky Survey-V program mapping the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds spectroscopically. The survey targets the kinematic and chemical structure of our two largest satellite galaxies using two instruments with complementary strengths.

In the Clouds' inner regions, high-resolution near-infrared spectra cover about fourteen thousand bright oxygen-rich giant stars with contiguous spatial coverage. Optical spectroscopy of fainter red giants, selected with Gaia data, reaches the diffuse outer structures that stretch twenty degrees across the sky. Inner-region optical data add elements the infrared cannot see and cross-calibrate the instruments. Roughly three hundred evolved massive stars and a small set of symbiotic binaries round out the sample. The overview describes design, target selection, and science goals, with first results previewed.
arxiv-2602-02893:
Ziming Liu and 3 co-authors estimate signal directions over a full circle in a 2026 paper. Their setting uses STAR-RIS, a surface that both transmits and reflects radio signals. Such surfaces could support sensing and communication together in future wireless networks, using only one sensing chain.

The authors show the received signal has a structure that turns direction finding into a low-rank recovery problem. No fixed angle grid is needed. Their algorithm alternates projections and gradient steps to recover angles robustly. Two surface designs are handled, each with its own lifting method. A theoretical error bound benchmarks performance. Simulations beat grid-based methods, reaching sub-degree accuracy near the surface's forward direction.
arxiv-2602-03293:
Anomalies reveal themselves by how far they drift toward density, offers Pritam Kar, with 3 co-authors, in a fully unsupervised finding system. Earlier detectors excel only under given structural assumptions and degrade under noise, so results varies sharply across anomaly types. Their Mean Shift Density Enhancement instead watches each sample's geometric response as a density-driven process iteratively pulls points toward nearby modes on the data manifold over many steps.

Normal samples, well supported by local density, stay comparatively stable. Anomalous samples undergo large cumulative displacements. A weighted mean-shift procedure with changing, sample-given weights from a fuzzy neighborhood graph operationalizes the idea. Review spans dozens of real tabular datasets, several anomaly output mechanisms, and multiple noise levels. Against many established earlier methods, displacement-based scoring stayed consistently strong and balanced.
arxiv-2602-03493:
Fine-tuning a large model with LoRA raises a trade-off: adapt well to the new task, or forget less of the old knowledge. Alessio Quercia and 3 co-authors analyze that balance in a 2026 paper through the lens of principal components of the weight matrices. Existing methods initialize adaptation from the first components or the last, with inconsistent advice.

Their analysis finds that the intermediate components hit the sweet spot. Tuning them balances task gains against forgetting and tolerates higher learning rates better than the extremes. The authors turn the finding into practical initialization guidelines for LoRA-style methods. A broad empirical study across vision and language tasks confirms higher accuracy with reduced forgetting.
arxiv-2602-03593:
Do AI coding assistants actually make developers more productive, and how would anyone know? Valerie Chen and 4 co-authors study that measurement problem inside BNY Mellon in a 2026 paper. They combine a survey drawing nearly 3,000 developer responses with 11 in-depth interviews, a mixed-method design.

Survey answers conflict with each other about whether the tools help. The interviews explain why, surfacing six distinct factors that span short-term output and long-term dimensions. Unlike earlier frameworks, theirs stresses slow-moving measures like technical expertise and ownership of work. The authors argue that industry needs a multifaceted, human-centered scorecard rather than commit counts. They hope the work steers future research the same way.
arxiv-2602-03993:
Nikita Arskyi and 1 co-author settle an algebraic question about symmetries of Clifford algebras. Clifford algebras package quadratic forms into algebraic forms used across geometry and physics. Any orthogonal transformation of the underlying space extends to a Bogolyubov automorphism of the algebra. Their 2026 paper asks when such an automorphism is inner, meaning generated from inside the algebra itself.

Working over an infinite-dimensional vector space, they derive exact conditions. The answer matters because inner and outer automorphisms behave in very unlike ways in representation theory and quantum field theory. The result completes a natural sorting question for these transformation groups.
arxiv-2602-04093:
Interpretable models need concept labels that no single hospital owns enough of. Dario Fenoglio and 8 co-authors merge concept-based models with federated learning in a 2026 paper. Concept-based models predict through human-understandable concepts, but annotating concepts is expensive and scattered across institutions.

Their Federated Concept-based Models aggregate concept information across sites without moving raw data. The architecture adapts as the shared concept set evolves, a mismatch ordinary federated learning cannot handle. Experiments kept accuracy and intervention quality comparable to centralized training. The approach suits medicine, where interpretability is mandatory and data cannot travel.
arxiv-2602-04393:
Craft tools should learn from materials, not flatten them into inputs. Ritik Batra and 6 co-authors interviewed expert woodworkers, fiber artists, and metalworkers about computer-aided making tools in a 2026 study. Mainstream tools treat materials as passive, which puts off communities built on reciprocal relationships with their materials.

The authors name three orders of convivial relations: between individuals, tools, and materials; between communities and platforms; and between institutions and ecologies. Craftspeople work across all three, struggling where tools abstract them away. Design principles follow for tools that support autonomy and material learning, aiming at creative uptake rather than mere speed.
arxiv-2602-04593:
Nitesh Jaiswal and S. Shankaranarayanan model Hawking radiation, the faint emission predicted from black holes, inside a chain of quantum spins in a 2026 paper. A sudden quench, meaning an abrupt change, triggers a transition that mimics gravitational collapse and forms an analogue horizon.

Mapping the chain to a Dirac fermion in curved spacetime, the authors study the radiation two ways. Localized wave packets acting as detectors found a spectrum close to thermal but with frequency-dependent distortions. Its statistics signaled lost information about formation. A coupled qubit sensor worked as a faithful temperature probe only when weakly coupled. Strong coupling made it thermalize with the whole environment instead. The protocol helps separate real analogue radiation from noise.
arxiv-2602-04993:
Krzysztof Frączek and Łukasz Kotlewski wrote this 2026 mathematics paper on interval exchange transformations, systems that cut an interval into pieces and rearrange them. A central question is how smooth the change of coordinates is that links such a system to a generalized version of itself, and to the inverse map.

Intuition says the map and its inverse should lose smoothness together. The authors show the opposite can happen. For self-similar systems of a certain hyperbolic type, along a natural family of deformations taken to a freezing limit, the conjugacy grows arbitrarily rough while its inverse stays uniformly Hölder continuous. Their tools come from thermodynamic formalism and renormalization. They also obtain sharp estimates for the dimensions of invariant measures and for the best possible Hölder exponents on both sides.
arxiv-2602-05093:
Virtual reality is often used to calm people down, yet most calming apps speak only to the eyes and ears. He Zhang and 3 co-authors add touch in this 2026 human-computer interaction paper, conditionally accepted at CHI 2026. Their system, VR Calm Plus, pairs an immersive virtual scene with a pressure-sensitive plush toy that users squeeze.

Squeezing changes the virtual atmosphere in real time, giving users a physical way to steer their own relaxation. In a study with 40 participants, the squeeze version beat a visual-only baseline on positive mood and perceived relaxation. Body measurements told a subtler story: heart rate fell further while autonomic flexibility held up, a pattern the authors call active relaxation, with emotional engagement sustained. The paper offers design lessons for VR mental health tools that engage the body.
arxiv-2602-05293:
Turning a single photo into a 3D scene is now possible with SAM3D, but the rebuild is slow. Weilun Feng and 12 co-authors present Fast-SAM3D in this 2026 computer vision paper, accepted at ICML 2026. Their first step was diagnosis: a systematic study of where the inference time goes, which showed generic acceleration tricks fail because the pipeline is heterogeneous at several levels.

Shape and layout evolve differently, texture refinement is intrinsically sparse, and geometries vary spectrally. The scheme answers each trait with its own mechanism. Caching splits structural updates from delicate layout updates, token carving that concentrates refinement on high-entropy regions, and token aggregation that adapts decoding resolution to the spectrum. The result is up to about 2.67 times faster end-to-end generation with negligible fidelity loss, a new speed-quality frontier for single-view 3D generation. Code is public.
arxiv-2602-05693:
In federated learning, many parties train one shared model without pooling their data, and each party role in the result matters for pay and trust. Arno Geimer, Beltran Fiz Pontiveros, and Radu State note that estimates of each party contribution swing wildly depending on the aggregation strategy used. That instability can scare off participants and hide free riders or malicious actors.

Their method, FedRandom, treats contribution estimation as a statistical problem and generates extra samples beyond what standard strategies give. More samples yield contribution values that are more consistent and reliable across runs. Tests across four image data sets, including CIFAR and MNIST variants, and across different data distributions support the claim. The authors show the approach reduces the instability that earlier work documented. The paper targets industry federations with few, data rich members. Fairer credit, they argue, is a condition for keeping such federations alive.
arxiv-2602-05993:
Flow and diffusion models make fine samples, but steering them toward a user's taste after training is slow and fragile. Peter Holderrieth and nine co-authors argue that easy steering should be built into the model, not bolted on later. Their answer is Diamond Maps, stochastic flow-map models that line up with any reward at run time, with no retraining.

The trick is to fold many simulation steps into a one-step sampler while keeping the randomness that good alignment needs. That keeps search, sequential Monte Carlo, and guidance cheap, since the value function can be estimated cleanly. The maps learn well by distillation from GLASS Flows, align more strongly than current methods, and scale better as effort grows. The work points to generative models that bend to new tastes on demand.
arxiv-2602-06193:
Turning a biased coin into a fairer one, using only the coin itself, is the classic Bernoulli factory problem. Tanay Roy demonstrates a quantum version in the lab. Two identical quantum coins, called quoins, are measured together in the Bell basis on IBM superconducting hardware.

From those measurement outcomes alone, with no outside randomness, the setup produced a doubling function that no classical factory can build. The same statistics also yielded an exactly fair coin and another classically impossible function. Measured biases were compared against ideal predictions, and device noise effects were discussed. The result offers a simple building block for quantum-enhanced random sampling.
arxiv-2602-06293:
Two measures of how fast the universe expands disagree, a clash called the Hubble tension. Prakhar Bansal and Dragan Huterer test whether tweaking only the recent expansion history can fix the clash. They check simple late-time models against local distance measurements, galaxy spacing data, and supernova distances.

A good fit, they show, demands one of two drastic moves. Either supernova brightness jumps sharply at very low distance, or a basic relation between two kinds of cosmic distance breaks. Both moves work by cutting the local measurements loose from the rest. A gentler change at a somewhat larger distance helps only modestly. Adding another distance method leaves the verdict intact.
arxiv-2602-06493:
Reasoning models that search at run time lean on reward models to score partial paths, but those scores turn unreliable off the training distribution. Zeen Song and 4 co-authors analyze that uncertainty problem and propose Uncertainty-Aware Tree Search. Standard search, they prove, piles up regret linearly when scores mislead, while uncertainty-aware search can keep regret sublinear.

Their method estimates scoring uncertainty with Monte Carlo dropout, which samples the reward model with random units dropped. A reinforcement learning controller then shifts compute toward paths where the score can be trusted and away from dubious ones. Experiments showed the approach reduced the harm of out-of-distribution scoring errors across reasoning tasks.
arxiv-2602-06693:
Robert Ganian, Fionn Mc Inerney, and Dimitra Tsigkari study split learning, where small internet-connected devices hand part of their model training to stronger helper machines. The scheduling problem is to assign clients to helpers and order the work so total training time, the makespan, is as small as possible. Helpers can only hold a limited number of clients in memory.

For the uniform-task version, the authors rule out exact fast algorithms and even approximation schemes, yet still design a polynomial-time method guaranteed to land within a factor of five of optimal. For the harder version with varied memory costs, they prove no good approximation can exist in general, but adapt their method into a heuristic that beat earlier ones in extensive experiments. The work pairs hard theoretical limits with a practical scheduling tool.
arxiv-2602-06793:
Anastasia Shlentsova and nine co-authors examine the X-ray glow of the most luminous quasars known that also drive strong outflows. Winds from active galaxies are usually linked to weak coronal X-ray emission, which is thought to let radiation push the gas outward. To test that link without selection bias, the team studied ten extremely luminous, radio-quiet quasars chosen for their ultraviolet brightness and fast blueshifted emission lines.

Seven of the ten turned out to have fairly normal, steep X-ray spectra, and only two of the fastest-outflow objects were X-ray weak, a rate similar to ordinary quasars. One apparent weak case is probably just a normal quasar hidden behind heavy obscuration. The team finds only a tentative hint that truly weak X-rays pair with the fastest winds, above 3,000 kilometers per second, and calls for larger samples to settle the question.
arxiv-2602-06893:
Mohammad Bakhsh, Victor Trinquet, Rogério Almeida Gouvêa, Gian-Marco Rignanese, and Samuel Poncé hunt for stable forms of a lead-free solar material, the double perovskite Cs2KInI6. Its cubic form has a direct band gap near 1.94 electron volts, well suited to solar cells, but first-principles calculations show that cubic phase is dynamically unstable. The team combined genetic algorithms with machine-learned potentials to search for stable structures.

The search found 42 dynamically stable structures, and first-principles checks confirmed 11 of them. The most stable phase has Cmc21 symmetry with 20 atoms per cell, though it lacks octahedral cation coordination. The most stable perovskite-like form has a different symmetry with 10 atoms per cell and low octahedral connectivity. Distortions generally widen the gap, turn it indirect, and flatten the band edges, a trade-off the paper maps for future material design.
arxiv-2602-06993:
Shashank offers a new part to swap in for the dense feed-forward layers of transformers. Dense layers spend the same compute on each token. They also spread capacity evenly, though language contexts cluster in tight groups. And when a model keeps learning, a small update touches shared weights and disturbs old skills.

His design, Attractor Patch Networks, keeps a bank of patch experts. A router that matches by similarity picks a few patches for each token, using learned prototypes. Each picked patch sends out a low-rank residual update tied to a compact code. In tests on character-level text, scores nearly matched a dense baseline. Yet old-domain retention was over two and a half times better, and new-domain adaptation nearly three times better, than global fine-tuning.
arxiv-2602-07193:
Millions of people form emotional bonds with AI companions, and when a model changes, a safety update lands, or a platform shuts down, those bonds end without closure.  Rachel Poonsiriwong and two co-authors study that loss through companion communities, finding grief comparable to human loss.

How users explain the ending shapes the pain: strong anthropomorphism tracks with intense grief. Endings seen as reversible trap users in cycles of trying to fix things, and endings users choose themselves bring more closure.  The paper turns grief psychology and self-determination theory into four design principles for psychologically safer endings.  It is essential reading for platforms that will increasingly have to end these relationships.
arxiv-2602-07593:
Benchmarks that rank models across accuracy, robustness, and efficiency often produce incoherent or unstable rankings when the model set changes. Polina Gordienko and three co-authors formalize multi-criteria benchmarking as a vote problem: each metric ranks models, and an operator aggregates the votes.

Rather than stopping at Arrow's impossibility result, they name sufficient settings under which it fades. On single-peaked, group-separable, and distance-restricted preference combinations, it supports well-behaved pooling. Evaluation teams get a constructive answer to a foundational worry, with settings under which multi-metric rankings can be trusted. The checks cover several modern suites, including HELM and MMLU.
arxiv-2602-07693:
Abelian covers of the projective line branched at three points reduce modulo primes to curves whose Newton polygons and Ekedahl-Oort types encode deep arithmetic.  Darren Schmidt studies those reductions and the density of primes giving supersingular and superspecial curves.

Supersingular and superspecial cases appear much more often than expected, and unlikely Newton polygons and Ekedahl-Oort types in the moduli space of curves turn up frequently.  A final theorem supports Oort's claim on Newton polygons in certain cases and constructs new supersingular curves.  Arithmetic geometers get density results and constructions that sharpen understanding of a classic moduli problem.
arxiv-2602-07893:
App logs help developers debug, but they can also leak private information, and no comprehensive picture of Android log leaks existed. Zhiyuan Chen and six co-authors build a large dataset of Android app logs and study the problem from three angles: developers' concerns, the leaks themselves, and the traits of logs that leak.

They identify five categories of developer concern about log privacy and analyze the severity and causes of leaks in real logs. The findings give platform designers, app developers, and privacy auditors concrete evidence about where sensitive data slips into logs and why. Anyone shipping Android apps should read it as a checklist for what never to log.
arxiv-2602-07993:
Instruction-based image editing handles simple commands well but falters on complex, compositional instructions and often damages the background. Xuehai Bai and five co-authors propose MCIE-E1, a multimodal language-model-driven editor with two attention modules: one aligns instructions to spatial regions during denoising, the other preserves features in unedited areas.

A dedicated data pipeline supports training, and new evaluation protocols target the failures of earlier methods. The design tackles the two central weaknesses head-on, instruction compliance and background consistency, rather than scaling up a single mechanism. Image-editing researchers and product teams gain a system aimed at the messy, multi-part edits real users actually request.
arxiv-2602-08293:
Speech recognition from audio alone degrades in noise, and lip movements can rescue it, but fusion must let audio reach visual cues without drowning clean-speech performance. Seaone Ok and four co-authors propose CoBRA, a cross-modal bottleneck framework that routes exchange through a compact set of learnable tokens.

Regulating information flow through the bottleneck lets the audio stream reliably access essential visual cues even when noise is adverse or out of domain. Despite limited training data, the model beats comparable baselines and rivals large-scale systems, with ablations showing fusion depth matters most. Audio-visual speech researchers gain an efficient, noise-adaptive fusion design that works where data are scarce and conditions are harsh.
arxiv-2602-08493: Piecewise fractional linear maps with three or more branches are well studied, and for many such maps the invariant density can be written exactly. Fritz Schweiger notes that the two-branch linear case resists that treatment: no explicit form is known. His arXiv paper offers a partial solution for maps where just two branches are linear, narrowing a stubborn gap in the theory of these dynamical systems.
arxiv-2602-08593:
Smallholder farmers often have sensors and weather data but no easy way to turn them into decisions. Muhammad Saad Ali and six co-authors present Kissan-Dost, a multilingual conversational system that delivers plain-language farm guidance over WhatsApp text or voice. It pairs off-the-shelf soil and climate sensors with a retrieval-based language system, guarded by grounding and traceability checks.

In a ninety-day, two-site pilot with five participants, dashboard use faded while chatbot use stayed near-daily and drove concrete actions. Controlled tests on ninety-nine sensor-grounded crop questions topped ninety percent correctness with subsecond latency. Readers learn that careful last-mile design, not new hardware, unlocks the value already sitting in farm sensors.
arxiv-2602-08693:
Do language models decide under uncertainty the way humans do, and does step-by-step reasoning change that? Gonçalo Guiomar and six co-authors test humans and many models on an active probabilistic reasoning task that separates gathering evidence from integrating it. Their arXiv paper finds that extended reasoning is the key driver of strong performance.

Longer reasoning yields large gains in inference and belief trajectories strikingly like humans', while improving active sampling only modestly. A mechanistic model with four interpretable factors, memory, strategy, choice bias, and occlusion awareness, places humans and models in a shared cognitive space. Readers learn that reasoning aligns models with humans in inference, while a gap in information gathering persists.
arxiv-2602-08793:
Column type annotation assigns types to table columns, powering data integration and search over data lakes. Yushi Sun and five co-authors tackle cross-lake adaptation, where annotators trained on one lake degrade on a new lake with different tables and type sets. Their arXiv paper recasts adaptation as knowledge management, splitting source knowledge into parts to discard, realign, or acquire.

LakeHopper works under an annotation budget. It realigns label sets, uses a language model to verify gaps, and spreads labels by cluster. Rehearsal tuning turns each flagged column into a labeling batch while keeping shared knowledge intact. Casting the language model as verifier rather than annotator keeps outputs inside the target type set, avoiding hallucinated types. Across three lake transfers, the method lifts backbones by up to 71.4 percent relative macro-F1, nearing full-data quality with under six percent of target labels. Readers get a fast adaptation recipe.
arxiv-2602-08893:
Can an AI helper inside a game teach quantum ideas without overloading the learner? Caroline Wermann and ten co-authors test three kinds of help in Qookies, a serious game about quantum technology. The three kinds are: no help, chat-only help from an AI character, and combined chat plus visual demos of the next step. A total of 152 school pupils, students, and members of the public took part.

All three groups learned a significant amount, confirming the game itself works. Learning scores did not differ between help styles, but mental effort was lower when players got both chat and visual help rather than chat alone. Players mostly asked the AI about level goals and actions, suggesting demos give the most accessible support.
arxiv-2602-08993:
Password-authenticated key exchange promises login without a public-key infrastructure, but Eloise Christian and three co-authors expose a hole on the other side of the handshake. In reverse online guessing, an attacker impersonates the server and tests password guesses against clients. The logic mirrors classic client-impersonation guessing, yet defenses built for that direction do not transfer, since detection now falls on clients.

The attack bites hardest against indiscriminate targets, as in phishing or password spraying, and against automated logins or shared passwords, including WPA3-SAE. The authors urge stakeholders to authenticate servers by stronger means by default, keeping password-only operation as a last resort against catastrophic failure of other mechanisms.
arxiv-2602-09293:
Emeric Roulley sets local and global split findings for moving repeat answers of the one-dimensional two-species Vlasov-Poisson equation. The answers form strip-like zones of ions and electrons in phase space which move as one, rising from even, speed-tied balance layers. Based on balance shape and Fourier mode, the split chart shows two or four arms.

In all cases the split is of pitchfork type, with curved local shape in mirror setups, and locally built arms stretch world-wide. The work stretches the author's earlier purely electron case, where ions formed a still balancing backdrop; letting both species change over time calls for a more tangled, higher-way study. A straight change of factors also links the model to the two-part Euler-Poisson system, yielding moving waves there too.
arxiv-2602-09393:
Quantum logic with linear optics appeals because the elements are comparatively easy to handle, yet controlled gates have often demanded extra photons or measurement tricks. Gui-Long Jiang and three co-authors present deterministic schemes for controlled-NOT and controlled-swap gates using linear optics alone. Control qubits ride on photon polarization, while target qudits ride on spatial modes, a hybrid encoding that keeps the construction lean.

No borrowed ancillary photons and no measurement-induced nonlinearities are needed. A controlled-NOT gate takes a single polarization beam splitter, a generalized controlled-swap gate takes one per spatial level, and every scheme holds optical depth at one regardless of dimension. The three-qubit controlled-swap gate also holds very high fidelity under realistic conditions, beating earlier schemes. The paper offers a compact route to high-dimensional photonic logic.
arxiv-2602-09893:
For a robot, touch is a working sense, not a luxury. It lets a machine judge grip, texture, and slip while it handles an object. But touch sensors produce varied, fast-changing signals, and sending them in real time strains limited links. A 2026 paper led by Zhengxue Cheng, with four co-authors, takes up that gap. It presents TaCo, a test bed for methods that shrink tactile data, with or without loss.

The team tests thirty existing and learned methods on five sets of readings from different sensor types. It scores them on four jobs: storing data without loss, showing it for people, sorting materials and objects, and guiding a dextrous grasp. Two new codecs trained on touch data, TaCo-LL and TaCo-L, come out ahead. The result gives robot builders a clear way to weigh size against task success.
arxiv-2602-09993:
The supernova remnant known as Veliki, in the Large Magellanic Cloud, wears a puzzling shape in multi-wavelength images. A 2026 paper by Noam Soker reads that shape as point-symmetric, shaped by at least three pairs of energetic jets in the jittering jets explosion mechanism. Two pairs of ear-like lobes, north and south blowouts, and a pair of dents make up the pattern.

Because symmetry axes pair opposite features inside the ejecta, Soker argues jets, not ambient material, did the shaping. On his reading, the rival neutrino-driven mechanism cannot produce such symmetry. The study is presented as strong support for jittering jets as the primary explosion mechanism for core-collapse supernovae.
arxiv-2602-10193:
Galaxies grow stars inside dark matter halos, but how stellar content tracks halo mass has stayed uncertain, especially for low-mass groups. A 2026 paper led by Victoria Toptun, with eleven co-authors, presents the stellar-to-halo mass relation for brightest central galaxies across three orders of halo mass. Halo masses come from eROSITA X-ray data, stellar masses from SDSS photometry, with stacked X-ray spectra yielding average gas temperatures converted via a mass-temperature relation.

The relation peaks near a trillion solar masses, with stellar fraction declining at higher masses. That trend reflects weaker star formation efficiency in massive halos, through active galactic nucleus feedback, reduced cooling, and ex-situ assembly, even as halos keep growing by mergers. Measurements agree with earlier studies across the range, but simulations diverge at cluster scales, exposing feedback sensitivity.
arxiv-2602-10293:
Ranking stats need metric geometry that handles incomplete ballots, not just full rankings. A 2026 paper by Moon Duchin and Kristopher Tapp develops that geometry. It proves the two major permutation distances, Kendall tau and Spearman footrule, carry over to incomplete rankings with both coordinate placements and graph realizations. The single framework connects metric likes and distortion, polarization, and proportionality in computational social choice.

Metric structure makes spotting voter blocs and slates of liked candidates fast. Since the rules work for partial ballots, methods run not only on fake elections but on real-world elections. The resulting grouping often lines voters up identically, even though one method family follows a Condorcet-consistent rule and the other does not.
arxiv-2602-10393:
Mean value bounds are basic tools in geometric analysis, but the classical Schoen-Yau result for superharmonic functions carried a radius restriction. A 2026 paper led by Zixuan Chen, with two co-authors, proves a sharp general mean value inequality for these functions, with its rigidity, removing that restriction. The authors also obtain an explicit formula for a scaling invariant integral of weighted scalar curvature, taken asymptotically. It applies to complete three-dimensional Riemannian manifolds with non-negative Ricci curvature that grow at maximal volume.

As an application, the formula re-proves Hamilton's pinching conjecture for this setting. The paper thus sharpens a classical inequality to its general form and gives a concrete integral formula for a geometric invariant. It shows that formula doing real work by re-proving a known conjecture through a new route.
arxiv-2602-10593:
Mas Nurul Achmadiah and four co-authors test fast person finding for train station safety in a 2026 paper. Passengers crossing the yellow line at stations face real danger, and automated finding could warn before accidents happen. The study compares edge AI hardware running the YOLOX sensor for this safety task.

The Hailo-8 accelerator outperformed the Jetson Orin Nano in the tests, improving scores by more than twelve percent while running with lower latency. That combination matters at a station: detections must be both right and fast enough to act on. The paper presents the comparison as evidence for choosing dedicated accelerators where safety decisions ride on every frame.
arxiv-2602-11393:
Robots can learn from human videos, but value functions struggle across embodiment gaps. Mrinal Verghese and Christopher G. Atkeson model human preferences by predicting motion of tracked points between images. Reward is defined as agreement between predicted and observed object motion in robot conduct at each step.

A modified soft actor-critic recipe, seeded with ten on-robot demonstrations, values value from that reward and optimizes policy entirely on the robot. Policies learned this way match or beat prior work across tasks in simulation and on a real robot. The method sidesteps long-term value value from video distance, replacing it with a motion-agreement signal grounded in human preference.
arxiv-2602-11893:
Weather outlooks at low detail need sharpening into high-detail chance-based outlooks, usually with model-specific tuning. Roberto Molinaro and six co-authors introduce a universal diffusion-based downscaling framework that lifts fixed low-detail outlooks into chance-based high-detail outlooks without any model-specific fine-tuning. A single conditional diffusion model trains on paired coarse inputs at about 25 kilometer detail and high-detail local targets at about 5 kilometer detail.

Applied zero-shot to fixed outlooks from varied upstream weather models, the framework is tested on near-surface values against station readings over lead times up to 90 hours. Across AI-based and numerical weather prediction systems, the ensemble mean of the downscaled outlooks improves on each model raw fixed outlook in test after test, with much larger gains in chance skill. This downscaling thus offers a scalable, model-free bridge for daily forecast work.
arxiv-2602-11993:
Random spanning-tree chains shape how analysts judge fairness in political redistricting, where districts must hold equal population. Hugo A. Akitaya and five co-authors address a bottleneck in the Up-Down walk, which adds then deletes a random edge: rejection to maintain balance grows exponentially with the number of parts. ReCom, the most widely used alternative, merges and splits district pairs, running fast but sometimes exploring poorly.

Their Balanced Up-Down walk runs Up-Down on trees while requiring every step to preserve splittability into balanced subtrees. It samples from a known invariant measure under exact balance and proves irreducible in several cases, including a regime where ReCom is not. Efficient implementation needs a subroutine testing splittability into near-balanced subtrees; the authors improve its analysis and prove the associated counting problem is number-P-complete. Empirical comparisons confirm the walk's usefulness for sampling partitions.
arxiv-2602-12193:
Networks of quantum sensors promise sharper field measurements than single sensors, especially when the estimate draws on the whole network at once. Luis Bugalho led this work with two co-authors, setting out a frame for spatial quantum sensing. Given sensors fixed in place, the task is to estimate a field trait, such as a source, a value, or a slope at any point.

Polynomial fields are handled as interpolation, while analytic fields lead to general least-squares estimates. The paper gives exact rules for when sensor layouts make those estimates well-defined and error-free, and shows that entangled, non-local sensing beats the best local plan under shared resource limits. Prior field knowledge can also shrink the sensor count through error-free subspaces.
arxiv-2602-12293:
Grid operators run N-1 contingency checks daily, yet static checks hide which lines and transformers matter most during fast post-fault swings. Ayrton Almada led this work with five co-authors, building a real-time dynamic N-1 screening frame. For each counterfactual single-phase fault, it estimates the chance of transient overcurrent on critical elements.

The output is a dashboard ranking faulted lines that most often trigger dangerous transformer overloads, and transformers that overload across many top-risk cases. Post-fault dynamics use a linear stochastic form of the swing equations, with analytic transient checks plus importance sampling for rare, severe events. On the IEEE 118-bus system, it exposes hidden high-risk elements far faster than brute-force Monte Carlo.
arxiv-2602-12393:
DragDiffusion lets users edit images by dragging points, claiming precise spatial control from optimising a single diffusion latent plus identity-preserving tuning and spatial regularisation. Ali Subhan led this work with one co-author, Ashir Raza, reproducing that method from the authors' released code and the DragBench benchmark. Reproduction studies matter because a striking demo may hide fragile settings.

The team reproduces the main ablation studies on timestep choice, LoRA fine-tuning, mask strength, and UNet feature supervision, finding close agreement with reported trends. At the same time, performance hinges on a few hyperparameters, above all the optimised timestep and the feature level for motion supervision, while other parts tolerate wider ranges. A multi-timestep variant adds cost without improving spatial accuracy, clarifying when the central claims hold.
arxiv-2602-12693:
Prediction intervals should widen where data are noisy and narrow where they are calm, but the standard split conformal method hands out one fixed width everywhere. Shreyas Fadnavis offers a fix that needs no extra model: weight each score by statistical leverage, a measure of how unusual a data point's inputs are. The resulting method, called leverage-weighted conformal prediction, borrows its sense of scale from the shape of the data itself.

The author proves the method keeps its finite-sample coverage promise for any weight choice, and that it can reach near-ideal coverage across regions at almost no width cost when noise tracks leverage. Under normal assumptions it recovers the classic interval form while keeping distribution-free guarantees. Tests on made-up and real data confirm the theory, with much smaller gaps in coverage between regions.
arxiv-2602-12793:
Most radio telescopes hunt fast bursts lasting milliseconds, but slower transients lasting seconds have been hard to search for systematically. Sujay Mate and colleagues describe CHIME/Slow, a new real-time backend for the CHIME telescope built to catch second-long radio transients, plus results from a pilot survey on archival data. Over 17 days on sky in late 2022 and early 2023, the prototype found nine bursts.

Eight came from the hyperactive repeater FRB 20220912A, and one from a new non-repeating source; two repeater bursts had been missed by the main CHIME/FRB search. From the pilot, the team estimates an all-sky rate of 184 to 4,556 bursts per sky per day. That rate covers pulses between 16 milliseconds and 5 seconds above a set brightness at 600 megahertz. The paper also reports sensitivity, completeness, and plans to improve the pipeline.
arxiv-2602-12893:
Thermal correlators in holographic theories show bulk-cone breakdowns where bulk null straight paths connect edge points. Ignacio Araya and four co-authors extend that picture to spacelike separations on a plane, where the stress-tensor part of the correlator shows matching breakdowns. They show these breakdowns are tied to complex null straight paths, curves that leave the real space-time behind.

A phase transition separates real from complex spacelike straight paths in the picture, and a phase-shift calculation pins down where the generalised breakdowns sit. The work deepens the dictionary between edge correlators and bulk shape, showing that even spacelike breakdowns carry shape meaning once complex straight paths are admitted. It is a technical advance in holographic duality with clear shape intuition.
arxiv-2602-13093:
Thinking models ace complex tasks, but multi-turn adversarial pressure may still break them. Yubo Li and two co-authors test nine frontier thinking models with adversarial attacks. Thinking helps: most models beat instruction-tuned plain rivals by a clear margin, yet every model shows distinct vulnerabilities, with misleading suggestions working universally and social pressure working in model-given ways.

Trajectory analysis spots five failure modes: self-doubt, conformity to social pressure, hijacking by suggestions, emotional susceptibility, and fatigue from thinking, with the first two causing half of failures. Confidence-aware response making, which helps standard models, fails for thinking models because long thinking traces induce overconfidence; surprisingly, random confidence embedding beats targeted extraction. Thinking, the paper warns, does not automatically confer adversarial toughness.
arxiv-2602-13193:
Pretrained vision-language models hold rich commonsense for robots, but grounding that knowledge in low-level behaviour is hard. William Chen and eight co-authors introduce Steerable Policies: vision-language-action models trained on rich synthetic commands at multiple abstraction levels, including subtasks, motions, and grounded pixel coordinates. Natural-language task instructions alone limit how much high-level reasoning can steer low-level action, so richer command channels unlock more pretrained knowledge.

Steerable Policies answer to two controllers: a learned high-level embodied reasoner plus an off-the-shelf vision-language model prompted to reason over command abstractions in context. Across extensive real-world manipulation experiments, both approaches beat prior embodied reasoning models and hierarchical baselines, including on challenging generalisation and long-horizon tasks. The result suggests controllability, not just reasoning, is the bottleneck for robot generalisation.
arxiv-2602-13293:
Vision-language models now help cars perceive the road, but they can be fooled by small physical patches or by invisible tweaks spread across a whole image. NutVLM defends the full perception-to-decision chain with a self-adaptive design. A sentinel called NutNet++ first sorts inputs three ways, into benign samples, local patches, and global perturbations, then local threats are cleaned by grayscale masking while global ones trigger expert-guided prompt tuning.

That tuning builds corrective driving prompts through gradient-based optimization, refocusing the model's attention without retraining the whole model. On the Dolphins driving benchmark, the framework improved overall metrics by 4.89 percent, and its code is public. Xiaoxu Peng leads the work with five co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13393:
Dark matter is usually pictured as weakly interacting particles. This paper explores a bolder fluid picture: a strongly interacting hidden sector described holographically by a braneworld in a five-dimensional linear dilaton spacetime. In that frame, dark matter comes from a bulk black hole. It is fed by energy leaking from our brane after inflation, a natural freeze-in production route.

The black hole phase is shown to be thermodynamically favored at all temperatures, and the model carries just two free parameters. One, the horizon position, is fixed by the observed dark matter abundance, while the other, the five-dimensional Planck scale, survives all current bounds above about three hundred thousand TeV. Sylvain Fichet leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13493:
Differential entropy measures the uncertainty in a continuous distribution, but when does it converge as densities converge? This paper answers with a direct appeal to Vitali's convergence theorem: when densities converge in measure, entropy converges whenever the entropy terms are uniformly integrable and tight.
