An entropy-weighted Orlicz condition with a single fast-growing function is given, strictly weaker than the fixed-alpha condition of Godavarti and Hero from 2004.

The paper also disproves the Godavarti-Hero conjecture that alpha above one could be replaced by alpha tending down to one. Prior conditions of Godavarti-Hero, Piera-Parada, and Ghourchian-Gohari-Amini fall out as corollaries, and on bounded domains uniform integrability alone is shown both needed and enough. Mahesh Godavarti is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13693:
Corneal imaging sensitively reveals small-fiber damage in diabetic nerve disease, but auto diagnosis is limited by scarce labeled data and fine-grained variation in corneal nerve shape. Foundation image models excel at natural images yet struggle with medical anatomy. This framework adapts them with Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation, splitting size and direction weight updates so the model separately learns nerve shape and stromal contrast. It is conditioned jointly on nerve masks and disease-specific clinical prompts.

A three-part check found state-of-the-art visual quality, with a Frechet Inception Distance of 5.18, and shape soundness, with a shape similarity index of 0.630, beating GAN and standard diffusion baselines. Synthetic images preserved gold-standard clinical biomarkers, matched real patient data in stats, and improved diagnostic accuracy by 2.1 percent. Xin Zhang leads the work with seven co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14193:
Yue Chen and seven co-authors present a 2026 arXiv method for robots handling jointed objects. Doors, knobs, and handles tell a robot where and how to act, but generalizing across object types is hard. Prior features were mostly two-dimensional and ignored functional parts.

Their Part-Aware 3D Feature Field, or PA3FF, predicts a dense 3D feature field from point clouds in one forward pass. It trains on 3D part proposals from a large labeled set, using contrastive learning. That part-aware field should let robots transfer manipulation skills across diverse articulated objects, a key step for real-world tasks.
arxiv-2602-14393:
Zongle Huang and three co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv pipeline framework for multi-chip-module neural network accelerators. Such chips pack huge compute, but they suffer idle goods and heavy off-chip talk. Old side-by-side plans, in-layer split and inter-layer lining, fail to break both jams at once, capping scale-up.

The authors note prior work fields layers apart, ignoring a joint multi-layer size. Scope, a merged line setup, uses that size to ease trade-offs among compute, talk, and memory costs, lifting throughput and scale-up. That new size tangles design-space search, so the paper also tackles search over the wider space, aiming for real gains as hardware and software scale.
arxiv-2602-14493:
Xinpeng Liu and one co-author offers a 2026 arXiv lightweight differentiable mesh renderer. Three-size Gaussian splatting enables high-truth novel view making with fast drawing, but triangle meshes, still liked for face rebuilding, suffer slow or heavy tuning in old mesh-based smooth drawers. The Gaussian Mesh Drawer, or GMR, tightly joins the Gaussian and mesh forms.

Each Gaussian bit is drawn analytically from its matching mesh triangle, keeping shape truth and enabling gradient flow. Weighed against old mesh drawers, the method gains smoother gradients, lifting tuning with smaller batches under tight memory. The build is public, offering a real bridge between Gaussian splatting speed and mesh-based face modeling.
arxiv-2602-14693:
Sharp electron images need beams that stay in step, yet stray loss can break that step. Cruz I. Velasco, with Valerio Di Giulio and F. Javier García de Abajo as co-authors, builds one theory of this loss for free electrons near bulk matter and flat faces. The frame spans all matter types through their wave response.

This decoherence theory finds bulk plasmons ruling the loss in gold and aluminium, while in salts like lithium fluoride, high-gap electron kicks lead. Heat-fed waves make loss spike at low-frequency, with a sharp heat link the team turns to tiny-scale heat gauging. Filtered holography, they predict, can sense fringe shifts near a tenth of a percent. The work ties image blur to matter physics.
arxiv-2602-14993:
Tungathurthi builds an open elevation model of the Chandrayaan-3 Vikram landing site from Chandrayaan-2 orbital stereo images. ISRO's own terrain products guided the first landing in the lunar south polar region, but they rest on a proprietary pipeline and were never released in public. This paper offers a fully open workflow using ISIS, the Ames Stereo Pipeline, and ALE, reaching 30 centimetre pixels comparable to mission products.

The model covers a patch roughly two kilometres on each side, with over 91 percent valid pixels and a median triangulation error near 8 centimetres. Both the Vikram lander and the Pragyan rover are resolved on their own. Alignment to an LROC NAC stereo model gives about 30 metre horizontal accuracy, and the method promises independent hazard mapping for Chandrayaan-4, LUPEX, and Artemis.
arxiv-2602-15093:
Cabral and colleagues study Bhabha scattering in non-Hermitian quantum electrodynamics at finite temperature. In this theory, the usual hermiticity demand is replaced by an unbroken symmetry condition. Hermiticity normally secures real physical observables. The swap favors an axial mass term and a vector-axial gauge coupling, changing the process picture.

Using the Thermofield Dynamics formalism, the team derives and analyzes the thermal differential cross section for the process in full. They also explore the high-energy limit of the amplitude. From that limit they set bounds on the axial coupling constant, offering insight into how the system behaves under extreme conditions.
arxiv-2602-15193:
Lemaire studies equivalence between mixed and nonconforming methods on general polytopal partitions for a variable diffusion problem. Mixed methods are conforming, while the others are primal, and both live on general grids of that kind. This first paper of a two-part series focuses on multiscale and projection methods.

For multiscale work, Lemaire shows first-level match between four oversampling-free approaches, going beyond results from Chaumont-Frelet, Ern, Lemaire, and Valentin in 2022. For projection work, he gives a simple test, checkable in practice, for primal and mixed well-posedness and match to hold. Along the way, the paper sheds new light on self-stable hybrid methods. Part two will address general element methods of that kind.
arxiv-2602-15293:
Park and colleagues ask how AI systems encode meaning structure into the shape of their code spaces. The driving point is that the true shape of these spaces should mirror how models use codes to produce acts. They focus on codes defining softmax spreads, saying the natural shape there is information geometry. Their focus is the role of information geometry in meaning storing and the linear representation idea.

As a sample use, they build dual guiding, a method for firmly guiding codes to show a chosen idea using linear probes. They prove dual guiding best changes the target idea while cutting shifts to other ideas. In tests, dual guiding lifts the control and calm of idea handling.
arxiv-2602-15493:
Cappelli and Ferrara offer a fingerprint tool that runs end to end, with no separate clean-up steps before or after. Their LEADER network reads a raw fingerprint image and returns minutiae, the small ridge details used to match prints, with place, direction, and type. It does this with just 0.9 million weights, helped by a new ground-truth code the authors dub Castle-Moat-Rampart and by two linked autoencoders joined through attention gating.

Tests show top accuracy on plain prints and strong transfer to hard latent prints, with a 34 percent higher F1 score than specialist latent tools on the NIST SD27 set. It ranks first on 47 percent of samples there, and it runs in 15 milliseconds on a GPU. Code and trained weights are public, so others can check and reuse the work.
arxiv-2602-15693:
Dahinden and de Pooter study how Hamiltonian trajectories behave when projected from a cotangent bundle down to its base. They show that projected paths from a typical submersive level set meet themselves only at separate, isolated points. With the fibres over the endpoints held fixed, they also show every crossing can be removed by a small shake of the paths once the base is three-dimensional or more.

Periodic orbits fall under the same results, and both results also cover Reeb flows on hypersurfaces that are star-shaped in each fibre, Finsler flows that cannot be run backwards included. That extension answers a question of Rademacher. The proof leans on a multi-jet transversality theorem, giving symplectic geometers a clean generic picture of projected orbit crossings.
arxiv-2602-15793:
Goodwin and colleagues extend the widely used SIMPSON software for runs, design, and reading of new pulse tests. Those tests cross nuclear magnetic resonance and electron paramagnetic resonance, including pulsed DNP. New tools address new pulse sequence testing through propagator splitting, high-order spin cross terms, and pulse phase transients.

These tools arrive in a C-plus-plus-based next version of SIMPSON. It speeds math in some aspects, is better ready for further growth, and eases group input to the open-source package. The paper will interest magnet resonance users who design pulse tests at the NMR-EPR edge and need run tools that keep pace with hybrid methods.
arxiv-2602-16193:
Physics-informed neural networks often struggle with multi-scale equations that mix smooth slow parts with local fast parts. Zhenzhen Huang and coauthors trace part of the trouble to fixed coordinate inputs, where shape misalignment with those parts induces gradient stiffness and ill-conditioning. Their mapping paradigm reshapes input coordinates through differentiable compaction maps, coupling PDE shape with spectral traits of leftover operators.

From that idea comes Geometric Compactification PINN, a framework with three mapping strategies: periodic boundaries, far-field scale expansion, and local singular parts. It leaves the underlying PINN design untouched. Tests on representative one- and two-dimensional PDEs show more uniform even spreads and higher solution accuracy, with better training stability and faster convergence. The work thus treats input geometry as a first-class design choice for physics-based learning.
arxiv-2602-16293:
Trung Loc Tang and coauthors study decay rates and global existence for a semilinear damped wave equation with a Riesz potential-type power nonlinearity. Their approach uses the decay character of initial data to establish global existence for several classes of initial data. A second objective uses a blow-up argument to show that conditions on the nonlinearity in the global existence theorem are sharp for initial data in a pseudo-measure space.

As a consequence, they derive a new critical exponent for low dimensions and a parameter range stated in the paper. They also establish a sharp lifespan estimate for solutions that blow up in finite time. The work thus gives both existence results for well-behaved initial data and precise limits: beyond the stated conditions, global existence cannot be expected, and blow-up timing is sharply estimated.
arxiv-2602-16593:
Chiara Esposito, Michael Heins, and Stefan Waldmann build a functorial frame for convergence of Drinfeld's Universal Deformation Formula on analytic vectors. They match the order of those vectors with an even-continuity rule on the twist behind the deformation. The work uses maps of finite Lie algebras by steady linear maps on locally convex spaces.

That setup yields more than convergence of a formal power series. It also gives steadiness of the deformed bilinear maps and full holomorphic ties to the deformation parameter. The theory is then used on explicit twists by Giaquinto and Zhang. There, the even-continuity rule holds and the analytic vector spaces are named, answering their query about a strict version in the affirmative.
arxiv-2602-16793:
Xingyu Dang and co-authors present an inference pipeline that reaches best-in-class scores on IMO-style math problems at far lower cost than rival routes, using only general-purpose off-the-shelf models. Custom and unreleased math models had reached gold-medal level, and large-scale inference on public models matched them only at prohibitive cost per problem. The new pipeline cuts that cost by orders of magnitude.

The key insight concerns grader failure in solver-grader pipelines, dubbed the Cognitive Well, where iterative refinement converges to a wrong solution that both solver and internal grader deem basically correct. The pipeline counters it by conjecture extraction: candidate lemmas are isolated and verified independently alongside their negations in a fresh context. On an advanced IMO proof benchmark, the pipeline scores about two thirds correct with a leading public model at modest cost per question.
arxiv-2602-16893:
Riku Arakawa and co-authors present CalmReminder, a watch-based design probe for parent engagement with children with hyperactivity, aided by real-time motion sensing. Families raising children with ADHD often face high stress and reactive parenting. Digital programs promise tailoring, yet many remain one-size-fits-all and miss parents' lived habits. CalmReminder detects children's calm moments and sends just-in-time prompts to parents.

Through a four-week trial with sixteen families, twelve finishing, the team compared alert plans from hourly to random to only-when-calm. Sensing-based alerts were often seen as arriving during calm moments. Parents used the system in varied ways, for praise, calm focus, activity planning, or conversation. The findings show parents as active designers reshaping programs to fit their own styles. The team contributes a calm detection pipeline and design lessons for systems that foster agency.
arxiv-2602-16993:
Selvi Kara and Ellie Lew study neural codes through homological invariants of polarized neural ideals. For a neural code, polarizing the standard form of the neural ideal yields a squarefree monomial ideal. That ideal, the polarized neural ideal, has a linked simplicial complex, the polar complex. The paper studies graded invariants, projective dimension and regularity, through the topology of the polar complex.

Simple shapes of the Hamming cube set their extremes. Regularity is at most twice n minus one, with equality just when the code comes from the full cube minus an antipodal pair. Projective dimension is at most twice n minus three, with a family reaching equality, each made of antipodal pairs. At the other end, regularity one forces a coordinate subcube, while projective dimension zero forces its complement. Families spanning large regions of the dimension-regularity plot for fixed n are constructed.
arxiv-2602-17093:
Mengjie Tang led a five-author team studying how blind people experience nature, a topic past research has largely passed over. Nature matters for health and well-being, but most accounts assume sighted engagement. The team surveyed blind and sighted adults on nature relatedness and interviewed blind participants in depth about their habits, values, and hopes for assistive tools.

Survey results showed lower nature relatedness among blind participants than among sighted peers. Interviews mapped current practices and barriers, the attitudes that shape engagement, and expectations for technology that supports safe, meaningful time outdoors. The paper offers design guidance for tools that widen nature access, framing blind engagement with nature as rich beyond vision rather than as a deficit to fix.
arxiv-2602-17193:
Juho Vepsäläinen, writing alone, makes the case for putting HTML first in web development. The web grew from a document platform into the largest application platform on earth, and HTML has anchored it from the start with tree-like, semantic pages. Frameworks later eased complex app building but pushed HTML aside, even as standards like HTML5 narrowed the gap between platform and framework.

HTML First development uses HTML wherever possible, embraces minimalism, hypermedia, and server-side logic, and leans on complementary tools like htmx. Case comparisons show smaller codebases, easier maintenance, and performance gains for content-oriented sites, including a converted public broadcaster site. Open questions remain about the size of the benefits and fit with AI-driven development, but the advantages for developers look clear.
arxiv-2602-17393:
Minxing Sun led a two-author team on camera-free, LiDAR-free odometry for legged robots. Reliable odometry without cameras or LiDAR remains hard due to IMU drift and noisy joint velocity sensing. The paper presents a purely proprioceptive state estimator using only IMU and motor data. It estimates body pose and velocity, with one form for quadruped and wheel-legged robots.

The key idea treats each reliable contact as a kinematic anchor: foot wrench estimation selects stance contacts, and footfall records supply world-frame constraints that suppress long-term drift. Height clustering and time-decay correction snap new footfall heights to observed planes, preventing elevation drift. For wheel-legged platforms, recorded contacts propagate by wheel rolling displacement with shank-motion compensation and slope-aware rolling direction. An optional Kalman filter refines velocity, and multi-contact consistency mitigates yaw drift as a soft heading prior.
arxiv-2602-17493:
Veit Elser led a two-author team on learning with Boolean threshold functions. The team trains neural nets on Boolean data, where each node holds strictly plus or minus one. Trained models tend to match nets with nonzero weights also plus or minus one. Loss chasing gives way to nonconvex constraints. Each node runs a Boolean threshold function, and training splits in two through divide-and-concur.

One constraint keeps each node locally sound across inputs, weights, output. The other forces network-wide accord, lining neuron outputs up with later inputs and holding weights equal across net copies. The reflect-reflect-relax projection algorithm settles the pair. With a big enough margin floor, learned forms turn sparse and match nets of plain logical gates. Tests on cellular automata learning, binary autoencoding, logic network inference, and multiplier circuit discovery give exact answers or strong generalization where gradient methods falter.
arxiv-2602-17593:
Sayak Dutta and team used the MUSEQuBES survey to map gas around isolated galaxies. They ask if the circumgalactic medium looks different along a galaxy's disk plane than above its poles. The sample spans more than a hundred galaxies, with dozens of new measures and a subset inside the virial radius.

For low-mass galaxies, hydrogen coverage peaks both near the disk plane and near the polar direction. That two-peaked shape is absent at higher mass. Oxygen gas shows a similar tentative two-peaked trend at low mass, but a more even spread at high mass. Velocity data add a twist: oxygen absorbers run narrower along the disk plane, as if the gas still recalls where it came from.
arxiv-2602-17993:
Mohan Tang and Sidi Lu argue that a Transformer can follow only a bounded number of steps along any hidden path. That cap limits models on problems solved step by step. Their answer is Turbo Connection, an architecture sending several backward links from upper-layer states of one token into the lower layers of the next token.

Fine-tuning language models with the method lifted accuracy by under one percent to over ten percent on grade-school math, parity, and multi-step arithmetic tests. Dense backward connections mattered, clearly beating sparse variants that pass only a single hidden state or vector. On parity, one fine-tuned small model scored only about fifty-four percent, but the modification carried it to full accuracy without retraining from scratch or elaborate curriculum learning. The results point to path depth as a key factor in reasoning ability, at little latency cost.
arxiv-2602-18393:
Vernon Barger organizes flavor hierarchies with a single number. His 2026 paper builds a single-flavon Froggatt-Nielsen framework in which each effective Yukawa entry sums three unit-magnitude messenger chains, and all hierarchies follow one parameter near five point three six. Benchmark complex matrices of order one reproduce quark and charged-lepton masses at the Z mass as powers of the inverse of that parameter.

A two-over-two lattice of four-sided mass ratios organizes the picture, mapping directly to a rational lattice of Froggatt-Nielsen exponents. Sequential dominance keeps the leading-power exponent matrices, while subleading chains generate entry-dependent complex coefficients and offer a UV-friendly source of CP violation. Neutrino masses are treated at the eigenvalue level within the same power counting. The paper gives flavor model builders a compact, single-parameter lattice to test.
arxiv-2602-18593:
Aidan Mason-Mackay and team solve dynamic inverse problems with sparse dictionaries. Their 2026 paper notes ill-posed dynamic inverse problems benefit from expected spatial features and temporal links, especially with limited data and large unknowns. One approach encodes spatial and temporal traits into dictionary entries, seeking the solution as a sparse mix of atoms.

To promote vanishing coefficients, the team uses a stochastic extension with a hierarchical sparsity prior. They compute the Maximum A Posteriori estimate with the Iterative Alternating Sequential method, shown to solve inverse problems with minimal tuning. Tests on dynamic CT and MRI data, compared with the Alternating Direction, show the method is competitive for compressed sensing with lower sensitivity.
arxiv-2602-18693:
Fact-checking tools often trust one source and ignore the rest, which hides exactly the disagreements a reader most needs to see. Md Badsha Biswas, with one co-author, builds a 2026 claim-verification system that gathers evidence for a claim and for its negation, from Wikipedia, PubMed, and Google.

The retrieved sets are filtered, deduplicated, and pooled, then fed to large language models for a verdict, with confidence scores used to show where sources disagree. Tests on four benchmarks with five models show the pooled evidence improves checking and makes source-specific reasoning visible. The point is not just better scores, but a more honest picture of contested information.
arxiv-2602-18793:
Most graph anomaly detectors are trained for one dataset at a time, which is costly, hard to transfer, and awkward where labels or full data cannot be shared. Yixin Liu, with six co-authors, proposes in 2026 a generalist alternative: one model that can spot anomalies on unseen graph datasets with little or no dataset-specific training.

Their method, ARC, uses in-context learning with only a few labelled normal samples at inference. A feature alignment module unifies features across datasets, a residual graph neural network encoder captures dataset-agnostic anomaly patterns, and a cross-attentive context module scores anomalies against the few-shot normal context. A further variant, ARC_zero, picks representative pseudo-normal nodes itself, enabling fully label-free inference. Tests on seventeen real-world datasets show strong generalisation in both few-shot and zero-shot settings.
arxiv-2602-18893:
Graphene on hexagonal boron nitride has band gaps that depend on twist angle and on how atoms relax. Jiaqi An, with four co-authors, assesses those effects in 2026 for the primary gap at charge neutrality and the second valence gap.

At zero twist, the primary gap falls sharply as relaxation is restricted. Fully relaxed bilayers show the largest gap. Keeping the remote substrate rigid cuts it greatly. Fully rigid structures cut it further still. With relaxation, the primary gap peaks near a small twist angle, where moiré alignment stabilises the system. The secondary gap falls to zero beyond about one degree. A small primary gap persists across a wide twist range for all sliding setups, then switches sign at larger twists.
arxiv-2602-19193:
Pushing is one of the simplest ways a robot can move things without grasping them, yet most systems still chain together fixed push moves planned in advance. That habit limits how well a robot copes with new layouts. Hieu Bui and three colleagues answer with a single learned policy that reacts on the fly instead of following a preset script.

A short visual prompt steers the policy, and a higher-level planner can supply that prompt for each job. The policy builds on flow matching, a method that turns noise into smooth actions step by step. Because one policy covers many push styles, the same system can be reused across tasks rather than rebuilt for each new scene.
arxiv-2602-19593:
Beatrice Costeri and three co-authors talk over distribution germs on smooth d-size Riemannian manifolds, working out multi-level Schauder bounds with no extra shape rules. As a first step, ideas of coherence and sameness get defined for germs on open bits of flat space. The rebuild theorem and Schauder bounds then get stated in this setting.

Using traits of the exponential map, the results reach Riemannian spaces. A twin of the earlier rebuild theorem gets devised, with smoothness of the rebuilt spread proved in fitting Hölder-Zygmund spaces. A new idea of beta-smoothing kernels on Riemannian manifolds then yields Schauder bounds for germs in that setting.
arxiv-2602-19693:
Tiny crystals of a cesium lead bromide perovskite can emit single photons, which makes them of interest for quantum light sources. A 2026 arXiv paper by Marina Cagnon Trouche and seven co-authors reports a gentler way to make them, using a modified ligand-assisted reprecipitation route instead of the usual hot-injection method.

The team trimmed particle size after synthesis with an amine step and coated the dots with ligands that steady their surfaces. Single dots made this way gave stable emission at low temperature, with little drift in colour, and showed the fine structure of the bright exciton plus related states. Time-resolved tests confirmed clean single-photon emission. The result offers a more flexible path to high-quality dots without strict heat and atmosphere control.
arxiv-2602-19793:
Magnetic sensing, nonreciprocal photonics, and optical isolation all lean on materials that rotate light strongly in a magnetic field. A 2026 arXiv paper by Megan H. Dransfield and six co-authors reports bismuth-substituted lutetium iron garnet films with exceptionally strong magneto-optical response in visible light.

The films combine bismuth's large spin-orbit coupling with the stable lattice of lutetium iron garnet, made by pulsed laser deposition and tested at room temperature across the visible range. Their Verdet constant, the standard gauge of magneto-optical strength, peaks in the visible spectrum at an exceptionally high value. That combination marks the material as a strong candidate for sensitive cryogenic detection and hybrid quantum applications.
arxiv-2602-19893:
Newton methods for optimization need second-derivative information, but in stochastic settings only noisy function values may be available. A 2026 arXiv paper by Soumen Pachal and three co-authors builds Hessian estimators from random-direction sampling using only those noisy values.

Each estimator's shape, and how fast its bias shrinks, depends on how many function values it uses. More values mean faster-shrinking bias. The authors prove the estimators become unbiased in the limit. They also analyze convergence of stochastic Newton methods built on them, both in the limit and for finite samples. Numerical tests back the theory. The work gives practitioners a family of estimators whose accuracy improves predictably with measurement effort.
arxiv-2602-20293:
Karthik Elamvazhuthi and two co-authors propose a discrete diffusion method for generative modeling over discrete state spaces. Instead of approximating a discrete analogue of a score function, their 2026 approach treats single-site conditional probabilities as the core objects of the reverse diffusion process. Those conditionals are estimated with a sample-efficient method called the Neural Interaction Screening Estimator, paired with round-robin noising and denoising dynamics.

Controlled tests cover synthetic Ising models, MNIST, data from a D-Wave quantum annealer, a synthetic Potts model, and one-dimensional quantum systems. On binary data, the method beats popular ratio-based approaches on total variation, cross-correlations, and kernel density estimates. The work shows that estimating conditionals directly can be a strong basis for discrete diffusion models. It offers a practical route for discrete-data domains.
arxiv-2602-20393:
A large team led by L. Pantoni maps dust properties across the face-on M99, with NIKA2. Large grains dominate far-infrared light, but contamination makes their properties hard to pin down. New millimetre continuum data from IRAM, in two bands, with ultraviolet-to-radio data, feed a spatially resolved analysis.

HerBIE splits the infrared-to-radio spectrum into dust, free-free, and synchrotron parts. Dust follows a modified blackbody with a varying millimetre index, compared with the THEMIS model at fixed index. Fits show the index rising from under two in diffuse regions to above two in dense star-forming areas, likely from grain clumping and changing makeup. Dust masses from varying index run up to about four times higher than fixed masses, biasing dust ratios. The small-grain share rises from ten percent in the center to fifteen percent in the diffuse disc.
arxiv-2602-20493:
Self-run agents team up more and more, but today's models pass notes while leaving each agent's running space alone. Xiaohang Nie and four co-authors offer the Agent Workspace Collaboration Protocol. It bridges that gap through short-term workspace sharing drawn from the Unix idea that all is a file. A lightweight control plane stays split from pluggable transports, letting a sender project its workspace to a remote doer who works on shared files with as-is local tools.

A fully open-source sample build with MCP tool hookup backs the system, tested through live demos of uneven teamwork between agents with matching skills. By adding the missing workspace layer to the agent system stack, the authors argue, teamwork can transcend message walls toward a fully linked agent world.
arxiv-2602-20693:
Recent terahertz experiments hint at ferroelectricity and multiferroicity in strontium titanate, a band insulator. Andri Darmawan and two co-authors use real-time density functional theory runs to study carrier and magnetization dynamics of that crystal under linear and circular polarized light. Runs show charge transfer from oxygen p states to titanium d states that depends on site and orbital.

Linear light wobbles electron lobes at oxygen and titanium and breaks mirror balance. Circular light spins charge dipoles around oxygen, producing a twist-dependent transient moment, flipped at oxygen and titanium. Mostly, angular momentum moves from light to electronic orbits, then from orbits to spins via spin-orbit link. The first is about ten times larger. Real-time timing splits the inverse Faraday effect from light aim. Purely electronic steps without lattice motion can induce ultrafast switching in a non-magnetic insulator, a tunable route to light-controlled uses.
arxiv-2602-20793:
Isaac Rudich and one co-author speed up decision diagrams, layered graphs used to bound and solve discrete optimization problems. Building a restricted diagram now costs width times log width per layer. A relaxed one costs width squared. Wider diagrams buy better bounds at a steep price in time and memory.

Their implicit diagrams store arcs implicitly rather than explicitly. That cuts both cases to width per layer, which they prove optimal when state updates and merges are treated as black boxes. The team also shows how implicit diagrams can drive a MIP solver, and releases ImplicitDDs, an open-source Julia solver that beats Gurobi on Subset Sum in their tests.
arxiv-2602-21293:
Beaming logic quantum states across a surface code is a landmark for tough work. Yiren Zou and thirty-four co-authors show it in this 2026 arXiv paper on a super-cold chip with one hundred twenty-five qubits. They beam a shape rotated surface code built by a linear-depth circuit, with code spans up to seven.

Tuning local linking gates evenly maps a beaming phase map across a finite threshold. In-step turns feeding magic goods beyond the Clifford regime boost that threshold and restore duality pattern of the shape phase, guiding least linkage goods use. The work lights up shape quantum matter on real devices and pushes spread-out tough quantum work.
arxiv-2602-21493:
Job Feldbrugge and two co-authors apply resurgence and hyperasymptotics to wave optics in astronomy. With gravity waves and fast radio bursts found, wave optics matters more in astrophysics. The paper studies random gravity and plasma lenses, giving refractive and diffractive series with higher-order terms that allow error bounds.

The diffractive series converge for a broad class of bounded lens models and describe wave patterns well across bands. Building on Picard-Lefschetz tools, the authors derive the full refractive series to any order, set out as a transseries. Near caustics, uniform asymptotics add to the series. Borel and hyperasymptotic summing then yield orderly values for lensing sums at all bands, including the strong wave-optics dimming of off-axis caustics.
arxiv-2602-21593:
Zheng Gao and four co-authors expose a flaw in meaning-aware image marks via LLM-guided coherence-preserving meaning injection. Made images spread on web platforms, and meaning marks bind mark signals to high image meaning in diffusion models for origin tracking and forgery blocking. Older noise-layer marks stay open to reverse attacks that recover hidden signals.

Recent content-aware mark designs bind signals to meaning, blocking local edits that break fit. Yet large language models can think in structured ways about meaning spaces, enabling locally fine but globally coherent changes that break bindings. The proposed Coherence-Preserving Semantic Injection attack uses LLM-guided changes under closeness limits. This match keeps visual-meaning fit while hand-picked shifts to mark-relevant meaning induce wrong calls. Wide tests show it beating leading older attacks, revealing a deep flaw in meaning mark designs when facing LLM-driven meaning shifts.
arxiv-2602-21693:
Jiafeng Lin and four co-authors built TiMi to help time series forecasting use text as well as numbers. Text like emergency reports and policy news can push a series up or down, yet most forecasters fail to fold such text into their numbers because aligning words with values is hard. TiMi uses large language models to infer how events will unfold, then feeds those inferences into the forecast.

A plug-in module called MMoE merges the outside factors with the series itself, so Transformer forecasters gain multimodal skill without an explicit step to line up words and numbers. TiMi led the field on sixteen real-world multimodal forecasting tests, beating strong rivals while staying adaptable and open to inspection.
arxiv-2602-22293:
Reliable river forecasts protect water, food, and energy, but sparse gauges have confined machine learning to isolated basins rather than connected river systems. Hancheng Ren and fourteen co-authors introduce GraphRiverCast, a topology-informed foundation model for reach-level prediction across the global river network. It exploits river links and energetics, training on sparse gauges to predict daily water flows with no prior river conditions.

The model outperforms strong physics-based and machine-learning rivals. Tests of what drives it show it rebuilds river states from topology and forcing, learning the flows themselves rather than leaning on time recurrence like standard autoregressive models. Water managers gain a global, connected forecasting tool that inherits rivers' self-correcting behavior.
arxiv-2602-22393:
Infinite-type surfaces, with endless handles or ends, need analogues of the finite-type tools topologists rely on. Manvendra Somvanshi defines one: for each natural number, a complex for such surfaces with non-planar ends, mirroring the Hatcher-Thurston complex. The build extends a classical combinatorial object into the infinite setting.

Somvanshi proves the complex is connected and simply connected, and that its automorphism group is exactly the extended mapping class group. Those three properties make the complex a faithful model of the surface's symmetries. The field gains a Hatcher-Thurston theory for surfaces whose ends never settle down.
arxiv-2602-22693:
Xinyi Ren and fourteen co-authors set a chip-scale record for squeezed light, the quantum-noise-suppressed light that sharpens optical measurement. Most on-chip sources lean on Kerr nonlinearities and stall on pump power and loss. Quadratic platforms promise stronger interactions, lower pump needs, and freer spectral design.

The team built a dual-resonant amplifier in a single periodically poled lithium niobate microresonator on thin film. Escape efficiency topped ninety percent, quality factors passed two and a half million, and squeezing was measured just under one decibel below shot noise at modest pump power. Inferred on-chip squeezing reached about seven and a half decibels across a spectrum over ten terahertz, the best yet for integrated quadratic cavity platforms.
arxiv-2602-22893:
Tanmoy Biswas asks how much work information can buy from an unknown quantum state. Extractable work tracks knowledge of the state, as Maxwell's demon and the Gibbs paradox illustrate. Standard protocols use system-bath contact, where maximum work equals the free-energy gap to the Gibbs state at bath temperature.

In closed systems without a bath, work comes from unitary operations driven by a time-dependent Hamiltonian, and ergotropy names the maximum under full state knowledge, usually demanding full tomography. With only partial knowledge, observational ergotropy, tied to the chosen measurement, rules instead. The paper shows it falls under classical post-processing, so fine-grained measurements beat coarse ones, and maximizing over measurements recovers standard ergotropy, split into classical and coherent parts. Coherence in measurement projectors thus powers quantum advantage.
arxiv-2602-23193:
Elzo Brito dos Santos Filho proposes ESAA, an architecture for autonomous language-model agents that build software. It targets three structural weaknesses: agents have no native state, their context degrades over long runs, and probabilistic generation clashes with the need for deterministic execution. The design splits the agent's intent from changes to project state, borrowing the event-sourcing pattern from software engineering.

Agents emit only structured intentions in validated JSON. A deterministic orchestrator checks them, stores events in an append-only log, applies file-writing effects, and projects a verifiable roadmap view. Boundary contracts, metaprompting profiles, and hash-based replay checks guard completed work and give forensic traceability. Two case studies, a nine-task landing page and a 50-task clinical dashboard built by four agents over eight phases, both finish with success and verified status. That shows the design scales to concurrent, multi-model teams.
arxiv-2602-23693:
Harry-Dean Kenchington Goldsmith and six co-authors compare tri-coupler shapes for color-free nulling beam mixing. Light tech drives next-generation sky tools with compact circuits for ground and space use. 

Two-guide light mixers rely on even leaky coupling, color-based. A three-guide tri-coupler promises deeper, broader, more stable color-free nulls. The work tests mock scores of leaky tri-couplers and a multi-mode mixer across the one point five to one point eight micron band. Scored traits include alien-world throughput, starlight dimming, sensing traits, and making slack. All three tri-couplers hit over 40 dB dimming over a 270-nm bandwidth. With part loss, the tapered tri-coupler has the highest throughput, mean ninety-seven percent, while the one fell to 50 percent at the band edges. The multi-mode mixer, limited to 40 dB by loose light, showed the greatest slack to making errors.
arxiv-2602-23893:
Bowen Yang and seventeen co-authors present AoE, an always-on egocentric video collection system for embodied AI, built on people and their phones. The 2026 paper argues that embodied models need vast real-world interaction data, but current collection demands costly hardware and narrow settings, while humans are already ideal embodied agents.

AoE uses an ergonomic neck-mounted phone holder for low-barrier first-person recording, a cross-platform app that processes video on-device, and cloud pipelines that label and filter raw footage into training data. The cloud-edge design lets anyone collect anywhere, at low cost and at scale. Tests on preprocessing quality and downstream tasks show that high-quality egocentric data markedly improve real-world generalization. The system offers a sustainable path past the data scarcity that limits embodied models.
arxiv-2602-24093:
Graziano Crasta and Ilaria Fragalà strengthen a classical result on the shape of the first Dirichlet Laplacian eigenfunction on a bounded convex set. The 2026 paper builds on the Brascamp-Lieb theorem, which states that the ground state is log-concave, meaning its logarithm is a concave function.

The authors prove a stronger power-log-concavity property. When the eigenfunction is normalized so its maximum stays below a threshold set by the domain's diameter and principal frequency, a certain transformed function is concave. That function is the negative square root of the negative logarithm. That refinement sharpens control over how the ground state decays from its peak toward the boundary, where it vanishes. Results of this kind matter for spectral geometry and for estimates that depend on the profile of the lowest vibration mode of a convex domain.
arxiv-2603-00393: Siahkoohi, Aghazade, and Gholami sample posterior beliefs for inverse problems ruled by hard physical laws, such as the wave equation in seismic imaging. Noisy, partial data leave many models plausible, yet hard laws resist standard sampling priors. Their dual space scheme turns laws into penalties through an augmented Lagrangian, tightening them step by step with multiplier updates. Pairing alternating direction splitting with a particle sampler lets far off models still improve. Tests on a toy problem and seismic benchmarks show physical uncertainty estimates that tighten as data grow.
arxiv-2603-00493: Che and three colleagues estimate the six degree pose of a new object from a single reference view, where occlusion, viewpoint shifts, and outliers break one to one matching. Their COG framework treats correspondence as a confidence aware optimal transport problem, predicting per point confidences that weight transport and suppress non overlapping regions. Vision foundation model priors steady the matches further. Unsupervised COG matches supervised rivals, and supervised COG beats them.
arxiv-2603-00593: London studies partitions of bipartite graph edges into induced 2K2 free subgraphs, also called Ferrers or chain graphs. He defines fp as the smallest part count in such a partition. General bounds come from induced matchings and Dilworth widths of neighbourhood posets. Exact values cover paths and even cycles, while separations show both bounds can sit far from tight. A host induced conflict graph bound, a zero one matrix view, and complexity remarks round out the paper.
arxiv-2603-00693: Ager-Hart and four colleagues count Fubini rankings by parking outcome, where tied rankings encode race results and double as parking lists. Rankings with n competitors sharing a fixed parking outcome number two to the power of n minus k, where k counts runs in the outcome permutation. That formula reproves the total Fubini count. For l-interval rankings, where at most l plus one tie at any rank, the count becomes l-Pingala numbers multiplied by a power of two, set by run lengths alone.
arxiv-2603-01193: Viswanath and five colleagues train neural PDE solvers without costly data sets or unstable higher-slope losses, using Walk-on-Spheres Monte Carlo guesses as weak coaching. Their WoS-NO scheme spreads walk costs across PDE cases, fitting a neural operator against cheap noisy answer guesses in a data-free physics goal. It carries over zero-shot to new settings and domains. It cuts error nearly nine times, speeds training over sixfold, and uses about a third of the GPU memory of standard physics training.
arxiv-2603-01293: Javanmard, Mirzasoleiman, and Mirrokni study data quality and synergy in pre- and post-training thought models, using models on an in-context weight guessing task for linear fit. They find even pretrain data can induce latent skills later woken during post-training. Guided fine-tuning learns best from a small set of cases hard for the pretrain model, while overly large fine-tuning data sets may dilute useful pretrain signals. In contrast, reward learning works best on large-scale data not overly hard for the pretrain model.
arxiv-2603-01393: Otsuji, Fulla, and Fukunaga prove NP-completeness for the logic puzzle Hotaru Beam and give a physical zero-knowledge proof for it. In Hotaru Beam, players connect circles on a grid by drawing lines from set starting points with set bend counts. A zero-knowledge proof lets one player persuade another they hold a piece of information without revealing it. Their physical proof, implementable using physical items, proves knowledge of a puzzle solution without revealing it.
arxiv-2603-01493:
Tianyi Xu, Rong Shan, Junjie Wu, and colleagues built a test set for finding photos in personal albums in this 2026 work. Real albums hold years of images tied to places, people, and life events. Most past tests use lone web images, so they miss the rich links that shape real user requests.

Their set, PhotoBench, draws on real personal albums and builds a profile for each image. Profiles join what the image shows with time, place, people, and event facts. Queries built from life paths then ask for multi-step thought, not just visual match. Tests expose two flaws: fused models fail on non-visual limits, and agent systems juggle search tools poorly. Both flaws point to what photo search must fix next.
arxiv-2603-01693:
Issei Niwata, R. Kumar, Aswathi Chakkingal, and colleagues map the magnetic layout of the mineral rouaite at low field. Their 2026 work studies a copper-based crystal with chains that alternate between opposing and aligned spin pulls. Such clashes can force spins into layouts that are hard to guess from rules alone.

The team used nuclear magnetic resonance on single crystals, with hydrogen nuclei as tiny local probes. Internal fields in the ordered state were read directly from those probes. By matching the readings to model calculations, they fixed the directions of the ordered moments. The found layout points to a key role for Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions, a twist-like coupling between spins. The map sharpens theory for low-field states and sets up study of stranger states at high field.
arxiv-2603-01893:
Zijin Yin, Tiankai Hang, Yiji Cheng, and colleagues teach an image editor to reason visually before it edits. Their 2026 work faults editors that guess where to edit from text alone, which fails in busy scenes with subtle spatial requests. Their framework, GVCoT, first generates spatial cues that locate the target, then performs the edit.

Visual tokens from both phases train together end to end, so spatial reasoning grows inside the model itself. Labeled edit regions are scarce, so the team built a data set with millions of samples across many tasks. Training moves from supervised fine-tuning for basic localization to reward learning for polish. A new benchmark with complex scenes and fine referring phrases stress-tests the skill. The method beats top models on that benchmark and on a standard edit test.
arxiv-2603-02093:
Francesco Lin and Michael Lipnowski construct families of hyperbolic homology spheres with controlled spectral gaps. Their 2026 work concerns the coexact one-form spectrum of hyperbolic three-manifolds, a topic tied to homology growth conjectures. The spectral gap here is the first positive eigenvalue for coexact one-forms, a subtle invariant.

Their construction keeps that gap uniformly bounded below across the whole family of spheres. The family is also well suited to explicit computation, a rare practical virtue in this area. Several disjoint intervals are shown to contain a limit point of such spectral gaps. The rightmost interval is pinned down numerically at the top of the range. An arithmetic family of examples rounds out the work, answering a question posed by five named researchers.
arxiv-2603-02493:
Stefano Profumo tests quantum gravity with high-frequency gravitational waves in this 2026 paper. Tiny black holes from the early universe evaporate and emit Hawking radiation, gravitons included. Gravitons stream away without rescattering, unlike every other emitted species. They thus keep a clean record of how black hole temperature depends on mass.

Six beyond-standard frameworks predict different temperature-mass relations. Profumo computes the wave spectrum for each one with numeric methods. Suppressing temperature shifts the peak by up to ten orders of magnitude in frequency. Some shifts land inside future detector bands. Models with a hard cutoff for evaporation leave distinct peak shapes. Spectral shape, not peak position, proves the cleanest probe, since it ignores early universe conditions.
arxiv-2603-02593:
Radhika Kulkarni and Brani Vidakovic build stronger denoising transforms from wavelet matrices in this 2026 paper. Wavelet transforms are a cornerstone of signal and image cleaning. They preserve energy, reconstruct perfectly, and represent data at many scales. The authors ask whether combining several wavelet bases beats using one.

Composite transforms multiply, stack, and block wavelet matrices into new unitary transforms. These leave the strict filterbank class yet stay invertible and stable. Their key effect is concentrating signal energy into fewer coefficients than classic wavelets. Sparser codes denoise better under identical thresholding rules, quantified with Lorenz curves. Simulations on benchmark signals show steady error reductions. Tests on turbulence data and a classic image confirm cleaner results with salient structures preserved.
arxiv-2603-03393:
Amit Suthar extends a modern amplitude formula to surfaces that have only one side. Colored scalar scattering amplitudes can be computed by a curve integral formula, which assigns one shared set of parameters to every contributing Feynman diagram. Extending that neat combinatorics past orientable surfaces was open. His 2026 paper uses quasi-cluster algebras, built for non-orientable surfaces, to do it.

Each non-orientable surface is embedded in a doubled orientable one, and the needed features are projected back down. A strong check follows: a superstring amplitude with Möbius strip topology, pushed to its field-theory limit, reproduces exactly the diagrams the new formula gives. The construction generalizes to any higher-genus non-orientable surface. A two-loop example lists its curves and dual momenta and builds the surface version of the Symanzik polynomials.
arxiv-2603-03493:
Ihor Kendiukhov measures how easily gene network rankings flip when the scoring rules change. Benchmarks rank methods that infer gene regulatory networks from single-cell data, and papers cite those rankings as proof of quality. His 2026 study asks whether the order survives plausible changes in evaluation protocol, using existing benchmark outputs for six methods across three human tissues.

Four protocol choices were varied: which candidate genes count, which tissue, which reference network, and how gene symbols map. Rankings reversed for roughly one pair in six under candidate changes, one in five across tissues, and one in three across reference networks, while symbol mapping changed nothing. A permutation test shows the order is far from random, yet far from fixed. Reversals trace to genuine shifts in discrimination ability, not base-rate inflation. Kendiukhov proposes stability-aware reporting practices and releases a diagnostic toolkit.
arxiv-2603-03693:
G Shibukawa and S Tsuchimi present a new special function by pushing an old one to its limit. The general mu-function, due to Zwegers, sits inside the theory of mock modular forms. Their 2026 paper defines its degenerate descendant, the little mu-function, and develops its theory in parallel with the parent function's known traits.

The little function is derived as the q-Borel summation image of a divergent solution to the Ramanujan formula, the most degenerate second-order linear q-difference formula of Laplace type. Symmetries and connection formulas follow, mirroring the general theory. Two further families of relations appear: contiguous relations tied to a two-parameter Fibonacci sequence, and Wronskian relations involving the Rogers-Ramanujan continued fraction, one of the most famous objects in partition theory.
arxiv-2603-03993: Sagitova and others model specialization of softmax focus heads using a high-dimensional single-location method. Multi-head focus lets models represent several patterns at once, yet heads specialize in stages while many stay redundant. The first analysis tracks multi-head softmax focus under random gradient descent, finding an unspecialized opening phase followed by multi-stage specialization where heads sequentially align with latent signal directions. A second analysis studies how focus activation functions affect results, introducing Bayes-softmax focus, which reaches optimal output results in this setting.
arxiv-2603-04093: Sevenants and others reduce hyperparameter sensitivity in measurement-feedback Ising machines. Their evolution is often described with time-steady motion, yet most experimental setups use time-discrete measurement-feedback designs. The authors observe the working hyperparameter range is much smaller in such setups than in planned time-steady machines. They analyze this gap and its real impact, then propose and verify in tests a method reducing hyperparameter sensitivity.
arxiv-2603-04293: Prokopiou and colleagues present LabelBuddy, an open source tool for tagging music and audio with AI help. Rich human aligned representation is replacing static tags, but open annotation infrastructure has lagged behind. LabelBuddy decouples interface from inference with containerized backends, letting users plug in custom models for pre annotation. Several annotators can work jointly toward consensus, each model isolated in its own container, with agents and large audio models on the roadmap. The tool is free to use and open to all.
arxiv-2603-04593: Li and Stolyarov build PulSKASim for SKA scale pulsar work. Existing tools skip integration time and related observing settings, hurting realism in full pipeline tests. Their simulator tracks flux across period, peak flux, duty cycle, and noise, including smoothing inside each dump from finite integration. Snapshots from OSKAR and Pyuvsim functions carry pulsars at set flux levels, supporting per slot experiments. Calibration, imaging, and detection pipelines can then be judged under lifelike SKA like conditions, bridging variability modeling with interferometric simulation in a way past tools cannot match.
arxiv-2603-04693: Gao and Jackson study regulated partitions. The paper treats rectangular partitions of free Z to the n actions on Polish spaces. Main concepts are regulation numbers, defined as the maximum rectangles meeting at a point. These numbers are the minimum values over rectangular partitions. For n equal to 2, both numbers equal 3. For n at least 3, the Borel number exceeds n plus 1 and the number is at most 3 times 2 to the n minus 2. For n equal to 3, both numbers equal 5, showing a striking difference from dimension 2.
arxiv-2603-04893: Sean Lamont and colleagues tackle wasted computation in diffusion language models, where independent samples often collapse into the same failure modes. Their training-free method reshapes each sample in a batch in turn, pushing it away from earlier samples' feature space so redundancy is penalized. The intervention needs no retraining or beam search and adds negligible overhead, yet every sample contributes a distinct perspective. Tested with LLaDA-8B-Instruct on HumanEval and GSM8K, it lifts both diversity and Pass@k scores across temperature settings.
arxiv-2603-05193: Vésteinn Snæbjarnarson and team formalize a new class of language models built by transforming a model's output deterministically. A byte-pair model does not yield word guesses, nor a DNA model amino-acid chains, yet a change converts outputs to the desired form. Their method uses finite-state transducers, with algorithms composing model and transducer to marginalize over source strings and condition on transformed outputs. Tests converting tokens to bytes, tokens to words, and DNA to amino acids show models adapting at inference time to output needs.
arxiv-2603-05393: Nilanjana Chanda and Alessandro Lunghi stretch spin relaxation to three-phonon processes, applied to chromium nitride van der Waals crystal. Spin-lattice theory built over almost a century with unverified key interaction assumptions. Weak coupling enables small-step dynamics and one- and two-phonon accounts. Three-phonon contributions only matter at temperatures inaccessible to tests, giving unprecedented weak-coupling validity evidence. Number results show a small coupling lift would make a crossover between three- and two-phonon leanness at room temperature, illustrating possible three-phonon effects and strong-coupling exploration.
arxiv-2603-05493: Sundaralingam and colleagues present cuRoboV2, a unified dynamics-aware motion generation framework for high-DoF robots. Its B-spline trajectory optimization enforces smoothness and torque limits. A GPU-native distance-field perception pipeline runs up to 10 times faster while using 8 times less memory, with up to 99% collision recall. Scalable whole-body computation reaches up to 61 times speedup and extends to high-degree-of-freedom humanoids. It achieves 99.7% success under a 3kg payload and collision-free inverse kinematics on a 48-DoF humanoid.
arxiv-2603-06293: Hazra puts forward a wrapped Gaussian Markov random field for large spatial directional data, tackling compute challenges of wrapped Gaussian processes at large domains and high resolutions. With a sparse precision structure, the model gains much compute speed while keeping flexible spatial dependence on the circular scale. Key traits include identifiability and dependence characteristics, and fitting uses standard Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques.
arxiv-2603-06393: Ray and Skoric set out an epsilon approximate unitary 2-design for p and q quadratures in continuous variable systems, alternating q hat and p hat based unitaries. The design acts live on a finite discretisation of that space and operate on the full space, a first for such systems. Epsilon equals 1 over d to the power ell, with d the truncated Hilbert space dimension. An Unclonable Encryption scheme uses the design acts. Security follows from recent decoupling results, giving unclonable hidden security for such encryption.
arxiv-2603-06493: Kadhem asks how the Finite Selection Model's augmentation parameter affects estimator scores, through full Monte Carlo runs. The study tracks how bias, spread, and mean squared error respond to varied such values. Mid tuning lifts group balance and keeps gauge efficiency, while heavy tuning may raise spread and reduce gauge steadiness. The findings offer plain guidance on choosing that parameter for applied trial design.
arxiv-2603-06593: Sorokin and team present Hierarchical Embedding Fusion for repository view in code completion, a two-stage approach, where leaning on retrieved snippets ties inference cost to code size and adds noise. An offline cache turns code chunks into dense-vector trees with a fuser model. An online interface maps few found vectors into pseudo-tokens consumed by the code generator. On RepoBench and RepoEval, HEF hits snippet-based-baseline-comparable exact-match accuracy, at median sub-second latency on one A100 GPU.
arxiv-2603-06693: Joohyung Lee and colleagues propose Soft Equivariance Regularization, a small add-on that splits two training goals. The main self-taught goal stays on the final code, while a soft push toward shape-aware behavior acts on an earlier map of image parts. That split eases a trade-off seen when both goals share one layer. Tests show gains on image sorting, warped images, and object finding.
arxiv-2603-06793: Pham and colleagues propose Optimistic Policy Regularization, which turns high-return episodes that on-policy agents discard into a closed-form reward bonus. They build an elite action prior from the best quarter of episodes, then add a bounded transform of its log-ratio to the action distribution. The method needs no extra network, value gate, off-policy fix, or adversarial loop, amounting to a one-line change to PPO rewards. On many Atari games it reaches strong human-normalized scores with far fewer agent decisions than long baselines.
arxiv-2603-06993: Ni and colleagues present AdaGen, a learnable framework that sets the schedule for image synthesis per sample. Recent gains come from strong generative models that split synthesis into many steps, but that split creates many step-specific settings such as noise level or temperature. Past methods use hand-designed rules to manage them, needing expert skill and trial and error. Static schedules also fail to adapt to each sample, so AdaGen learns the schedule instead, giving better performance.
arxiv-2603-07393: Xu and colleagues review underwater robot autonomy through the lens of tightly linked physical limits. Thin communication, scarce energy, partial observability and hydrodynamic uncertainty interact inside the sense-plan-act loop and amplify each other over time. The review synthesizes progress in learning-based planning, belief-aware planning, hybrid control and multi-robot teamwork under this view. A cross-layer failure taxonomy then traces how errors cascade, pointing toward physics-grounded, verifiable autonomy.
arxiv-2603-07793: Vignat writes an identity by Ramanujan using polar coordinates, with its proof reduced to checking an elementary trigonometric identity. Polar form describes points by distance from an origin and angle, rather than by sideways and up-down spots. The trig fact at the heart of the proof uses only basic sine and cosine links. This approach produces a few spinoffs on the original, each following the same polar route.
arxiv-2603-07893: Aitken and colleagues address farmers facing uncertain weather at planting time, where no single forecast fits every farm. They build a decision-theory framework for shaping forecasts when advisers cannot simply prescribe the best action, then apply it to the seasonal start of monsoon rains. Their system blends benchmarked AI weather models with a new statistical model of evolving farmer expectations, using Bayesian inference. In 2025 a government program used it to send onset forecasts to 38 million Indian farmers, catching that summer's unusual dry spell early.
arxiv-2603-07993: Amano constructs a family of exact vacuum black brane solutions to 5D Einstein gravity with a negative cosmological constant. They center on a homogeneous horizon with Bianchi VI_h symmetry, generalizing the Solv geometry through a steady anisotropy parameter. The field equations reduce to a cohomogeneity-one system, letting the author derive the metric analytically. They are not asymptotically anti-de Sitter, yet their thermodynamics yield scaling links between entropy and heat. A new branch of Ricci-flat, hyperscaling-breaking vacuum solutions appears when the cosmological constant is zero.
arxiv-2603-08393: Bamidele and colleagues present a hybrid graph and spatial system for space-time risk mapping. Good spatial forecasts and strict error bars are central to modern spatial disease tracking and eco risk analysis. The system joins curved learning of a dynamic graph network with a latent Gaussian spatial process from model-based spatial stats. It jointly captures graph links encoded in graph shapes and smooth spatial links ruled by real nearness. Tests on mock data and malaria spread data compare it against older spatial models and solo graph nets.
arxiv-2603-08493: Jonathan Wurth and colleagues propose judging tuning methods by rank over time, not by raw score. That route needs no set bounds or known best score, and it holds steady when rivals join or leave. Their PolarBear plan uses a ranking model with calibrated doubt to drop beaten rivals early and keep only those no rival beats at every point in time.
arxiv-2603-08593: Lei Hu and colleagues speed up transient hunting for the Dark Energy Camera with graphics processors. The pipeline differences images, filters candidates with a neural real-or-fake check, and sends alerts and light curves to community brokers. It catches nearly all true transients while tossing most subtraction junk, and each exposure takes about fifty seconds from image to alert.
arxiv-2603-08993: Tony Mason presents Arbiter, a framework that detects interference in LLM agent system prompts. System prompts steer agent behavior but miss the test rigs ordinary software gets. Combining formal rules with multi-model scouring across three major coding agents, Arbiter finds 152 undirected findings and 21 hand-labeled patterns, showing prompt architecture tracks failure class but not severity.
arxiv-2603-09393: B. Michel Döhring and colleagues report on a new fast scan system that steps electron energy in fine increments for crossed-beams work at Giessen. The aim is to measure electron-impact ionization cross sections with a high-power electron gun built over recent years. Its multi-electrode design lets beam energy and beam density be set apart from each other. The paper describes the control system that sets the electrode potentials, plus the key technical features.
arxiv-2603-09593: Klaus Thomsen describes an extended future cover for sofic shifts, built as a cover of the future cover itself. The new cover is canonical in the same spirit as the future cover. In some cases it is isomorphic to the future cover, while in others it is a genuine extension of it. Thomsen then uses this construction to define the desynchronization of sofic shifts and describe it.
arxiv-2603-09993: Jon Chun and coauthors release CEI, a benchmark for pragmatic reasoning, the skill of reading meaning past literal words. Each scenario pairs a setting and speaker listener roles, with clear power relations, against an unclear utterance. Cases span sarcasm, mixed signals, strategic politeness, passive aggression and deflection in work, family and service settings. Human labels often disagree, and the authors treat that spread as informative rather than as noise.
arxiv-2603-10293: Patrick Bennett and Alan Frieze study when a random set of k-subsets, each kept independently with high probability, forms the bases of a matroid. They pin down a sharp threshold, with the chance tending to one, to a stated limit, or to zero as a tuning term moves. When the event occurs, the matroid is sparse paving with high probability. A greedy construction then improves known counts of matroids and their paving and sparse paving kinds, letting rank grow slowly with ground set size.
arxiv-2603-10393: Yeji Jo and Sang-Sung Lee study radio and gamma-ray changes in PKS 1222+216, a flat spectrum radio quasar, using monitoring data plus Fermi-LAT records. After a gamma-ray flare in late 2014, radio flux at several bands fell exponentially over a year. Fitting jet components gave cooling times of weeks to months, small viewing angles, and magnetic fields that decline slowly with distance. Timing suggests the flare came when a moving jet component hit a stationary feature, placing the gamma-ray site well beyond the broad-line region.
arxiv-2603-10893: Yuzhou Ji and coauthors introduce S2D. This pipeline rebuilds scenes as 3D Gaussian splats from very few input captures. Point clouds render poorly. Splatting also degrades under sparse views. S2D lifts a sparse point cloud with a one-step diffusion model. That model repairs image artifacts. A fitting strategy then keeps the reconstruction consistent across dense novel views. It uses random sample dropping and weighted gradients. The pipeline tops sparse-view quality tests at several sparsity levels.
arxiv-2603-11493: Shi and co-authors present OrthoEraser, a concept erasure method for text-to-image models that spares benign content. Erasing by silencing neurons can wound benign traits that share the same tangled activation space. OrthoEraser first uses sparse autoencoders to split activations and single out sensitive neurons. It then finds coupled neurons, the benign features at risk from the edit. The erasure vector is projected onto the null space of those coupled neurons. Harmful content drops away, the benign manifold stays intact, and safety scores beat prior best methods.
arxiv-2603-11693: Kim and Ting present pyKurucz, a pure Python rebuild of the Kurucz codes for stellar spectrum synthesis. ATLAS12 and SYNTHE, the standard tools, are decades-old Fortran that fights modern toolchains. The rebuild translates both engines line by line, dropping the Fortran need for good. NumPy, SciPy, and Numba power the loop, from opacity sampling to line broadening. Against the original, it matches to a median below 0.01 percent across 100 atmosphere models. The range runs from cool giants at 2500 K to O stars at 44,000 K.
arxiv-2603-11893: Tran presents a one-body perturbation method, OBMP2, applied to K-edge excitation energies. The method reshapes the Fock operator with a one-body correlation potential built from double-excitation MP2 amplitudes, then optimizes orbitals under correlation. This dodges convergence and accuracy troubles that hit plain MP2 on open-shell systems and stretched bonds. On closed-shell and open-shell test sets, the OBMP2-based approach beats ΔDFT, EOM-CCSD, and USTEOM-CCSD, the author reports. It stands as a robust new tool for K-edge states.
arxiv-2603-12093: McRobie extends graphic statics to rigid-jointed frames in three dimensions using homology theory. Graphic statics draws equilibrium in geometric form, unlike matrix-based structural analysis. Older versions need flat polygonal faces between bars, which many real frames lack. Cell complexes from CW homology replace polygons and polyhedra, so curved loop shapes fit too. Any frame splits into a union of closed loops made of bar circuits. Shear, bending, and torsion enter naturally in this second part of the series.
arxiv-2603-12593: Li-Yu Yu and co-authors tune bright broadband light in a multimode fiber by bending it, not by mixing its modes. They launch a high-order mode and apply programmed bends near the input. The bends shift group delay and dispersion while the mode stays fixed. With a standard pump, the output tunes smoothly across 700-1350 nm and keeps a clean Bessel-like profile. The team also used the source for multiphoton microscopy with a deep focus.
arxiv-2603-12793: Yichen Zhang and co-authors present Cheers, a single model that both understands and generates images. The two jobs want mismatched decoding styles and visual features, which makes joint training tricky. Cheers decouples patch details from semantic tokens to keep meaning stable. A unified tokenizer compresses image states for the language model core. A cascaded flow head then adds gated detail back for crisp output. On key benchmarks, Cheers matched or beat advanced unified models at far lower training cost.
arxiv-2603-13193: Dong Xiao works with Zahra Sharif-Khodaei and M. H. Aliabadi on tracking modes in elastic waveguides. Mode labels can swap near close crossings, which breaks SAFE dispersion analysis. The team uses perturbation theory for the single-parametric Hermitian case. They find how mode shapes change and how strongly modes couple. Veering, crossings guarded by symmetry, and equal modes each pose distinct tracking risks. A two-level scheme with an error flag and tests on sample cases back the theory.
arxiv-2603-13293: Rodrigo Tertulino and Laércio Alencar present FedCVR, a case study in secure cardiovascular risk prediction. Clinical data sit split across institutions under strict privacy rules, which blocks joint model building. Their framework uses federated learning with differential privacy across mixed clinical networks. Server-side adaptive optimization acts as a denoiser against statistical noise. In a synthetic test built to mirror real datasets, FedCVR held a stable F1 score and high AUC. It beat FedAvg, FedProx, and other adaptive methods under the same privacy limits.
arxiv-2603-13393: Daan Korporaal and co-authors present Colony Grounded SAM2 for finding bacterial colonies on agar plates. Detection and classification matter in microbiology, but labeled datasets are scarce. Their zero-shot pipeline joins Grounding DINO and Segment Anything Model 2, fine-tuned for the microbiology domain. No further training is needed for new settings, which aids robustness when data change. Mean Average Precision reached 93.1 percent, with a strong Dice score at detection. The full pipeline and model weights are shared open access for annotation work.
arxiv-2603-13593: The MicroBooNE Collaboration reports a new measurement of the electron neutrino cross section on argon, for events with no pions in the final state. It uses the full MicroBooNE booster beam dataset from Fermilab. Events are split by whether a proton passes the kinetic energy visibility threshold. Cross sections are given as a function of proton and electron energy and angle to the beam. The angle between the proton and electron is also studied. Most models match the lepton data well, with some gaps on the hadronic side.
arxiv-2603-13893: Perez and Fusco present UVLM, a shared loader that runs several vision-language models through one interface on Google Colab. Model families differ in vision encoders, tokenizers, and decoding, which makes fair comparisons hard. UVLM hides those gaps behind a single inference function with identical prompts. It supports LLaVA-NeXT and Qwen2.5-VL so far. Features include four answer types, majority-vote checks over repeat runs, and a chain-of-thought reference mode for benchmarking.
arxiv-2603-13993: Genilotti and co-authors test visual anomaly detection on real planetary images from the Moon and Mars. Space missions return far more imagery than people can inspect by hand. Rare features matter most, yet labeled examples are scarce and odd finds cannot be listed in advance. The team builds two benchmarks: lunar orbiter images with fresh and worn craters, and Mars rover surface images. Feature-based methods flag rare terrain well and stay light enough for onboard use.
arxiv-2603-14293: Bhore, Gupta, and Kumar improve online hitting set algorithms for structured and geometric set systems. Sets arrive over time, and the algorithm must keep a chosen set of elements that meets every set seen. For general systems, the best known ratio is doubly logarithmic and cannot be beaten. For systems with linear shallow-cell complexity, their weighted algorithm reaches a near single-log bound. The result gives the first bounds for natural geometric families, which closes open questions on the gap.
arxiv-2603-14593: Abubacar, Bauer and Kanojia test tiny recursive models for translation quality estimation. Recursive models refine answers by looping one shared network. The team checks if that loop helps score translations in low-resource languages. Tests span eight language pairs. Outside iteration hurts scores, they find, and inside recursion helps only in narrow ways. Frozen pretrained embeddings match fine-tuned ones while cutting trainable weights 37-fold. Their frozen model ties fine-tuned scores and beats a plain transformer of equal depth.
arxiv-2603-14893: Cacioli casts language models as signal detectors and tests a temperature-criterion analogy. Calibration scores mix two skills: telling right from wrong, and leaning bold or shy. Signal detection theory splits those parts cleanly. Three models face 168,000 factual trials in a pre-registered design. Temperature should act like a payoff shift if the analogy holds. It breaks instead, moving sensitivity and criterion at once. Evidence spread stays unequal, with z-ROC slopes from 0.52 to 0.84. Instruct models skew more than the base model, Cacioli finds.
arxiv-2603-15293: Rajendran and co-authors test a standard shortcut used to extract the Wigner delay from two-color photoionization. The shortcut splits the measured delay into a Wigner part and a universal infrared part. Their self-check setup uses spaced extreme ultraviolet harmonics instead of consecutive ones. Measured sideband phases missed the shortcut forecast by a few tens of milliradians, a few attoseconds in time. Full simulations matched the measured miss.
arxiv-2603-15393: Tong and co-authors characterize self-oscillations in discrete-time relay feedback systems with a dead zone. They focus on unimodal cycles, where the output peaks once per period. The linear part is stable, with an impulse response that falls in a strict monotone way. A total positivity framework drives the analysis. Such cycles can exist only when positive and negative loop gain values balance in count within the period, a sign-symmetry rule. The authors then give existence conditions, tight period bounds, and uniqueness results.
arxiv-2603-15893: Kumar and co-authors drive a phononic crystal cavity with electrostatic forces. Phononic crystals steer sound-like waves for filters and sensors. Cavities inside the bandgap trap motion and cut loss. The team embeds a double-ended tuning fork in a 1D crystal. Two flexural modes, in-phase and out-phase, share the device. The in-phase mode sits inside the bandgap. Its quality factor roughly doubles against an anchored twin. The out-phase mode gains little at low thermoelastic loss. The design suits sealed, low-loss phononic devices.
arxiv-2603-16193: Lama studies complementary edge ideals and asks which of them are licci. He gives a full description of that class in terms of the underlying graph. The description lets him link the licci property to other algebraic traits of the ideal. He also studies random graphs. For them, he finds two probability regimes. In one, the ideals are licci with high probability. In the other, they are not.
arxiv-2603-16293: Borca and co-authors report a survey of young physicists on training quality. The focus is software and machine learning for high-energy physics instruments. A 2021 study found most young researchers used open-source tools with no training. The new survey drew 174 participants. This report details what they said about access and quality.
