arxiv-2604-20093: Dobre, Wang, and Yang present FurnSet, a framework that rebuilds 3D scenes from a single view by exploiting repeated objects. Past methods rebuild objects alone or lean on implicit scene context, missing the repeats common in real rooms. FurnSet groups identical instances with per-object tokens and set-aware self-attention, pooling complementary views across repeats for joint reconstruction. Scene-level and object-level conditioning plus layout optimization over point clouds then align the scene, improving quality on 3D-Future and 3D-Front.
arxiv-2604-20293: Aly and Sharpanskykh test whether synthetic flight data can stand in for confidential real records and pad rare events. Their four-stage check rates two generative models, TVAE and Gaussian Copula, on statistical likeness, fidelity, diversity, and predictive use. Gaussian Copula wins on likeness and fidelity but costs too much compute for large data sets, while TVAE scales well. Synthetic-trained delay prediction matches real-trained accuracy, opening a path to richer predictive modeling in air travel.
arxiv-2604-20393: Zhang and six colleagues present MLG-Stereo, a vision Transformer pipeline for stereo matching that pushes global modeling past the encoder stage. A multi-granularity feature network balances global context with local geometric detail, handling images of any resolution and bridging train-inference scale gaps. A local-global cost volume captures locally correlated and globally aware matching clues. A local-global guided recurrent unit then refines disparity step by step under global guidance, with top results on Middlebury, KITTI-2015, and KITTI-2012.
arxiv-2604-20493: Yang, Xu, Zhao, and Li use a multi-phase transport model to trace a nonlinear flow signal in nuclear collisions. The signal probes quark-gluon plasma, hot freed-quark soup, in uranium-uranium and gold-gold crashes at 200 GeV. They track it through partonic flow, quark joining, and later particle scattering, watching shape quirks turn into motion patterns. The signal grows as the system expands, while its ratio between the two crash types stays nearly flat, keeping a cleaner read on the starting nuclear shape, including hexadecapole deformation.
arxiv-2604-21093: Bhavana Sajja offers a configurable testbed for spotting fraud rings on travel platforms, where gangs share devices, fake reviews, or chain loyalty transfers. Her simulated graphs cover three ring shapes across networks from 500 to 200,000 nodes, with each ring kept whole in one data split to stop answer leakage. GraphSAGE tops the tested methods and recovers every ring type fully, while device and IP sharing prove the strongest clues.
arxiv-2604-21193: Vipula Rawte and three colleagues make language-model claims checkable with DAVinCI, a two-stage framework. It first traces each claim to model parts and outside sources, then verifies it with entailment checks and tuned confidence. Across datasets including FEVER and CLIMATE-FEVER it lifts accuracy, attribution precision, recall, and F1 by 5 to 20 percent over verification-only baselines. A modular release lets existing pipelines adopt the approach.
arxiv-2604-21493: Rui Marques-Chaves and four colleagues present deep JWST spectroscopy of two UV-bright galaxies at redshift about 8.7, seeking very massive stars in the reionization era. Spectra show strong P-Cygni wind profiles and broad HeII emission. Models with very massive stars fit markedly better than models without them, and local very-massive-star spectra support the reading. Best-fit models imply stellar ages of roughly 2 million years and an initial mass function beyond 100 solar masses, evidencing an overabundance of very massive stars at high redshift.
arxiv-2604-21793: Awuklu and four colleagues build a logic-based method to detect high-level events from timestamped data and background knowledge. Logical rules capture when simple temporal events start and end, then combine them into meta-events. In medicine, disease episodes and therapies are inferred from diagnoses and drug use in patient records. Constraints weed out clashing events, with a fix that picks the best fitting sets. Limits keep data handling in polynomial time. A lung cancer test matches what doctors say.
arxiv-2604-21993: Xu and seven colleagues study detection of short-lived liquidity erosion, or crumbling quotes, in electronic order books. Seen quote decay may reflect mechanical withdrawal or repricing. Using the ABIDES simulator, crumbling emerges from random regime switches in a market maker, giving ground truth. A detection pipeline identifies mechanical quote erosion using order book features, and a neural model gives calibrated crumbling odds. Tests show the framework identifies crumbling events against agent ground truth, with the neural model beating rule-based baselines by 36 percent AUC.
arxiv-2604-22293: Sun and six colleagues make lookup-table neural networks practical on FPGAs, chips whose logic blocks map arithmetic onto hardware. Earlier lookup-table-aware training was far slower than standard training and needed manual tuning. Their HGQ-LUT method trains dense and convolution layers with regular tensor operations, then compiles them into tables. Fine-grained mixed-precision quantisation plus a resource estimator explores accuracy-versus-resource trade-offs with no manual tuning. It trains over 100 times faster on modern graphics processors, suiting CERN collider experiments.
arxiv-2604-22493: Jedelský studies first-order model checking, whether a graph satisfies a logical sentence, parameterized by variable-name count. That parameter is far stricter than quantifier rank, since a sentence can reuse few names across many quantifiers. Earlier work showed hardness by quantifier rank and a slower algorithm by variable count. Fast algorithms were known only for special graph families under the rank parameter. Jedelský asks which families admit such an algorithm, characterizing them in the monotone setting and proving a weaker result for hereditary families.
arxiv-2604-22593: Bulling and three colleagues analyze stability limits for gravity-induced entanglement in shielded setups. Proposed setups suppress electromagnetic forces between two masses with a Faraday shield. Superconductors need magnet shielding against dipole forces, given their diamagnetism. Residual particle-shield forces, both Casimir and dipole, can badly limit entanglement tests by imprinting phases. Run-to-run place and tilt shifts of parts, including shield, traps, and detectors, turn these phases into decoherence, reducing detectable two-party entanglement. Magnetic particle-shield forces emerge as a noise source, especially for levitated superconductors.
arxiv-2604-22993: Borysov and four colleagues present PHIN-GAN, a physics-informed generative network for high-fidelity simulation of particles passing through matter. Generating synthetic data sets at lab scale has become far too expensive. They derive analytical probability density functions for the straggling function and apply them at any point in phase space. Those forms enforce a distribution-level learning objective, yielding a generalizable proof of concept that matches GEANT4 fidelity at a fraction of the cost.
arxiv-2604-23093: Husain and three colleagues analyze a rare multiple open cluster system using Gaia DR3 astrometry and photometry. Clustering methods find a compact core of seven known open clusters plus two extra parts, including a fresh candidate, forming a nine-member group. Membership odds are refined by statistical modeling, including methods for tidal tail spotting. Backward orbits confirm matching motions over 20 to 30 million years, hinting a common origin in the same massive molecular cloud.
arxiv-2604-23293: Otsubo, Kido, and Mori study the hump-shaped strategy, in which players match others' contributions up to a threshold, then lower their own beyond it. Through agent-based simulations spanning group sizes and production shapes, they find this partial exploitation adaptive for the individual, especially in middle groups with step-like production functions. Exploitative as it is, the hump strategy lifts group-level cooperation. It forms a stable equilibrium with unconditional cooperators that jointly exclude defectors across many settings, showing that neglected behavioural variety can sustain large-scale cooperation.
arxiv-2604-23393: Chen and Li develop the large-sample theory of rerandomization for survival analysis, where outcomes are censored and the target is a whole survival curve rather than a single number. They prove that standard survival estimators converge to tight limits with smaller variance under rerandomization, while a debiased machine-learning estimator keeps its variance unchanged. Simulations and a real example illustrate the theory.
arxiv-2604-23493: Yadav presents K-SENSE, a system that spots stress and depression in social media posts by combining commonsense reasoning about mental states with a contrastive training scheme that sharpens its representations. A three-stage pipeline draws on a commonsense model, fuses two encoding streams into a shared anchor, and aligns same-class examples while suppressing irrelevant knowledge. It beats the strongest prior baselines on both stress and depression benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-23593: Wang and nine colleagues audit AI refereeing for security and trust as language models move into peer review. They map attacks across the whole review process and run controlled probes on ICLR papers with two advanced model referees. The probes isolate effects of prestige framing, strong assertions, rebuttal flattery, and poisoned context. Hidden prompt injections and other biases emerge as real failure points needing targeted, testable fixes.
arxiv-2604-23793: Mazumdar, Malakar, and Bhuyan test a gravity theory coupling non-metricity to matter across cosmic history, from Big Bang nucleosynthesis to late-time acceleration. Fitting DESI and earlier baryon acoustic data, cosmic chronometers, and gravitational-wave sirens with a nucleosynthesis constraint, they find strong agreement with observations and a clean transition from deceleration to acceleration. The model behaves like quintessence and stands as a viable rival to standard cosmology.
arxiv-2604-24193: Lall and three colleagues build a low-cost vision system for early detection of destabilized containers at sea. Vessel motion, wind, and heavy seas can slowly loosen stacks despite securing manuals, and new IMO reporting rules make early evidence urgent. The system segments container stacks in onboard camera footage, tracks them with optical flow, and extracts residual motion per container to quantify relative movement. Tests on real ship footage isolate container-level motion across sea states and visibility, giving early crew alerts and course adjustments.
arxiv-2604-24293: Hou and Tang show graph neural ODEs with positive irreducible mixing operators fall into a one-state trap. Information leaks and dynamics converge to one global consensus attractor. They propose the Hysteresis Graph ODE, coupling feature evolution with a latent potential from learned pairwise forces. A double-well edge potential and two-way gate let edges split into connected or insulated phases while keeping smoothness. The authors analyze the collapse cause and looping topology dynamics, testing the model on made-up diagnostics and graph benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-24393: Muthivhi and van Zyl track how linear regions evolve in self-taught deep ReLU networks. Taught, contrastive, and self-taught methods are tested on MNIST and FashionMNIST, using SplineCam to pull flat shapes. Region counts, areas, shapes, and edges are tracked, and region change tracks with model quality. Self-taught methods build far fewer regions for accuracy like that of taught models. Contrastive methods grow regions fast, while self-taught methods merge nearby regions. Region shape reveals model collapse early, suggesting shape scores show model quality and performance.
arxiv-2604-24493: Rana and Debnath introduce CA-IDD, a diffusion-based face swap method that moves a source face identity onto a target face while keeping pose, expression, and setting intact. Gaze cues, identity codes, and face-part maps guide the process through layered attention, replacing the less stable training of older adversarial systems. On standard checks it scored 11.73 on the face-quality scale used by the authors, beating known rivals, and kept identity steady across varied poses.
arxiv-2604-24693: Hsu, Beaglehole, Radhakrishnan and Belkin improve linear activation steering, a way to elicit model capabilities and specialize behavior with little labeled data. Fixed steering strength for all tokens gives uneven quality across prompts. Their Contextual Linear Activation Steering adapts strength to context. On eleven steering benchmarks spanning four model families, it consistently beats standard linear steering and matches or exceeds ReFT and LoRA with limited labeled data. The authors present it as scalable, interpretable and accurate.
arxiv-2604-24993: Lin and four colleagues propose Laplace-Bridged Smoothing, an analytic rework of randomized smoothing. Randomized smoothing gives promises for any classifiers but needs noisy training. Certification is costly, typically needing tens of thousands of passes per input, hindering edge deployment. Laplace-Bridged Smoothing replaces input-space Monte Carlo sampling with fast computations in a low-dim space. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, it beats the method and cuts per-sample cost by an order of magnitude. On Jetson Orin Nano and Raspberry Pi 4, speedups reach up to 494 times for edge use.
arxiv-2604-25093: Gushiken and three colleagues show energy absorption in silicon can be tuned by two-color double pulses. Using density functional theory, they examine wavelength effects on energy. They cover intensities and wavelengths of 515, 1030 and 2060 nm. At low intensity, multiphoton effects dominate, favoring short pairs. At high intensity, tunneling and intraband effects matter more, favoring long pairs. At mid intensity, a short pulse before a long pulse gives strong boost. The first pulse sets a nonequilibrium state shaping the second pulse's effect, raising energy gain.
arxiv-2604-25193: Keshvari, Tuxbury and Lin study adaptive sensing beyond non-adaptive information limits through end-to-end co-design of geometry, policy and inference. Information missed by hardware is lost downstream, yet existing approaches optimize hardware or adaptive measurement alone, rarely both. They formulate the co-design as joint dynamic programming over sensor geometry and a Bellman-optimal adaptive measurement policy. The outer hardware gradient comes from dynamic programming with a sharp Bellman maximum. Relaxations extend the framework from small discrete POMDPs to freeform light-based layouts with over 100,000 design pixels.
arxiv-2604-25293: Piene and Shapiro study families of plane algebraic curves sharing the same set of foci. They reformulate confocality via a focal map on equiclassical families and analyze its fibers using deformation theory. A family is confocal when all its curves share the same foci, a classical geometric condition. The focal map assigns to each family its focal data, and its fibers collect families sharing the same focal data. Deformation theory, the study of how geometric objects vary in families, provides the tools for analyzing these fibers.
arxiv-2604-25493: La Riviere and Chepiga probe single-ion anisotropy in the spin-1 J1-J2 chain, and transitions out of trimer order. Using large-scale simulations, they uncover five gapped phases and two floating phases. These liquid phases emerge from spreading zero-states and dimers in a trimer background. They are kept where net spin is zero, while spin excited states stay gapped. The Haldane-to-floating shift follows a mixed line with central charge c equal to 2, matching joint spin and spin-zero modes.
arxiv-2604-25893: Jing and Mudgal prove a structure theorem for integer sets with doubling at most 4 plus a small delta. Doubling compares a set's sumset size with the set's own size. Their result extends Eberhard, Green, and Manners, who handled doubling strictly below 4. It advances a question of Green about near-extremal sets. The paper is brief and technical, for additive combinatorics readers.
arxiv-2604-26093: Mohanty and Ro study diffusion with conservation at the part level, not for multi-pole groups. They ask whether the flow rules stay nonlinear. Part patterns yield curved rules with shear-only transport. In those rules, clumping in the initial edge distributions survives at long times because they are conserved. A linear regime appears only for small wobbles around a uniform background. They also derive rules for any dimensions, stable states under set limits, and a reading where the overall link keeps falling even when pairwise mutual information does not.
arxiv-2604-26393: Liu and Li simulated stellar clusters inside fuzzy dark matter halos to test wave dark matter through dynamical heating. Earlier work bounded the particle mass with a diffusion picture valid only when the de Broglie wavelength stays well under the galaxy's half-light radius. For very low masses, where the wavelength dwarfs the cluster, tidal heating dominates instead. A lighter soliton and a tidally stripped halo can damp that heating, so halo structure and environment matter for any mass bound.
arxiv-2604-26493: Mvondo-She studied log modes in critical topologically massive gravity at the chiral point, where massive and left-moving graviton modes merge into one another. Building the log mode as a parameter derivative, he showed that complexifying the radial coordinate gives it a many-valued structure with nontrivial monodromy. Left-moving and log modes then form an indecomposable Jordan-block representation, and monodromy alone fixes the two-point functions' log form up to normalization. The picture casts log modes as sources of branch-like bulk behavior.
arxiv-2604-26593: Haywood-Alexander, Duthé, and Chatzi built PiGGO, a physics-guided graph Kalman filter for virtual sensing of nonlinear structures. Digital twins struggle with unknown nonlinear dynamics and sparse sensing, undermining online state tracking. A learned graph neural ordinary differential equation serves as the state-transition model inside an extended Kalman filter, with physics-guided biases encoding structural links. The mix enables uncertainty-aware virtual sensing that spreads across similar topologies. Case studies beat open-loop graph models and standard filters under model doubt and sensor noise.
arxiv-2604-26693: López and seven colleagues run a model grid for Be X-ray binaries in the Small Magellanic Cloud. They seek the evolution parameters that reproduce both the count and the joint period and magnitude spreads. The best match comes from models where Roche-lobe overflow mass transfer stays always stable. Tides recycle angular momentum into the orbit as the accretor nears peak rotation. Favored models use low natal kicks under 100 kilometres per second, mass transfer rate near three fifths, and strong propeller blocking of neutron-star accretion.
arxiv-2604-26993: Moon builds a state-based Lyapunov framework for gradient descent on rank-one matrix factorization, a method that splits a matrix into simpler factors. A quadratic certificate orders nested level sets, and each point gains a state that moves inward along descent paths. That geometry pins down the limiting motion even when nearby stationary points are unstable, giving convergence to a global minimizer below a stability threshold and a balanced two-cycle beyond it.
arxiv-2604-27293: Gao and Hang propose ALC-YOLOv8s, an improved model for recognizing student classroom behavior from video, built on YOLOv8s. Classroom behavior reflects learning state and participation, aiding teaching quality analysis. Real scenes pose dense targets, many small objects, frequent occlusions, and imbalanced classes. Their model adds SPPF-LSKA for contextual feature extraction, CFC-CRB and SFC-G2 for multi-scale feature fusion, and ATFLoss for minority classes and hard samples. Against baseline, it improves mAP50 by 1.8 percent.
arxiv-2604-27593: Parisot updates DeepSpaceYoloDataset, a collection of annotated images for training YOLO models to detect deep-sky objects with smart telescopes. Published in 2023, the data set targets Electronically Assisted Astronomy for a wide audience, not just major observatories. The update adds a new evaluation split, test2026, with a greater diversity of images. It aims to give detection models a broader test than the earlier splits allowed.
arxiv-2604-27693: Ghasemi and Grange introduce cluster first-order logic, a narrow slice of first-order logic built to probe order invariance. Whether such a formula holds stays fixed no matter how its order reads, even though its vocabulary contains an order. While this logic can define properties beyond plain first-order logic in general, its power falls inside first-order logic for graph classes of bounded degree. They prove this by building linear orders that keep similar structures similar when expanded with those orders.
arxiv-2604-27893: Nunes, Coutinho, Bezerra, and Machado hunt code smells in Angular apps, where React smells are mapped but Angular ones are not. From blogs, docs, and shop talk, they gather 11 Angular smells, six also found in React, and sort each by shape. They build an auto static checker for these smells, test it on a hand-checked set, and score accuracy above 0.88 with strong F1 marks. Repeat offenders include overloaded parts, copied logic, and wasteful template links, and the catalog gives studies a base for cleaner front-end code.
arxiv-2604-28193: Gupta and colleagues present GenWildSplat, a feed-forward system that rebuilds outdoor 3D scenes from sparse, unposed internet photos. From learned geometric priors it estimates depth, cameras and 3D Gaussians in a common space, adapts appearance to target lighting, and segments transient objects away. Trained by curriculum on synthetic and real data, it generalises across lighting and occlusion patterns. It renders in real time with state-of-the-art feed-forward quality on two benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-00293:
Artem Petrov, Guillermo A. Hernández-Mendoza, and Alfredo Alexander-Katz study tiny droplets of block copolymers stuck to a surface. These droplets, only tens of nanometers wide, can arrange themselves into ordered patterns useful for electronics, sensing, photonics, and even cryptography. Whether a single droplet could switch its inner pattern on demand was unclear.

Using large-scale field theory calculations, the team mapped a full diagram of droplet shapes across wetting and separation conditions, without assuming the answer's form in advance. The patterns matched published experiments closely. Crucially, droplets could switch back and forth between patterns when the interaction between their two components changed, as it does with added surfactant or shifted temperature. The finding points toward smart coatings whose fine structure answers to outside signals.
arxiv-2605-00393:
Haichen Hu, Jian Qian, and David Simchi-Levi attack the computing cost of reinforcement learning in large environments. Standard regret-minimizing algorithms call planning and estimation subroutines again and again, and the bill grows with the number of states and actions, which rules out huge or continuous settings. Oracle-efficient methods try to call those subroutines rarely, but earlier versions still scaled with the environment's size.

Their algorithm, built on log-barrier and log-determinant regularization, keeps the optimal square-root regret rate while making only a doubly-logarithmic number of oracle calls when the horizon is known. Crucially, that count does not depend at all on how many states or actions exist. The framework extends from tabular problems to linear ones with infinite state spaces and arbitrary actions, still with sublinear regret. The authors call it the first doubly oracle-efficient method of its kind for such large problems.
arxiv-2605-00493:
Maksym Nechepurenko presents ForesightFlow, a framework for detecting informed trading on decentralized prediction markets. Its Information Leakage Score measures, for a market settled by a public event, how much of the final price move was already priced in before the news broke. Three scope conditions must hold before a score can be interpreted at all.

A pilot evaluation produced uncomfortable findings. A cheap proxy for the news timestamp failed to separate event-settled markets from matched controls, with the separation running backwards, proving proxy quality is a binding constraint. On one high-stakes case, a timestamp taken from articles shifted the score dramatically and flipped its sign. Auditing documented insider cases showed they are systematically settled by deadline, outside the original scope entirely. The paper therefore introduces a deadline-based extension of the score, and releases its case inventory, market classification, and code.
arxiv-2605-00693:
Sumanta Chakraborty, M. V. S. Saketh, Tanja Hinderer, and Jan Steinhoff study how spinning black holes respond dynamically to tidal fields, the stretching forces from a companion in a binary system. Tidal response shapes the gravitational waves a binary emits, so it must be modeled with care. The authors work within effective field theory, where each compact object is a worldline carrying internal degrees of freedom for finite-size effects.

They analyze Kerr black holes under generic-spin perturbations, mainly for scalar and gravitational cases, to linear order in frequency. Matching the field theory description to full perturbation solutions yields the dynamical Love number and an approximate response with both dissipative and conservative parts. Mode mixing caused by spin proves essential for a consistent match.
arxiv-2605-00793:
Zhilin Guan and Wei Zhang address noise in low-dose liver CT scans. Lower radiation dose protects patients, but the extra noise can hide detail and affect diagnosis. Clean paired examples from real clinical care are hard to obtain, so supervised training is limited. The authors build an unsupervised system inspired by Cycle-GAN to clean the scans without such pairs.

Their framework combines a U-Net for features at several scales, attention for fusing them, and a residual network for transforming them, plus a perceptual loss tuned to medical images. They also build a real low-dose dataset and run many comparisons. Scores and reviews by imaging doctors suggest the results meet clinical needs.
arxiv-2605-00993:
Katja Fahrion, Michael Hilker, Avinash Chaturvedi, Juan P. Carvajal, and Thomas H. Puzia reconstruct the history of NGC 1427A, a star-forming low-mass galaxy near the center of the Fornax cluster. Such galaxies show how ram-pressure stripping, tidal forces, or mergers shape star formation. The team combines integral-field spectroscopy from MUSE with multi-band imaging, using both the integrated spectra and star clusters as surviving tracers of past episodes.

Ages and masses are fitted for more than two hundred cluster candidates, with spectra added for a subset and good agreement between methods. Cluster ages and the reconstructed history both show multiple star formation episodes, including a very young population and an intermediate-age one. The authors infer stripping plus tidal interaction or a minor merger.
arxiv-2605-01393:
Abhishek Vivekanandan, Ahmed Abouelazm, and J Marius Zöllner ground self-driving motion forecasts in a bank of real, readable example paths. Standard systems either hide their guesses in opaque learned queries, which can collapse to sameness, or sample paths naively, which limits variety.

Their framework builds a motion bank, a structured space of physically possible paths learned by contrast. At run time, a retrieval layer picks fitting example paths from the bank using adapted queries and a sampling trick that keeps training smooth. A decoder then refines the picked paths, trained with a winner-takes-all mixture model and extra terms that reward variety and close endpoints. Because each forecast starts from a named, sensible path type, the output stays open to inspection. On the Argoverse 2 and Waymo motion data sets, scores stay competitive with the best opaque systems.
arxiv-2605-01593:
Ammar A Ellaboudy, Valentin V Karasiev, and S X Hu simulate shocked hydrogen-helium mixtures to test a claimed sign of planet-interior physics. Laser-shock experiments on a mix with a small helium share suggested the two elements unmix inside Jupiter, reading breaks in reflected light as the fingerprint of separation.

The team run first-principles molecular dynamics along the main shock curve. One modern thermal functional handles the equation of state and ionic shapes. A range-separated hybrid covers the optical traits, chosen for its band-gap accuracy in warm dense matter. Their reflectivity tracks the measured values well overall, yet shows no break at high temperatures, and the mixed system's values sit inside the range where unmixing was inferred. The moral is diagnostic caution: at low helium shares, reflectivity alone may not uniquely betray demixing under these conditions.
arxiv-2605-01693:
Khalid Mahmud Labib, Inayat Rasool, and Shabbir Ahmed race two data-driven models of lithium-ion battery voltage against each other on pulse-test data. Voltage behavior bends with load and age, and a faithful model underpins charge estimation, control, and health tracking.

One contender is operator-theoretic: delay-stacked snapshots of voltage and current feed a control-aware mode decomposition, which returns an interpretable state-space model for step-by-step prediction. The other is a physics-guided transformer that splits voltage into a computed open-circuit part and a learned dynamic leftover, with a pathway shaped for the known pulse profile. On a thirty amp-hour cell both catch the sharp pulse transients. The operator model wins on error and on toughness as the cell degrades, at least on this small data diet, while the transformer shows more flexibility that larger data could feed.
arxiv-2605-01793:
Anirudh Shankar, Avhishek Chatterjee, and Anjan Chakravorty price the memory appetite of artificial intelligence in energy terms. Models keep growing, and with them the data they must store and move. Memory traffic in data centers is a major and rising share of AI's carbon footprint, yet it lacked a general measuring frame.

Their framework estimates the memory cost of a model analytically, giving a foundational count of the ecological bill that training and inference run up through memory alone. A shared yardstick of this kind is what sustainable design needs. Architects can compare layouts before building them. Operators can attribute footprint to the memory system rather than to compute in the lump. The authors offer the framework as groundwork for architectural strategies that treat energy per remembered bit as a first-class design target.
arxiv-2605-01993:
Paola Testa and colleagues review why elements in the Sun's corona differ in abundance from those in its visible surface. Elements that ionise easily are often enhanced, a pattern called the FIP effect. Evidence points to the chromosphere, the layer where those easy elements are mostly ionised while harder ones stay neutral, as the place where the sorting happens.

The authors discuss recent studies that looked for signs of coronal abundance patterns in the lower atmosphere. They also note the limits of current observations. Open questions remain about how the lower layers leave such a footprint, and future data should help separate competing accounts of fractionation, the process that changes element shares by height.
arxiv-2605-02093:
Octavio Arizmendi and Katsunori Fujie revisit the finite R-transform, Marcus's finite free analogue of Voiculescu's R-transform in free probability. They take an analytic route, linking the finite free Fourier transform to the Laplace transform. That link lets them study the finite transform through log potentials and Legendre transforms, tools from classical analysis.

Under suitable assumptions, they prove the finite R-transform of a polynomial differs from the Voiculescu transform of its root distribution by a term of order one over the degree. As an application, they give an analytic proof that finite free additive convolution tends to free additive convolution. The work grounds a finite theory in its limiting free counterpart.
arxiv-2605-02293:
Krzysztof Lider and Marek Góźdź model the Deutsch algorithm, a basic quantum algorithm, with a two-level harmonic oscillator in the second quantisation formalism. Their aim is a physical description of how quantum gates transform states, rather than a purely abstract circuit account. Within that frame, they derive the evolution operators for the algorithm.

The authors present a projection evolution model that characterises state transformation inside quantum gates. The method gives a systematic way to find evolution operators for gates. It also allows a full description and prediction of how a state evolves, including projection errors that an ideal circuit model would hide. The Deutsch case serves as the worked example for the approach.
arxiv-2605-02593:
Costa Georgantas and Jonas Richiardi build risk scores that a person can compute by hand, without giving up predictive power. Risk scores assign points for a short list of traits and are used in medicine, insurance, and risk work. Most are built from linear regression, which can miss curved effects in the data.

Their algorithm uses gradient boosting, a method that builds many small trees in sequence, to capture nonlinear patterns, then compresses the result into a compact score. Software is provided in C++ with bindings for Python and R. Across twelve datasets covering regression, classification, and time-to-event tasks, the method matched rivals on accuracy while using far fewer rules. Shorter scores are easier for practitioners to apply and explain.
arxiv-2605-02693:
Marcos Matabuena and Mateo Cámara develop a random-effects method for repeated measurements whose outcomes are not numbers but objects, such as distributions or graphs. Many studies measure the same unit several times, and random effects capture each unit's own tendency, improving estimation and personal prediction. Such models are standard for scalar outcomes and workable for curves, but general metric-space objects lacked a full framework.

Their algorithm builds on Fréchet methods, which extend averages to metric spaces, and is framed as an M-estimation problem. Conditions are given under which the prediction target is consistently estimated. Tests on synthetic data and digital health datasets, including distributions and random graphs, show good performance. Notably, the method can beat approaches built for Hilbert spaces, even though it assumes less structure.
arxiv-2605-02993:
Mark M. Bailey, Matthew J. Hasenjager, and Nina H. Fefferman test a spectral method for slowing contagion on hypernetworks, where contacts involve groups, not just pairs. Their hypergraphs are built from three classic random graph families by promoting full cliques to hyperedges. The question is which hyperedges to remove so a spreading process dies down most, per removal spent.

For each network they build a line graph whose nodes are hyperedges, linked when they overlap enough. Spectral clustering of that graph gives a cut-persistence score, used to rank hyperedges for removal across scales. Simulations show the payoff depends strongly on topology. The spectral ranking beat random removal in one family, but only matched or trailed it in the other two. Structural importance alone, the authors caution, does not guarantee the best suppression.
arxiv-2605-03093:
Dushmanta Sahu reports the first identification of the Einstein-de Haas effect in hot QCD matter, the state made in heavy-ion collisions. In that classic effect, aligning spins under a magnetic field forces a compensating rotation so total angular momentum stays conserved.

Using an equilibrium hadron gas in an external field, Sahu finds even leftover fields at freeze-out induce rotation at levels matching typical vorticity estimates from hyperon data. No starting vorticity is needed; the field alone creates it. The result frames QCD matter as a self-vortical magnetofluid and adds spin-rotation coupling to its angular momentum story.
arxiv-2605-03393:
Riddhiman Bhattacharyya, Sayak Chakrabarty, and Imon Banerjee give the first adaptive estimator with strong guarantees for offline contextual Markov decision processes. No stationarity is assumed. Contextual processes guide decisions from biostatistics to machine learning. Yet offline use lacked robust, theory-backed methods.

Context from inside the system breaks standard tools. It brings drift and model irregularity. Using T-estimation, they build a selector and prove oracle risk bounds under two losses. They then use the density estimate for optimal control. Finite-sample guarantees for the cost follow, under broad conditions, not narrow special cases.
arxiv-2605-03693:
Pietro Colombo and five co-authors build a framework for fusing environmental data from sources of different quality, such as noisy satellite products and sparse but accurate ground sensors. Their tool is multi-fidelity Gaussian processes, extended to handle cases where patterns change across space or time. The goal is sharp maps rebuilt with full likelihood-based inference.

A split covariance form lets the Vecchia approximation act directly on the low-fidelity and gap processes. A Woodbury-based step then keeps the likelihood math stable and fast, without ever forming the full covariance matrix. A least squares step with fidelity-specific offsets stops bias from leaking into the cross-fidelity links. Tests include synthetic data and a large-scale wind speed case.
arxiv-2605-03793:
Lauri Lovén proves an honesty property for scored oversight mechanisms. In these systems, an agent reports private information to a principal who scores the report. Such systems appear in AI oversight, forecasting, and expert surveys. The agent's type captures its information quality relative to a reference, and reports pass through an outcome interface with many dimensions, scored by a power-p pseudospherical rule.

Honest reporting is dominant-strategy optimal for every dimension and every allowed power, without any prior over the agent's type, with a quadratic loss rate for misreports. The quantitative core, the True-KL0 property, certifies one curvature margin for the misreport channel. The margin comes through a Rayleigh quotient bound. The proof uses a substitution that simplifies the loss integral. It also uses log-concavity arguments, algebraic in two dimensions.
arxiv-2605-03893:
David Gamarnik, Miklós Z. Rácz, and Gabe Schoenbach study the problem of finding large common induced subgraphs of two independent random graphs. Chatterjee and Diaconis recently showed the largest such shared structure has size about four times the base-two logarithm of the number of vertices. The question here is what online algorithms, which must commit to vertices as they arrive, can achieve.

A simple greedy online algorithm reaches about half the optimal size, two times the logarithm. The main result proves no online algorithm can do better: none finds a common induced subgraph of size above that threshold with probability bounded away from zero. The proof uses a version of the overlap gap property plus an interpolation argument, suggesting a genuine computation-to-optimization gap.
arxiv-2605-04293:
Daniel Verscharen and eight co-authors review how electrons travel through tangled magnetic fields in space plasmas. Cosmic fields are rarely smooth; plasma flows, turbulence, and instabilities twist them, and electrons mostly follow the field lines in tight spirals.

The review explains the basic principles first, then how tangled fields form and how waves and particles interact along the way. It covers electrons becoming trapped and escaping again, plus movement and energy gain across the field. Because spacecraft measure these electrons directly, their behaviour helps map how field lines connect across space.
arxiv-2605-04693:
Waseem Akbar and Michał Zegrodnik compare two theories of the superconductivity recently observed in twisted bilayers of a transition metal dichalcogenide, focusing on tungsten diselenide. In these moiré materials, two atomic sheets rotated slightly create a pattern that strongly reshapes electron behaviour.

One approach uses a negative-U Hubbard model, a fairly conventional pairing picture where strong repulsion barely touches the paired state and a uniform s-wave gap emerges. The other uses a t-J-U model that builds in strong correlations, renormalises the electrons heavily, and allows unconventional gap shapes. The authors compare the two states' key properties and weigh them against the available experimental observations.
arxiv-2605-04893:
Dominik Dahlem, Diego Maniloff, and Mac Misiura study what can truly be learned about a language model from the spectrum of its attention operators. Each attention head moves information between tokens, and a growing set of diagnostics reads behaviour, including hallucination, from that movement's spectrum. The authors split the operator into a symmetric part for capacity and an antisymmetric part for direction.

They prove a hard limit: any diagnostic unchanged under transposing is blind to the direction of information flow. On the capacity side, they derive exact bounds that differ for full and windowed attention. Their two-axis diagnostic makes a testable prediction that held in sign under controlled checks.
arxiv-2605-04993:
Vasilis Perifanis and four co-authors forecast electric vehicle charging demand early in each session, using only information available at plug-in and in the first minutes. Knowing a session's total energy early helps grid stability, planning, and live charging decisions. Their data come from the Adaptive Charging Network at a single depot, Caltech.

The authors build session features covering user intent, timing patterns, and early charging behaviour, splitting stations into separate clients. Models are then trained in a federated way, keeping data at the depot instead of pooling it centrally. Federated models approached centralised accuracy, showing early estimates can be reliable with very little data.
arxiv-2605-05093:
Jia Wei He, Ayesha Ali, and Gerarda Darlington propose a regression method for high-dimensional data where predictors themselves form a network. Sparsity saves computation and highlights the predictors most tied to the response. When predictors can be drawn as a Gaussian graphical model, that graph structure can guide the regularisation instead of being ignored.

Their model splits the coefficient vector into latent parts, one contribution per graph node, and penalises those parts directly. A penalty balancing two common norms, plus a new projection step during optimisation, avoids duplicating predictors and saves resources. Simulations across graph shapes and sizes, plus real data, suggest stable performance from the approach.
arxiv-2605-05193:
Paata Ivanisvili and Xinyuan Xie report five mathematical discoveries made in collaboration with the Grok language model, each subsequently verified by the authors themselves. The findings span several areas of analysis and combinatorics. They include an improved lower bound on the largest Gaussian perimeter of convex sets and sharper moment comparison inequalities on the Hamming cube.

The remaining results strengthen an autoconvolution inequality, improve asymptotic bounds on the size of the largest special Sidon-type sets, and give an optimal balanced form of Szarek's inequality. As a short note, the work doubles as a case study in machine-assisted discovery, with human verification supplying the mathematical guarantee behind each claim.
arxiv-2605-05493:
Joshua C. Chang introduces a family of statistical models borrowed from physics. The renormalization group idea behind them stacks effects from coarse scales to fine ones. His models split the input space into a lattice, and each cell of the lattice adjusts the regression parameters at its own scale.

The same models can be read as piecewise linear models, mixed-effects regressions, or structured regression trees. Using replica analysis from statistical physics, Chang studies the WAIC score as a stand-in for generalization error. He derives guidance on lattice size and on how strongly to penalize finer terms, and tests the method on public data.
arxiv-2605-05693:
Quantizing a large model for use usually sets each layer to rebuild the layer below it as closely as possible. Yanlong Zhao and eight co-authors question that aim on broader grounds. The tuning data are limited and possibly unrepresentative, so pure rebuild error can drag quantized weights away from the originals and hurt real performance.

Their regularized tuning scheme adds saliency awareness, weighting what matters for the model's behavior. The approach covers both scale-search and Gram-based tuning styles. The aim is quantized models that keep their full-precision behavior on data nobody calibrated for.
arxiv-2605-05893:
Verifying a model's reasoning usually means paying humans or teachers to build labeled datasets. Xinyu Wang and six co-authors propose LoVer, an unsupervised verifier disciplined by logical rules instead. The verifier is treated as a latent judgment over multiple reasoning paths, constrained three ways: negated answers must score oppositely, paths within an answer group must agree, and groups must differ.

Those constraints let LoVer learn from unlabeled examples and attach to any off-the-shelf model. Experiments across ten datasets show the logic-regularized verifier eliciting stronger reasoning. Supervision, the work suggests, can be partly replaced by consistency.
arxiv-2605-06093:
Vishal and Malay Nandy study whether quantum cosmology can resolve the big bang singularity in a relational time framework. Their setting is a plane symmetric Bianchi type I universe described by the Wheeler-DeWitt equation of quantum gravity. That equation has no built in time variable, which is the classic problem of time in this field.

The Page-Wootters formalism supplies time by conditioning the global state on a clock subsystem. The authors build an entangled global state as a Gaussian superposition and derive the matching conditional probability density. That density vanishes at zero volume for all clock values, which they read as quantum resolution of the classical singularity. Positivity of the density also limits which clock values are admissible.
arxiv-2605-06693:
Irshadullah Khan and Bilal Khan give a quadratic-form representation of the scalar Casimir trace, a spectral quantity tied to vacuum energy, using a codimension-three reduction of a Riesz operator. Under a fixed heat-regularized Gaussian source covariance, they track how a product operator splits into a brane part and a transverse part. They identify the critical exponent where the reduced operator becomes the ordinary Green operator.

With that kernel, the expected quadratic energy of the source equals exactly the heat-regularized Casimir trace. In the classic parallel-plate geometry the formula reproduces the standard finite part. The authors stress the result is a scalar spectral representation only, with no claims about electromagnetism, gravity, or fundamental constants.
arxiv-2605-06993:
Tobias Maringgele and Jalal Etesami ask which experiments are worth running when a causal effect cannot be fully pinned down from observations alone. Experiments can tighten the bounds on an answer, but they cost money. The authors define a measure of how much an experiment is guaranteed to narrow those bounds.

They show choosing the best set under a budget is computationally hard. Two graph-based pruning rules, using only the causal graph and the question, discard half to most candidate experiments in their tests. A demonstration on health survey data selects experiments for estimating how physical activity affects diabetes, showing the full workflow end to end.
arxiv-2605-07093:
Zezheng Lin, Fengming Liu, and Handi Li audit what they call the translation tax in multilingual benchmarks. Translated tests are often assumed to inflate scores by keeping helpful English cues, treated as one simple number. The authors check that claim on benchmarks translated from English into Chinese.

Three estimation methods disagree with each other, pointing to model-family effects rather than a uniform tax. A stress test that rewrites Chinese wording while holding content fixed finds an effect tied to leftover English residue. High-residue items benefit, low-residue ones do not. The authors release their evidence, checks, and a reporting checklist for translated benchmark work.
arxiv-2605-07193:
Fred Zhangzhi Peng and three co-authors generate discrete data, like text or designed sequences, in a single step. Generation usually needs step-by-step decoding or many refinement rounds. Their Coupling Models learn a direct pairing between discrete sequences and Gaussian noise variables, then train a decoder to invert that pairing in one pass.

Unlike distillation methods, nothing starts from a pretrained multi-step sampler, and no continuous flows over probability simplices are needed. Across text generation, fly brain enhancer design, and binary image generation, the model improved on the strongest one-step baselines in each domain. The gains suggest the pairing between data and noise matters greatly.
arxiv-2605-07393:
Hongqiang Lin and five co-authors tune robot policies from fixed offline data without the excessive pessimism that usually guards against unknown ground. Model-based offline learning must avoid using model errors outside the data, yet heavy pessimism sacrifices reach. Their PSPO method treats the dynamics model as a random variable drawn from a posterior, not a single estimate.

That framing allows careful probing of new regions that still fit real dynamics. Trading off posterior and policy updates gives a tuned method that provably settles. On standard benchmarks PSPO beat leading rivals, and checks confirm it stays robust without pessimism, with each part helping in removal tests.
arxiv-2605-07493:
Khulan Tumenbayar studies a geometry problem about plane curves of degree four, called quartics, that have two nodes and one cusp as their only rough points. Against such a curve she considers conics that touch it in a special even way at every meeting point. The question is which conics can occur for a given quartic.

Tumenbayar answers by passing to a rational elliptic surface, a related curved space that arises naturally from the quartic and one smooth touching point. Reading the geometry there lets her list every possible conic. As a payoff, she builds Zariski pairs, two curve arrangements of degree seven and eight that look alike combinatorially but differ in deeper geometric ways.
arxiv-2605-07693:
Shaoheng Yan and five co-authors improve the representations behind molecule generation, where a model first encodes a molecule and then builds a three-dimensional structure conditioned on that encoding. The bottleneck is the representation space itself: popular pretrained encoders like UniMol produce jagged, non-smooth codes that generative training does not fully exploit.

Their framework, LENSEs, adds a jointly trained head. It also adds a perceptual loss measured in the learned space, and an alignment loss tying the generator's hidden states to the encoder's. On the hard GEOM-DRUG dataset it reached validity above ninety-seven percent and stability above ninety-eight percent, beating leading methods. Probing tasks and smoothness measures confirmed the refined codes carry more usable information.
arxiv-2605-07793:
Allya Nurul Islami Pasha and four co-authors present a compact sentiment analysis study for Indonesian social media text, classifying posts as positive, negative, or neutral. Their practical baseline pairs TF-IDF text features with three lightweight numeric metadata features and a balanced multinomial logistic regression classifier. A two-layer neural network over the same features serves as the comparison.

After cleaning, the dataset held just over seven hundred samples with a strong positive skew, drawn from a much finer-grained emotion dataset. Logistic regression reached about eighty percent accuracy and the better weighted F1 score, while project notes report a higher-accuracy neural model that was not production-ready. The lesson: careful preprocessing and class balancing keep simple models competitive on small datasets.
arxiv-2605-07993:
Nikita Dhawan and three co-authors make sensitivity analysis for causal inference less pessimistic and more honest. Causal conclusions rest on untestable assumptions, and the standard check asks how badly things could go in the worst case. The authors argue that worst-case thinking often becomes uninformative, or demands changes to the world no one believes, contradicting prior knowledge.

They generalize the s-value framework to three common causal assumptions and add a Bayesian sensitivity value. The new value is the expected sensitivity of an estimate to assumption violations, averaged under priors built from real-world evidence rather than adversarial extremes. Monte Carlo approximations make it computable. An observational study of diabetes treatments and weight loss illustrates the method in practice.
arxiv-2605-08093:
Maribeth Rauh and coauthors score the five most popular AI companion phone apps. These apps are built to mimic close personal bonds. Big chat platforms draw research and legal heat, but apps made for closeness remain little studied, even as their use grows fast.

The team coded each app's user flow by hand. They counted design tricks that push one-sided attachment or steer users. They logged dark patterns, human-like cues, stereotypes, erotic content, and tech faults. Every app held many dark patterns aimed at revenue and time spent. Erotic content and game-like leveling were also common. The results feed debates on emotional reliance and user safety.
arxiv-2605-08193:
Youssef Saied and François Fleuret generalize a robustness property for image-to-image models. A normalization equivariant function scales its output when the input is scaled. It shifts its output when the input is shifted. That helps when test images differ in brightness or contrast from training data.

Older methods forced every internal layer to obey the property. That added cost and ruled out standard parts such as softmax attention. Their Wrapped Normalization Equivariance takes a simpler route. It normalizes the input, runs any backbone untouched, and denormalizes the output. They prove the wrapper captures the whole class of such functions. On blind denoising, it improved robustness with no added GPU cost.
arxiv-2605-08493:
Haroon Wahab, Irfan Mehmood, and Hassan Ugail bring vision-language learning to capsule endoscopy, where a swallowed camera films the small bowel. One exam yields a flood of frames, and subtle abnormalities hide under wildly varying imaging conditions, so vision-only tools trained on narrow disease sets transfer poorly between hospitals.

CapCLIP aligns capsule frames with clinically grounded text built from standardized nomenclature and pathology-aware caption templates. The shared embeddings are therefore semantically informed rather than purely visual. The framework is evaluated against relevant open models for recognition and retrieval, aiming at decision support that survives the move across datasets and clinical centers.
arxiv-2605-08693:
Min Yang and six coauthors teach language model agents to master skills on their own rather than borrow them from teachers or fixed rules. In current frameworks, skills stay external tools that agents merely invoke. SkillMaster trains agents to create new skills, refine old ones, and pick among them while solving tasks, learning from evidence in finished episodes.

Candidate skill edits earn their keep by proving useful on related probe tasks, and a dual advantage training method scores task actions and skill edits separately for stability. On household and shopping simulations, success rates beat leading baselines clearly. Agent research moves toward systems that grow their own reusable know how.
arxiv-2605-08793:
Yixuan Qiu builds cuRegOT, a solver for best cost mass moves on a graphics chip. Such moves sit at the heart of much machine learning today. At large scale they cost too much. The plain Sinkhorn plan is slow on hard cases. A newer Newton style plan stalls on chips. Its sparse steps run in a line, and its memory reads jump around.

Qiu cuts the chip waits by reusing past work on the plan's frame. Live updates keep the chip fed as old ones finish. A fused core step counts slopes with lean memory use. Proofs back the whole plan. On test tasks, it beats top chip solvers by clear gaps.
arxiv-2605-09093:
Anika Tabassum Orchi and eighteen co-authors present HyDRA Scorpion, a low-cost underwater robot built for inspection, intervention, and object detection. Commercial remotely operated vehicles are capable but expensive, and cheaper platforms often lack smart sensing, which shuts many teams out of underwater work.

The robot moves in four directions, carries two manipulator arms, and sits in a custom housing tested to stay dry at pressures like those hundreds of meters down. In trials it held its position within a tight margin despite pushes from outside. Its onboard AI spotted underwater objects with high accuracy in real time and measured distances and lengths, while the arms could grip and rotate without tangling.
arxiv-2605-09393:
Khan and three colleagues build and test a model for cheap ways to bring large language models into software engineering teaching. It is based on what pushes teachers toward them and what holds them back. They turn 19 factors, 9 motivators and 10 demotivators from an earlier survey list, into a poll answered by 126 people in software teaching across several countries.

Poll answers feed two chance-based models, Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression, that guess high LLM familiarity. The pooled guesses feed a genetic-algorithm plan weighing guessed familiarity against cost, at whole and group levels. People polled see gains in programming help and debugging aid and in tailored, adaptive learning. Worries centre on copying and ownership rights, leaning too hard on AI, and weaker critical thought and problem-solving. Under tight budgets, rules and ethics safeguards come first, while teaching-centred work gives more gain per cost than deep structural reforms.
arxiv-2605-09493:
Amir and Lazarovich build simple uniform lattices inside products of chosen Davis complexes. That extends a landmark build of Burger and Mozes for products of trees. Simple groups are the building blocks of group theory. Yet finitely presented infinite simple groups remain rare and hard to find. Their setting is lattices inside products that pair trees with two dimensional Davis complexes tied to right angled Coxeter groups with odd defining graphs.

Their proof builds a counterpart of the Burger Mozes universal groups for this setting. They also supply a local check for when a vertex transitive group sits densely inside the universal group. That machinery yields the new simple lattices. It widens the known families of finitely presented infinite simple groups beyond tree products into the world of Davis complexes and their symmetries.
arxiv-2605-09793:
Pi and five colleagues studied how AI gets challenged in real life, through close reading of 43 cases where affected people, workers, and public-interest groups pushed back on AI systems. Failures, harms, and public rows prompt demands, yet how such pushback actually unfolds was underexplored. Drawing on Bovens's relational model of accountability, the authors frame contestation as accountability-seeking from below.

Actors from below direct explicit demands at actors from above, who answer by accepting, resisting, or dodging responsibility. The study yielded grounded types of pushback moves, institutional response tactics, outcome types, and shaping context factors. Those being challenged often deploy varied moves to limit how much they must answer for. The paper offers guidance for anticipating and countering such evasion.
arxiv-2605-09893:
Rakshit and two colleagues studied pseudo-deliberation in language models: reasoning that looks principled while actions drift from stated values. Models are often judged by stated values, yet values do not reliably govern actions, a discrepancy called the value-action gap. The gap persists even under explicit reasoning, the paper argues, revealing a deeper failure mode.

To measure it, the team built Valdi, with 4,941 human scenarios across five domains, three tasks covering value stating, reasoning, and action, and five metrics of value fit. Across closed and open-source models, expressed values often clashed with downstream dialogues. A multi-agent value checker, ViValdi, stepped in at several stages. Post-hoc auditing and rewriting of final dialogues beat fixes aimed at middle reasoning, hinting action-level fit at output time matters most.
arxiv-2605-09993:
Liu and two colleagues proposed R-GFM, a Riemannian Graph-of-Graphs foundation model for graph learning. Graph foundation models pretrained on massive graph data support general-purpose reasoning across diverse tasks. But existing models pretrained with fixed-hop subgraph sampling impose a fixed receptive field. That causes scale mismatch on tasks needing heterogeneous, unknown structural contexts beyond a fixed sampling scale.

R-GFM treats structural scale as a first-class citizen. It builds a multi-scale Graph-of-Graphs over sampled subgraphs at different hop distances. It learns shape-adaptive representations from Riemannian manifolds. Theory shows R-GFM reduces domain generalization error versus fixed-scale models. Experiments showed state-of-the-art performance, with up to 49 percent relative gains on downstream tasks.
arxiv-2605-10193:
Temmer and four co-authors combine remote-sensing and in-situ data of coronal mass ejections colliding with the heliospheric current sheet, the wavy boundary separating solar magnetic sectors. The event sequence peaks in the largest directly seen flare of solar cycle 25 on 3 October 2024. It produced a fast halo ejection from a nested active region that lasted across several solar rotations. Such durable regions reflect deep magnetic structures shaping the global field.

A drag-based travel model links near-Sun observations to spacecraft measurements. One ejection passed on the far side of the current sheet from Earth and left no local signatures. Over 5 to 10 October 2024 a complex of current-sheet and ejection structures moved together with a shock ahead. The current sheet appears locally replaced by ejection signatures, producing a sector reversal lasting over forty-eight hours, a vivid link between surface structures, global field and eruptive change.
arxiv-2605-10393:
Marco Sälzer, Pascal Bergsträßer, and Anthony W. Lin map what message passing neural networks can count. These graph networks have been shown to express logic with counting up to a threshold, or more generally linear arithmetic constraints. Their 2026 paper pushes beyond linear arithmetic, studying extensions of graded modal logic with polynomial counting constraints, using local and global mean aggregations.

The authors show mean message passing networks can check global polynomial counting constraints in node-labeled graphs under mild assumptions. Local constraints are also checkable for formulas without nested modalities, if either sum or max aggregations are allowed or graphs are restricted to regular ones. Formulas with nested modalities fall within reach of mean networks on tree-like graphs given similar assumptions. Readers get precise conditions for when polynomial counting lies within these networks' expressive reach.
arxiv-2605-10893:
Reza Khanmohammadi and six colleagues tackle a quiet failure of vision-language models: fluent, confident answers driven by language habits alone, with the image adding nothing. Standard confidence scores cannot catch this, since they watch only normal inference and never test whether the picture mattered.

Their BICR framework trains a light probe on hidden states from a frozen model, shown twice: once with the real image and once with it blacked out. A ranking loss punishes confidence that stays high when the picture vanishes, teaching the probe to treat visual grounding as a reliability signal at no extra inference cost. Across five models and tasks from medical imaging to finance documents, BICR leads on calibration and discrimination together.
arxiv-2605-11193:
Raphael Bertrand-Delgado and three co-authors present new data-grounded outlooks for detecting stochastic gravitational-wave background anisotropies from stellar-mass compact binary coalescences. The team sizes up discovery prospects with simulations based on the Euclid Flagship Galaxy Catalogue and LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA constraints, plus theory work.

For compact pairs up to redshift below 3, an angular resolution of about four degrees is required for a find within five years. The cross-correlation uses a galaxy list complete to limiting magnitude below twenty-four point seven, with redshift errors of three thousandths times one plus z. Stretching to ten years relaxes it to about six and a half degrees. Binning them in redshift allows mapping of the anisotropy signal. GW astronomers get concrete angle and time needs for multi-messenger work.
arxiv-2605-11493: Nunes and Almeida show that the Aharonov-Casher effect can coexist with exact supersymmetry. The effect is the phase gained by a neutral particle with a magnetic dipole moment moving in an electric field. Exact supersymmetry is often said to force anomalous magnetic dipole moments to vanish, suggesting incompatibility in four dimensions. Their N-equals-1, D-equals-4 gauge model uses a Lorentz-violating Kalb-Ramond background plus a Fayet-Iliopoulos term. This induces the dipole interaction dynamically, while supersymmetry stays intact and the nonrelativistic limit reproduces the Aharonov-Casher Hamiltonian.
arxiv-2605-11693: Ali, Mollá-Aliod and Naseem present MM-Eval, a unified tool for scoring multi-mode digests by quality, match and range. Multi-mode summary pairs concise text with salient visuals, but current scoring checks quality, match and range alone. MM-Eval mixes text quality from OpenFActScore and G-Eval for truth, flow and fit. Image-text match comes via MLLM-as-judge, and range via CLIP entropy. Tuned on mLLM-EVAL news, it reveals a text-first ladder where truth drives seen quality. It beats rule mixing rivals.
arxiv-2605-12493: Wu and six colleagues build a benchmark for long-term agent memory in specialised web settings, where success rests on recalled workflows, interface quirks and past failure modes. Earlier tests focused on user histories, short traces or final task success, leaving memory itself unjudged. LongMemEval-V2 offers 451 hand-made questions across five memory skills, covering static recall and dynamic tracking plus workflow knowledge, environment gotchas and premise awareness. Each pairs with histories of up to five hundred trajectories and over one hundred million tokens.
arxiv-2605-12893: Glover and Hoffmann give a modern, self-contained account of LFPL, a functional language from 1999 that captures exactly the functions computable in polynomial time. Despite its influence on cost analysis and type theory, no full presentation or machine-checked version existed. They streamline the strongest known soundness and completeness proofs and mechanise both in the Istari proof assistant, adapting a 2002 technique to bound expression costs with explicit polynomials.
arxiv-2605-13093: Nguyen, Wu, Alvarez and Liu fix two flaws in feed-forward pixel-wise Gaussian Splatting: over-bright renders when input view counts vary, and hole artifacts from weak supervision of Gaussian scale. They trace over-brightness to varying numbers of overlapping Gaussians and propose simple alpha normalisation to hold brightness steady. An auxiliary 3D sampling-based regulariser improves scale estimation and mitigates holes in high-resolution renders. Benchmarks show significant gains over baselines under varying views and high resolution.
arxiv-2605-13293: Tan and colleagues present Img2CADSeq, a pipeline that turns a single image into a CAD model. Boundary models are the standard CAD form, but rebuilding them from one view is hard. The method codes CAD steps into a three level codebook, valuing outlines over fine detail, and links image features to 3D steps through point clouds. Backed by two new datasets, it beats current methods and outputs standard STEP files for commercial CAD tools.
arxiv-2605-13493: Jiaxin Yang and seven colleagues introduce PhysEditBench, testing whether image editors can predict physical maps from one RGB image. Image editors need prompts, examples or textual cues rather than directly outputting a map. The benchmark covers depth, normal, albedo, roughness and metallic maps, with fixed protocols for input, output and scoring. Data come from OpenRooms-FF, InteriorVerse and a new procedural source for metallic maps, with quality checks. Specialised models stay much stronger on depth, normal and albedo, while editors match or beat baselines on some roughness and metallic metrics.
arxiv-2605-13693: Eneko Atxa Landa and three colleagues offer StayStill, a large-scale collection of 3D idle moves from 50 subjects with about 6 hours of data. Idle moves show real motion during still states, yet idle motion has drawn little attention for lack of own training sets. They also propose a shared evaluation plan for number and user-based metrics, a first step toward standard checks for future systems. StayStill is openly shared with check code and a pre-trained baseline model making idle moves via link chaining.
arxiv-2605-13793: Paulo Pirozelli and three colleagues present an end-to-end word-model-based system tracing arguments from natural word text into abstract case graphs. The pipe spots case-based parts, selects apt elements, and finds logic links. These form one-way acyclic graphs with premise and verdict components and support, attack and undercut links. Results show fair shape finding and fair test scores across datasets when adapted to different schemes, showing LLM pipe potential for large argument mining.
arxiv-2605-13893: Jacques Raynal and three colleagues introduce Level 4, centred on seen long-run health, in a multi-level study of gait motion under bite limit. Using a trial single-case design in a patient with Parkinson's disease, gait was tracked with sensor insoles under three probes. Two sessions eleven weeks apart used a common PCA map to compare M1-M2 centroid shift. The findings are trial and non-causal, proving no distinct body states, causal bite effect, proven health line, healing optimum, or spread-free ranking.
arxiv-2605-13993: Gao, Shaikh and Kissinger introduce Graphical Algebraic Geometry (GAG), a family of diagram languages that extends the Graphical Linear Algebra program. They build several members and prove them universal and complete for the span semantics of commutative algebra and affine varieties. Polynomials, ideals and shapes gain clear diagram forms for strict diagram proofs. Counting constraint problems reappear as rewrite problems for closed diagrams, making rewrite checks #P-hard.
arxiv-2605-14093: Jain and four co-authors give new Parity-SAT algorithms, including bounded-occurrence versions. Parity-SAT asks whether a CNF formula has an odd number of satisfying assignments, a canonical complete problem for parity counting and a variant of exact model counting. Under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, no algorithm beats the two-to-the-n or two-to-the-m barrier generally. The paper revisits that barrier through structural limits and sharper use of parity, for formulas where each variable appears in at most d clauses.
arxiv-2605-14193: Bracale and Michailidis study monopoly pricing on consumer networks. A consumer's utility depends on their own price and peers' choices, spread through a one-way and signed social graph. The setup covers logit choice, isoelastic and Stone-Geary utilities. Equilibrium exists and is unique under contraction and variational terms, allowing one-sided and signed network effects. Price discrimination in community and influencer markets is studied. Last, isotonic regression learns unknown utilities, with strict no-regret bounds.
arxiv-2605-14293: Goss and thirteen co-authors show a Z3 discrete time crystal in a chain of 15 superconducting qutrits using a Floquet chiral clock model. Periodically driven quantum systems can break discrete time-translation symmetry, forming discrete time crystals. Prior work focused on period-doubling in Z2 qubit time crystals, since stabilizing higher-symmetry order is hard. Unlike Ising, a tunable chiral angle governs domain-wall dynamics and the stability of time-crystalline order. With disordered chiral interactions, the team observes robust subharmonic period tripling across drive strengths, independent of initial state.
arxiv-2605-14393: Junho Kim and colleagues study analogical trajectory transfer, moving motion paths between matching spots in different 3D scenes. Because similar scenes differ in placement, scale and layout, semantic matching causes collisions or distortions. The team splits scenes into object clusters and predicts cross-scene maps from 3D features. Cluster maps are assembled and refined to remove collisions and distortions, giving a trajectory without training. It runs in about 0.6 seconds and beats language, vision and scene-graph baselines. Uses shown include virtual co-presence, camera transfer and human-to-robot motion.
arxiv-2605-14493: Simon Scheidegger offers a hands-on guide to deep learning for solving and estimating dynamic models in economics and finance. Big state spaces strain old grid methods, from economies with diverse agents to climate-economy models. The guide centers on four tools: deep equilibrium nets, physics-informed nets, deep surrogates with Gaussian processes, and Gaussian-process dynamic programming. Uses run from business-cycle models to continuous-time macro-finance and structural estimation.
arxiv-2605-14793: Menescardi and de Gironcoli study melting in calcium oxide under extreme conditions with a machine learning interatomic potential. Trained on about twelve thousand configurations from ab-initio molecular dynamics, the potential feeds large-scale simulations. Two melting methods give about three thousand and fifty-five kelvin and about two thousand eight hundred and forty-seven kelvin at ambient pressure. The enthalpy of fusion near seventy-three kilojoules per mole matches thermodynamic assessments, and a high-pressure melting curve to twenty gigapascals is computed.
arxiv-2605-14893: Grzywaczewski and team study the covariance spectrum of contrastively trained vision-language models. Shared latent spaces hold non-semantic multi-modal noise with meaning. Spectral split divides the latent space into a signal part and a shared noise subspace. The noise shape shows strong subgroup invariance across data subsets. Pruning shared noise dimensions is claimed to be mainly harmless, preserving or improving downstream scores, hinting much latent shape reflects design-level noise rather than task meaning.
arxiv-2605-15093: Jess Jones and four others present CoralLite, a micro-CT dataset rebuilding whole coral colonies from single corallites, the skeletal cups around each polyp. Colony history sits in growing skeletons that may span centuries, while living tissue is only a thin outer layer. CoralLite pairs fully measured 3D segment maps with cross-slice linking into 3D models per corallite. A hybrid V-Trans-UNet model, pre-trained weakly and fine-tuned on over 8 thousand manual labels, reaches 0.94 topological accuracy on unseen slices.
arxiv-2605-15193: Tuna Han Salih Meral and four others align latent geometry for spherical flow matching in image generation. Latent tokens gather in thin shells, yet linear paths between noise and data leave those shells. Component-swap probes show decoded content rides mainly on direction, not radius. The team projects data latents to a fixed radius and uses the radial projection of noise as prior. It tunes the decoder with the encoder frozen, and swaps linear blending with spherical interpolation. Class-based ImageNet FID lifts across token tools at matched training.
arxiv-2605-15393: Philipp Mondorf and three others offer logic-preserving difficulty scaling for evaluating language-model robustness. A model that solves a problem should not fail merely because names, numbers, or context changed while logic stayed fixed, yet current models often do. Existing evaluations sample changes at random, which can inflate toughness. Their framework quantifies variation difficulty and searches methodically for the hardest logic-keeping variants. As difficulty rises, performance falls and reasoning-chain errors grow sharper, and the search fast exposes failures per model.
arxiv-2605-15793: Qitan Lv and seven colleagues propose reshaping complex partial differential equation operators into simpler, better-aligned forms before modeling them jointly. Their AOT-POT method splits hidden states into parallel streams, merges and spreads them around each sub-layer, and mixes streams via Sinkhorn-projected doubly stochastic matrices for stable training. On 12 PDE benchmarks it tops rivals with only 3 percent extra parameters, cutting relative L2 error by up to 77.6 percent, 40.9 percent on average. Fine-tuning cuts error further, by up to 92 percent in-domain and 89 percent out-of-domain.
arxiv-2605-16093: Sasmal, Kanjilal, and Das ask how long information in a single qubit stays useful after repeated decoding. In the standard two-to-one random access code, one receiver gains a quantum edge, but decoding destroys the encoded data. Preparation distinguishability plus measurement incompatibility can offset that disturbance. The authors show an arbitrarily long sequence of receivers can each keep a quantum advantage, so the qubit's information need not be exhausted.
arxiv-2605-16393: Valdivia Ortega, Peng, and Jasnin introduce ViTC-UNet, which conditions a UNet on frozen pretrained ViT features for biomedical segmentation. Promptable ViT models rely on lightweight pixel decoders that may lack the local bias needed for sparse targets. ViTC-UNet uses learnable tokens and a two-way attention decoder to combine ViT global priors with UNet local bias and high-resolution decoding. It avoids end-to-end ViT fine-tuning and beats baselines across MRI and CT tasks. Structure-conditioned UNet decoding adapts visual priors to biomedical segmentation.
arxiv-2605-16593: Langevin shows how to derive treatment policy rules from observational data when several actions are possible and patients differ.
