Phase retrieval asks whether a signal can be recovered, up to a sign or phase, from the magnitudes of its measurements. Norm retrieval asks the weaker question: can just the signal's length be recovered? Their generalized versions replace measurement vectors with operators between Hilbert spaces, covering ordinary frames and Sun's generalized frames in one framework.

The authors develop properties of both notions in general Hilbert spaces, with emphasis on finite-dimensional Euclidean space. The main result concerns generalized norm retrieval there: it is stable. If a family of operators performs the retrieval up to a small error, then a nearby family performs it exactly. Approximate success can always be cleaned into exact success by a small perturbation. That robustness matters practically, since real measurements are noisy.
arxiv-2606-12693:
Ogonowski develops a reconstruction scheme to derive one Standard Model generation's carrier structure from a geometric defect, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The starting point is a codimension-three Codazzi defect, a singular worldline whose surrounding link is a sphere read as a projective line. A self-reconstruction loop treats configurations as fixed points, and its failure to close becomes a list of residuals that must vanish in sequence.

Reconstruction of the defect's 2 boundary charge types, with a visibility condition from quantisation on the projective line, selects a support built from blocks of dimensions 3 and 2. A determinant condition on that carrier then yields the group S(U(3) times U(2)) divided by a 6-element centre. That group is the form of the Standard Model gauge group, with the one-generation representations, hypercharge normalisation, and passing anomaly checks. The Koide relation among charged-lepton masses appears as a zero-correction balance diagnostic.
arxiv-2606-12993:
Liu and colleagues audit Chinese legal case retrieval benchmarks and show the criminal charge is a powerful construct-validity confound, in this 2026 arXiv paper. These benchmarks call a reference judgement relevant when its characterisation matches the query's, and neural systems score near eighty-five hundredths on NDCG at 10.

Ranking candidates by shared charge, tie-broken by BM25, closes just over 99 percent of the BM25-to-trained-system gap on LeCaRDv2. There is no detectable difference from that system. The reason is definitional. LeCaRDv2 defines relevance by matching key constitutive elements of the crime. Those elements encode the charge. The lift is about four and a half. Holding charge fixed leaves a within-charge NDCG residual near twenty-six thousandths, about a quarter of the trained reranker's advantage. The charge-only rule recovers only about 84 percent of the gap on LeCaRDv1, with the charge signal weakening across the 3 benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-13093:
Schwarz and colleagues define extensive-form games with stochastic action sets, in which actions can become unavailable during play due to exogenous randomness, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Extensive-form games are the standard model for sequential decision-making under imperfect information, but they assume every action is always available at every decision point.

Given a base game, the authors define the stochastic availability of action subsets at each information set, with laws known to all players. An expansion procedure converts such a game into an extensive-form game, proving that strategy notations can blow up in size. Under an independence assumption, compact strategy representations polynomial in the size of the game exist. They present SI-CFR, an algorithm minimising sleeping regret, a regret notion that only counts rounds where an action was available. It converges to Nash equilibria with probability in 2-player zero-sum games of this type.
arxiv-2606-13193: Added to arXiv in 2026, this scientific paper communicates fresh results. The title points to A Dual-Mode Faust-to-CLAP Compilation System as its subject. The paper works the ground of science and technology — careful study of how the natural and built world works. The work reported here becomes part of the open literature.
arxiv-2606-13493:
Boxelaar and colleagues analyse the low-frequency radio emission of radio galaxies in this 2026 arXiv paper. Jets from active galactic nuclei inject energy into their surroundings, shaping galaxy evolution. The radio glow of their lobes comes from synchrotron radiation, emitted by electrons spiralling in magnetic fields, and its spectrum records the plasma's energetic history. The oldest populations shine below 100 megahertz, a band where well-resolved observations have been scarce. The team performs the first multi-frequency analysis of the 3CRR catalogue down to 58 megahertz.

With that coverage they study how they are accelerated, measure the low-frequency spectral shape, and constrain the injection index, the spectrum's slope at birth before ageing distorts it. Absorption processes and energy losses, long entangled at higher bands, can be separated cleanly at these wavelengths. The results feed models of jet duty cycles, how long active phases last.
arxiv-2606-13693:
Kokubu asks whether expensive reasoning models earn their cost in corporate sustainability scoring in this 2026 arXiv paper. Automated scoring of environmental, social, and governance disclosures with language models is gaining traction. Kokubu evaluates ten Japanese listed firms on three rubric axes: quantitative targets, progress-tracking, and alignment with standards. A four-model consensus design compares a reasoning-heavy frontier model against three contemporaries with reasoning off, producing 120 firm-axis-model scores. The deviation between the reasoning model and each counterpart averages well under half a point on a five-point scale.

Only a small fraction of comparisons differ by two points, and none by more. Meanwhile the reasoning arm costs roughly five to six times as much as the three-model ensemble. Kokubu concludes the benefit of reasoning-heavy deployment is limited for this task. The study is a template for cost-aware model selection in scoring tasks.
arxiv-2606-13793:
Lee and Teyssier implement a fast multipole Poisson solver in an astrophysics code in this 2026 arXiv paper. Simulating cosmic structure requires solving the Poisson equation for gravity at every step. The RAMSES code's multigrid solver is iterative, needing multiple passes through a hierarchy of grids. The fast multipole method instead makes one upward pass, accumulating and shifting multipole expansions, summaries of distant mass, then one downward pass propagating local terms. The authors build a hierarchy of multipole grids on RAMSES's Cartesian grid, keeping the solver's cost linear in problem size.

Tests show the solver attains accuracy comparable to multigrid for smooth potentials. It is well suited to boundary conditions, since it avoids the rough treatment multigrid needs at domain edges. This paper presents the algorithm; adaptive refinement is the sequel. Solver choice shapes what simulations are feasible, and a linear-scaling gravity solver widens the range cosmologists can afford.
arxiv-2606-13993:
Houghton and colleagues test whether language models store common phrases as wholes, like humans appear to. Linguistics debates storage against computation: do speakers retrieve ready-made chunks or build phrases from rules? The team probed verb-plus-up phrases, such as give up, in text language models and the Whisper speech recognizer. They varied phrase frequency and predictability and watched internal representations. Their 2026 arXiv paper reports clear signs of holistic storage.

All models formed distinct whole-phrase representations, driven by frequency and predictability. That supports usage-based theories, where exposure shapes what gets stored. Effects appeared even in models trained on data amounts comparable to human experience. Larger models showed stronger predictability effects, emerging in earlier layers; smaller models showed them later. Whisper, which hears audio rather than reading tokens, behaved similarly in encoder and decoder. The parallel suggests a shared strategy.
arxiv-2606-14993:
Baldick proposes a market design that treats energy storage through its state of charge in a 2026 technical reference. Storage is growing fast as renewable output rises and dispatchable thermal plants retire. Current United States markets model storage as a paired generator and load. Owners must forecast prices across the whole dispatch horizon, and forecast errors make dispatch suboptimal.

The proposed design has the system operator optimize state of charge directly, with round-trip efficiency built in. Storage owners submit no bids inside the horizon at all. They give only one end-of-horizon bid for ending above or below the starting charge level. Small examples illustrate how the clearing works, and appendices sketch extensions such as charge-dependent power limits. The author notes the design would need major changes to existing market structures. Ancillary services markets are left for a companion paper.
arxiv-2606-15093:
Zhang and coauthors build fuzzy private set intersection protocols from cheap symmetric primitives in a 2026 cryptography paper. Private set intersection lets two parties find common items without revealing their sets. The fuzzy version matches items that are merely close, within a distance threshold. Prior protocols scaled linearly with that threshold or needed expensive homomorphic encryption. Cost also ballooned for general distance metrics beyond the simplest one. The new protocols use only oblivious transfer and symmetric-key operations.

Their trick encodes values by prefixes and checks equality conditions interactively. That yields exactly logarithmic dependence on the threshold, provably the best possible scaling. Two variants cover low- and high-dimensional data under different assumptions. Implementations beat the prior state of the art by up to about forty-four times in runtime. Communication improved by up to about thirty-one times as well. Applications include genomic matching, credential checks, and similar-image retrieval.
arxiv-2606-15393:
Perets and coauthor build a false discovery rate framework for testing many hypotheses with scarce reference data, in a 2026 statistics paper. False discovery rate control limits the expected share of false alarms among claimed discoveries. Two obstacles collide here: each hypothesis's p-value is estimated from only finitely many null samples, leaving it uncertain. The hypotheses also carry structure, such as spatial layout, that should let neighbors share strength.

The framework uses a count-based likelihood that works with the null draws directly, and a kernel-based prior that pools information across the structured hypothesis space. Two decision rules trade exactness for power: one guarantees exact control, the other adapts a mirror-statistic method for more discoveries, with analysis of the slack when symmetry fails. The same machinery suggests where to spend extra null samples. Simulations show better performance than baselines under budgets common in genomics and imaging.
arxiv-2606-15493:
Baltz and coauthors challenge how model stealing success is measured in a 2026 machine learning paper. In model stealing, an attacker queries a prediction service and trains a surrogate mimicking it, walking away with the provider's asset. Success is usually scored by fidelity, how often surrogate and target agree. But queries reveal only part of the target's behavior, so the surrogate is not uniquely pinned down: a whole Rashomon set of near-equally faithful models exists around it.

Computing such sets across tabular, medical imaging, and language tasks, the authors find surrogates with matching fidelity yet wide spread in ambiguity, disagreement rates, and group fairness outcomes. A stolen model can thus behave differently from its victim where deployment matters. The practical moral cuts both ways: victims should not equate high fidelity with total loss, and risk assessments should measure the multiplicity and fairness spread of extracted models, not agreement.
arxiv-2606-15793:
Zykova-Myzina and colleagues bring proximal policy optimization, reinforcement learning's workhorse, to Generative Flow Networks in 2026. GFlowNets train a policy to sample structured discrete objects, like molecules, in proportion to a reward. Their objectives are usually bespoke, but connections to entropy-regularised reinforcement learning suggest standard policy gradient tools should transfer.

The authors derive policy gradient versions for GFlowNet training, experimenting with baselines and advantage estimates. Even vanilla policy gradient, with variance reduction, beats standard GFlowNet objectives on small problems. Their adapted algorithm, Ent-PPO, converges faster and uses data better, beating the baselines across the benchmark set, from synthetic energies to molecular graph generation. One ingredient proves essential: the KL penalty that falls out of the entropy-regularised formula. Removing it makes naive PPO collapse over many epochs. The work is the first to apply PPO to GFlowNets, narrowing the gap between sampling and reinforcement learning.
arxiv-2606-15893:
Li and colleagues present BALTO in 2026, a reinforcement learning framework that fights hallucination in language models at the token level. Response-level faithfulness rewards have a granularity mismatch: one localised hallucination can drag penalties onto fully supported content, and unbalanced fine-grained rewards bias length and verbosity instead. BALTO extracts checkable factual claims from a response, verifies them against the reference context, and projects the claim-level judgments down to token-level labels.

Its balanced credit assignment then redistributes probability mass from unsupported content toward faithful content, rather than suppressing the whole response. Theory backs the design: balanced token-level assignment reduces needless updates and gradient variance, giving bounded, stable optimisation signals. Across ConFiQA, RAGTruth, and a finance benchmark, with two Qwen3 models, BALTO achieves the highest faithfulness in all six settings and the best trade-off against both baselines. Fine-grained honesty, balanced properly, beats blunt punishment.
arxiv-2606-16093:
Torlak and colleagues propose a hybrid language model in 2026 that runs its components side by side instead of in sequence. Transformers read long texts well through self-attention, but their cost grows quadratically with length. State space models scale linearly, yet their compressed states struggle to retrieve precise details.

Their Parallel Hybrid Architecture runs three branches at once: Gated State Spaces for global context, Grouped Query Attention for selective retrieval, and feed-forward networks for extra processing. A learnable mixing mechanism fuses the outputs, letting each branch specialize. On WikiText-103, the model reaches a perplexity of 16.51 at 125 million parameters, beating the named baselines. A larger variant beats a baseline with roughly twice its parameters. Ablations confirm the parallel layout beats sequential designs on quality and runtime.
arxiv-2606-16293:
Hodzelmans and co-authors test isogeometric analysis in 2026 for simulating waves through poroelastic media, materials that mix a solid skeleton with fluid in its pores. Higher-order finite element methods, the standard tool, produce spurious optical modes in their wave spectra beyond linear order. Isogeometric analysis, which builds the simulation from smooth spline functions, is known to avoid them in elastic problems.

The team checks whether the advantage carries over to poroelasticity, studying both a primal form with pressure kept and a reduced form with pressure eliminated. Using divergence-conforming spline spaces, they prove and demonstrate that the two formulations coincide. In the spectra, higher-order finite elements show non-physical optical branches, while isogeometric analysis computes only acoustic modes, apart from a few removable outliers. With outliers removed, the allowed timestep becomes nearly independent of the method's order. Fewer degrees of freedom then buy the same accuracy.
arxiv-2606-16393:
Kucharski calibrates a borrowed statistic in 2026, turning the Brody exponent into a ruler for how strongly points repel each other. The Brody distribution began in quantum chaos as a blend between Poisson and Wigner spacing statistics. Its exponent beta measures short-range exclusion, the tendency of points to keep distance.

First, the complete-spatial-randomness baseline in 2D is recalibrated to beta equal to 0.96, plus or minus 0.15, replacing the wrong one-dimensional Poisson reference. Second, a measured beta-to-exclusion-radius calibration validates against the effective hard-core radius with a Spearman rank score of 0.988. Demonstrations span 58 test surfaces, surface scans of a roundness standard, and 2D embeddings of prime numbers. The primes give beta of 2.15, a truly arithmetic signal standing 0.68 above a sparse-integer control. A Cantor-set embedding, by contrast, shows exclusion created by the embedding itself. The test is cheap to run on any flat point pattern.
arxiv-2606-16593:
Dai and co-authors estimate the pose of industrial parts in 2026 from point clouds alone, without the 3D models that factories often refuse to share. Pose estimation drives tasks like robot spray painting, but confidentiality concerns frequently block access to object models. The team's insight is that rotational symmetry, a property many industrial objects visibly have, can substitute for the missing model. Pose and point cloud are refined together in iterations, driven by a loss built from the symmetry constraint itself.

Each 3D point is rotated under the current pose estimate, and nearest neighbor search finds the multiple correspondences the symmetry implies. The identified correspondences define the symmetry loss that pulls the pose toward consistency. Occluded regions can even be compensated: symmetry fills in areas the sensor never saw, yielding more complete estimates. Symmetry is usually treated as a nuisance that makes poses ambiguous; here it becomes the measurement.
arxiv-2606-16693:
Beck and colleagues build hybrid neuron models in a 2026 computational neuroscience paper. Biophysical models tie a neuron's voltage traces to the ion channels that produce them. Trouble comes from channels whose kinetics, the rules for opening and closing, are poorly known. Leaving channels out or shrinking cell detail creates systematic gaps between model and real cell.

Their framework inserts a neural ordinary differential equation, a learned continuous-time model, inside a conductance-based neuron model. The learned part replaces only the unknown currents or faulty channel rules. Written through voltage-dependent steady-state and time-constant functions, it stays readable as gating dynamics rather than a black box. The hybrid fits thousands of ion channel models and recovers hidden gating from single voltage recordings. It also compresses a detailed cortical neuron into one compartment at up to ten times lower computing cost.
arxiv-2606-16793:
Chen, Cheng, Wan and Yao prove decay estimates for a two-dimensional beam equation in a 2026 analysis paper. The equation governs vibrating plates; a decaying potential perturbs the bilaplacian operator that drives it. Decay estimates say how fast vibrations spread out and fade, and they hinge on delicate behavior near zero energy.

When zero is a regular point or a mild, first-kind resonance, the authors prove sharp bounds: the solution operators decay like one over time. In logarithmically weighted spaces they do better, gaining an extra logarithmic factor the free equation cannot achieve. The potential, it turns out, shifts the bilaplacian's built-in zero resonance and buys that gain. Second-kind resonances are harsher: a nonzero trace moment creates threshold singularities that worsen decay by a squared logarithmic factor. The paper maps all cases carefully. Such sharp rates feed scattering theory and stability arguments for plate models.
arxiv-2606-16893:
Ranta outlines the Informath project in a 2026 paper on turning formal mathematics into fluent prose. Machine-checked proofs are precise but hard for humans to read in raw logical form. Informalization, translating formal statements into ordinary mathematical language, promises readable text with no loss of precision.

The project uses an interlingual design. Dedukti serves as a hub between proof systems such as Agda, Lean and Rocq, while Grammatical Framework handles grammar and wording in several natural languages. Rich vocabulary, compression tricks like aggregation, and symbol tables with a large lexicon make the output read like textbook mathematics rather than a controlled language. Ranta reports fluency is strong for definitions and statements, though ranking many phrasing options and rendering whole proofs remain open problems. The same machinery could also explain, in plain words, what an AI system has actually proved after autoformalization.
arxiv-2606-17093:
Haroon and colleagues diagnose why a 3D scanning network cheats, then repair it, in a 2026 computer vision paper. Fringe projection profilometry recovers shape from one projected striped pattern. At long range, past a meter, light falloff weakens the fringes and the single-shot problem turns ill-posed. Learning-based systems fill the gap somehow, but how?

On a photorealistic synthetic benchmark of thousands of fringe images, the best baseline UNet plateaus at a stubborn error level. Three mechanistic probes converge with conformal uncertainty estimates on one verdict. The network is not decoding fringe phase at all; it leans on object-boundary shape priors, a shortcut that caps accuracy. The repair, PhiCalNet, is architectural, forcing genuine phase use, and the same diagnostics verify the fix. The broader contribution is the template itself: interpretability and uncertainty tools locate the failure, guide the redesign, and certify it.
arxiv-2606-17193:
Cohen and Pakianathan present 2026 arXiv lecture notes on configuration spaces, the spaces of unordered point sets on a surface, and their ties to braid groups and mapping class groups. Braids arise as the fundamental groups of such spaces, so topology and group theory meet directly here. The notes pursue three threads: special spaces built from these connections, a function space reading of the results, and the cohomology of the groups involved.

Cohomology is worked out for surfaces of genus zero, one, and two, with marked points allowed, and for related function spaces. A running example treats particles moving on a punctured torus up to a natural modular group action. The notes recall that most surface configuration spaces are of a special type whose topology is fixed by the fundamental group. The sphere and projective plane need Borel constructions to reach the same form.
arxiv-2606-17393:
Green and Xu present a 2026 arXiv paper using perfect matchings and labelled Fano planes to study the orthogonal bases hidden in the E8 root system. The E8 lattice packs spheres as densely as possible in eight dimensions, and its minimal vectors form the roots. Among the positive roots sit just over two thousand orthogonal bases, a set with a rich graded order that also appears in quantum foundations through parity proofs of a famous no-go theorem.

The set of bases forms a Bruhat-like graded poset whose rank can be read from generalised Rothe diagrams. The authors characterise those diagrams purely through matchings and Fano planes, with no root system language needed. Ranks then follow from statistics such as the weights of perfect matchings assigned to each basis. Simple formulas emerge for the rank generating functions of the whole set and its fifty congruence classes.
arxiv-2606-18593:
Kwon and colleagues examine the human cost of the United States Food and Drug Administration's new food traceability rule, in a 2026 paper in human-computer interaction. The rule, part of a food safety law taking effect in 2026, requires farmers, fishers, retailers, and others to keep detailed tracking records so contaminated food can be traced and pulled faster.

Reading the rule through a data feminism lens, the authors analyzed nearly twelve hundred public comments submitted during rulemaking. Three tensions stood out. The rule turns supply chain workers into data laborers bearing individual labor, financial, and educational burdens. In some settings tracking is infeasible, blocked by infrastructure limits, cultural contexts, and the realities of production. And flexibility meant to help instead bred confusion through ambiguity. Smaller, under-resourced producers are hit hardest, and the authors argue such stakeholders should be treated as policy partners, not just compliance targets.
arxiv-2606-19393:
Nazarov introduces graph linear notation in 2026 as an alternative way of defining finite graphs. The notation is a complete graph invariant, built by an algorithm akin to canonical labeling. A complete invariant captures a graph fully, up to relabeling. Storing it instead of a regular graph form promises simpler tooling for two classic hard chores in graph databases and drawing software.

The first chore is drawing pictures that respect a graph's symmetries. The second is testing two graphs for isomorphism. The author shows classical concepts transfer to it. Colorings and paths have natural counterparts, as do abstract vertices, edges, and subgraphs. Converting back to an ordinary graph runs in polynomial time, which justifies storing graphs this way. The proposal reframes a graph as its canonical code, making identity and symmetry properties that usually need search into properties readable from the stored form itself.
arxiv-2606-19493:
Andrew Lesniewski gives an exact account of Ricci flow for the Bures-Helstrom metric in 2026. The metric is the smallest monotone way to measure distance between quantum states of a qubit, a two-level quantum system. With the quantum Fisher scaling used here, the qubit state space becomes a hemisphere of the round three-sphere. Ricci flow is a process that smooths a shape by letting its curvature drive the change over time.

Lesniewski shows the flow simply shrinks the metric, since the metric is Einstein. The squared warping function obeys a linear forced heat equation in a Hamilton-DeTurck gauge. Curvature grows as the shape shrinks, and the flow ends at time one quarter. A volume-normalized version instead holds the metric fixed, with a spectral gap of five after scaling is removed. The exact solution gives a clean test case for flow methods in quantum geometry.
arxiv-2606-19593:
Aditi Awasthi, Gokul Subramanian Ravi, and Jonathan Baker pipeline fault-tolerant quantum computing in 2026. Fault tolerance needs three systems in step: classical control logic, quantum hardware, and error decoders. Current schedulers treat each logical operation as one atomic block, hiding long idle stretches.

The framework splits every operation into Control, Execute, and Decode stages. Stages from many operations can then overlap, like stations on an assembly line. Speculation strategies let later operations start before earlier decoding finishes. Wrong guesses trigger partial rollback, yet the penalty stays small next to the parallelism gained. On common benchmarks, pipelining with speculation cuts total steps by 20 to 40 percent. The boldest strategy wins most often, beating cautious variants. Speculation also evens the load across the unlike subsystems, turning idle time into useful work.
arxiv-2606-19993:
Nico Harder, Daniel Becking, Karsten Mueller, and Wojciech Samek present AIR in 2026, an SVD method that compresses large language models while respecting what each layer actually does. Plain low-rank truncation treats all weights alike, but activations and backward signals show which directions matter. Starting from the activation-aware optimum of SVD-LLM, AIR runs one closed-form alternating least squares sweep that folds a backward-signal influence score into every element.

A monotone-descent property guarantees the sweep only improves its objective. Perplexity beats the activation-aware baseline by over eighteen percent at sixty percent parameter retention, with about ninety percent less calibration data. Savings convert into fewer operations, lower peak memory, and faster tokens, and the method stacks with LoRA fine-tuning. Cheaper deployment of large models is the direct payoff.
arxiv-2606-20093:
William Guey and Pierrick Bougault test whether language models protect their own writing against valid corrections, a cousin of self-preference bias in model judges. Their 2026 paper builds the test on IFEval, a benchmark with a deterministic checker, so a fix counts as good only when the checker proves it repairs a violation. A model drafts a response and receives a verified fix. It then accepts or rejects the fix, either as the genuine author or as a fresh reader.

Across four model families and eighty-five matched comparisons, authors rejected good fixes at nearly the rate fresh models did, a gap of about five points. When authors did refuse, nearly all their stated reasons flagged supposed flaws rather than loyalty to their own text, and a hint of self-skepticism from a small pilot vanished at scale. Effects under thirteen points remain possible, but strong self-preference looks absent.
arxiv-2606-20493:
Liu Zewen measures how evaluator preferences spread through networks of interacting language model agents. The 2026 paper introduces Contagion Networks, a formal framework for tracking that spread. When LLMs judge each other in multi-agent systems, their strategy preferences, whether prompted or built into shared priors, do not stay put.

In a controlled three-agent experiment with DeepSeek-chat, three evaluator profiles, structured, balanced, and evidence-based, show preferences propagating between agents, with contagion strengths between 0.157 and 0.352. A neutral-prompt control delivers the surprise: shared architectural priors dominate explicit prompts as the contagion channel. Multi-agent pipelines can thus drift toward one house style without anyone instructing them to. Checking evaluator bias becomes a network problem, not a single-model one.
arxiv-2606-20693:
Maulik Srivastava, Esha Saha, and Hao Wang build a model in 2026 to forecast wildfire spread in Canada from satellite and weather data. Canadian fires threaten ecosystems, towns, and infrastructure. Many older models scale poorly or miss how fire changes over time. Their goal is a deep learning system that captures both space and time patterns in public data.

Their design pairs a Video Swin Transformer encoder with a U-Net decoder. It reads three-day sequences of weather and environmental variables. Data come only from public sources through Google Earth Engine. Training uses major Canadian fire events from 2014 to 2023. The system forecasts next-day fire incidence maps. Strong test results suggest attention over space and time helps capture complex fire dynamics. A transparent data pipeline also matters, because forecast tools for emergency planning must be open to checking and reuse.
arxiv-2606-20793:
Ignacio Ruiz and five colleagues report in 2026 that the nearby galaxy Messier 74 is much larger than previously known. Galaxy models predict growth from the inside out. Observations support that view broadly, but timing and scale remain unclear. Deep optical imaging from the TST telescope at Teide Observatory reaches very faint surface brightness limits. It reveals stellar light far beyond the known disc radius of about 14 kiloparsecs.

The new component is faint and young, about 600 million years old. It reaches about 30 kiloparsecs from the center. That doubles the known size of the stellar disc and matches the hydrogen gas disc. Its youth suggests recent disc growth, possibly in under one billion years. A past flyby with another galaxy is discussed as one cause. Messier 74 becomes a strong case for studying how galaxies gain size late in their lives.
arxiv-2606-20893:
Sameek, Bharath, and Ajita propose a generative attack in 2026 that uses neural audio codec latent space to fool audio classifiers, with given names alone where surnames are not recoverable. Audio systems, including speaker verification, can be fooled by crafted inputs. Optimization attacks need costly step-by-step updates on full waveforms. Generative attacks make one-shot synthesis, but often add audible artifacts or run slowly.

Their conditional generator works in the compressed latent space of a neural audio codec. It creates class-specific perturbations in a single forward pass. A decoder turns them into adversarial waveforms. Targeted attack success reaches very high rates. Inference takes only a few milliseconds. That is far faster than diffusion or autoregressive baselines. Fast, hard-to-hear attacks change threat assessment, because real-time systems such as voice login may face attacks that are both quick to make and hard for users to notice.
arxiv-2606-20993:
Milan Miletić, Julie Kallini, and Ekaterina Shutova propose phoneme-based tokenization in 2026 to reduce language gaps. Gaps can start at tokenization. Common subword methods favor high-resource languages. Their fix uses the International Phonetic Alphabet as a shared input, based on sounds not scripts.

The alphabet offers a compact symbol inventory and greater overlap across languages. Byte balance across languages improves. Matched text and phonetic tokenizers are trained across many languages and scripts. Phonetic tokenizers consistently improve tokenization quality. Gains are largest for non-Latin scripts. Generalization to unseen languages and scripts is also stronger. Fairer input units could narrow gaps for languages that current tokenizers split into long, costly sequences.
arxiv-2606-21293:
Silvia Ferro, Fabio Bacchini, Giuseppe Arro, Francesco Pucci, and Pierre Henri use kinetic models in 2026 to link reconnection with electron heating at plasma shear layers. The Kelvin-Helmholtz instability rolls such layers into vortices, a process seen at Earth's magnetopause. As the vortices evolve, thin current sheets form, fragment, and reconnect, but how that activity energizes electrons was not fully mapped.

In their two-dimensional runs, ions act as the main energy reservoir and feed the electromagnetic fields, while electrons gain the most net energy. That gain is strongly directional, concentrated inside thin current sheets with intense field-particle exchange. Electron spectra there grow fast tails, evidence of nonthermal heating. Both shear layers behave alike despite opposite vorticity, tying localized heating directly to reconnection sites.
arxiv-2606-21493:
Hongyang He, Jiuming Liu, and Victor Sanchez present SemiVLA in 2026, a way to adapt robot vision-language-action models when only a few demonstration trajectories carry action labels. Labeled robot data are costly, yet unlabeled trajectories still show scenes and instructions. The missing piece, the action, must be visually grounded, physically feasible, and steady over time, which ordinary semi-supervised learning does not check.

SemiVLA is a teacher-student setup that learns from pseudo-actions the teacher proposes for unlabeled runs. A reliability controller scores each pseudo-action on vision-language alignment, feasibility, and temporal consistency, and a projected update rule keeps noisy feedback from corrupting the teacher. With only ten percent labeled data, SemiVLA with selective LoRA tuning reaches 89 percent average success on LIBERO, eight points above supervised tuning alone.
arxiv-2606-21593:
Linara Adilova, Henning Petzka, Asja Fischer, and Bernhard Geiger test a widespread assumption in 2026 about what neural networks keep in their hidden representations. Two kinds of squeezing are often conflated: information compression, meaning low mutual information between inputs and internal codes, and geometric compression, meaning tightly clustered codes. The authors ask whether one reliably implies the other, using class-wise clustering as the geometric yardstick.

Experiments on classification tasks with controlled noise, in conditional entropy bottleneck and continuous dropout networks, give a nuanced answer. Low mutual information does not reliably track the geometric kind, and the relationship found is negative and nonlinear, even reversing when the training setup changes. The authors hypothesize that generalization confounds the link rather than resulting from either form, a caution for representation-based explanations of why networks generalize.
arxiv-2606-21793:
Chen and colleagues analyze pseudo-sonic curves in 2026, boundaries that arise inside self-similar solutions of the Euler equations for compressible potential flow. Along such a curve the governing equation changes type, behaving hyperbolically on one side and elliptically on the other, and degenerates exactly on the curve itself. The curve's shape matters for problems such as shock wave reflection.

The authors first prove the curve must be a circle when the pseudo-velocity at each of its points points along the curve's normal. They then study the general case, and prove two theorems giving conditions that force the normality property to hold. Applying the theory to shock reflection with non-uniform incoming flow, they show the pseudo-sonic curve is an arc for solutions close to a known uniform-flow case. They also prove smoothness up to that arc, apart from one corner point.
arxiv-2606-22093:
Kitover and Orhon work, in 2026, in functional analysis, extending classic results about compact disjointness preserving operators from Banach lattices to a broader setting. Disjointness preserving operators are linear maps that keep disjoint elements disjoint, and compact ones admit a tidy series representation on lattices. The authors ask whether the same structure survives for finitely generated Banach modules over C(K), the continuous functions on a compact space.

They show it does. A series representation analogous to the de Pagter-Wickstead and Arenson-Kitover theorems holds in the module framework, expressing such operators as sums built from disjoint atoms and disjoint positive elements. The paper also provides details about the spectra of these operators, the sets of values governing their invertibility. The extension matters because module-valued analysis covers function spaces that lattice theory alone cannot reach, and representation formulas make concrete computations with these operators possible.
arxiv-2606-22393:
Yuzhen Song and colleagues, including Qi Wu and Wei Hong, tackle chip design in this 2026 paper. Their subject is on-chip inductive elements, such as spiral inductors, which set the size and performance of millimeter-wave circuits. Designing their layouts is hard because geometry maps to performance in a nonlinear way, and checking candidates needs slow full-wave simulation.

The team proposes HFORD, a hybrid of forward optimization and reverse design, which works backward from target performance to a layout. Its core combines a random forest that picks a topology, a variational autoencoder that generates spectral features, and a mixture density network that maps targets back to designs. Particle swarm optimization then searches the design space, and sparse-fitting sampling improves coverage of key performance regions. The generated layouts respect design rule constraints more often. Two examples show the design cycle shrinking from hours to minutes.
arxiv-2606-22593:
Igor Santos-Grueiro measures how software releases gain authority in this 2026 paper. Dependency graphs show where released code can flow, but not how a release reached users. A package can keep identical exposure while its authority path quietly changes: a new publisher account, a relinked repository, a moved signing key.

Santos-Grueiro defines a predecessor-aware record comparing each release with the previous one across publisher, repository, workflow, provenance, signing, and mediation evidence. Applied to an audited cohort of nearly forty-six thousand releases from five major registries, transparent rules flagged two hundred four release-path discontinuities as a review queue. One selection rule covered most triggers; a regime-specific rule covered all of them. In a blinded test, practitioners rated most triggers as needing immediate review and every control as needing none. Known malicious versions showed zero overlap with the triggers, marking the method's boundary.
arxiv-2606-22693:
Vladimir Müller and Yuri Tomilov open a new line in operator theory in this 2026 paper, the first systematic study of numerical ranges on sequence spaces. The numerical range collects the values an operator produces on unit vectors. Its essential variant ignores compact perturbations, and both objects help describe an operator's spectrum and behavior.

Working on spaces of p-summable sequences, the authors first lay Banach-space foundations, including a description of the essential numerical range using finite-codimensional subspaces. In finite dimensions they find star-shapedness in some cases and explicit two-by-two counterexamples in others. On the full spaces, they prove the essential numerical range is compact and convex. It also equals the algebraic numerical range of the operator's image in the Calkin algebra, and the closure of the numerical range is star-shaped. Examples cover tridiagonal Toeplitz operators and the discrete Hilbert transform.
arxiv-2606-22993:
Ioannis Kalogridis builds a theory of generalized regression inside reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces in a 2026 statistics paper. These spaces are function families where each point evaluation behaves like an inner product, which makes fitting smooth functions practical. Regularized M-estimation chooses the function balancing fit against roughness across many possible loss functions. Earlier theory covered only narrow loss choices. Kalogridis aims for one framework spanning convex losses and non-convex ones, including the bounded robust losses used against outliers.

Kalogridis proves the estimator exists and is measurable under mild conditions. He derives sharp convergence rates with an explicit split between bias and variance. The variance does not depend on whether the model is wrong, while the bias follows a source condition on the true function. For tensor product Sobolev spaces, new rates explain how these estimators dodge the curse of dimensionality. Numerical experiments and a C++ implementation support the theory.
arxiv-2606-23593:
Roodabeh, Li, and Alemzadeh detect technical mistakes during robot assisted surgery in real time, in a 2026 paper on medical robotics. Such surgery gives surgeons fine control, but errors still occur, even for experts, and catching them matters for safety. Video only detectors often miss the fine context of what task is underway. Surgery unfolds in steps: procedures break into gestures, and gestures involve tools touching tissue or objects.

The framework fuses three inputs: video, kinematics, the recorded motion of the tools, and text prompts. Prompts spell out gesture-level tasks and error definitions, a method called activity prompting. Vision encoders pretrained on surgical activity labels supply activity aware features, compared against standard language image embeddings. On the JIGSAWS and SAR-RARP50 datasets, the fused system beats prior baselines clearly, raising its F1 detection score by up to five points on one and about seventeen on the other.
arxiv-2606-24193:
Luo and colleagues secure drone computing networks with a blockchain-managed reputation system. Drones offering aerial services share computing through decentralised networks. But resource-limited agents in untrusted settings face a trilemma among autonomy, security, and efficiency, with malicious agents in the mix. Their 2026 framework, SkyChain Intelligence, combines agentic AI, a consortium blockchain, and multi-agent deep reinforcement learning in one design.

A lightweight blockchain trust system tracks reputation scores for the drones, updating them as behaviour changes. A hybrid-action-space learning algorithm embeds those on-chain scores into its reward function. Offloading decisions, resource allocation, and three-dimensional drone paths are thus optimised jointly, with trust in view. Simulations show the framework beating strong baselines on task completion latency and energy use. It holds a high completion rate in the baseline case, and converges stably within a few hundred training rounds.
arxiv-2606-24393:
Godard, Waters, and Moulton model a tendon as waterlogged tissue whose fibres wake only when straightened. Tendons are mostly water. Poroelasticity, the mechanics of fluid-saturated solids, is thus a natural framework. Their collagen fibrils are crimped at rest, unloaded until stretching pulls the crimp flat. Earlier models included fibres but not this recruitment process. The 2026 one-dimensional model adds it.

Crimped fibrils sit in a soft neo-Hookean matrix. They straighten progressively as the tissue stretches, joining the load-bearing skeleton one by one. Dynamics obey a diffusion equation whose coefficient depends on stiffness. Within realistic tendon parameter ranges, the fibre model is softer than a purely neo-Hookean comparison tissue. It nears steady state more slowly under constant load, and relaxes far more slowly on unloading. Recruitment also lets the tendon stretch further without overstraining fibrils or matrix. This is a natural protection mechanism, matching experiments.
arxiv-2606-24493:
Klemenc and Scagliotti prove that weighted sum problems almost never leave their answer ambiguous. Multi objective problems juggle several rival goals at once. The standard trick scalarises them: assign positive weights, add the objectives into one number, and minimise. The setting here is bare. Any set carries a vector valued objective, with no topology, convexity, or continuity assumptions to lean on.

A trade off invariance principle for such sums yields generic uniqueness in objective space. For almost every weight vector, in the measure theoretic sense, all minimisers of the weighted sum share the same objective vector. Excluding another tiny set of weights, all minimising sequences converge to that same limiting objective vector, regardless of the sequence chosen. In geometry terms, for almost every positive weighting the sum exposes at most one nondominated point of the reachable set. Klemenc and Scagliotti's 2026 result says ties are the exception, not the rule.
arxiv-2606-24593:
Hammoud and colleagues teach weather models their surface fluxes from simulated turbulence, instead of hand derived formulas. Turbulent fluxes of momentum, heat, and mass between ground and atmosphere shape the boundary layer, and coarse weather and climate models must parameterise them. The problem is nastiest under unstable conditions, where transport is strongly nonlocal, and stable ones, where turbulence turns patchy.

A novel formulation represents nondimensional fluxes as a linear convolution, acting on scaled mean state profiles. The flux at each height can thus draw on the whole profile, rather than local values alone. A large eddy simulation dataset, spanning ideal flow over uniform surfaces across stability regimes, supplies training and test cases. Several first order versions of the scheme are derived, and tested against the simulations. Hammoud's 2026 team, anchored at Princeton, aims at a data driven flux law honest about nonlocality, the property classical surface layer theory assumes away.
arxiv-2606-24693:
Jarkko Kari, Sébastien Labbé, and Pieter Mostert build aperiodic sets of Wang tiles tuned to any chosen quadratic irrational. Wang tiles are squares with coloured edges that must match when tiling the plane. An aperiodic set tiles the plane but never in a repeating pattern. The authors first give a sufficient condition for non periodicity in striped tile sets. The proof uses a quadrilateral drawn around a parabola.

From that geometry, the stripe densities in any valid tiling must be irrational numbers. The condition yields fresh proofs for known examples. Those include an encoding of Penrose tilings into 24 Wang tiles and the metallic mean tile family. The converse direction is the headline. For any two irrationals in the same quadratic number field, the team constructs a finite striped tile set. It admits a tiling whose vertical stripe density is the first number and whose horizontal density is the second.
arxiv-2606-24793:
Anne-Laure Basdevant and Arvind Singh study a random colouring process on trees. Vertices are revealed one by one in random order. Each new vertex copies the colour of the closest vertex revealed before it. Earlier versions were studied in Euclidean spaces by Preater and by Aldous. On trees, the authors track the genealogy of colour inheritance: who copied whom.

The tree case differs sharply from the Euclidean one. The genealogical graph on an infinite regular tree is disconnected. It splits into infinitely many endless components, each heading in its own asymptotic direction. Every vertex, meanwhile, has only finitely many descendants. The authors also describe what changes with finitely many starting seeds. Finally they take local limits on finite regular trees as height grows. Two seed layouts are analysed: two fixed seeds, and a blue root seed against red leaf seeds.
arxiv-2606-24893:
Zheyuan Zhang and six colleagues introduce AgentOdyssey, a benchmark that generates endless text games to test agents that keep learning while deployed. Most evaluation assumes learning stops at test time. Continual learning agents instead must explore, gain world knowledge, remember episodes, and plan far ahead, all during use. AgentOdyssey procedurally builds open ended text games with rich entities and world dynamics. Its tasks stretch over long horizons.

Evaluation goes beyond game progress. Diagnostic tests probe world knowledge acquisition, episodic memory, exploration of objects and actions, action diversity, and model cost. Diverse agent designs were run in the generated games. Results expose sharp limits in the key abilities. Stronger base models scale performance up, yet even the best agent stays far below human play. Short term memory helps several agent designs at once. Zhang and colleagues map which factors lengthen an agent's meaningful horizon, and how much headroom remains.
arxiv-2606-24993:
John Sweeney shows that the order in which training data is presented to a model can be predicted from geometry. Sequential learning is order dependent: the number of possible curricula explodes. Sweeney proves the order effect is governed by a computable quantity, the Lie bracket commutator of gradient update fields. It yields a pairwise score for whether source A should precede B or the reverse. From that primitive he builds a tournament method that ranks all sources cheaply.

The tournament needs one Hessian vector product per source and a fast sort, never the full pairwise matrix. Empirically the planner shines: about 98 percent pairwise accuracy for single step instruction tuning and preference optimisation, and about 73 percent twenty steps out. It recovers the best of all six schedules for three sources in about 88 percent of trials. On 85 programming language domains aimed at a Python target it ranks in the 99th sampled percentile.
arxiv-2606-25093:
The odd odd nucleus promethium 150 sits in a transitional region near the edge of beta stability, and its low lying states are poorly mapped. A. Pal and twenty one colleagues probe it with a proton induced reaction, watching the emitted gamma rays with an array of five Compton suppressed Clover germanium detectors plus one segmented planar detector. Measurements at beam energies of 8 and 9 MeV feed excitation functions and coincidence data.

Sixteen new gamma rays and fifteen new levels enter the level scheme. Relative intensities come from total and gated projections, and limited angular distribution data support tentative spin parity assignments for a few states. Lifetimes for two excited levels are estimated in the nanosecond range. Large basis and projected shell model calculations interpret the scheme. It shows a ground state, a nearby state around 50 keV, and a low lying isomeric state, with bands built on two quasiparticle configurations.
arxiv-2606-25493:
From any graph, build a new one by linking vertices exactly k steps apart, and repeat: does the sequence ever cycle back to its start? Gregory Demo, David Lund, and Oleksiy Al-saadi study that periodicity question in 2026 for the k distance graph operator. They also examine clique numbers, the sizes of the largest fully linked sets in the derived graphs. Period behaviour turns out to depend sharply on whether k is two or larger.

For every k, some k distance graph is weakly periodic with any prescribed period length. The main theorem goes further for k above two: strongly periodic examples exist at every size period as well. For the borderline case of two distance graphs, the authors gather evidence that connected examples have periods bounded by a function of the vertex count, a ceiling the higher cases escape.
arxiv-2606-25693:
Uncertainty quantification runs thousands of simulations whose runtimes vary wildly, and ordinary schedulers built for uniform jobs waste the cluster. Chung Ming Loi, Mario Wille, and Anne Reinarz present an improved dynamic load balancer in 2026 inside UM-Bridge, a language neutral bridge coupling uncertainty software to simulators. Their test case is deliberately nasty: Bayesian inversion of tsunami simulations arranged in a multilevel hierarchy, where sampling requests arrive with loose dependencies and runtimes spanning orders of magnitude. The balancer must hand work to nodes without knowing job lengths in advance.

In trials it kept average node idle time near a millisecond, essentially eliminating scheduling waste on the test problem. No prior assumptions about the workload were needed, which matters because Bayesian samplers reveal their costs only as they run. Faster turnaround for such inversions feeds hazard assessment, where posterior answers are only as useful as the compute schedule allows.
arxiv-2606-26093:
Botao He leads a team teaching robots to feel force through a wristband. Robot policies learn well from human demonstrations. Standard demos record motion and appearance, though. Contact forces, vital for squeezing and placing fragile objects, go missing. ForceBand is a low-cost wrist-worn system based on surface electromyography. Muscle signals from the forearm stand in for the forces fingers apply.

Ten hours of multimodal data anchor the system. Video, muscle signals, motion data, and fingertip force readings were captured together. A model named EMG2Force learns to predict per-finger forces from the muscle and motion signals. After brief personal calibration, a user records demos wearing only the band plus a camera. Predicted forces then enrich each demo automatically. Force prediction error drops by over half versus vision-based rivals. Policies trained on the enriched demos hit eighty-seven percent success on pick, squeeze, and place tasks.
arxiv-2606-26493:
Fitsum Reda, John Kamalu, and four colleagues at NVIDIA present Nemotron-Labs-TwoTower, a diffusion language model. Autoregressive models write text one token at a time, which limits speed. Diffusion models draft blocks of text in parallel and refine them over several passes. Existing diffusion models use one network both to read context and to clean up drafts. That forces one network to serve two different jobs.

TwoTower splits the jobs into two towers. A frozen autoregressive tower reads the clean text so far. A trainable diffusion tower refines the next block, attending to that context. The system builds on an open-weight thirty-billion-parameter model. Training covered roughly two trillion tokens. The result kept nearly all of the original model's answer quality. It also generated text more than twice as fast in wall-clock time. Code and model weights were released publicly.
arxiv-2606-26893:
Kim, Grebennikova, and Perchet study online stopping problems where reward values come from an unknown formula family. In a prophet inequality, a decision maker sees random rewards one by one and must pick one on the spot. Here rewards follow an exponential-type family, covering cases like exponential and Pareto distributions, with one hidden parameter. The authors first pin down the best possible long-run competitive ratio when that parameter is fully known.

With full knowledge, the limiting ratio takes a closed form for unbounded rewards and reaches one for bounded rewards. Learning must then match that bar using only rewards seen so far, with no practice data. Their confidence-based dynamic programming policy does exactly that as rounds grow. It reaches the same best long-run ratio purely from online observations. Worked rates for standard examples and simulated tests confirm the policy performs as theory predicts.
arxiv-2606-26993:
Qi Cheng gives a fast, deterministic algorithm for a basic task in number theory with crypto stakes. An ideal in a number field is a structured set of algebraic integers. Many applications want just two elements that generate the whole ideal. Older methods are either randomised or too slow at cryptographic sizes, where lattice-based cryptography now lives.

Cheng's algorithm runs in polynomial time with no coin flips. It applies when the ideal's norm is coprime to a certain index measuring how far a simple ring sits inside the full integer ring. All ideals qualify for an important polynomial family that includes the cyclotomic polynomials of lattice cryptography. A broadened Dedekind test is the key tool. The result removes chance from a routine step in ideal math.
arxiv-2606-27193:
Unger and Soker propose a triple-star route to the merging black hole pairs that gravitational wave detectors hear. Three massive stars evolve together, and two shared-envelope phases do the tightening. In a common envelope phase, one star swallows a companion, and friction shrinks the orbit. First, a growing star engulfs a low-mass companion. In the 2026 proposal, the third star then spirals in, spinning up the core that collapses into the first black hole.

Later, the second star engulfs that black hole in a second shared-envelope phase, then explodes to form the second black hole. Spins end up mostly aligned with the orbit, giving a positive average effective spin with a negative tail. Predicted merger rates, though, run up to twice the observed share of supernova rates. The channel can still significantly feed the observed population of merging black hole binaries.
arxiv-2606-27293:
Bhattacharjee and colleagues give deterministic algorithms for factoring sparse polynomials when each variable's degree stays bounded. A sparse polynomial has few terms relative to its size, and factoring one is a core problem in computational algebra. The new algorithm runs in polynomial time and outputs a list of circuits guaranteed to contain every factor. In the 2026 algorithms paper, extra spurious circuits may appear in the list, a caveat stated plainly.

Each circuit in the output list can be kept at constant depth, which suits complexity analysis. A corollary recovers all factors with no spurious entries at modest extra cost, using interpolation and divisibility tests. A second algorithm handles unbounded individual degree in quasipolynomial time, still listing every low-degree factor. That result also bounds how many bounded-degree factors a sparse polynomial can have. Deterministic factoring thus catches up with the randomised state of the art.
arxiv-2606-27593:
Sridhar Mahadevan argues that foundation models should be built for checking. Their claims should be verified locally, not trusted wholesale. His 2026 tutorial paper introduces a framework called Odyssey. Odyssey assembles models from components called foundries. Each foundry covers a local context. It carries its own evidence and rules for joining with neighbours. It also carries policies for handling contradictions.

Five named agents run the system. Scylla handles human inspection. Homer ingests sources. Athena builds and audits the foundries. Prometheus tracks causal and predictive state. Toulmin supplies the reasoning layer. That layer states why a claim is warranted and where it would fail. A typed query language, Foundry SQL, exposes the stored artifacts. Mahadevan also describes a method called Ticket. Ticket converts outside pretrained models into durable foundries. Throughout the system, consistency, provenance, and failed joins stay visible as explicit artifacts.
arxiv-2606-27993:
Andreas Thom studies the Howe–Moore property for groups acting on buildings in 2026. A building is a highly symmetric combinatorial geometry. Its automorphism group can be a totally disconnected locally compact group. The group acts strongly transitively on a locally finite building of finite rank and minimal non-spherical type. The question is when representation coefficients must vanish at infinity.

Once thickness is large enough, every weakly mixing strongly continuous unitary representation is of C0 type. If the group also has no non-trivial finite-dimensional unitary representations, it has the Howe–Moore property. Concrete cases include rank-three compact-hyperbolic types of large thickness, absent compact quotients. An application follows for Kac–Moody lattices of Caprace–Rémy type. Those lattices, simple, finitely presented, and Kazhdan, are character-rigid. Their only extremal characters are the regular and trivial ones.
arxiv-2606-28193:
Hiren Kakkad, Rémy Larue, and Alexander Ochirov derive quantum anomalies, places where a classical symmetry breaks once quantum effects enter, using a bootstrap approach. Instead of computing with a full theory, they start from scattering particles treated as on-shell, meaning every particle is real and physically allowed.

Working at the simplest level of three interacting particles, Kakkad and colleagues feed in only the classical symmetry and the symmetries of the effective action. Helicity spinors and on-shell versions of the discrete symmetries then fix the Weyl, chiral, diffeomorphism, and Lorentz anomalies up to overall constants. They recover the known conditions under which gauge anomalies cancel. They also find that the Weyl anomaly cannot involve Pontryagin densities, certain geometric terms one might have expected.
arxiv-2606-28293:
Mor Rozner, Alejandra Rosselli-Calderon, and Enrico Ramirez-Ruiz ask where the heaviest gravitational-wave sources come from. Black holes and neutron stars sitting in gas-rich surroundings keep swallowing gas and growing, and the team wondered how that growth reshapes a whole population over time.

Rozner and colleagues treat accretion as transport through mass space, governed by how the growth rate scales with mass. When growth rises faster than mass itself, evolution runs away and builds long high-mass tails. Slower scaling squeezes the population into a narrower range instead. Simulations show sustained accretion can populate the heavy end of gravitational-wave catalogs and even produce events like the very massive GW231123. Inside binaries, shared accretion also pushes the two masses toward equality.
arxiv-2606-28393:
H. Ibrahim Gulluk, Max Van Puyvelde, Wim Van Criekinge, and Olivier Gevaert improve how artificial intelligence picks the best chest X-ray report among several candidates. Radiologists read each new scan against the patient's prior exam, and much of a report describes change. Existing report generators, however, score candidates without any sense of that before-and-after transition.

Gulluk and colleagues embed each report's sentences as a set, compress the prior-to-current shift into one directional vector, and score candidates by closeness to real transition vectors banked from training data. They try four set-distance designs, from mean shift to optimal transport. Across three prompts and three vision-language generators, transition-aware selection beat random choice everywhere, with the largest relative gains in the Impression section, where change matters most.
arxiv-2606-28593:
Anya Ji, Abhijith Varma Mudunuri, David M. Chan, and Alane Suhr test whether vision-language models understand motion, not just appearances. Models have improved at turning a static picture into code for webpages and charts, but rebuilding an animation from video demands recovering how things change over time, a different and harder skill.

Their Animation2Code benchmark holds over a thousand web animation videos with their original HTML, CSS, and JavaScript implementations. Two human-aligned metrics score appearance similarity and temporal similarity separately, so a pretty but wrongly timed reconstruction cannot hide. State-of-the-art models, even with fine-tuning and iterative refinement, score well on appearance while struggling to keep temporal consistency. Reconstructing what moves, the results show, remains a sharp weakness of current multimodal systems.
arxiv-2606-28693:
Kishimoto and Tong extend a discrete version of homotopy theory from graphs to cubical sets, which are structures built from cubes of many dimensions. Homotopy groups measure the holes and loops in a shape at different dimensions, and a discrete version tries to capture them by purely combinatorial moves. Their setting covers quasisymmetric cubical sets, where coordinates can be permuted in ways compatible with faces and degeneracies, though not necessarily with extra connection structure.

Their main result says the discrete groups of such a set match the ordinary homotopy groups of the shape it realises. They build a purely combinatorial left adjoint, a best-fit construction, for the functor that forgets the symmetry. Its unit map proves to be a weak equivalence on every object. As a payoff, homotopy groups of any cubical set's realisation gain a combinatorial description. A Hurewicz theorem, linking homotopy to simpler homology invariants, follows.
arxiv-2606-28893:
Dessmann and eight colleagues measure how quickly excited donor atoms in silicon lose energy to lattice vibrations, and use those rates to test basic facts about silicon itself. Donors are impurity atoms whose bound electrons mimic hydrogen atoms inside the crystal, with Rydberg states, meaning highly excited levels, that spread widely and react sensitively to the lattice. Such states are candidates for quantum devices, but vibration shortens their lives far more than for free atoms.

Their theory combines the shapes of the Rydberg states with tabulated coupling strengths for all six branches of lattice vibration across the whole momentum space. Time-resolved measurements with a free electron laser then tested the predictions under controlled conditions. The widely quoted position of silicon's conduction-band minimum disagreed with the observed rates. A value further from the reference point matched well, turning donor relaxation into a precision tool for silicon band parameters.
arxiv-2606-28993:
Knigge, Scaringi, Castro Segura, de Martino and Veresvarska dissect the light of ASKAP J1745-5051, a system that is both a long-period radio transient and a magnetic cataclysmic variable. Such variables pair a white dwarf with a donor star whose gas it steals. This system's radio bursts repeat on a period of about 1.3 hours, matching its orbit, and it also emits X-rays.

Building the energy distribution from far-ultraviolet to near-infrared light, the team fit two components. A white dwarf at about fifteen thousand degrees dominates the ultraviolet and optical bands. A sub-stellar donor, about a twentieth of the Sun's mass and far cooler, dominates in the near-infrared K band. Their fit corrects the discovery paper's dust reddening treatment, drops data contaminated by a nearby star, and adds archival infrared photometry. The donor's tiny mass suggests the system has bounced past its minimum period.
arxiv-2606-29493:
Ammanamanchi, Bhat, and Biderman audit benchmarks for language-model theorem proving in Lean, a proof assistant whose kernel machine-checks every proof. That checking creates false comfort. The kernel verifies that a proof establishes a formal statement, not that the statement faithfully encodes the intended problem. Evaluation harnesses can also fall for trivial or adversarial solutions.

The team audits five widely used Lean benchmarks, together with their forks, using corpus-scale static checkers. Their scan surfaces thousands of findings, including hundreds of issues certified by machine checking, such as counterexamples, vacuous theorems, and unsound axioms. Semantic defects include missing hypotheses, simplified problems, and incorrect translations from informal statements. On corrected subsets, these defects push reported prover scores in both directions. The authors propose a fault taxonomy, automated checkers, and release standards. They publish their checkers, audit prompts, and corrected dataset snapshots for the community.
arxiv-2606-29593:
Dereziński and Dong tell how artificial intelligence settled the worst-case complexity of the Kaczmarz algorithm, proposed in 1937 for solving systems of linear equations. That method counts as the oldest known example of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Its last-iterate convergence had resisted decades of analysis.

The authors initiated and facilitated a collaboration between Gemini Deep Think and ChatGPT Pro. Gemini found a novel link to a branch of functional analysis that the authors did not know. ChatGPT then derived an elementary proof from that link. The result shows the last iterate reaches a given error in a number of steps that grows only in inverse proportion to that error, the optimal rate. The authors verified the proof independently and wrote the paper themselves.
arxiv-2606-29693:
Nguyen asks a sharp question about decoder-only transformers, the models behind modern chatbots: between which two layers is a predicted token's probability actually produced? Existing layer-wise readout tools give only approximate answers. The logit lens reports per-layer levels but no additive split. Other methods are additive only in logit space, not probability space.

His method, IG-Lens, applies Integrated Gradients along one path through the hidden states, from a baseline up to the final layer. Each segment is credited to the layer it ends at, giving attributions that sum exactly to the change in target probability. The softmax sits inside the integration path rather than being linearized away. Completeness holds exactly at any step count, down to floating point. Nguyen proves the identity behind this and describes a single-pass implementation.
arxiv-2606-29893:
Bojović, Salzo, and Pontil give a negative result about AdaGrad, a widely used optimization algorithm that shrinks its step size as it accumulates past gradients. The question is whether it adapts automatically to Hölder-smooth objectives, functions whose slope changes at a controlled rate.

The authors build a simple one-dimensional convex problem with a composite objective, a smooth part plus a non-smooth part, where AdaGrad fails to reach the classical fast convergence rate for such objectives. The reason is a mismatch: the smooth part's gradient need not vanish at the optimum, so AdaGrad keeps shrinking its steps too aggressively and converges slowly. They also explain why variants based on gradient mappings or successive gradient differences avoid this trap.
arxiv-2606-29993:
Pierre Germain and Mickaël Latocca prove decay estimates for a basic kinetic equation on flat tori. The Liouville equation describes particles moving freely without collisions. Its space-time density is what their Strichartz estimates control. Such estimates quantify how the density spreads and evens out. Applications reach toward the X-ray transform and Kakeya problems.

In dimension one, they obtain the optimal range of estimates. The density is bounded purely by norms of the initial data. Higher dimensions behave differently, and they prove estimates cannot hold as-is. A weight involving particle speed must be added to the data. They conjecture the optimal range for these weighted estimates. Part of that conjectured range is proved in the paper. The results then feed into problems on Euclidean cylinders. Both the X-ray transform and Kakeya type questions benefit.
arxiv-2606-30093:
Gianluca Bonifazi and seven colleagues speed up retrieval-augmented generation with a graph built from raw tokens. Retrieval systems ground language model answers in external documents. Standard versions struggle when answers need multi-hop reasoning across chunks. Graph-based rivals rely on costly, error-prone extraction by language models. Their system, TIGRAG, builds its graph without any such pipeline.

TIGRAG constructs a knowledge graph from token co-occurrence statistics. A sliding window records which tokens appear near each other. This makes graph construction cheap and scalable to large corpora. At query time, graph-based expansion widens the search semantically. Neural reranking then orders the retrieved evidence for the model. An iterative strategy expands the query using bridging entities from earlier results. On three multi-hop question answering benchmarks, TIGRAG wins consistently. It beats dense retrieval and graph rivals while cutting indexing time.
arxiv-2606-30393:
Nguyen and three colleagues build the first benchmark for deciding which objects in a photo should be erased. Photographs often contain distractors that steal attention from the subject. Editing tools can remove objects easily once chosen. Choosing them is still mostly manual work. Existing saliency tools ignore what the user intends as subject. Removing the wrong object can also break a scene's sense.

The task is formalized as subject-aware distractor localization. Their benchmark, SADL, holds eighteen hundred cases over one thousand photographs. Nearly fifteen thousand candidate objects carry annotations. A hard negative set stress-tests when models should exclude objects. Five inclusion factors and three exclusion rules structure the labels. Seven vision-language models run a two-stage pipeline on it. Models spot distractors well but then over-apply the exclusion rules. True distractors get wrongly suppressed at scale as a result.
arxiv-2606-30493:
Konstantinos Kampourakis and three colleagues argue that labeling control-system attacks as simply attack or normal hides what operators need to know. Intrusion detection for industrial control systems leans on binary labels. Real attacks bend processes in varied concrete ways. A valve slam and a slow sensor drift demand different responses. Their framework characterizes behavior beyond the binary split. Raw process traces map onto five physical primitives.

The primitives are drift, spike, oscillation, repetition, and switching. Three public benchmarks receive the treatment: SWaT, WADI, and HAI. Attack windows shift clearly away from normal operation. The datasets occupy largely distinct regions of that space. WADI leans on repetition; HAI favors drift and oscillation. SWaT shows stealthier frozen-telemetry behavior instead. A random forest baseline exposes the stakes. Fine-grained scores fall far below the flattering binary scores. Stratified evaluation would expose such blind spots routinely.
arxiv-2606-30593:
Omran Ahmadi and Hassan Norouzi sharpen a bound in combinatorics, the mathematics of finite collections. A sunflower is a set of subsets whose pairwise overlaps are all identical, like petals sharing one core. Families with no sunflower cannot grow too fast, and Naslund and Sawin had bounded their size using the slice-rank method for diagonal tensors, a tool from algebra.

Ahmadi and Norouzi define a new class of tensors, called i-triangular tensors, and prove a slice-rank-style lemma for them. Feeding that lemma into the Naslund-Sawin argument improves the bound by a polynomial factor. In plain terms, the power of n in front of the main exponential term drops from one half to one sixth. The gain is modest next to the exponential term, but it is the first progress of its kind on this bound.
arxiv-2606-31193:
McOrist tackles heterotic moduli, the coupled shape and field choices that define a family of string theory vacua. In a heterotic vacuum, complex structure, Hermitian form, gauge bundle, and B-field deformations mix rather than forming separate sectors. Corrections at second order in the string scale make that mixing harder to ignore.

McOrist organises the problem with an extension bundle whose sections gather all the deformation types in one object. A nilpotent differential acts on that bundle, and its square vanishes exactly when key conditions such as anomaly cancellation hold. This universal geometry gives one frame for supersymmetry and anomaly equations, instead of treating each modulus apart, and it stays in force even when parts of the curvature fail simpler conditions.
arxiv-2606-31293:
Kubík and three colleagues present ToothForge, a generative framework for dental crown shapes learned from small datasets. Crown shape guides diagnosis, orthodontic planning, and restoration design, yet training data stay scarce. Models also face teeth whose surface connections differ from clinic to clinic, which breaks many shape methods.

ToothForge works in the spectral domain, describing each crown with compact intrinsic coefficients from the Laplace-Beltrami operator. Spectral synchronisation steadies those eigenbases across samples, so shapes with varying connectivity share one low-dimensional learning space. Benchmarks against statistical shape models and point-based generators show reconstruction and generation quality that matches or beats spatial methods. The compact form suits limited medical datasets and keeps the geometry readable for clinical use.
arxiv-2606-31693:
ShopX Team presents ShopX, a foundation model built to turn a shopper's stated intent directly into items. Many AI shopping systems wrap a language model around older search and ranking tools. That split forces rich requests through narrow interfaces and loses detail. ShopX instead unifies intent understanding, planning and item-level actions inside one model.

Items are handled through semantic IDs, compact codes a model can generate and act on. ShopX composes operations such as beam-search retrieval, listwise ranking and product bundling within a serving harness. Tests on tasks drawn from anonymized Taobao production logs show better fulfillment than tool-mediated agents, especially on complex or ambiguous requests. A capability breakdown yields practical guidance on ID design and training choices.
arxiv-2606-31893:
Xiao proves that generalized Medvedev logics can never be captured by finitely many axioms. Medvedev's logic of finite problems is characterized by products of two-element chains with the greatest element removed. A classic theorem says that logic is not finitely axiomatizable. Bezhanishvili conjectured the same failure for topless products of arbitrary chains and frames.
