Michael and co-authors review how the dose of exercise shapes the heart's nerve control during and after a workout. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Physiology. One common gauge tracks how much the heart rate varies. That gauge reflects the calming branch of the nerve system. It does not track the arousal branch well. Timing measures from each heartbeat fill that gap. Most past studies took these measures at rest.

Intensity proved the key factor for heart rate variation. Harder exercise lowered it during the effort. Past a fairly high level, the drop leveled off. A harder session also slowed recovery afterward. The exact dose pattern stayed unclear. Session length mattered only in narrow cases. Evidence on exercise type was thin and mixed. The timing measures were seldom reported at all. The authors advise tracking both gauge families together in future work.
europmc-pmc548793:
Kulldorff and co-authors present a methods paper in PLoS Medicine on detecting disease outbreaks early. Health departments increasingly scan daily data such as emergency visits and pharmacy sales. Such data lack a clear population base for rates. Older scan methods need that base to judge clusters. The authors propose a scan that uses case counts alone.

Their space-time permutation method shuffles dates and places among known cases. Real clusters then stand out against that shuffled backdrop. Daily runs on New York City emergency data flagged local outbreaks early. Four of the five strongest signals preceded citywide waves, they report. False alarms stayed modest in the test period.
europmc-pmc5501393:
Wei and co-authors report a methods comparison in PLoS ONE on disease coding for health record studies. Phenome-wide studies scan many diseases for gene links at once. They rely on billing codes to define each disease. Raw ICD-9 codes are often too fine or poorly grouped, though. The team compares three grouping systems head-to-head.

Hand-built phecodes matched 83 of 100 target diseases exactly. Raw ICD-9-CM codes matched 53, and CCS groups matched 32. Phecodes also replicated more known gene and disease links. Their signals tended to be stronger as well. All three systems can serve such studies, they conclude. Phecodes simply align best with real clinical diseases.
europmc-pmc5514393:
Anil and Anand present a review in Frontiers in Pediatrics on early childhood caries. This tooth decay strikes infants and preschool children worldwide. It starts as white spots along the gumline of upper front teeth. Untreated, it can destroy whole crowns. Prevalence reaches 85 percent in some disadvantaged groups.

Risk factors span microbes, diet, and family circumstances, they report. Sugary feeding habits and poor oral hygiene drive the damage. Low income and limited dental access raise the odds further. Pain, infection, and trouble eating or sleeping can follow. The disease is largely preventable, the authors stress. Fluoride and feeding guidance anchor their prevention advice.
europmc-pmc551593:
Morse and co-authors report a phase I trial in the Journal of Translational Medicine on a lung cancer vaccine. The vaccine uses dexosomes, tiny vesicles shed by dendritic cells. These parcels carry tumor antigens plus signals that wake immune cells. Thirteen patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer enrolled. Their tumors expressed MAGE antigens, the vaccine's targets.

Nine patients finished four weekly doses, the authors report. Side effects stayed mild: mostly sore injection sites. Some patients held stable disease for many months. Skin tests and lab assays showed immune activation in a few. Making the vaccine proved feasible, so larger trials could follow.
europmc-pmc5519493:
Braga and Buckner report a brain network study in Neuron. Group averages blur the fine layout of each person's brain networks. The authors scanned four people 24 times each instead. Such deep sampling exposes detail that group maps erase. The famous default network became their test case.

The default network split into two side-by-side networks, they report. Only one of them couples to the hippocampus. Neighboring networks split in similar paired ways. The pairs repeat across many cortical zones in a broad gradient. Their exact spots vary from person to person. Brain stimulation plans may need that personal detail, they argue.
europmc-pmc5539193:
Bitto and co-authors report a microbiology study in Scientific Reports on bacterial membrane vesicles and DNA. Gram-negative bacteria shed tiny sacs called outer membrane vesicles. These carry proteins and toxins to other cells. DNA rides along too, but its placement and purpose were unclear. The team examined vesicles from five diverse pathogens.

Most DNA clung to the vesicle surface, they report. A protected share sat inside the sacs. In Pseudomonas vesicles, that inner DNA was enriched for virulence and resistance genes. Vesicles delivered their DNA into human cells, even reaching the nucleus. The route may shape host responses and vaccine design.
europmc-pmc5569093:
Ali and co-authors design a dengue vaccine on the computer in Scientific Reports. Dengue kills people across the tropics each year. No fully effective prevention exists yet. The team turned to immunoinformatics instead of the wet lab.

They scanned dengue proteins for promising fragments. B-cell, killer T-cell, and helper T-cell epitopes were predicted. The final construct joins T-cell epitopes with a beta-defensin adjuvant. Checks found it antigenic and non-allergenic. Its folded structure was modeled and refined. Docking placed it against the TLR-3 immune receptor. Dynamics simulations supported a stable fit. europmc-pmc5585393:
Bertoni and co-authors present a modeling study in Scientific Reports. Cell work often depends on proteins joining into complexes. Lab structures for such assemblies lag far behind interaction data. Their method models whole complexes by homology, starting from amino acid sequences alone.

The approach must guess both the partner count and the overall shape. The team scores how well contact surfaces are conserved across evolution. They also cluster known complex structures to measure shape variety. Blending those scores with classic surface traits improved template choice. That gave more reliable models of protein complexes. Readers see how sequence clues can stand in when no lab structure exists.
europmc-pmc5622393:
Chouhan, Sharma, and Guleria review antimicrobial essential oils in Medicines. Plant essential oils kill a wide range of microbes. Drug resistance keeps rising in the meantime. Shoppers also distrust synthetic preservatives more each year.

How the oils attack microbes is only partly mapped. A few components have clear mechanisms. Most blends remain poorly understood. The review covers what is known about their action. It also weighs how oils interact with food components. Two fixes answer the oils' weak points. Nano-encapsulation shields them from fast evaporation and decay. That wrapping boosts stability and stretches their release. Pairing oils with antibiotics can add synergy as well. But additive and hostile pairings are hard to predict. Readers get the status and the open questions for fighting resistant pathogens.
europmc-pmc5671593:
Egamberdieva and co-authors present a review in Frontiers in Microbiology. It covers plant hormones and helpful microbes under stress. Crops face drought, salt, heat, and heavy metals. Such abiotic stresses cut growth and yield. Plant hormones strongly shape metabolism and defense responses. Adding hormones from outside can improve growth under stress.

Root microbes also make these hormones. Recent work shows their output can raise host tolerance. Hormone pathways have been mapped by genetic and chemical methods. The review focuses on crop plants and recent successes. It names plant traits that reveal positive hormone effects. The aim is better microbial inoculants for farming in harsh settings. That would support steady crop production.
europmc-pmc5707393:
Drewes and co-authors pool many studies to find shared microbes in colorectal cancer. Their work combines a new patient group from Malaysia with eleven public datasets. Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer in the world. Past studies tied gut microbes to the disease, but few links held across studies.

The team used fine-grained 16S rRNA gene profiling and checked for biofilms. Cancer tissues held more invasive biofilms, mostly on right-sided tumors. Certain bacteria turned up again and again across datasets. These included Bacteroides fragilis and several oral pathogens. Species from the mouth as a group were strongly enriched. No single feature appeared in all cases, but overlap was high.
europmc-pmc5720393:
Kortlever and co-authors show how two cancer genes team up to shield lung tumors. Their study uses a mouse lung model driven by the oncogene KRas. Adding Myc activation turned mild growths into fast, invasive cancers at once. The new tumors had inflamed, blood-rich tissue that blocked immune attack.

Two signals from the tumor cells drove that change. One, CCL9, drew in macrophages and helped push T and B cells out. The other, IL-23, kept out T cells, B cells, and natural killer cells. Blocking both signals halted tumor growth. Switching Myc off reversed the tissue changes and shrank the tumors. Returning natural killer cells played a key part in that reversal.
europmc-pmc5733393:
Clift and co-authors present Trim-Away, a fast way to destroy a chosen protein inside cells. Gene knockout and RNA methods act slowly, through DNA or RNA. Long lived proteins can resist both for days. Cells also gain time to mask the loss.

Trim-Away uses antibodies to tag the target protein where it sits. A cell receptor, TRIM21, then sends the tagged protein for breakdown. Removal takes minutes, with no change to the genome. The method works in many cell types, even cells that no longer divide. Ready made antibodies make it usable for a wide range of targets.
europmc-pmc5768693:
Fang and co-authors study how liver cancer spreads to the lung. They focus on the niche, the tissue that receives the cancer. Aggressive liver cancer cells turn normal fibroblasts into cancer linked ones. The team traced the signal that does this work.

The signal is a small RNA carried in exosomes from the tumor, they report. It switches on a pathway inside fibroblasts. The changed fibroblasts then release factors that feed cancer growth. In patients, high levels of this RNA in blood track lung spread. The chain offers targets for blocking metastasis, the authors say.
europmc-pmc5773593:
Risso and co-authors present a model for pulling signal from single-cell RNA data. Such data read gene activity one cell at a time. The tiny RNA amounts mean some active genes go unseen, a flaw called dropout. Standard tools can blur the picture such data should give.

Their model, ZINB-WaVE, builds compact summaries of the data. It accounts for dropouts, wide spread, and the count nature of the reads. It needs no first pass of normalization. On test and real data, it beat two rival tools for stable, accurate summaries, the authors report.
europmc-pmc5792493:
DeWaal and co-authors test what happens when liver cancer cells lose the enzyme hexokinase-2. Cancer cells favor this high grip form, while normal liver cells use another. Silencing it in human cancer cells slowed tumor growth and raised cell death. Mouse work pointed the same way.

Without the enzyme, sugar burning fell, they report. Cells leaned more on oxygen based energy making. That shift made them far more sensitive to the drug metformin. Pairing the loss with metformin or with sorafenib shrank tumors more. A shared signaling switch was blocked only by the pair.
europmc-pmc5827693:
Bhattacharya and co-authors describe ImmPort, an open trove of immunology study data. Immune studies yield rich, layered data on people and model animals. Reuse of that data can test old claims and spark new ones. ImmPort was built to make such reuse easy.

The system splits into private data, shared data, analysis, and resources. Over 300 studies sit free in the shared portal. Topics run from allergy and autoimmunity to transplants and vaccines. The team also pushes standards for assay data. Shared formats let separate studies be pooled and rechecked. Readers get a guide to a public engine for immune research.
europmc-pmc5868293:
Ferreira and co-authors profile the microbes that live in the stomach in gastric cancer. Their article appeared in Gut. Gastric cancer is triggered by Helicobacter pylori. Long infection cuts the acid the stomach makes. That shift may let other bacteria grow there. The team compared 54 cancer patients with 81 patients who had chronic gastritis. They read the microbes with 16S rRNA gene sequencing.

Cancer stomachs held a less varied mix of microbes, they report. Helicobacter was scarcer, while gut bacteria grew more common. A combined score split the cancer cases from the gastritis cases well. The cancer-linked mix did more nitrite-forming work. Such work can harm DNA, the authors note. Groups from other regions showed the same pattern.
europmc-pmc5885893:
Aung and co-authors pool trials of omega-3 supplements and heart risk. Their meta-analysis appeared in JAMA Cardiology. The team combined ten randomised trials. Together they held 77,917 participants at high heart risk. Supplements were marine omega-3 fatty acids, taken for 4.4 years on average. Outcomes included fatal and nonfatal coronary heart disease. Major vascular events were also tracked across trials.

The authors report no significant link to lower heart deaths. Nonfatal coronary events showed no clear drop either. Any major vascular event likewise showed no benefit. The results give no support for current advice, they say. High-risk patients should not count on these supplements. The finding weighs against routine use for prevention.
europmc-pmc5930493:
Lesyuk and co-authors review cost-of-illness studies in heart failure from 2004 to 2016. Their systematic review appeared in BMC Cardiovascular Disorders. They searched five databases for such studies. Sixteen studies met their rules for inclusion. Heart failure takes 1 to 2 percent of health budgets. Its prevalence keeps rising with ageing populations.

Methods and results varied widely across studies, they report. Hospital admission was the priciest part in most work. Yearly costs per patient ranged from 868 to 25,532 dollars. Only three studies counted indirect costs at all. Lifetime cost was estimated near 126,819 dollars per patient. Better methods could guide policy more firmly.
europmc-pmc5998893:
Zhang, Rabiee, Sayyari, and Mirarab introduce ASTRAL-III, a faster method for rebuilding species trees from gene trees. Their paper appeared in BMC Bioinformatics. Gene histories often disagree across the genome. Species trees must account for that discordance. ASTRAL searches for the tree sharing the most quartets with the gene trees. The new version guarantees polynomial running time. It also handles unresolved gene trees more efficiently. Several search shortcuts skip parts that cannot hold the best tree.

Simulations showed that cutting very weak branches improves accuracy, they report. Over-aggressive filtering hurt instead. On a bird data set of 14,000 genes the gains were large. The method scales to 10,000 species.
europmc-pmc6023993:
Watts and co-authors review how the brain manages energy and oxygen. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience. Neurons burn most of the brain's energy at synapses. Activity drives fast, local shifts in metabolism. Those shifts change the oxidative state of the cell.

Stress signals like reactive oxygen species shape neuron function. Low oxygen, called hypoxia, also plays a role. The review covers how metabolism is regulated in neurons. It links metabolic genes to learning and plasticity. It then turns to diseases where metabolism fails. Such failure marks many disorders tied to cognitive decline. Readers get a framework that treats metabolism as a driver of brain function, not just fuel.
europmc-pmc6040293:
Enogieru and co-authors review rutin as a possible brain protectant. Their article appeared in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. Rutin is a plant flavonoid found in buckwheat and citrus. Many brain diseases share oxidative stress as a driver. No current drug stops neuron loss in these diseases.

Studies in lab models link rutin to several helpful actions. It lowered inflammatory signals in those models. It raised antioxidant enzyme activity as well. It also restored activity of mitochondrial enzyme complexes. Gene changes touched both cell death and survival pathways. The authors sum up this evidence across disease models. They include Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's disease. Readers get a case for rutin as a candidate treatment. Human proof remains a task for future trials.
europmc-pmc6073093:
Weller and Budson review the current state of Alzheimer's disease diagnosis and care. Their review appeared in F1000Research. Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia worldwide. Its hallmarks are amyloid plaques and tau tangles in the brain. Cases keep rising as populations age.

Diagnosis now rests on clinical criteria plus biomarkers. Fluid tests and brain scans support the judgment. Two drug classes ease symptoms for a time. Neither slows the underlying decline. Trials now aim at cutting amyloid production and burden. The review sums up evaluation steps stage by stage. Readers get a clear briefing for clinic and family decisions.
europmc-pmc6098093:
Roager and Licht review microbial tryptophan catabolites in health and disease. Their review appeared in Nature Communications. Gut microbes break dietary protein into small products. Tryptophan yields a family of these compounds. They were long dismissed as waste.

New data give them active roles. Several switch on the aryl hydrocarbon receptor in immune cells. Others tighten the gut barrier or speed gut motion. Some calm inflammation in the blood. A few turn toxic instead. Effects reach gut hormones and microbial balance too. Most proof still comes from animal studies. Readers get a map of diet-microbe signals needing human tests.
europmc-pmc6273793:
Brglez Mojzer and co-authors review polyphenols, from extraction to cancer care. Their review appeared in Molecules. Polyphenols are plant compounds found in most fruit, herbs, and vegetables. They guard plants against sun, pests, and disease. In people they may help prevent several cancers. Low toxicity and wide availability add to their appeal.

Extraction methods open the review, with a green fluid method highlighted. That method protects fragile compounds from damage. The main problem is poor uptake in the body. Polyphenols break down fast after eating. Nano packaging can shield them until they reach target cells. Mixing polyphenols can also boost effect through synergy. Pairing them with standard drugs may cut drug toxicity. The review weighs each fix with care. It gives a realistic map of promise and limits.
europmc-pmc6340993:
Muller and co-authors review how cannabinoids act on TRP channels. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience. TRP channels are membrane gates for ions. They sense heat, pressure, acidity, and pain signals. Faults in them drive pain and inflammation. Cannabis compounds were found to switch some of them.

Six channels across three families respond to cannabinoids. Those are four TRPV channels, TRPA1, and TRPM8. Both plant and lab-made compounds act on them. Endogenous cannabinoids made by the body do too. The review maps each channel and compound pair. It explains how activation shapes sensation and disease. That detail matters for designing pain drugs. It also clarifies why cannabis effects vary so widely.
europmc-pmc6342893:
Williams and co-authors link coronary plaque traits to later heart events. Their analysis appeared in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology. It uses data from the SCOT-HEART trial. CT angiography can describe plaque types in artery walls. The team checked scans from 1,769 patients. All had suspected coronary artery disease.

Scans were scored across 15 artery segments. Adverse plaque meant outward bulging or low-density deposits. About a third of patients had such features. Those patients faced the worst outcomes over five years. Their rate of heart death or heart attack was highest. It was about tenfold the rate in clean arteries. The authors say plaque character adds warning value. It goes beyond simple narrowing or calcium scores.
europmc-pmc6344493:
Deshpande and co-authors present a tool that rebuilds amplified DNA regions in cancer. Their paper appeared in Nature Communications. Tumors often copy cancer genes many times over. Those copies can sit in tangled, rearranged blocks. Whole genome sequencing shows the raw pieces. AmpliconArchitect, or AA, assembles their fine structure.

The team validated the tool on simulated and real data. It handled a wide range of copy numbers and depths. Applied to a pan-cancer set, it found new patterns. Many amplified regions matched DNA circles outside chromosomes. Such circles form and copy themselves in tumor cells. In virus-linked cancers, many circles mixed human and viral DNA. The work gives a sharper view of how tumors evolve.
europmc-pmc6371893:
Babayan and co-authors present a data descriptor in Scientific Data. They release the LEMON dataset, built to study how mind, brain, and body interact. Data were collected in Leipzig between 2013 and 2015 from 227 healthy adults in two age groups.

The younger group held 153 people aged 20 to 35, and the older group held 74 people aged 59 to 77. Over two days, each person had MRI scans and a resting 62-channel EEG recording. Heart and breathing measures ran during the scans. The set adds blood and urine tests, six cognitive tests, and 21 questionnaires on emotion, personality, and habits. The data are public for reuse.
europmc-pmc6372693:
Albanna and co-authors present a proof-of-concept study in Scientific Reports on printing skin into wounds. Large full-thickness wounds heal slowly and can scar badly. Skin grafts need healthy donor skin, which may be scarce after major injury.

Their mobile system scans a wound, then prints the patient's own skin cells into it in place. Layered printing places the right cells at the right depth. In their tests, treated wounds closed faster and healed with less scarring risk. The work points toward on-site wound care at the bedside. Larger trials would be needed before routine use.
europmc-pmc6408493:
Cullot and co-authors report a cautionary study in Nature Communications on CRISPR editing. CRISPR-Cas9 can cut DNA at a chosen spot to fix a faulty gene. The team used it at a gene tied to a rare blood disorder, porphyria.

Clean repair proved rare next to rough, error-prone repair. More worrying, a single cut sometimes removed a huge stretch of chromosome. That loss appeared in cell lines and in primary cells, through a p53-linked route. A nicking version of the tool looked safer in their tests. The authors warn that gene therapy plans must screen for such damage.
europmc-pmc6448993:
Allin and co-authors compare gut microbiota in 134 Danish adults with prediabetes against 134 matched adults with normal glucose control, asking whether microbial shifts precede diabetes itself. Earlier diabetes signatures were muddied because the drug metformin reshapes the gut community. These participants were drug-naive, keeping the picture cleaner.

Five genera and 36 finer units differed between groups. Clostridium fell, while Dorea, Ruminococcus, Sutterella, and Streptococcus rose; the mucus-eating Akkermansia muciniphila was notably scarcer in prediabetes. Yet transplanting prediabetic stool into germ-free mice failed to disturb their glucose control. The altered community mirrors low-grade inflammation states, but this study could not show it causes the condition.
europmc-pmc6456593:
Kang and co-authors follow up the 18 children with autism and gut problems who completed Microbiota Transfer Therapy two years earlier, checking whether the gains of the original open-label trial endured. The therapy stacked antibiotics, a bowel cleanse, acid suppression, and fecal transplant from healthy donors. Gastrointestinal and behavioral symptoms had both improved by treatment's end.

Two years on, most gut improvements held, and autism-related symptoms had improved further still. Microbial changes persisted too, with greater diversity and more Bifidobacteria and Prevotella than before treatment. The authors read the durability as evidence of long-term safety and effect, while calling plainly for a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial next.
europmc-pmc6492693:
Jørgensen and co-authors review the sulfur cycle turning over beneath the seafloor, where microbes burn buried organic matter by reducing sulfate to sulfide, the dominant terminal pathway in anoxic sediment. Most sulfide is reoxidized through a tangle of in-between forms, elemental sulfur, polysulfides, thiosulfate, and sulfite, each fair game for further oxidation or reduction by other microbes.

New actors keep tangling the wiring further, including cable bacteria that ferry electrons over long distances to oxidize sulfide. Because many steps run partly in reverse, isotope patterns blur in informative ways, and the review shows how tracer results and splitting patterns must be read again once back-reactions are admitted. Ecology, chemistry, and isotope geochemistry are treated as one system.
europmc-pmc6498593:
Yang, Zhang and Wang review new treatments for small cell lung cancer in the Journal of Hematology & Oncology. This cancer grows fast, spreads early, and has long had few treatment options. Chemotherapy is still the standard first and second treatment, but most patients relapse, and survival rates stay low.

The review covers recent drug results by class. Checkpoint immunotherapy drugs such as nivolumab, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab and durvalumab have improved patient outcomes. Lurbinectedin won orphan drug status after tumors shrank in 39.3% of patients in a phase II study. Anlotinib, a targeted drug, lengthened the time before the cancer grew in its trial. A three-drug metronomic chemotherapy plan also beat topotecan on survival in a Japanese trial. The authors see the future in pairing immunotherapy with targeted drugs, tested in smarter trial designs.
europmc-pmc6503493:
Haslam and Prasad estimate how many US cancer patients could use, and gain from, checkpoint inhibitor drugs, writing in JAMA Network Open. These immune drugs drew wide praise, but no one had measured their reach across all cancers. The authors used FDA approval labels plus national cancer death counts as a stand-in for advanced disease.

Eligibility grew fast as approvals piled up. It rose from 1.54% of patients in 2011 to 43.63% in 2018. The share expected to respond rose from 0.14% to 12.46% over the same years. That tops the under-5% benefit once estimated for genome-driven drugs. Yet the authors stress the gains stay modest next to the hype around this drug class.
europmc-pmc6515593:
Myers, Amend and Pienta review TAM receptors on tumour-associated macrophages. Their review appeared in Molecular Cancer. These macrophages are abundant around tumours. They help cancers grow and suppress immune attack. The TAM family has three members: Tyro3, Axl and MerTK.

TAM receptors share the ligands Gas6 and Protein S. In macrophages, they push cells toward a pro-tumour M2-like state. They also drive efferocytosis, the clearing of dead cells. After that clearing, macrophages release more suppressive signals. Blocking TAM receptors could shift macrophage behaviour against the tumour. The authors survey therapies in preclinical work and trials. Effects on macrophages may add to direct effects on cancer cells.
europmc-pmc6516193:
Palmer and co-authors test whether clearing senescent cells eases obesity-linked metabolic harm. Their study appeared in Aging Cell. Senescent cells build up in the fat tissue of obese humans and rodents. Their causal role in diabetes was still unproven.

The team cut senescent cell burden in obese mice two ways. One used drug-activated suicide genes under the p16Ink4a promoter. The other used senolytic drugs such as dasatinib plus quercetin. Both routes improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity. Inflammatory signals in blood fell, and fat formation improved. Kidney and heart measures also got better. The authors read senescence as a causal driver worth targeting.
europmc-pmc6589893:
Li and co-authors show how the m6A writer METTL3 keeps a stemness gene alive in colorectal cancer, writing in Molecular Cancer. Colorectal tumors kill mainly by spreading, and a small pool of stem-like cells drives the relapse. Screening patient data and tumor samples, the team found METTL3 raised in metastatic tissue, marking patients for worse outcomes.

The mechanism runs through SOX2, a master stemness gene. METTL3 stamps SOX2's RNA with m6A marks, and the reader protein IGF2BP2 grips those marks and shields the message from decay. With SOX2 sustained, cancer cells renewed themselves, migrated, and seeded tumors and metastases in mouse models; removing METTL3 collapsed the chain. A three-protein panel of writer, reader and target predicted patient prognosis best.
europmc-pmc6625793:
Maeda, Otomo, and Otomo show that a membrane tether also moves lipids. Their research article appears in eLife. Cells build the autophagosome, a double-membrane sac, from a small precursor. That precursor, the phagophore, must gain lipids to expand. The protein ATG2 links the phagophore to the endoplasmic reticulum.

The team tested human ATG2A in lab assays with membrane vesicles. The protein pulled lipids out of one vesicle and unloaded them into another. Transfer ran faster between tethered vesicles than free ones. Partner proteins WIPI4 and WIPI1 held ATG2A on PI3P-rich vesicles. That grip sped both tethering and transfer. The authors propose that ATG2 ferries lipids from the reticulum to the growing phagophore. This supply line, they argue, drives its expansion.
europmc-pmc6651993:
Zheng and co-authors track how the gut microbiome relates to anti-PD-1 therapy in liver cancer. Their study appears in the Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer. Eight patients received anti-PD-1 antibodies after sorafenib failure. Stool samples were sequenced across the treatment course. Responders carried richer gut communities with more genes. Non-responders diverged in composition by week six. Their Proteobacteria rose from week three onward. By week twelve that group predominated.

Twenty species were enriched in responders. Akkermansia muciniphila and Ruminococcaceae species stood out. Functional genes matched their likely activities. The authors suggest stool dynamics could predict outcomes early. Such signals would aid monitoring and treatment choices.
europmc-pmc6705893:
Senkomago and co-authors estimate cancers caused by human papillomavirus in the United States for 2012 to 2016. Their surveillance report appears in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. CDC analysts used national cancer statistics data. Registries covered the full population. An average 43,999 HPV-associated cancers occurred yearly. An estimated 34,800 were due to HPV. That is 79 percent of the total. Most such cases involved vaccine-targeted types. The 9-valent vaccine covers those types. They accounted for 32,100 cancers annually.

Oropharyngeal cancer was the commonest type due to HPV. It contributed 12,600 cases per year. Cervical cancer followed at 9,700. Anal, vulvar, penile, and vaginal cancers completed the list. Only half of adolescents were vaccinated at the time. Prevention potential remains largely untapped.
europmc-pmc6719893:
Ghurye and co-authors present SALSA, a tool that assembles genomes to chromosome scale. New sequencing methods yield long reads, but joining them into full chromosomes is error-prone. Hi-C data, which shows which DNA parts sit near each other, can guide the joins. Open tools for this task were scarce, and errors stayed high.

SALSA uses the assembly graph, not just finished pieces, to guide its choices. It needs no advance guess of the chromosome count. Tests across Hi-C library types and assembly sizes showed fewer errors than leading methods. The code is free in Python and C++, at a public address given in the paper.
europmc-pmc6758693:
Pei and Wu asked whether online learning beats classroom learning for medical undergraduates. Technology has made online teaching common, but its value was unproven. The pair searched five databases and four key journals for studies from 2000 to 2017. They pooled knowledge and skill outcomes in a meta-analysis.

Sixteen studies emerged from 3,700 articles. On post-test scores, online learning came out clearly ahead for both knowledge and skills. The single retention comparison also favored online learning. But gains from pre-test to post-test showed no real difference. Nothing suggested offline learning works better. Online methods, the authors conclude, can strengthen what medical students learn.
europmc-pmc6829293:
Mantha and co-authors review smart hydrogels in the journal Materials. Hydrogels are water-rich gels that can hold cells and support growing tissue. They resemble the soft matrix that surrounds cells in the body. Smart versions also react to cues such as heat, acidity, or light. Regenerative medicine hopes to use them to rebuild lost tissue and organs.

The review covers how these gels are made and tuned. It explains how their firmness and breakdown rate can be matched to a target tissue. Uses range from cartilage and bone to the discs between spine bones. The authors also note the slow repair of some tissues as a design limit.
europmc-pmc6851393:
Baldassari and co-authors report a large genetic study of focal cortical dysplasia, in Acta Neuropathologica. In this condition, part of the brain's cortex forms wrongly before birth. It is a major cause of severe childhood epilepsy that drugs cannot control, so surgery is often the only option. The malformed tissue holds swollen, abnormal neurons.

The team enrolled 80 children whose removed tissue confirmed one of these malformations. They sequenced target genes at very high depth in matched blood and brain samples. Both inherited variants and changes found only in the brain played a part. Sorting which genes drive which form of the condition should guide diagnosis and future treatment.
europmc-pmc6889193:
Wang and co-authors report a study in Cell Death and Differentiation on a lung cancer RNA that blocks a form of cell death. Ferroptosis kills cells through iron-driven damage to their membranes. A nuclear long noncoding RNA, LINC00336, runs high in lung cancer and acts as an oncogene. It protects cancer cells by soaking up microRNAs. It also does something more direct.

LINC00336 binds a stabilising protein, ELAVL1, at a defined stretch of its sequence. That binding helps it hold back ferroptosis. In a feedback loop, ELAVL1 also steadies LINC00336 itself, raising its level. A chromatin factor, LSH, feeds the loop through the p53 pathway. Interrupting the circuit, the authors suggest, could expose lung tumours to ferroptotic death.
europmc-pmc6891893:
The Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer pools the world evidence in The Lancet on hormone therapy and breast cancer. Menopausal hormone therapy eases symptoms such as hot flushes. Reports on its breast cancer risk had conflicted for decades, and long-term effects were murky. The group gathered individual data from every eligible prospective study, published and unpublished.

Studies were tracked from January 1992 to January 2018. Nearly all therapy types raised risk somewhat, and the risk grew with years of use. Combined oestrogen-progestagen carried higher risk than oestrogen alone. Even progestagen-only therapy showed a raised risk ratio of 1.39 during years 5 to 14 of use. Some excess risk lingered after stopping, the analysis found.
europmc-pmc6918593:
Heinzinger and co-authors turn a language model into a tool for protein sequences. Their study appeared in BMC Bioinformatics. Predicting protein structure and function from sequence is a core task in computational biology. Classic methods rely on evolutionary data from related proteins. Finding those relatives is slow, and small protein families give weak signals.

The team adapted ELMo, a model built for human language, to amino acid sequences. Their embeddings, called SeqVec, were learned from unlabeled data in UniRef50. Simple neural networks using SeqVec predicted structure, disorder, and cell location well. Speed was the striking gain. Embeddings took about 0.03 seconds per protein, against roughly two minutes for a standard search tool.
europmc-pmc6938793:
Schoeler and Caesar review how dietary fat interacts with gut microbes and body fat handling. Their review appeared in Reviews in Endocrine and Metabolic Disorders. Gut microbes act as central regulators of host metabolism. What we eat, including the amount and type of lipid, reshapes that community.

Lipids feed some bacteria and poison others, shifting the mix. In turn, microbes affect lipid levels in blood and tissues, in mice and humans. Their products include short-chain fatty acids, secondary bile acids, and trimethylamine. Inflammatory bacterial factors also play a part. Disorders tied to faulty lipid levels, such as fatty liver disease and atherosclerosis, show altered gut profiles. Diet, microbes, and metabolism, the pair argue, form one linked system.
europmc-pmc6942593:
Guan and Liu review how microbes survive acid stress, and how industry can use that skill. Their review appeared in Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology. Microbes meet harsh acid during many production processes. Acid can wreck metabolism and kill cells, so species have evolved layered defences.

Cells protect themselves by holding their inner pH steady. They keep membranes intact and fluid, adjust metabolism, and repair damaged molecules. Such tolerance has practical value. It helps probiotic bacteria survive stomach acid on the way to the gut. It also boosts output of organic acids made by fermentation. The authors argue that systems and synthetic biology can sharpen these traits further, building hardier cell factories for useful chemicals.
europmc-pmc6960993:
Ho and co-authors identify disease-causing bacteria in minutes using light fingerprints and deep learning. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Raman spectroscopy can read a bacterium's chemical signature without labels. Weak signals and the sheer number of species have slowed its clinical use.

The team built a large library of bacterial Raman spectra, then trained deep learning models on it. The system named 30 common pathogens with average accuracy above 82 percent, even on noisy spectra. It also chose the right antibiotic treatment with about 97 percent accuracy. Resistant and sensitive staphylococcus strains were told apart at 89 percent accuracy. Tests on samples from 50 patients held up, reaching 99.7 percent treatment accuracy from just 10 spectra each. Culture-free diagnosis, the authors argue, is within reach.
europmc-pmc6997393:
Reiman and co-authors show that people with two copies of a protective gene variant almost never develop Alzheimer's dementia. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The APOE gene shapes Alzheimer's risk. Its E4 version raises risk with each copy, while E2 lowers it. Whether two E2 copies give special protection was unknown.

The team built odds from more than 5,000 cases and controls, all checked clinically and by brain examination after death. People with APOE2/2 had far lower dementia odds than those with one E2, and exceptionally lower odds than E4 homozygotes. The gene-dose effect ran stronger in brain-confirmed cases than in a comparison set of over 24,000 unconfirmed ones. Finding how APOE variants protect or harm, the authors argue, could transform prevention.
europmc-pmc7007693:
Qin and co-authors present Lisa, a program that infers which regulators drive a set of genes. Their paper appeared in Genome Biology. Gene sets from expression studies hint at the transcription factors and chromatin regulators behind them. Guessing those regulators well takes more than the gene list alone.

Lisa builds a chromatin model for the input genes from public histone-mark and accessibility data. It then tests candidate regulators by deleting their binding sites in the computer and watching the model change. Regulators whose removal hurts most rank highest. In benchmark tests on gene sets from targeted knockdown experiments, Lisa beat rival methods at naming the perturbed regulator. In stem cells it correctly flagged NANOG, SOX2, and POU5F1 as masters of the downregulated genes. The tool is freely available online, backed by a large uniform database of public experiments.
europmc-pmc7069093:
Liu and co-authors review magnetic hyperthermia for cancer in Theranostics. The method heats tumours from inside: magnetic nanoparticles lodged in the tissue make heat when an alternating magnetic field is applied. Its draws are high safety, deep reach into tissue, and selective killing of tumour over healthy tissue. The field has about 60 years of history, yet clinical impact still trails the theory.

Most work has chased higher heating power from the particles, the basic lever for stronger therapy. Newer proof complicates that picture: nanoparticle heating can damage cell structures at nanoscale hot spots with no measurable rise in overall tumour temperature. Grasping those local effects could explain, and improve, the treatment's power. The review gathers current strategies for raising antitumour efficacy, from better particle design to pairing magnetic heating with imaging and other therapies, and maps the hurdles still blocking wider use.
europmc-pmc7140093:
Pottier and co-authors review tyrosine kinase inhibitors in cancer, in Cancers. Receptor tyrosine kinases are signalling proteins that govern cell growth and spread, and they are faulty in many cancers. Over the last two decades, drugs blocking them have become first- or second-line treatments for several tumor types.

Their success is limited by resistance and side effects, which the review explains in detail. New tools, including artificial intelligence, chemoproteomics, and microfluidics, may yield sharper, more selective inhibitors. Combining different kinase blockers, or pairing them with other drug types, is discussed as a route to personalised treatment with less collateral damage. The authors frame the field as a breakthrough still working through its challenges.
europmc-pmc7164393:
Sheahan and co-authors test an oral antiviral compound against SARS-CoV-2 and several other coronaviruses, in Science Translational Medicine. The compound, NHC, is a ribonucleoside analog that corrupts viral RNA copying. Its prodrug form, EIDD-2801, can be swallowed rather than injected, a practical advantage in an outbreak.

The drug worked against SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV, and related bat coronaviruses in lab cultures, including human airway cells. It even kept potency against a coronavirus resistant to remdesivir. In mice with SARS or MERS, preventive and treatment dosing improved lung function and cut virus levels and weight loss. Viral RNA accumulated mutations, supporting a lethal mutagenesis mechanism.
europmc-pmc7171193:
Lindestam Arlehamn and co-authors track immune responses to alpha-synuclein in Parkinson's disease. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Alpha-synuclein is a protein that builds up in the brains of people with Parkinson's. The team measured T cells that react to this protein. They compared healthy donors with patients before and after diagnosis.

Responses were strongest shortly after a motor Parkinson's diagnosis. They then faded over the following years. One patient showed high responses before motor symptoms began. The pattern suggests the immune reaction starts early in the disease. It may later quiet down as the illness advances. The authors argue this timing matters for early detection. It could also shape when immune-based treatments might help most.
europmc-pmc7297793:
Shang and co-authors design a single-atom catalyst for the oxygen reduction reaction, a key step in fuel cells and metal-air batteries. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Platinum catalysts work well but are rare and costly. Cheaper catalysts built from single metal atoms offer a way out if their atomic surroundings can be controlled.

The team anchored single copper atoms in porous carbon derived from a metal-organic framework, arranging each site with one sulfur and three nitrogen neighbors, an unsymmetrical pattern. The catalyst reached a half-wave potential of 0.918 V, showing excellent activity. X-ray tests during operation showed the low-valent copper site is the true working center. The design offers a general scheme for tuning single-atom catalysts for energy devices.
europmc-pmc7308593:
García, in a solo-authored review, argues that the wide range of COVID-19 severity mirrors the wide range of immune responses to the virus. The review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Infection can pass without symptoms or proceed to severe pneumonia and multi-system failure. Every arm of the immune system takes part in clearing the virus and recovering.

The same responses, the review stresses, can drive the disease's lethal turn. The critical point comes when regulation between protective and damaging responses is lost and inflammation escalates. Comparing SARS-CoV-2 with the earlier SARS and MERS viruses sharpens the picture. García sets out the open questions in how the disease develops, aiming to guide better diagnosis, treatment, and prevention.
europmc-pmc7319493:
Weiskopf and co-authors follow the T cells that recognize SARS-CoV-2 in intensive care patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome. Their study appeared in Science Immunology. Severe COVID-19 mixes two puzzles: patients often have too few lymphocytes, yet their immune systems are hyperactive, a pattern dubbed cytokine storm. Which T cells actually target the virus, and how they change over time, was little known.

By stimulating blood cells with pools of viral peptides, the team tracked virus-specific CD4 and CD8 T cells over the course of illness. Such cells, aimed at the spike, membrane, and nucleoprotein, were found in patients and could be followed as disease progressed. Earlier work in one recovering patient showed activated T cells rising just before symptoms resolved. The study gives a longitudinal picture for the sickest group.
europmc-pmc7331093:
Clark and co-authors, working with the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium, profile kidney cancer in Cell. Their subject is clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the most common kidney cancer form. The team combined gene, protein, and chemical-tag data from tumors and matched healthy tissue.

One group of tumors stood out for genomic instability, meaning their DNA carried heavy damage. Protein data showed changes that gene data alone missed, in energy pathways, protein building, and cell signaling. The team also sorted tumors into four immune types, based on which immune cells had moved in. Readers get a deep map of how gene damage plays out inside these tumors, and hints for matching treatment to type.
europmc-pmc7331793:
Britton and co-authors model herd immunity to SARS-CoV-2 in Science. Herd immunity is the point where enough people are immune that spread slows on its own. Classic estimates assumed everyone mixes alike, which real populations do not.

Their model splits people by age and by activity level, since active people catch and pass the virus more. With that uneven spread, immunity builds first among the most active, and the threshold falls to about 40 percent of the population infected. That is far below earlier estimates. They also warn that very strict controls can block immunity from building at all. If controls lift too fast, infections surge back.
europmc-pmc7335093:
Li and co-authors search for one shared stimulation target for obsessive-compulsive disorder in Nature Communications. Deep brain stimulation, which sends pulses through implanted electrodes, had been aimed at several different brain sites for this condition. The team pooled data from four patient groups, 50 people in all.

Whether electrodes sat near the internal capsule, the nucleus accumbens, or the subthalamic nucleus, the same fiber bundle tracked the best response. That bundle connects frontal regions to the subthalamic nucleus. A model built from one group predicted improvement in the others, across centers. The authors share the target openly so surgeons can use it. Readers see how network maps can unify rival surgical approaches.
europmc-pmc7392393:
Tenforde and co-authors report how long milder COVID-19 keeps people unwell, in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Telephone interviews reached a random sample of outpatients who had first tested positive at 14 academic health systems in 13 states. Interviews ran 14 to 21 days after the test, and 292 adults responded.

Of those with symptoms at testing, 35 percent had not returned to their usual health by interview, a median of 16 days later. Even among 18 to 34 year olds, 26 percent were still unwell. Cough lingered in 43 percent of those who had it, fatigue in 35 percent, and breathlessness in 29 percent. Mild illness, the report stresses, is not always brief, even for the young.
europmc-pmc7400693:
Borcherding and co-authors present scRepertoire in F1000Research, a software toolkit for single-cell immune receptor data. Single-cell sequencing can read both a cell's gene activity and its immune receptor, the identity card T and B cells use to recognize targets. Software for the gene side was plentiful, but receptor analysis lacked options.

Their R package processes data from 10x Genomics immune profiling runs, covering both T cell receptors and immunoglobulins. It slots into popular expression tools such as Seurat, so receptor and activity data can be studied together. The package is open source on GitHub with in-depth tutorials and processed example data. Readers get a practical methods paper for a fast-growing corner of immunology and cancer research.
europmc-pmc7403393:
Touret and co-authors screen a library of approved drugs for activity against SARS-CoV-2 in Scientific Reports. With no approved treatment existing, repurposing known drugs offered the fastest route to the clinic. Their screen used the Prestwick Chemical Library of 1,520 approved compounds in infected cells.

Ninety compounds scored as hits, including some already known to work in such assays, which validated the screen. From a shortlist, 11 compounds showed real antiviral potency, among them macrolide antibiotics, proton pump inhibitors, antiarrhythmic agents, and nervous system drugs. Potency sat in a modest range, so none was a ready cure. Still, the catalogue gave trial designers a vetted starting list instead of guesses.
europmc-pmc7407193:
Naeem and co-authors review ways to curb off-target damage in CRISPR gene editing, in Cells. CRISPR-Cas9 is simpler, cheaper, and more efficient than older editors, but it sometimes cuts DNA at look-alike sites. Those stray cuts are the system's crucial shortcoming for medicine.

The review sorts the fixes. Some detect stray cuts better. Others use gentler editors that swap single letters without full cuts, or prime editing, or tamed Cas9 forms. Paired nickase enzymes cut only when both halves agree. Delivery as short-lived protein complexes limits exposure time. Shortened guide RNAs also sharpen aim. Each approach trades some efficiency for safety. Readers get a current catalogue for judging how cleanly a given editing job can be done.
europmc-pmc7473193:
Yuen and co-authors find which SARS-CoV-2 proteins block interferon, the cell's antiviral alarm. Early immune suppression is a hallmark of this virus. The team compared its proteins with known blockers from SARS-CoV.

Four viral parts, nsp13, nsp14, nsp15, and orf6, strongly shut down interferon making and signaling. The unique orf8 protein did not. Of 27 viral proteins tested, orf6 was the strongest blocker of all. In contrast, the SARS-CoV-2 PLpro protein lost blocking powers that its SARS-CoV twin holds. A virus missing orf6 might serve as a live but weakened nasal vaccine. The study maps the virus's stealth tools. Such maps help design drugs that restore the alarm in infected cells.
europmc-pmc7505693:
Wang and co-authors survey mental health among college students in a large United States university system during COVID-19. The team worked at Texas A&M University with an online survey. Standard scales measured depression and anxiety.

Of 2031 participants, 960 showed moderate-to-severe depression levels and 775 showed moderate-to-severe anxiety levels on the scales used. A further 366 reported suicidal thoughts in the survey responses. Most participants said their stress and anxiety had risen in the pandemic. Less than half felt able to cope well with the strain. Worries spanned studies, health, and daily life changes. The authors call the shares alarming for one campus system. They urge more work to grasp and meet student needs in long crises.
europmc-pmc7513993:
Groarke and co-authors measure loneliness in the UK during the first COVID-19 lockdown. Lockdown cut social contact across the country. The public feared harm to mental health from the rules.

The team analyzed baseline survey data from 1964 UK adults gathered in the COVID-19 Psychological Wellbeing Study. Loneliness prevalence was 27% in the sample, or 530 of 1964 adults surveyed. Younger adults faced the highest risk by far. Being separated or divorced raised risk, as did depression-level scores. Poor sleep tied to the crisis also raised the odds. Marriage, living with more adults, and strong social support protected against loneliness. The authors urge support aimed first at younger people. Better sleep and emotion control may blunt lockdown harm, they add.
europmc-pmc7726193:
Budreviciute and co-authors review how to manage and prevent non-communicable diseases. These chronic diseases, such as heart disease and diabetes, cause 71% of deaths worldwide each year. Risk factors span habits, genes, surroundings, medical state, and social position. Food choices sit at the heart of risk control.

The authors sort prevention by level: the person, society, the nation, and the globe. Lifestyle change is the strongest lever, through diet, activity, quitting smoking, and control of metabolic risks. They call for joint work across sectors and better flow of knowledge. New tools and clear policy round out their proposed plan.
europmc-pmc7728293:
Arevalo-Rodriguez and co-authors review how often a first COVID-19 test misses true cases. The test is RT-PCR on a swab sample. A false negative frees an infected person from isolation and risks spread. The team searched major databases and COVID-19 evidence hubs, current to July 17, 2020.

They kept 34 studies with 12,057 confirmed cases. All studies carried bias risks or limits in how far results apply. Miss rates varied wildly between studies, with no clear cause for the spread. Proof quality was rated very low. The authors warn that a single negative first test should not rule out infection when suspicion runs high.
europmc-pmc7780693:
Madden and co-authors review efforts to block c-Myc directly as a cancer treatment. c-Myc is a transcription factor. It is switched on at abnormal levels in over 70% of human cancers.

Blocking c-Myc in mice caused fast tumor regression. Side effects were mild and fully reversible. Those results mark direct inhibition as a plausible treatment path. The authors weigh the known hurdles in targeting this protein. They assess lessons from current inhibitors. Future routes include shrinking the inhibitor Omomyc into a smaller form. Another route targets how c-Myc binds E-box DNA sites. The aim is to move c-Myc blockers toward clinical use.
europmc-pmc7804893:
Huang and co-authors review how inflammation in the body can break the blood-brain barrier. The barrier seals the brain off from blood flow. It controls what passes between vessels and brain tissue. A sound barrier keeps the brain stable and working well.

Body-wide inflammation can loosen that seal by several routes. A leaky barrier then feeds many brain diseases. Recent cases include brain problems after SARS-CoV-2 infection. CAR-T cell therapy can trigger the same kind of cytokine storm. The authors first set out how the barrier works in health. They then list the factors that disrupt it. The goal is a base for shielding the brain during severe inflammation.
europmc-pmc7829493:
Ravens-Sieberer and colleagues studied how the COVID-19 pandemic affected children and teens in Germany. School closures, closed leisure sites, and distance rules changed daily life. Early reports from abroad hinted at harm to mental health. No nationwide study had asked German children. The COPSY study set out to fill that gap.

The team surveyed 1586 families with children aged 7 to 17 between May 26 and June 10, 2020. They compared the replies with pre-pandemic data from the BELLA study. Two-thirds of the children said they felt highly burdened. The authors reported low quality of life in 40.2 percent of the children, up from 15.3 percent before the pandemic. Mental health problems rose to 17.8 percent from 9.9 percent, and anxiety rose to 24.1 percent from 14.9 percent in the years before. Children with low socioeconomic status, a migration background, or limited living space were affected more. Readers get breakdowns by age and sex, plus the survey tools.
europmc-pmc7877493:
du Plessis and co-authors report a genomic study of how the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic took hold in the UK. They drew on one of the largest virus sampling efforts of the early pandemic. Their aim was to trace the lineages that entered the country and spread within it.

The team analysed 50,887 virus genomes, including 26,181 from the UK first wave. They combined family-tree analysis with travel and case data. The authors report more than 1000 separate UK transmission lineages. Lineages that arrived before the national lockdown tended to grow larger and spread wider. Imports and local diversity fell after lockdown began. The study shows how genome data can reveal the fine structure of an epidemic while it is still unfolding.
europmc-pmc8128293:
Lythgoe and co-authors sequence SARS-CoV-2 deeply inside more than a thousand hospital patients. Consensus genomes show only each infection's loudest variant. The full within-host swarm is where new variants are born. Most samples carried just one or two variants apiece. A few patients carried many at once. Strong purifying selection pruned the swarm, even in the spike protein.

Household clusters and likely superspreader events left linked patterns. Shared rare variants traced those transmission threads between people. After jumping to a new host, most variants simply fizzled out. Occasionally one caught hold and seeded ongoing spread. The bottleneck at transmission is tight, the data show. That tightness slows how fast within-host experiments escape. It also means surveillance catches most successful mutants late. Deep sequencing fills the gap between birth and spread. Evolution's workshop floor is now partly visible.
europmc-pmc8157593:
Wang and Qian assess phthalates and their impacts on human health. Phthalates are widely used chemicals that can disrupt hormones. They turn up in many goods that touch plastics during making, packing, or shipping.

Though each dose clears fast, steady exposure can harm many organs. The review links phthalates to risks in pregnancy, child growth, and fertility. It sets out toxicity paths and risk assessment methods. Harms to children get their own section. The authors review current limits and urge wider curbs or safer substitutes. Feasible steps to cut exposure close the article.
europmc-pmc8203293:
Nicolas-Boluda and co-authors test whether softening a tumour helps T cells and immunotherapy. Dense matrix in tumours can wall T cells out. Only a share of patients gain from checkpoint inhibitors.

Across five mouse tumour models, stiffness rose with growth and matrix crosslinking. Stiffer tumours showed less T cell movement inside. Blocking lysyl oxidase cut collagen stabilisation and softened the tumours. T cell migration improved after that change. Anti-PD-1 treatment then worked better. The study ties a physical trait of tumours to a drug strategy. Matrix change, not just immune drugs, did part of the work.
europmc-pmc8382893:
Xu and co-authors present ggtreeExtra, a software package for drawing rich data onto phylogenetic trees. Trees are used in genomics, epidemiology, and microbiome work. Adding outside data layers to a tree helps readers spot patterns and form new ideas.

The package draws trees in circular or rectangular layouts. It supports more data types and display methods than rival tools. Users can add annotated layers with grammar of graphics syntax. Results from common evolutionary software can be merged with outside data sets. The authors present the package as a general tool that widens the use of trees across fields.
europmc-pmc8424393:
Kurian and co-authors review GelMA hydrogels strengthened with nanomaterials for tissue repair. GelMA, a methacrylated gelatin, is a popular scaffold for growing cells in three dimensions. It can also carry drugs and cells into damaged tissue.

Adding nanomaterials gives the gel new powers. Mixes can be stiffer, easier to print, or able to conduct electric or magnetic signals. Some mixes release their cargo in response to cues. Others add direct healing effects, such as calming oxidation. Gains have been shown in bone, skin, heart, and nerve tissue. The authors present these blends as next-generation platforms for tissue therapeutics.
europmc-pmc8639093:
Lin, Deng, and Pan propose a new method for Mendelian randomization that blends two standard tools. The method uses gene variants to test if one trait causes another. One tool is strong when all variants are valid. The other stays sound when some variants act through side paths, but it loses power.

Their model mixes both regressions in one frame. It counts valid and invalid variants at the same time. Tests showed it often beat each tool alone on power and error control. The team added steps to handle doubt in model choice. They applied it to 48 risk factor and disease pairs and 63 unrelated trait pairs. Results held up well.
europmc-pmc8903393: Raman, Bluemke, Lüscher, and Neubauer examine the lasting effects of COVID-19 with a focus on the heart and blood vessels. Their subject is long COVID, the post-acute phase when symptoms and organ effects persist after infection, from heart muscle injury to vessel and rhythm problems. The hosted text for this record is fragmentary: front matter and the reference list survive, but the article body does not. The record is therefore described only by its stated focus, authorship, and scope.
europmc-pmc9086893:
Chennamadhavuni and co-authors offer a practical guide to side effects from immune checkpoint inhibitors. These cancer drugs free the immune system to attack tumors. They can also cause immune harm to the gut, lungs, skin, and other organs. Bad cases can be life threatening and can end cancer care.

The guide lists risk factors by age, sex, weight, past illness, and drug use. It also sorts blood tests and other markers that may warn of harm ahead. Some markers, like blood counts and thyroid tests, are easy to get in daily care. The authors add advice on when a patient might safely restart these drugs. Clinicians get a hands-on aid for spotting high-risk patients early.
europmc-pmc9344793:
Duan and co-authors review how the body keeps cholesterol in balance, and how that balance can be drugged. Cholesterol balance rests on making, taking in, moving, storing, and clearing the fat. When control fails, heart disease, brain disease, and cancers can follow. Lowering LDL cholesterol is proven to protect the heart.

The review traces the history of cholesterol science, Nobel prizes included. It maps the control paths gene by gene, from the SREBP switch onward. Current cholesterol-lowering drugs are sorted by how they act. New targets in trials get their own survey. Benefits reach beyond heart disease to diabetes, fatty liver, and even virus infection. The authors argue the same pathways serve many diseases at once.
europmc-pmc9385493:
Cao and co-authors ask whether antibodies from Omicron infection can stop its newer branches. They studied plasma from triple-vaccinated people and from those who had BA.1 infection after vaccination. Structural comparisons of the spike proteins framed the tests. A library of 1,640 spike-binding antibodies was profiled for escape patterns.

Infection after vaccination mostly recalled memory aimed at the original virus. Those antibodies cover the old virus and BA.1 but fail at the newest spike changes in BA.4/BA.5 and its kin. New antibodies specific to the first Omicron branch were narrow and weak elsewhere. Two drug antibodies, bebtelovimab and cilgavimab, still neutralized the new branches. The authors conclude that boosters built on the first Omicron branch may not give broad cover against later ones.
europmc-pmc9613693:
Wang and co-authors show that Wnt and beta-catenin signaling shields gastric cancer cells from ferroptosis. Chemotherapy resistance is the top block to success in this cancer. The Wnt pathway is often faulty in gastric tumors. Ferroptosis is an iron driven death that chemo can trigger.

Active Wnt signaling cut lipid reactive oxygen in the cells. That drop blocked ferroptosis and let cells survive. The beta-catenin and TCF4 complex binds the GPX4 gene promoter. Binding switches GPX4 on, and GPX4 mops up lipid damage. Lack of TCF4 had the reverse effect on cells. It made cisplatin spark more ferroptosis in lab and animal tests. The authors propose breaking this shield to restore drug sensitivity. Such a move could help patients with advanced disease.
europmc-pmc9905093:
Hirz and co-authors dissect the immune-suppressive setting inside human prostate tumors. Low-risk prostate cancer often needs only active surveillance. High-risk disease needs surgery, radiation, and hormone treatment combined. Recurrence and spread remain common problems with unclear immune causes.

The team combined single-cell RNA sequencing with high-resolution spatial transcriptomics. They compared tumor tissue with nearby normal tissue and healthy controls. Tumors showed suppressive myeloid cells and exhausted T cells. Stromal areas showed strong new vessel activity. Ligand-receptor analysis traced cell-to-cell signals inside intact tissue sections. The result is a detailed resource on the prostate tumor setting. It may guide work on immune escape and tumor growth.
freeman-giles-corey-1893:
Freeman turned to drama in Giles Corey, Yeoman, a play printed by Harper in 1893. The cast lists Giles and Martha Corey, minister Samuel Parris, and judges Hathorne and Corwin. Act one opens in Corey's Salem Village home, with daughter Olive at her spinning.

Little Phoebe Morse knits nearby while old servant Nancy Fox pares apples. A strange clatter in the chimney scares the child at the very start. Behind the scene stands the true Salem horror of 1692. Corey, an old farmer, was pressed to death under stones rather than confess to witchcraft, and his last words were a call for more weight.
french-constitution-1793:
The National Convention adopted a new French constitution in June 1793, drawn up by the Mountain, the Revolution's radical party. France was at war and near civil war, and the charter promised more democracy than any law of its age. It was approved by a popular vote, then set aside until peace should come. Peace never came in time.

The text grants the vote to all adult men and declares work, public help, and education to be rights of every citizen. It even blesses the people's right to rise against a government that betrays them. No charter ever offered the people more on paper. Its makers never dared to put it into force, ruling instead through the Terror. The constitution stands as the Revolution's boldest dream of self-rule, written down but never tried in life.
frus-1861-d193:
John Appleton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 April 1861. The dispatch is document 193 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Appleton held the St. Petersburg post until Clay could reach it. His April report came four days before Fort Sumter. It shows the old envoy serving the new chief through the last days of peace, with Russia friendly but far away. Russia's goodwill, though real, could not send ships or gold across the world in time. Goodwill that could not send aid still denied aid's hope to the other side.
frus-1861-d293:
The State Department sent word to Mr. Harvey on 30 July 1861, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 293 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d93:
On 29 October 1861, William H. Seward closed the month with a letter to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 93 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's last October letter to Adams keeps the routine of the autumn intact. Neither man knew that a Union warship was about to stop a British mail ship at sea. The letter's calm close to the month makes the crisis that followed stand out all the more. Within a month the two envoys seized from the Trent would fill every London talk. Every London talk that winter would turn on the names of those two envoys.
frus-1862-d193:
The last Adams letter in this run, Document 193. Is a Seward dispatch of 21 November 1862 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It closes the autumn sequence of the London file in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

By late November the danger of Britain and France acting together on the war had passed for the year. What remained was the slower fight over ships, trade, and opinion, which ran on into 1863. This letter stands at the point where the record turns from emergency to endurance, a fair summary of the Union's foreign war. Adams reported home at least once a week, and oftener when the news was hot.
frus-1862-d293:
On 9 July 1862 William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report printed as Document 293 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The report came after a gap in the Paris file.

By the time Dayton wrote, news of McClellan's retreat from Richmond was reaching Europe, and French talk of stepping into the war revived. His report from Paris in that week carried the court's first reactions. For Washington, such letters answered a vital question: would failure in Virginia bring foreign action, or only foreign talk? A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d393:
On 16 September 1862, the day before Antietam, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Simon Cameron in St. Petersburg. The dispatch is printed as Document 393 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

A letter to Russia on the eve of the war's bloodiest day could not mention it, and would not be read for weeks. That lag gave the Russian correspondence its reflective tone: policy stated as principle, not reaction. This dispatch closes the Seward-Cameron run in the file, written at the hinge of the autumn campaign. The Russian route was the longest in the file, crossing an ocean and then half of Europe.
frus-1862-d493:
On 8 April 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. It is Document 493 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

Seward wrote two days after Shiloh, though full word of that battle had yet to settle. His orders to The Hague that spring kept returning to the same Dutch questions. Those were port rules and colonial harbors. They also included the standing of Confederate agents in Europe. Pike's task was to be pleasant, exact, and immovable on the Union's rights. The dispatch is one of a steady spring run in the Dutch file, in which neither side let a month pass in silence.
frus-1862-d593:
On 28 June 1862 Thomas Corwin sent this report from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 593 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Corwin's end-of-June report came as the Seven Days battles opened in Virginia, though no word of them could reach him for weeks. In Mexico his subject was the French advance and the endurance of the Juárez government, which the Union supported in word. The isolation of his post is part of the record's interest: a minister arguing America's case with month-old news, in a capital itself under threat. His letters home remain the volume's fullest American account of the Mexican crisis of 1862.
frus-1862-d693: On 23 May 1862, a Mr. De Long sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 693 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, his first letter in the file since March of that year. The evidence gives the writer, the date, and the place in the volume, but not his post or what the letter covers.
frus-1862-d93:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 8 July 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 93 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d193:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 May 1863. It is document 193 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Adams dealt most often with Lord John Russell, Britain's foreign secretary. His letters home summed up those talks and the mood of the British government. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d293:
The mail from London dated 17 September 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 293 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

British yards were building two ironclad rams for the Confederacy in the summer of 1863. The fight to stop those ships reached its peak that autumn, filling the London mail. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d393:
A note dated 18 February 1863 carried the British position from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 393 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d493:
Among the day's business on 7 May 1863 was a letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d593:
In the flow of wartime mail, Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington wrote to Secretary William H. Seward on 22 July 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d693:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, on 12 November 1863. The letter stands as document 693 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863, part one of that year's printed papers.

By mid-November the two men had a set rhythm of notes, replies, and fresh notes. That rhythm was itself a kind of peace work. It gave both capitals a calm way to raise sharp points about the war at sea and on land. For the reader, this dispatch fills in one more day of that rhythm. Its plain, brief form is typical of how the work got done.
frus-1863p1-d93:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 February 1863. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date, and a Seward letter shares it too. Adams was the American minister in London; this letter is document 93 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Late February was one of the thickest points in the whole file, with both men writing in bunches. Adams's sheets reported the London scene as the month closed: officials, papers, and Southern men all in motion. This one opens his set of three for the day. The pile itself tells the story of a post at full stretch.
frus-1893:
Brazil swells to the front of the 1893 volume. Its file dwarfs the rest of the alphabet. A naval revolt drives the Rio correspondence. Turkey takes the second-longest run.
