Mexico's legation papers outweigh its main file. Haiti and Persia hold solid places. Hawaii appears without a document count, a sign of unsettled business. Britain's embassy file carries a Canadian thread.

Its mid-volume paper advises a reciprocity proclamation. A privy council clerk submits the report for approval. The act would take force on June 1, 1893. Ottawa expects Washington to answer in kind. Cleveland's message opens the volume in formal terms. The files show republics in flux. Brazil's fleet and Hawaii's throne both hang in doubt.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d193:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff, the joint British-American high command, issued paper C.C.S. 380/2 at Washington on 6 November 1943. It lays out the basic strategy and policies meant to guide the next Anglo-American staff conference, held alongside the Cairo and Tehran meetings.

The stated aim is the unconditional surrender of the Axis, first in Europe and then in Japan, with steady pressure on Japan in the meantime. A list of first-charge tasks follows: guard the home bases, beat the U-boats, bomb Axis Europe harder. The list goes on: aid Russia and China, help French and Italian forces fight, and prepare to shift forces to the Pacific once Germany falls.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d293:
President Roosevelt sent an urgent telegram to James Byrnes, director of war mobilization, on 23 November 1943, from Cairo. Copies went to Admirals Horne and Nelson. Landing craft, the boats needed to put armies ashore, had become the tightest bottleneck in Allied planning, and Roosevelt wants the numbers at once.

He asks whether the present schedules for building and finishing landing craft can be increased in each month from January through May. He also asks how many extra craft, by type, could be delivered month by month. The question assumes that landing craft take precedence over all other munitions of war. Byrnes is told to call a conference of all interested departments, and the message is marked very urgent.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d393: President Roosevelt sent Secretary of State Cordell Hull a one-sentence telegram from Tehran on 29 November 1943, answering Hull's message of 27 November about the American seat on the European Advisory Commission. Hull had offered three names: Grew, Caffery, and Johnson. Roosevelt replies that he thinks it more advisable to appoint Winant, the ambassador in London, as the American representative. The editors note that Winant had cabled Roosevelt on 2 November saying he would like the chance to serve on the commission.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d493:
On December 6, 1943, the closing day of the Second Cairo Conference, President Roosevelt sent a message to King Farouk of Egypt. Cairo had hosted two Allied conferences in a fortnight, with the meetings held under the King's own roof at the Mena House by the pyramids. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Egypt was formally neutral, yet its capital had become the stage for the alliance's most secret talks. A presidential message to Farouk on the final day belongs to the courtesies and calculations owed to a host whose country held Allied bases and supply lines. It shows summit diplomacy remembering the ground it stood on.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d93: Ambassador Winant wrote to Roosevelt from London on November 4, 1943, and his letter is Document 93 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Winant wrote often in those weeks, and the president read his reports as a window into British plans. The catalog record supplies the date and the two men and nothing narrower. The letter belongs, in the Foreign Relations series, to the last fortnight before the leaders sailed and flew east.
frus-1944-quebec-d193:
Naval minutes of September 15, 1944, record Admiral Cunningham arranging bases for the British Fleet in the Pacific. He asked whether the United States Navy planned to evacuate its facilities at Brisbane and Sydney. If so, he wanted repair facilities for fleet units and shore aviation facilities for the Fleet Air Arm, arranged directly with the Australian government.

Admiral King said the American Navy was generally moving out and ordered a "roll-up" plan prepared for Sydney and Brisbane. Espiritu Santo, he suggested, was the most forward usable rear base, and Majuro's anchorage might also serve. Cunningham said Sydney would do as the rear base; forward, the fleet needed only an anchorage, living off its train. The talk also covered Torres Strait and Avenger aircraft for British carriers.
frus-1944-quebec-d293: Harry Hopkins, the president's closest aide, received this note on 16 September 1944 from H. Freeman Matthews, deputy director of the Office of European Affairs. Kept as document 293 in the Foreign Relations volume on the 1944 Quebec Conference, it belongs to the staff traffic running behind the Roosevelt and Churchill talks. The full text appears as published by the Office of the Historian.
frus-1944-quebec-d93:
Robert Murphy prepared a memorandum dated September 9, 1944. Murphy served as political adviser on Germany for the Americans. His paper appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume. It was written three days before the conference opened.

Few Americans knew occupied Europe's politics better than Murphy did at first hand. He had served in North Africa and Italy during the war. His advice concerned the political handling of a beaten Germany. For readers, the memorandum shows a field expert briefing Washington. Summit choices about Germany rested on hard judgments like his. The conference opened at Quebec City three days later.
frus-1945-50-intel-d193:
A text titled "Circular Instruction From the Department of State" bears the date 15 April 1947. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 193 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

Orders of this kind turned broad policy into daily rules. They name the office in charge and the work to be done. They name the office in charge, the work to be done, and the limits that apply, line by line. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d293:
Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter addressed a memorandum to the Chief of Naval Operations (Denfeld) on 18 June 1948. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 293 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d393:
W. Park Armstrong, the Secretary of State's special assistant for research and intelligence, wrote to Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter on 2 August 1949. His letter is document 393 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series.

Armstrong ran the State Department's own intelligence office, the unit that read world events for the Secretary. A letter from him to the head of the CIA shows the two shops talking at the top. It helps readers see how the State Department tried to keep its own strong voice in intelligence work.
frus-1945-50-intel-d93:
Eddy wrote to Under Secretary Acheson on 30 January 1947. The intelligence chief's channel to the department's second-ranking man was by then a well-worn path. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

McCormack had used the same channel in the office's first autumn, and Eddy now used it in its steadier second year. Acheson remained the ear that mattered for the department's inner business. Readers can compare the two chiefs' papers to Acheson across fifteen months: the first pleading for an office's life, the second conducting its affairs. That contrast is the State intelligence story in two letters, and the volume prints both ends of it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d193:
“United States Policy Toward Italy” is a full briefing book paper, prepared for the conference trip and printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its summary states the aim in one breath. Italy is to grow into a democratic and constructive force in the Europe of the future.

Washington also wants Italy politically independent and able to support itself as soon as possible. Six questions may be raised with the British and Soviets. They run from ending the state of war by convention, in place of the surrender terms, to letting Italy join world bodies as an associated nation. Italy might share in the German surrender instrument, hold national elections once the Germans are expelled, and even join the war against Japan.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d293:
A day-by-day work program for Malta is set out in this British Chiefs of Staff memorandum of 30 January 1945. Annexed to the combined chiefs' minutes, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It tells the staffs what to settle, and in what order, before the leaders arrive.

Tuesday the 30th takes coordination of operations and bomblines, the combined bomber offensive, and the planning date for the end of the German war. Wednesday turns to strategy in the Mediterranean, then to Japan: Southeast Asia, and the split of resources between that command and China. Thursday covers Pacific operations, the Japanese war's planning date, and the U-boat threat. Friday is left for cargo shipping, oil stocks, and basic undertakings. The paper is signed from the Auberge de Castile in Valletta.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d393:
Air bases in the Far East brought Roosevelt and Stalin together on February 8, 1945, in Bohlen's minutes of a smaller meeting. With Manila fallen, the President said, the Pacific war entered a new phase. America hoped for bases on the Bonins and near Formosa. The time had come to plan heavier bombing of Japan.

Roosevelt said he hoped invasion of the Japanese islands would not be needed. Japan had four million men under arms; bombing might destroy its army and save American lives. Stalin raised no objection to American bases at Komsomolsk or Nikolaevsk, on the Amur River. Kamchatka, he said, would take more talk.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d493:
Roosevelt took the hint and wrote to Churchill on February 10, 1945, about Article VII of Lend-Lease. He had hoped, he wrote, to find a quiet moment in the conferences for a brief word. The importance he attached to resuming high-level talks on the clause was his subject. No quiet moment had come, so he would not let the meeting close without writing.

Talks on commercial policy under Article VII had run between the two governments since the fall of 1943. Roosevelt judged it most important that they be reinvigorated. He proposed naming full delegations on both sides promptly, headed by men of standing. The letter pushes postwar trade onto the summit's crowded desk.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d93:
Voting in the Security Council gives this briefing book paper its title and its problem. The briefing books armed Roosevelt with papers on each question he would face. This one defends the voting formula he sent Stalin on 5 December 1944. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Under that formula, the permanent members must agree in most kinds of decisions. The one break comes in peaceful settlement, where a member party to the dispute does not vote. The paper warns that the Soviet demand for a straight veto in all cases would hurt at home. It would alienate fair supporters of Dumbarton Oaks and arm the isolationists. It would also look like surrender to Russia.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d193:
Ambassador Kirk reported British support for a Trieste settlement in a telegram from Caserta on July 7, 1945. The message is document 193 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It relays word of a Foreign Office telegram to the British representative dealing with General Morgan, the Allied commander in Venezia Giulia.

London fully backs Morgan's view, Kirk reports. A final settlement of the Venezia Giulia problem should be attempted at the Big Three meeting. And Britain favors such a settlement before the peace conference as a matter of principle. The question is on the summit agenda, but London expects great difficulty persuading the American government to accept its view. The Foreign Office also warns that the procedure will be complicated, since the port of Trieste itself needs some special arrangement apart from the region.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d293:
Melbourne, the acting American representative in Rumania, wired from Bucharest at noon on June 23, 1945. His short note told the Acting Secretary of State about talks held just before Mr. Berry left for the United States. Berry had discussed a possible peace treaty with Rumania with the British political representative, Le Rougetel.

Because Berry would reach Washington within days, Melbourne suggested the Department hear his views in person. He added that General Schuyler, back soon from an inspection trip, might send his own views on the Allied Control Commission. The cable is a small link in the chain, passing field judgment up before Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d393:
Paragraph four of a draft agreement on the treatment of Germany in the first control period deals with war criminals and dangerous Nazis. War criminals, and all who took part in planning or carrying out Nazi enterprises that involved atrocities or war crimes, were to be arrested. Nazi leaders, influential Nazi supporters, and any other persons dangerous to the occupation were likewise to be arrested and interned.

The extract also preserves the drafting fight in the margins. Secretary Byrnes, by hand, replaced the closing words with a harder phrase: the arrested men were to be prosecuted to final judgment. Matthews's copy reads, more mildly, brought to judgment. The draft formed part of the briefing book's paper on Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d493:
A message from Warsaw's new Premier reaches Harriman in his Moscow cable of June 29, 1945. The Polish ambassador that afternoon handed him a note addressed to President Truman. It was signed by Prime Minister Osóbka-Morawski. Harriman was asked to send it to his government, and its translation follows in his next telegram.

Modzelewski, Harriman reports, explained the note's second paragraph. The new government, at its first meeting, had accepted the Yalta decisions in full. That covered the holding of elections, as well as all other matters in them. Harriman also caught an omission: the word Provisional had been left out of the new government's title, a point later corrected.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d593:
Archibald MacLeish, an Assistant Secretary of State, wrote to Secretary Byrnes on July 6, 1945. His top secret memo is document 593 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It questions how the State Department was framing Japan's surrender terms.

MacLeish cites a June study holding that Japan's irreducible terms are two. The present Emperor must not be harmed, and the throne itself must survive. Japan, the study said, would bear harsh hardship if those terms were met. MacLeish then presses a point of honesty in public language. Surrender on terms, he argues, is not unconditional surrender, and the U.S. people have a right to be told plainly if the policy has changed. He also asks why Germany's ruling party is to be stamped out while Japan's throne is spared.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d693:
Extracts from a wire by Ambassador Kirk in Italy, dated June 29, 1945, report Russian pressure in the Balkans. They form document 693 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Kirk relays findings by General Oxley, head of the British team on the control commission in Bulgaria.

Oxley had toured from Sofia to Varna and found everyone speaking freely of Russian aims at the Dardanelles. As proof he cited a drunken Russian corporal, delighted to meet the British party. The man said he had just been told a bargain had been struck. The English would let the Russians have the Dardanelles, in return for a free hand in Austria. Oxley also noted that Bulgaria's army was not being demobilized. Its officer cadre was in fact being increased. His summary impression was of Russian forces massing in depth north of the Greek and Turkish frontiers.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d93:
Major General Floyd Parks reported on his first trip into Berlin in a memorandum dated June 24, 1945. The excerpt is document 93 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Parks flew from Frankfurt to Tempelhof airfield on June 22, where Soviet officers met him, and drove through the ruined city to Babelsberg.

Parks met General Kruglov, Stalin's security chief, who was running the conference arrangements. Kruglov explained that the Russians had meant to host the meeting and chose Babelsberg for its grand houses and light bomb damage, close to the Crown Prince's palace at Potsdam. He promised radio links to SHAEF and full care for the American planes. But he could not discuss U.S. troops entering the Berlin district itself, which lay outside his authority.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1093:
Charles Yost, executive secretary of the conference secretariat, summed up the Potsdam talks on Italy in this memorandum of August 9, 1945. Only the Italy sections are printed here. Stalin, Yost records, raised no objection in principle to easing Italy's surrender terms. His motive was to detach former enemy states from Germany and align them with the Allies.

Stalin still blocked any easing for Italy alone. Whatever was done for her must apply equally to Rumania, Bulgaria, Hungary, and Finland, he held. Churchill, for his part, indicted Italy's wartime record and would ease terms less far. He also wanted treaty drafting to wait on free Italian elections. The result was only the communiqué's general words on peace treaties.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1193:
Carnwath of the maritime board's London branch wrote jointly with regional chief Monroe on 21 July 1945. Their message went to shipping chief Land and his aide Morse. A companion cable of the same date covers the same joint world of Allied shipping.

Merchant fleets faced a vast re-routing. Ships were needed for the Pacific war, for troops sailing home, and for food bound to freed Europe. A joint note from the London end of the system lined up the chiefs behind that shift. It shows the shipping world reordering itself for the war's last act, in plain office language.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1293:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to Ambassador Hornbeck in the Netherlands on 23 July 1945. The message answered the Hague post from Washington, in the circuit of guidance that bound the embassies to the home office during the summit.

Orders to a newly freed country had to match what the talks were deciding in Germany. The home office kept its envoys in step as stands shifted. This cable is that keeping-in-step at work. It preserves a moment in the traffic between the two governments, caught in the American files at the height of the conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1393:
Mikołajczyk wrote another diary entry on 31 July 1945, the day before the Potsdam leaders signed their protocol. His file of papers is the longest single-author run in this section of the volume. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

On the eve of the settlement, a diary entry holds a special charge. The writer knows the decisions are nearly fixed, yet not announced. Mikołajczyk's page for that day lets readers stand where he stood: informed of much, able to change little, still writing. Set against the dry protocol printed nearby, the diary restores the fear and hope that the official text leaves out entirely.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-93:
Delegation staff member Thompson kept these minutes of a Potsdam meeting on July 24, 1945. Thompson's sets of minutes run through the whole conference in the second Potsdam volume. Note-takers like him gave the American side its own written record of each session. That record mattered when the sides later disputed what had been said or agreed.

The minutes follow the talk in the order it happened. Readers meet claims, replies, and points put off for later work. The style is plain because the aim was accuracy, not drama. Read across several days, Thompson's pages show the talks slowly narrowing toward the deals struck at the end.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d793:
General Schuyler, chief of the American military team on the Allied Control Commission for Rumania, wrote to the War Department on July 16, 1945. Document 793 opens the volume's Rumania military thread. The Commission supervised the armistice in a former enemy state. Schuyler reported from Bucharest on the eve of Potsdam.

A control commission officer saw occupation from inside. Schuyler dealt daily with Soviet partners and a wary local government. Readers get the friction of joint control in plain military prose. The document grounds the summit's Balkan arguments in one city's reality. It shows why Rumania's file at Potsdam was so hard to close.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d893:
Edwin Pauley, the American representative on the Allied Commission on Reparations, wrote to the Secretary of State on July 16, 1945. He argues that reparations must cover property across the whole German Reich as it stood at the end of 1937. That scope raises a question: how should reparations relate to German land ceded to other nations?

Pauley attaches four provisions he wants inside any deal that confirms such a cession. Goods from ceded land would first serve Germany's own needs, then pay for approved imports. Remaining value would count as reparations deliveries. Property left inside ceded territory would also be counted as reparations.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d993:
Edwin Pauley cabled the American minister in Sweden on July 25, 1945, about German external assets. A declaration of Allied power over those assets is under study at Potsdam, he reports, but its early issue looks doubtful. A second tool is also in draft: a decree vesting all right and title in German external assets in an agency working under the Control Council.

The decree text is going to Stockholm by pouch. Pauley plans to hand it to the American Control Council group, for presentation to the other members. Formal action matters most, he argues, for big German properties in Spain, Portugal, and Switzerland. The cable was cleared with William Clayton.
frus-1964-68v06-d93:
A memorandum for the record, dated Washington, February 29, 1968, argues for sending more U.S. troops to Vietnam. It is document 93 in Volume VI of the Foreign Relations series for 1964-1968, which covers Vietnam in the first part of that year. The writer backs the Wheeler recommendation on four grounds. More forces would cut risk in Vietnam. They would also calm fears that the United States was stretched too thin in other regions.

The memo says the enemy now fights at more than twice the rate of 1967. It urges firm demands on Saigon, with set tasks and dates. It warns against being pushed toward wider war moves, such as strikes on Haiphong.
gao-gaoreports-b-298293:
Air Products Healthcare protested a Veterans Affairs award for home oxygen in GAO decision B-298293, dated August 11, 2006. The winner was Rotech Healthcare. The zone was New England, in six states. The work was to bring oxygen to homes and back that care. The firm's bid was ruled not fit on tech grounds. Talks were also hit.

GAO denied the protest. The not-fit call was sound on the record. The agency had told the firm its fears in clear terms in talks. That gave the firm a fair shot to fix them. Past work marks were also sound. A firm told its flaws in talks that still falls short can be cut.
gao-gaoreports-b-298993:
Gear Wizzard, Inc. protested a Defense Logistics Agency award to Ruta Supplies, Inc. The contract covered propeller shafts for vehicles. The shafts were classed as a critical application item. GAO ruled in B-298993 on January 11, 2007.

The agency cast the firm's bid out on source grounds. The firm had offered the part of an approved source. Fresh facts, though, showed the part would be made by a distinct shop. That shop sat outside the scope of the source clearance. A part's badge alone does not prove an approved build path. The rejection fit the source rule. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299393:
Northern Sealcoating & Paving protested the rejection of its low bid by the Federal Highway Administration. The work covered road and parking work at Cape Cod National Seashore. A restroom building formed part of the job. GAO decided B-299393 on March 30, 2007.

The bid failed to note a key amendment. That change was material to the job. It set the color of exterior shingles. It also called for cedar lap siding and a color additive for concrete. A bid that skips a material change does not match the terms. The rejection as nonresponsive was proper. No cure was owed. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-307693:
Relief from a money debt is refused in this GAO letter, B-307693, dated April 12, 2007. Jeffrey Elmore was a certifying officer for a Defense Logistics Agency center. He certified four bad purchase card payments. The payments came to $402.81 in total. The center asked GAO to lift his duty to repay the sum.

GAO first held it had power to hear the plea. Elmore served a defense agency, not the armed forces as such. But GAO then refused relief on the merits. It found he did not act in good faith when he certified the payments. The case warns card certifiers that a careless stamp can leave them holding the debt.
gao-gaoreports-b-310093:
Charles Kendall & Partners, Ltd. lost its protest in GAO decision B-310093, dated November 26, 2007. The Army sought all-terrain vehicles and trailers. The gear serves guard forces in Afghanistan and Iraq. The award went to Polaris Sales, Inc. at a high price. The loser held a clear price edge in the race.

GAO denied the protest. The call scored price, ship speed, and small-firm share in a trade-off. The pick chief found the winner's fast ships worth more than the price gap. That sort of trade call sits well inside a chief's free hand. Speed can beat price when troops wait for gear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-293:
Defense Management, GAO-05-293 of May 5, 2005, checks the bill for fixing war-worn gear when troops come home. Iraq and other hot zones wear out trucks, guns, and kits at a fast pace. Units must restore each item so they can train and sail out again. The fix bill runs to many billions of dollars. It is built in two steps for each add-on budget.

GAO tests the fiscal year 2004 round of that work. It asks if the two-step path gave sound sums for the fix need. It asks if the Pentagon tracks and tells the true cost as work goes on. Both steps can be made sharper.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-393:
Internal Revenue Service, GAO-05-393 of April 29, 2005, is the yearly ledger of what the tax arm has done with GAO's past advice. Since the first audit of its books in fiscal year 1992, GAO has flagged flaws in how the arm runs its cash. Each flaw drew a tip for a fix. Each year, GAO asks what state each tip stands in.

The ledger helps IRS chiefs track each tip and the acts still owed. Some fixes stand done. Some crawl. Some wait for cash, tools, or a chief's call. The book is thick by need: it is the score card for a decade of audit work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-793:
U.S. aid to foreign forces in Southeast Asia is scrutinized in GAO-05-793, released July 29, 2005. Aid grew to the Philippines, Indonesia, and Thailand after 2001. Law bars funds to units with credible proof of gross human rights abuse. GAO sized the aid first. Then it tested the checks used to screen trainees. It also judged whether a clear aid strategy exists.

The United States allocated about $265.7 million from fiscal years 2001 to 2004. GAO found no proof that about 6,900 trainees were screened for abuse. They included 32 men from an Indonesian unit once barred for past abuse. Defense-run training showed better screening proof. New State guidance came in February 2005, with a database of abuse claims. GAO also found no clear, coherent aid strategy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1093:
Child welfare in the District of Columbia is reviewed in GAO-06-1093, issued on September 28, 2006. The Child and Family Services Agency has a long record of poor results. A 1989 court case set strict performance duties the agency must still meet. Court monitor reports showed many duties unmet. GAO checked whether the agency could meet the terms by December 2006, and what blocks progress.

The agency improved from December 2005 to April 2006 and met some benchmarks. Still, GAO judged it would not meet all duties by the deadline. Other measures stayed well below the court's marks. Complex cases strain caseworkers, and health care providers are scarce. GAO urged the Mayor to order training that fits complex cases. It also urged the city to widen the provider pool. The agency agreed with the findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-193:
Joint urban combat training is reviewed in GAO-06-193, a report issued on December 8, 2005. Urban fighting in Iraq made city warfare skills vital for U.S. forces. The Defense Department stresses training that mixes services under one headquarters. In May 2002 the Senate Armed Services Committee told the department to set facility needs for urban training. In May 2005 it set a November 1, 2005 deadline for a requirements baseline. GAO checked the department's strategy, its exercises, and its use of lessons from the field.

Since 2002 the department has made only limited progress on a joint urban training strategy. A study for Joint Forces Command, finished in early 2005, named facility and training needs. A full strategy and firm requirements still lagged. GAO made recommendations to sharpen the approach. The department rejected one of the two, but GAO held that both remain valid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-293:
Bank customers and their complaints about the national bank regulator anchor GAO-06-293, published February 23, 2006. In January 2004 the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency set rules on how far federal law overrides state banking law. State officials and consumer groups feared weaker protection for the public. GAO compared the office's complaint handling with that of sister regulators.

The process resembles those of other bank regulators, GAO found. One gap stood out: the office never asks the people it helps how satisfied they were. Two other regulators do collect such feedback. GAO urged the office to measure satisfaction and fix how it tracks speed. It also urged wider outreach so the public knows where to turn. The regulator agreed with the findings and the advice. The report links turf fights over banking law to a plain question: can a wronged customer get heard?
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-593:
The Army wanted its own unmanned aircraft rather than buy an existing one. GAO's May 19, 2006 report, GAO-06-593, reviews the Warrior unmanned aircraft system. The Defense Department plans to spend $20 billion on such systems through 2011. Congress worried that some systems cost more and took longer than predicted. That concern prompted this review. The Warrior is the Army's entry in the field.

GAO describes the Army's requirements behind choosing Warrior. It compares that choice with existing systems such as the Air Force's Predator. It then assesses whether the Army set a sound acquisition strategy. A better strategy is needed for success, GAO found. Readers get requirements and strategy side by side.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-793:
Lists meant to flag vital military technology are faulted in GAO-06-793 (July 28, 2006). Keeping an edge in technology underpins the Defense Department's force transformation plans. If critical technologies leak, foes could clone or neutralize United States weapons. The department keeps two lists for this purpose, a military critical technologies list and a developing science list. GAO judged whether the lists guide real decisions.

GAO found that updates to the two lists produced documents of limited value. Agencies tended to rely on other information when judging critical technologies. As a result, the lists rarely informed export control or other policy decisions. GAO urged the department to make the lists useful or stop investing in them. The report questions a paper safeguard that few officials actually use.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-93:
Nuclear safeguards run by the International Atomic Energy Agency are assessed in GAO report GAO-06-93, dated October 7, 2005. That agency's checks form a base of U.S. efforts to stop the spread of nuclear weapons. The base treaty dates to 1970.

Since then the agency has toughened its checks. It has also helped states guard nuclear and radioactive stock against theft or attack. GAO listed the steps taken to firm up safeguards. It weighed the strain of putting them in place. It tracked U.S. money behind the work, and the agency's aid to states. Gains were real, yet weak points still called for action.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-993:
Weather satellite buys, and lessons from past space work, are reviewed in GAO report GAO-06-993, dated September 6, 2006. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration plans a new set of geostationary weather satellites, the GOES-R series. The data they send is vital for forecasts through the year 2028.

GAO set out the state of the GOES-R buy, and its plans. It judged the steps the program team takes to dodge flaws seen in past satellite buys. Some steps draw on those lessons, the title notes. Others remain to be built in. The report suits readers who track big federal tech buys and their risks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1093:
Bird habitat buying in the Prairie Pothole Region lags its goals, GAO reports in GAO-07-1093, dated September 27, 2007. The 64-million-acre region in the north-central United States breeds over 60 percent of key migratory bird species. Draining and plowing cut that habitat through much of the 20th century.

Under a small wetlands program, the Fish and Wildlife Service buys top habitat for good. Farm reserve deals guard some land for a time. GAO tracked the state of the buying program and the service's goals for the region. It weighed hurdles to those goals. At the current pace, GAO found, the service is unlikely to reach them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-193:
Workers who cleaned up after Hurricane Katrina faced fouled water, debris, and wrecked buildings. GAO checked how well they were protected in GAO-07-193, dated March 28, 2007. The workplace safety agency coordinates federal worker protection in big disasters. GAO asked how many response workers went to the Gulf Coast. It asked whether injuries and illnesses were tracked. It also judged how well worker needs were met.

No one counted the total workforce, GAO found. Agency estimates put about 49,000 federal workers in the Gulf on October 1, 2005. The safety agency could not build usable injury data. It had no collection process ready before the storm. The disaster agency tasked it more than 3 weeks after landfall. Data that did arrive was partial and unreliable. Nine work-related deaths were reported. GAO urged clear roles and data systems before the next disaster.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-293:
A homeland security data mining tool can link people, groups, and events from vast files. GAO warned its privacy risks went unmeasured in GAO-07-293, dated February 28, 2007. The tool, called ADVISE, scans structured and free-text data. It draws maps of relationships for analysts. Four department components plan to use it. None was fully running at review time. GAO asked what the tool would do and what privacy issues it raises.

The department skipped a required privacy review, GAO found. Officials said the tool itself holds no personal data. But its planned uses do involve such data. Risks include tying innocent people to crime or terror. Similar names could be confused for one another. Data gathered for one purpose could serve another. Security controls like access limits were in place. GAO urged an immediate privacy impact assessment. It also urged controls built from that review. The department generally agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-93:
Counting volunteer reservists is faulted in GAO-07-93, dated October 31, 2006. Defense leaders worry about how often volunteers serve. The department's request for volunteer levels nearly doubled in one year. The fiscal year 2005 estimate missed many who were serving. No shared definition of operational support existed then. The definition arrived on April 26, 2005, months after the limits were set. Components counted heads by differing rules. GAO traced why the numbers jumped. It checked how each component reports its volunteers.

Bad base data explains most of the surge, GAO found. Early figures borrowed counts kept for other purposes. Those counts excluded whole groups of serving volunteers. Once real monitors supplied the numbers, requests rose sharply. Reporting still varies across the reserve components. Categories of support work mean different things to different units. GAO urged clear written guidance on what counts. Shared definitions should govern every report. The Defense Department agreed with the advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-993:
Legal Services Corporation governance is the subject of GAO report GAO-07-993, dated August 15, 2007. Congress asked GAO to review how the corporation's board watches over its work. The corporation is a private nonprofit set up by the federal government. It funds legal aid for low-income people in civil cases. It relies heavily on federal funds.

GAO compared the corporation's rules with those for federal bodies and other nonprofits. It found weaker governance and accountability rules than current practice elsewhere. Board members took an active part, but the board had no charters and had not judged its own work. GAO urged four steps, among them a full risk review and a stronger ethics code. It also asked Congress to weigh new legal duties for the corporation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-593:
Dated May 23, 2008, GAO report GAO-08-593 looks at making nuclear weapon pits. Pits are a core part of a warhead. The nation lost pit production when the Rocky Flats Plant closed in 1989. Los Alamos National Laboratory was told in 1996 to rebuild a small capability for the W88 warhead.

The lab met the stated goals: capacity for 10 pits a year from 2007 and one war reserve pit delivered that year. It made 11 pits in 2007, 8 of them war reserve grade. But goals for war reserve output shifted across documents, and over $1 billion in support costs sat outside the $1.29 billion spent against a $1.55 billion estimate. Lab limits bar any real capacity growth soon. GAO urged a firm cost and schedule baseline.
gifford-dialogue-concerning-witches-engl:
George Gifford, an Essex minister, published his Dialogue Concerning Witches and Witchcrafts in 1593. Villagers in the dialogue debate a local witch scare, and Gifford speaks through them. His subtle claim is that the devil deceives the accusers even more than the accused.

Panicked neighbors see pacts and familiars where malice and melancholy suffice. Gifford does not deny the devil; he relocates his cleverest work into human fear. The result is often called the subtlest Elizabethan demonology. Doubt here wears a pastor's tender heart and a keen eye for village life. Modern readers still admire how Gifford turns a witch panic into a lesson about its makers.
gissing-odd-women-1893:
George Gissing published The Odd Women in 1893, taking his title from the many women of his time who could never marry for lack of men. Gissing wrote about the Madden sisters, left poor by their father's sudden death. The novel asks what unmarried women were supposed to do with their lives.

Two sisters scrape by as teachers and shop workers, while their younger sister Monica is courted by an older, controlling man. Nearby, Rhoda Nunn runs a school training women for office work and preaches independence. Love tests every one of these positions. The novel is now read as a founding text about women's work and freedom.
haddock-holt-s-delineator-1893:
Allen Haddock and Charles P. Holt copyrighted their Delineator in 1893, for the use of scientific phrenologists in describing the character of their patrons. Orders went to Haddock and Holt, at the Office of Human Nature, 1008 Market Street. The book is a working form: pages on which the practitioner could mark a client's head and write the reading. It claims the most advanced knowledge of phrenology, physiognomy, physiology, psychology, and psychometry.

A blank delineation opens the volume, with space for the patron's name, the giver, the place, and the date. The rest gives the scales and terms by which bumps and features were turned into character. Phrenology was a trade as well as a theory, and this book is its shop counter. As an artifact of the business of reading heads, it is complete and curious.
hale-collection-modern-relations-1693:
Judge Matthew Hale presided over the famed Bury St Edmunds witch trial of 1664, and a 1693 book gathers his thoughts on such cases. A Collection of Modern Relations concerning Witches and Witchcraft is tied to his name. It links Bury with a run of other trials of the age.

The book collects modern cases of witchcraft and adds Hale's own meditation on the Bury trial. A chief judge of England sets out why he held witchcraft to be real and its proof sound. The volume shows the law's highest minds still firm in belief late in the century. It helps explain why trials ran on so long.
hermetic-museum-vol-2-1893:
A. E. Waite put out The Hermetic Museum, Restored and Enlarged, in 1893. Book Two ends the pair. The Museum is a store of old tracts on alchemy in English dress. Waite was the great voice of the occult age in Britain.

Tracts by famed hands of the art fill the book, some in print for the first time. The texts deal with the stone, the elixir, and the purge of base metals. Waite adds heads and notes to guide the new hand through the maze. The pair is a chief store of the alchemy of the West.
histoire-de-l-alchimie-xivme-siecle-nico:
Albert Poisson wrote this French history of alchemy, printed at Paris in 1893. Its subject is Nicolas Flamel, the famed Paris scribe of the fourteen hundreds. Poisson gives Flamel's life, his good works, and his writings. The book belongs to a series called the Hermetic Collection.

Appended are two older texts in reprint. One is Flamel's Book of Hieroglyphic Figures, with its strange signs. The other is a letter from Dom Pernety to the Abbé Villain. The text is in French throughout. Readers get the Flamel legend sorted by a scholar of the art.
histoire-des-sciences-la-chimie-au-moyen:
Marcellin Berthelot, the French chemist, led this history of medieval chemistry, issued in 1893. It opens his series on the history of the sciences. Berthelot had just edited the old Greek alchemists in text and translation. Here he traces how ancient science passed to the Middle Ages.

The first volume studies manuscripts and translations with care. Berthelot examines alchemy texts of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries at Paris. He tracks Greek lore through Arabic hands into Latin Europe. The text is in French and densely learned. It shows a great chemist rebuilding his own science's deep past from the shelves.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r:
Edward Gibbon's fourth volume, in the transcription produced by David Reed and Dale R Fredrickson, treats the half century between Rome's western fall and Justinian. The text itself calls those years faintly marked by the obscure names of Zeno and Anastasius. Chapter thirty-nine then gives Theodoric's Gothic kingdom of Italy in full.

Basiliscus betrayed, Verina raising armies of seventy thousand, and empresses intriguing fill the eastern chapters. Later, Tribonian and ten lawyers reshape Roman law under Justinian's absolute commission, finishing faster than the emperor demanded. This record duplicates the library's other volume four in content while differing in production, so readers may choose their transcription of the same Milman text.
hort-way-truth-life-1893:
Fenton John Anthony Hort was the Cambridge textual critic who, with Westcott, rebuilt the Greek text of the New Testament. His Way, the Truth, the Life, published in 1893, prints his Hulsean Lectures on the words of Jesus in John's Gospel. The book shows the great critic as a theologian.

Hort takes Christ's claim to be the way, the truth, and the life as a key to the whole faith. He reads the Gospel's images of light, bread, and the shepherd as one unfolding self-revelation. The lectures' quiet depth reveals why Cambridge trusted Hort with its hardest textual questions.
hudson-law-psychic-phenomena-1893:
Thomson Jay Hudson split the mind in two in The Law of Psychic Phenomena, his hit book of 1893. Hudson was a law man and news man in the United States. His scheme gives each man two selves: one that thinks and weighs, one that takes bids, holds all past, and can act in trance, dreams, and strange cures at a word.

On that split he builds cures, faith, and tales of ghosts. The book sold in droves and shaped how his land spoke of the hid self. Its terms roamed far past its field. It is a folk text of mind lore.
inter-caetera-1493:
Pope Alexander VI issued Inter Caetera in 1493, the year after Columbus reached the Americas for Spain. The bull drew a line down the Atlantic Ocean, west of the Azores and Cape Verde islands. Lands west and south of that line were granted to Spain's rulers.

The text urges Spain to spread the Catholic faith among the peoples it met overseas. Portugal objected to the line, and the two kingdoms soon moved it by treaty. Even so, the bull supplied a legal claim behind Spain's growing empire. It shows how European powers used church law to divide lands they barely knew.
jabir-ibn-hayyan-oeuvres-berthelot-1893:
Jabir ibn Hayyan, known in Latin as Geber, was the great name of early Arabic alchemy, a scholar of Kufa in the eighth century. A vast body of work bears his name. Marcellin Berthelot printed six of the Arabic treatises in French in 1893, in his study of Arabic alchemy. The text here gives those six.

The treatises set out the sulfur and mercury theory of metals and the search for the elixir that perfects them. Jabir teaches balance, weights, and careful furnace work, a turn toward the measured side of the art. His name ruled alchemy in both Arabic and Latin for centuries. Berthelot's French pages let modern readers meet the Jabirian corpus at its source.
jean-darras-melusine-1393:
Jean d'Arras wrote this romance of Melusine for a French duke in 1393. The text here is the 1895 Early English Text Society print of the Middle English form, set in print by A. K. Donald. Melusine is the famed maid who is part woman, part fish or snake.

She weds a knight on one term: he must not see her on the one day each week. When he breaks the term, she flies off in her strange form and is lost to him. The tale is the root stock of a vast line of fairy bride tales in Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-selig-ben: Aaron Selig ben Moses of Zolkiev was an author who flourished in the seventeenth century. His "'Amude Sheba'," or Seven Pillars, was published at Cracow in 1637. It gives commentaries and glosses on the old and the new Zohar, and explains the foreign words found there. It also lists treatises left out of the old Zohar, points readers to other commentaries, and adds remarks on the style of the Zohar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abdan-or-abidan:
Abdan, a short form of Abba Yudan, was a Palestinian scholar of the first amoraic age, about the start of the third century. He served Rabbi, that is Judah I, as disciple and clerk. The entry shows him too full of his place. When Ishmael ben Yose, a very stout man, pressed into the college hall, Abdan mocked him in sharp words.

The clash ended with Rabbi ordering Abdan to stay at the door, while Ishmael proved his skill in the Law. Legend in the entry adds a hard price for the pride. Abdan was struck with eczema, and two of his sons were drowned. Yet his memory was kept in honor as a good man, spared worse punishment in the world to come.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abigdor-ben-sim:
Abigdor ben Simḥa, who wrote under the name Abigdor Levi, was a German author born in Glogau. He worked as a tutor in Berlin, then moved to Prague in 1768. Early in 1773, on a trip through Saxony, he was seized on a false charge. He sat in the prison of Pirna for ten months with no hearing at all.

From prison he sent a Hebrew letter on his plight to Moses Mendelssohn. The reply, in German, was opened by the authorities, as he had hoped. Seeing their prisoner was a friend of Mendelssohn, they cleared and freed him. Back in Prague he brought out a Hebrew grammar in 1783. He later edited Mendelssohn's letters to him, in 1792 and again in 1797.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-of-augs: Abraham of Augsburg was a proselyte to Judaism who died a martyr's death on Nov. 21, 1265. He seems to have taken his new faith with such zeal that he spoke out against Christianity in public. He also attacked images of the saints, and for that he was sentenced to torture and death. The case drew wide notice at the time. Elegies on him were written by Mordecai ben Hillel and by the liturgical poet Moses ben Jacob.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adelaide-793:
Adelaide is the capital city of South Australia. Its Jewish story ties to a first settler, Jacob Montefiore. He helped found both the colony and the town's Jewish body. That body dates from 1840 and now counts about five hundred souls. Its synagogue on Rundle street was opened in 1871. It stands on the site of the small hall used in the first days.

Jews of Adelaide have held high posts in the state. Four have sat in the lower house, and one in the upper house for nine years. V. L. Solomon became premier in November, 1899. A tangle of party deals kept him in the post just seven days. Three Jews have been mayor of the city. One minister, A. T. Boas, has served the flock since 1871. A school at the synagogue teaches sixty children. Four aid groups serve the town's Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agen-893: Agen is a town on the Garonne, southeast of Bordeaux. Jews settled there early in the twelfth century. Its Jews were the first hit by the Shepherds' raids. Those bands of friars claimed to free the French king from Saracen hands. From Agen the bloodshed spread to more than 120 towns in Guienne and Gascony. Jews sent envoys to the king to beg his shield. In 1250 the local lord was told to hunt banned Hebrew books. A hamlet of Jews called Agenais stood near the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahithophel-993:
Ahithophel was a native of Giloh, in the highlands of Judah, and a privy councilor to David. He had rare sagacity and insight in political affairs. Yet he joined the rebellion of Absalom against the king. His counsel to chase the fleeing David at once was sound as war craft. Absalom chose Hushai's delay instead.

Stung by the slight, Ahithophel went home to Giloh and hanged himself. Rabbinic tales add much more. They say his wisdom was consulted like an oracle, and that David cursed any man who hid a needed remedy. They also say astrology misled him: the kingship he foresaw belonged to his granddaughter Bath-sheba, not to himself. He died at thirty-three, warning his children never to take sides against the house of David.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alcaniz-1093:
Alcaniz is a town in the province of Teruel, in Aragon, Spain. It lies sixty-three miles southeast of Saragossa. Jews lived there as early as the thirteenth century. In 1306 the king of Aragon gave the town to the grand master of the Order of Calatrava. With the king's leave, the master took thirty Jewish families under his care. They were likely refugees from France.

For the conquest of Naples, the Jews of Alcaniz lent King Alfonso V. a sum of 2,225 florins in gold. At the Tortosa debate of 1413 the town was represented by Joseph Ardot and Meir Alcoya. A local law also fined any Jew seven sueldos for leaving the town to settle elsewhere.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alfasi-isaac-be: Isaac ben Reuben Alfasi is often linked by name to the great Isaac Alfasi. Some writers called him that scholar's grandson. The entry treats that link with doubt. It credits him with a work in twenty chapters on oaths. That work is often printed with the Halakot of Alfasi. The entry suggests the true author may have been Isaac ben Reuben of Barcelona.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almoravides-al-:
Almoravides were a Moorish line in northwest Africa and Spain. They ruled in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Their founder was Yusuf ibn Tashfin. He did not know Arabic, the entry notes. He was the first non-Arab to hold a Moslem throne. His rule was mild toward those of other faiths.

Jews had little cause for complaint under Yusuf. He founded Morocco and Tlemçen in 1062. Those new towns gave Jews fresh homes. Under his son Ali, Jews held high posts. One Jew served as the ruler's physician. The line fell in Spain in 1149. The Almohades took its place there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-american-sadie-:
Sadie American was a leader in charity and club work. She was born at Chicago on March 3, 1862. She served as the writing secretary of the Council. That body is the Council of Jewish Women. She took that post at its birth and kept it. She spoke for the Council at meets of women's groups.

Her posts reach far past that one Council. She sat on the board of the Chicago Civic Federation from 1896. She led a league for shared worship in 1897 and 1898. She chaired a board for school yards and rest schools. She went as a voice to a London meet in June 1899. She also edited the books of the Council.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ancona-jacob-be: Jacob ben Elia d'Ancona was a copyist who lived at the end of the fifteenth century. Steinschneider, as quoted here, says he copied some anonymous commentaries. One set glossed Ezobi's Ka'arat Kesef, and another glossed the Behinat Olam. The second copy bears the date 2d Adar, 5255, or 1495. The codex, forty-six folios long, sits in the Royal Library of Turin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antiochus-viii-:
Antiochus VIII Gryphus owed his nickname, Gryphus, to the hook shape of his nose. Born in 141, he was king of Syria from 125 to 113 and again from 111 to 96 B.C., the year he died. A rival, Alexander Zabinas, fought him for the throne for three years.

That contest forced him to keep Jewish friendship, since the Jews held a balance of power. Even after Zabinas fell, eight quiet years did not make him strong enough to press the hard treaty terms of Antiochus Sidetes on the Jews. His later wars with Antiochus IX won him only inland Syria, never the borderland near Palestine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arad-alt-arad-1:
Arad is a royal free city and market town of Hungary, on the Maros, 145 miles southeast of Budapest. Its Jewish community holds a high place among Hungary's, the entry says. Its history starts in the first half of the eighteenth century.

The oldest known record is a passport of May 1, 1717, issued to two Jews living in the suburbs. In 1741 a single Jew, Mandel, held the right to sell groceries, then liquors, under a colonel's protection. Others followed; by 1754 there were 24 Jewish families. The year 1789 turned the story, when Aron Chorin became rabbi. From then on, the entry says, the community's struggles and fame center on him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-army-1793:
Fighting forces of Israel across all stages of the nation's history form the subject here. Hebrew had several words for them, from a broad term for force to terms for an army in the field and an army in battle order. The entry sorts the subject by how each force was raised and organized. Its turning point is the standing army set up in the time of King David, alongside the kingdom itself.

In tribal days, clan chiefs levied their own able-bodied men, as Abraham mustered his household servants in Genesis chapter 14. Later sections follow armies under kings and foreign rule, and Jewish soldiers abroad. One passage tells of Jews in Surinam fighting bravely for their colony, and of David Nasi, who died in 1743 in his thirty-first campaign. Polish and Lithuanian Jews, the entry adds, served beside their neighbors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ascher-anton-18:
Anton Ascher, a German actor, was born at Dresden on July 15, 1820, and died at Meran on April 24, 1885. Ludwig Tieck trained him for the stage. He first appeared in 1838 at Hainichen in Saxony, playing that year at Merssen, Bautzen, and Zittau as well. In 1839 he reached Wiesbaden and then the court theater at Dresden, where he stayed until 1844.

Years of touring followed: Hamburg in 1845, Konigsberg and Cassel in 1846, Potsdam in 1847. From 1848 to 1860 he played light, gallant roles at Berlin's Friedrich-Wilhelm Theater and ended that engagement in charge of the stage. From 1866 to 1872 he directed the Carl Theater in Vienna. His best parts included Thorane in Der Konigslieutenant and Bolz in Die Journalisten.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-solom:
Solomon ben Nathan Ashkenazi served as court physician to King Sigismund II Augustus of Poland, who reigned from 1548 to 1572. He was also a Turkish diplomat. Born probably about 1520, he died in 1602. From a German family settled at Udine in Italy, he came young to Cracow, likely in the train of Queen Bona, and rose to first physician to the king.

Later he moved to Constantinople and joined the staff of Grand Vizier Mahomet Sakolli. During the Turkish war with Venice over Cyprus in 1570, he worked on the preliminaries of peace. At the Polish royal election of 1572 he practically ran Turkey's foreign affairs and swung the choice to Henry of Anjou. His influence helped revoke the banishment of Jews from Venice on July 19, 1573. In 1576 the Porte sent him to Venice as envoy with full power to make peace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azal-r-v-azel-2: Azal is a place near Jerusalem. Its exact position cannot be fixed, the entry says. The name occurs in Zechariah, in a passage about the Mount of Olives splitting in a day of judgment. Some take Azal to be the same place as Beth-ezel, named in Micah. Clermont-Ganneau, a scholar cited here, places it at the Wadi Yasul.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bach-emilie-229: Emilie Bach was an artist and journalist. She was born at Neuschloss in Bohemia on July 2, 1840. She died at Vienna on April 29, 1890. She directed the royal school for artistic embroidery. On that craft she published two works, one a two-volume set of patterns for school and home. She wrote for many daily papers, among them the Neue Freie Presse. She also gave many lectures on arts and handicrafts, most of which were printed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bakst-ossip-isa: Ossip Isaakovich Bakst was a son of Isaac Bakst and brother of Nicolai. He died on Oct. 8, 1895. He worked as an interpreter in the Asiatic Department of the Russian Foreign Ministry. The entry knows him chiefly as a publisher of Russian versions of science books by men such as Helmholtz, Schleiden, Claude Bernard, and Draper. He also issued Emanuel Hecht's history of Israel in Russian at St. Petersburg in 1866, with a second edition in 1881, and the last volume of Grätz' history of the Jews in 1884.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bekorot-in-bibl:
Bekorot is the fourth treatise of the Mishnah order called Holy Things. It deals with the first-born of man and beast, a law repeated often in the Pentateuch. A first-born son is bought back with five shekels paid to a priest.

Seven of its nine chapters treat first-born animals: doubts, blemishes, and flaws made on purpose. One chapter treats the first-born son, one the flaws that bar a priest from service, and one the tithe of cattle. The entry also covers the companion Tosefta and the treatise's place in each Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-wolf-b: Benjamin Wolf ben Isaac Levi was a cabalist who lived at Leitmeritz, in Bohemia, in the middle of the seventeenth century. He wrote Amarot Tehorot, or Pure Words, a work explaining hard words in the Zohar. His son Saul brought it out at Lublin in 1745. A second work, Torat Mosheh, still rests in manuscript at Oxford. It treats the thirteen articles of belief and gathers views from Spanish, French, and German scholars, with his own additions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berlin-nahman-b: Nahman ben Simḥah Berlin was a writer who fought the Reform movement from Lissa, in Germany. He worked at the turn of the nineteenth century. All his writing served the orthodox cause, set steadily against each new bid to reform Judaism. His first book, printed in 1796, struck at the editors of a Hebrew journal and at Aaron Wolfssohn in particular. Five more titles followed, all at Berlin, on the oral law, on prayer in Hebrew, and on unity in religious affairs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bikkure-ha-itti:
"Bikkure ha-'Ittim" means First-Fruits of the Times. It was a Hebrew annual printed at Vienna. S. J. Cohen edited it from 1820 to 1831. It began as a calendar supplement for young people. In 1822 it became an independent magazine. Galician Maskilim adopted it as their organ. It fostered culture and education among Galician Jews.

The entry calls its influence inestimable. It worked like a college of Jewish learning. Great scholars wrote for it for years. Luzzatto, Rapoport, and Reggio all contributed. The young stylist Isaac Erter published there. The magazine helped revive modern Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-ludwig-33: Ludwig Bloch was a German dramatist. He was born at Berlin on December 6, 1859. His father Eduard published theatrical works. Ludwig entered that business in 1875. He traveled through Britain, France, and America in 1881. In 1883 he resumed work with his father. His comedy "Dekorirt" heads his works list. A farce appeared under the name R. Elbe. Two musical pieces and a piano work follow. He also edited popular stage publications.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bosor-3593: Bosor is given two short senses here, and little more. First, it is a city of Gilead, which Judas Maccabeus conquered. The entry cites First Maccabees, chapter five, for that fact. It may be the modern place named in Buhl's geography of ancient Palestine. Second, Bosor is the Septuagint reading for Besor in First Samuel, chapter thirty. The entry gives no history, people, or later fate for the city beyond those two notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bresslau-harry-:
Harry Bresslau was a German historian born in Dannenberg, Hanover, on March 22, 1848. He studied history at Göttingen from 1866 to 1869. He taught in Frankfort and Berlin and rose at Berlin's university.

In 1890 Bresslau became professor at the University of Strasburg. He joined the board of the Monumenta Germaniae Historica in 1888. For that series he edits its journal on old German sources. He also helped found a society for the sources of Jewish history in Germany. He serves as its president, the entry notes. His essays there proved a tale about Charlemagne and Rabbi Kalonymus was made up. He also showed a charter of Henry IV. for Speyer's Jews was spurious.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-buczacz-abraham:
Abraham David Buczacz, son of Asher Anshel, was a Galician Talmudist born in 1770 at Nadworna. His sharpness as a boy drew the notice of leading scholars. One chose him as a son-in-law when he was ten. At twenty he was ready to serve as rabbi at Goslowitz. He died at Buczacz in 1840.

His central struggle set Talmud against Cabala. Skeptical of Hasidic miracle tales, he still took his sick son to Levi Isaac of Berdychev. That rabbi led him into Cabala study and nearly cost him his reason before winning him over. From 1813 he served as rabbi of Buczacz. In legal rulings he stayed with Talmud, not Cabala. The entry lists eight of his works, most printed after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caceres-also-sp:
Caceres was a family whose members lived in Portugal, Holland, England, Mexico, Surinam, the West Indies, and the United States. The name likely came from the Spanish city of Caceres. Its earliest figure here, Antonio Dias de Caceres, appears on a Mexico list of heretics in 1590. His wife did penance as a Judaizer while the family practiced Jewish rites in secret.

Numbered notices follow for many kin. Samuel de Caceres, a poet and preacher at Amsterdam, edited the Spanish Bible translation printed in 1661. Simon de Caceres worked as a merchant and military planner across Hamburg, London, and the Americas. Later notices reach Surinam and Curacao, and kin still lived in New York and Philadelphia in 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cantor-moritz-3:
Moritz Cantor was a German historian of mathematics born at Mannheim on Aug. 23, 1829. Sickly as a boy, he was schooled at home before joining an advanced gymnasium class. At Göttingen, Gauss and Weber taught him, and Stern woke his love of historical research. He took his doctorate at Heidelberg in 1851 and began teaching there in 1853.

Cantor rose to honorary professor at Heidelberg in 1877. He helped edit journals of mathematics and physics and ran their history sections. His masterwork, lectures on the history of mathematics, ran to three volumes from 1880 to 1898. It covers the field down to 1758. The entry calls it the fullest and most trusted work of its kind and Cantor the head of the revived field.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-casal-maggiore-: Casal Maggiore is a town in Italy, about twenty-two miles east-southeast of Cremona. Its place in Jewish history rests on one printing episode. In September 1485, Joshua Solomon and Moses, sons of Israel Nathan of Soncino, began printing a large prayer book there. The book followed the Roman ritual. The next year they set up a press in the town and finished the second part. The finished work ran to 320 folio leaves. Some copies were printed on parchment. No other work was printed at Casal Maggiore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chemarim-4293:
Chemarim is a Hebrew word kept untranslated in Zephaniah i. 4 and in margin notes at two other passages. Elsewhere the versions render it as idolatrous priests or priests. In Zephaniah it may be a later insertion, the entry argues, from the verse's shape.

Its sense, though, is sure: priests. Semitic inscriptions use it so, and Aramaic uses a like word for priest with no bad sense. In the Bible passages it carries a stain. It names the idol-worshiping priest. The word's root is debated. Links to black garments, to sadness, and to prostration before an idol are all offered.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-circus-4393:
Circus, in the ancient world, was a large grounds for horse and chariot races and at times for gladiator fights. Because games and theater shaped Greek and Roman life, Jews of that age had to settle their stance toward them. The entry treats circus and theater as one question, as rabbinical writing so often does.

Hellenistic Jews had brought gymnasia into Jerusalem before the Maccabees, to orthodox disgust. Herod the Great built a theater and amphitheater there and staged games for the emperor. Pious Jews recoiled at men fed to beasts for sport and at the images set up in theaters. Later pages gather rabbinic mockery of circus crowds and rulings on attending such shows.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-lionel-lo:
Lionel Louis Cohen, an English financier, politician, and communal worker, was born in London in 1832 and died there on June 26, 1887. Son of the founder of Louis Cohen and Sons, he led that firm from 1882 after rising through Stock Exchange posts. He retired in 1885 on winning a seat in Parliament for North Paddington.

Work on the Turkish debt won him a nomination to the order of the Medjidie. In Jewish life his mark was deeper still. His 1860 scheme for managing relief of the Jewish poor became the working charter of the board of guardians, which he led from 1878 until death. He also drove the union of London's city synagogues in 1870 and raised England's first fund for persecuted Russian Jews in 1881.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-commercial-law-:
Commercial law, under Jewish law, starts from capacity. Whoever can contract at all can make trade contracts, the entry says. Girls reach majority at twelve and boys at thirteen. Three classes are barred: the deaf-mute, the unsound in mind, and the minor. Bondmen lack standing since their goods and earnings belong to their masters.

Married women pose a harder case, lacking full control of property. Yet the law allows the wife who trades within the house with her husband's leave, and a marriage pact can shield her property outright. Partnership law, freight, and bills of exchange fill the rest. The Talmud shows little trace of joint-stock companies, the entry notes, and few rulings on sea trade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-costa-joseph-da: Joseph da Costa is a very short entry, and it covers two men of the name. The first was a younger brother of Uriel Acosta. He lived at Amsterdam. Manasseh Ben Israel dedicated the Spanish edition of his Hope of Israel, from 1650, to him. The second man was a relative of the first. He wrote a work titled Tratado de Cortesia y Politica, printed at Amsterdam in 1726. No dates of birth or death are given for either man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cuckoo-a-v-cuck: Cuckoo is the Authorized Version rendering of a Hebrew word in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. In both places the bird stands in the list of unclean birds. The entry warns that the identification is only a guess. No certain tradition supports it. The Targum simply copies the Hebrew word. The Septuagint gives sea-gull, and the Revised Version gives seamew. Leading commentaries accept that reading. The entry still closes with a fact about the real bird: the cuckoo does summer in Palestine, in two varieties, common and spotted.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dante-alighieri:
Dante Alighieri was a Florentine poet, born in 1265. He died at Ravenna on Sept. 14, 1321. Caught in his city's feuds, he was banished in 1302. He spent the rest of his life in exile, a guest of northern princes. His chief work is the Divina Commedia. A few Hebrew words in the poem raised a question. Did Dante know Hebrew? His own words say no, the entry holds.

The Comedy shaped Jewish poets who read it. Immanuel ben Solomon modeled the last chapter of his Divan, Hell and Paradise, on Dante's work. The two poets likely knew each other well. Contemporaries treated their friendship as common knowledge. Whether Dante hides in Immanuel's guide, a figure named Daniel, is left open for the reader.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-davidson-benjam: Benjamin Davidson was an English Orientalist of Jewish birth who died in 1871. He worked for the British Society for the Propagation of the Gospel Among the Jews. When that society founded a London college in 1847 to train its missionaries, he became its principal. He wrote an analytical Hebrew and Chaldee lexicon and reading lessons in Syriac and Chaldee. He also helped edit a Hebrew concordance. His chief work appeared after his death: a concordance of the Hebrew and Chaldee Scriptures, printed in London in 1876.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-digne-hebr-5193: Digne is the capital of the French department of Basses-Alpes, and it held a Jewish community as early as the thirteenth century. In 1299 a Jew of Digne named Salve served as one of the commissioners who divided among the Jews a tax promised to the Count of Provence. In 1305 Baruch of Digne, an eminent rabbi, quarreled heatedly with his old teacher and was excommunicated by him. Baruch refused the sentence and left for France. Jews named for Digne appear later at Carpentras and Forcalquier.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dositheus-5293:
Dositheus founded a Samaritan sect and probably lived in the first century. Church writers call him the first to deny the Prophets. Hippolytus opens his list of thirty-two heresies with Dositheus. The Samaritan chronicler Abu al-Fath puts the sect's rise before Alexander the Great.

Rabbinic sources pair Dositheus with Sabbaeus as founders of Samaritan parties. Their teaching kept Mount Gerizim holy, rejected the prophetic books, and denied the resurrection. Some writers make Dositheus the teacher of Simon Magus. Others treat him as a Samaritan messiah figure. The entry shows his followers still active and argued with in the sixth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-earring-5393:
An earring is a ring or hook worn through the ear lobe. Hebrew has no word for the earring alone. One term covers both ear ornaments and nose rings. Writers added a word when they needed to be exact.

Early pendants may have been strings of pearls or beads. Drops is one old name for their shape. Gold earrings appear in Exodus and Judges, alongside rings of other stuffs. Round earrings show up only by Ezekiel's time. Jacob's sons gave up their earrings with their idols, which hints the ornaments carried a sacred air.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eisler-leopold-: Leopold Eisler was an Austrian rabbi born at Boskowitz, Moravia, on Feb. 11, 1825. He studied Talmud under Abraham Placzek. At Prague he read Oriental languages and heard Rapoport lecture. In 1856 Eiwanowitz chose him as rabbi. In 1892 he added the new Wischau community, serving both. His chief work, on rabbinic language and antiquities, came out at Vienna in four parts. They appeared between 1872 and 1890, with a later volume of studies in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elias-samuel-55: Samuel Elias was an English prize fighter known as Dutch Sam. He was born in London on April 4, 1775. He died there on July 3, 1816. The entry lists his bouts with dates and foes. Of three fights with Tom Belcher he lost one and won one. Men of his day called him the hardest hitter the ring had seen. He made the upper cut his own mark in the sport. He left the ring with his health ruined and died in deep poverty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elkind-arkadi-d: Arkadi Elkind was a Russian doctor and student of man. He was born in Mohilev on the Dnieper in 1869. He took his medical degree at Moscow in 1893. His bent was the study of the human body by group. A learned society sent him to study the Poles of Russian Poland. His reports came out in that society's journal. His book on the Jews of the region is his chief work. The entry calls it the largest such study of any Jewish group.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephraim-5793:
Ephraim was the younger son of Joseph in Genesis. His name is tied to a root that means fruitful. Joseph's elder son was Manasseh by birth order. Yet Jacob, in his blessing, set Ephraim above his brother. He gave the younger the rights of a firstborn son. That scene, the entry argues, dresses a fact of tribal growth. Ephraim and Manasseh were once one tribe with Benjamin.

Manasseh split off first from that old Joseph tribe. Hence he counts as the elder in the tale. Ephraim then grew in strength and in number year by year. In time he passed his brother clan in weight. The birthright of Reuben passed to Joseph's sons as well. That grant marks the slow fall of Reuben's tribe. Tribal lists show the shift in their mixed order. At times Manasseh leads the list, and at times Ephraim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ferreolus-6093: Ferreolus was bishop of Uzes, France, from 553 to 581, and the entry tracks his swing from kindness to force. He tried to convert the town's many Jews, at first gently, even asking them to his table. Complaints got him banished to Paris for three years. Cleared in 558, he came home changed. A synod he called pressed the Jews to convert by words or by force. Many yielded, and the rest were driven out. Some converts returned to Judaism after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankel-jonas-6:
Jonas Fränkel was a German banker and philanthropist born at Breslau at the end of the eighteenth century. He died there on January 27, 1846. He was a grandson of David Fränkel, the commentator on the Jerusalem Talmud. By great business skill he rose from deep poverty to wealth. He became one of the leading bankers of Breslau. The Prussian government gave him a councilor's title for his services to German trade and industry.

Busy as he was, Fränkel worked without rest for the community. He directed many charities and gave freely to them. At his own cost he built a hospital, with an orphanage, a study house, and a synagogue attached. Being childless, he left part of his fortune to a family fund for dowries. The greater part went to charities, above all to a Jewish seminary at Breslau. That school opened in 1854.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friendship-6393:
Friendship, in Jewish thought, means a close bond built on shared interests and trust, not on gain. Bible stories and wise sayings give the topic high rank. God speaks to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. Isaiah also calls Abraham the friend of God.

True friendship, the entry holds, must be free of self-seeking. Selfish ties end when the gain ends. Jonathan and David stand as the chief case, since Jonathan chose loyalty over royal interest. Later rabbis add sharp warnings about picking friends with care. Frank reproof between friends counts as a high duty, not a breach of love.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gamaliel-6493: Gamaliel is a name that in the Bible marks only the prince of the tribe of Manasseh, in Numbers. After Bible times the name turns up most often in the family of Hillel. One tale tells of a convert made by Hillel whose two sons took the names Hillel and Gamaliel in thanks. Six patriarchs bore the name. Other men called Gamaliel lived in Palestine in the third and fourth centuries and rank among the amoraim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gittith-6693: Gittith names a musical instrument mentioned in the headings of Psalms viii, lxxxi, and lxxxiv. Gesenius took the word to mean a "striking instrument," but the entry says it is now generally held to be a zither. Rashi, following the Targum, linked the name to Gath, making it an instrument made by Gath's people. Ibn Ezra instead tied it to the descendants of Obed-edom the Gittite, a Levite. The entry also records, and questions, readings that connect the word with wine-presses or with Edom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gomez-de-sosa-s:
Isaac Gomez de Sosa was a Latin poet, and De Barrios called him a famous one. He was the son of Abraham Gomez de Sosa. In 1677 he served as arbiter at Don Manuel de Belmonte's academy of poetry.

He wrote the Latin epitaph on his father's tomb. He also wrote a Latin poem honoring Jacob Judah Leon's "Las Alabanças de Santitad." Two more poems honored a work by Joseph Penço de la Vega. He further arranged a translation of the work "Divinidad de la Ley." The entry rests on de Castro's tombstone book and Kayserling's bibliography.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grossmann-louis: Louis Grossmann was an American rabbi and author. He was born at Vienna, Austria, on Feb. 24, 1863. He came from a family of rabbis. Cincinnati's university and Hebrew Union College gave him his degrees. In 1884 he became rabbi of Detroit's Temple Beth El. He kept that post until 1898. He then succeeded Isaac M. Wise at Cincinnati's B'nai Yeshurun. He also took Wise's theology chair at Hebrew Union College. His books include "Judaism and the Science of Religion" (1889) and "Maimonides" (1890).
