Four scenarios vary how fast quotas tighten and auctions are introduced. Fast tightening with high auction shares overloaded firms, collapsed prices and forced early fossil plant closures. Gradual auction growth with smooth quota cuts kept prices steadier and supported phased low-carbon investment. The findings favor stepwise reform for markets pursuing deep decarbonization without supply shocks.
pmc-13264193:
Hassan Asadigandomani and colleagues describe three children with a rare inflammatory eye socket disease in a 2026 case series. IgG4-related disease fills tissues with immune cells and scarring, and in the orbit it forms masses that push the eye outward. Adult cases are recognized, yet reports in children are exceedingly scarce, so each well-documented case helps doctors consider the diagnosis earlier in young patients.

The girls, aged five to sixteen, all showed progressive bulging and displaced eyes, with scans revealing tissue involving the tear gland. Biopsies confirmed dense immune infiltrates rich in the defining cell type. Steroids and immune-calming drugs formed the main treatment. One stubborn case improved substantially after rituximab, a targeted antibody therapy.
pmc-13264293:
Yang Yang and colleagues study how grazing and burrowing animals jointly shape soil carbon in high Tibetan meadows in a 2026 field paper. Alpine soils hold most of the ecosystem carbon and respond slowly, so disturbance effects matter for climate accounting. Grazing alone raised organic carbon and nitrogen while lowering inorganic carbon. Plateau zokors, burrowing rodents, mainly shuffled carbon and nitrogen between soil layers across seasons through their digging.

Combined grazing and burrowing did not simply add their separate effects. Together they suppressed inorganic carbon more than expected yet blunted gains in organic carbon and nitrogen. Such interactions complicate predictions from single-disturbance studies. Meadow management for carbon storage should treat grazers and burrowers as an interacting system.
pmc-13264393:
Eamonn Tweedy and colleagues wrote a 2026 study on warning signs that a child in hospital may soon need intensive care. Late moves to intensive care harm outcomes, and current bedside scores are often too slow or too weak. The team built a machine learning tool from health record data.

Their F-WIN model used records from one large children's hospital, with more than 72,000 ward stays. Of those stays, 816 ended in an unplanned move to intensive care. The model flagged risk up to a full day ahead and beat the standard bedside score and two watch programs. A short version with far fewer inputs kept nearly the same skill, which may ease use in wards.
pmc-13264893:
Julia Jieyu Fu and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review of diabetic retinopathy care in the United States, using a cascade view that tracks patients step by step. This eye disease, a diabetes complication, can blind if screening and follow-up lapse. The team measured where patients drop out of the care chain.

From nearly 15,000 studies screened, 46 met the rules. Screening every two years ranged widely, with a median near 59 percent of people with diabetes. Among people found to have the eye disease, a median of about 70 percent did not know they had it. Only about half of diagnosed patients first linked to care, and many later lapsed in follow-up. The authors name awareness, linkage, and follow-up as the three big leaks to fix.
pmc-13264993:
Rui Hu and co-authors wrote a 2026 narrative review on blending Western medicine with Traditional Chinese Medicine for older patients around hip fracture surgery. Pain, poor sleep, and nausea after surgery form a linked trio that slows recovery in this frail group. Western enhanced-recovery plans are proven, and Chinese methods may complement them while cutting drug load.

The review examines nerve blocks and drug prevention from Western care, and electroacupuncture, skin-point electrical stimulation, and ear therapy from Chinese practice. It traces the shared brain pathways tying pain, sleep, and nausea together. The proposed plan phases the blend: conditioning before surgery, nerve block with point stimulation during, and mixed pain care with acupuncture after. The authors call for rigorous trials and mechanism studies to firm up the approach.
pmc-13265593:
Andy Jacobson and colleagues published a 2026 study on cheaper ways to monitor pesticides in surface water. Daily sampling gives the best exposure estimates but costs too much for most programs. The team reused rare daily data sets to test whether pooled weekly or two-weekly samples, or a statistical model called SEAWAVE-QEX, could match daily results.

Both weekly and two-week pooled samples estimated long-term pesticide exposure accurately. A trial run of the model with weekly pooled samples reasonably estimated short-term peaks at one site. Rain data worked as a cheaper stand-in for streamflow data in the model, with little loss. The authors offer the findings as practical guidance for designing monitoring programs that balance accuracy against cost and effort for risk assessment.
pmc-13266193:
Shota Wada and co-authors present 2026 cell biology findings on ATF6 alpha, a sensor that helps cells cope with stress in the endoplasmic reticulum. When unfolded proteins build up, this sensor must pair up and travel to the Golgi apparatus before it can switch on protective genes. The team asked which helper enzymes control that pairing step.

Several oxidoreductase enzymes shaped the outcome in opposite ways. ERdj5 and PDIR promoted pairing at one cysteine site, while ERp18 held it back. Pairing also stabilized the sensor and protected it from disposal inside the cell. Clarifying these controls helps explain how cells tune their stress response and avoid damage.
pmc-13266593:
Nesibe Aydogdu and Emel Sabaz Karakeci report a 2026 study of belly fat measures and nerve damage in diabetes. The study covered 562 people with type 2 diabetes seen between 2022 and 2024. Nerve damage was judged by electrical nerve tests and a pain score scale.

Of the group, 213 patients tested positive for nerve damage and 349 did not. The nerve-damage group had higher body mass, blood fats, and blood sugar control markers. Three fat-based scores were also higher in that group. Waist size and one fat score, along with blood sugar control, stood out as separate risk factors. The authors suggest these scores can flag patients at high risk.
pmc-13267593:
Abdullahi Hassan Elmi wrote a 2026 letter on bringing modern recovery pathways and AI support into surgery in poor settings. Surgical safety is hard where staff, monitoring, and record keeping are thin. Enhanced Recovery After Surgery, a set of proven steps around an operation, speeds healing. Elmi argues the two tools should be treated as partners, not rivals.

AI could flag risky patients, watch for complications, and feed back audit results to teams. Combined with recovery pathways, that could make care more reliable and catch risk earlier. But Elmi insists the rollout must be gradual, fitted to local needs, and ethically governed. Basics come first: checklists, team work across professions, staff training, and honest audit of results.
pmc-13267893:
Emmanuel Kissiedu Antiri and Ivy Adwowa Efiefi Ekem present a 2026 case report on a leukemia that first showed in the gums. Acute promyelocytic leukemia is a fast blood cancer with a known gene fusion and a high early death risk if treatment lags. Their patient was a 26-year-old man whose gums grew steadily larger over three weeks. Swollen gums are a rare sign for this subtype.

He was treated for gum inflammation for two weeks before blood work was done. Marrow tests and gene probes then confirmed the leukemia, in its microgranular form. Blood counts were low, but there was no severe bleeding disorder, which made the picture atypical. The standard targeted drug was unavailable locally, so standard chemotherapy was given. He died one week into treatment. The authors stress fast referral when gums swell oddly.
pmc-13268793:
Xuefen Cai and colleagues look in 2026 for blood markers measured before embryo transfer that predict whether a frozen-thawed transfer will lead to pregnancy. Their retrospective study compared 404 patients who became pregnant with 313 who did not. Newer blood indices, including markers tied to insulin resistance and inflammation, were tested with several statistical methods.

Patients who did not conceive were older, heavier, and had higher insulin resistance markers. Two combined indices built from triglycerides, glucose, and body mass stood out, with pregnancy chances clearly lower in the highest group than the lowest. Adding one index modestly improved prediction beyond standard clinical factors. Checking these simple measures before transfer may help flag women at higher risk of failure.
pmc-13269593:
Maajid Mohi Ud Din Malik and Rajesh Prasad Jayaswal wrote a commentary in 2026 on a small trial of clot-busting treatment for dangerous lung clots in intensive care. The trial tailored low-dose treatment using a clot firmness test. The commentators praise running such a trial in very fragile patients, then raise design concerns.

Twenty-two patients were assigned, 8 to standard care and 14 to the guided method, but only 7 and 12 were analyzed. One control patient stopped treatment after severe chest pain and was dropped, which the authors say should have been counted and tested in a check analysis. Two guided-group patients were also removed later, though only one removal appears in the trial's flow figure.
pmc-13270493:
Elias Bitzer and colleagues published a 2026 journal article on alpha-gal syndrome, a meat allergy gained after tick bites, in patients seen for gut symptoms. Their work came from a gastroenterology clinic, the clinic for stomach and bowel care, at Cairns Hospital in Far North Queensland, Australia.

The team audited blood test requests before and after a local testing guideline began in March 2025. Of 19 patients tested, five, or 26 percent, showed sensitivity, most often with diarrhea and belly pain and with no severe whole-body reaction. All three patients who finished a meat-free trial saw their symptoms clear. Testing yield rose sharply after the guideline, though one clinician ordered most tests.
pmc-13271893:
Johanna K. Freundt is lead author of a 2026 journal article on titin, the largest human protein, which forms the elastic backbone of heart muscle cells and gives the heart its passive stiffness. Titin mutations cause inherited heart disease, and injury can also cut titin's elastic segment, but the effect of suddenly losing that spring was unknown.

The team engineered mice whose cardiac titin could be cut on demand. Cutting did not stretch the heart open; instead chambers shrank and filling worsened. Isolated cells lost elastic recoil, cell junctions broke down, gaps between cells widened, and scar-forming cells activated, driving fibrosis, stiffening of heart tissue. Compensation failed and heart failure followed, showing the spring is essential to mechanical balance.
pmc-13272093:
Xiaobei Liu and coauthors trial in 2026 a new teaching model for nursing students on placement in gut surgery wards. The model uses a six-step lesson plan called BOPPPS and adds story-based teaching, with values content woven into the course. Ward training must build both hands-on skill and a strong sense of the nursing role.

Ninety-two students were split between standard teaching and the new model during placements from 2023 to 2024. The new-model group scored higher on role identity, core nursing skills, ward performance, and how much they liked the teaching. The authors offer the model as a guide for reform in clinical nursing courses.
pmc-13272693:
Shiqiong Zhou and Qinghua Ke wrote a 2026 comment on skin-scope signs for acral lentiginous melanoma, a melanoma on palms, soles, or nails. They respond to a meta-analysis that confirmed the parallel ridge pattern as a strong sign of this cancer. That pattern had 79.6 percent sensitivity and 99.4 percent specificity in the review.

The authors warn that about 20 percent of these melanomas lack that pattern, so its absence cannot rule out cancer. They also question the high specificity, since only 25 percent of benign lesions in the studies were confirmed by tissue tests. They call for future studies to record lesion site and pressure from walking or use.
pmc-13272893: Correction notice from Hsiao-Ling Chen and co-authors. It concerns a cost study of a lung cancer drug. The drug is atezolizumab, used for advanced small cell lung cancer. Tables 1 and 2 had errors when first published. Cut-off screen images were printed in place of clean tables. Those images also showed word processor marks. Full original tables are shown in the notice. The paper has now been corrected.
pmc-13273393:
Xiaoyun Zhang leads a 2026 multiomics study of risperidone, a widely used drug for schizophrenia that can cause weight gain and blood sugar problems. The team combined genetic, gene activity, and DNA methylation data to find genes that link the drug's benefits to its metabolic harms. Patient blood cells were used for validation.

They found 120 genes changed by risperidone, and three, including DKK3, linked causally to both schizophrenia and metabolic traits. DKK3 fell after drug exposure and its promoter gained methylation, a silencing mark. Lower DKK3 tied to worse sugar and fat control. The authors propose DKK3 as a marker for personalizing schizophrenia treatment.
pmc-13273593:
Loris Mannino and a large team tested a biohybrid implant for spinal cord injury in a 2026 study. A hard blow to the cord causes lasting loss of movement and feeling, first from the impact and then from inflammation that follows. The team combined electrical stimulation with stem cell delivery in one device.

Their implant sits under the cord's outer membrane and delivers pulsed fields for ten days, then steady current for five more, while carrying two kinds of stem cells. Stimulation helped implanted cells migrate and settle, and it sharply cut the number of reactive microglia, the cord's immune cells. Stimulated animals also ran faster in tests. The treatment did not worsen scarring, pain, or neuron loss, and both wired and wireless versions worked.
pmc-13274393:
Zhi Qiu, Yanyan Ma, and Hongju Liu report a 2026 case report of a hip fracture that healed without more surgery. The patient was a forty-four-year-old manual laborer whose broken femoral neck, the narrow bridge below the hip ball, had failed to unite nine months after metal fixation. Poor blood supply makes this break prone to nonunion.

The man refused revision surgery, so doctors injected his own platelet-rich plasma, a blood concentrate rich in growth factors, into the gap three times under ultrasound guidance. A phased exercise program followed. Over seven months, X-rays showed the bone knitting together. His rest pain vanished, and he returned to walking unaided and to light work.
pmc-13274593:
Xiaolei Hao and a large team present a 2026 journal article on how vitamin C helps the immune system tolerate the body's own tissues. Using CRISPR screening in living mice, they singled out the vitamin C transporter Slc23a2 as a brake on naive T cell reactivity. T cells that cannot import enough of the vitamin become trigger-happy against self.

Without the transporter, T cells lost internal ascorbate, gained extra DNA methylation tags, and turned into fighter and memory cells too readily, causing low-grade autoimmune inflammation. The vitamin keeps TET enzymes active, and those enzymes hold a master gene, Tcf1, in place. The same pattern appears with vitamin deprivation and aging, linking diet to immune tolerance.
pmc-13275493:
Andi Mai and many co-authors review data errors in AI-driven precision nutrition in a 2026 article. Personal diet advice increasingly draws on wearables, lab profiles, behaviour tracking, and self-reported food intake. Errors in any of those inputs can bias advice and widen gaps for underserved groups.

The review compares older statistical fixes and Bayesian models with newer machine learning tools. Autoencoders and related deep learning tools can clean noisy inputs in different ways. Uncorrected error can also bake group bias into deployed systems. The authors propose a practical framework for researchers, developers, and regulators who build fairer nutrition tools.
pmc-13275593:
Depanshi Pandit and colleagues present a 2026 journal article profiling the DNA maintenance protein DNA2 across all major cancers. DNA2 helps cells copy and repair DNA, and overactive repair can help tumors survive stress. Using national cancer genome cohorts and other public databases, the team ran the first pan-cancer multi-omics study of this gene, spanning expression, mutations, survival, and immune patterns.

DNA2 was overexpressed in seventeen tumor types compared with normal tissue, and endometrial cancer showed the most frequent genetic changes, about seven percent. High DNA2 tracked with worse survival in several cancers, most sharply in adrenocortical carcinoma. It also tracked with more regulatory immune cells and fewer killer cells. Two drugs, tozasertib and daporinad, hit high-DNA2 tumor cells harder in drug-response data.
pmc-13275793:
Anna Westwig and co-authors ask how listeners piece together spoken words in a 2026 journal article. Hearing a word draws on the sound itself and on the meaning of the sentence around it. The team compared human choices with ideal observer models, math models of the best possible decision maker.

Two experiments had people judge a target word inside a sentence while the team varied its sound, the sentence meaning, cue order, and noise. Listeners combined the two cues in a mostly additive way, meaning each added its own push. Swapping cue order changed little when the information stayed the same. People also reweighted cues based on how reliable each cue was on its own. Overall, listeners came close to the ideal model's performance.
pmc-13276593:
Chuang Liang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a brain network pattern that changes during long-term dialysis. End-stage kidney disease patients on hemodialysis often develop thinking problems, depression, and dementia risks. The brain biology behind those risks, beyond waste buildup, is unclear.

The team fused functional and structural brain scans of thirty-nine patients followed for a year. Unsupervised analysis isolated a pattern joining the default mode network, active at rest, with the insula, a deep integration hub. The pattern shifted over the year of treatment and tracked patients' cognition. Genes tied to it clustered in DNA repair, energy use, and cell activation. The starting pattern also predicted cognition a year later. The same brain-cognition links held in separate depression, mild impairment, and Alzheimer's cohorts. The authors hope the pattern clarifies how dialysis-era kidney failure affects the brain.
pmc-13277193:
Freda Zhi Yun Chua and colleagues report five years of kidney-doctor-led dialysis catheter placement in a 2026 study. Peritoneal dialysis needs a working abdominal catheter, and delays block patients from starting. A fluoroscopy-guided service run by nephrologists at one centre offered a faster route than surgery.

Records covered 253 insertions in 243 patients between 2019 and 2023. Dialysis started successfully in nearly every case, and urgent starts began a median of one day after placement. Serious bleeding was uncommon, and no early infections, leaks, or organ injuries appeared within thirty days. Six patients with polycystic kidney disease, usually a hard group, were also treated successfully.
pmc-13278793:
Qing Yi Fang leads a 2026 case report of a lung tumor that spread to the heart and disrupted its rhythm. The patient was a 69-year-old man with a Pancoast tumor, a lung cancer at the top of the lung. He arrived with ECG changes mimicking a heart attack and a 2-to-1 atrioventricular block, where every second electrical signal fails to reach the lower heart chambers.

Heart ultrasound and PET imaging revealed metastases inside the heart. A permanent pacemaker was implanted for the symptomatic block. He died of advanced cancer shortly afterward. The case raises hard questions about when pacing helps at the end of life. Such decisions should be shared, weighing prognosis and patient preference, the authors stress.
pmc-13278993:
Hanmo Zhang and colleagues published a 2026 study hunting for gene markers that link cell aging to acute myocardial infarction, a heart attack. Working from gene-expression data on 106 patients and 76 controls, the team combined network analysis with four machine learning methods to find senescence-related genes that separate patients from healthy people. Senescence here means the worn, inflammatory state that aged cells enter.

Four genes — FOS, SOD2, MXD1, and GRN — held up across blood gene data, single-cell data, protein data, and mouse models of heart attack. A classifier built on them reached an accuracy score of 0.808 in testing, respectable for a four-gene panel. The authors also split patients into low- and high-senescence groups; the high group carried more inflammatory neutrophils. Their models offer a starting point for diagnosis and for sorting patients by aging-related risk.
pmc-13279393:
Haolan Xiong and colleagues report a 2026 case series on fixing hip socket breaks that reach the back column. Such breaks are hard to fix due to deep, three fold anatomy and a tight surgery path. Their method fixes a plate along the inner back column through a front approach. The plate is a standard rebuild plate, bent by hand in surgery to fit each pelvis.

The series held thirty six back to back patients treated from 2019 to 2022. Two front routes were used, one in twenty six cases and one in ten. Mean age was near forty three years. Staff logged surgery time, blood loss, bone union, side effects, joint fit grade and hip function at one year. Low plate cost and easy bending make the route open to most hospitals.
pmc-13280593:
Elizabeth Catherine Conti and colleagues report a 2026 longitudinal study of faith and meaning on quality of life in United States women with breast cancer on chemotherapy. Women newly diagnosed and undergoing chemotherapy at a large tertiary cancer centre enrolled. One hundred fourteen women completed measures of spirituality and health related quality of life at study entry and three and fifteen months later. Spirituality was scored in three subscales: Meaning, Peace and Faith.

Baseline Faith was positively associated with Meaning and Peace at three months. Both Meaning and Peace mediated the association between Faith and mental quality of life at fifteen months. When baseline Meaning was controlled, the indirect effect of Faith on mental quality of life remained significant. Increases in Meaning over the first three months also carried effect. Faith may lift later mental well being by building early meaning and peace during chemotherapy.
pmc-13280693:
Jihua Hu and colleagues led a 2026 gene study on anxiety that split results by sex. Anxiety disorders strike women about twice as often as men. Past gene studies mostly mixed the sexes, which can hide real signals. The team pooled two huge health banks, one British and one American. They had tens of thousands of cases in each sex, plus far more controls.

They found twenty-one key gene variants tied to anxiety in women and five in men. The gene patterns overlapped a lot but were not the same. Gene effects explained more of the risk in women. Links to other traits also split by sex. The authors say studying the sexes apart can reveal gene clues that pooled studies miss.
pmc-13280893:
Xiongheng Bian and colleagues published a 2026 study of droplet tweezers, a tool that picks up microscopic objects using the capillary grip of a liquid bridge, not hard jaws or laser beams. Mechanical grippers can crush delicate samples, and optical traps adapt poorly to varied weights. The team's tweezers use two surfaces with contrasting water affinity, one hydrophilic and one hydrophobic, forming a bridge whose shape can be tuned. They derived the balance conditions that keep the bridge stable, identifying contact angle, opening distance, and height as settings.

Experiments confirmed the analysis: pulling the tweezers up and widening the lower opening favored transfer. By adjusting the bridge's curvature to match the wetting contrast, they handled objects of different weights with one device, from light cell clusters toward heavier micro-components. The authors present the liquid bridge as a damage-free route to micromanipulation for biomedicine, analytical chemistry, and micro-assembly.
pmc-13280993:
Nuha M Alhazmi published a 2026 study producing the enzyme tannase from a soil fungus, Aspergillus terreus, and testing it on textile dyes and fruit juices. Tannase breaks down tannins, plant compounds that cloud juices. The strain was grown two ways: submerged fermentation yielded 136.8 units per milliliter, more than double the 62.7 from surface culture. Production peaked at mildly acidic pH, 30 degrees, and a tannic acid concentration.

Purification sharpened the enzyme's activity, and gel analysis suggested it forms a multi-unit complex above 250 kilodaltons. Kinetic testing on tannic acid followed the saturation pattern used to benchmark enzymes. In trials, the enzyme bleached textile dyes in a dose-dependent manner on agar plates. Added to pomegranate, pineapple, and guava juices, it hydrolyzed tannins, cutting cloudiness and thickness while improving clarity and lowering microbial counts. The author presents the enzyme as a versatile green processing aid for beverage and textile industries.
pmc-13281493:
Aarushi Ahuja and colleagues reviewed lung safety signals for a fast-growing drug class in a 2026 paper. The drugs mimic a gut hormone and treat diabetes and obesity. Their gut side effects, like nausea, are well known. Their effects on the lungs are far less clear, even as use soars worldwide. The review gathers every kind of human proof, from trials to single case reports. Safety watch databases, which log harm reports, were part of the hunt.

The authors sort reported lung events by type and severity. They grade how strong the proof is with a standard tool. They also weigh how bias may bend each kind of study. Possible paths by which the drugs could harm or help the lungs are laid out. The team frames the work as signal hunting, not proof of cause. Its map shows where firm trials are most needed.
pmc-13281593:
Jonas Töpfer and colleagues piloted a blended course on doctor talk skills in a 2026 study. Good talk with patients is core to good care. New digital and smart tools now demand fresh talk skills too. The course mixed online units with in-person practice for medical students. Online parts covered story-based talk and talk about smart tools. In class, students practiced with trained actors playing patients and got structured feedback. Six students took the pilot.

All six finished the course, which marks it as workable. Self-ratings rose in every skill area after the course. Gains were largest for digital and smart tool topics. In a graded role-play exam, the pilot group matched peers overall. Their edge showed most in advising on smart tools and in closing the visit well. The authors call for a larger run to test the gains.
pmc-13281893:
Yangyang Xu and colleagues hunted blood markers for schizophrenia in a 2026 study. Schizophrenia still lacks any lab test, so diagnosis rests on talks and observation. Long gene strands that never build proteins can steer brain programs. Some ride in tiny blood sacs that echo brain states. The team mined a public dataset for such strands in patient sacs. Fifteen candidates were then checked in a clinic group. Blood cells and blood sacs were both tested.

Two strands stood out, raised in both blood sources in patients. Each alone sorted patients from healthy peers fairly well. Paired, they sorted better still. One sits in the cell body and may tune learning-linked paths. The other rides the sacs and may carry signals cell to cell. Both are strongly conserved across species, a hint of core roles. The authors call them candidate markers that need wider proof.
pmc-13282193:
Omar Salim and co-authors report a 2026 study on whether one brain surgeon could safely switch epilepsy surgery technique in children. The operation, hemispherotomy, disconnects one side of the brain to stop drug-resistant seizures. It can be done from the side or from the top. Recent reports hinted the top route might work better, raising the question of switching safely.

Thirty-six children treated between 2016 and 2025 were compared, twenty-three with the side route and thirteen with the top. About nine in ten in each group were seizure free after one year. Complication rates did not differ clearly. The top route took much less time and caused less blood loss, while hospital stay was similar. Adjusting for time period and other factors did not change the results. The authors say an experienced surgeon can switch without harming outcomes.
pmc-13282693:
Niamh Wilson and co-authors present a 2026 study defining the inner environment of the human spinal disc core, and testing how disc cells respond to it. Disc degeneration is the leading cause of low back pain worldwide. Yet the core's chemistry, its glucose, oxygen, acidity, salt balance, and signal proteins, was not fully charted. The team profiled tissue from disc surgery patients across degeneration grades.

Against expectations, the measured values and tissue makeup held broadly steady as degeneration worsened, though donors varied a lot. Disc cells grown as tiny tissues, primed with a growth factor, then stressed for fourteen days with disc-like glucose, acidity, and signals, proved resilient. They stayed alive and kept building matrix, the tissue's scaffold. The authors say the defined ranges give cell therapy designers realistic targets, and that disc cells tolerate the harsh disc environment better than feared.
pmc-13282993:
Skin microbes and autoimmune skin disease may push on each other, a two-way genetic probe undertaken by Junlin Wang's team in 2026. Three diseases are covered: psoriasis, localized scleroderma, and lupus of the skin and body. Skin microbes help keep immune balance, but cause and effect were unclear.

Gene data for 1,656 skin microbe traits were paired with disease data from FinnGen. A method that uses genes as natural tests probed links in both directions. Some microbe traits raised disease risk, while others lowered it in the results. Disease also appeared to shift microbe levels in return. Most strong links showed no clear bias in checks. Results point to two-way links, not one-way cause.
pmc-13283393:
A waist-and-lipid index flags hormone and pregnancy risk in polycystic ovary syndrome, Baichao Shi's reanalysis shows in 2026. The index mixes waist size, body mass, and blood fats in one score. It may flag hormone and pregnancy risks in this common condition.

Data came from 956 women in a prior trial of the syndrome. Higher index scores tracked with higher weight, pressure, and blood sugar problems. Scores also tracked with insulin resistance, fatty liver, and metabolic syndrome rates. Top-score women had far higher insulin resistance odds than bottom-score women. The index predicted both conditions with fair accuracy in curve tests. Higher scores also tracked with lower pregnancy success.
pmc-13283993:
Mengyao Liu and co-authors ran a single-centre phase 2 trial in 2026 of a drug pairing for advanced bladder-area cancer. Patients with locally advanced or metastatic urothelial cancer often cannot take cisplatin, the standard backbone drug, which leaves few options. Thirty such patients received gemcitabine chemotherapy plus tislelizumab, an immune checkpoint drug, as their first treatment.

About 47 percent of tumours shrank measurably, and disease was controlled in about 77 percent. Median time without progression reached about fourteen months, and median survival about twenty-three months. Blood-related side effects were most common, led by low white cell counts. Tumours holding organised immune cell clusters, called tertiary lymphoid structures, responded more often, though the gap was not statistically firm. The authors call the pairing tolerable and promising.
pmc-13284093:
Meriem Derkaoui and colleagues sequenced bacteria in 2026 from a newborn ward in Chlef, Algeria, to test whether the ward itself spreads drug-resistant germs. Klebsiella pneumoniae is a major hospital infection threat. The team sampled the ward environment, checked drug sensitivity with an automated system, and read whole genomes, comparing them against thousands of public genomes to place the strains.

Every isolate resisted multiple drugs, and sequencing found twenty-two resistance genes, with a core set shared by all samples, including genes against common antibiotic families. Three isolates carried virulence genes tied to iron capture and belonged to a high-risk clone, ST13, whose matching profiles suggest spread within the hospital. One strain was a novel type. The authors warn the ward environment acts as a reservoir.
pmc-13284493:
Asma El Ayeb-Zakhama and colleagues assess plant oils as insecticides against the green peach aphid in a 2026 study. Oils came from sage, Ormenis africana, and pennyroyal mint, tested alone and in mixtures. Chemical profiling showed distinct main parts, with pulegone dominant in mint oil and camphor plus thujone strong in sage oil.

In lab fumigation, the three-oil mixture killed aphids at the lowest dose of the blends tested by the team. Greenhouse work showed spraying killed more aphids than fumigation but also harmed plants at higher strength, while fumigation caused no plant harm. The authors present the blends as a possible natural swap for synthetic sprays in greener pest control.
pmc-13284593:
Ngo Thi Thu Thuy, Le Van Thieu, and Tran Vuong The Vinh measured body composition against bone density in 2026 in surgical patients. Weak bones and low muscle worsen surgical results, from implant failure to slow recovery. The cross-sectional study enrolled 199 patients, using whole-body DXA scans for regional muscle, fat, and bone density, plus blood tests for two fat-related hormones, leptin and adiponectin.

Trunk and hip-region muscle mass showed the strongest positive ties to bone scores. Fat mass linked weakly, while adiponectin linked inversely with density. In combined modelling, trunk muscle, hip-region muscle, body mass index, and adiponectin each independently predicted bone score, together explaining about 45 percent of its spread. The authors advise adding muscle checks and metabolic tuning to care around surgery.
pmc-13284893:
Oliver Nilsen and co-authors present a 2026 case report of triple M syndrome during cancer immunotherapy. The rare overlap joins heart muscle inflammation, muscle inflammation, and myasthenia gravis, and can threaten life. An 80-year-old woman with spread bile duct cancer grew weak, with drooping eyelids and trouble swallowing, after maintenance treatment began.

Her care combined durvalumab, an immune checkpoint drug, with olaparib. Tests pointed to the triple syndrome plus breathing failure from muscle weakness. High-dose steroids, immune globulin, and breathing support brought early gains, but a fatal bleed behind the belly ended the course. The authors stress fast action when such overlap signs appear during immunotherapy.
pmc-13285593:
Tumors school nearby immune cells to help them colonize lungs, María Rosado-Sanz and co-authors reveal in a 2026 study of triple-negative breast cancer. This subtype spreads early and shrugs off many drugs. Cancer cells rewire fresh macrophages into tumor helpers that pour out four signaling proteins.

Those signals push cancer cells to change shape, crawl, slip through vessel walls, and seed lungs. The helpers also flip naive defender T cells into suppressor cells, building a self-feeding shield. Blocking three signal receptors with known drugs broke the loop and cut lung seeding in mice. The authors call the paired blockade a workable plan to curb spread and drug resistance.
pmc-13285993:
Yuta Hieda and co-authors report a silent lung clot found by a new X-ray method after hip replacement in a 2026 case vignette. The 58-year-old woman at its center had her worn hip joint replaced and felt fine in the days that followed. Blood clots in the lung often hide without symptoms after such surgery, and standard scans carry costs that limit their use for screening.

A week after surgery, moving X-ray images that map blood flow through the lungs showed fresh dark patches on both sides. A contrast scan then confirmed clots in both lungs, matching the patches spot for spot. Blood-thinning treatment cleared the clots in full, and the patient stayed well throughout. The authors present the contrast-free method as a gentle early warning tool that could catch hidden clots before they turn dangerous.
pmc-13286093:
Xintong Jiang and Xueman Wang describe how they kept a drainage tube from slipping out of a dangerous leak between the esophagus and the chest cavity. The 2026 case report concerns a 74-year-old man receiving cancer treatment who developed the leak with an abscess. Such leaks carry high death rates, and drainage tubes often migrate when the opening is wide.

The first tube indeed slipped within a week. The team rebuilt it with side holes and two small coils, then clipped the coils to healthy tissue beside the opening so it could not move. Frequent salt-water flushing followed, and the leak shrank steadily. After thirty days the opening had narrowed greatly, showing the anchoring trick worked.
pmc-13286393:
Claunara Schilling Mendonça and Ana Luiza Ferreira Rodrigues Caldas comment on thirty years of Brazil's Family Health Strategy in a 2026 editorial. The program grew from a coverage drive into the backbone of primary care inside the national health system, steering extra funds toward quilombos, indigenous villages, river communities, and other long-neglected groups. Their commentary takes stock of that arc and asks what quality demands next.

Money, staffing, and coordination remain the stubborn trio after three decades, they argue. Most municipalities are tiny and cannot run referral networks alone, while the standard panel of 3,500 people per team strains against complex territories. They press for smaller panels, valued staff on fair terms, and digital tools treated as core care rather than garnish. Care that merely expands, they warn, is not yet care that works.
pmc-13287293:
Alexandra Lautarescu and colleagues ran a co-designed survey in 2026 with 709 people in the United Kingdom. Both neurotypical and neurodivergent people took part. They ranked what research on mental health around pregnancy and birth should tackle first. A smaller group of 253 people also gave written answers.

Treatment studies ranked first, followed by better diagnosis for birthing parents. Effects on the parent and baby relationship ranked third. Written answers added care experiences, trauma, and neurodiversity itself as missing topics. The authors read the pattern as a sign of layered barriers to getting a diagnosis and support. They urge funders to follow the priorities set by affected people.
pmc-13288393:
Maurizia Palummo and co-authors model a protective oxide skin for lead-free solar materials, in a 2026 study. Halide perovskites promise cheap solar cells, but the best versions contain toxic lead. Tin and germanium versions avoid lead yet degrade quickly. The team used first-principles calculations to test a germanium oxide coating on a mixed tin-germanium perovskite. They asked whether the coating could protect the surface without spoiling light response.

Adding germanium lowered the energy that binds electron pairs, which helps free charges for collection. Model slabs with one quarter germanium were capped with the oxide in several surface arrangements. Band alignment and surface reshaping depended strongly on both mix and surface ending. Some arrangements kept the traits wanted for efficient solar conversion. Models with disordered oxide matched real coatings more closely. The work gives growers specific recipes to try for stable lead-free cells.
pmc-13288693:
Louisa Redeker leads a 2026 German multicenter study building computer-readable rules that flag harmful drug events inside electronic health records. Multidisciplinary teams at ten university sites, working within the national Medical Informatics Initiative, drafted the rules from published literature and expert agreement, then put them through a standardized review round.

The group produced 82 algorithms covering 48 adverse events, most built fresh and the rest adapted from earlier versions. Diagnosis codes did most of the work, appearing in 65 algorithms, with laboratory, drug, and procedure codes filling gaps where records were richer. All rules run inside a publicly available phenotyping framework and export in several formats, ready for validation studies and drug safety research.
pmc-13289193:
Elin Orbeck Vallevik and colleagues set infant blood pressure norms in 2026. Their cohort study spans Norway and Sweden. Mothers were recruited during pregnancy. Babies were checked at 3, 6, and 12 months. A cuff method called oscillometry was used for all readings.

In all, 2,100 infants had readings in infancy. Good readings came from 1,778 infants. Median top pressure sat near 95 at each age. Bottom pressure sat near 56 or 57. Mean pressure sat near 69 to 72 at the three checks. Values held steady across the first year. The norms can help spot odd readings early. They give clinics a shared yardstick for the first year.
pmc-13289293:
José Victor Bortolotto Bampi and coauthors present a 2026 cross-sectional study on tuberculosis symptom reporting in Brazilian prisons. Active case finding can catch tuberculosis early in crowded settings, but many programs first ask about symptoms. The authors test whether answers change with who asks, and when, during screening.

The program ran in two male prisons from February 2023 to February 2025, testing sputum every four months with GeneXpert Ultra and culture. Among 6919 people screened, 448 had lab-confirmed disease, and 292 with full data entered the analysis. Only 38.7 percent reported symptoms to nurses at first screening, while 65.8 percent did so with a doctor later in the process. Timing and trust clearly shape what gets reported.
pmc-13290093:
Blood-borne vesicles and their adenosine-making activity in melanoma patients form the subject of a 2026 study led by Yana Najjar. Tumors release tiny extracellular vesicles that can carry the enzymes CD39 and CD73, which produce adenosine, a molecule that calms immune cells.

Najjar and colleagues separated vesicles from melanoma cells and from healthy cells in plasma samples from patients with metastatic disease or with no sign of disease. Against their expectation, vesicles from non-malignant cells showed the stronger enzyme activity. Still, CD73 activity across all plasma vesicles tracked with disease stage and ran higher in metastatic cases. Measuring that activity, they argue, could give a personal read on adenosine-driven immune suppression.
pmc-13290393:
Juri Sugiyama, Yasuhiko Takegami, and Satoshi Muto compare wound suction therapy with plain dressings after severe infection surgery, in 2026. Necrotizing fasciitis and gas gangrene are flesh-destroying infections needing urgent tissue removal. The study pooled records from eleven Japanese tertiary hospitals between 2015 and 2024. Seventy-four adults with leg or trunk disease were split by wound care method. Twenty-eight received negative pressure therapy and forty-six received conventional dressings.

The suction group stayed in hospital far longer, about eighty days against about forty-three. They also needed more repeat debridement operations on average. Skin grafting closed their wounds far more often, while direct closure was commoner with plain dressings. Walking function at discharge did not differ between groups. The authors caution that sicker wounds may have drawn the suction therapy, skewing the comparison. They advise careful patient selection rather than routine use after debridement.
pmc-13290893:
Twelve weeks of care retuned how self-injuring adolescents' brains handle negative images, Jianqiang Bi and colleagues report in an EEG study from 2026. Teenagers who engage in nonsuicidal self-injury often over-detect negative information automatically yet regulate it weakly later, and the team tested whether routine clinical care shifts both stages.

Thirty-two adolescents completed an emotional oddball task with EEG before and after the intervention. Self-injury thought days and episode counts both fell significantly. The early brain response to negative images (mismatch negativity) shrank, suggesting softer automatic alarm, while the later response (P3) grew, suggesting stronger deliberate evaluation. Responses to positive and neutral images and task performance stayed stable. Bi and colleagues propose the two signals as candidate markers for tracking treatment response.
pmc-13291193:
Kubra Yildirim and co-authors test whether heavier bacterial loads distort tuberculosis drug testing, in a 2026 lab study. Susceptibility results guide TB treatment, and uneven sample preparation can mislead them. The team ran the agar proportion method on five reference strains and twenty-four patient isolates. Six inoculum sizes were compared, from the standard dilute reference up to thick suspensions. A commercial automated system provided a cross-check.

For most isolates, results at every load matched both the reference test and the automated system fully. Streptomycin told a different story in seven isolates. Those looked susceptible at the standard load yet resistant in the automated system and at heavier loads. Bigger samples thus exposed hidden resistance that the standard missed. The authors conclude that raising inoculum does not spoil testing and may help for some drugs. Labs could catch more streptomycin resistance with modest protocol changes.
pmc-13291293:
Soccer can break face bones and hurt eyes. Anaas M Mergoum leads a 2026 review of these injury patterns. Such harm can scar looks and threaten sight. Few past reviews covered face and eye harm together.

The cheek bone broke most often in soccer cases. Nose and jaw breaks came close behind. Head-to-head clashes caused most face breaks. Elbow hits were rarer but more likely to crack bone. Eye harm most often meant bruises and cuts. Blood inside the eye was also common. Ball strikes drove most eye cases. Small case sets limit firm claims, the authors warn.
pmc-13291493:
Steady selection on size may explain fly wing patterns at two scales. Haoran Cai presents a 2026 study of this evolution puzzle. Wing shape lines up closely across strains and species. Yet shape changes far more slowly than genes suggest.

That mismatch breaks a simple constraint story. Cai shows one-axis selection can solve the paradox. Selection on size alone drags other traits with it. Shared growth links make side traits move as one. Variety thus hides along a single line. Broad patterns may often reflect such simple selection. Complex adaptive landscapes may be rarer than assumed. The work reframes how to read aligned evolution patterns.
pmc-13291993:
Chaimae El Aoufir and colleagues report POEMS syndrome announcing itself through gut vein clots, in a 2026 case. POEMS is a rare disorder tied to abnormal plasma cells, named for its five feature groups. A 38-year-old woman arrived with acute belly pain and worsening limb nerve damage. Scans found clotting of the superior mesenteric vein reaching into the portal vein. Her liver and spleen were enlarged, fluid had gathered in her abdomen, and her bones showed sclerotic patches.

Blood tests revealed a monoclonal IgA lambda protein, the syndrome's signature antibody product. PET imaging lit up the bone lesions and armpit lymph nodes, with extra uptake in the heart. Heart ultrasound showed a stretched right ventricle and possible raised lung pressures. Taken together, the findings fit disseminated POEMS syndrome rather than a simple clotting disorder. The authors urge doctors to think of POEMS when odd vein clots arrive with systemic signs.
pmc-13292593:
Yaxian Yang, with co-authors, tests a 2026 herbal upgrade for broiler chickens hit by acute cold stress, which stunts growth and damages lungs. Sini Decoction is a classic warming formula; the team enriched it with ginger oil, rich in 6-gingerol, to make SNDO. Ninety-six day-old broilers split into control, cold-stressed, decoction, and enriched-decoction groups.

Both formulas eased lung damage and cell death, but the ginger version pulled ahead. Enriched birds gained weight faster with better feed conversion, showed lower lung wet-to-dry ratios, and carried less IL-1beta and IL-6 with more IL-10 in lung tissue. Barrier proteins occludin, ZO-1, and claudin-1 rose, oxidation eased, and lung microbes shifted toward Firmicutes, Faecalibacterium, and Lactobacillus. The authors credit the oil boost for the stronger protection.
pmc-13293393:
Zoe R Rand leads a 2026 study of killer whale use of Washington waters in the Salish Sea, comparing two types with unlike diets. Fish-eating Southern Resident whales are endangered, while Bigg's whales hunt marine mammals and face other pressures.

Sightings from 1978 to 2022 fed models of where each type appears over time. Bigg's presence climbed steeply across the period, while Southern Resident presence varied and fell in recent years, driven by two of the three family groups. Summer presence of residents dropped after 2016, and overlap between the types grew, above all in Puget Sound. Seasonal shifts may call for place-based care plans.
pmc-13293793:
Judith Jantine Willemijn van Beek and colleagues set out, in a 2026 protocol, a feasibility study of a wearable sensor that estimates bladder volume by electrical bioimpedance. People with spinal cord injury often cannot feel bladder fullness, yet must drain on fixed schedules that fit daily life poorly.

The three-phase study across centers will test the sensor first in people without cord injury, then against catheter measures in 60 participants with chronic injury, then in six hours of daily wear. Body fat and muscle activity effects will also be checked. A working wearable could let drainage follow actual fullness, not the clock.
pmc-13293893:
Torsak Tippairote and coauthors map how energy failure in cells is described across aging research in a 2026 evidence synthesis. Mitochondrial trouble covers many processes, from redox imbalance to weak repair, and links to resilience against stress. Rather than a fresh full review, the team recoded a curated set of 433 reports by aging hallmark, impairment stage, mechanism, and evidence tier.

Mapped work clustered in communication between cells, chronic inflammation, and nutrient sensing. Common labels were redox imbalance, substrate shifts, limited ATP supply, and faulty quality control. Adaptive, functional, and structural stages often overlapped in one domain instead of forming neat steps, which complicates simple stage models.
pmc-13294193:
Hua-jun Zhang and coauthors ask why CAR T cell therapy keeps failing in kidney cancer in a 2026 review. The treatment transformed blood cancer care, and kidney tumors respond to immune drugs and carry targetable markers, yet engineered cells give no lasting benefit. Blaming marker variety alone no longer fits the trial record.

Across studies, cells reach tumors poorly, tire fast, and vanish quickly, with little sign that marker loss drives escape. Three linked barriers stand out: shut-out vessels with low oxygen and suppressive myeloid cells, fierce metabolic competition, and missing support for lasting function. Future designs must improve homing, fitness, and oxygen tolerance while reshaping the tumor setting.
pmc-13294293:
Abdullah Ali Al Ameer leads a 2026 meta-analysis of heated chemotherapy washed inside the abdomen during ovarian cancer surgery. Standard care pairs major debulking surgery with systemic drugs, while the heated wash remains contested. Only randomized trials through February 2025 counted, drawn from three databases with quality checks by two reviewers.

Six trials held 773 patients, split between first-time and recurrent disease settings. In primary cancer, adding the heated wash improved overall survival in pooled hazard terms. Complication checks accompanied the survival pooling. Evidence quality was moderate, so the authors present benefit as real but still needing careful patient selection and safety tracking.
pmc-13294493:
Shensi Shen introduces a 2026 review collection on cancer metabolism and treatment openings. Tumor energy use, long a side topic, now sits at the center of cancer biology. Pathways span sugar burning, fat reshaping, nucleotide building, redox balance, iron handling, and mitochondrial motion, all tangled with growth signals, cell identity shifts, and the tumor neighborhood.

Hard problems remain: metabolic needs flip by tumor type, growth stage, and local crowding, and hardy persister plus stem-like cells exploit that flex to survive drugs. Death by ferroptosis can cut both ways. Multi-omics and spatial tools now map hunger cell by cell, suggesting paired attacks tuned to place and state.
pmc-13295093:
Ryan Nguyen and colleagues build a software tool that catches a common mass spectrometry mix-up, in a 2026 methods paper. When scientists profile thousands of small molecules at once, some compounds shatter inside the instrument before measurement, and those fragments can be mistaken for separate molecules. The team's tool, IMFrag, runs in a Jupyter notebook and uses ion mobility, a technique that sorts ions by how they drift through gas, to tell true compounds from in-source fragments.

Tests on tryptophan, an amino acid that fragments heavily, showed that identical fragments carry different mobility signatures depending on where in the instrument they formed. The same logic held across a varied set of small molecules, and the data revealed extras like dimers and protonation sites that standard analysis misses. Applied to human plasma, the framework helped resolve ambiguous candidates, and the authors offer it for pipeline use and library building.
pmc-13295293:
Chiara Del Prete and colleagues test antioxidant feeding in breeding stallions in a 2026 study. Intensive semen collection during the breeding season strains horse metabolism and can tilt the body toward oxidative damage. Hay loses many natural antioxidants in drying and storage, widening the gap.

Stallions given a supplement showed better overall antioxidant standing, with lower damage markers and stronger defences in testing. No harm appeared in general health measures during the trial period. Gut fermentation measures shifted as well, hinting that the supplement also touched intestinal microbe activity. The authors present feeding support as a practical management tool for the season.
pmc-13295493:
Saleh M Al-Sager and colleagues shine ultraviolet light on rice seed to fight fungi in a 2026 study. Seed-carried fungi spoil germination and weaken seedlings, while chemical seed dressings raise health and environment worries. Three Egyptian rice varieties were exposed for different lengths of time.

Light treatment cut fungal contamination clearly and lifted germination and seedling vigour over untreated seed. Thirty minutes of exposure gave the best balance, with longer sessions adding energy cost but no further gain. The authors offer the method as a residue-free, chemical-free way to raise seed quality and trim fungicide use in rice production.
pmc-13296693:
Cristina Cioti and colleagues describe lung cancers that grow in old tuberculosis scars in a 2026 study of past cases. Tuberculosis can heal yet leave deep scarring in the lung, and cancers at times grow in that scarred tissue. No agreed rules name this pattern, so the team looked for the traits that mark it.

Records of 844 lung cancer patients with signs of past tuberculosis were studied. Lasting lung damage, with dense scarring and hollowed areas, clustered close to the scar cancer profile. Symptoms, scan patterns, and tissue findings together sketched its form. Spotting the pattern could sharpen checks for people whose lungs carry such scars, the authors suggest.
pmc-13297093:
Maria Colomar-Roig and colleagues validate, in 2026, a home-grown lab workflow for testing ovarian tumours for a DNA repair flaw. That flaw guides use of platinum drugs and PARP inhibitors. Thirty high-grade cases went through the local partly automated pipeline and two commercial kits.

Results matched both commercial systems closely, with instability scores matching strongly, and the local workflow left fewer cases unclassified. Disagreements clustered at borderline scores near cut-offs, and mutation calls agreed within shared regions. Flexibility and local reruns add appeal. The authors back the workflow for routine molecular diagnostics in hospital laboratories.
pmc-13299193:
Nurses who staff front-line clinics in five lands in Europe back full health checks for old patients, but say their training lags the task. Evangelos C Fradelos and a team from many lands report that view in a 2026 talk-based study. Talk groups in Greece, Iceland, Finland, Estonia, and Latvia drew 29 nurses in all.

Three themes came out of the talks. Nurses prized checks that look at the whole person. They tried to hold set forms and free judgment in balance. And they asked for clear paths to build real skill. Set tools and team work won praise. Gaps in school training, thin staff and funds, and scant skill with unlike ways of life held the work back. The team urge school plans built on team work and hands-on skill.
pmc-13300193:
Falguni Khan and co-authors report a 2026 study turning an insect immune molecule into a targeted crop insecticide. EpOME is a lipid signal that calms insect immune responses late in infection, and its cell-killing effect suggested pest control potential. The team chemically altered the molecule, methylating one end and swapping its epoxide group for an alkoxide, to create a compound called AS56.

Earlier analog work had singled out AS56 as especially potent against moth and butterfly pests, so the study probed which structural features drive that activity, including double bond position and alkoxide shape. Applied to cabbage in field conditions, AS56 controlled beet armyworm and diamondback moth at levels similar to a commercial insecticide. The authors present the compound as a broad yet lepidopteran-specific option for pest management.
pmc-13300393:
N Drapier and colleagues examine the safety of ajmaline testing in Brugada syndrome in a 2026 study, asking whether mutations in the SCN5A sodium channel gene raise the danger. Drug challenge testing unmasks the syndrome's hidden electrocardiogram pattern but can provoke serious rhythms. The retrospective series covered 3,192 patients tested with ajmaline or flecainide at their centers between 1994 and 2025, with genetic results and complications recorded.

Sustained fast ventricular rhythms were rare overall yet clearly concentrated among mutation carriers. Ventricular fibrillation occurred in four patients, split between the carrier and uncertain-variant groups, with none among non-carriers. Adjusted analysis left mutation status, a longer PR interval, and a wider QRS pattern as independent predictors of complications. The authors conclude that carriers need heightened caution, while non-carriers face an extremely low risk during testing.
pmc-13300593:
M Hozman and colleagues measure left atrial function before and after pulsed field ablation for persistent atrial fibrillation, in a 2026 imaging study. The procedure isolated the pulmonary veins and ablated the posterior wall, raising the question of what that extra work costs the atrium. Twenty-nine patients in sinus rhythm received ultrasound strain imaging and magnetic resonance scans around the procedure, with follow-up at three months.

Both imaging methods agreed: reservoir and contractile strain fell right after ablation and stayed depressed at three months in the twenty-three patients who completed follow-up. Magnetic resonance imaging found new scar signal on the posterior wall in twenty-eight of twenty-nine patients. The conductive phase of atrial function drew less attention in the reported contrasts. The authors present the decline as a lasting mechanical price of the broader ablation set, relevant when weighing how much tissue to treat.
pmc-13301093:
Ruiqi Zhao and co-authors hunt for the shared genetic machinery behind primary sclerosing cholangitis and ulcerative colitis in a 2026 multi-omics study. The bile duct disease and the bowel disease travel together in most patients, implying common roots. The team layered genome wide association meta-analyses, tissue enrichment, spatial mapping, and single cell atlases, then cross checked candidate genes through five separate algorithms.

Tissue analyses kept pointing at intestine and immune tissues for both diseases. Natural killer cells emerged as the core shared effector cell type across the prioritization methods. One gene survived every algorithmic filter: STAT3, a signaling hub expressed widely across immune cells and spliced differently between tissues. Fine mapping flagged a high risk variant in its locus plus dozens of further independent signals. The authors name the natural killer cell and STAT3 pairing as a candidate therapeutic target for the comorbidity.
pmc-13301393:
Samantha Mairesse and co-authors review how well artificial intelligence diagnoses voice box disorders in a 2026 integrative review. The synthesis covered eighty-eight studies from 2015 to 2025, spanning acoustic features, recording databases, model architectures, and validation habits. Laryngeal disease is common and hard to pin down without specialist scopes, which is exactly the gap these systems promise to fill.

On the easy task, telling a healthy voice from a disordered one, accuracies ran high, roughly eighty-eight to ninety-nine percent inside the lab. Sorting disorders into categories proved much weaker, and performance sagged further when models faced outside data. The authors blame narrow vowel based databases, skewed class and demographic mixes, and validation that rarely leaves home. They propose a three level framework casting AI as decision support beside the clinician, not an autonomous diagnostician, and they call for multicenter data and honest external testing before deployment.
pmc-13301593:
J Diaz and co-authors hunt for predictors of response to left bundle branch area pacing in a 2026 cohort study. The series held 230 heart failure patients with ejection fractions under forty percent who received this approach to resynchronization between 2020 and 2025, followed a median of about 583 days. Super response was graded three ways, from a ten point ejection fraction gain up to recovery above fifty percent.

The strong definitions still caught plenty: about fifty-two percent gained more than ten points, thirty percent more than twenty, and about twenty-four percent crossed into normal range. That top group skewed female, started with higher ejection fractions and smaller, faster hearts, and showed quicker activation times during pacing. Super responders then suffered fewer heart failure hospitalizations and deaths, with the strongest definitions faring best. The authors argue these traits can flag super responders before implant, sharpening expectations and follow-up planning.
pmc-13301693:
Manesh A. Yewale and co-authors marry two metal oxides into a supercapacitor electrode in a 2026 materials study. Copper oxide stores charge but conducts poorly and degrades with cycling; zinc oxide conducts well yet stores little. The team grew both oxides and their composite hydrothermally, then ran the electrochemical gauntlet of voltammetry, charge discharge cycling, and impedance spectroscopy to see whether the pairing beats its parents.

The composite won, posting a specific capacitance of about 513 farads per gram against 416 for zinc oxide and 190 for copper oxide, with energy density near twenty-six watt hours per kilogram. Impedance showed solution resistance, and kinetic analysis found the mixed storage mechanism the authors wanted. Built into an asymmetric device against activated carbon, it delivered about forty-nine farads per gram and kept seventy-six percent of its capacitance after ten thousand cycles. The authors credit the heterointerface for charge movement and endurance.
pmc-13302293:
M Shurrab and colleagues document rural-urban gaps in atrial fibrillation care across Ontario in a 2026 population study, despite Canada's universal health coverage. Patients reaching emergency departments with this rhythm problem should receive a standard set of heart tests and treatments. The authors compared what rural and urban patients actually received within a year.

The cohort held more than one hundred thousand emergency patients seen between 2012 and 2022. Rural patients received fewer ECGs, heart ultrasounds, wearable rhythm monitors, and stress tests than urban patients on every measure. Rhythm-control procedures such as cardioversion and ablation were also less common in rural areas. Device implant rates, by contrast, matched closely. The authors call for system-level fixes to close the gap.
pmc-13303293:
Linli Cai and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, a plant-based nanoparticle treatment aimed at the oxidative damage driving diabetic kidney disease. High blood sugar floods kidney tissue with reactive oxygen, feeding inflammation and scarring that current glucose and pressure drugs only partly slow. Grape seed polyphenols were polymerised by enzymes into particles, then assembled with resveratrol.

In diabetic animal models, the platform restored kidney shape, structural proteins, and working function in a coordinated way, beyond brief chemical improvements. The particles stayed stable and tissue-friendly in testing. The authors argue that engineered natural polyphenols can rebalance the kidney's chemical environment for longer-term protection, a claim needing further development toward clinical use.
pmc-13303893:
Wongi Hong and co-authors fit, in a 2026 engineering study, a soft air-driven gripper with a flexible pressure sensor so it can judge the size of what it holds. Soft grippers handle odd shapes gently but usually cannot measure their catch. The sensor blends carbon nanotubes into silicone rubber, changing resistance as it is squeezed.

One recipe, with one percent nanotubes, proved most sensitive in the gentle pressure range where contact begins. When the gripper closed on balls of different diameters, the resistance patterns separated clearly by size, with larger balls registering at lower air pressures. Size could therefore be read from the pressure at first contact alone, without cameras. The authors aim at grippers that adapt their squeeze automatically.
pmc-13304693:
Gertrude Nembot Messah heads a 2026 study of root bark compounds from Pithecellobium dulce, a plant long used against diabetes. Which exact chemicals drive the effect, and how they act, had stayed poorly defined.

Bark extract was split into parts and cleaned step by step, yielding seventeen compounds. One proved new to science, and another had never been found in nature before. Bench tests measured antioxidant power and blocking of sugar-breaking enzymes, while computer docking checked fits against human targets. The authors flag that yeast enzyme results are early screening only and need human enzyme confirmation.
pmc-13305393:
Po-Feng Huang heads a 2026 meta-analysis asking whether wet suction beats dry suction when sampling solid lesions through endoscopic ultrasound. Filling the needle with saline first may yield cleaner, richer tissue for diagnosis under the microscope.

Seven randomized trials covering 784 patients and 1,566 samples were pooled under standard review rules. Wet suction cut blood contamination and raised cell yield in samples, with steady results across trials. Sample wholeness and overall diagnostic accuracy ran similar between methods. In the needle aspiration subgroup, though, wet suction diagnosed more accurately, favoring its use there.
pmc-13305693:
Yingqi Yao and Lin Zhu wrote a 2026 narrative review on what active people know, choose and buy in sports nutrition foods. They searched Chinese and international databases for work published between 2001 and 2025 on ingredients, needs during exercise, public understanding and product design.

After screening, 45 articles and four official documents shaped the synthesis. A persistent gap appeared between knowledge and use, with mistimed supplements, random product choice and loose dosing on the consumer side. Industry problems included look-alike products and weak standards. The authors propose joint education by experts, media and regulators, plus cleaner labels and more precise products.
pmc-13306293:
Onur Uysal recovered lost detail from simple cow collar signals in a 2026 livestock study. Collars using low-power radio compress motion into one number per interval, which separates walking from grazing but confuses resting with cud chewing.

Data held 9222 labelled records from 24 cows across four breeds. Adding past values, rolling summaries and a previous-behaviour feature lifted four-class macro-F1 from 0.647 to 0.94 in reported tests, with strong scores for each behaviour. The gain shows that time context can restore much of what heavy compression removes on remote pasture. The team says time aware tools can run on cheap collars in the field.
pmc-13306693:
Şükrü Mustafa Kaya tested bearing fault finders for motors when working conditions change in a 2026 study. Models that shine on random data splits can fail badly once speed or load shifts away from training settings.

Raw signal networks, image-based networks and a fused vibration plus current method were compared on Paderborn bearing data under one shared protocol. Simple early fusion gave the best balance of robustness and size in reported results, with only 73,891 parameters in the chosen model. Harder tests hiding whole bearing types still proved tough, marking the next frontier.
pmc-13306993:
Taylor Clark and colleagues map in 2026 the extra training states demand before pharmacists may prescribe hormonal contraception. Thirty-one states plus the District of Columbia allow pharmacists to prescribe, and each sets its own rules. The team checked pharmacy board sites, laws, rulebooks, and prescribing protocols.

Most states require training beyond standard schooling before prescribing begins. The rules were grouped by level and type, showing wide spread across the country. Extra training is typical when a trade gains new power, since rule-makers must assure skill and manage legal risk. The authors expect extra rules may fade as prescribing content enters normal pharmacy training. Drugstores could widen contraceptive access, above all in rural areas, and the paper shows what prep states now demand for that role.
pmc-13307193:
Chibuike Daniel Onyejesi reviewed quality improvement for child emergency care where resources run low in a 2026 narrative review. Weak buildings, staff shortages and broken supply chains drive avoidable harm and death in such settings, the authors argue.

Sources came from two databases plus World Health Organization and aid group guidance, covering trials, reviews and field reports. Included work reported better triage reliability and other safety gains from structured improvement efforts. Barriers and helpers for lasting change are weighed alongside telemedicine, task shifting and community worker roles. The team says gains held best where staff were trained and backed by clear local leads.
pmc-13307693:
Ning Jiang and co-authors weigh in 2026 the global, Asian, and Chinese burdens of malaria and dengue with Global Burden of Disease 2021 data. They compared rates of new cases and years lost to ill health from 1990 to 2021, and they built an index for the risk of cases entering China from abroad.

Dengue rates rose worldwide and in China, most of all in middle income settings, while malaria rates and lost years fell sharply. Dengue harm hit young children hardest for lost years, and women caught it more often than men in these data. Southeast Asia posed the top entry risk for both diseases. Forecasts see dengue still rising to 2030 while malaria keeps falling.
pmc-13309193:
Jiebo Chen, Jinzhong Zhao, and Caiqi Xu report in 2026 a no contact knee injury in a boy aged 16 years during a basketball game. A small bone flake on his scan gave away a torn front cruciate ligament. He landed, felt his knee twist in and bend, and heard a pop, with pain, swelling, and wobble at once.

Plain films showed a Segond fracture, a tiny pull off flake at the upper outer shin bone on the films. That flake rides with a torn front ligament in 75 to 100 percent of cases in past counts, and scans plus laxity tests confirmed the tear. Ligament rebuild plus standard rehab followed, and by six months he had begun no contact drills.
pmc-13309493:
Hodias S Oliveira Filho and colleagues describe a 2026 case of severe ear infection by worms in a stranded melon-headed whale in Brazil. Whales rely on hearing and echo location, so ear disease can threaten survival and may help explain strandings. The adult male whale was found dead on the coast.

Examination showed both middle ears packed with roundworms that blocked the ear canal and pressed on the eardrum. Tissue study found long-standing swelling and sores with worms inside the tissue. Microscopy named the worm as Stenurus globicephalae. Other findings included fluid in the belly and an empty gut. The authors judge the ear infection the main disease and a likely factor in the stranding and death.
pmc-13309793:
Hirotaka Matsumoto and co-authors map repeated protein patterns across protozoan parasites in a 2026 study. These single-celled parasites cause major diseases and increasingly resist drugs. Repeated stretches inside their proteins help them face hosts and dodge immunity, yet repeat layouts vary far beyond simple copies.

Standard repeat finders were joined by a new algorithm, Drepper, which scores how complex each repeat layout is. Grouping proteins by many repeat traits split them into clusters tied to parasite lineages. One high-complexity cluster centered on malaria parasites, while a low-complexity cluster centered on two other parasite groups. Trait, history, and shape analyses set the clusters apart. The authors offer the map for drug and vaccine target hunting.
pmc-13309993:
Ian M. Fearon and co-authors chemically analyse the aerosol of a leading disposable-style pod vape in 2026 against smoke from a reference cigarette. Seventeen harmful constituents were measured across four flavour variants. The work was funded by the product's manufacturer, a disclosure the authors make plainly in the abstract.

Most listed toxicants were undetectable or below quantification in the vape aerosol. Aldehyde levels ran roughly 99.6 to 99.9 percent below the reference cigarette under standard machine puffing. Metals such as cadmium and lead were also largely absent. The authors argue the results support harm reduction discussions for smokers who switch completely. Smokers face well documented disease risks from burning tobacco. Independent replication outside industry funding would strengthen confidence in these numbers for regulators weighing product standards.
pmc-13310193:
Manaka Moro and co-authors study sleep apnea during pregnancy in Japanese women in a 2026 cohort article. Breathing pauses in sleep are common in pregnancy, and repeated oxygen dips may affect fetal growth. Diagnosis-based data for East Asian pregnant women were scarce.

Questionnaires and a portable sleep monitor assessed 185 women at 28 weeks of pregnancy or later, and newborn growth was compared by apnea status. Apnea at the set threshold appeared in 15.7 percent of women, mostly at mild levels in the cohort. Women with apnea started pregnancy heavier, while their weight gain rate during pregnancy ran lower. The authors set out newborn outcome contrasts to guide screening talks.
pmc-13310393:
Sharan K Rai and co-authors ask rheumatoid arthritis patients what they want from a decision aid on biologic drugs in a 2026 interview study. Biologics can control the disease well, yet some patients hesitate over risks, costs, and injections. A decision aid tool exists to walk patients through the choice.

Fourteen patients across the United States who were starting or switching a biologic reviewed the aid, then took part in deep phone interviews. Five had never used a biologic before. Four themes covered how patients hunt for treatment facts, what in the aid helped, gaps it left, and broader needs such as peer contact. The authors use the themes to argue for aids that answer real daily questions.
pmc-13310493:
Huilin Li and co-authors test whether simple nutrition scores predict survival in advanced throat-area cancer in a 2026 study. The cancer, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, had returned or spread in these patients, who received an immune drug after at least two prior chemotherapy rounds. Nutrition shapes tolerance and outlook, yet its weight beside immune therapy was unclear.

A second look at a trial of 153 patients scored nutrition three ways at baseline, mixing blood proteins, cholesterol, and cell counts. Worse scores on each index tied to shorter overall survival in adjusted models of the analysis. Two indices also tied to shorter time without growth. The authors propose baseline nutrition scoring as a cheap guide for prognosis talks.
pmc-13310793:
Ghassan Habash and co-authors describe dental repair of a badly shrunken gum area near a front side tooth in a 2026 case report. Loss of an upper lateral incisor often collapses ridge bone and gum, which harms later tooth replacement. The tooth sat in a wrong place and had severe tissue loss around it.

Care used gentle removal, socket saving with coral graft material, and a turned gum flap to build height. A bonded bridge then filled the gap without an implant. Tissues stayed stable, with good looks and function over time. Planned soft tissue work can rescue looks even when bone loss is severe.
pmc-13310893:
Hongzhi Du and Liling Shi review swallowed foreign bodies in children in a 2026 hospital study. Coins, beads, and other objects can block or pierce the gut, and harm depends on type, place, and delay. The team mapped scan findings and risk factors for severe harm.

Records covered 71 children with 78 stuck sites from 2020 to 2025. Magnetic beads were the most common object and caused most gut holes. Water swelling beads always caused blockage. Ultrasound found clear objects that plain X rays missed. Sharp or corrosive items, delay past a day, upper gut site, and symptoms each raised harm risk. Most children needed surgery.
pmc-13311193:
Carlos E. Valdivia and José I. Orellana study nectar robbery in a Chilean shrub by native and invasive bumblebees in a 2026 field paper.
