Bees that pierce flowers to steal nectar are often blamed for cutting plant breeding success. In Desfontainia fulgens, robbed by a native bee and an invasive bee, true fitness costs were untested.

Robbery peaked when flowers were most plentiful, and pierced flowers held about nine times less nectar than intact ones, with sugar strength near unchanged. Bees visited more flowers per plant while robbing than while pollinating fairly. Seed output held steady when pollinators were present, while barred pollinators cut seeds sharply.
pmc-13311293:
Sirui Liu and colleagues report a 2026 rat study testing photoacoustic-ultrasound imaging for watching the placenta in preeclampsia. The method pairs light-based sound imaging with standard ultrasound to read oxygen and blood flow.

In the rat model, the combined imaging tracked placenta oxygen levels and tiny vessel flow over time. Its measures matched well with tissue markers of low oxygen and vessel density under the microscope. An odd dip and rise in the measures appeared on gestation days 10 to 12 in this work. The approach could one day let doctors watch placenta health without any cut or needle.
pmc-13311693:
Jamison P Geracci and co-authors review access to blood products before hospital arrival in a 2026 narrative article. Early transfusion saves lives in severe bleeding, yet few American ground ambulances carry blood.

The review joins clinical studies, guidelines, and system reports on prehospital transfusion. Only about 3 percent of the 11,450 eligible ground EMS units in the United States offer it, and access tracks local wealth more than patient need. Blocks include supply logistics, lack of steady payment, weak data systems, and a scattered national blood supply. The authors argue state-level coordination within trauma systems could widen access fairly.
pmc-13311793:
Sébastien Nicolas and colleagues, in 2026, present a field study on how grapevines answer water shortage across wine regions. Pinot noir and Chardonnay fruit from thirteen regions in Europe and Argentina supply the test.

Up to 256 grape juices from three vintages were checked for water status by carbon isotope reads and for hundreds of small molecules. Both varieties coped with wide water shortage, some matching a two-degree warming case for Burgundy. Chardonnay answered steadily across the range, while many Pinot noir markers faded under severe shortage. The contrast hints Chardonnay may weather hotter, drier seasons better.
pmc-13311993:
Peng Sun and co-authors give a 2026 study on deep learning to tell ankle avulsion fractures from harmless subfibular ossicles on X-rays. The two look alike but need different care.

The two-stage system first finds bone fragments near the ankle with a detection network, then classifies them with a tuned MobileNetV2 model. Data covered X-rays from 2121 patients at two centers. The classifier reached an accuracy area of 0.887 on outside test data, beating rival models and two experienced radiologists. Radiologists given the AI output and heat maps improved clearly, supporting first-visit triage use.
pmc-13312093:
Phannathat Tanthanapanyakorn and co-authors describe a 2026 participatory study that built and tested a holistic health program for inmate health volunteers in a Thai prison for young offenders. Nurses carry most care inside prisons, yet little evidence exists on training inmate volunteers to help, so the team designed the program together with the volunteers themselves.

One hundred well-behaved inmates took part as co-participants in ten training sessions over five weeks, covering physical, mental, social, and environmental health. Questionnaires given before, after, and one month later showed large gains in knowledge, attitudes, health practice skills, and data handling, all statistically significant. The authors conclude that the program strengthened the volunteers' ability to support health promotion and record keeping inside the institution.
pmc-13312493:
Simona Denaro and co-authors investigate, in a 2026 study, the enzyme PARP1 as a driver of neuropathic pain. Inflammation, oxidative stress, and metabolic derangement feed each other in this condition, keeping spinal glial cells in a reactive state. PARP1, which switches on after DNA damage, sits at the crossing point of all three.

They showed sustained PARP1 activity pushes cells toward death pathways and reactive gliosis, tightening the knot between inflammation and redox imbalance in the spinal cord. Blocking PARP1 eased touch-evoked pain and improved movement in injured rats. Protein and metabolite profiling showed broad recovery of disturbed signatures, especially around glutathione and amino acid handling. Cell-specific knockdown tied the effect causally to microglia priming.
pmc-13312793:
Ligia J. Dominguez and co-authors review, in a 2026 narrative synthesis, what lifestyle and diet can do to prevent cognitive decline and dementia. Against that backdrop, evidence suggests up to 45 percent of cases trace to modifiable factors spread across the life course.

The review weighs diet, physical activity, smoking, alcohol, sleep, and social and mental engagement, drawing on large cohorts, meta-analyses, umbrella reviews, and multidomain trials. Mediterranean, DASH, and MIND eating patterns associate with better cognitive outcomes, while unhealthy patterns raise risk. Their synthesis maps where prevention advice stands on firm ground and where it does not.
pmc-13313793:

Cultural sensitivities around intimate examinations shape who gets hands-on practice, in a country carrying one of South Asia's highest maternal death burdens. A split pattern emerged. Men scored higher on the written examination, averaging 70.46 against 68.69 in the reported comparison. The authors read the divide as an educational signature of cultural gender norms, with patient preferences channeling practical experience toward women. They tie the issue to simulation and culture-aware teaching in women's health.
pmc-13313993:
Noor Adil Abood and colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, whether peptides from buffalo milk whey can kill the drug-resistant bacteria lurking in dairy products. The products yielded 136 isolates spanning twelve species, spread fairly evenly across the three food types. Most isolates scored above the 0.2 index threshold that signals dirty origins. Resistance to ampicillin was prominent. Gene sequencing confirmed what the isolates were. The treated whey and several fractions then killed the resistant isolates strongly, backing whey peptides as natural protection for the dairy chain.
pmc-13314493:
Jue Wang and colleagues trace a rare skin disease from its first marks in a 2026 case report. Acquired reactive perforating collagenosis is often misread, most of all before its hallmark, collagen pushed out through the skin, shows plainly.

She also had long-standing type 2 diabetes and other metabolic ills, as the report notes. Close skin viewing of early red bumps showed subtle, repeatable signs unlike full-blown lesions, yet classic marks of perforation were missing even where the surface had begun to break. A biopsy of early bumps showed clumped, disordered collagen in the deep skin layer. The case gives doctors a pre-perforation stage to watch for, which could speed a correct call.
pmc-13314793:
Kaiying Hou and co-authors investigate, in a 2026 study, an unexpected villain in Parkinson's disease: p53, the famous tumor suppressor. The authors thus place p53 upstream of both hallmark pathologies, stimulating toxic aggregation while degrading mitochondrial quality control. The work suggests dialing p53 activity could be a therapeutic angle, handled carefully given its cancer-guarding day job.
pmc-13315093:
Christoph J Siepe and colleagues tally complications of full-endoscopic spine surgery in a study dated 2026. The one-portal scope method is a gentler swap for open or microscope surgery, yet forward-looking data on its risks were thin and past reports clash.

The team followed 304 straight-line patients having first-time scope surgery. The mix held 111 wide decompressions, 196 disc removals, and 30 side recess cleanouts, with some patients in more than one class, as the counts in the report show. Every complication and return to theater was logged, and traits tied to bad events were hunted. Honest tallies matter here, since scope fans may underreport harm. The cohort gives patients and surgeons a grounded risk picture for a fast-spreading method.
pmc-13315193:
Aubrey L. Galusha and many colleagues describe a workforce program in 2026 at the Wadsworth Center, the large state public health laboratory in New York. Their CARE effort aimed to rebuild links with schools, support staff learning, improve new-staff orientation, and set up a steering group to guide the work.

Over 18 months the program reached more than 1,000 students through outreach. Most orientation participants answered all check questions correctly, staff in learning groups used modules far more often, and the steering group finished 13 goals in its first term. Satisfaction was at least 70 percent for each activity. The authors offer the low-cost model for other laboratories.
pmc-13315893:
Chiamaka Nwachukwu and co-authors evaluated in 2026 a transition program that moves young people with sickle cell disease from child to adult care at Tulane's center in southern Louisiana. The move years are known for care gaps and poor outcomes, so a multidisciplinary clinic was built to bridge them.

Records covered 49 patients aged 18 to 25 years treated from 2021 to 2024, with 39 in the transition clinic and 10 who transferred directly. Only 12 clinic patients, or 30.7 percent, had completed transfer at analysis. Being at least 21, finishing high school, and attending five or more visits each linked strongly with successful transfer, while mental health diagnoses raised acute care use.
pmc-13316193:
Amy C. Ogilvie and colleagues used Colorado claims data in 2026 to learn who with Huntington's disease actually reaches specialty neurology care. Using the state all-payer database from 2019 to 2022, they compared patients seen by a movement disorders specialist with those seeing a general neurologist.

About half of patients, 49.9 percent, saw any neurologist in a given year, and a third, 33.8 percent, saw a movement specialist. No measured traits differed between the specialist and general groups. The authors say practice features and patient views on access need further study to explain the gap in specialty reach.
pmc-13316693:
Govinda Adhikari, Nischit Baral, and Dipendra Dahal studied 2026 national hospital data on stage D heart failure, the end stage of the disease, in the United States during 2019. Hard numbers on these sickest patients have been scarce.

They found 28,356 such hospital stays, with a mean patient age of 66 years and women making up 31 percent of the group. Kidney injury struck over half, one in four fell into cardiogenic shock, and 14 percent died during the stay in the reported figures. About eight percent returned within thirty days, most often for heart failure again, and stays averaged 11.59 days. The burden argues for better late-stage care planning.
pmc-13316993:
Magda Škaloudová and a large team report, in 2026, three new red pigments from a freshwater alga that lives in peat bogs. pmc-13317393: Naila Mir Baz and co-authors published a 2026 correction to their review of carotenoid building in Prunus fruit species. The notice is a correction only: back-matter sections including author contributions, funding, and data availability were mismatched during production. It states plainly that the science, findings, and conclusions stand unchanged, and the original article has been updated.
pmc-13318593:
Zhuoman Chen and co-authors report a 2026 retrospective study of carotid web, a shelf-like growth inside the neck artery that can trigger strokes, in Chinese patients. They reviewed CT angiography scans from 9,220 patients at one southern China centre between November 2005 and February 2021.

Webs were found in 34 patients, almost all men, giving a prevalence of 0.37 percent in the scanned group studied. Most webs sat at the common carotid artery split, were one-sided, and caused only mild narrowing, yet brain infarction was the commonest diagnosis among these patients. Wider artery diameter at the web and high blood pressure each tracked with infarction, underlining careful scan reading and tailored management.
pmc-13318993:
Pushpa Gehlot, Jyoti Yadav, and Tripta Jain review, in 2026, microbe-based biofertilisers for chilli, an important spice crop. Heavy chemical fertiliser use has degraded soils and disturbed ecology. Helpful root bacteria and fungi offer a greener route. The review weighs how they work together.

These microbes free nutrients by fixing nitrogen and dissolving phosphate. They also make plant hormones and enzymes that shape roots. Some fight crop diseases directly. Mixed bacterial-fungal teams outperform single strains, the evidence suggests. They improve nutrient availability, root structure, and stress tolerance at once. Practical topics include carriers, shelf stability, and field performance. The authors present combined biofertilisers as a path to productive, soil-friendly chilli farming.
pmc-13319693:
Joshua W Tashman, Chris Gorman and Emilio Madrigal describe, in 2026, an automated pipeline that prepares pathology slide scans for research while stripping out private information. Whole-slide images are huge scans of entire glass slides, prized for teaching and training algorithms. Privacy law requires careful removal of identifying details from images and their metadata, a task often done slowly by hand.

Their system converts scans from many proprietary formats into open de-identified formats using the DICOM standard. Requests arrive through a web portal, a human reviewer verifies each job, and finished archives are shared from cloud storage. Since November 2024 the pipeline has handled thousands of slide files from several scanner models. Processing scaled predictably with request and image size, avoiding rescanning.
pmc-13321393:
Chiara Molinelli and co-authors revisit a breast cancer trial to test a dosing question in a 2026 analysis. Dose-dense chemotherapy, given more often than standard, is standard for high risk early breast cancer without HER2. The GIM2 trial data were rechecked to see whether benefit differs between tumours scored HER2-zero and HER2-low.

Among 1243 patients followed for a median of 14.9 years, no interaction appeared between dosing benefit and HER2 score. Dose-dense treatment helped in both groups, with the clearest gain in HER2-zero tumours. The authors read the result as support for dose-dense care across the HER2-negative range, while noting the analysis was exploratory.
pmc-13321793:
Charlotte Charpentier leads a 2026 French national study of people with HIV starting lenacapavir treatment. Lenacapavir is the newest capsid blocking drug, approved in December 2022, but real world data were scarce. The retrospective study covered 96 people who began lenacapavir based care, with a median follow-up of 12 months.

Half were already virus suppressed at the start. At last follow-up, 94 percent of that group and 64 percent of those with active virus stayed below 50 copies per millilitre in blood tests. Treatment failure occurred in 8 people, and 12 people stopped the drug. The authors read the results as support for lenacapavir in heavily treated patients with advanced resistance.
pmc-13322093:
Hanka Brangsch and co-authors report a sheep disease case in Germany in a 2026 veterinary case report. Ovine contagious epididymitis, caused by Brucella ovis, must be reported in European Union states, yet cases are seldom logged and spread data are thin. Unlike other Brucella types, this germ does not infect people, so the stakes are animal health and farm income.

In 2024 the germ was isolated from two stillborn lambs in one flock, with antigen found in their airways and liver damage in one lamb. Genome reading tied the strain to other European lines. Two rams tested positive in blood checks, though flock abortion rates had not risen. The case shows how quietly the disease can circulate.
pmc-13322393:
Yoshihito Saijo and co-authors test a fully automated AI system for heart ultrasound in breast cancer care in a 2026 study. Cancer drugs can injure the heart, and a stretch measure called global longitudinal strain catches that harm early. Patients on anthracyclines or HER2 targeted therapy from 2022 to 2025 had scans at baseline and every 12 weeks.

A total of 92 patients and 456 scans were analysed, with strain read by two experts and by the AI system. AI values ran slightly lower, and agreement between methods was moderate. Harm was flagged in 31.5 percent of patients by experts and 34.8 percent by AI, at similar times. Automation may ease workload in cardio-oncology clinics.
pmc-13322493:
Isabela Cristina Monteiro de Lira and co-authors test whether poor sleep links to swallowing risk in older intensive care patients in a 2026 study. Screening at admission gathered 221 patients, and 66 met the study rules of age over 60 with clear thinking and stable condition. Sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, and swallowing risk were each scored with standard tools.

Women made up 65.2 percent of the group, and 30.3 percent were admitted for breathing problems in the study. Most reported good sleep, at 62.1 percent, while 16.7 percent scored at risk for swallowing trouble, with choking the top warning sign. Poor sleep was not clearly tied to swallowing risk in this sample.
pmc-13323293:
Hongkai Li, Xingyun Liu and Hanshu Zhang run three experiments on age and stroke misinformation on social media, reported in 2026. They used signal detection methods. The tests asked how age, past stroke experience and claim frequency shaped whether people accepted false stroke claims.

No main age effect appeared on judgement thresholds. Claim frequency alone did not shift them either. Younger adults with past stroke experience proved more likely to accept false claims. Such experience often came through family illness. Those readers used looser criteria for truth. Prompt corrective feedback made judgements more cautious, above all in that group. Repeated feedback also improved task accuracy one week later in the third experiment.
pmc-13323593:
Tazeen H Jafar leads an interview study of hypertension care barriers in two rural North Carolina counties, from 2026. Blood pressure deaths run higher in rural areas than in cities. The gap is worst in the southeast, yet local barriers and fixes are poorly mapped.

Interviews with 62 community and health system informants covered Pamlico and Robeson counties. A standard framework sorted barriers by setting. Outer barriers covered money strain, weak insurance, food hardship and transport gaps. Poor digital access also came up. Clinics faced staff gaps and poor contact between teams. Residents reported low health literacy, chronic stress and mistrust. Informants backed co-planned task-sharing with community outreach and help with healthy food costs.
pmc-13324293:
Shangbin Kao and team made a highly sensitive blood test for finding IgA nephropathy, a kidney disease that still depends on invasive biopsy. Their 2026 study built a time-resolved glow immunoassay around MH33, a new monoclonal antibody against galactose-deficient IgA1, the disease's key marker. Current serologic markers, including that IgA1 form itself, have limited test accuracy, leaving biopsy as the standard.

Surface plasmon resonance showed MH33 recognizes a distinct glycoepitope on the IgA1 hinge region, different from the epitope seen by the established KM55 antibody. The team tested the MH33 assay in healthy controls, non-IgA kidney disease controls, and patients with the disease. Because antibodies against distinct glycoepitopes may capture different disease-linked subsets of circulating marker, the authors argue that MH33 could complement current tests and sharpen noninvasive testing.
pmc-13324493:
Zhixin Zheng and colleagues pin down a driver of lung adenocarcinoma spread in a 2026 study of the protein S100A10. The protein is abundant in this lung cancer and tracks with poor patient outcomes.

Lab and animal work shows S100A10 switches on the JUND and TNC pathway, pushing cells through epithelial-mesenchymal transition, a change that helps tumors invade and spread. The team also singled out a small molecule, [D-Leu-4]-OB3, that binds S100A10 directly. That compound curbed cancer growth and spread in cell tests and in living models. The results nominate S100A10 as a drug target for a cancer where many patients still lack workable targeted options.
pmc-13325993:
Yili Jin and team made a nucleic acid carrier that brings resveratrol to the retina to fight both abnormal vessel growth and inflammation. Their 2026 study targets retinal neovascular ills such as retinopathy of early birth and diabetic retinopathy, which threaten vision through harmful vessel growth and chronic inflammation. Current anti-VEGF drugs mainly attack vessel growth, control it poorly, and require repeat dosing.

The team loaded it into four-sided frame nucleic acids, a body-safe, stable carrier that gets in well and boosts the drug's ocular delivery and activity. In hypoxia-induced retinal vessel-growth models, the construct markedly reduced lesion area, vascular leakage, and immune cell infiltration. Mechanistically, it suppressed HIF-1 signaling and inhibited the p38 MAPK and NF-kB p65 pathways. The authors present the platform as a promising dual-action treatment for retinal vessel disease.
pmc-13326893:
Anna Behler and colleagues studied how gaze adapts when movie viewers lose the soundtrack and must rely on captions. Their 2026 eye-tracking study had participants watch a 20-minute movie with audio alternating on and off. It tested whether more caption use meant more frequent switching between captions and scene, longer unbroken reading, or both. Closed captions, once only for hearing-impaired audiences, now add a second visual stream to a multisensory experience.

Viewers integrated both streams by frequently shifting gaze between captions and scene. Without sound, the balance shifted through more frequent switching, not longer reading: increased caption engagement reflected more frequent sampling of captions rather than extended reading. Caption eye movements were more consistent and focused than on the scene, and those differences held with or without sound. Dialogue presence and emotional content also shaped caption engagement, showing how viewers adapt to missing audio by sampling text more often.
pmc-13327393:
Narayana Manjunatha and many co-authors put forward a 2026 proposal for a World Psychiatry Day. Psychiatry joins body, mind, and social science in treating mental disorders, yet public campaigns speak mostly of mental health in general. The authors argue the specialty itself stays poorly seen and its role in medicine stays unclear.

They propose marking the day each year on February 20, the birth date of Johann Christian Reil, who coined the term Psychiatrie in 1808. A fixed day could strengthen the field's identity, link mental care with general health care, cut stigma, and support policy and research. Other specialties already use such days, and the authors say psychiatry should stand as a third main branch of medicine.
pmc-13327893:
Vipul D Yagnik, Prema Ram Choudhary, and Pankaj Garg review artificial intelligence for anal fistula care in a 2026 article. Fistula anatomy is intricate, recurrence is common, and treatment must protect continence, leaving standard routes limited. The authors sort published AI work by the IDEAL stages used to judge surgical innovation.

Four areas emerged: imaging before surgery, help during operations, outcome prediction, and wider anorectal testing such as pressure studies. MRI and CT deep learning models reported strong diagnostic results in early studies, mostly at proof-of-concept to exploration stages. Small samples, thin outside checking, and workflow fit remain barriers, so the authors urge staged, careful adoption rather than quick rollout.
pmc-13327993:
Tinghui Zhang and co-authors review a paired sensing method for studying brain-muscle coupling in a 2026 article. Near-infrared light sensing tracks brain activity while surface electrodes track muscle signals, and together they promise a fuller view of real movement control and rehabilitation. The authors sum up principles, coupling measures, and uses.

Healthy movers show stable, repeatable links between motor and sensory cortex areas and their matching muscle groups, with link strength tracking accuracy and force. In nerve diseases, coupling weakens and rhythms break while other cortex areas overwork in compensation, and chronic pain shows its own tangle of brain control and muscle firing. Coupling laws differ by group, guiding tailored rehabilitation checks.
pmc-13328093:
Victoria Olivé and co-authors survey burnout among medical residents after the COVID-19 pandemic in a 2026 single-center study. An anonymous online questionnaire in 2023 drew 197 residents, a 43.5 percent response, and results were set against an independent 2018 survey using the same tool at the teaching hospital.

Burnout affected 28 percent of residents, with no gender gap, and ran higher in surgical fields and later training years. Role strain, behavior stress, job satisfaction, and training year all raised burnout odds, while supervision and role conflict explained much of the variation in felt health. Compared with before the pandemic, work variety and attention effort had worsened, showing strain that outlasted the emergency years.
pmc-13329793:
Yixin Sun and colleagues study school burnout among Chinese primary pupils in a 2026 report. Harsh parenting, such as rejection or overprotection, may feed burnout, and the team asks whether inner resilience carries that effect. Pupils in grades 4 to 6 at a public school in Hebei took part, with 853 students included.

Children rated each parent's behaviour, their own resilience, and burnout on standard scales. Harsh parenting from both fathers and mothers linked to more burnout and lower resilience. Resilience partly carried the effect for both parents, at closely alike shares of the total in the reported models. Building resilience could thus protect pupils no matter which parent's style is in view, the authors suggest.
pmc-13330793:
Sumanjit Midha and team linked implant placement factors to prosthetic failure in full-arch fixed false teeth. Their 2026 retrospective matched case-control study used records from January 2020 to December 2024 in a dental department. It studied how implant angulation, anteroposterior spread, and cantilever extension influence stress spread and prosthetic failure. Good full-arch rebuild needs implants to last and long-term false-tooth stability and bite harmony, yet false-tooth problems remain big.

Cases showed much greater mesiodistal tilt, buccolingual tilt, up-down implant place, distal arm length, and arm-to-spread ratio than controls, with all gaps significant. Greater front-to-back spread and inter-implant distance shielded against false-tooth failure. The team concludes that increased implant tilt and arm extension raise false-tooth failure risk, while greater spread and distance improve stability. Exact false-tooth-driven placement may reduce breakdowns and improve long-term false-tooth success.
pmc-13331693:
Tomoyuki Gurita and co-authors report a 2026 endoscopy case of a 71-year-old man with a small surface cancer in the mid esophagus. Scarring from earlier chemoradiotherapy had narrowed his throat so much that standard scopes with attachments could not pass.

The team instead used gel immersion mucosal resection, filling the view with gel and snaring the 10 mm lesion out in one piece through a slim 7.9 mm scope. The whole procedure took 18 minutes with no adverse events. Tissue study showed squamous cell carcinoma limited to the mucosa with clear margins. The authors offer the gel method as a workable fallback when dissection or cap-assisted resection cannot be done.
pmc-13331993:
Ritu M Ramamurthy and colleagues test 2026 safety and efficacy of liver-directed gene therapy using lab-grown human liver tissue. Hemophilia A, the focus of the therapy, stems from low factor VIII activity and can cause life-threatening bleeds. The team built tissue equivalents from the main liver cell types at ratios that mirror real liver structure and function.

They tested two virus serotypes, AAV5 and AAV3b, carrying a marker gene, plus AAV5 carrying an engineered factor VIII gene. AAV5 gave higher marker expression, and both serotypes entered lining and star-shaped cells more readily than liver cells or Kupffer cells. Both also shifted liver function markers, and gene readouts flagged inflammation and liver stress pathways. The platform offers a human-based way to probe vector safety before trials, without relying only on animal models.
pmc-13332793:
Luís M Cardoso dos Santos and Magnus Bäck wrote a 2026 editorial on whether inflammation-resolving molecules can serve as heart disease biomarkers. They comment on a study of resolvins measured around heart surgery. Omega-3 fats have long been studied for heart protection. Yet big trials gave mixed results and hinted at more atrial fibrillation, a paradox needing explanation.

The body converts omega-3 fats into molecules that actively switch inflammation off. These include resolvins, maresins, protectins, and lipoxins. In the study discussed, patients who developed atrial fibrillation after surgery showed lower predicted resolvin D2 but higher resolvin D1. The pair moved in opposite directions despite sharing most of their production path. The editorial asks whether single agents can act solo or must be read as an orchestra. It lays out step-wise ways to profile whole mediator families rather than single members.
pmc-13333293:
Francesco Emma and colleagues map a 2026 phenotypic spectrum for HNF4alpha-associated Fanconi renotubular syndrome. Fanconi renal tubular syndrome type 4 is an uncommon, dominant disease passed down in families, caused by gene changes touching the arginine spot at position 85 of HNF4A. The team gathered worldwide, doctor-reported, anonymous data via a European rare kidney disease network and other sources, with a focus on symptoms, treatment, and chronic kidney disease progression.

Data covered 25 patients, 24 carrying the classic p.R85W variant and one a new p.R85L variant. Early births and oversized births were frequent, and congenital hyperinsulinism with postnatal low blood sugar appeared in fourteen of twenty-one patients. The middle age at renal Fanconi syndrome diagnosis was about one and a half years. Common features included failure to thrive, rickets, nephrocalcinosis, and chronic kidney disease before age ten.
pmc-13333393:
Yafei Guo and colleagues present a defined case report in 2026 of a blood cancer that broke the pattern for its family. Cancers with PDGFRB gene rearrangements typically flood the blood with eosinophils, but this patient had almost none of that signature.

A 60-year-old man with no symptoms showed high white cell counts and low platelets at a routine check. His marrow was packed with maturing granulocytes without blasts, and his blood was dominated by neutrophils with only mild eosinophilia. Chromosome study found a t(5;14) swap. RNA sequencing revealed the engine: an in-frame fusion joining CCDC88C exon 12 to PDGFRB exon 11, plus an ATM frameshift mutation. Low-dose imatinib at 200 mg daily normalized his counts within one week, and the remission held through follow-up. The authors say RNA sequencing deserves a place in odd presentations, because it can find drug-targetable fusions that other tests miss.
pmc-13334793:
Lisanne Duizer and colleagues test 2026 whether app ease of use influences post-birth weight loss in the INTER-ACT trial. The secondary analysis examined whether perceived app ease of use influences post-birth weight loss, and whether app use, drive, and lifestyle uptake carry that effect. Dutch-speaking women aged eighteen or older who delivered a single infant and exceeded Institute of Medicine pregnancy weight gain guidelines were recruited from May 2017 through April 2019 across six Flemish hospitals.

The analysis included 138 women from the INTER-ACT program arm. At six months post-birth, women completed a process review survey assessing app ease of use with the system usability scale, perceived drive, and perceived uptake of lifestyle recommendations. Pearson links and parallel middle-step analyses, adjusted for maternal age, parity, and pre-pregnancy factors, test whether a usable app actually helps new mothers lose weight.
pmc-13336493:
Hui Zhao and colleagues study 2026 SC CO2-induced porous MXene films for EMI shielding and IR stealth. Lightweight and flexible porous MXene films have emerged as hopeful picks for EMI shielding and IR stealth. However, current foaming methods remain a challenge in keeping the built-in traits of MXene while reaching eco-friendly foaming.

SC CO2 foaming tech is used for green foaming of dense MXene films without harming the built-in shape of the MXene nano-sheets. The phase shift of SC CO2 sparks bubble birth and growth, well opening the stacked MXene nano-sheets into a porous shape. This strategy is widely usable and can also be spread to other 2D films, such as graphene oxide. Thanks to highly-conductive porous frame, the foamed porous MXene film shows an EMI shielding power of about 73.2 dB, which is 21 percent higher than that of plain MXene films.
pmc-13336593:
Estela Carvalho de Sousa, Monica Melchio, and Malgorzata Mikulska review drug-resistant infections in a 2026 article on stem cell transplant care. Recipients have weak immune defenses, and resistant bacteria are infecting them more often. Rates vary widely by place, and these infections raise illness and death.

New drugs, including fresh beta-lactam pairs and cefiderocol, now widen choices for hard Gram-negative infections, the authors note. Much proof still comes from general patients, since transplant recipients are often left out of trials. The review weighs when to combine drugs, when cefiderocol fits, and how shorter, stepped-down courses can help. Careful drug use remains central to protecting this fragile group.
pmc-13336793:
Junhong Yu and colleagues showed in 2026 how packing lead halide perovskite nanocrystals into supercrystals speeds the cooling of hot charge carriers. Slow cooling helps solar cells but hurts light emitting devices, and past tuning tricks often damaged the material or added competing effects. The team used long range electronic coupling between crystals instead.

Transient absorption tests found supercrystals cooled hot carriers twice as fast as lone nanocrystals at low carrier density, near the limit set by phonon theory. Stronger shared electronic states explain the gain. The result gives device makers a cleaner knob for balancing solar and light emitting performance in perovskite optoelectronics.
pmc-13336893:
Madiha Habib and co-authors review nanomaterials for allergy care in a 2026 article. Allergic diseases such as food allergy, asthma, and eczema affect an estimated 10–30% of people worldwide, driven by skewed immune responses and IgE antibodies. Current tests vary in accuracy and cannot predict real reactions well.

Immunotherapy is the only treatment that tackles causes, yet it demands frequent doses and carries reaction risks. The review covers nano-based tests that sharpen IgE detection and cell assays, plus nano-delivered therapies that meter allergens and tune immunity more safely. It also weighs the hurdles blocking clinic use, from safety proof to scale-up. Tiny carriers could make allergy care both more precise and easier to stick with.
pmc-13337093:
Fanrong Liu leads a large 2026 team exposing a shield that keeps bone cartilage tumors drug-resistant. Chondrosarcoma resists chemotherapy, and ferroptosis, an iron-driven death from fat oxidation, offers a possible way through. The shield protein REG gamma was high in tumors and tied to poor patient outcomes.

REG gamma destroys a partner, WDR6, without the usual tagging route, which mutes a ferroptosis pathway run by the STK11-AMPK axis. Removing REG gamma let fat oxidation and death signals rise. A blocker of the REG gamma proteasome partner, RLY01, suppressed tumor growth and made cells sensitive to cisplatin again in models. Hitting this shield could revive standard chemotherapy for a stubborn bone cancer.
pmc-13337393:
Victor Cardoso Oliveira and colleagues measure how potholes and cracks raise car emissions in real city driving in a 2026 study from Fortaleza, Brazil. A portable emissions system logged exhaust second by second while a windshield camera filmed road obstacles once per second across five urban segments.

A detector trained on 1,812 labeled images with 3,158 marked obstacles from a pool of 44,175 road images in the project scanned the routes. Segments with more obstacles showed higher emission rates for carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and nitrogen oxides. Rough surfaces force braking and acceleration that burn extra fuel. The work gives city managers a pollution argument for road repair beyond comfort and safety.
pmc-13337493:
Nadezhda Azbukina and colleagues built a single cell atlas in 2026 to improve lab grown models of the midbrain and hindbrain. Those brain regions coordinate movement, senses, and cognition, and their failure underlies many neurological disorders. Organoids promise a window on development and disease, but existing recipes produce limited cell types.

Pairing single cell RNA and chromatin data, the team mapped cell types and control circuits in midbrain and hindbrain organoids. A screen of patterning signals then found doses that expand the models, including conditions yielding medulla and cerebellum neuron types. The atlas and screen give researchers a guide for engineering region specific brain organoids for disease modelling.
pmc-13337693:
Michele Poletti, Antonio Preti, and Andrea Raballo set out a 2026 framework for spotting severe mental illness risk much earlier. Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depression are viewed here as conditions rooted in brain development. Warning signs may appear long before clear symptoms, as subtle thinking and behavior changes.

Current high-risk services mostly catch the late, near-onset phase, and only some people they flag go on to develop illness. The authors argue for developmental high-risk criteria that track earlier premorbid features instead. Such criteria could widen early detection beyond help-seeking clinics. They could also help separate paths that lead to illness from those that do not.
pmc-13338693:
Qi Zhang and colleagues gathered ten cases of late-onset sepsis from Clostridium ramosum in preterm infants, in a 2026 case series with a literature review. The gut bacterium rarely causes invasive disease in newborns, and preterm cases were almost unreported. The team reviewed infants admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit from birth between 2022 and 2024, plus published cases from 2010 to 2025.

All ten infants were preterm, with a median gestational age of 32 weeks plus 3 days, and most showed feeding intolerance and bloody stool. Eight in ten had necrotizing enterocolitis, and all received meropenem-based treatment, with four in ten needing surgery. No infant died of the acute infection, a reassuring outcome that still calls for vigilance in fragile newborns.
pmc-13339193:
Jinyan Lei and colleagues compare stand-in measures of insulin resistance for multiple heart-metabolic diseases in a 2026 study. Having two or more such diseases at once is rising worldwide. Twelve simple index formulas were tested head to head in survey data.

The group drew 9,756 adults from United States nutrition surveys spanning 1999 to 2020 as reported. Among them, 4,383 people, or 44.9 percent in the reported share, had multiple cardiometabolic diseases. Every index rose in steps alongside disease odds after adjustment. Curve and accuracy analyses ranked which cheap blood-based scores best flag people carrying several conditions at once.
pmc-13339893:
Mary Rao and Sandeep Tamber studied Salmonella risk in 2026 in tahini paste and sauces, a low moisture food tied to 20 salmonellosis outbreaks since 1995 with over 1,600 cases. When tahini paste is mixed into high moisture foods such as hummus, bacteria can grow and risk rises. The team tested three naturally contaminated pastes and tracked growth under varied preparation and storage.

Naturally contaminated paste carried low Salmonella levels near 0.4 most probable number per 100 grams, with no link to background microbes. Sauces made from spiked paste showed how diluent and storage shape growth. The findings guide safer recipes, storage times, and controls for tahini based foods.
pmc-13340693:
Rebuilding a shinbone with the patient's own recycled bone is described by Viet Nhuan Ngo and colleagues, in their 2026 case report. The 36-year-old man had adamantinoma, a rare slow-growing bone cancer, forming a 20-cm lesion in the middle of his left tibia.

Surgeons removed a 25-cm segment, froze it in liquid nitrogen at −196°C for 20 minutes, then thawed, washed, and reimplanted it. Fixation combined a nail and plate, helped by bone cement, hip bone graft, and a calf muscle flap. Only two earlier cases used this method for adamantinoma. The authors report good cancer and function outcomes, with lifelong checks still required.
pmc-13341493:
Infected fat cells can seed the liver with virus, in a 2026 study by Cinthya Alicia Marcela López and colleagues. Human fat cells grown from stem cells were infected with the Wuhan strain of SARS-CoV-2, which entered through surface ACE2 and replicated productively.

Infected fat cells swelled, secreted more IL-6, shifted their leptin-to-adiponectin balance, and stored extra lipid droplets. Fluid from these cultures made liver cells accumulate fat and switch on scarring programs. Blocking spike protein or ultraviolet-inactivating the virus erased the effect, proving live virus, not just fat cell signals, drove it. The pathway may help explain worse COVID-19 in obesity.
pmc-13341593:
Two gene variants raise newborn jaundice risk in a 2026 case-control study by Wen-Fang Wang and colleagues in Haikou, China. The study compared 210 babies with hyperbilirubinemia against 195 healthy newborns admitted between January 2024 and January 2025, genotyping seven sites in the UGT1A1 and SLCO1B1 genes.

Cases included more preterm births, at 16.9% in cases versus 9.5% among the healthy controls. Risk alleles appeared about twice as often in cases, for example UGT1A1 rs4148323 at 22.14% in cases versus 11.79% in the control group. Both genes govern bilirubin handling, one by processing it and one by transporting it. Combined and cumulative allele analyses explored how risks stack in this subtropical population.
pmc-13341793:
Janet E. Burke and colleagues reconstructed ocean oxygen zones in 2026 during the Miocene Climatic Optimum, 14.7 to 17 million years ago, the last time atmospheric carbon dioxide stayed consistently above today. Dissolved oxygen is generally falling as global temperatures rise, with broad implications for carbon cycling and marine animal habitats. The team used a foraminiferal iodine redox tracer to map oxygen deficient zones and nearby low oxygen waters.

Pacific lowest oxygen waters were confined to a narrow band from about 10 degrees north to 20 degrees south, substantially contracted versus today. Atlantic oxygen deficient zones, minor today, showed a different spatial pattern in the warm past. The ancient warm world offers a test bed for how ocean oxygen may shift under future warming.
pmc-13343993:
Ottavia Romoli and co-authors test what gut microbes do for mosquito larvae beyond handing over vitamins in 2026. Aedes aegypti larvae need living microbes to grow, so the team stripped the microbes away and profiled small molecules in larvae and dissected guts hours later.

Germ-free larvae showed sagging levels of energy cycle and nitrogen waste compounds, plus less gut cholesterol and altered long-chain fatty acids. Adding back a little cholesterol slightly improved survival to adulthood, while heavy doses harmed development. Larvae fed bacteria that cannot burn fatty acids also fared poorly. Microbes, the team concludes, underpin energy making, waste handling, and sterol balance, likely through the vitamins they supply.
pmc-13344593:
Qun Zhang and co-authors build a real-time beam watching platform for the High Energy Photon Source in 2026. Fourth-generation synchrotrons squeeze beams brighter and smaller, demanding fast, trustworthy alignment checks, so the team tied fluorescent-target imaging to the facility's control system with synchronized cameras and online analysis.

Thirteen cameras ran steadily together, extracting beam parameters in under 20 milliseconds with total delay below 50 milliseconds. Data flows run through the EPICS areaDetector framework with a Mamba Data Worker handling management. The platform supports daily beamline tuning today and points toward data-driven optimization at other large light sources tomorrow.
pmc-13347693:
Modou Ndongo, Ibrahima L. Sarr, and Sidy M. Seck write a letter, issued in 2026, flagging kidney failure patterns near gold mining in southeastern Senegal. A new dialysis unit at the regional hospital in Kedougou opened in May 2023, letting the authors map where patients starting long-term dialysis between August 2023 and August 2025 had come from.

Of 59 starters, 38 lived inside the region. Half of those came from the Kedougou area while 42.1 percent came from Saraya and only 7.9 percent from Salemata in the reported split. Mining communes such as Bembou supplied more patients than their population share would predict, so the letter calls for full study of mining links rather than claiming proof.
pmc-13347893:
Alexandra Munns and colleagues ask whether drive and confidence foretell sticking with home exercise in older adults, in a 2026 study. Eighty-eight adults with a mean age of 67.2 years followed a 26-week home program, wearing heart monitors so adherence came from real effort minutes. Grouping by motivation type and self-belief gave two profiles.

One group was keen and highly confident while the other was middling on both. Yet sticking rates were high and near equal, at 129 percent and 116 percent of set volume in the reported means. Fitness, grip strength, and flexibility gains also matched across groups, which suggests set home programs can carry less driven starters further than expected.
pmc-13350193:
Ruyue Deng and colleagues studied how a modified starch rescues irradiated fresh rice noodles in a 2026 food science analysis. Irradiation extends noodle shelf life but chops starch chains, changing texture and cooking behaviour.

Adding hydroxypropyl starch at several levels was compared, and 6 percent gave the most balanced result. The additive enlarged starch molecules, improved order and crystallinity, and raised peak thickness on cooking, while easing other traits. Chain pattern analysis tied good pasting behaviour to a balanced mix of short and long starch branches. Tuning one ingredient could let producers keep irradiation's shelf-life gains without losing noodle quality.
pmc-13351693:
Yang Li and co-authors wrote in 2026 about family-integrated care in child intensive care. The piece moves from concept to practice. Family engagement backs children and parents through critical illness. Post-intensive care syndrome in children gives one rationale for involvement. Yet family-integrated care extends far past it.

Hunting five bases with focus on work from 2015 onward, the review sums up many uses. These span bedside participation, talk, shared picks, rehab, psychosocial backing, and transition planning. Reported gains, blocks, and future priorities are also covered. The review helps teams move from family-centred talk to workable routines. Parents can then join as partners with no harm to safety or workflow.
pmc-13354993:
Megan Clemens and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how problem-based learning is used in family medicine residency training across four countries. In this method, learners work through a clinical case in a group, raise questions, and build a solution, rather than sit through lectures. The team screened six databases and kept 12 studies.

Programs used the method alone, as an add-on, or mixed with lectures, and groups often mixed specialties and seniority. Learners liked the sessions and felt they knew topics better, yet tests of knowledge showed no clear gain. Hints of gains for behavior and patient care were thin. The authors call for stronger studies on where the method fits best.
pmc-13355193:
Geun-Hee Cho and co-authors compared in 2026 the official lab methods of Korea, China, and Japan for measuring vitamin E esters in food additives. These esters fortify foods and guard against spoilage, so exact measures matter for rules and quality. The team ran each country's method and checked it against shared standards.

All methods passed the checks, but they differed in sensitivity, recovery, and exactness. A titration method gave the tightest results, while a gas-based method varied the most. Error margins ran from about 5 to 10 percent, traced to steps like calibration and sample prep. The study shows why cross-country checks help keep food standards aligned.
pmc-13355693:
Lan Lan and co-authors report in 2026 that tuning the gap between two gene switches in a virus-based production system greatly improves gene therapy making. Making adeno-associated virus in insect cells often yields many empty shells with no gene cargo, due to unbalanced protein output. The two switches sit back to back and interfere with each other.

The team found that a gap of a precise length boosted both switches beyond separate controls, with the best result at one sharp length. Built into the production system, genome copying tripled and empty shells fell from about 85 percent to about 20 percent. Cell infection strength stayed intact, giving makers a simple design rule.
pmc-13356493:
Mabel Moreno and co-authors explored in 2026 three atomic-scale methods to add zinc oxide to chitosan, a natural polymer used in medical materials, to build multifunctional surfaces. The methods lay down zinc in vapor or plasma steps, each shaping the surface in a distinct way. Checks with imaging and X-ray tools confirmed even zinc spread in all three.

One method smoothed the surface, another raised a rough, high-area texture with the finest crystals. The plasma method gave the highest surface energy and swelling. In cell tests, growth matched controls, and germ killing was tuned by method. Implants in animals spurred blood vessel growth with a balanced immune response.
pmc-13357093:
Yuxin Han and co-authors review in 2026 what is known about tiny plastic particles and cancer. Microplastics and nanoplastics turn up in water, soil, air, food, and human tissue samples. Evidence from cells, animals, and small human studies links them to several solid tumors and some blood cancers, through routes like cell stress, long-term inflammation, and DNA damage.

Yet direct proof that the particles alone cause human cancer is still lacking, and lab particles differ from aged, chemical-coated ones in the real world. The authors favor a cautious view: the particles more likely modify tumor behavior than start it, and better methods are needed.
pmc-13358793:
Jianfei Lin and co-authors present a 2026 study on spotting who will develop serious COPD, a chronic lung disease. Many people at high risk still show normal results on standard breathing tests, so the window for early action is missed. The team built a model that reads the whole lung on CT scans for early warning signs.

They used records from 806 patients at two hospitals, treated from 2021 to 2025. Software cut out the lung tissue on its own, then pulled both measured features and deep learning patterns from the images. A combined chart joined these with patient facts. Catching high-risk people early could focus quitting support and treatment where it counts.
pmc-13358993:
Yohei Yatagai and co-authors share a case and a question about sarcoidosis in older patients in a 2026 letter. Sarcoidosis can settle into lasting quiet, called clinical remission, where signs vanish without treatment. A prior study found remission less common when the disease starts late in life. The authors describe a 61-year-old woman whose remission has held for more than three years.

Her case began with swollen chest lymph nodes found on a screening X-ray, though she felt no symptoms. The authors note that doctors lack shared rules for how long remission must last, or how to check it. Their letter asks the field to agree on clear definitions.
pmc-13360793:
Jakub Wiśniewski and co-authors propose a scoring framework for spinal cord stimulation in a 2026 review. The treatment uses mild electric pulses on the spinal cord to ease stubborn nerve pain. Results vary a lot between patients, so picking the right candidates matters. The authors read trials, registries, and expert guidance to build a bedside tool for sorting who should get a trial of the device.

Their score, called STSS, rests on six domains a clinician can check in normal practice. These include the main pain cause, mental health state, smoking, and opioid use level. The authors are clear that this is a sorting frame, not a proven prediction model. Its job is to make selection talks more open and uniform, without claiming more precision than the proof allows.
pmc-13365493:
Mohammad Mehrabinasab and co-workers build in 2026 a full shape sim of bore cuts in metal, to guess the fine skin a bore tool leaves on a part. Skin grade rests on tool shape, move path, frame bend, and shake in the cut. Their sim joins force math with bar bend tests and lab cut checks.

Sim forces match lab forces in calm and shake prone cuts. Sim skin maps match scope shots of real cut skins as well. The tool can flag bad shake and poor skin prior to a real cut, which saves stock and time in shops.
pmc-13372193:
Angel Geromin Pérez Queb and co-authors profiled bowel surgery patients in Mexico in a 2026 study. The patients had long-term colon swelling and had the colon removed, with a new pouch built from small gut. The work was done at one large referral clinic.

The team read charts to log age, sex, surgery facts, and pouch troubles. Pouch sores, long drug need, pouch loss, and a late shift in the disease label were the main woes tracked. Reports from Mexico and the wider region are rare, so even plain counts help. They give local teams a base to judge their own results and plan pouch follow-up.
pmc-13374093:
I. Avery Bick and co-authors mapped heat illness claims across California in a 2026 study. Heat is now the top weather killer in the United States. Claims for state health aid from 2011 to 2019 were mapped by ZIP code and set next to wealth, job, and home facts.

The top claim zones had lower pay, more farm staff, and more mobile homes than the state mean. Claim rates rose faster per heat step in farm zones than in built zones. Of three risk scores in use, just one matched the claim map well. State grant cash did not always reach the top zones, the team finds.
pmc-13374293:
Fatemeh Aliasghari and colleagues lay out a plan to build and test a web app for the mental health of infertile women in a 2026 protocol paper. Infertility brings high rates of anxiety, depression, low quality of life, and low resilience, yet psychological support is often blocked by cost, social pressure, and stigma. Web-based support offers a private, lower-cost route.

The multi-phase study will first assess needs through literature reviews and interviews with infertile women and experts. A user-centred app will then be built with psychoeducational content, interactive exercises, and support resources for depression, anxiety, stress, quality of life, self-efficacy, and resilience. A later evaluation phase will test effectiveness. Because this is a protocol, no results are reported yet.
pmc-13375093:
Amal Moukhtari and co-authors report a rare two-part ovary cancer in a 2026 case report. A woman aged 58 had a swollen belly and pelvic pain that grew week by week. Scans showed a left ovary lump, belly fluid, and spread through the belly.

Fluid and tissue tests showed two parts in one tumor. One part was a fast gland cancer, and one part was a cartilage-type growth, a rare mix. The spread was too wide for a cure cut, so drug care was planned. Such mixed tumors act fast and treat hard, which makes each logged case of use to the next team.
pmc-13380193:
Jehan Al Fannah argues in a 2026 paper that health systems fail to count much of the clinical work now done away from the bedside. Doctors review monitoring data from home, join remote team meetings, and follow patients up digitally. Measurement systems, built for in-person work, rarely credit that time fairly.

The author calls the result a productivity illusion: services look busy and accountable while missing the outcomes they claim to deliver. Current measures can even punish efficiency and discourage new ways of working. Examples span video consultations, computer-supported decisions, and remote follow-up. Redefining what counts as a unit of health care work, the paper argues, is a basic fix, not a technical tweak.
pmc-13380493:
Zhicheng Xu and co-authors report a 2026 study of a simpler suction system used after surgery to rebuild a missing ear. Rebuilding an ear from the patient's own rib cartilage needs the skin to hug the new framework closely, which requires good drainage of fluid after surgery. Their system applies controlled suction to achieve that.

The team reviewed patients operated on between January 2021 and August 2025. One group received the suction system with full dressings in the usual way, while the other received suction without full dressing cover. Each group held close to two hundred patients. Follow-up showed advantages for the uncovered approach, which the authors detail, making aftercare simpler.
pmc-13383093:
Kecia N. Carroll and co-authors link a mother's lifetime stress to mutation load in placental mitochondrial DNA in 2026 research. The study drew on 496 participants in the PRISM cohort and sequenced placental tissue to count distinct mutations. Stress and trauma history came from a standard life stressor checklist.

Across all participants, higher stress showed only a modest link to higher mutation load. The link looked stronger in women who were not obese, and within racial groups it appeared only in Black women. In non-obese Black women the link was clearest, a pattern the authors say needs further study of how body and social factors interact.
pmc-13383393:
Sanni Peltola's team reconstructed the life of a 16th-century Sámi individual buried at Kitka, Finland, in a 2026 bioarchaeology study. The burial, from the turn of the 16th and 17th centuries, is the oldest known in a region where Sámi semi-nomadic life later gave way to Finnish farming. Genes, isotopes, and grave context were combined to read one life.

The individual showed clear genetic affinity with modern Sámi, closest to present-day people in northeastern Lapland. Isotopes placed childhood farther north or northeast of the burial site and recorded diet shifts tied to long-distance mobility. The study gives a rare personal window onto a community whose language and way of life later faded through assimilation.
pmc-13383493:
Huihui Yang's team mapped how childhood trauma reaches impulsive behavior through mood and stress pathways, in a 2026 study. Trauma and impulsivity co-occur in disorders such as borderline personality and bipolar disorder, but the chain of mediators was unclear. The team surveyed 637 clinical patients on trauma, impulsivity, neuroticism, perceived stress, and depressive symptoms, then modeled the links.

Trauma showed both direct and indirect paths to impulsivity, with a total indirect effect of 0.210 across three pathways running through depressive symptoms, stress perception, and neuroticism in sequence. Emotional and physical trauma were also modeled separately to test distinct effects. The chain points to mood and stress care as levers for curbing impulsivity after early trauma.
pmc-13383893:
Mostafa Javanian and colleagues challenge a study linking simple blood count ratios to blood sugar control in a 2026 commentary. The study under review used data from 3,545 Saudi adults and proposed the ratios as markers of poor sugar control. The commentators praise the large dataset but raise several cautions about its reading.

Missing data on weight, infection, and medicines could skew the ratios, they note, and many subgroup tests lacked correction. One table value looks implausible, and sampling time was not addressed, though the ratios can shift within hours. Their letter urges tighter methods before such ratios guide diabetes care.
pmc-13384593:
Jingjing Su and Daqing Zhang trace a century of the Chinese Medical Journal and its association in a 2026 history article. The journal was formally set up in 1932 by merging two earlier titles, one rooted in missionary medicine from 1887. That merger shifted China's modern medical voice from foreign doctors to Chinese scholars.

The companion association, founded in 1915, published in both Chinese and English from the start. Across name changes and eras, journal and association grew like a double helix, spreading knowledge nationwide. The authors frame the pair as twin engines in the building of China's modern scholarly medical community.
pmc-13385793:
Olga Vera's team identified a protein pair that drives melanoma state switching, in a 2026 study. State switching fuels melanoma growth and therapy resistance under the lineage factor MITF. The team found the small MAF factor MAFG as a key regulator of MITF activity, often high in melanoma and tied to poor survival.

MAFG binds MITF and redirects where MITF sits on the genome, reshaping MITF-driven gene programs. Lab and animal tests showed MAFG promotes a dedifferentiated state, speeds growth, supports cell division, and enables the shift from moles to melanoma in mouse models. The MAFG-MITF pair thus offers a fresh target for blocking melanoma plasticity.
pmc-13386893:
Li and colleagues identify the cholesterol transporter Niemann-Pick C1 as a doorway for porcine epidemic diarrhea virus, a coronavirus devastating to pig herds, in 2026 veterinary virology research. Screening cholesterol-modulating compounds against the virus, the team found the NPC1 inhibitor U18666A potently blocked virus genotypes in cell lines and pig intestinal organoids. Knocking out the NPC1 gene with CRISPR in human cells inhibited infection, while restoring the gene partly restored the virus's ability to infect cells.

NPC1 helps the virus at the internalization step, the moment it slips inside the cell, the experiments showed. The transporter binds to the S2 fusion subunit of the spike protein, and its partner NPC2 participates, placing the cholesterol transport complex inside the entry mechanism. Adding cholesterol partly canceled the inhibitor's effect. Li argues host-directed drugs against NPC1 could resist viral mutation better than vaccines, since the virus cannot replace a doorway.
pmc-13387793:
Hung-Hua Chen and colleagues test a combined blood index for outlook after oral cancer surgery in a 2026 study. The index joins lymphocyte count, albumin, and neutrophil count into one ratio reflecting immunity and nutrition. Records covered 660 patients who had radical surgery between 2007 and 2017, split into training and validation groups.

A cutoff value split patients into clearly different survival paths in the analysis. Low values independently predicted worse overall and disease-free survival at five years in their models. A chart built on the index predicted well in both groups, which supports its use in pre-surgery counseling.
pmc-13387993:
Chiara Ragusa and Valentina Oliveri survey copper-driven cell death as a cancer treatment route in a 2026 review. The death mode, cuproptosis, exploits cancer cells' dependence on copper handling, a possible weak point. Metal-based drugs and copper-carrying systems that trigger this death form the core of the survey.

The authors first lay out how cuproptosis works and where it may link to ferroptosis, another metal-tied death path. They then test inducer systems against varied cancers, weighing gains against limits and drawbacks. Open questions on selectivity and resistance frame where the young field must go next.
pmc-13388993:
Lulu Lin's team shows that energy units cast out from cells act as immune alarms during viral illness, with a viral protein driving the release. In African swine fever virus, the protein B66L pushed damaged energy units into cell sacs. It blocked their fusion with breakdown sacs, so the units piled up outside cells.

The same outside-cell energy units turned up in the blood and lung fluid of mice carrying B66L and in the blood of sick pigs. Cleaned samples triggered immune signals and lung injury in mice. The workings also showed up across several other viruses, pointing to a shared early trigger of body-wide inflammation.
pmc-13389893:
Benjamin Sims, Meghan Oram, and Joshua Startup report, in 2026, a single rehabilitation case where correcting low blood calcium shortened a heart interval that had blocked a drug choice. A 70-year-old man recovering from strokes in several brain areas showed a prolonged QTc interval, which delayed use of donepezil for his language loss.

His mild low calcium was treated with calcium carbonate by mouth. After that, the QTc fell from 464 to 412 milliseconds. The authors note that causation stays uncertain, since many factors shift this interval. Rehabilitation and pharmacy readers gain a practical reminder: check and correct calcium before judging a patient unfit for a drug that itself can lengthen the QTc interval.
pmc-13390293:
Rui Xu's team built a CT-based chart to estimate inner pleural spread before surgery in solid lung gland-cancer nodules touching the pleura. Spread into the pleural lining worsens outlook, yet a before-surgery guess remains shaky, so the team studied 162 treated patients from 2018 to 2025.

Spiky edges, pleural dents, and length of pleural contact emerged as independent signs, and a chart from those three traits sorted well, with areas under the curve near 0.90 in training and 0.86 in testing. Surgeons can use the tool alongside staging to refine surgery planning. All 162 patients had solid nodules touching the pleura.
pmc-13390493:
Mackenzie Hull, Michelle King, Abigail Decker, and Marianna A Patrauchan investigate, in 2026, how calcium steers the metabolism of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This common opportunist causes life-threatening lung infections, above all in people with cystic fibrosis.

Calcium is unusually high in cystic fibrosis airways, and earlier work showed it boosts the bacterium's virulence factors and pushes it toward surface-bound biofilm growth. The new study maps how calcium reshapes the bacterium's wider metabolic network during airway colonisation. The work may show weak points for drugs that disarm the germ. Such drugs would not need to kill it at all. That kind of drug could spare good germs too. One salt, found in all airways, acts here as a cue.
pmc-13392393:
Sarvesh Ram Kumar and colleagues present, in 2026, a learning-based route planner for electric vehicles on real charging networks. Range limits, sparse chargers, and variable energy use make electric trip planning harder than shortest-path routing, and classic algorithms ignore charger availability and connector fit.

Their framework blends reinforcement learning with graph methods, centred on a dual model that weighs gain against cost as it learns, tuning its own weights by a primal-dual scheme. Transport software engineers gain an optimiser designed around charging reality, aiming to cut both travel time and stranding risk as charging networks evolve.
pmc-13393293:
Veronica Masawe, Modesta Makungu, and Antonio Ortega-Pacheco X-rayed the front legs of seven southern giant pouched rats to document the normal radiographic anatomy of the shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints. These large African rodents appear in research and detection work, yet imaging references for them are thin. Anaesthetised adults of both sexes supplied the films, and selected forelimb bones were measured.

Every rat showed a well-developed collarbone, coracoid process, and shoulder blade spine, with the humerus knobs sitting lower than in familiar domestic species. A hole above the elbow condyle appeared in all animals, the forearm gap ran wide, and the wrist held eight small bones with two rudimentary digits visible on the palm side. Five slim, well-spaced hand bones completed the picture. One female showed shoulder dysplasia. The authors offer the atlas for rodent research and welfare-minded care.
pmc-13393793:
Laurie Clauzon and colleagues review epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity in cancer in a 2026 paper. Cancer stem cells drive tumor start, spread, and treatment resistance by shifting between stem-like and mature states, and this flexibility is central to their danger.

The review explains transitions between epithelial and mesenchymal states, including hybrid forms that combine invasion with continued growth. Regulatory networks of transcription factors, signaling routes, and non-coding RNAs steer these shifts, while the tumor microenvironment stabilizes them. Readers gain a framework for why some tumors resist therapy and where new treatments might intervene.
pmc-13394193:
Christine L Shrock leads a twelve-author multicentre study, called VISTA. It tests whether smartphone videos can triage infantile epileptic spasms. Fast treatment protects the developing brain in this dangerous seizure type. Yet brain-wave testing is scarce in many regions. Clinicians worldwide watched nine videos of children with confirmed spasms or look-alike movements three times: cold, after brief training, and with clinical history added, answering diagnosis and management surveys each round.

Starting accuracy averaged just under two thirds. Training plus history lifted it clearly, raising the odds of a correct call by over four fifths, with strong sensitivity and overall discrimination. Confidence and willingness to treat without a brain-wave test both grew, and accuracy rose with confidence. Experienced physicians outperformed trainees. The authors back video triage, boosted by short training, for settings with limited testing access.
pmc-13394393:
Amaia Ochandorena-Saa and colleagues report, in 2026, how mice set left and right sides without the usual flow cue. In normal embryos, tiny hairs sweep fluid left in a pit called the node, and that flow guides organ layout. The team studied mutant mice whose hairs cannot move. To their surprise, most pups were born with organs in the normal places.

Gene studies pointed to two signal sets, Wnt and Nodal, sorting embryos into layout groups. Some mutants showed a fully mirrored body, and some showed mixed layouts with heart and lung faults. Drugs that nudge Wnt backed its role. The authors propose that flow only biases a choice the embryo can make alone.
pmc-13394593:
Emma M. Swift leads a 2026 survey in Iceland on aspirin use in pregnancy to ward off preeclampsia. That illness raises blood pressure and can turn severe, yet aspirin can cut the risk. An online survey drew replies from 887 women in mid or late pregnancy. The team sorted women by risk and scored how well they stuck to the pills.

About one third of women at risk did not recall being told to take aspirin. Among those told, few reported poor use, and poor use did not track risk level. The authors say the weak point is the advice step, not the taking step. A more set routine in clinics could help.
pmc-13394693:
Xiaofeng Ma and others test whether lone feelings, gene risk, and old risk habits shape bone, joint, and muscle illness in a 2026 UK Biobank study. Lone feelings were thought to lift such illness risk, but their weight next to old risk habits and gene scores was unclear.

Among 315,197 people tracked for a middle span of 13.3 years, 79,689 bone and joint cases arose, from joint wear, gout, joint attack illness, low back pain, and neck pain. Risk models tested lone feelings, cut-off living, old risk control, and gene scores side by side. The paper puts a number on how much social health counts for backs, joints, and bones.
pmc-13395393:
Ebere-Bank and co-authors review, in 2026, the proof for feeding peanut early to stop peanut allergy. Old advice told parents to delay peanut, fearing early contact would spark allergy. A landmark trial named LEAP flipped that view: babies at high risk who ate peanut early had far fewer allergies. Follow-up into the teen years found the guard effect held.

Other trials and pooled reads back the early feeding path. The body seems to learn tolerance through the gut in a key early window. The review gives risk-split steps for clinics, drawn from major allergy and child health bodies. Safety checks and family habits remain the main adoption hurdles.
pmc-13395993:
Hayat Hamzeh and colleagues mapped the content of cancer quality-of-life questions onto a World Health Organization framework in a 2026 content analysis. The questions come from the EORTC Item Library, a pool of items that researchers use to build custom questionnaires for cancer studies.

Trained reviewers applied the official linking rules of the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, which sorts health into body functions, activities, participation, and surroundings. Counts of the links show which parts of daily life the item pool covers well and which it barely touches. That map helps trial teams pick items with fewer blind spots when they judge how treatment affects patients' lives.
pmc-13396093:
Veyrier and colleagues report, in 2026, a qualitative study of what long-term treatment feels like for people with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. They interviewed 20 French-speaking adults who had used disease-modifying therapies for at least ten years, recruited through patient associations and neurology clinics in France. Participants averaged 52 years of age, 60 percent were women, and their average disease duration was 20 years.

Patients strongly preferred oral medicines or infrequent infusions because those regimens felt less burdensome day to day. Frequent home injections, by contrast, were linked with anxiety and a loss of autonomy in participants' accounts. Voluntary treatment pauses were common, driven by fatigue or social needs, yet fear of relapse constrained how freely people took them. Treatment had woven itself into identity and daily organization for most interviewees. The authors call for personalized care that acknowledges treatment fatigue and shares decisions with experienced patients.
pmc-13396393:
Qi Li and co-authors review how to build human blood vessels in the lab that match the cause of the disease being studied, in a 2026 article. Animal vessels often miss the human steps of disease, and new United States policy now pushes research toward human-based methods.

Their framework sorts vascular disease into six classes, by origin: present at birth, metabolic, cancerous, inflammatory, wear-related, and driven by risk factors. Each class is matched to the lab system that best copies its setting, from flat cell cultures and organoids to chips, engineered grafts, and printed vessels. The guide aims to help researchers pick a model by cause rather than by habit.
pmc-13396693:
Ahmed I. A. Mansour and co-authors fed young mullet fish diets laced with nano-sized spirulina to see whether the algae, ground ultrafine, improves growth and health. Their 2026 feeding trial ran 63 days and used fish starting at about 14.75 grams each.

Five groups of 30 fish, each in triplicate, received the nano supplement at three doses, plain feed, or feed with one percent ordinary spirulina. The lowest nano dose, 0.05 percent of the diet, gave standout final weights and growth rates. Gut and liver tissue, antioxidant defenses, and immune measures were checked as well, letting the authors judge whether nano-sizing beats the ordinary powder it derives from.
pmc-13397593:
Khulud Mahmood Nurani and colleagues meta-analyze RTS,S and R21 malaria shots for African children under five in a 2026 systematic review. Malaria remains a major burden in this age group, and consolidating trial evidence was needed to guide programs.

Eleven randomized trials enrolling 27,178 children were pooled with random-effects models, covering first and multiple malaria episodes, severe malaria, and severe adverse events. RTS,S showed about 32 percent efficacy against first clinical episodes, with R21 results pooled alongside. Health programs gain a comparative evidence base for deploying childhood malaria vaccines.
pmc-13397693:
Mohammed Sani Gaddafi and others review climate change and drug resistance spread in farm animal systems in a 2026 paper. These joining threats threaten farm animals, food security, and public health, yet their causal links were spread out across studies.

Rising heat weakens farm animal defenses, lifts disease and antibiotic use, and boosts sideways gene transfer through plasmid toughness and stress effects. Rainfall shifts, floods, and droughts move hardy bacteria and drug leftovers among manure, soil, water, wildlife, and humans. The review offers joined curb plans and flags little-studied factors such as damp air and soil workings.
pmc-13397793:
Ghaith Mohsen and colleagues explore whether how much patients drink before heart surgery links to kidney injury afterward. Their 2026 single-centre study calls itself hypothesis-generating: a first careful look rather than a verdict. Kidney harm after bypass surgery is common, lengthens hospital stays and raises death risk, yet few preventive levers are known.

Patients reported their fluid intake between admission and elective surgery, and a cutoff near 51.5 mL per hour split low from high drinkers. The team then compared kidney injury rates across the split, hunting for a pattern worth testing properly later. Because intake was self-reported, the measure stands as a rough stand-in for true hydration, a limit the design accepts openly.
pmc-13398293:
Sheila Fernández García and colleagues use ultrasound to profile the deep belly muscle of female rugby players and probe its link to urine leakage. Their 2026 study covers 34 players without children, drawn from two competitive clubs. Rugby's collisions, sprints and trunk bracing load the pressure system of the abdomen, and the transversus abdominis is a key pressure manager.

Scans measured the muscle's thickness at rest and during set tasks, while a validated Spanish questionnaire logged leakage. The team also tested whether seeing live scan feedback, playing history or body mass changed the picture. They caution that thickness shifts show tissue behaviour, not proof of nerve activation, keeping claims tied to what ultrasound can truly say.
pmc-13398493:
Fengxue Duan and colleagues shape a potato-spiral nanomaterial that guides zinc into smooth layers for rechargeable pouch batteries.
