Their 2026 study builds a covalent organic framework with curled, spiral form and zinc-loving sites. Amp-hour zinc pouch cells demand high metal use with even growth; rough, spiky deposits normally kill such cells early.

The spiral framework forms an even surface film that spreads deposition in all directions, matching ideal growth curves. Test cells plated and stripped zinc stably for over 2,800 hours at a current of 10 milliamperes per square centimetre in the reported runs. A triple-stacked 1.2 Ah pouch cell then cycled more than 200 times while using 40 percent of its zinc, a mark toward practical zinc storage.
pmc-13399293:
Ana Camila de Castro Gandolfi and co-authors translated the SCAT-5 concussion assessment tool into Brazilian Portuguese, reporting in 2026. The SCAT-5 bundles quick sideline checks of memory, consciousness, balance, and thinking. Clinicians use it to follow athletes after a head injury and judge when they can return to play. No such tool existed in Portuguese, which the authors say can compromise care for Brazilian patients.

Concussion is the commonest form of traumatic brain injury and usually resolves on its own. Yet more than 30 percent of patients still report symptoms a year later, as the introduction notes. The study followed the standard translation and cultural adaptation route. Items were rendered into Portuguese, checked against the original, and adjusted so instructions and symptom terms make sense locally. The adapted tool gives Portuguese-speaking doctors the same structured follow-up the English version provides, including baseline testing before injury.
pmc-13400093:
Connor G Oltman and Issam D Moussa profiled patients receiving renal artery denervation in routine United States practice. Their 2026 study covers a nerve-disrupting procedure for resistant high blood pressure, recently adopted after trials showed durable pressure reductions. Trial patients were highly selected, so real-world users and early results had remained unclear.

Using the Epic Cosmos records database, the team identified 722 adults treated between November 2023 and March 2025, mean age 64, with 58.2 percent having resistant hypertension and many carrying heart failure or sleep apnea. After the procedure, prescriptions fell for most drug classes, and the share reaching systolic pressure under 140 rose by 24.3 percent overall, with smaller gains in heart failure and advanced kidney disease. The paper gives clinicians a real-world baseline, while uncontrolled records cannot prove the procedure caused the change.
pmc-13400193:
Liangdong Sun and colleagues assembled the deepest molecular portrait yet of pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinoma, a rare and vicious lung cancer, in a 2026 multi-omics study. Eighty-six patients contributed tumors for whole-exome, transcriptome, proteome, and phosphoproteome profiling. Three more, treated with chemoimmunotherapy before surgery, gave single-cell data. Sarcomatoid tumors mix ordinary carcinoma with spindle-shaped sarcoma-like elements and shrug off standard treatment.

The tumors carry a strong ferroptosis-suppression signature, a shield against iron-driven cell death. The team showed that attacking two of its components, FTL and SLC3A2, makes the cells vulnerable to ferroptosis after all. Proteomics split patients into three subtypes with distinct microenvironments, mutations, and candidate drug targets. Single-cell analysis caught carcinoma cells mid-transition into sarcomatoid cells. The authors offer the dataset as a resource and the subtype map as a starting point for trials.
pmc-13400593:
Killian Rigaux, André Ferreira Castro and Lida Kanari introduce, in 2026, a method for charting how nerve cells grow their branching shapes over time. Modern time-lapse imaging can follow developing neurons in detail, but turning those movies into numbers is hard. Manual tracing is slow and error prone.

Their framework, called TTMD, blends persistent topology, a way to summarize shape, with time-resolved imaging. Applied to fruit fly sensory neurons, it decoded growth stages and branching events directly from shape, without hand-picked features. A simpler static version caught major transitions, while the time-aware version revealed subtle branch changes caused by mutations in actin control genes. The authors present topology as a readable language for neuronal growth.
pmc-13400693:
Byrne H and co-authors explore, in 2026, the dental difficulties faced by cancer patients receiving bone-modifying agents. These drugs protect bones during cancer care but raise the risk of a serious jaw problem where bone dies after dental work. Care sits awkwardly between oncology teams and ordinary dentists.

Ten patients joined a focus group or interviews, and twenty general dental practitioners took part in three focus groups. Four shared themes emerged: awareness of the jaw risk, the sheer burden of dental care, how to plan treatment for this group, and the need for coordinated multidisciplinary care. The authors offer the findings as a practical template for joining dental services into cancer care.
pmc-13401193:
Tsutomu Hayashi and Takaki Yoshikawa wrote a 2026 review on whether removing the spleen still belongs in surgery for scirrhous gastric cancer. This aggressive stomach cancer subtype spreads diffusely and often seeds the abdominal lining. Spleen removal can clear lymph nodes near the splenic hilum, yet it raises complications after surgery.

Newer drug treatments, including immune checkpoint inhibitors and targeted agents, have improved control of disease beyond the stomach, weakening the case for routine splenectomy. Spleen-preserving dissection of the hilar nodes has also become a workable alternative. The authors argue the operation should be selective and tailored to each patient, while noting that diffuse growth, heavy scarring. Hard intraoperative judgments still complicate decisions, and the best extent of node removal after drug therapy stays undefined.
pmc-13401593:
Naseema Gangat and Ayalew Tefferi wrote a 2026 commentary on selinexor, an oral cancer drug. They ask whether it truly has a place in treating myelofibrosis, or whether it is a drug still searching for its disease. Selinexor blocks exportin-1, a protein that ferries materials out of the cell nucleus.

Blocking that export traps tumour suppressor proteins inside the nucleus, reactivating them and pushing malignant cells toward death, a mechanism that could work across many blood cancers. The drug is approved for multiple myeloma, and lab studies found exportin-1 to be a weak point in myelofibrosis cells carrying the JAK2 mutation, sparing healthy progenitors. Myelofibrosis itself brings heavy symptoms, poor quality of life, and shortened survival, leaving real unmet needs that the authors weigh the drug's promise against.
pmc-13401693:
Zaki Farhana and colleagues explored contraceptive use among married adolescent girls in Bangladesh in a 2026 study drawn from the 2019-20 Adolescent Health and Wellbeing Survey. Bangladesh has raised contraceptive use overall but still aims to cut unmet need to 6 percent by 2030.

The sample held 4,802 married girls aged 15 to 19. Overall use was just over 65 percent, higher in urban areas at about 71 percent. Modern methods dominated at nearly 89 percent of use, with traditional methods at about 10 percent. Pills were the leading method at roughly 65 percent, followed by condoms and injections. The team mapped geographic disparities with GIS tools and modelled determinants with logistic regression, comparing regions and user groups to find where adolescent use lags and why.
pmc-13401893:
Qingqing Liu and Hui Zhao built machine learning models to identify patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease who produce excessive mucus. Their 2026 study combines clinic data with airway microbiome profiles. Heavy mucus secretion drives symptoms and flare-ups, but it is not always obvious from routine measures.

At Changzhi People's Hospital, 319 patients enrolled between May 2020 and March 2024 were divided by sputum amount and character. That gave 173 high-secretion and 146 comparison patients. The two groups were then split randomly into training and test sets. Airway bacteria were profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing, and seventy features in total were extracted from clinical and microbial data. Six algorithms, from support vector machines to neural networks, were tuned with cross-validation and judged on sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and discrimination. The high mucus group was older, had longer disease, and showed worse lung function and a distinctly depleted airway microbiome.
pmc-13401993:
Zivile Jacike and colleagues tested how handling before analysis changes routine blood chemistry results, in work published in 2026. Blood came from 20 healthy adults, giving 960 measurements across glucose, albumin, liver enzymes, cholesterol fractions, triglycerides, and electrolytes. Each sample was spun for 5, 10, or 15 minutes, tested within two hours, then retested after storage for up to 14 days.

Storage ran at room temperature, in a fridge, and frozen, and the team compared groups with the Kruskal-Wallis test. Heat and storage time shifted most analytes, with p values below 0.001 for several of them. Spin time mattered far less, affecting only chloride and glucose in a clear way. For laboratory staff, the practical point is that where and how long a sample waits counts more than small changes in spinning.
pmc-13402093:
Wang Chun Kwok and colleagues compared two diabetes drug families for people in Hong Kong who live with both diabetes and asthma. Using territory-wide records, they followed adults who started a GLP-1 receptor agonist or a DPP-4 inhibitor in 2018 and stayed on it at least six months. Matching methods balanced the groups, which held 3193 people on DPP-4 drugs and 102 on GLP-1 drugs.

Follow-up ran to the end of 2023, counting asthma flare-ups from clinic visits to hospital stays. Those on GLP-1 drugs had clearly fewer severe flare-ups needing hospital care, with a mean ratio of 0.513 against the comparison group. Emergency visits and steroid-treated clinic flare-ups also ran lower. The authors say a trial should test the signal, since the GLP-1 group was small and the data came from routine records, not random assignment.
pmc-13402693:
Wang and co-authors map, in 2026, the collateral weaknesses that drug resistance creates in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. They use genome-scale CRISPR interference to dampen every gene in drug-resistant strains and drug-sensitive parents side by side. Resistance mutations carry fitness costs, and those costs may expose new drug targets. Their essentiality calls agreed with a screen at 92.3 to 93.4 percent across the parent strains, validating the approach.

Most resistant strains proved more sensitive than the parent to knockdown of tRNA synthetases, the enzymes that charge transfer RNAs, marking them as high-value shared targets. The rifampicin-resistant RpoB S450L mutant was instead vulnerable through sulfur metabolism, owing to distorted transcription, and isolates had evolved lineage-specific mutations in sulfur genes that soften this cost. Cultures ran for 14 days with or without the inducer in the screens. The authors argue functional genomics can pinpoint where resistant tuberculosis is fragile.
pmc-13402893:
Song Su and co-authors report new variants in the ALG13 gene and a wider range of brain outcomes than the gene was known for. ALG13 helps build N-linked glycans, the sugar trees attached to new proteins that decide whether they fold, travel, and work properly. Its catalytic part partners with ALG14 in the endoplasmic reticulum to run an early step of that assembly line.

Faults in the gene were already tied to congenital glycosylation disorders and to developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, with severe seizures and regression. Isolated developmental delay and other milder pictures, by contrast, were barely explored. By lining up variant position and protein domain against clinical features, the authors expand the spectrum and sharpen genotype-phenotype links. Such maps help families and clinicians read a new ALG13 result with better foresight.
pmc-13402993:
Andrea Portacci and co-authors comment on new UK Biobank evidence linking dietary salt to asthma development, asking whether sodium truly belongs in asthma biology. The study under discussion followed 420,041 adults for a median of 10.9 years, estimating salt excretion from spot urine. Risk rose step by step across salt quintiles, reaching a hazard ratio of 1.50 in the highest group against the lowest, with no clear safe threshold.

Table salt habits told the same graded story, and higher sodium tracked with worse lung function. Links ran stronger in women, never-smokers, leaner participants, and those with low eosinophil counts, while genetic risk scores did not reshape the pattern. Portacci and the team weigh mechanisms and caveats, framing salt as a plausible, modifiable trait in a disease defined by airway inflammation and hyperreactivity.
pmc-13403593:
Tram Bich Thi Ha headed a 2026 case where a special MRI view found a tiny brain aneurysm that standard vessel imaging missed. A 49-year-old woman arrived with sudden bleeding around the brain from no clear source. First scans of the vessel channel showed nothing sure.

Wall-focused MRI showed a small neckless bulge on one brain artery segment. Dye made the bulge wall light up, a sign tied to fresh rupture. Nearby wall thickening suggested a tear with trapped blood in the artery wall. Looking at the wall, not just the channel, can expose such blister-like weak spots.
pmc-13404193:
Chih-Chuan Yang and co-authors built a tiny coated particle in 2026 aimed at nerve pain that current drugs only dull. Nerve pain grows from cell stress, swelling, and cell death acting together. Their particle pairs cerium oxide, a redox-active mineral, with L-theanine, a calming tea compound.

The coating left the mineral's crystal form and mixed charge states intact. In stressed nerve support cells, the particles cut harmful oxygen by-products and kept more cells alive. In rats with a pinched nerve, repeated doses eased touch and heat sensitivity. Spine stress marks fell, and swelling signals dropped as well.
pmc-13405093:
Kevin Mekulu, Faisal Aqlan and Hui Yang present a 2026 voice test that screens for dementia in about a minute. Standard checks such as the MMSE and MoCA take time and trained staff, which limits screening in assisted living. Their model listens instead to how a person describes a picture.

Speech features include pause rate, pronoun use and sentence complexity, drawn from DementiaBank transcripts. Language model embeddings added meaning-based axes with names like Drift and Hesitation, which ranked among the strongest signals. A sparse ElasticNet classifier reached an AUC of 0.858 in the reported testing, beating the MMSE comparison. The authors picture deployment in phone apps or room monitors for low-burden early screening.
pmc-13405493:
Giancarlo A Turri-Vasquez and colleagues report a rare twin pregnancy in 2026 where one twin was a partial molar pregnancy beside a live normal fetus. Such pregnancies seldom progress to aggressive trophoblastic disease that resists standard drugs. Their patient was 28 and had never been pregnant before.

After miscarriage and womb clearing, tissue tests supported the partial mole diagnosis with reassuring markers. Yet the patient developed large ovarian cysts with twisting, then disease that resisted two single drugs and spread to her lungs. A five-drug combination, EMA-CO, brought full remission, and three years of follow-up show no return. The case warns against trusting calm pathology alone.
pmc-13405693:
Adriano Scibilia and Luigi Fortuna read sleep through the mathematics of chaos in a 2026 analysis. Sleep control loops mix pressure that builds while awake, the daily clock, and signals that switch brain states. Such feedback systems can wobble, split rhythms or tip into disorder, which their tools expose.

Beyond reviewing classic models, they build a four-part system linking cortical activity, sleep-promoting activity, sleep drive and the circadian pacemaker. Maps of bifurcations and Lyapunov exponents chart where steady cycles double, break into chaos or show hyperchaos with two expanding directions. Intermittency patterns are matched to real sleep-wake behaviour. The work offers a dynamical vocabulary for fragmented sleep.
pmc-13407893:
Peili Hou and co-authors uncover, in 2026, a helper role for a protein previously filed under cancer biology in the fight against RNA viruses. PAWR was known from tumour research. The team shows it strengthens the cell's virus alarm. It raises production of RIG-I. That sensor detects viral RNA and triggers interferon defences.

The mechanism runs through a stress-pathway factor, XBP1. PAWR increases its active form. A partner kinase switches that form on chemically. The factor then sits on the RIG-I gene's promoter and drives expression. Silencing PAWR blunted interferon responses in human immune cells and macrophages, and mice lacking the gene succumbed more readily to RNA virus challenge. A small molecule that activates PAWR suppressed a test virus in a PAWR-dependent way, marking a candidate drug target.
pmc-13408193:
Nantharat Wongfaed and team built a hybrid trapping system for biohydrogen output from Napier grass and oil palm fronds. Their 2026 work joins polyvinyl alcohol, alginate, silica, and chitosan to trap cellulose-breaking microbes and hydrogen-making germs apart, testing four process set-ups. Earlier dual-matrix systems kept only 83.8 percent activity over four cycles, curbing economics.

Set-up mattered greatly: apart hydrolysis with free degraders plus trapped producers yielded 81.5 milliliters of hydrogen per gram from Napier grass, 2.2 times the joint process, while another set-up showed strong co-digestion synergy. Five-cycle testing kept 84.0 to 89.1 percent hydrogen output with beads intact, beating dual-matrix durability. Medium costs led at 57.3 percent, but five-cycle steadiness gave a fivefold money edge. The platform backs farm biohydrogen scale-up.
pmc-13408493:
Yaqiong Wang, Jiong Zhang, Yin Zhang, Fang Wang, and Lipeng Wu report in 2026 a titanium-catalysed route to silicon compounds carrying both a reactive hydrogen and a boron group. Molecules holding boron and silicon together promise unusual reactivity, yet building them selectively has been awkward. Their starting materials are strained four-membered silicon rings whose carbon-silicon bonds the catalyst cuts open.

The reaction worked across many ring variants and left both new handles free for later chemistry, which the team demonstrated by assembling silicon-containing drug-like molecules. Swapping the boron reagent for hydrogen gas gave a broader family of mixed hydrosilanes, including deuterium-labelled versions useful as tracers. Calculations revealed an unusual two-electron process at titanium and explained why the catalyst picks carbon-silicon bonds of one type over another.
pmc-13408693:
Maria Guarnaccia and Sebastiano Cavallaro argue in 2026 that brain tumour diagnosis has become a precision science that much of the world cannot afford to practise. Gliomas are now defined by molecular fingerprints, such as IDH mutation and chromosome losses, which decide prognosis, treatment, and trial entry under the current World Health Organization classification. The review lines up the major international guidelines and the testing toolbox behind them.

Immunostaining, targeted PCR, large sequencing panels, and methylation profiling each answer different questions at different prices. Wealth gaps, thin infrastructure, regulation, and workforce shortages keep integrated diagnosis out of reach in many regions. Using health-economic evidence, the authors contend that failing to test costs society more than testing does, and they propose a tiered framework that reserves expensive methods for cases that truly need them.
pmc-13410193:
Charlotte Wendelboe-Nelson and colleagues write in 2026 about neighborhood climate projects that quietly improve health. Cities usually run climate work and health work apart, so gains that cross over go uncounted. Many local projects draw people into parks, riversides, and gardens, places tied to better body and mind.

Across 32 community climate projects, health gains showed up even though no project had set health as a goal. Projects rich in green or blue space contact reported gains most often, and even short outdoor time beat longer indoor programs. The team offers a framework linking local control, time in nature, and health gains. Funders could use it to plan projects that pay off twice.
pmc-13410393:
Anne Sumner and co-workers report in 2026 on whether a one-hour glucose test gives the same diabetes answer when repeated. The test checks blood sugar one hour after a sweet drink. A stable test matters, since a label of diabetes shapes care for years.

The study enrolled 154 people of African descent who took the test twice, about ten days apart on average. Diabetes was found in 34 people, and about 65 percent of them tested positive both times. The rest switched status between visits. Agreement overall was rated substantial. People who stayed positive both times tended to show more insulin resistance, hinting that the test settles better when resistance is present.
pmc-13411293:
Kim and colleagues ask whether a bipolar streak, even below diagnosis level, worsens the clinical picture in insomnia. Sleep clinics rarely screen for bipolar traits, yet the conditions share restless rhythms. Their 2026 study sorts 338 adults from a phenotyping project: 252 with insomnia and 86 good sleepers. It sorts them by sleep status and by a bipolarity cutoff on a questionnaire. It then compares fourteen scales of symptoms and function.

Insomnia status drove differences on thirteen of fourteen scales, sharply on sleep quality and body rhythm disturbance. Bipolarity acted on its own across ten scales, with its strongest marks on anxiety, anxiety sensitivity, and depression, in good sleepers as well as patients. The two factors added up rather than amplifying each other, since no interaction survived correction. Screening for bipolar traits in sleep medicine, the authors argue, would catch a load of distress sleep treatment alone will not lift.
pmc-13411393:
Felix Trautner and colleagues built a saddle-shaped carbon sheet in 2026 that holds a stable twist. Chiral nanographenes with non-six-sided rings are prized yet hard to make, so the team used stepwise oxidation of an anthracene-based precursor to install two seven-sided rings carrying helical twists.

Crystal analysis confirmed the saddle shape and separable mirror-image forms. Those forms gave strong chiral light signals and gripped soccer-ball carbon molecules with some of the highest binding strengths reported for curved sheets. Materials chemists gain both a new chiral building block and a host that cradles fullerenes in a striking one-to-three pattern.
pmc-13413393:
Carlos Luques Fonseca and colleagues re-examine in 2026 whether the questionnaires used for chronic low back pain actually register change well. Their secondary analysis of a randomized trial split patients into active and placebo groups and tracked scores at baseline, after treatment, and at follow-up. Internal responsiveness, meaning change within groups, was judged by effect sizes, while external responsiveness tested whether scores could spot patients who truly felt better.

Pain and quality-of-life scales showed large internal effects, so the tools detect group-level movement easily. Yet every instrument scored below 0.70 on the curve test for telling apart individual improvers, and the Bournemouth Questionnaire did best of a weak field. The authors recommend combining measures rather than trusting any single score for decisions about one patient.
pmc-13414393:
Marcelo Ortega-Silva, Pablo Navarro-Cáceres, and Mariano del Sol measure in 2026 how common hip dysplasia is among Chilean infants and what travels with it. The condition, where the hip socket forms too shallow, affects up to three percent of babies worldwide, and Chile reports one case per 500 births, among South America's highest rates. One hundred pelvic X-rays of infants aged ninety to one hundred fifty days were read alongside recorded risk factors.

Dysplasia appeared in 12 percent of the radiographs, higher than most published figures, and the left hip suffered more often. Girls were affected more frequently, matching the known pattern across the literature. Uneven hip opening, a tilted socket roof, and taller stature at two months each tracked significantly with the diagnosis in their analyses. The authors call for wider local screening studies.
pmc-13415593:
Xiaojuan Zhong and colleagues show that a vessel growth factor called AGGF1 slows aging in endothelial cells, the lining of blood vessels, in 2026 cell work. AGGF1 levels fell in worn out human vein cells aged two ways, by repeated division and by drug exposure. Removing AGGF1 sped up aging signs, while adding it back prevented drug induced aging.

Gene reading pointed to a chain: AGGF1 raises TGFB3, which activates TAK1 and then AMPK, a metabolic switch. That chain kept mitochondria from breaking into fragments, a pattern seen in aged cells. Blocking any link with drugs or gene silencing erased the protection. Microscopy confirmed fewer fragmented mitochondria when AGGF1 ran high.
pmc-13416193:
Mwajuma Bakari Mdoe and colleagues measure unintended pregnancy in Tanzania from the 2022 Demographic and Health Survey, in a 2026 analysis. Their sample held 1,182 women chosen through two stage sampling. Weighted regression hunted factors tied to pregnancies women described as unintended.

Prevalence reached about 28 percent, nearly three in ten women. Older women and women who were married, cohabiting, or previously married had markedly lower odds than younger unmarried women. Households with at least six members carried higher odds. Eastern Tanzania and Zanzibar exceeded the western mainland zone. Youth friendly services and help for large households and unmarried women are the authors' prescriptions.
pmc-13417293:
Niklas Schmickler and co-authors merge titanium catalysis with electrochemistry to attach aromatic rings to epoxide derived radicals, in a 2026 methods paper. The titanium route stalled at a step needing a coupled proton and electron move. Their fix splits that step across two electrodes in a paired electrolysis, meaning both electrode reactions do useful work.

At the anode, the radical intermediate loses an electron to become a cation that can restore the aromatic ring. At the cathode, the active titanium catalyst is freshly made by reduction. Titanium is abundant and low in toxicity, adding appeal. The setup generalises a reaction class that earlier methods handled narrowly.
pmc-13418493:
Khan and Poolos surveyed families in 2026 about seizure drugs for children with epilepsy caused by HCN1 gene variants. HCN1 variants cause a syndrome of early epilepsy and developmental disability that often resists drugs. The team built a registry of ten children through a parent community and reviewed surveys plus medical records.

Five of the children's variants had never been reported before. Variants sitting in the channel's membrane-spanning region caused more severe disease than variants elsewhere. Children given lamotrigine or oxcarbazepine had more frequent seizures. Children given valproate or clobazam improved, and two became seizure-free on those drugs. The authors note the pattern resembles Dravet syndrome, another severe early epilepsy, hinting at shared mechanisms. They present the survey as practical guidance for drug choice in this rare syndrome, while urging confirmatory studies.
pmc-13418793:
Shemarah Lindo and Edward Mensah audit clinic records for stress tied to artificial intelligence and its link to suicidal thoughts. Their review covers patients seen from April to August 2025 at a psychiatry and primary care clinic in Ibadan, Nigeria. Each person in the set had come in with anxiety, low mood, or stress complaints.

The records came from routine care and were stripped of names before the audit began. Because the group was small, under 30 people in the analysis set, the team used a scoring method suited to small samples for its ranges. Fresh stress tied to fast-spreading AI tools is only now entering clinic view, and this audit gives an early count of how often it shows up. The authors set out what clinics might watch for as these tools spread further.
pmc-13418893:
Thu Tran Minh Le and colleagues report real-world results for microwave treatment of heavy underarm sweating with body odor, followed for a full year in Southeast Asia. Adults with confirmed primary underarm sweating and odor took part, all having agreed in writing to the treatment. Check-ins at one week and then every three months tracked sweat area, severity scores, and life quality.

One week after treatment, the stained sweat area on the left side had shrunk from 49.1 square centimeters to 0.3 in the same measure, with a like gain on the right side. Gains held across the twelve months of follow-up visits. The most common side effects were pain and swelling, both mild and short-lived, with no serious problems reported. The year-long record supports microwave care as a lasting option for this condition.
pmc-13419893:
Michael J Franco builds a decision model for surgery on cubital tunnel syndrome, the second most common trapped-nerve problem of the arm. Two operations compete: a simple release of the tight tunnel, and a bigger move that reroutes the nerve through muscle. Trials have not shown the bigger operation to be clearly better overall, so the cheaper, gentler release is often favored.

The model follows patient cohorts through five yearly cycles, split by whether nerve tests show coating damage or deeper fiber damage. A nerve injury near the elbow that can linger as its own health state is counted, a detail older models skipped. Cost views came from the wider social angle, with future values discounted yearly. The split by severity lets surgeons match the choice to the nerve in front of them.
pmc-13420293:
Sayuri Kajitani and colleagues report a child whose severe food reaction syndrome was pinned to short-neck clams with help from a blood cell test before any food challenge. The syndrome brings delayed, violent gut reactions hours after eating, and clam triggers are rarely reported in children. A lymphocyte test, which watches immune cells multiply against a suspect food, came back positive for the clam.

Guided by that result, doctors ran a low-dose food challenge, which confirmed the diagnosis with less risk than a full serving. No firm diagnostic route other than challenge feeding exists for this syndrome, so a useful blood test would spare children harsh tests. False positives in healthy people remain a caveat the authors note. The case gives allergy teams a worked sequence they can adapt for other rare triggers.
pmc-13420493:
Beatriz Rodríguez-Martín and colleagues gather what adults aged 50 years and older think about wearable health trackers meant to raise their activity. The review searched eight databases for work in English or Spanish from January 2013 to January 2024. Ten papers passed the screen and were woven together with a method that builds fresh themes from qualitative findings.

Older adults weigh trackers by comfort, trust, ease, and whether the numbers feel useful rather than nagging, the synthesis suggests. Activity in later life guards against high blood pressure, diabetes, falls, and heart death, so uptake matters beyond gadget fashion. Standard review guidelines governed the reporting. Designers of health wearables get a grounded list of what this age group welcomes and what makes them leave a device in a drawer.
pmc-13421593:
Yuto Moritake, Masato Takiguchi, Takuma Aihara and Masaya Notomi report, in a 2026 paper, light diffraction from a pattern built on the famous aperiodic monotile. That is the single tile shape, found in 2023, that covers a plane only in arrangements that never repeat. Their structure keeps perfect threefold rotational symmetry while dropping mirror symmetry for good.

Diffraction experiments showed sharp Bragg peaks that did not depend on where the light fell, the signature of a quasicrystal. The pattern twisted into a pinwheel, and the response differed for left- and right-circularly polarised light — chiral behaviour absent from conventional mirror-symmetric quasicrystals. The authors offer chiral quasiperiodic structures as a new platform for studying order that never repeats.
pmc-13422093:
Schmidt and co-authors follow new parents in eastern Germany, in this 2026 longitudinal study. They ask how work-privacy conflict relates to relationship satisfaction two years after childbirth. Work-privacy conflict is the feeling that work invades private life. They also ask whether personality changes the answer. Data came from 686 mothers and 702 fathers, with personality measured at eight weeks postpartum, conflict at fourteen months, and satisfaction at two years.

For fathers the story was simple: more conflict predicted lower satisfaction regardless of personality. Mothers showed an interaction with neuroticism, the tendency toward negative emotion. Mothers with average or high neuroticism reported low satisfaction whether their conflict was high or low, while low-neuroticism mothers were satisfied unless their work-privacy conflict ran high. The authors read neuroticism itself as a risk marker for new mothers and recommend stronger work-family supports after childbirth.
pmc-13422293:
Ferrao-Malheiro and colleagues followed in 2026 French registry patients given eptinezumab, a preventive antibody drug by infusion, for a full year in real-world care. All 302 patients had at least eight migraine days a month and had failed at least three earlier preventive treatments. None had tried this drug class before. Three quarters also overused acute pain medicines.

Strong responses, a cut of three quarters or more, more than doubled over the year. Scores for headache impact, mood, burden between attacks, and quality of life all improved at every check. Most patients still in follow-up at a year called themselves much or very much improved, and results ran alike in episodic and chronic migraine.
pmc-13423293:
François Moutou reviews, in French, how environmental change is reshaping the emergence of zoonoses, infections that pass between humans and other vertebrates. Planetary shifts in climate and ecosystems have sped up sharply. Suspected for decades and confirmed since the late twentieth century, these shifts already show health effects in people, animals, and the wider world.

The short synthesis first stresses a practical problem: judging these links needs reliable, accessible data, which often does not exist. Worked examples then show how altered landscapes and ecosystems help infections spill over. Moutou closes with a call for awareness at the highest decision levels, arguing that only then might the trend be reversed.
pmc-13423493:
Jin and co-authors review in 2026 how light itself can stamp chirality, a left- or right-handed twist, into nanomaterials. Handedness controls how materials interact with polarized light and with living tissue, and making it by chemistry alone is slow and rigid.

The review organizes the optical toolbox into several families. These include laser direct writing, optical manipulation, symmetry breaking with circularly polarized light helped by surface plasmons, swirling light beams called optical vortices, and direct momentum transfer. It compares the routes by resolution, scalability, suitable materials, and equipment demands, giving readers selection guidelines. A further section covers light-switched chirality that can be reconfigured after fabrication. Applications span medicine, sensing, polarization optics, and chiral displays. The authors present light imprinting as the most promising route to scalable chiral manufacturing, while listing open challenges.
pmc-13423793:
Sardar Karash leads a thirteen-author study showing that bacteria infecting the lungs can swap resistance genes inside a patient, producing sudden, extreme drug resistance. The usual donor was a species from nature, and the most common gene passed was one never before linked to clinical resistance. The work changes how doctors should read sudden resistance during therapy.
pmc-13424493:
Kim and colleagues report a 2026 laboratory study on moving mitochondria, the cell parts that make energy, from one cell type to another. The results suggest mature heart cells are strong donors for repairs aimed at faulty mitochondria.
pmc-13425993:
Leyla Kara and colleagues studied body composition and two blood proteins in adolescent girls with polycystic ovary syndrome in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Their sample held 54 girls with the syndrome and 69 controls, assessed with hormone and biochemical testing plus bioelectrical impedance for body makeup. Irisin and FABP4, proteins tied to metabolism and fat tissue, were measured alongside standard markers.

Girls with the syndrome showed higher total testosterone and luteinizing hormone, and a higher muscle mass index, while other body measures did not differ clearly. Regression kept testosterone and luteinizing hormone as independent predictors, tempering enthusiasm for the newer proteins as markers.
pmc-13426093:

Their method marks the spot with ultrasound before surgery even begins. The mark blends two surface guides, a tendon path and a ligament line. During surgery, a camera inside the knee confirms the marked spot matches. Early use showed the marks lined up well with camera-based anatomy checks. pmc-13426493:
Hongmei Zhao and colleagues assessed optimized nursing care for people on long-term hemodialysis in a 2026 retrospective before-and-after study of 112 patients at one center. Conventional care covered January 2022 to June 2023 with 53 patients, while an optimized program ran from July 2023 to December 2024 with 59 patients. Outcomes spanned dialysis adequacy, complications, hospitalization, laboratory values, quality of life, mental health, satisfaction, and nursing quality scores, adjusted for age and sex. Dialysis units gain a structured template for upgrading routine nursing. The gains span body signs and felt health, which counts for sick men and women who spend most days tied to a chair and a pump.
pmc-13426993:
Kambayashi, Suzuki, and Hirohara reviewed in 2026 how pharmacists and veterinarians work together in animal care. Pharmacists are joining veterinary teams in roles beyond handing out drugs, but the shape of that teamwork differs widely by region. The authors searched four databases plus grey sources for studies in English or Japanese, and screened the results against set rules.

Kambayashi found 239 records and kept 16 studies published between 2007 and 2024, most from the United States, New Zealand, and Japan. Making and dispensing drugs for animal patients was the most common pharmacist role, in about six of ten studies. Drug advice, stock control, client teaching, and safety work came next. The authors say wider use needs better mutual grasp of each role and more veterinary training for pharmacists.
pmc-13427393:
Ruedl and Burtscher warn that collisions between skiers and snowboarders are a growing injury risk in Alpine resorts, worsened by climate-driven snow shortages that crowd traffic onto fewer, harder artificial slopes. A 13-year Austrian registry analysis counted 30,503 collisions involving 52,430 skiers and 8,576 snowboarders between 2005 and 2018 across the country. Collisions once caused about 10 percent of Alpine ski injuries, but a German evaluation office estimates the share may now approach 20 percent under changed slope conditions. Similar increases appear in Italy, Switzerland, and France, according to the authors. They argue preventive action is overdue and discuss slope rules requiring speed adjustment and safe overtaking under the international federation's code of conduct.
pmc-13428393:

In the overproduction group, higher platelet counts tracked with greater loss of the factor's largest, most active forms. Antibodies against the factor appeared in some lymph and autoimmune cases. Two distinct mechanisms, the authors show, need two distinct treatment logics.
pmc-13428793:

Their 2026 study reanalyzes NUPRESS, a Brazilian trial in adults with high blood pressure. It compared a DASH diet, rich in produce and low fat dairy, with a lifestyle program over 180 days. The dietary program showed no effect on pressure change in this analysis. Nor did genes and diet interact: a high genetic score raised or lowered the expected change the same way in both arms. Genetic profiling, the authors suggest, could one day forecast who responds to lifestyle care, pending checks in cohorts.
pmc-13429693:
Giovanna Weykopf and colleagues show, in a 2026 study, that disease genes can hide their damage in alternative versions of a protein. Most genes can be read in several forms, called isoforms, yet variant checks usually consult only the standard form. The team found that exons unique to alternative forms carry more population variants, and those variants more often change the protein. Many alternative forms appear only in specific tissues and stay invisible in standard genome references.

Their worked example is a lung-specific form of DPP9, a protein that regulates inflammation. A common variant in its unique first exon, tied to severe COVID-19 and lung scarring, swaps one building block for another and measurably alters the enzyme's activity. Deep sequencing of full-length transcripts confirmed the hidden form exists. Genetic counselors are warned that the reference form alone can misread a variant's meaning.
pmc-13430193:
Seun Jung and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, machine learning forecasts of mosquito numbers meant to warn control teams before populations surge. Their framework does double duty: short-term forecasts driven by weather predictions, and long projections under climate scenarios reaching toward the year 2100. Models were tested across landscape types against the current monitoring system.

Forecasts fed with predicted weather performed nearly as well as those fed with observed weather, which makes advance warning realistic. Accuracy beat the existing monitoring setup by a clear margin in every landscape. Yesterday's mosquito count and the day's maximum temperature mattered most to the models. Under warming scenarios total numbers fell, yet spring growth sped up, pulling the season earlier. Control programs may need to start their year sooner.
pmc-13431693:
Yoshikuni Kawaguchi and co-authors answered a 2026 letter about amino acid plans in vein feeding right after gut cancer surgery. Readers had pressed on whether protein doses and the balance between fuel and protein also shape results.

A split study of theirs found that higher mean protein doses in the first week went with fewer bad events, and matched groups showed lower in-hospital deaths for the higher dose band. Fresh trials must settle the point, they add.
pmc-13432793:
Ssengooba, Andrew, and Fernandes review inorganic nanoparticle delivery systems for medicine in this 2026 article. Applications span cancer, infectious disease, and noncommunicable conditions, the authors report. They discuss the obstacles of toxicity, clearance, and manufacturing consistency, and close with current trends aimed at making these systems more effective and safer.
pmc-13432893:

pmc-13434293:

Because the molecule is released and reused, small doses can clear many targets, including proteins long classed as undruggable.

Turning bench success into trials, they say, should be the field's next push.

pmc-13434593:

pmc-13434793:

pmc-13435193:

pmc-13436093:

pmc-13437193:
Myong-Hwan Karm and co-authors update how clinicians measure feeling and pain in diseases of the mouth lining. The conditions covered include burning mouth syndrome, oral lichen planus, mouth sores from cancer care, and repeated aphthous ulcers.

Such illnesses often change sensation in ways a plain exam misses, the review explains. Careful testing can reveal small nerve fiber problems and show whether a treatment truly helps. Testing inside the mouth is tricky, though: the space is wet, crowded, richly supplied with nerves, and always moving. The authors gather current trial practice and point out what each method can and cannot show. Their aim is a clearer base for diagnosis, for tracing how these diseases work, and for judging new therapies.
pmc-13437293:
Yangchun Yan and Panpan Ren explore whether learning from younger coworkers can spark fresh ideas in older staff. They call this upward flow knowledge counterflow, since knowledge usually runs from senior to junior workers. Their 2026 study surveyed 323 older employees at separated points in time. The team tested whether fresh input loosens set thinking, and whether hard-to-absorb knowledge dulls that benefit.

Older workers who received more knowledge from younger colleagues showed greater mental flexibility, meaning they could switch angles and reframe problems more easily. That flexibility, in turn, tied to stronger creativity at work. When knowledge was sticky, meaning tangled, hard to take in, or hard to use, the helpful effect weakened. Instead, they suggest firms waste a resource when they keep knowledge flowing one way. Pairing generations so tips and tools travel upward may unlock ideas that years of experience alone cannot supply.
pmc-13437393:
Yujing Zhang and colleagues tested an unusual idea: signs of hip bone death in lupus might show up in nearby bone that still looks healthy. Their 2026 study mined MRI texture features, called radiomics, from the greater trochanter and the ilium rather than the hip ball itself, in 123 patients at one hospital and forty-four at another.

The texture-only model proved steadier, and adding clinical facts did not clearly help. They call the signals a possible early marker, not a test ready for use. Prospective studies, they say, must confirm that healthy-looking bone really carries a readable warning of damage nearby.
pmc-13437493:
Kinga Kramarczyk and co-authors build a circular model of fever, treating it as a weapon against bacterial infection rather than a symptom to crush at once. Their 2026 review groups scattered findings into a loop. Invading bacteria release fever triggers, the host answers with inflammation and heat, and the heat itself then works on both sides of the fight, spurring immune cells while stressing the germs.

They also weigh the everyday habit of reaching for fever reducers, asking whether cooling the patient too fast can cost the body a useful defense. The model is offered as a frame for new findings, and as a caution against treating every fever as an enemy by default.
pmc-13437793:
Esha Pal, Sovan Chakraborty, and Aishwarya Guha frame breast cancer growth as a contest among cells, where the fittest clones win. Their 2026 review gathers evidence that this competition, more than quiet mutation accumulation, steers how tumors progress and why they return after treatment. Cancer stem cells sit at the center, armed by boosted genes and rewired growth pathways.

Immune cells referee and rig the match at once. Some macrophages, killer cells, and suppressor cells starve rivals or mute attacks, tilting the field toward hardy clones. Fuel rivalry matters too: cancer cells ferment sugar even with oxygen present, and their acid weakens immune challengers. Support cells and the matrix send signal parcels adding further handicaps. The authors merge these contests into one framework. Their closing claim is practical: if fitness drives relapse, fitness itself is a target, and treatments rigging the contest against stem-like cells could cut the lethal returns.
pmc-13438393:

The authors argue the record contradicts a public safety story told at the top. pmc-13438593:
Mengjie Zhao's team tracked frailty paths in 2026 among postmenopausal Chinese women to predict painful knee osteoarthritis. pmc-13439193:

pmc-13440693:

pmc-13442393:

pmc-13442593:

pmc-13444293:

pmc-13444493:

pmc-13445493:

pmc-13445693:

pmc-13445793:

pmc-13446093:

pmc-13446193:

pmc-13446293:

pmc-13446493:

pmc-13447093:

pmc-13447193:

pmc-13447493:

pmc-13447793:

pmc-13448193:

pmc-13448293:

pmc-13448693:

pmc-13448893:

pmc-13449093:

pmc-13449393:

pmc-13449493:
Anisa Saleh and co-authors grade in 2026 the maturity of KenyaEMR, the electronic medical record system serving much of Kenya's public care. The authors say workforce and financing need the most attention to get there.
pmc-13449793:

pmc-13449993:

Though tuned on this one muscle, the authors say the approach adapts to other muscles, other models, and human samples, serving studies of age-related muscle decline.
pmc-13450093:

The authors frame the salt as a recycling hinge: one reliable intermediate that turns waste streams into feedstock.
pmc-13450293:
