Dislocations, line defects in a lattice, are usually treated as pure damage in electronics. Yet theory predicts they might host useful behaviors. The team grew germanium-tin sulfide core-shell nanowires by a vapor method. Phase separation naturally produced a wire whose base holds one helical dislocation, part screw and part edge, while its tip stays perfect.

Using nanometer-scale light spectroscopy, the team found efficient emission from the tip segment. Emission dimmed with distance into the dislocated stretch, and the fall in efficiency was pinned on the defect's edge component. The growth process lets the mix of screw and edge character be tuned. The authors present these wires as a testbed for a larger ambition: installing dislocations as elements in future devices rather than tolerating them.
pmc-13450493:
Nan Wu and a large team describe in 2026 a gel system built to kill brain tumor cells left behind after surgery. Their tiny spheres mix a heat-making iron compound with two drugs, one that blocks blood vessel growth and one standard chemo drug. The design copies the self-mending ducts found in pine resin.

In mouse models of tumor removal, one dose placed in the cut space and warmed by a magnet held regrowth down sharply. Tumors shrank to roughly five percent of the size seen in untreated mice, and survival time doubled. Gene checks on tens of thousands of cells showed immune cells shifting toward attack states, with weaker signs of stem-like tumor traits.
pmc-13450693:
Ting Zhang and co-authors outline in 2026 a lab method that reads two layers of cell control at once, in place, from a frozen tissue slice. Most cell tests lose where each cell sat, yet place shapes what a cell does. Their workflow stamps location codes on cell cores inside a brain slice, then frees the cores for study.

Each core yields both its gene activity list and marks on a histone that flags active gene switches. Keeping both reads from the same core sharpens cell type labels and shows how control zones are laid out across the tissue. The authors present the flow as a simple route to maps that link gene use with gene control.
pmc-13451593:
Xinzhi Yang and co-authors test in 2026 whether a shrunken thigh nerve flags poor wound healing after vessel-opening treatment for limbs at risk. Past work hinted that a slim sciatic nerve tracks slow healing and limb loss. The team measured the nerve on scans in 52 patients with tissue loss, then followed healing for months.

Nineteen patients fell in the shrunken group, where only about a sixth of wounds healed by six months, versus near nine tenths in the normal group. The mark also split survival without limb loss at one year. Math checks kept the nerve mark as a stand-alone risk sign, and the authors call for larger trials.
pmc-13451793:
Sara Lyckner and co-authors follow in 2026 how Swedish patients feel recovery goes after major belly surgery that spares the heart. The study nested inside a wider Swedish surgery project at two hospitals and tracked 124 adults for a year. Poor recovery meant a set drop on a fifteen-point recovery scale from the pre-surgery score.

Over half of patients felt unrecovered a week or so after surgery, near half at one month, and a quarter at a year. Problems after surgery hit half the group and doubled the odds of poor recovery at one month. Early poor recovery also cost close to four days alive and out of hospital in the first month. Most patients still regained their base by a year.
pmc-13451893:
Junmo Xu and a large team report in 2026 that light thinning of a mixed timber stand grows bigger trees and more wood than no thinning at all. Fast eucalyptus stands in south China give quick wood but small logs, so growers mix in a slow native tree for long-term timber. Five years after strip cuts that removed from none to all of the eucalyptus, the team read tree maps of who stood where.

Light thinning left a random tree spread with mild mixing, and total wood volume beat the uncut stand by about an eighth. Big eucalyptus thrived under that light touch, while heavy cuts favored big native trees. The authors turn the map logic into a thinning guide.
pmc-13452093:
Nash and Domke improved how the United States counts carbon stored in harvested wood. The wood ranges from furniture in use to lumber rotting in landfills. They fed national forest inventory harvest data directly into the wood products accounting system for the Northern Lake States. Earlier estimates relied on separate production statistics. Those did not line up cleanly with forest ecosystem accounts.

Over 1900 to 2024, products in use from Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin harvests accumulated an estimated 277.0 million metric tons of carbon. Another 155.2 million tons rested in waste disposal sites. The region's wood products still acted as a net carbon sink of 4.9 million metric tons in 2024 by their accounting. The figures include exports but exclude imports into the region's product pool. The authors say the method allows finer geographic breakdowns and tighter integration with forest carbon estimates nationally.
pmc-13452193:
Zhang and colleagues screen a drug library in this 2026 study for compounds that persuade bone-forming cells to lay down mineral, hunting fresh options for repairing bone defects. High-throughput screening surfaced adelmidrol, a compound related to a natural anti-inflammatory molecule, as a standout promoter of osteoblast mineralization, the hardening step that turns new tissue into real bone.

Cell experiments showed adelmidrol raised two master bone genes, RUNX2 and OSX in the authors' notation, by activating the Notch signaling pathway. For delivery, the team loaded the drug into a printed hydrogel scaffold of silk protein and gelatin reinforced with treated bioactive glass particles. Implanted into critical-size skull defects in mice, the loaded scaffold boosted mineralization, shrank the defect area, and repaired damage that would not heal alone. The authors offer both a candidate drug and a delivery platform for bone repair.
pmc-13452393:
Ewoud T Jansma and three co-authors ask whether schooling gaps in disability last into the final year of life across Europe. Their 2026 study tests two rival views: one says gaps keep growing with age, the other says they shrink near death. The data come from end of life interviews for 6,957 people who had died.

People with more schooling were expected to face fewer limits in daily tasks such as washing, dressing, and handling money. The gap was clear for basic self care tasks and larger still for tasks such as shopping and cooking. Gaps also changed with each country's welfare system, showing up in some regimes but not in Nordic or Southern European ones. The pattern backs the view that early advantage keeps building across a whole life.
pmc-13452493:
Marcell Papp, Chiara Morelli, Sarah Khawaja, and Paolo Arosio review how droplet like cell compartments shape the growth of amyloid fibrils, the stiff protein fibers tied to brain disease. Cells build these open droplets, called biomolecular condensates, to hold proteins at high local levels. Their 2026 review asks why droplets have been reported both to speed and to slow fiber growth.

Inside the droplet bulk, the review argues, proteins can stay dissolved and fiber growth can stall despite the crowding. The danger zone sits at the droplet surface, where the dense inside meets the thin outside fluid. Conditions at that border suit the first seed of a fiber unusually well. The split view helps explain clashing past reports and points drug work toward the droplet edge.
pmc-13452993:
Mgeyi and colleagues analyze six years of national records in this 2026 study of childhood tuberculosis in Tanzania, where globally about half of child cases are thought to go undiagnosed. Drawing on the national electronic TB register for 2018 through 2023, they tracked case notifications and treatment outcomes across ten regions.

A total of 25,449 childhood cases were notified over the period. Annual notifications climbed from 2,688 in 2018 to a peak of 5,421 in 2022 before easing to 4,493 in 2023, suggesting improving detection. Treatment success was high overall, with 97.2 percent of children achieving favorable outcomes in the register. Encouragingly, the share of cases co-infected with HIV fell from 28.5 percent of notifications in 2018 to 8.9 percent by 2023, although HIV-positive children and the youngest and oldest age bands still faced the worst outcomes.
pmc-13453693:
Jiye Pan, Juan Shi, Yating Ai, Ming Lu, and Huahui Wang grade the risk prediction models built to warn of infection after hip fracture surgery. Their 2026 review searched nine databases to February 2026 and kept 17 papers with 21 models. Infection rates in the source studies ran from a low of 1.61 percent to a high of 24.56 percent across the set.

The models scored well on raw accuracy, with area under the curve values from a low near 0.699 in the weakest model to a high near 0.946 in the strongest. A pooled look named low protein, diabetes, lung disease, smoking, and long surgery among the true risk drivers. Yet every study rated high for bias risk under a standard tool, and reporting quality ran low across the board. Most came from one center with no outside check. The authors call for large shared studies before these tools guide care.
pmc-13453993:
Amanda M. V. Pinto and others made three new oxime drugs in 2026 that may wake up a nerve-blocked enzyme hit by an A-242 nerve agent copy. Nerve agents jam acetylcholinesterase, and wake-up drugs are key antidotes, yet old drugs fall short on new agents. Three new 2-oxime forms, AM01 to AM03, were set next to past 4-oxime forms.

Unlike their 4-oxime kin, the 2-oxime forms woke the jammed enzyme at 100 micromolar and even beat the shop drug HI-6 in the tests. Docking and motion sims probed how the drugs sit in the enzyme-agent knot. The new forms show a wake-up style like obidoxime and trimedoxime. Defence medics gain lead drugs for A-242 antidotes.
pmc-13454093:
Hanrui Guo, Hao Wen, Yian Hou, Nan Li, and Yingli Cao improve a vision model that spots whether rice spikelets are flowering, a key window for hybrid rice breeding. The targets are small, densely packed, and lost in busy backgrounds. Their 2026 study rebuilds the compact YOLOv11n detector with four changes, including a softer downsampling step and a fusion block that mixes convolution with attention.

On the test set the rebuilt model hit 88.8 percent precision and 84.7 percent recall, gains of 8.0 and 3.4 points over the base model. Its average precision score rose to 84.0 percent and beat a rival detector by clear margins. The model stays tiny, with 2.14 million parameters and low compute cost, so field gear can run it. The team offers the tool for flowering window tracking in breeding plots.
pmc-13454493:
Nawal Khattabi, Axel Ros, Matthew Carey, and Aled Jones argue, in a 2026 perspective, that hospitals learn the wrong lessons from safety incidents. Reviews often claim a systems view yet end by blaming a worker's deviation and ordering more training. The authors ask a sharper question: was the flagged act rare, or was it how work normally gets done?

Their Safety-II model reads each incident through three lenses. Work-as-imagined is the official plan, work-as-done is the real routine, and work-as-experienced is what patients and families alone witness over time. They propose checking electronic records to learn whether a practice was the norm or an outlier. The piece closes with concrete steps for regulators, hospital leaders, and researchers. Its aim is learning from everyday success, not only from failure.
pmc-13455293:
Bram Veldman and colleagues study a milder inherited form of Fabry disease in a 2026 cohort from one gene variant. Fabry disease stems from GLA gene faults that leave a key enzyme short. Wider gene testing now finds many carriers whose illness looks far milder than classic cases. The team followed 42 carriers of the same p.I319T variant and tested that variant in lab cells, where it kept about 7 percent of normal enzyme activity.

Most patients showed heart disease rather than the full classic picture. Men all developed heart disease from age 50, with a blood marker called lysoGb3 clearly raised. Women varied more, with heart trouble after 60 when that marker sat mid-range, rarely at all when it stayed low. With 86 percent of the group also carrying ordinary heart risk factors, the authors argue that tight control of those risks matters as much as disease-specific drugs for many carriers.
pmc-13456193:
Claudia Riccardi and six colleagues test, in a 2026 chemistry study, rust-colored ruthenium compounds fitted with fatty tails against the protein clumping behind brain diseases. Clumped peptides drive Alzheimer and Parkinson diseases and prion disorders. Two ruthenium drugs first built for cancer had already shown anti-clumping promise, so the team tried a cousin compound and its fat-tailed versions.

Two tailed versions, named for their myristic and palmitic tails in the study, stopped amyloid peptide clumping at low doses, around five micromolar. Closer study showed the metal anchors to histidine spots near the peptide's start. In human nerve-like cells, the compounds caused no meaningful harm at the doses that blocked clumping. The authors present the fat-tailed design as a route to brain-friendly anti-aggregation drugs, marrying the metal's grip with tails that may aid delivery.
pmc-13457193:
Xinrui Ren and nine colleagues published this 2026 study building a prediction model for hepatitis B cure under interferon treatment. Losing the hepatitis B surface antigen, called HBsAg loss, is the ideal endpoint for chronic hepatitis B. The drug Peg-IFNα-2b is the preferred route to it, though results vary widely between patients. The multicentre retrospective study enrolled patients treated for at least 48 weeks and modelled who reached that endpoint.

Among 859 patients, 133, or 15.5 percent of the cohort, achieved HBsAg loss by week 48. Four factors independently predicted success: combining treatment with traditional Chinese medicine, lower starting HBsAg level, lower starting AST liver enzyme level, and not using entecavir as the partner antiviral. The model's discrimination scored 0.884 in the training group and 0.866 in the validation group on the accuracy curve measure. Calibration was also strong. The authors offer the model to help clinicians judge which patients suit this demanding therapy.
pmc-13457393:
Akira Iwanami and colleagues validate a Japanese version of the Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale, a clinician-run interview that grades symptom severity and treatment response in adult ADHD. No validated Japanese edition existed, so the team translated the scale and checked its wording with clinicians. They then ran a multicenter longitudinal study with 61 adults who have ADHD, average age 34.

Scores held together well. Its Cronbach's alpha reached 0.83 for the full scale, with the inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity halves close behind. Repeat testing gave an intraclass correlation of 0.77, the same rater agreed with themselves at 0.76, and different raters agreed at an excellent 0.96. The scale also matched the Japanese self-report version closely, at 0.89 overall. The authors conclude the instrument is reliable and consistent enough for assessing ADHD symptoms in Japanese adults in clinics and trials.
pmc-13458893:
Atsuko Suzuki and colleagues externally validate a European risk score predicting heart damage from anthracycline chemotherapy in Japanese patients, a population the tool has barely touched. Anthracyclines cure cancers and injure hearts, and the HFA-ICOS score, endorsed in the 2022 European cardio-oncology guidelines, estimates risk from history before treatment. The check draws on Japan's AIC Registry: anthracycline patients enrolled between 2016 and 2021, with imaging before and during treatment.

Patients with reduced heart function or major valve disease were excluded, leaving a cleaner test. The endpoint is cardiac dysfunction within two years, defined as a ten-point ejection fraction drop below 55 percent. The team grades the score three ways. Discrimination uses Uno's C statistic with death as a competing risk, and calibration compares predicted against observed rates across the low, moderate, and high strata. Clinical utility comes through decision curve analysis weighing net benefit at varied thresholds.
pmc-13459293:
Malith Kumarasinghe and co-authors reviewed how women's bodies change after childbirth and what shapes that path. The focus is body makeup: the shares of fat, muscle, and water, not just weight. Studies measure it with tools from skinfold calipers to X-ray scans. Their 2026 review searched six databases through September 2025 and kept long term studies that measured mothers at least twice after delivery, screening 1,273 abstracts to find the eligible work.

Eighty six studies were kept, with sixty one reporting changes and forty four examining what drives them. Researchers used seventy three different body measures across studies, with fat mass percentage the most common. Waist size dropped a lot during the first month after birth in the findings summarized. Measurement timing and technique varied widely between studies, and 59 percent finished follow up at or before nine months after birth, limiting long term conclusions.
pmc-13459693:
Ivetka W. Noon, Marie Ojeh, Giovanni Melandri, and Rebecca A. Schomer present in 2026 draft genomes for twelve bacterial isolates gathered from sorghum leaves in central Arizona. The bacteria belong to the Methylobacteriaceae, pink-pigmented microbes that live on leaf surfaces, feed on one-carbon compounds such as methanol, and can promote plant growth. Leaves came from a 2023 field trial at the Maricopa Agricultural Center.

Colonies were grown on a selective medium with methanol as the only carbon source, purified, and sequenced with either short-read or nanopore technology. The twelve drafts span several Methylorubrum species. Because these microbes thrive in a hot, arid farm setting, their genomes offer material for studying how plant-associated bacteria adapt to dry conditions and handle single-carbon foods.
pmc-13460193:
Yue Lan and colleagues ran in 2026 a randomized, double-blind trial of Anshen Buxin Liuwei Pill, a Mongolian medicine, for cardiac neurosis with a palpitation pattern called heyisheng type. Cardiac neurosis brings real symptoms without structural heart disease, and this trial judged success mainly on a Mongolian medicine symptom scale. Two hundred patients enrolled between 2021 and 2022, split evenly between the pill and a placebo for eight weeks, with follow-up to twelve weeks.

In the analyzed set of 182 patients, nine withdrew from each arm. Secondary measures covered anxiety, depression, and insomnia alongside safety monitoring, and two blood markers were checked for balance at entry. The trial was designed to give Mongolian medicine a fair, blinded test in a condition where evidence has been scarce.
pmc-13461493:
Jie Wang and colleagues examined in 2026 whether a gum disease bacterium, Porphyromonas gingivalis, found inside oral cancer tissue tracks with the inflammatory climate around the tumor. Their retrospective study enrolled 201 patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma. Tumor samples were stained for the bacterium to split patients into high and low expression groups. Four composite inflammation indices were computed from routine preoperative blood tests.

Tissue analysis also counted helper T cells and measured several immune signals, including a chemokine pair and the suppressive marker FOXP3. That let the team compare bacterial load against both blood markers and the tumor's local immune makeup. Clinical stage and grade were weighed alongside. The authors aim to learn whether a chronic oral infection quietly shapes the environment that oral cancers grow in.
pmc-13461893:
Abdirahman Mohamed Jimale and colleagues reviewed what blocks or enables use of maternal, newborn, and child health services among displaced people in Somalia. Displaced families carry heavy health burdens from conflict, repeated moves, poverty, and weak health systems.

Barriers stacked up on both sides: transport costs, distance, insecurity, and low female say-so kept families away. On the supply side, shortages of skilled and female workers, drug stock-outs, and weak referrals broke care chains. Helpers included community health workers, women's groups, mobile outreach teams, and aid programs that treat displaced people as a priority. Jimale argues services alone will not suffice without linked data systems tracking families across the whole care path.
pmc-13462093:
Charalampos Filippatos and colleagues pool clinical trial data, in a 2026 review written as a letter, on the safety of engineered immune cell therapy for myeloma that has returned or stopped responding. The treatment, CAR T-cell therapy, rebuilds a patient's T cells to hunt the cancer, and can bring deep, lasting responses in heavily treated patients. Its side effects are unusual and can be severe. A pooled safety picture was missing.

The team searched three databases for trials of the therapy, following review guidance. Trial results were combined with models allowing for variation between studies. Sub-analyses split results by region, phase, product type, and how the cells were made. Extra analyses tested whether study size, age, prior treatments, or gene traits shifted the results. The authors argue a pooled account of harms is essential as the therapy moves into wider real-world use.
pmc-13462793:
Howard and colleagues proposed in 2026 a single standard name, MFRE, for the root-dwelling fungi known as Mucoromycotina fine root endophytes. These fungi partner with plants much like the better-known arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, but they branch earlier in fungal evolution and have collected several competing names, which muddies the growing literature. The proposal follows debate at the twelfth International Conference on Mycorrhiza in Manchester in 2024.

The authors trace the group's obscure history: likely sightings date to 1963 in a New Zealand tree, where the fungus was misnamed for its look-alike arbuscule structures. Those are the tiny trees fungi build inside root cells, and it resisted lab culture for decades. A shared short name with a defined meaning, they argue, will sharpen communication and set the group apart from its coarse-rooted cousins. The piece is a consensus call to the research community rather than a data report.
pmc-13463093:
Neil Ramsay and colleagues present, in a 2026 review, the first pooled summary of functional visual loss covering its frequency, features, outlook, and treatment. In this condition vision falters without structural eye damage; the problem lies in nervous system functioning and sits within the family of functional neurological disorders. Diagnosis has drawn many studies, while the basics of who it strikes and how it ends were scattered. The team searched a database back to 1951.

Forty-four studies with 2,284 patients qualified, two thirds female, with a median age in the early forties. Common companions included eye or face injury, other eye disease, headache, and functional symptoms. Outlook data from thirteen studies varied widely, and children seemed to fare better than adults. Most studies blurred true symptom loss with test signs that cause no symptoms. Treatment data were very thin. The authors map the gaps that better care must close.
pmc-13463293:
Claude Simon A Naco leads a 2026 plant study of spearmint seeds that spent six months aboard the International Space Station, testing whether they withstand a high-tech fertilizer water. The water, plasma-activated water, is treated with cold plasma so it carries reactive oxygen and nitrogen species that feed plants. Two strengths were brewed, with five and ten minutes of plasma discharge, then used on the flown seeds.

The stronger water harmed germination and growth over a fourteen-day test. The milder water caused no such harm, pointing to a dose-dependent response. Chemical profiling found a drop in a phenolic defense compound in flown seeds given the strong water. The authors speculate the space-flown seeds shifted toward enzyme-based defenses, a pattern seen in other plants. They raise spearmint as a promising space crop and note that prior space exposure seemed to grant extra tolerance.
pmc-13463893:
Jesús Pedro Paredes Cotoré and Fernando Fernández López test whether simple clinical scores can foretell which rectal cancers will vanish before surgery. Radiation with chemo makes a minority of tumors disappear fully, and those patients fare well. A good forecast could spare some patients major surgery.

The pair ran two published scores on 425 of their own patients treated across ten years. Neither score foretold full response with useful accuracy. Rebuilding one score on local data failed to help, which points to routine clinical facts being too weak for the task. Only the treatment actually given swayed the outcome, so the authors back imaging and scope checks after treatment instead.
pmc-13463993:
Jalali and co-authors mapped the worldwide literature in 2026 on informal payments in health care. These are the under-the-table cash or gifts patients hand over for services they are officially entitled to receive. The review followed established scoping methods across five databases through January 2025. Two reviewers independently screened the records. Findings were grouped thematically.

The 68 included studies sorted the causes into five stacked levels. They span frightened or hurried patients and underfunded, weakly regulated systems. Underpaid providers short on supplies form another level. Cultures where such gifts feel normal, and organizations lacking accountability, complete the set. Reported prevalence swung wildly, from 2 percent to 80 percent of patients depending on country and service. Proposed fixes also fell into five families. They range from teaching patients their rights to raising provider pay, widening insurance, and tightening oversight with real sanctions.
pmc-13464393:
Cummings-John and co-authors ran a randomized trial in 2026 at Connaught Hospital in Sierra Leone. They asked whether antibiotics alone can treat uncomplicated appendicitis, sparing patients an operation. Sixty patients were assigned evenly. The non-operative group received two days of intravenous antibiotics, then five days of pills. The other group underwent open appendix removal. Follow-up checks ran out to 90 days.

Antibiotics succeeded in 18 of the 30 patients, a 60 percent success rate. Only one successful patient relapsed within a week of discharge. The failures mostly declared themselves during the first admission and proceeded to surgery. Successful antibiotic treatment beat surgery on nearly every practical measure. Quality-of-life scores were higher, and the mean stay was four days. Mean cost was about 49 dollars, with no family pushed into catastrophic health spending. The authors see a real role for antibiotics where surgical capacity is scarce.
pmc-13464793:
Padilla-Cerda and colleagues surveyed in 2026 cold-loving Acinetobacter bacteria in raw milk from Ecuador, where they spoil refrigerated dairy goods. The team collected 400 raw milk samples from farms in two provinces across dry and rainy seasons. They screened the samples with gene tests for the genus and ten target species, then grew and confirmed isolates by gene sequencing.

Padilla-Cerda detected the bacteria in about eighty-six in a hundred samples, a strikingly high share. Prevalence ran higher in Pichincha province than in Manabí. One species, A. lwoffii, dominated, appearing in nearly nine in ten positive samples. Five species were isolated in total, including A. baumannii, a species also known from hospital infections. The authors warn that such wide spread in local dairy systems threatens milk quality and shelf life, and they call the genus a hidden microbial risk for dairy products.
pmc-13464993:
Yao Xiao, Fang Liu, Guixia Xu, and Xi He assemble the first mitochondrial genomes for five members of the Aquilegia ecalcarata flower complex. The group is a prized model for parallel evolution, where the same trait arises apart in kin lines. Nuclear and chloroplast data were rich, yet the mother-passed mitochondrial record was missing.

Long-read sequencing built all five genomes for side-by-side comparison. The two spurless lines did not group together on the mitochondrial tree. Each instead sat beside a different spurred relative, which fits spur loss arising twice on its own. Gene order, gene sets, and stray chloroplast pieces in the genomes all backed the split. The new record adds an independent witness to a classic evolution puzzle.
pmc-13465693:
Tunsi explores why Saudi women with heart disease struggle to eat heart healthy diets in this 2026 study. Cardiovascular disease kills more people worldwide than any other cause, and Saudi women face rising risk from obesity and inactivity. Diet change is central to preventing further events. Yet women's roles as family cooks and caregivers shape what they can eat.

Tunsi interviewed 19 women individually and analysed their accounts thematically. The influences fell into individual, social, institutional, and environmental groups. Serving family preferences first, thin dietary counselling, and poor access to healthy food all blocked change. Serious illness and family backing motivated it. Tunsi argues that diet programmes must be built around these gendered realities rather than simply telling women what to eat.
pmc-13466593:
Abdullah Golbasi and colleagues refine prostate cancer prediction by splitting a blood marker's density by gland zone, using artificial intelligence to outline the zones on MRI, in a 2026 study. The group held 354 men biopsied for raised PSA between 2024 and 2026, most in the lower four-to-ten range. Standard PSA density treats the whole gland as one unit.

Density for the inner transition zone beat the whole-gland figure at spotting cancer in both PSA bands, with the edge growing in the higher band. At the chosen cut point, the zone measure missed more cancers yet rarely flagged healthy men. Readers scored the scans without seeing biopsy results, keeping the test honest.
pmc-13466693:
Wen Pan and colleagues study why bone defects heal poorly in old mice, focusing on a macrophage signal called IL-34, in a 2026 study. Young and aged male mice received matching shin bone defects, then healing was tracked with scans, tissue stains, cell sorting, and gene readouts. Aging thinned bone, slowed new bone cell formation, and left defects unhealed.

Macrophages at the defect were fewer in old animals and less often in their healing, repair-oriented state. IL-34 stood out among genes turned down with age, and its protein drop was confirmed. The signal seems to govern whether immune cells arrive, survive, and settle into the repair mode that bone rebuilding needs.
pmc-13466793:
Lu Tong and colleagues report a 2026 staged rescue of a 58-year-old man whose heart attack and shock resisted weaning from heart-lung support. Veno-arterial ECMO plus a balloon pump kept him alive, but prolonged ECMO breeds inflammation, organ harm, and device complications. Transferred on day 14 of ECMO, he still showed poor pumping despite optimised drugs, and his balloon pump came out on day 18.

An interventional Extra-VAD device on day 19 mimicked a permanent assist pump, letting the team test right heart function while organs recovered. When pumping stayed poor, a definitive LVAD went in on day 25 and the Extra-VAD came out. He left hospital on day 38 with LVAD support, showing staged bridging can move shock patients safely from temporary to durable support.
pmc-13466993:
Magdalena Nowak, Tomasz Kamizela, Angelika Skorupa, and Małgorzata Worwąg grow duckweed in synthetic waters of rising human contamination to model pressure on aquatic ecosystems, in a 2026 study. Four made-up media stood in for two river waters with different loads and two wastewaters, one spiked with caffeine as a marker of municipal sewage. Two fourteen-day runs tracked water chemistry and plant condition.

Duckweed grew best in the river-like media, especially the more heavily loaded one. Wastewater versions stunted growth, worsened the plants' look, and made the water chemistry swing more. Final biomass and nutrient uptake rounded out the read on how a common floating plant handles the gradient from river to effluent.
pmc-13467193:
Yuedong Wu and colleagues dose self-compacting concrete with a corrosion inhibitor and track what changes, in a 2026 study aimed at protecting steel bars inside concrete from rust. Fresh concrete grew more viscous and slumped less as inhibitor rose. Strength generally fell, with the smallest loss at a two percent dose.

Every inhibitor mix resisted chloride penetration better and drank less water through surface pores than the plain mix. Two imaging tools, one magnetic and one X-ray based, counted pores by size, and microscope views filled in the microstructure story. The trade is explicit: some strength is exchanged for longer life of the steel skeleton, a bargain many structures would accept.
pmc-13467293:
Szczerbakow and colleagues review machine learning for forecasting how severe acute pancreatitis will become, in 2026 gut medicine research. The disease, sudden pancreas inflammation, ranges from mild and self-limiting to organ failure with high mortality, and early sorting of patients guides treatment levels. Older scoring systems need many inputs, apply late, and reach only fair accuracy. The review weighs studies training algorithms on patient, lab, clinical, and imaging data to forecast severity and complications.

Models in the reviewed literature target severity grading, organ failure, ICU admission, and death, often beating the standard scores they were compared against. Methods that show which inputs drove a forecast get special focus, since clinicians distrust black boxes. Flaws recur across studies: small datasets, overfitting, poor fit, and scarce outside testing. Szczerbakow argues multi-input models and forward testing must come before these tools can safely support routine decisions.
pmc-13467393:
Aurélie Mialhe and colleagues present a 2026 cell study on whether resveratrol, a compound found in grapes, can make colorectal cancer cells easier to kill with chemotherapy. Resistant tumors often rebuild their fat metabolism, and one enzyme in that rewiring helps cancer cells store fat droplets and survive treatment. The team tested resveratrol on a resistant colon cancer line and on cells engineered to overproduce that enzyme.

Resveratrol triggered cell death and slowed growth in both cell types. It also lowered the levels of key enzymes that build and remodel phosphatidylcholine, a major fat in cell membranes. Because the compound attacks the fat-handling machinery that resistance depends on, the authors argue it deserves study as a partner for standard drugs in hard-to-treat colon tumors.
pmc-13467893:
Nazire Esra Ozer and colleagues ask in 2026 whether cow teeth can stand in for human teeth when testing dental adhesives. Labs often use bovine teeth because human teeth are scarce, but the swap needs evidence. The team bonded modern universal adhesives to enamel and dentin from 144 human and bovine specimens, using two application protocols. The samples were aged with 5,000 temperature cycles, and then the bonds were sheared apart.

Both tissue type and tooth species significantly affected bond strength, while the adhesive protocol alone did not. One combination stood out: the top group enamel bonded significantly more strongly than another group enamel and its own dentin. Failures were mostly at the glue interface rather than inside the tooth. The detailed breakdown tells dental researchers where cow teeth behave like human teeth and where the substitution may mislead.
pmc-13468893:

These cases were slightly younger and showed lower cell growth indices and lower rates of another mutation in the reported comparisons. Scans showed less swelling around the tumour and lower internal texture grades for that group, while enhancement and diffusion measures matched. Survival trended longer for these cases without reaching significance, and subtype was not an independent survival predictor after adjustment. Imaging can raise suspicion but cannot replace molecular testing.
pmc-13500693:
Hu and colleagues present a new way to profile turbulence in the air from a laser wind instrument, information that wind farms and weather models need. A coherent Doppler lidar sweeps its beam in a cone and measures wind along it, but extracting how turbulence strength varies with height normally leans on tower instruments. Their 2026 method works from the scan geometry itself, computing energy dissipation rates and then adjusting the spectral analysis window by altitude to sharpen measures of turbulent kinetic energy.

Checked against ultrasonic anemometers, the lidar method reproduced the same ups and downs in dissipation across heights. The team also mapped where the method strains. Fitting residuals and sensitivity to frequency choices varied with altitude and wind component. Energy values shifted by up to roughly a quarter in the touchiest layers. They offer the technique for wind resource assessment.
pmc-13501093:
Brendan Masi leads a five-author team with a 2026 case of cardiohepatic syndrome, liver injury caused by heart failure congestion, in a 48-year-old man. He had hypertension, high cholesterol, type 2 diabetes, and recently diagnosed heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. He arrived with worsening breathlessness, worse when lying flat, swollen legs, and falling exercise tolerance. Blood tests showed low sodium with excess body water, kidney injury, raised bilirubin, and a cholestatic pattern of liver injury.

Heart ultrasound showed normal pumping function but severe thickening of the left ventricle wall and signs of high right-sided pressures. Catheterization confirmed a greatly raised filling pressure despite open coronary arteries. Imaging of the abdomen found an enlarged liver, large-volume ascites, bowel congestion, and fluid around the lung, without bile duct blockage. Strong intravenous diuretics plus standard heart failure therapy improved him, supporting congestion rather than primary liver disease as the cause.
pmc-13501593:
Yinghui Guan leads a seven-author team with a 2026 scoping review of gamified interventions for children with type 1 diabetes, who face daily self-management demands around insulin, food, and glucose checks. Following the Arksey and O'Malley framework, the team searched six databases for work published from January 2010 to January 2026 and also tracked citations. Of 762 records retrieved, 23 studies met the inclusion rules and were mapped for design, delivery, and outcomes.

Mobile apps delivered 52 percent of the interventions and websites 17 percent. Goal setting, challenges, and fun elements each appeared in 96 percent of studies, while social features appeared in only 35 percent. Most studies, 70 percent, named no explicit theory behind the design. Reported benefits covered blood sugar control, self-management, knowledge, and mental distress, though quality of life effects were mixed. The authors call for theory-driven designs and longer evaluations.
pmc-13501693:
Somayeh Momenyan and others estimate the economic burden of road trauma in Canada by road user type. In 2026, the study looks at 1,372 survivors from July 2018 to March 2020. It costs healthcare and lost productivity over the following year in 2023 Canadian dollars, with productivity measured at four follow-up points. Injury gravity and type shape costs differently.

Mean healthcare costs ranged from about 14,840 dollars for cyclists to 27,369 dollars for pedestrians, while total costs were highest for pedestrians, followed by motorcyclists, passengers, drivers, and cyclists. Higher injury gravity raised total costs for all groups, with age, prior health, pain catastrophizing, and coma scores mattering for certain groups. Policymakers gain group-specific targets for prevention and support.
pmc-13501793:
Seyyed Ruhollah Seyyediyan, Mansureh Ghavam, and Ali Tavili report a 2026 field and laboratory study of spearmint essential oil in the mountains around Kashan, Iran. Mentha spicata, locally called Naana Dashti, is used traditionally for breathing and digestive complaints, and its oil is an industrial product. The team collected plants at four sites, Barzok, Hosnarood, Kamoo, and Viduj, distilled the oil with a Clevenger apparatus, and profiled it by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. They tested antibacterial strength by diffusion and dilution methods.

Oil yield swung widely, from 5.04 percent at Hosnarood down to 1.08 percent at Kamoo, tracking altitude and the water plants could draw from the soil. Carvone dominated everywhere, peaking at 63.98 percent in Viduj oil and bottoming near 46.85 percent at Barzok in the site comparison. Barzok oil hit Bacillus subtilis hardest, while Kamoo oil led against E. coli. Site choice, the authors argue, decides oil quality.
pmc-13503693:
Shanshan Yi and a large team study why cloned placentas grow poorly, in a 2026 paper. Cloning by nuclear transfer often yields placentas with grave faults, yet the cause has stayed unclear. The placenta moves food and oxygen from mother to fetus, so its faults shape the whole pregnancy.

The team mapped single cell cores and found that early placental cells stall and keep traits they should shed. Blood vessel growth signals were weak, so the exchange zone formed poorly. They trace the faults to DNA damage picked up during reprogramming, tied to loss of a protective mark from the donor cell. When repair paths were boosted, cell growth and vessel transport both improved.
pmc-13504993:
Shangjie Zheng leads a team mapping low-risk HPV infection among women screened in Jingzhou, central China, in a 2026 study. Low-risk types of the virus cause warts rather than cancer, yet their local patterns guide vaccine and screening choices. Regional data for this city were lacking.

Records covered more than twenty-four thousand women tested over three years for 27 virus types. One in ten carried a low-risk type. Three types led the list, HPV81, HPV61, and HPV44, while the classically common wart types were rare. Rates peaked in the youngest women and in those over sixty, a two-humped age curve. Most women carried a single type. The authors urge prevention plans built on local type patterns.
pmc-13505093:
Jie Tao leads a team showing how low oxygen and lactate switch off a protective protein in lung adenocarcinoma, in a 2026 study. The protein, SIRT2, had been cast as both friend and foe in lung cancer, which muddied its value. The team set out to learn what controls it and what it does.

In tumor tissue the protein ran low, and low levels tracked with poor outlook for this lung subtype alone. Low oxygen raised lactate, which pushed SIRT2 down. Cells stripped of SIRT2 grew and spread faster in dishes and in mice; extra SIRT2 did the reverse. The protein binds fuel-burning enzymes and strips their tags; without it, one enzyme's tag at a key spot raised sugar burning sharply. Many other fuel paths shifted as well.
pmc-13505293:
Pandya and colleagues synthesized a family of radical probes for magnetic resonance by building a pyridine ring into the trityl framework, in a 2026 chemistry study. Trityl radicals, long-lived molecules with an unpaired electron, are prized as oxygen sensors and polarization agents because their resonance lines are narrow and they survive in fluids. All existing versions use benzene-based arms, limiting ways to tune them.

Pandya's versions produced a three-line resonance signature from the ring's nitrogen atom while keeping the narrow line widths that make these probes useful. Water-friendly derivatives dissolved better and stuck less to the blood protein albumin, a source of signal distortion. The probe stayed stable in air-saturated buffer at room temperature, and its line broadened with oxygen at a sensitivity for measuring tissue oxygen levels. The authors present heteroatom rings as a tuning strategy for biomedical magnetic resonance probes.
pmc-13506793:
Yuma Togashi and colleagues present a 2026 case report of stubborn lymph fluid leakage after thigh sarcoma surgery in a 53-year-old man. Wide removal of a myxoid liposarcoma also took the femoral artery and vein, later rebuilt with a vein graft and flap cover. Drainage and pressure care failed to stop the leak.

Early joining of surface lymph vessels to small veins did not help, and a placed tissue graft failed. Special scans showed the leak came from the deep lymph system. Joining deep vessels to veins at three sites cut drain output from about 200 to 19 milliliters per day within a week. Scans then showed no leak, with no return within 94 days.
pmc-13508193:
Selvarajan Valsa Shiby Kripa leads an eight-author team exploring how people in Kerala, India, cope with living with several long-term illnesses at once, in 2026 work. Care for multiple conditions can pile up visits, drugs, and costs until the load outruns what a person can manage. The team held in-depth interviews with 42 such patients in primary care clinics. Answers were read through two frameworks that weigh treatment burden against patient capacity.

Illness complexity, money strain, and cultural habits all shrank patients' room to cope. Family support, reachable care, and a hopeful outlook expanded it. Clinics tended to treat single diseases in slices, which added to the burden. Paying out of pocket for medicines was a sharp pain point. The authors say services should be designed around total load, not single conditions, if patients are to keep up with care.
pmc-13508293:
Jingyan Li and six co-authors examine a protein called SPP1 in head and neck cancers and its link to spread into lymph nodes, in 2026 work. Node spread is a key marker of poor outlook in these cancers. Public data sets first showed how SPP1 levels relate to tumor features and patient survival. The team then checked forty surgical samples, covering normal tissue, tumors that stayed local, and tumors that had spread to nodes. Lab tests used gene silencing and extra protein to probe effects on cancer cell growth and invasion.

SPP1 ran much higher in tumor tissue than in nearby normal tissue. High levels tracked with node spread, later stage, and worse survival. Gene reading in silenced cells pointed to a signaling route involving two well-known growth switches. The authors cast SPP1 as both a warning marker and a possible drug target for these cancers.
pmc-13508393:
Yu Li, Qingyu Dai, Guoxiang Liu, and Qian Xiong sequence the chloroplast genomes of nine green algae to settle a family tree dispute, in 2026 work. The algal order Oedogoniales holds over 600 species in three genera, sorted mainly by shape traits like branching and hairs. A past proposal split the largest genus by the shape of its base cell into two sections. The team sequenced four genomes from one section and five from the other, then compared their full gene sets.

The nine genomes kept the same structure and gene count known for the order, with modest variety in size and repeats. Family trees built from 64 shared genes backed the two-section split by base cell shape. Twenty-seven genes evolved at different speeds between sections, and three showed signs of positive selection. The authors read the round-based section as a fast-spreading group that kept older traits.
pmc-13509193:
Mengru Cai leads an eleven-author review of plant-made nanoparticles as delivery trucks for cancer drugs, in 2026 work. These particles, squeezed from edible and medicinal plants, are natural sacs carrying fats, proteins, genetic scraps, and plant chemicals. The review asks what shapes their quality: which plant they come from, how they are isolated and cleaned, how cargo is loaded, and how they are given. Gentler column and filter methods give purer batches and a better path to factory scale.

Stronger loading tricks like electric pulses or sound waves pack more cargo yet can clump or damage the sacs. Lab and animal studies suggest the particles can fight tumors, retune the tumor neighborhood, and ferry standard drugs. Proof that they home to tumors in living bodies is weaker than proof they enter cells, the authors stress. Shared naming, making standards, and safety tests must come before clinic use.
pmc-13510893:
Pedro Alexander Velasquez-Vasconez, Marina de Lima Nogueira, Carlos Betancourth García, Claudia Elizabeth Salazar-González, and Angie Fernanda Riascos-España study rice plants with two protective genes turned down, in 2026 work. The genes make enzymes that clear harmful peroxides and help manage the cell's redox balance, meaning its mix of damaging and protective chemistry. The team compared normal plants with five silenced lines for growth, enzyme activity, and DNA methylation, a chemical tagging system that helps set gene activity.

Silenced plants started poorly, flowered late, and built far less leaf, root, seed, and total mass, with roots hit hardest. Activity shifted for the target enzymes and one partner enzyme, while three other defense enzymes stayed unchanged. Total methylation fell by about two fifths in silenced groups, yet detailed digestion tests showed the changes were uneven across the genome rather than uniform.
pmc-13513493:
Aslı Doğan Sarıkaya measures sex differences in the back plate and wing covers of a Turkish longhorn beetle using both classic and shape-based methods, in 2026 work. The beetle, Dorcadion parilis, is flightless, found only in Turkey, and sits in a genus where species lines are hard to draw. Eighty-five specimens were measured, and raw sizes were also compared after adjusting for body size.

Some raw gaps between males and females weakened or vanished once size was accounted for. Relatively longer back plates in males and broader wing covers in females stayed as the clearest classic patterns. Shape analysis exposed further differences hidden from rulers, spread widely across the back plate yet localized on the wing covers. The two structures also changed shape in a coordinated way. The author says splitting size, proportion, and shape gives taxonomists a cleaner base for this tricky genus.
pmc-13514193:
Tiziana Ruggiero and eight co-authors pool patient-level data from two randomized trials of hyaluronic acid gels boosted with amino acids for healing after tooth extraction in people with diabetes, in 2026 work. Diabetes slows wound repair, and mouth surgery is a common test bed. Each trial paired the gel against its own control, and one formula carried six amino acids that feed collagen building while the other carried a different set.

Healing scores improved over time across the pooled group. Against its matched control, the six-amino-acid formula produced a clearly larger healing gain over time than the rival formula, after age and diabetes duration were counted. Neither age nor how long a patient had lived with diabetes bent the healing path in a reliable way. The authors say amino acid choice inside the gel matters more than patient age for early socket healing.
pmc-13518093:
Mohamed and co-authors review a quiet convention behind kidney testing: results are scaled to a standard body surface area. Their 2026 paper traces why glomerular filtration rate, the kidney's filtering speed, is reported per 1.73 square metres of body surface. That indexing lets clinicians compare people of different sizes and stage chronic kidney disease consistently.

The authors argue the indexed number is not always the right one. For drug dosing, the non-indexed value, reflecting actual clearance, should be preferred. They also discuss transplant decisions and patients whose weight changes severely, where indexing can mislead. Alternative scalings based on lean body mass or body water look theoretically attractive but show no established clinical benefit. For general assessment and monitoring, they conclude, body-surface indexing remains the clinical standard.
pmc-13518793:
Claudia Ollauri-Ibáñez and seven colleagues ask in 2026 whether high levels of endoglin, a protein also called CD105 that helps blood vessels grow, mark lung tumors that resist immunotherapy. Such resistant tumors are often called cold because few killer T cells enter them and suppressive cells dominate.

Using mice engineered to overproduce human endoglin, the team grew lung tumors that showed more oxygen shortage and fewer CD8 T cells. The tumors also carried more suppressive M2 macrophages and regulatory T cells than normal-mouse tumors. Human lung adenocarcinoma samples told the same story, with cold tumors carrying higher endoglin. The protein could help doctors predict immunotherapy response and tailor treatment.
pmc-13518893:
Satoshi Ikemura leads an eleven-author comparison in 2026 of two stem designs used in cementless hip replacement. Fractures around the thigh implant and sinking of the stem are the main early complications, yet head-to-head evidence adjusting for patient differences was scarce. Records covered 753 fit-and-fill stems and 526 tapered-wedge stems.

Propensity matching balanced age, sex, body mass, and bone shape, leaving 478 operations in each group. Fractures during surgery occurred in 2.3 percent of fit-and-fill cases versus 0.6 percent with tapered wedges. Stem sinking of at least 2 millimeters hit 7.2 percent versus 1.5 percent. Ikemura and colleagues conclude tapered-wedge stems carry lower early risk.
pmc-13520193:
Jie Xiong leads a nine-author review in 2026 of what predicts failure when doctors try to unfold a child's telescoped bowel with a fluid enema instead of surgery. Ileocolic intussusception is a common pediatric emergency, and ultrasound-guided hydrostatic reduction succeeded in 199 of 231 children treated at two centers between 2021 and 2025.

Five factors independently predicted failure: age under 12 months, symptoms lasting over 48 hours, a previous episode, constipation, and bowel wall thickening on ultrasound. Each carried a large odds ratio in the adjusted model. Every child ultimately recovered uneventfully. Xiong and colleagues advise early surgical consultation or transfer for children showing these warning signs.
pmc-13520293:
Bo Dong, Li Wang and Yifan Li present a 2026 study of depression patterns among older adults living in rural China. Using survey data from 2022, they group people by symptom pattern rather than by a single total score, then ask which health and daily-life factors separate the groups.

Records for 3,114 older adults yielded four groups, ranging from low symptoms to high risk. Long-term illness, body discomfort, poor self-rated health, higher medical costs and smoking marked the higher-risk groups. Daily exercise marked lower risk. Network maps placed discomfort and self-rated health near the centre, which helps readers see which factors travel together.
pmc-13522393:
Mahani and colleagues tracked how brain network connections change over four weeks after two kinds of stroke in mice, asking whether lesion size and location steer the trajectory. Their 2026 study used resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging, which infers connections from synchronized activity. Scans ran at one, two, and four weeks after either a small surface stroke or a larger stroke reaching deep brain structures.

Mahani found opposite patterns. The small cortical stroke triggered over-connection in the first two weeks, with about nine in ten connections strengthened, before partial normalization. The larger cortico-striatal stroke caused widespread under-connection from week one that largely persisted at week four. movement-network connections changed in opposite directions between the models and separated the groups at every time point. Larger lesion involvement meant larger connectivity shifts, suggesting timing and targets for network-rebalancing therapies after stroke.
pmc-13522593:
Yue Ma and Liangke Cao propose a deep learning model for judging staff performance in tourism firms in a 2026 study. Performance data in tourism shift quickly and involve many linked criteria, which makes older static methods unstable. A twenty-four-item index was built from literature and interviews with more than three hundred managers and employees at four firms, followed by expert screening.

The model updates its weights continuously, smooths them across network layers, and carries past learning forward through a momentum mechanism. Tests on data from the four firms showed deviations staying within a narrow band and close agreement with historical records. Under heavy load and unstable network conditions, the model beat two fuzzy decision methods on accuracy and speed, supporting real-time performance management.
pmc-13522693:
Ying Luu, Hamid Hajmomenian, and Reza Khorsan present a case report, published in 2026. It describes one woman in her seventies with end-stage kidney disease. Her blood became dangerously alkaline. This is the opposite of the acid build-up typical in kidney failure. Her alkalemia came mainly from over-breathing. Over-breathing blows off acid as carbon dioxide.

She received regular haemodialysis. The team could treat the problem through the dialysis fluid. They lowered its bicarbonate level. Her blood chemistry was gently pulled back toward normal. The case shows a flexible lever for clinicians. Dialysate adjustment can address rare acid-base emergencies in dialysis patients.
pmc-13522793:
Chen Zhang and colleagues engineer a probiotic bacterium to deliver gene editing into the gut in a 2026 study of inflammatory bowel disease. The disease involves excess reactive oxygen species, unstable molecules that damage the intestinal barrier. A harmless gut bacterium was equipped with CRISPR editing tools aimed at a gene that helps produce those reactive molecules, then wrapped in a protective gel for oral delivery.

The gel raised bacterial survival sharply in tests. In immune cells, the system cut the target gene's expression by nearly half and reduced reactive molecules by most of their level. In mice with induced colitis, oral treatment eased inflammation and activated protective pathways that boosted antioxidant defenses. The authors present the living delivery system as a promising strategy for bowel inflammation.
pmc-13523193:
Nusrat Jahan Mim leads a team measuring obesity among women working in small and cottage industries in Bangladesh in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Three hundred fifty workers aged eighteen to sixty were interviewed across handloom, shrimp, pottery, and stitched textile sectors between 2023 and 2024. Height and weight were measured directly, with obesity defined by a regional body mass threshold.

Thirty-six percent of the women met the obesity definition. In adjusted analysis, obesity linked to middle age, sedentary work, sitting for eight or more hours daily, stomach complaints, physical inactivity, and long screen time. Daily soft and energy drink consumption also raised the odds. The authors note that purposive site selection limits wider generalizability and call attention to an understudied workforce beyond the garment industry.
pmc-13523293:
Chengwei Li and colleagues review how lung injury early in life may affect brain development in a 2026 article framed around a lung-brain axis. Conditions such as chronic lung disease of prematurity, childhood asthma, repeated chest infections, and tobacco smoke exposure are each linked to higher risk. The risks cover thinking skills, autism-related traits, attention, and emotional disorders. The developing brain is especially sensitive during infancy and childhood.

Several connected pathways are described. Low oxygen and oxidative stress can disturb white matter formation. Lung vessel injury can disrupt brain energy supply. Body-wide inflammation can weaken the blood-brain barrier, and lung inflammation can trigger brain inflammation. The authors urge clinicians to add developmental screening and early intervention to the care of children with early lung disease.
pmc-13524193:
Jonathan C. Horton reports, in a 2026 case account, the euthanasia of a lab macaque that began harming itself in a vision neuroscience lab. Such conduct in primates is poorly grasped, with sparse settings, limited social contact, lack of novelty, nursery rearing, and temperament all possible causes. The threshold for euthanasia is rarely debated.

The healthy five year old monkey was put down eleven days after the behavior began. Bouts took up about half a percent of the time and scored in the mild category of a national primate center scale. Horton reviews possible causes, attempts to help, and the choice, then urges management steps for future cases. He argues that euthanasia wait until behavior reaches moderate or severe levels, so milder cases get fuller chances at recovery.
pmc-13524593:
Agnieszka Kaczmarska-Such and Adam Reich propose, in a 2026 review, a framework that treats chronic itch as a neuroimmune disorder rather than a simple skin feeling. Research history moved from histamine and mast cells to nerve circuits and then to cytokine signaling, yet no single signal explains lasting itch.

Their model, called the immunopathogenic spiral of itch, links barrier damage, immune firing, and nerve rewiring into layers that feed on themselves. Histamine signaling, sensory neurons, type 2 immune skewing, an IL-17 pathway, and a shared JAK-STAT signaling hub are treated as linked layers, not rivals. The framework helps explain why single target drugs give real but incomplete relief, and it supports multi target treatment plans for chronic pruritus.
pmc-13524793:
Shuangqing Wang leads a large team in a 2026 study revealing an unexpected route for energy transfer in purple photosynthetic bacteria. Light harvesting depends on carotenoid and bacteriochlorophyll pigments passing captured energy swiftly to reaction centers. The complementary colors they absorb make their teamwork central to photosynthesis.

The team shows that transfer can run through singlet fission, where one high-energy singlet excitation splits into two lower-energy triplet excitations. In these bacteria, a carotenoid singlet splits into triplet excitations sitting on neighboring carotenoid and bacteriochlorophyll sites. The long-lived, spin-protected triplet pair then transfers cooperatively onward to bacteriochlorophyll and the reaction center. Because the path starts and ends in singlet states, it adds a protected detour that augments solar harvesting, with implications for artificial light-harvesting design.
pmc-13524893:
Evelyn Iriarte leads a large team in a 2026 cross-sectional analysis linking neighborhood conditions, mapped from home addresses, with physical function in older people with HIV. This group loses function and becomes frail faster than peers without HIV. Baseline data came from an exercise trial enrolling 120 sedentary adults aged fifty or older at sites in Colorado and Washington.

Function measures included a 400-meter walk, chair rise time, a self-report scale, daily steps, and frailty status. In Colorado, higher neighborhood deprivation tracked with slower chair rises. In Washington, higher social vulnerability tracked with slower walks, and frailer participants lived farther from parks. Pooled results showed frailer participants in more vulnerable neighborhoods. The authors call for larger studies to guide place-based interventions.
pmc-13525093:
Tripathy and colleagues describe a single striking case from 2026: a fifty-nine-year-old man whose acute hepatitis E infection set off three separate immune complications during one hospital stay. Hepatitis E is a liver infection usually spread through contaminated water, and it normally clears on its own. In this patient, the immune response turned against his own blood cells, immune system, and nerves in sequence.

He arrived with autoimmune hemolytic anemia, a condition where antibodies destroy red blood cells, and within a week he developed secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, a dangerous immune overactivation. On day seventeen he developed Guillain-Barré syndrome, where immune attack on nerves causes weakness. The team treated each complication as it appeared, and the man recovered completely. They present the case as a warning that hepatitis E can trigger a chain of immune disorders needing close monitoring.
pmc-13526093:
Glen M. Blake leads a large team in a 2026 analysis of the REASURE study. Two scan measures were compared, a simple uptake value and a metabolic flux measure, against MRI diffusion changes as a reference for tumor response.

Thirty-four men received up to six radium cycles, with scans and MRI at baseline and at four, twelve, and twenty-four weeks. Diffusion values rose while both PET measures fell over time. Baseline uptake and radium dose predicted the MRI response, yet changes in the PET measures failed to track MRI changes at any point. The authors warn that falling uptake after therapy likely reflects effects on bone-forming cells, not tumor kill.
pmc-13526793:
Dong and a large team open a nose-to-brain drug route in this 2026 study of glioblastoma, the most aggressive brain tumor, in mice. The nasal lining normally blocks drugs bound for the brain. So the team used low-intensity pulsed ultrasound to loosen its tight junctions for a time. Then they sent in engineered vesicles carrying two immune drugs. One is a PD-L1 antibody. The other is the beta-blocker carvedilol, which fights T-cell exhaustion.

Reactivated T cells shrank tumors by 40 percent, extended survival, and left long-term immune memory in the treated mice. The vesicles, cloaked in macrophage membrane, needed no microbubbles to work. The authors present the approach as a general platform for delivering biologics to the brain.
pmc-13527993:
Claudia Herrera-deGuise and ten colleagues measure fungi in stool samples from ulcerative colitis patients in a 2026 prospective study. Gut bacteria get most research attention in this disease. Fungi are far less studied. The team counted fungal and bacterial gene copies in three groups. Twenty-nine patients were in long remission, twenty in short remission, and thirty-eight were flaring.

Fungal copies were vastly outnumbered by bacterial ones in every sample. The ratio was about one to 461,000. Still, fungal counts were higher during flares than in long remission. The fungal share also rose in flare samples versus both remission groups. Bacterial loads stayed steady across states. Over eight weeks the fungal ratio dipped modestly. The authors say fungal shifts track disease activity and deserve study alongside bacteria.
pmc-13528093:
Miguel Marcelo Freire de Melo and seven colleagues report leprosy mistaken for lupus in a 2026 case study and review. Leprosy can copy the skin, joint, and lab signs of systemic lupus erythematosus. Most patients were women, with a median age of thirty-five. Every patient had skin signs. Butterfly rash, sun sensitivity, and nodules were common. Joints were hit in about seventy-eight percent of cases. Nerve signs appeared in about forty-three percent. Most had tested positive for antinuclear antibodies. Two-thirds met formal lupus criteria before the truth emerged. Nearly half waited over a year for the right call. The authors give clues: nerve damage and poor response to immune drugs should raise doubt.
pmc-13531793:
Murat Celebi and co-authors test in 2026 whether a citrus plant compound called hesperidin shields rat testes from the drug gentamicin. Hesperidin softened most of those shifts, restored protective enzymes, and revived a growth signaling pathway that the drug had quieted. Sperm quality improved in parallel, supporting a protective role.
pmc-13531893:

Bilibili videos scored higher than TikTok videos on both scales. Videos from professional sources beat amateur ones clearly, and professional origin predicted quality most strongly in adjusted models. Length and sharing mattered weakly at best. Overall quality stayed below par, prompting calls for tighter platform review.
pmc-13536693:
Kübranur Çebi Karaaslan and colleagues analyze barriers to health care among older adults in Türkiye in a 2026 study using a nationally representative 2023 survey. A statistical model links reported difficulty reaching care to income, daily function, health status, and practical problems such as booking visits and moving inside clinics. Adults who rated their health as good or moderate reported fewer problems, as did high school and university graduates and adults who did not live alone. The authors urge health policy that targets literacy, transport, and clinic access together.
pmc-13538493:
Ronghua Wang and colleagues examine how health anxiety links disease views to self-care in bowel inflammation disease in a 2026 hospital survey. Older patients and those ill for over five years scored lower on self-care, while higher income scored higher. Mediation modeling split direct and anxiety-carried paths.

Most of the perception effect ran direct, with a smaller yet real share carried through anxiety. The authors suggest adding mental assessment and support to routine bowel care, while noting that one-time data cannot prove cause.
pmc-13538693:
Jingyue Guo and colleagues pin down social and mind factors tied to taking drugs as told among older adults in a 2026 survey study. A total of 1,102 adults aged 60 years or older on long-term treatment filled proven scales on drug habits, drug know-how, beliefs, self-belief, and social support under a behavior change frame. Higher self-belief and drug know-how each lowered the odds of poor drug taking. Stronger worry beliefs about drugs raised those odds, as did past bad drug reactions in the final model. Living alone or with children, versus with a spouse, sharply raised poor taking odds. The authors advise joined support spanning teaching, self-belief building, and social backing.
pmc-13539893:
Changjian Lin and eight colleagues test, in a 2026 pilot study, a new way to sample swollen glands inside the chest when doctors suspect a benign cause. Needle sampling through an ultrasound bronchoscope often returns too little tissue to name conditions such as sarcoidosis.

Fourteen patients first had needle sampling, then a biopsy taken with small forceps passed through a tract opened by an electric knife at the same spot. The forceps method produced a diagnosis in twelve patients, against three for the needle alone, and accuracy rose sharply. No serious bleeding, lung collapse, or infection occurred. The authors urge larger trials before the method enters routine care.
pmc-13543493:
Yuqiong Yang and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study of pain catastrophizing, the tendency to magnify pain and feel helpless against it, in women giving birth vaginally. Participants were 282 women at a hospital in Sichuan Province, China, assessed during the latent phase of labour and again in the second stage. Questionnaires measured catastrophizing, pain intensity, social support, mood, and confidence in coping with pain.

About twenty-nine percent of women met the catastrophizing threshold at each stage. Risk rose with longer gestation, stronger pain, and depressive symptoms. Confidence in coping protected against it, and women accompanied by someone other than their husband were more likely to catastrophize than those with a husband present. Cross-lagged analysis probed whether pain drives catastrophizing or the reverse. Screening for this mindset during labour, the authors imply, could identify women who need extra support before pain spirals.
pmc-13543593:
Mackingsley Kushan Dassanayake's team studied Cleistanthus bracteosus in 2026, a tree of Malaysian rainforests, as a source of germ-fighting compounds and antibiotic helpers. Extracts of bark, stem, and wood were made in three solvents and tested against seven harmful germs, alone and paired with standard antibiotics. The most active extract was split into parts and its makeup charted, and treated bacteria were viewed by electron microscopy.

The chloroform stem extract worked best alone, chiefly against Bacillus cereus. Pairings shone brighter: wood extract with ampicillin strongly blocked the stubborn Acinetobacter baumannii, and a clavulanate partner gave wide clear zones against E. coli and Salmonella typhi. Lab analysis found twenty bioactive plant compounds in the chloroform extracts, among known groups such as flavonoids and tannins. Rainforest plants, the authors argue, may rescue failing antibiotics rather than replace them.
pmc-13545793:
Yilin Chen and colleagues explored in 2026 how medical trainees in a Chinese program for rural practice come to see themselves as doctors. Trainees in such low-resource tracks often leave early, and a weak professional identity is part of the problem. The researchers ran nine focus groups with 42 trainees at different training stages and analyzed the conversations for recurring themes.

Eleven themes emerged, grouped into society, relationships, and the individual. Working conditions and policy sit in the first group, role models and patients in the second, and reflection and personal values in the third. Identity appears to shift over training from outside pressures toward internal commitments, though early outside experiences weigh heavily. The framework is offered as a guide for programs trying to keep rural doctors.
pmc-13547293:
Sümeyye Şen-Alpay and colleagues tracked listeners' eyes in 2026 to see whether pupils and gaze follow the rhythm of natural speech, and whether the emotion in a voice changes that following. One hundred volunteers first rated segments of two TED talks for pleasantness and intensity, confirming the talks swung widely in mood. Forty-one others then listened while pupil size and eye movements were recorded.

Every eye signal tracked the slow rhythm of speech. Intense passages strengthened pupil tracking while weakening gaze tracking, and negative passages strengthened tracking in pupils and vertical eye movements. The listener's own mood and empathy bent the patterns further. The authors read the eyes as active sensing tools that tune themselves to emotional speech.
pmc-13547393:
Seonghu Jung and Do-Kyeong Ko demonstrated in 2026 a faster way to characterize quantum states carried by twisted light, where each photon's spiral pattern can encode far more than a single bit. The standard approach counts rare photon pairs one coincidence at a time, so measurements crawl, especially for high-dimensional states. Their alternative, stimulated emission tomography, shines a bright seed beam through the same process and reads the amplified result.

Rebuilding the state from these bright measurements gave a fidelity of about 91 percent against the expected state, with each projection taking a single second. The reconstructed state's purity measures matched theory well. The authors present the technique as an efficient replacement for slow tomography in quantum optics laboratories.
pmc-13547993:
Fedor Moiseenko and a large Russian team asked in 2026 whether cutting out leftover tumor masses during targeted drug treatment helps patients with EGFR-mutated lung cancer live longer. These patients normally stay on mutation-blocking pills until the disease progresses. The retrospective study covered 230 people with locally advanced or spread disease on first-line therapy. Of these, 57 looked operable and 41 actually had surgery after a median of about seven months on the drug.

No one died from the surgery, though about a fifth had complications. Operated patients went a median of about 28 months before progression and lived about 47 months overall, clearly ahead of comparable patients who were not operated on. Resistant clones already lurked in some removed tissue. Nearly a third of operated patients remained disease-free at analysis.
pmc-13548493:
C. M. Dieteren and colleagues report a 2026 qualitative study of maternal mental health in western Kenya. Mothers, fathers, nurses, and community health workers from three hospitals in Kisumu County took part in ten focus group discussions. The team asked what drives distress during and after pregnancy, what blocks women from seeking help, and what kinds of emotional support people would accept.

Participants largely agreed on the main pressures, naming poverty, stigma, partner violence, and weak social support. Fathers raised household disputes that mothers did not stress, while nurses focused on medical effects and community workers took a broader view. Groups favored care led by community health workers, offered in groups with partners included. Their answers shaped an intervention later tested in the same setting.
pmc-13548593:
Melinda M. Ashcroft and colleagues track infections from environmental mycobacteria among First Nations people in Queensland, Australia, in a 2026 analysis of laboratory notifications. These bacteria live in soil and water and cause lung and other infections, while First Nations communities carry higher illness burdens and face barriers to care. The team examined records spanning more than two decades, calculating rates by region and comparing them with the non-Indigenous population.

Notifications rose steeply, reaching a rate more than five times higher in 2024 than in 2011. Lung infections dominated, and one prison outbreak of a fast-growing species drove a sharp jump in non-lung cases after 2020. The absolute rate stayed below the non-Indigenous figure, yet it climbed more than four times faster, which the authors read as under-detection. They call for culturally appropriate surveillance and quicker diagnostic access.
pmc-13548693:
Erin Nolan and colleagues rerun two completed school trials inside a computer simulation to test a leaner trial design, in a 2026 methods study. Trials that fine-tune strategies for delivering programs, such as getting schools to run physical activity sessions, are slow and cluster-hungry. The team merged two earlier cluster trials of the PACE program into one virtual three-arm trial, then let Bayesian adaptive rules drop arms or stop early along the way.

Every adaptive version stopped early and crowned the cheaper strategy best, matching the original trials' verdict while needing half to a quarter fewer schools and about forty percent less time. A catch appeared: early schools happened to be Catholic schools that favored the cheaper option, skewing interim decisions. Balancing school types at each checkpoint shrank that bias. The authors endorse adaptive designs with demographic guardrails.
pmc-13550093:
Andres Heigl and colleagues compare set rapid-recovery care in planned versus emergency bowel surgery, in a 2026 registry analysis. Enhanced recovery plans cut complications and stays after planned bowel operations, yet emergencies arrive unstable with no time to prepare the patient, so their place there was doubtful. The team studied more than eight hundred cases from audit records spanning 2016 to 2024. They then matched emergency and planned-surgery patients two to one on background risk.

Emergency patients followed the plan less fully than planned-surgery ones, about seventy-one percent against seventy-six percent adherence. They also needed open surgery more often.
