Despite that handicap, rates of leaking bowel joins, major organ problems, and death matched the planned group. The authors conclude emergency recovery care can work. They argue for care plans written just for the emergency setting.
pmc-13550493:
Chiung-Ray Lu and colleagues test whether the gut microbiome can betray a hidden blood clot in the deep veins, in a 2026 case-control study. Deep vein thrombosis often stays silent, and current tests lack precision. Stool came from fifty-eight clot patients, fifty-six heart disease patients, and five hundred healthy controls, all sequenced at species level. A random forest model then learned to separate clot cases three ways: using microbes alone, clinical data alone, or both together.

The combined model clearly beat the clinical-only model on discrimination. Ninety-five candidate microbial features were winnowed to ten that carried the signal, and the microbial pattern stayed tied to clot risk after accounting for clinical factors. Pathways for making vitamin K2 and bacterial endotoxin ran hot in clot patients, hinting at microbial routes into clotting and inflammation. Healthy guts instead favored vitamin-making pathways.
pmc-13551193:
Cody Spadaccini and Kai Schweizer published a 2026 first-person account of conversion practices in hospital care. Such practices try to change a person's gender or sexuality. They are linked to faith settings, yet they can occur in health care too. Spadaccini tells of his stay in an eating disorder unit as a young trans man. He maps the events to agreed definitions of conversion practices.

Staff treated his gender as an illness, he reports. Coercion and ward power enforced cisgender norms. Gender-affirming care was delayed, withheld, or framed as a problem. Lasting harm and a long pull away from care followed. The pair call for safeguards in inpatient units and for affirming eating disorder care.
pmc-13551693:
Tengfei Qi, leading five colleagues, published a 2026 mouse study of how gastric bypass surgery reshapes fat tissue. Roux-en-Y bypass reliably improves obesity and type 2 diabetes, yet the fat changes behind that benefit are incompletely understood. Obese diabetic mice were assigned to bypass, sham surgery, or no surgery, then followed for eight weeks with body composition scans and tissue examination.

Bypass mice lost weight steadily, normalized blood sugar, and improved insulin sensitivity and blood lipids, losing fat while preserving lean mass. Their white fat cells shrank across depots, a pattern the authors read as browning toward a more active, brown-like state, while brown fat reversed its obesity-related whitening. Liver fat also eased, supporting fat plasticity as a central mechanism.
pmc-13551793:
Ian W Baumgart, leading eleven colleagues, published a 2026 case report of a wearable sleeve that delivers intention-timed electrical stimulation to stroke survivors' arms. Functional electrical stimulation can retrain movement, especially when timed to the user's own effort and practiced across several tasks. The NeuroLife sleeve packs a dense electrode grid into a forearm garment, switchable by software and triggerable by the wearer's muscle signals.

Two people with chronic stroke trained for eight weeks, twice weekly under operator control and once weekly under their own muscle signals. Both improved on standard arm and hand tests in the reported scores, with one regaining a peg test previously impossible, and gains held through ten weeks of much reduced therapy. The authors call it proof of concept.
pmc-13552593:
Ana Morillo Palomo and three colleagues report a 2026 Spanish study of parents whose babies died in newborn intensive care. Fifty-one babies died after care turned toward comfort alone. Of 102 parents who could take part, fifty-two filled in a structured survey. Questions covered how news was shared, how choices were made, and how comfort care felt.

Parents rated honest, gentle communication very highly, at a mean near the top of the scale. Most wanted guidance from staff while still sharing in the choice. Yet only half felt the final choice matched what they had wanted. Chances to pick where death occurred were rare. The authors stress time to think, steady support, and a real chance to say goodbye.
pmc-13556093:
Liping Ning and five colleagues gather risk factors for kidney injury after surgery for Stanford type A aortic dissection in China. Postoperative acute kidney injury threatens recovery, yet its drivers in Chinese patients were scattered across studies. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis searches eight databases through September 2025. It pools 47 studies covering 9,077 patients.

Older age, higher body mass, hypertension history, renal artery involvement, cardiac tamponade before surgery, and raised creatinine, myoglobin, and cystatin C all linked to kidney injury. Longer bypass, operative, arrest, and clamp times, transfusion volume, and ventilation time also linked, while higher urine output protected. Evidence certainty was mostly low or very low. The findings still map warning signs for clinicians.
pmc-13557793:
Zijing Huang and colleagues hunted for the mechanism by which cordycepin, a compound from Cordyceps fungi, attacks stomach cancer, publishing the study in 2026. Gastric cancer remains common and deadly once advanced, and cordycepin had shown anti-tumour effects without a clear target. The team combined gene-expression data from stomach tumours with a database of cordycepin targets, narrowing 649 tumour genes and 336 candidate targets to one key intersection.

That gene, fibronectin 1, was overactive in tumours and linked to poorer survival. Cordycepin slowed cancer-cell growth, triggered cell death, and lowered fibronectin 1 while switching off a growth pathway, and forcing fibronectin 1 back on reversed those effects. The work names fibronectin 1 as a promising new target for cordycepin-based stomach-cancer treatment.
pmc-13558593:
Anning Wang and five colleagues surveyed in 2026 more than a thousand teenagers to see how exercise relates to fitting in socially. Social adaptability matters for adolescent wellbeing, and the team tested whether confidence and resilience carry the effect of exercise. A total of 1,280 adolescents completed surveys, and path analysis sorted direct links from indirect ones.

Exercise showed a modest direct link with social adaptability. Three indirect routes also proved real: through self-confidence alone, through resilience alone, and through a chain in which exercise raised confidence, confidence raised resilience, and resilience lifted social adaptability. The resilience route carried the largest share. Because the survey captures one moment, the authors speak of links rather than proof of cause. Schools aiming at social gains, they suggest, might pair sport with confidence and coping building.
pmc-13558893:
Aye M Thaw and seven colleagues modelled in 2026 the web linking traits, resilience, and two kinds of compassion to depression in older stroke survivors. Post-stroke depression is common and drags down recovery, yet how these inner strengths connect was unmapped. Their study enrolled 142 survivors aged fifty and over from clinics at Chiang Mai University Hospital in Thailand. Standard scales captured every construct, and a chain of path models sorted the links.

Neuroticism linked to more depression and less resilience, while resilience itself linked to fewer symptoms. Part of that harm passed through eroded resilience. That path hinged on compassion levels: kindness toward others eased the link between resilience and low mood. Self-compassion in turn changed how compassion acted. The authors suggest rehab programmes should build resilience and both forms of compassion rather than treating mood alone.
pmc-13559093:
Du and colleagues describe infant-onset inflammatory bowel disease in northern Chinese children, a severe form of gut inflammation beginning in the first years of life, in a 2026 ten-year retrospective study. Beijing Children's Hospital treated 98 such children between January 2016 and December 2025. Records were sorted into Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis patterns, and 77 children received genetic testing to separate single-gene causes from ordinary inflammatory disease, which responds differently to treatment.

Sixty-four children, 65.3 percent of the cohort, showed the Crohn's pattern, against 34 with the ulcerative colitis pattern overall. Median onset age was just 4 months for the whole group. Perianal lesions and penetrating disease behavior occurred significantly more often in the Crohn's group. Genetic testing found definite single-gene mutations in 39 of the 77 children tested, a share of 50.6 percent in that subgroup. Du argues early genetic testing should be routine, since monogenic cases need different management.
pmc-13559293:
Taiwei Sun and colleagues set out to map how tumors evolve inside treatment-naive small cell lung cancer, a fast-growing cancer where inner diversity fuels drug resistance. Their 2026 analysis used whole-exome sequencing from 41 patients who had not yet received treatment. A probabilistic model sorted each tumor's cell populations into four layers so patterns could be compared across patients.

Clustering split the cohort into two architectures. Twenty-eight tumors were clonal-dominant, shaped mainly by tobacco-related mutation patterns. Thirteen were subclonal-rich, marked by a late-appearing defect in DNA mismatch repair that spawned many small branches. The second group responded to platinum chemotherapy far less often and survived for less time overall. A similar pattern appeared in lung squamous cell carcinoma, a smoking-related cancer used for cross-checking, but not in lung adenocarcinoma. The authors frame heterogeneity itself as a possible early warning marker.
pmc-13559393:
Taek Yong Ko and colleagues describe a method for growing a lung tumor at a chosen spot near the edge of a rabbit's lung, a platform for testing surgery and focused radiation. Their 2026 paper tackles a practical problem: injected tumor cells often leak and spread through the chest instead of forming one local mass. The team paired a bronchoscope inside the airway with a thoracoscope watching from outside.

New Zealand White rabbits received VX2 tumor cells through a thin catheter placed under direct vision. Cells mixed with lipiodol, an oily contrast agent, behaved best: four of five rabbits on the refined protocol grew tumors, and three tumors sat exactly at the intended peripheral site. Cells injected alone grew invasively without staying local. Tissue examination confirmed cancer at the target. The authors offer the model for preclinical testing while noting it still needs refinement.
pmc-13560193:
Ying Liang and colleagues review tertiary lymphoid structures in breast cancer, organized immune cell clusters that form inside tumors and stir local antitumor immunity. Their 2026 article maps how these structures vary by breast cancer subtype, how they arise, how they can be spotted, and whether treatment can coax them to form.

Mature structures concentrate in triple-negative and HER2-positive tumors, where they track with a better outlook and stronger response to pre-surgery therapy, and greater sensitivity to checkpoint drugs. Hormone receptor-positive tumors often lack organized structures and show weaker immune activity. Formation runs through cytokine and chemokine networks plus specialized blood vessels, yet control mechanisms remain murky. Detection ranges from microscopy to spatial transcriptomics and scan-based radiomics, with shared standards still lacking. Treatments including chemotherapy and checkpoint blockade can induce or mature the structures. The authors call for shared scoring standards before bedside use.
pmc-13560393:
Akhil Kapoor and colleagues systematically review perioperative immunotherapy for resectable head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, where nearly half of patients relapse within five years despite aggressive standard treatment. Their 2026 PRISMA-compliant review searches four databases and conference proceedings from 2018 onward. Twenty-five studies qualified, and heterogeneity ruled out a pooled meta-analysis.

Checkpoint inhibitors before surgery proved safe and did not delay operations, but single-drug treatment produced major pathological responses in only about six percent of patients. Doubling up helped: one trial doubled that response rate by adding a second checkpoint drug. After surgery, adding nivolumab to chemoradiotherapy lifted three-year disease-free survival in a major trial. A perioperative pembrolizumab trial improved event-free survival enough to win regulatory approval for certain tumors. The authors describe a fast-moving frontier still refining biomarkers and drug sequencing.
pmc-13560793:
Morgan Ye and colleagues present a methods paper, published in 2026, clarifying how atopic dermatitis, the common itchy eczema, should be counted in a major British birth cohort. The Avon study of parents and children holds twenty-two rounds of relevant data, but different questions produce very different prevalence figures, so the team catalogued them to promote consistent definitions.

Reported rash in the past year ranged widely across rounds and reached eighty percent of children cumulatively by age eighteen, while reported eczema gave far lower figures, twenty-nine percent cumulatively by sixteen. Crease-area dermatitis questions sat between the two. The authors show the definition chosen changes the answer and urge researchers to state theirs plainly.
pmc-13561493:
Danny Salka and Victor Ajluni make the case for gratitude as a clinical virtue in mental health care, in a 2026 letter. Writing as clinicians, they argue that anger, grievance, and ingratitude have spread widely. Gratitude, they say, offers a counterweight rooted in Aristotle's idea of flourishing and Aquinas's view of thanks as a matter of justice. Modern psychology, they note, links gratitude to well-being and fewer signs of mental illness.

They point to studies where mood and symptom journaling raised life satisfaction and eased depression. Practices such as gratitude letters, mindful notice of small positives, and modelling thanks within teams are cheap and easy to adopt. Such habits are tied to better coping, less stress, and greater life satisfaction. The letter urges psychiatrists to weave gratitude into everyday care as part of whole-person healing.
pmc-13562193:
Lanfang Guo and colleagues trace forty years of maternal hemorrhage deaths worldwide using Global Burden of Disease 2021 data. Their 2026 analysis covers women aged fifteen to forty-nine from 1982 to 2021, applying age-period-cohort modeling and grouping countries by sociodemographic development. Hemorrhage remains the main direct cause of maternal death, at over a quarter of the total.

Global deaths fell by 63.13 percent across the four decades. Progress split sharply by development level: high-middle regions cut deaths by over ninety percent, while low-development regions managed only about a fifth in the reported percentages. Nigeria, India, and Pakistan held the highest absolute counts in 2021, and Sierra Leone, Chad, and Niger the highest standardized rates. Cohort analysis shows younger generations in poor regions still face far higher risk. The authors call for targeted system strengthening.
pmc-13562693:
Mohamad Issa Ibraheem and four colleagues design a controller that keeps an islanded microgrid's frequency steady while attackers feed it false commands. Linking control systems to communication networks invites false data injection, where tampered signals can destabilise a grid with shifting loads and renewables. Their 2026 design uses fractional-order sliding mode control, a robust method with memory of past states. An observer watches the system, estimates its state, and flags injected signals, its settings solved through matrix inequality methods.

Stability was proven on paper with Lyapunov analysis, then tested on a real-time hardware simulation rig. The controller held frequency stable through several attack scenarios and disturbances. Dynamic response beat existing methods in comparisons. The authors stress that attacks on the command path can be sneakier than sensor attacks because watchdogs guard the data path. Their design aims to close that gap for critical energy infrastructure.
pmc-13563793:
Richard M. Oxborough and thirteen colleagues propose taking malaria test huts on the road. Bed nets remain Africa's main defence, with 2.2 billion insecticide-treated nets shipped since 2004, yet mosquito resistance is blunting them and new net chemistries need proof. The gold-standard test, the experimental hut trial, happens at fixed sites that often sit far from the hardest-hit villages. Their 2026 paper reviews those fixed sites, finding 34 across endemic Africa, most of the West African design and most parked beside rice fields for mosquito supply.

The team designs portable experimental hut tents: cabin-style tents echoing the hut, with a veranda and 3D-printed entry points for mosquitoes. Being movable, they can test the nets villagers use, aged and worn, against local mosquito populations. The authors extend the idea to spatial repellents, emergency camps, and military settings. Better local evidence, they argue, should drive net choices district by district.
pmc-13563893:
Chuan Qin and nine colleagues build a calculator for spotting osteoporosis in older people living with HIV, whose treatment itself thins bone. Years of antiretroviral therapy erode density until a fracture announces it. Their 2026 study assembled 256 patients aged fifty or over, or postmenopausal, all on therapy for at least a year at one centre. Bone density scans sorted them by the threshold, and a shrinkage regression picked predictors from clinical and blood measures.

Just under forty percent, 102 patients, had osteoporosis. Seven variables survived into the nomogram. Its parts: sex, the ratio of age to body mass, years on therapy, starting CD4 count, tenofovir in its older form, and two blood markers of bone turnover. The model separated cases from non-cases with a concordance of 0.709, held up under resampling, and calibrated. The authors pitch it as a triage tool for clinics that cannot scan every ageing patient.
pmc-13566393:
Peipei Feng and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, whether sleep apnea worsens the tiny blood vessels of the heart in people who also have high blood pressure. Patients received heart stress ultrasound or a vessel-based measure of microvascular resistance, plus portable sleep monitoring, and were sorted into five groups by blood pressure and apnea severity.

Patients with both hypertension and moderate-to-severe apnea had the weakest coronary flow reserve, the highest resistance in a major heart artery, and the highest inflammation markers. Statistical models tied that combination independently to microvascular dysfunction. Cardiologists get a reason to screen hypertensive patients for sleep apnea when small-vessel heart disease is suspected.
pmc-13568393:
Christoph Karl Hofer's team tells the story of A-QUA, Switzerland's national anaesthesia quality registry, in a 2026 analysis. Launched by the Swiss anaesthesiology society, the programme tracks anaesthesia processes, events, and outcomes, yet its scale, take-up, and data quality had not been described. The team analysed routine case-level data from 2017 to 2024 across public and private providers.

By late 2024 the registry held over two million cases from 54 centres in all language regions, mostly from large teaching hospitals. General anaesthesia accounted for three-quarters of cases. Plausibility checks caught recurring preventable errors, and case studies showed regional variation in technique, timing, and postoperative destination. The programme offers a validated platform for benchmarking and targeted quality improvement. The registry keeps growing as more centres join.
pmc-13569393:
Kaisa Saarinen and colleagues survey, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how veterinarians in Sweden, Finland, and Norway treat acute ear inflammation in dogs, a top reason for practice visits and antibiotic use. Surgeons in one corporate group registered their first twenty cases each in spring 2024, totaling 1,060 dogs with symptoms lasting four weeks or less.

Antibiotics were used in eighteen percent of cases, almost always as ear drops, while steroid treatment and ear cleaner covered most dogs. Norway and Finland used antibiotics in over a quarter of cases, against only two percent in Sweden. Microscope findings of certain cells and bacteria drove prescribing more than outward signs did.
pmc-13569893:
John Mark Wiginton and colleagues follow, in a 2026 cohort study, 572 sexual minority men in the United States. All completed surveys in 2019 and twice in 2020. The study tests whether stigma experienced before the pandemic predicted anxiety growth during its first months. Three stigma types were measured: from family and friends, expected in health care, and in general social life.

General social stigma before the pandemic predicted rising anxiety from April to July 2020. The link grew stronger in men with earlier psychological distress and in middle age groups, while family stigma mattered most for the youngest men. Crisis mental health planning, the findings suggest, must reckon with stigma carried into the emergency.
pmc-13570593:
Anes and colleagues produced the first profile of Microsporum canis complex fungal infections in the United Arab Emirates, in a 2026 study. The fungus is a major cause of ringworm in children. No gene check had been published since the nineteen eighties. The team studied 52 samples collected in Abu Dhabi during 2024 and 2025, using naming by appearance, gene sequencing, and drug response testing together.

Anes found sequencing assigned about nine in ten samples to Microsporum canis and the rest to a related clade. Sequencing fixed appearance-based calls in one case in ten, including one misread as a different fungus. Most patients were children, scalp ringworm was most common, and half reported cat contact. All samples looked highly drug-sensitive in the lab. Yet over four fifths of patients failed treatment or relapsed. That shows lab sensitivity poorly predicts outcomes and supports care matched to the species and pet-aware prevention.
pmc-13571393:
Qin and co-authors described a 2026 technique for reopening completely blocked, heavily calcified heart arteries when standard tools fail. In chronic total occlusion, a guidewire may cross but low profile balloons and microcatheters cannot follow through the rock hard plaque. Their method, shortened to IMAC, modifies plaque from inside the vessel.

First the wire's position inside the vessel is confirmed from several angles using calcification or a retrograde wire as landmarks. A special wire then follows the path the first wire created through the blocked segment. Qin explains that a spinning rotational atherectomy burr grinds the impenetrable plaque along that confirmed route. Afterwards a wire can cross from either direction to finish opening the artery. Precise wire control is crucial, since drilling outside the vessel wall risks perforation and rupture.
pmc-13572393:
Mohammed Tanveer Hussain, with 15 colleagues, led a 2026 study of drug-resistant gut bacteria in Rohingya camps in Bangladesh. Sludge from latrines and nearby drinking water can both carry E. coli that shrug off many drugs. The team looked for strains that make ESBL, an enzyme that breaks key antibiotics.

E. coli turned up in 88.1 percent of sludge samples and 40.2 percent of water samples. About a third of sludge strains and an eighth of water strains made ESBL. The gene blaCTX-M led the list, in 81.1 percent of the resistant strains picked for gene tests. Two gut illness types were most common among the strains. Drug tests showed wide resistance. The work shows why camp water and sludge need close watch and safe handling.
pmc-13572493:
Mahmoud Leila, with six colleagues, reports a 2026 lab test of carbon dioxide storage in sandstone that holds the green mineral glauconite. The rock comes from the Mangyshlak Basin in Kazakhstan, where a fine-grained layer runs 30 to 40 metres thick for hundreds of kilometres. Glauconite can lock carbon into minerals, but past work said the process takes geological ages.

The team ran a 30-day batch test at 100 degrees and 150 bar, with brine and rock at a ratio of 20. The fluid first gained iron, sodium, potassium, magnesium, and silicon as minerals dissolved. Late in the run, magnesium, iron, and silicon dipped, which hints that new minerals had begun to form and take up ions. Rock checks backed that read. The results test how fast mineral trapping can start in this rock type.
pmc-13573193:
Omkar Indari, Prashant Giri, Rebecca E. Tweedell and Thirumala-Devi Kanneganti published this 2026 genetic study of PANoptosis, an inflammatory form of programmed cell death used by the innate immune system. During PANoptosis, pore-forming executioner proteins rupture the cell and spill inflammatory signals. Three executioners, gasdermin D, gasdermin E and MLKL, were candidates for driving the process. The authors deleted each gene, alone and in combination, across several triggers of the pathway.

Deleting any single executioner did not fully block PANoptosis, showing the proteins can cover for one another. Removing all three protected cells more than any single or double deletion. Even then, 20 to 50 percent of cells still died under the conditions tested, pointing to further executioners not yet identified. The authors warn against defining cell death pathways by one executioner protein. For diseases driven by PANoptosis, they argue, drugs should target the upstream sensors that start the pathway instead.
pmc-13573393:
Zhifang Lin, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 study of a blood protein that might flag throat cancer early. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is common and aggressive in Southeast Asia, yet early screening lacks a solid marker. The team hunted for one by scanning blood proteins in patients and healthy controls.

Mass spectrometry profiled blood from 15 early-stage patients and 15 healthy people who carried a viral antibody marker. Computer analysis sorted the protein patterns for candidates that split the groups. One protein, SULT1A3, rose to the top of the screen. A second test method, ELISA, was then used to check the candidate in a fresh round of samples. A marker that holds up in both rounds could feed a blood test for early disease. The authors frame the work as a first step toward screening.
pmc-13575193:
Kai Feng and four colleagues present a lighter detection model for finding small warm objects in drone infrared images, in a 2026 paper. Tiny targets, messy backgrounds, and faint features make this task hard, and drone hardware needs fast, small models. Their design, DAN-YOLO-L, reworks the YOLO detection framework.

A new feature module sharpens detail across scales, an auxiliary head improves how features at different levels interact, and a revised loss function steadies box placement for tiny targets. Pruning then cut the parameter count by 20.8 percent while speed rose by 8.32 percent. On the HIT-UAV benchmark the model scored 81.9 percent on the main detection measure. A second infrared dataset confirmed the gains carried over.
pmc-13576093:
Mirary Mantilla-Morrón and colleagues studied sex life among one hundred old people with more than one long-term illness in Barranquilla, Colombia. The group had a mean age of 72.6 years, and just over half were men. Mood, daily function, and sex life were each rated with proven scales, and health records backed the diagnoses.

A sense of control and of choice stood out as the best signs of a good sex life, while self-growth showed the reverse link. Men scored lower on their own, apart from other factors. Care for old people should thus ask about mood, choice, and control, and not just about pills, pain, and blood tests.
pmc-13576193:
Steven Garcia and three colleagues test whether a wrist artery reading can stand in for a direct heart measure of squeezing strength, in a 2026 study of valve replacement patients. The direct measure, the rate of pressure rise in the left ventricle, is a standard gauge of heart muscle strength, yet it needs a catheter inside the heart.

Patients having a new aortic valve fitted by catheter had both measures recorded before and after the procedure. Before surgery the wrist reading sat far above the heart reading and tracked it weakly. After surgery the average gap shrank, yet agreement stayed poor. In 73 percent of patients the two measures moved in opposite directions across the procedure. The authors see the wrist signal as, at best, a rough guide to direction of change.
pmc-13576293:
Helder Hugo and Iain Douglas Couzin present a new arena for watching whole termite colonies build trails, in a 2026 methods paper. Trail formation is a classic case of collective behaviour growing from local rules. Past lab setups used small subgroups or tight boxes that cramp colony-level movement.

Their circular arena folds at the edge, staying connected to the intact nest while termites cross a central viewing surface and loop back. Colonies of a Neotropical species were filmed with no food or water added. Within six minutes, shared trail structure appeared in 15 of 16 colonies, seen as paths converging from the entrance. Automated tracking pulled fine movement data for workers and soldiers from dense crowds. Dark traces left on the paper lining gave a physical record of heavy routes.
pmc-13578693:
Manuel Rubio and colleagues find a shortcut for measuring how stiff a soft tube material is, in a 2026 study. Soft tubes show up in pumps, implants, and body passages, and knowing their stiffness guides design. The team paired computer models with bench tests on tubes of two materials, watching how volume swelled as inside pressure beat outside pressure.

For long, thin tubes the patterns lined up neatly. Cutting wall thickness tenfold cut the needed pressure tenfold for the same swell. Tube length stopped mattering once tubes ran long enough. All the curves for such tubes merged into one master curve when plotted the right way. Reading one pressure test against that curve then gives the stiffness, with just a simple pressure gauge.
pmc-13579993:
Jinlan Li and a large team of co-authors find a way to revive cancer killing T cells worn down by chemo aged tumor cells, in a 2026 study. Chemo can push lymphoma cells into senescence, an aged state where they ooze signals that tire immune cells. Two lymphoma cell lines were aged with a low drug dose, then treated with a blocker of a surface guide protein called CCR7.

Aging raised that protein and its partner signals, which latched onto a T cell brake and drained killing power. Blocking the guide steadied a key brake on inflammation inside the cells and rolled back the aged state. In mixed culture the blocker restored engineered T cell killing. Patient T cells carried less of the guide than healthy ones, and more of it meant fitter cells, a nuance the authors weigh.
pmc-13580393:
Lars K Burri, Svitlana Shishkina, and Martin Albrecht slip a two atom fragment into the spine of a platinum bound ligand. Such molecular editing usually moves one atom at a time. The ligand, a pyridinium amidate, offers a carbon nitrogen bond that platinum can pry open. A nitrile then donates its carbon nitrogen unit straight into the gap. The skeleton stretches by two atoms at once.

Marked atoms traced the break to the bond between nitrogen and the ring. Watching the mixture over time revealed several way stations before the final complex settled. The team frames the trick as a fresh route for reshaping ring compounds. Two atom inserts were nearly unheard of in that class, outside ring opening detours.
pmc-13583193:
Garyfallia Stefanou and colleagues surveyed people in Greece who live with psoriatic arthritis, a long-term illness that inflames joints and often comes with the skin disease psoriasis. Their 2026 survey traced the full path each patient took, from first symptoms through diagnosis and treatment, and priced the toll on daily life and on the wallet.

A total of 148 patients answered, most of them women with a middle age of 56 years. The middle wait ran past a year before treatment began, and nearly half were first given a wrong diagnosis. Skin rash was the most common first sign, ahead of joint pain. Work loss and care costs fell heavily on patients, with most yearly spending coming straight from their own pockets.
pmc-13585593:
Wei Cheng and colleagues present a tangled liver case in a woman treated for rectal cancer. She had her rectum removed and then received five rounds of chemotherapy containing oxaliplatin, a drug known to injure the liver. During treatment her liver cells were badly hurt, and a biopsy in June 2020 showed a pattern matching autoimmune hepatitis, where the immune system attacks the liver.

Over time her spleen swelled and twisted veins formed near her stoma and food pipe, bleeding again and again, even though her liver had no cirrhosis. Pressure in the portal vein measured far above normal. Doctors blocked one vein and treated others with foam, which slowed the bleeding without stopping it, then added a beta blocker and a steroid. The team reads the picture as high portal pressure with several causes acting together.
pmc-13586093:
Jae Hee Han and Joong-Hyuck Auh mine an edible beetle larva for peptides that might help blood sugar control. The rhinoceros beetle larva is approved as a food in Korea and is rich in protein. In their 2026 study, the pair broke that protein down with enzymes and split the mix into three parts. They were hunting for a part that blocks DPP-4, an enzyme that trims hormones which keep insulin working.

The third part blocked DPP-4 best by a clear margin. Fed to insulin-resistant liver cells, it raised sugar uptake and switched on a key insulin signal, along with more of the sugar gate protein GLUT4. Chemical reading found 22 compounds in the winning part, rich in water-shy building blocks, and computer fitting showed them gripping the enzyme's active pocket. The authors pitch the larva as a source of sugar-friendly food peptides.
pmc-13591693:
Arman Shekarian and six colleagues pool, in 2026, forty studies to ask how often thyroid failure shows up in people with metabolic syndrome. That syndrome bundles belly fat, high blood pressure, and poor sugar and fat control, all of which thyroid hormones help govern. Their search gathered data on more than 25,000 people with the syndrome. They split thyroid failure into overt disease and a milder, subclinical form.

Across all studies the milder form touched about one in five people, and overt disease about one in eleven. Studies judged sounder gave lower rates for both, near one in eight and one in twenty. Shekarian and the team say the milder form still looks common enough to justify thyroid testing in this group.
pmc-13591793:
Beatriz Oliveira leads a 2026 survey of how Portuguese family doctors handle prostate cancer screening and shared choices with patients. The PSA blood test can find cancer early, yet it can also spark needless biopsies and treatment. A survey across 25 health centers drew 107 doctors, most of them women under 40. Questions covered who gets tested, how often, and how risks and gains are discussed.

Most doctors said they explain the test, yet only about two thirds always walked through gains, harms, and patient wishes. Tools that aid such talks were barely known: just a handful had ever used one. Referrals hinged mainly on odd ultrasound findings rather than PSA alone. Oliveira and the team want clearer national guidance.
pmc-13592493:
Erica Cecchini and colleagues hunted gene clues in MOGHE, a child brain fault with too many small brain support cells that brings seizures. About half of cases hold SLC35A2 gene faults, which leaves the rest with no known cause. Brain bits from 29 kids, nineteen boys and ten girls, were tested with gene-copy reads, PCR, and glow tests on tissue.

Y-chromosome bits showed up in five of ten girls, and patchy Y-chromosome gains in sixteen of nineteen boys, backed by two tests and tied to sick tissue. Kids with both SLC35A2 faults and Y gains leaned to early seizures, wide brain spread, and thought harm, though not by a clear margin. Sex-chromosome faults may thus feed this brain fault's roots.
pmc-13592793:
Sebastian Schwab and five colleagues test, in 2026, whether insurance billing data alone can forecast kidney disease outcomes. Lab values drive most risk models, yet records often lack them. Their cohort held 29,144 insured people in Germany with stage three or four chronic kidney disease in 2016. Billing codes over the next six years fed forecasts for dialysis, death, hospital stays, and drug prescriptions.

Claims patterns predicted dialysis well and death very sharply, with weaker but real signal for kidney injury admissions and intensive care. Adding disease stage lifted every forecast. Two drug classes tied to prescriptions also tracked with better kidney and heart outcomes. Schwab and the team say claims data carry genuine prognostic weight even with no lab numbers attached.
pmc-13593693:
Lilly Josephine Bindel and Roland Seifert re-examined the drugs that have survived on the World Health Organization's Essential Medicines List from its first edition in 1977 to the twenty-fourth in 2025. Their 2026 assessment graded 129 long-retained medicines by present-day value, weighing guideline support, benefit and safety, how widely each is used, and what alternatives exist.

For most of these drugs the listed uses had barely changed across nearly fifty years. Just over half were judged to hold constant importance, a smaller share had grown more important, and nearly a third had declined. Nineteen drugs raised enough questions, through narrow use, weaker effect, resistance, or toxicity, that the authors say their place on the list deserves open debate. Staying on the list for decades, they argue, should not by itself certify a drug's worth.
pmc-13594893:
Jakob Nikolas Kather, Tobias Boettler, Daniela Sia, and Josep M. Llovet warn that AI-generated slide decks are quietly taking over scientific conferences. Writing in 2026, they point out that journals have built disclosure rules for AI in writing and reviewing. The conference talk has drawn far less attention. Yet it remains one of the last genuinely human exchanges in science.

General-purpose AI tools can now produce a polished deck in minutes, hard to tell from an afternoon of careful handwork, and invented references have become rare. The authors worry less about laziness than about what meetings are for: live human interaction, where new ideas form and integrity is on display. Attendance at hepatology meetings sits at record highs, partly because researchers crave that contact. The authors argue the community should decide deliberately how generated presentations fit. Waiting risks the human core of the meeting eroding unnoticed.
pmc-13595393:
Lisa Yamasaki and colleagues tested whether air-conditioning use changes how heat drives ambulance trips in the Tokyo area. Heat illness grows with rising temperatures, yet how seasonal adaptation shifts risk is poorly understood. Their 2026 study analysed 88,893 ambulance transports from June to September 2015 to 2019 across seven prefectures, using power use as a stand-in for air-conditioning use.

In June, hotter days raised risk more when power use was high, a pattern the authors link to delayed or patchy cooling early in summer. In July the pattern flipped, with high power use tied to lower risk, suggesting protection once cooling habits settle. No such modifying effect appeared in August or September. Yamasaki and colleagues urge early-season adaptation measures.
pmc-13602893:
Eetu Hakkarainen leads an eleven-author team designing deep-blue light emitters in 2026. Pure deep blue remains one of the hardest colors for organic light-emitting diodes. Their molecules pair two phosphane oxide units, strong electron pullers, inside an asymmetric donor-acceptor scaffold. Three related compounds were synthesized to map how small structural changes steer the glow.

The compounds fluoresced deep blue, at 385 to 418 nanometers in solution and slightly redder in solid form, with light yields reaching 95 percent. Swapping phenyl for biphenyl links and adjusting donor strength shifted the energy gap, brightness, and excited-state pathways. Two compounds kept high triplet energies and good heat stability, qualifying them as OLED emitters. A device using compound 2 reached 4.86 percent external quantum efficiency with color coordinates of (0.15, 0.07), a genuinely pure blue, at low turn-on voltage. Extra light came from triplet pairs merging, beating the usual singlet limit.
pmc-13603993:
Jie Hou leads a seven-author team surveying 5,764 Chinese college students about leaning on artificial intelligence and their sense of their own creativity. Dependence differs from ordinary use: it means habitually handing pressure and hard thinking to the tool. Their questionnaire measured dependence, self-reported creativity, four motives for using AI, and AI literacy.

Dependence tracked with lower self-reported creativity overall. The pathways split by motive in opposing directions. Dependence running through escape or social motivation dragged creativity down. Dependence running through instrumental or entertainment motivation lifted it. Feeling AI-literate changed how dependence fed the escape, social, and entertainment motives, but not the instrumental one or the direct creativity link. The authors argue that why students reach for AI matters as much as how much, which gives educators a finer target than simple screen-time rules.
pmc-13605693:
Carmen Lara-Apolinario leads an eight-author team charting drug test results at a Spanish university hospital across five years. From January 2021 to December 2025, the Dr. Negrín University Hospital laboratory logged every urine sample that tested positive for cannabis, cocaine, amphetamines, or opioids. Only age and sex were attached to each anonymized result. The series captured 5,019 positive findings, a first portrait for the hospital's population.

Women accounted for just 28.2 percent of positive patients. Age reshaped the drug mix completely. Cannabis dominated at 59.9 percent of positives and was overwhelming among teenagers, at 94 percent of under-18 positives, but faded to 16.2 percent past age 65. Amphetamine and opioid positives climbed steadily with age, reaching 61.3 and 23.1 percent in the oldest group. Cocaine peaked in middle age at 62 percent of the 36-to-55 group. The authors offer the patterns for aiming prevention and treatment at the groups actually showing up.
pmc-13608293:
Vigdís H. Viggósdóttir and five colleagues take stock of heart health in Icelandic adults who survived childhood cancer. Anthracycline chemotherapy drugs can damage the heart, so survivors should manage ordinary cardiac risks carefully. The team studied everyone treated with anthracyclines at Iceland's pediatric oncology service, 1981 to 2011. Of 76 eligible survivors, 60 took part, aged 20 to 48, giving records, questionnaires, and measurements gathered between 2016 and 2019.

A quarter of participants showed a widened left ventricle, mostly mild to moderate, with one severe case. Metabolic syndrome affected 20 percent, and 20 percent still smoked. About half had a heart ultrasound within the past ten years. Most striking, only 10 percent knew their cancer treatment could harm the heart. The authors call for systematic surveillance and targeted work on smoking and metabolic risk. Raising awareness among survivors and doctors is itself a treatment step, they argue: people cannot manage a risk never heard of.
pmc-13608493:
Sara Scilli and three colleagues measure how much occupational contact dermatitis goes unreported in Italy. This work-caused skin inflammation is among the most common occupational diseases, yet compensation data capture only a fraction of it. The team took official case reports filed with the national workplace insurer INAIL from 2020 to 2024. These were set against incidence estimates from published studies of high-risk trades such as healthcare, construction, and hairdressing.

Officially, about 182 cases a year were recorded. Literature-based estimates pointed instead to between 1,439 and 21,412 cases annually. Depending on which estimate is trusted, only 0.8 to 12.7 percent of expected cases are ever notified. The authors blame under-recognition of the work link, the habit of treating symptoms as minor, and clunky surveillance. Their remedies are practical: better monitoring, more awareness, and simpler reporting, so cases are caught before a passing rash hardens into chronic disease.
pmc-13612193:
Gülşah Altan and three colleagues dissect drug resistance in a hospital bacterium that shrugs off most drugs. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia infects sick patients and resists many drug classes by nature. The team tested 34 isolates against three key antibiotics, screened them with targeted DNA tests, typed their relatedness, and sequenced three genomes fully.

Resistance stayed uncommon: 5.9 percent to the first-line combination trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, 8.8 percent to levofloxacin, and 11.8 percent to minocycline. One screening target, dfrA27, lit up in 82.4 percent of isolates yet matched neither the resistance pattern nor the sequenced genomes, a mismatch the authors highlight. The two combination-resistant isolates shared the same fingerprint type and an identical 19,361-letter resistance island packed with drug genes and a mercury-resistance module. A third isolate lacked it entirely. Shared ancestry could explain the island's presence, they caution; sideways transfer was not demonstrated.
pmc-13612593:
Laura Redaelli leads a five-author team releasing an open sound library of toothed whales and dolphins from Madeira in 2026. Odontocetes live by sound, navigating, hunting, and socializing acoustically, yet public recordings from the region were scarce. Between 2022 and 2025 the team followed visually confirmed single-species groups by boat, recording at close range with a SoundTrap hydrophone.

The curated dataset covers seven odontocete species and three call families: tonal whistles, broadband pulsed calls, and echolocation clicks. Every file ships with metadata on species, group size, behavior, and environmental context, the labels automated detectors need. Madeira sits in a North Atlantic biodiversity hotspot, so the recordings fill a genuine geographic hole. The authors intend the resource for comparative repertoire research and for building acoustic monitoring tools that identify species automatically. Open access, they note, lets any group worldwide test algorithms against the same ground truth.
pmc-13613793:
Nicole B. Goecke, Þorbjörg Eva Ellingsen, Lars E. Larsen, and Nina D. Otten report a 2026 survey of germs found in young calves across Iceland. Lung and gut disease in calves causes deaths, money losses, and heavy antibiotic use, yet Iceland has had little lab capacity to name the culprits. Gut disease in newborn calves is common there, while lung disease is rare. Twenty herds joined, twelve in the northeast and eight in the west, with 197 calves in all.

Each calf had a health check plus nose swabs and dung samples, and owners answered questions on calf care and farm hygiene. Testing those samples shows which bacteria and viruses actually circulate in Icelandic herds. With names in hand, vets can aim treatment and prevention at the right targets instead of guessing.
pmc-13613993:
Per Winterdijk and co-authors present a narrative review, published in 2026. It argues psychological care should be built into routine diabetes services. It should not be added as an afterthought. The authors draw on studies and clinical experience. They also draw on the voices of people living with diabetes. They map the mental health burden of the condition. Service models that work are mapped too.

Psychological care works best in layers, they find. Routine screening for diabetes distress is the first layer. Frontline education and support form the next. Specialist therapy serves those who need it. Layered care reduced distress and depressive symptoms. Effects on blood sugar control were mixed. The authors set out innovation paths for care models, evaluation, and policy.
pmc-13615093:
Maki Uraguchi and Hideki Ohira test in 2026 a core claim of predictive processing, using the sense of time. That theory holds that the brain constantly predicts the world and updates when it is wrong. People judged lengths of time against an internal reference, and the authors watched whether that reference shifted in the direction that would shrink their error. Two experiments ran: one with 60 university students and one with 359 adults of wider ages.

Hearing longer or shorter durations often shifted the internal reference the expected way in the first experiment. In the larger second study, clear shifts appeared only when the prediction error was big enough. The work separates true updating of the time reference from a mere change in judgement sharpness. It gives the grand theory a concrete, checkable foothold in the split-second range.
pmc-13617393:
Yudai Kaneda writes a letter to the editor about a study of HPV knowledge, screening, and vaccination attitudes among three hundred two Brazilian women in primary care. The study found a striking gap: most women had had a Pap smear and most would certainly vaccinate their children. Yet few were screened as guidelines recommend, and few knew HPV causes cervical cancer. Kaneda raises three points to refine how those numbers should be read.

First, screening adherence should count only women in the guideline age range, since some younger participants were scored as off-protocol when screening was not yet due for them. Second, the study does not say how many respondents were mothers of vaccine-age children, so uncertain answers may reflect hypothetical choices, not hesitancy. Third, younger women's dimmer ratings of primary care seem driven by do-not-know answers, suggesting limited contact with services rather than distrust.
pmc-13617593:
Matthew J. Martin and eleven colleagues report a six-month study of asthma reliever strategies in the STIFLE trial. One group used a budesonide and formoterol inhaler for both maintenance and relief, a single-inhaler approach called MART. The comparison group took the same inhaler twice daily as maintenance and used salbutamol, a reliever, when symptoms struck. Forty-two patients with moderate asthma recorded symptoms, lung function, and inflammation daily through a phone app.

Adherence to home measurements topped eighty percent in both groups. Exacerbations struck about twenty-eight percent of the MART group against about seventy-one percent of the salbutamol group, and heavy reliever days were also less common with MART. Day-to-day swings in inflammation, symptoms, lung function, and reliever use were smaller under the single-inhaler strategy, with no unexpected safety findings. The authors read this as improved asthma control and plan larger confirmation.
pmc-13617993:
Charline Alleaume and eight colleagues document the first known cases of equine leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania martiniquensis in France, an emerging parasite species from a little-understood lineage. Three horses in different regions, with no link in place or time, developed localized skin lesions that first looked like common horse skin problems, including sarcoid-like tumors. Tissue examination under the microscope showed inflamed skin packed with immune cells carrying tiny parasite forms.

DNA testing of the tissue confirmed Leishmania, and sequencing pinpointed the martiniquensis species. Blood antibody tests disagreed between horses, negative in two and strongly positive in one, while one case yielded living parasites in culture. The disease stayed localized in all three animals: one healed on its own, one after surgical removal, and one after injections of an antimonial drug into the lesion. The authors provide guidance for veterinarians meeting this infection.
pmc-13620193:
Fabienne Ballanger and four fellow acne experts offer a consensus review on where non-ablative laser therapy fits in treating active acne. Standard creams and pills often run into resistance, side effects, and relapse, while lasers can target oil glands and the acne bacterium directly. The panel weighed fifteen published sources spanning two decades to place the technology honestly.

Limited trial evidence suggests the lasers reduce lesions safely, yet protocols vary widely and access is uneven, so the panel cannot endorse them as a replacement for standard care. Their proposed slot is narrower: an alternative first step for mild acne, or a supporting second-line option when standard treatments fail or cannot be used. Scars and dark marks sit outside the review's scope. Large, well-powered trials with settled protocols remain mandatory, the experts say, before the benefit can be confirmed.
pmc-13620293:
Lonneke H C Gremmen and three colleagues describe two fertility patients whose first sign of severe ovarian hyperstimulation was fluid around the right lung. This syndrome follows ovarian stimulation for in vitro fertilization, when leaky vessels let fluid escape into body cavities. Both women developed sharp chest pain and growing breathlessness days after egg collection.

One patient needed two fluid drainages from the belly and one from the chest, while the other needed a single chest drainage. Hospital care combined intravenous fluids, oxygen, correction of blood salts, and protection against blood clots. Stays lasted twelve days and two days, and both women recovered fully within three weeks of discharge. The authors review why fluid favors the right side and stress that chest symptoms after stimulation deserve quick attention, since the condition can worsen fast.
pmc-13621593:
Xiaowen Hu and five colleagues mapped HPV infection across more than one hundred twenty thousand women screened in Bengbu, northern Anhui, over a decade, published in 2026. Persistent infection with high-risk types causes most cervical cancer, and type patterns vary by region, so local data shape screening and vaccine choices. The team genotyped cervical samples collected at one teaching hospital.

About one woman in seven carried a high-risk type, and overall infection across twenty-eight genotypes ran higher. Infection peaked twice across life, among women under twenty-five and again near age sixty to sixty-four. Prevalence climbed in 2016 and 2017, fell back, and ticked up again by 2023. Type 16 led, followed by 52 and 58, and most positive women carried a single type. Older age raised risk for eight high-risk types even as most types faded over time. The authors offer it as the region's baseline for prevention planning.
pmc-13623093:
Qi Cheng and three co-authors build a gene-based picture of why some heart attack patients calm their inflammation after treatment while others do not. The attack type studied, STEMI, is the most severe form, and reopening the artery does not end the immune storm for everyone. The team worked from public blood gene data rather than new patients.

They combined six blood data sets and one single-cell data set, then built an axis running from acute inflammation toward recovery. Eighty-one patients in the main cohort split into recovery and recovery-failure groups by their gene patterns. An eighteen-gene module tied to monocytes, a frontline immune cell, marked the failure group and faded as patients recovered in other cohorts. Single-cell data confirmed the signal sat in monocytes. The authors stress the tool describes a pattern for testing, not a proven way to predict outcomes.
pmc-13623393:
Hevelyn dos Santos da Rocha leads a scoping review mapping safe practices for giving medicines by vein to adults in hospital. Intravenous drug therapy is common and risky, since errors reach the bloodstream directly. Following Joanna Briggs Institute methods, the team searched four information sources plus grey literature with a guiding question on safe administration.

Eighteen studies survived screening and deduplication. The reviewers sorted the safety practices into five stages of the process: sterile technique, preparation, labelling, administration, and recording. Hand hygiene, double checking each step, and confirming both the medicine and the patient stood out as core habits. Checking that the vein line is open before injecting, and recording each dose plus any bad reaction, completed the picture. The authors present steady use of these practices as a basic defence for hospital patients.
pmc-13624393:
Ruohui Mao led a randomized trial testing a toothpaste made with two plant extracts, Bletilla striata and Litsea cubeba, in people with gum disease caused by plaque buildup. Eighty patients used either the herbal paste or a plain control paste. Checks ran over twelve weeks after a two-week washout, with scores taken at the start and at weeks four, eight, and twelve.

The herbal group showed earlier and larger drops in plaque scores and gum bleeding scores, clear by weeks eight and twelve. Levels of some fluid markers of swelling also fell sooner or further, though one marker changed about the same in both groups. The trial offers early support for the blend in daily gum care.
pmc-13624693:
Grillo and colleagues published in 2026 the first year-round checklist of mesopelagic swimmers caught by an automatic sediment trap on a mooring in the Ross Sea, Antarctica. Swimmers are free-swimming animals that enter traps set to catch sinking particles, and they give rare clues about life in deep Southern Ocean water. The trap sat at about 500 metres depth in the Joides Basin and worked across three Italian Antarctic program periods, from 1995 to 2016.

Grillo recorded 210,411 individual animals in total, spanning 68 genera and 68 species across 905 occurrence records. Each record comes with mooring sensor data on temperature, salt content, and water density. Because Southern Ocean surveys are rare and costly, these accidental catches help sharpen species distribution models and forecasts of where each animal lives. The data set also offers a baseline for spotting climate-driven change in Antarctic food webs.
pmc-13626193:
Nikolaos Boumparis and a broad team review why teenagers drift away from digital lifestyle programs. Apps and online plans target activity, food, weight, alcohol, and smoking, yet fewer than half of young users finish them as designed. Searching four databases in March 2024, with an update in June 2026, the reviewers kept 116 studies holding 46,029 adolescents, and they pooled dropout across most of them in a meta-analysis.

About two-thirds of participants completed programs on a simple yes-no count, while day-to-day use of program parts averaged nearer half. Pooled dropout sat at roughly one in six, with wide variation between studies and no single factor explaining the spread. The synthesis sorts causes into program design and user traits, giving builders a checklist for stickier tools.
pmc-13626293:
Sameera Shridhar and co-authors listen to two brain regions talk while rats learn a maze. The hippocampus, a memory hub, fires sharp wave-ripples during learning, while the prefrontal cortex, a planning region, was less charted. Electrodes in both regions recorded activity as male rats learned spatial tasks over days, and the team tracked what changed as performance improved.

A beta rhythm near twenty cycles per second swelled in the prefrontal cortex whenever rats reached a goal, growing stronger as they got better, and it tracked the odds of reward. Ripples in the hippocampus moved the other way, shrinking in rate and size as the task grew familiar. The two signals, the authors propose, are partners: one marks fresh encoding, the other growing mastery.
pmc-13629793:
Augustus Osborne and four colleagues built a scorecard to judge how ready African lands are for the continent's health security agenda. The agenda is the Africa CDC framework drawn from COVID-19 and Ebola lessons. Their study coded 48 documents. They ranged from continental plans to national policies in twelve lands across five regional blocs.

Scored across ten strands, readiness looked strongest in governance and planning. Money detail lagged badly. So did digital health design, plus lab and drug systems. Only a few national money plans held the needed provisions. So did only a few drug policies. The authors offer the scorecard as a repeatable checking tool. The Africa CDC, governments, and partners can use it to aim help where bottlenecks bite hardest.
pmc-13637393:
Babasola Okusanya and eight colleagues published this 2026 protocol for a prediction tool against preeclampsia with severe features, the condition's most dangerous form. The severe form drives many maternal deaths, above all in poorer countries. Existing prediction tools were built elsewhere and may misread African patients. The PreSev study will follow at-risk pregnant women at four major Lagos hospitals, enrolling them in mid-pregnancy.

Clinical and background data will be gathered in a digital system. Five machine learning approaches will compete to predict who develops the severe form, tested with cross-validation and carefully tuned. The team will judge the models on how well they separate cases and how honest their risk numbers are, and will open the black box with importance scores for each predictor. The winning model becomes an online risk tool. The authors aim for a context-fit tool that helps Nigerian doctors flag risk early.
pmc-13638693:
Joshua Ierace and five colleagues report a 2026 experiment on how radiation dose rates from nuclear medicine patients can be modeled more accurately. Standard estimates treat the patient as a simple point source, which tends to overstate exposure for staff working close by.

The team measured four radioactive tracers with calibrated ionisation chambers, using point and line sources plus water-filled body and neck phantoms that mimic real patients. Their measured gamma factors matched published values closely, and the phantom work showed how much dose the body itself absorbs. The results give hospitals measured curves for shielding, scheduling, and staff safety checks.
pmc-13639093:
Angana De and five colleagues report a 2026 therapy study that silences the VEGFA gene directly in tumor DNA. VEGFA drives blood vessel growth in tumors and switches on when a hypoxia factor binds a control site in low-oxygen tissue.

The team built a gamma-modified peptide nucleic acid that blocks that binding site by sequence. In several solid cancer cell lines the treatment lowered VEGFA output and cell survival. In mice with triple-negative breast tumors, it slowed growth and extended survival. The authors present DNA-level targeting as a precise way to shut down a central cancer growth signal.
pmc-13641693:
Jake Colautti and four colleagues present a study of how Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a hard-to-treat bacterium, controls construction of its dividing wall. Cell division needs wall building at the septum, switched on by a protein chain whose details differ between species.

Working with bacteria missing the activator FtsN, the team found changes in a pedestal region of the wall enzyme FtsI that let division proceed anyway. Some of these changes slightly blunted several beta-lactam antibiotics, while one on the opposite face made cells strikingly more sensitive. Similar changes appear in patient isolates, tying division control to drug resistance.
pmc-13645393:
Samantha Teixeira led a 2026 study of how people in a large city public housing complex experience the four pathways linking housing to health: cost, conditions, consistency, and context. Public housing is meant to deliver decent, stable, low-cost homes, yet years of neglect have left many complexes poorly kept in poor neighborhoods. The authors spoke with sixty-one residents to learn how those four factors interact in daily life.

People described the four factors as tangled and reinforcing. Many endured poor conditions as the price of staying put, since moving costs too much and could mean leaving a neighborhood whose shops and family ties they valued. Planned rebuilding raised fears of broken stability that outweighed hopes for better conditions or surroundings. Officials get a warning: when residents must trade decent conditions for stability, the program's core promise of decent, stable, affordable housing is already failing.
pmc-13645593:
Yunqing Hou and three colleagues compare five large language models on how well they answer common patient questions about cataracts. The condition clouds the eye lens and are a leading cause of reversible blindness, mainly in older people. The team put twenty frequent questions to each model. Answers were scored for reading ease, information quality, and fitness for patient teaching.

Clear differences appeared between models on every measure the team used. One model earned the highest quality and teaching scores, though its answers were also harder to read. Topics differed too: aftercare and prevention answers taught well, while surgery topics read harder. The authors note that easy reading and high quality did not always go together. Their results can help clinics pick and supervise chat tools for patient education with more care.
pmc-13647093:
Yan Li led a 2026 Finnish cohort study of how mental disorders in childhood and adolescence relate to final comprehensive school grades, with attention to sex and age at onset. Earlier work was often small or single-disorder, leaving the scale and timing of the link unclear. The team used national registers for everyone born between 1990 and 2003 who finished comprehensive school in Finland between 2005 and 2019, a total of 837,546 students.

More than sixteen percent had a mental disorder diagnosis before graduation. Those students averaged 0.41 grade points lower than peers without a diagnosis, with a larger gap for girls than boys, at 0.45 against 0.37. Disorders diagnosed later in childhood tracked with poorer grades across most specific diagnoses. Educators and policymakers get large-scale evidence for targeted psychological support, especially for girls and adolescents, since school performance carries long-term economic consequences.
pmc-13648493:
Francis D. Semakuba and twenty-six colleagues introduce PfPHAST, a streamlined genetic sequencing panel for routine malaria surveillance of the parasite Plasmodium falciparum. A larger research panel exists, but public health programmes need a cheaper tool focused on drug resistance, diagnostic-evading deletions, vaccine targets, and strain diversity.

The fifty-six-target panel was benchmarked against its parent using laboratory strains, dilution series, and a five-strain mixture across a range of parasite densities. It passed quality control more often, spread reads more evenly, and matched the larger panel on resistance and diversity calls, though very minor strains at low density challenged both. The authors position it as a scalable option for routine monitoring.
pmc-13648593:
Jawad Akhtar and fifteen colleagues design drugs that destroy, rather than merely block, a protein called SMYD3 in HPV-negative head and neck cancer. That cancer still carries a poor outlook despite immunotherapy, and SMYD3 is overproduced in many tumours, driving growth, invasion, and resistance.

Ordinary inhibitors shut off the protein's enzyme activity yet barely slowed cancer cells, implying its harmful roles lie elsewhere. The team's degrader molecules, built to drag SMYD3 to the cell's disposal machinery, wiped it out at low doses and sharply cut proliferation and invasion. One compound also behaved well in animals and proved highly selective. The authors argue degradation is the right strategy here.
pmc-13649393:
Silvia F. M. Pizzoli and three colleagues put forward a new frame for building virtual reality places that feel truly personal. Most health uses of virtual reality rely on stock scenes that fit no one in particular. Deep personal designs can work well, but they take long interviews and costly rebuilding for each user.

Their frame, called the embodied meaningful place framework, joins three layers. One layer holds shared symbols and archetypes that many people grasp at once. One holds cues from a person's own life story. The last layer turns inner body states into scenes a user can see and explore. The authors argue this mix can scale personal care without losing depth.
pmc-13649693:
Constantin C. Ketz and two colleagues tested whether a classic law of flash vision also holds for reading shapes. Bloch's law says that, for brief flashes, what counts is total light: brightness times time. The team measured letter acuity in 19 healthy adults across 25 blends of brightness and flash length, from a split instant to half a second.

Within each of four strength bands, acuity stayed near flat, with shifts too small to span one chart line. In plain terms, a dimmer letter shown longer read as well as a brighter one shown briefly. Only at the top band did acuity jump by two lines. The authors say a Bloch-like rule governs shape reading too.
pmc-13649993:
Yanjun Yang and three colleagues introduce Views, a graph database model built for knowledge systems where relationships themselves carry labels and descriptions nest inside other descriptions. Ordinary graph stores strain under that kind of nesting, so the team reworks the graph into chains of link nodes that can label both points and connections at any depth.

The model also maps onto special associative hardware, a chip design that searches memory in parallel, and the authors convert two common graph styles into their format. Storage tests used a standard social network benchmark at three sizes, and traversal tests ran on a programmable chip implementation. Results showed that memory layout choices drove storage size more than the model itself, while wider searches returned more points at higher delay. Worked examples show how search steps can be combined, though full reasoning applications remain untested.
pmc-13650693:
Yoshiaki Takagawa and twelve colleagues, publishing in 2026, examine a second round of boron neutron capture therapy. They ask whether repeating the treatment is safe or worthwhile for head and neck cancer that returns after the first round. This specialized radiation uses a boron drug that concentrates in tumors before neutron exposure, and patients who receive it twice usually have no surgical option left.

Thirty-three patients treated twice at one Japanese center between 2020 and 2024 were reviewed. Tumors responded to the second course in seventy percent of cases, and median survival afterward ran close to three years, with about four fifths alive at one year. The price was high, though: serious late side effects struck roughly three fifths of patients, and local control faded to about a fifth by two years. One patient died of aspiration pneumonia. The authors restrict any recommendation to carefully chosen patients with no alternatives.
pmc-13651893:
Leroy D'Souza and eight colleagues pull together published cases of orthostatic tremor to test how well current classification rules fit real patients. Orthostatic tremor causes shaking in the legs while standing, and doctors sort it mainly by tremor frequency and by whether other neurological signs are present. The team gathered individual patient data from one hundred studies covering 244 people with tremor confirmed by electromyography.

Most patients fit the existing criteria, yet a small group fell outside them, with frequencies above the accepted range or values that shifted across the key threshold. People whose tremor came with other disorders tended to shake more slowly than those with isolated tremor, and frequency alone predicted that grouping fairly well. The authors conclude that frequency still matters, but it should always be read alongside the full clinical picture.
pmc-13675293:
Lukas Andereggen led a 2026 study of headache in prolactinoma patients, asking what drives it and whether upfront medical or surgical treatment relieves it better over the long term. Headache is common with these prolactin-secreting pituitary tumors, yet its determinants and lasting outcomes by first treatment were poorly documented. The team reviewed 145 patients at a tertiary center, tracking headache, hormone levels, tumor size, and cavernous sinus involvement over a median of eighty months.

At diagnosis, 42 patients, or 28.9 percent, had prolactinoma-associated headache. Those patients tended to be older and male, and more often had large tumors with cavernous sinus involvement. That involvement emerged as the only independent predictor, while prolactin levels alone did not predict headache. Headache prevalence fell to 2.8 percent over follow-up, with durable relief after both dopamine agonist therapy and transsphenoidal surgery and no significant difference between them.
pmc-1904193:
Schardt, Adams, Owens, and co-authors test whether the PICO framework improves searching PubMed for clinical answers. Modern evidence-based care needs quick access to trusted medical knowledge at the point of care. Many bedside questions go unanswered, though, often because searches are poorly framed.

PICO breaks a question into patient, intervention, comparison, and outcome parts before searching. The authors studied whether teaching that structure helps searchers find better evidence faster. Clearer questions lead to cleaner searches, which matters when a clinician needs a solid answer during a busy clinic.  Better searches mean fewer missed papers when evidence is gathered under time pressure.
pmc-2443193:
Hagmann, Cammoun, Gigandet, and co-authors map the structural core of the human cerebral cortex. The cortex is divided into specialised regions, yet those regions are joined by a dense web of fibre pathways. Using diffusion spectrum imaging, the team traced those pathways without surgery.

Their scans covered links within each hemisphere and across to the other side. From the full web, they identify a core set of highly connected regions that may anchor brain communication. A structural backbone helps explain how separate brain areas act as one system, and what fails when core links are damaged.
pmc-3965093:
Orchard and many co-authors reported the MIntAct project in 2013. At its heart is IntAct, a free and open database of how molecules interact inside cells. Its records come from careful reading of published papers and from data sent in by research groups.

MIntAct made IntAct the shared editing platform for eleven interaction databases at once. One web-based curation tool lets all partner groups enter and check records in the same way. That shared work cuts repeat effort and keeps records in a common form. Users gain a larger, cleaner pool of interaction data for studies of cell pathways and disease.
pmc-4342193:
Chang, Chow, Tellier, and their co-authors released a second generation of PLINK in 2015. PLINK is a widely used open source toolset for genome-wide association studies and population genetics. Data from imputation and whole genome sequencing had grown so large that the first version strained.

The new version was rebuilt for speed and scale on larger, richer datasets. It keeps the familiar commands that labs rely on while handling far bigger files. Association studies test millions of DNA variants against a trait or disease. Faster tools mean bigger studies can be run and re-run as methods improve, which sharpens the search for genetic effects.
pmc-5998893:
Chao Zhang, Maryam Rabiee, Erfan Sayyari, and coauthors presented ASTRAL-III in 2018. Genes within a genome can tell conflicting stories about how species split. A good species tree must allow for that discord rather than ignore it.

ASTRAL builds the species tree from many gene trees while modeling the conflict. The third version handles gene trees that are only partly resolved, a common real-world case. It also runs fast enough for large data sets. Evolutionary biologists use it to place new species and test how sensitive a tree is to gene choice.
pmc-6098093:
Henrik Roager and Tine Licht reviewed microbial products of tryptophan in health and disease in 2018. Tryptophan is an amino acid from food protein. Gut microbes turn part of it into small compounds that signal to the host.

Growing evidence links these compounds to immune balance, gut barrier strength, and even mood pathways. Some products calm inflammation, while others may harm when levels go wrong. The review sorts what is known from what is still guesswork. Diet researchers read it to see how protein choices ripple through microbial chemistry. Several of these compounds also reach the blood, which extends their reach beyond the gut wall.
poetry-and-prose-1893:
Submit Chesebrough Loomis, who wrote under the name Golden Rod, published a volume of poetry and prose in New York in 1893 with George H. Putnam. The surviving title pages are badly worn in transmission, yet the facts stand out: an artotype frontispiece by E. Bierstadt, copyright held by Mrs. L. J. Wing, and an author signing herself with a flower name, in the period's fashion for literary ladies of verse.

Golden Rod was a pen name of the sentimental school, and a mixed volume of poems and prose pieces was its natural form. Verses for consolation and occasion, prose sketches for reflection, gathered for the home market that bought such books as gifts. The record preserves a minor but real presence in 1890s American letters, the kind of woman writer whose work filled magazines and parlor shelves while the canon looked elsewhere.
revised-odd-fellowship-illustrated-1893:
John Blanchard, a minister and fierce critic of secret societies, published Revised Odd-Fellowship Illustrated in 1893. The Odd Fellows were a large fraternal order with lodges, degrees, and private ritual. Blanchard printed what he said was their full revised ritual so the public could judge it.

Pages give the opening and closing forms, oaths, prayers, songs, and degree work of the lodge, with notes attacking them. Blanchard argued that secret pledges and mock sacred scenes were wrong for Christians. Whether read as warning or record, the book preserves the exact forms of a major fraternal order at the end of the nineteenth century.
roosevelt-wilderness-hunter-1893:
Theodore Roosevelt hunted the Rockies and wrote it up in The Wilderness Hunter of 1893. Tucked in its tales is the Bauman story, told him by an old trapper. Bauman's partner was found dead in camp, his neck broken, with strange tracks all around.

Bauman said a great two-legged beast had stalked them in the woods and killed his friend. Roosevelt tells it straight, as a true tale of the wild, with no wink. The story is now read as the classic first draft of Bigfoot lore. It gains force from the teller: a hard hunter who became a president.
sallustius-gods-and-world-taylor-1793:
